She did it twice more, careful and slow, like a scientist and also like a dog chasing its own tail.

"Um, my glasses are haunted," she reported.

Ms. Okafor came over, and Kate demonstrated, tilting her head like a confused owl. "Ah," Ms. Okafor said. "Those are cylindrical lenses. They bend light more in one direction than in the other. Turn them sideways and everything stretches." Kate looked down at the lenses, turning them over in her hand, thinking that she was wearing tiny directional window washers on her face, and that this was the best school day she'd had in weeks.

"Can I keep them on for class?" she asked.

"Loaners are yours until your real pair comes in. Those will be permanent."

Kate slid them on and stopped in the doorway, staring at the hallway clock. "That's been there the whole year?"

"Since before you were born," said Ms. Okafor. On her way out, Kate noticed a teary first-grader waiting with an ice pack, and she handed him one of Ms. Okafor's drawer lollipops on her way past. "The nurse is really nice," she whispered. "And her glasses made my head look huge, so you'll feel great about your ice pack."

"Thanks," the boy said, squinting up at her. "Are you wearing a purple owl?"

"Close enough," said Kate.

The message lit up Caleb's phone at 9:14 on a Friday night, right in the middle of his math homework. It was from Marcus in the Beach Week group chat: a news story with the headline MAN BITTEN BY SHARK OFF CAPE COD, followed by six shark emojis and the words "I am NOT swimming this summer. Not happening. Cancel the whole trip."

"You can't cancel a trip we've been planning since October," Priya typed back. "My mom already bought the giant umbrella."

"Did you read this?" Marcus sent the link again, as if nobody had seen it the first time. "He needed forty stitches. FORTY."

Caleb frowned at his screen. He had read the story, and it was gross, and the detail about the stitches was going to stick in his brain like gum on a shoe. But something about it bothered him. He'd read about sharks before, in a library book, and he had a fuzzy memory of numbers that didn't match the panic. He typed, "Hold on, checking something," and went to the library website on his laptop.

Ten minutes later he exhaled slowly and pasted what he'd found into the chat. "Okay. So shark bites are crazy rare. Like, way more people get hurt by lawnmowers. And here's the weird part. I looked up why we all think they're everywhere, and it's an actual thing scientists studied. These two psychologists, Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman, wrote about it in 1973. They called it the availability heuristic."

"That sounds like a dinosaur," Marcus replied.

"It means people judge how common something is by how easily examples come to mind," Caleb typed. "One shark story jumps into your head because it's scary and vivid, so your brain says, see, it happens all the time. It doesn't."

Priya sent a thinking emoji. "Wait, that's why my grandma thinks all restaurants in other countries will poison her. She saw one news story about bad Mexican cuisine in 1998."

"Exactly," Caleb wrote. "That's the same thing happening."

Marcus's typing bubble appeared, vanished, appeared again. Finally he sent: "Okay but the ocean is dark and I would feel extremely vulnerable out there. Also I still want to go on the trip, I just want to sit on the sand and be hilarious, which is my job."

"Your job is carrying the cooler," Priya said.

"Fine. The cooler AND being hilarious."

"Deal," Caleb typed. "And if you get in the water up to your knees, I'll count that as a win. Baby steps. The shark in your head is way bigger than the real odds."

There was a long pause, and then Marcus sent one message: "Up to my knees. But if anything touches my leg, I'm launching straight out of the ocean like a dolphin and nobody gets to film it."

Priya replied, "No promises on the filming."

Theo spread his homework on the picnic table, weighted the corners with pinecones, and glared at the two climate graphs. Both showed a whole year of rainfall bars and a temperature line, and both had been sitting under his juice box on the drive up. The labels were now a purple smear. Somewhere in that mess was the Sonoran Desert and somewhere was a rainforest in Borneo, and on Monday he had to stand up and compare them, starting with the words "to evaluate the data, we look at rainfall and temperature together."

"Which one's which?" his little sister Priya asked, chewing a marshmallow she had not been given.

"The one where the rainfall bars are tall almost every month is the rainforest," Theo said, tapping the top graph. "And this one, where the bars are sparse, just a few stubs all year, that's the desert. Deserts get rain once in a while and then nothing." The desert temperature line also swooped like a roller coaster, scorching highs and shivery lows, while the rainforest line lay flat as a lazy snake. He wrote the names back on in pen and felt extremely scientific.

Priya had wandered off with the small globe from the camper, spinning it and narrating a pretend trip. "I'm flying north," she announced. "Following this line all the way to the top." Theo glanced over. The line she traced ran pole to pole, and he noticed something he had never seen before: up near the top, all those lines bunched together like spaghetti being pinched between two fingers.

"Wait," he said, and took the globe. He stretched a string across one degree of longitude at the fat middle of the globe, then up near the pole, where the gap had shrunk to almost nothing. He dug the globe's little fact card out of the box. "A degree of longitude is about a hundred and eleven kilometers at the equator," he read, "but it shrinks to zero at the poles, because that's where the lines meet."

"So I could walk across a degree at the pole in one step," Priya said. "I'd be a giant."

"Basically." Theo marked both poles with marshmallow-sticky fingerprint smudges, which he decided counted as scientific annotation.

That night rain hammered the tent, and Theo lay awake smiling. His rainforest graph had tall bars every month, and here was the proof falling on the fly of his tent, right on schedule. Priya's voice floated over from the other sleeping bag. "Theo, is this a rainforest?"

"No, it's Ohio," he said. "Go to sleep, giant."

The tryout sheet in Theo's hand had one line left open: defense, second squad. He'd been at Pine Hollow Ice Arena since six in the morning, and his legs felt like wet rope, but he could still skate, so he lined up for the final drill. The coach blew the whistle, and Theo bent his knees and cut hard around the first cone, imagining that the cone was Eli Marsh, the fastest winger in the district. He couldn't mimic Eli's full speed, but he could copy the way the boy changed direction late,欺骗ing defenders. So far it was working.

Then it stopped working for somebody else. Marcus Boyd, a stocky kid Theo knew from science class, raced backward to catch a breakaway, tangled skates with a winger, and went down. His helmet cracked against the ice with a sound like a dropped coconut. He stood up too fast, swayed, and grabbed the boards. Theo skated over because he was closest, and because last year he had done the same thing himself.

"Get away, I'm fine," Marcus said, blinking hard at the scoreboard as if the numbers were moving. "There's like ten minutes left. If I sit out, I don't make the team."

Theo remembered his own eighth-grade soccer tryout, when he'd bounced his head off a goalpost and stayed in because he was afraid of exactly that. He'd felt strange for two days, and his mother had been furious, and even now he couldn't decide whether staying in had been brave or just reckless. He had scored, though. That part he still thought about.

"Sit down a second," Theo said. "There's a rule about this. My uncle told me. It's called the Zackery Lystedt Law. Washington passed it in 2009, and it was the first state law in the country like it. If they even think you have a concussion, you're out until a doctor or somebody clears you." Marcus lowered himself onto the bench, still arguing, saying it was just a bump, that his whole body felt twisted up like a knot of intestine. Theo waved the coach over anyway.

The coach crouched in front of Marcus, looked at his eyes, and pulled the clipboard off the boards. "He's done for today," she told the assistant. "Protocol." Marcus put his head in his gloves.

Afterward, in the parking lot, Marcus was quiet for a long moment, helmet dangling from one finger. "Do you think I still have a shot? There's another tryout Thursday."

"There's a whole season after that," Theo said. "There's nothing after your brain."

Marcus snorted, then winced and touched his temple. "Okay. But if they take you instead of me, I'm blaming the law."

Sawyer had promised his mother he would clean the garage, and instead he had spent the whole Saturday drawing a giant periodic table on butcher paper. Now it was Sunday night, and the garage still looked like it always did, which was like a raccoon had moved in and given up halfway. He spread the paper across the kitchen table instead, over the spots where his little sister had glued glitter that morning, and looked at the row of boxes he had copied from the website. Somewhere in his backpack, his science test sat with a red 62 at the top, which felt like an ominous warning about what happened when you guessed.

He picked up his pencil and turned it over in his fingers. On the side, in tiny letters, it said graphite. He found graphite on the website and read that graphite was a form of carbon, which meant the gray stuff sliding across his homework paper was carbon too. He scrolled until he found carbon's square in the table. At the top of the box sat a bold 6, labeled atomic number.

"Six," he said out loud, and then, quieter, "six protons."

The kitchen was empty except for him, so nobody heard him talk to a pencil. He flipped through his notes from class, where he had written atomic numbers in one column and nothing useful anywhere else. He'd gotten a question wrong on the test by saying carbon had twelve protons, because he'd multiplied by two for some reason he could no longer reconstruct. His grandfather, a chemist before he retired, had said only one thing about it on the phone: "The atomic number counts the protons, Sawyer. Start there." He hadn't explained more. He never did. Sawyer half wished he had, and half liked that he hadn't.

He tried it out like an experiment. He ran his finger down the paper to oxygen, atomic number 8, and said, "Eight protons." Gold, atomic number 79, meant 79 protons, which seemed like a lot for something you could wear on a finger. It felt strange, counting things no one had ever seen, smaller than small, inside the graphite dust smeared on the edge of his hand. But the rule held every single time, like a pattern hiding under the table the whole while.

His mother came in from the garage, and he could tell from her face that she had seen the raccoon situation. Before she could speak, he slid the butcher paper toward her and pointed at carbon's box. "This pencil is graphite, which is carbon," he said. "Carbon has atomic number 6, so every carbon atom has six protons in its nucleus." She looked at the paper, then at the garage door, and then at him. "You convert one Saturday into this," she said, "and I'm supposed to be mad?" He grinned and picked the pencil up again.

Ryder slid his paper across the library table and watched Priya's eyes move down the page. The room smelled like pencil shavings and the lemon cleaner the librarian had used on the shelves, and the radiator under the window clicked like a slow clock.

"Three reasons," Priya said, tapping each heading with her pen. "One, the school needs a soccer goal because the old one has a hole. Two, a new goal would make recess better. Three, kids would have more fun at recess." She looked up. "Ryder, two and three are the same reason in disguise."

"They are not." Ryder grabbed the paper back. "Better and more fun are different words."

Priya folded her arms. "The three points in an argument have to be truly different reasons. If two points just say the same thing in different words, the argument really has only two." She said it the way Mr. Okafor had written it on the club poster last fall, like a rule you could hold in your hand.

Ryder sat back. He remembered October, the first club meeting, when he had frozen in front of a blank page while everyone else wrote. Maya had slid a pencil toward him and whispered, "Just put down anything. It's a draft, not a monument." He had written a story about a talking dog with dialogue so messy that every line ran into the next, and Mr. Okafor had circled nothing, only said, "Next time, commas and new paragraphs." Ryder had gone home and practiced until his quotation marks sat straight.

Now he read his two points again, mouthing them. "Making recess better" and "kids having more fun" both pointed at the same thing, the way two doors could open into the same room. That was the hidden problem, and no amount of prettier words would fix it. He tested it out loud. "If I cross out point three, does my argument still say everything?"

"Everything it already said," Priya said. "Two things."

"That's the dilemma," Maya said from across the table, without looking up from her own draft. "Find a third real reason, or turn in an argument that only has two."

Ryder tapped his pencil against his chin. He needed a reason that was truly different, one that touched something the first two did not. The broken goal, the fun at recess. What else did a goal do? He thought about the sixth graders who played with a rolled-up sweatshirt because the net had a hole the size of a basketball. He wrote a new heading: "A real goal would keep the ball from flying into the parking lot, so fewer games get interrupted."

"Ooh," Priya said, leaning over. "That's safety and time. Different from fun."

Ryder grinned and started a fresh page. At the top he wrote his lead, then a line of dialogue from a sixth grader named Tomás, with the comma tucked inside the quotation marks exactly where it belonged. For his climax he chose the moment Mr. Okafor read the finished argument aloud and paused at the third reason. Ryder watched his teacher's eyebrows lift, just a little, and waited.

"Three real reasons," Mr. Okafor said. "This one goes to Principal Deng."

The computer lab smelled like warm plastic and the janitor's lemon spray, and Isla had exactly forty minutes to finish her spreadsheet before the bell. Her chart was supposed to show something real, not pictures of cats like Marcus had turned in last week. She was typing numbers into column B when her best friend Priya leaned over, cracked her knuckles, and announced the problem.

"My new password is six letters," Priya said. "All lowercase. My brother says that's not enough, but he also thinks ketchup belongs on eggs, so I don't inherit his opinions." She typed her password invisibly into her own screen, as if the keyboard might judge it.

Isla almost let it go. Then she remembered the spreadsheet. She made a new column and started figuring, letter by letter, how many guesses a password could take. One letter was 26 possibilities. Two letters, 26 times 26. She kept multiplying, and by the time she got to six, the number had swollen so large that it filled half the cell. She made a bar chart and watched it climb like a staircase built by someone with a grudge against ground floors. Each extra letter made the bar 26 times taller than the one before, which was the part that got her. It wasn't adding. It was multiplying, over and over, invisibly, in a place nobody could see.

"Look at this," she said, and dragged Priya's chair over with one foot. Priya squinted at the chart, then at the formula in the formula bar, then back at the chart, as though one of them might blink first.

"So seven letters would be 26 times all of this?" Priya pointed at the towering sixth bar.

"That's what it does. Using only lowercase, every letter you add makes 26 times as many possibilities to guess."

Priya sat quietly for a moment. "My password is the name of a fish," she admitted. "Lowercase. Six letters."

"A fish nobody would guess?"

"Everybody would guess it. I talk about him constantly."

Isla saved her chart, which had gone from homework to evidence in under ten minutes, and decided this was the most credible thing she had ever produced for school, better than the volcano that had refused to erupt in fourth grade. Priya was already muttering candidate passwords under her breath like someone preparing for an audition she intended to win.

"Add a number," Isla said. "And a capital. Give the guessers a bad afternoon."

Priya typed. Somewhere on her screen, a small fish named after a noodle retired forever.

The first thing Muhammad noticed about Camp Willowood was the canopy of oak branches over the swimming dock, so thick that the water looked green instead of blue. The second thing he noticed was Dana. She sat at the end of the dock every morning, gripping the edge, staring at the lane ropes like they might bite her.

"They're doing time trials Friday," his cabin mate Theo told him. "Dana's the fastest swimmer here, but she won't get in the water. She's been like that for weeks. Won't eat breakfast, won't sleep. Just sits."

Muhammad knew about not sleeping. Back in the spring, before his big math exam, he had lain awake for a whole month, his stomach in knots, until his grandfather taught him a trick. Breathe in for four counts, hold for four, out for six, and do it in bed at the same time every night. The breathing was boring, but boring was the point. It told his body the day was over. His stomach had finally settled, and the night before the exam, he had actually slept.

On Wednesday, Muhammad's own jitters arrived. Time trials meant the whole camp watching, and when he stood on the dock for practice, his heart hammered and his hands shook. He almost climbed back down. Then he remembered what his grandfather had said, and he tried the breathing right there, four in, four held, six out, three times. His hands went still. His focus got sharp, sharp enough that he swam his fastest lap of the summer.

He climbed out, dripping, and an idea formed. A nervous feeling right before you perform wasn't the enemy. His jitters had made him faster. But Dana hadn't felt nervous for one race. She'd felt awful for weeks, and that was different. He couldn't see inside her any more than he could see the roots under the oak trees, but the pattern was there, hiding in plain sight.

He walked to the end of the dock. "You're going to think I'm annoying," he said.

"Probably," Dana said, not looking up.

"Jitters before a race are normal. They can actually sharpen you. But feeling this bad for weeks isn't the same thing." He sat down beside her. "That kind doesn't go away on its own. You should talk to the camp nurse. Or your counselor. Somebody."

Dana finally looked at him. "I thought it would just go away."

"I did too, for a month," Muhammad said. "It didn't. Then I talked to my grandpa, and we fixed the sleeping part first."

She stared at the green water for a long moment. Then she stood up, brushed off her shorts, and walked toward the office building, her flip-flops slapping the boards.

Friday came, and the camp gathered under the oaks where the ivy seemed to flourish even in the shade. Muhammad stood on the blocks, heart hammering, hands steady. In lane four, Dana pulled her cap on and shook out her arms. When the whistle blew, she hit the water first.

Romy pushed through the metal door of the Riverside Food Bank with a box of granola bars her mom had bought by mistake, thinking they were for school snacks. Inside she expected a line of people waiting for food, maybe folding tables and grocery bags. Instead she found a warehouse, plain and enormous, with pallets stacked to the rafters and a forklift beeping somewhere in the back. No customers anywhere. Just a woman in a green apron counting cans into a spreadsheet.

"You're early," the woman said. "Distribution's not here."

"Where is it?" Romy asked, because obviously it had to be somewhere. People didn't come to a warehouse to shop. Nobody wanted to walk past a forklift for a bag of rice.

The woman, whose name tag said DEB, pointed her pencil toward the door. "The pantry on Fourth Street. That's where people pick up their groceries directly. This is the food bank. We collect and store the large amounts first, then truck them out." She squinted at Romy's box. "You volunteering or just delivering?"

"Volunteering," Romy said, though she had only signed up because her friend Priya had bailed and Romy had already told her mom she'd gone.

Deb's own plan soon became clear. She wanted to finish inventory before her daughter's soccer game at noon, and she kept glancing at the clock like it might sneak ahead. "You can count soup or you can sort the eccentric donations bin," she said. "Somebody donated a hundred cans of pickled okra and one birdbath."

Romy chose the bin. The birdbath turned out to be ceramic, heavy, and inexplicably painted with the face of a cat. She carried it to the corner where the odd donations lived, next to a bag of hotel shampoos and a trombone mouthpiece.

Then she noticed something. The pasta shelf had a gap, and the gap had a shape: long, straight, and exactly the width of spaghetti boxes. On the far wall, the spaghetti boxes sat in a pallet, forty of them, waiting to be moved. Romy had an idea. If the warehouse stored large amounts and sent them out to smaller places, then whatever left the shelves fastest was whatever people actually needed most. The pasta gap was wide. The pickled okra pile was not moving at all.

She tested it by asking Deb, casually, which orders went out that morning. "Spaghetti, peanut butter, canned peaches," Deb said without looking up. "Nobody wants the okra. The pantry on Fourth has a whole shelf of it."

So the pattern held. The shelves were like footprints showing where the food would go next, and Romy spent the next hour counting the gaps instead of just the cans, calling out the low ones so Deb could mark them for the next truck. Deb finished her spreadsheet at eleven forty, ten minutes before the soccer game, and patted the cat-faced birdbath on her way out.

"Take the okra if you want it," she said. "Consider it a conservation effort. We've got to conserve shelf space somehow."

Romy carried home three cans and the trombone mouthpiece, which nobody had claimed. The mouthpiece turned out to fit nothing in her house, but it made an excellent, brass-toned doorstop, and every time she tripped over it she thought of the cat birdbath, still standing in the corner, waiting for its own truck to Fourth Street.

The marble soldier at the war memorial had one hand shading his eyes, looking west, as if he could see everything Evelyn could not. She sat on the bottom step with a photocopied settler's diary spread across her knees. Her project was due tomorrow morning, and the whole thing depended on one question: why had the Halloran family left Ohio in 1846? The diary said they wanted land of their own. But her teacher had written a note in red pen: "How do you know the diary is telling the truth?"

Her grandfather found her there after his walk, out of breath from the hill. "Still stuck?" He lowered himself onto the step beside her.

"The diary says a hailstorm ruined their crop on June 9th, so they gave up and left," Evelyn said. "But I found a newspaper from that same town, and it says the big hailstorm was in July." She turned the pages of the diary, her frustration growing acute. "The paper even printed a letter about it from a farmer two miles from the Hallorans. Same storm, different month."

"Which one is wrong?" her grandfather asked.

"That's the problem. I can't tell. I only have two things, and they disagree." She stared at the carved soldier. Then she flipped to the back of the folder, where she'd copied a page from the county government records. The Hallorans sold their land on June 2nd, a week before the diary's supposed hailstorm. She read it twice. "They sold the farm before the storm even happened. The storm can't be why they left."

"So the diary got the date wrong," her grandfather said.

"Or the diary got the whole reason wrong, and they wrote the storm in later to explain it." She sat back. The probability that the diary's date was right seemed small now, with two other sources pointing the other way. "I kept thinking the diary was automatically true because it was written by somebody who was there."

"You could write that," he said. "Show how you checked it."

The light was going orange behind the memorial when she began to write her new first paragraph. Letters, newspapers, government records: she listed them in her notebook like witnesses, each one confirming a piece of the story. The diary still mattered, but it had to answer to the others. When she finished the paragraph, she read it aloud to her grandfather and the stone soldier.

"That works," her grandfather said. "Now let's get you home before dark." Evelyn packed her folder, then looked back once at the soldier gazing west, toward all that land the Hallorans had gone chasing after all.

Mrs. Okafor's office smelled like lemon tea, and a poster on the wall showed a cartoon brain holding a red umbrella. Ivy sat on the squishy blue chair by the window, watching the door, because her brother Devon was supposed to arrive at three fifteen and it was already three eighteen. Her plan for today was simple: convince Mrs. Okafor that Devon needed help before his science presentation on Thursday, the one he had already tried to skip twice by claiming he was sick.

When Devon finally slid in, his backpack strap was twisted and his face was pale. Ivy had noticed a pattern at home. He was fine all morning, cheerful even, and then around first period he would go quiet, and by the time he had to speak in front of anyone his hands shook. "He had to give a book report last month," she told Mrs. Okafor. "His heart was pounding like he'd run a mile, and he was breathing fast, and nothing was even happening. Nothing dangerous, I mean. It was just a book report."

Devon glared at the umbrella poster. "That was one time," he said, but his voice wobbled, which illustrated the point better than anything Ivy could add. Mrs. Okafor asked him what the worst part was. "The humiliation," Devon said quietly. "Everyone looking at me like I'm going to throw up."

"Here's what I keep reading," Mrs. Okafor said, turning her chair toward him. "It's called fight-or-flight." Devon frowned, so Ivy leaned forward. "What's that?" Mrs. Okafor said it was the body getting ready for danger, and that during fight-or-flight the adrenal glands release adrenaline, which makes the heart beat faster and breathing speed up. Ivy sat back. So Devon's body was doing exactly what bodies were built to do. It wasn't broken. It was just loud.

"So it's like a smoke alarm," Ivy said, testing the idea out loud. "It's not a fire. The alarm doesn't know that." Devon chewed on the thought. Mrs. Okafor nodded slowly and mentioned that lots of kids called that feeling anxiety, that stress had a way of turning up the alarm, and that coping skills were basically ways to tell the alarm to settle down. She also said the word boundaries, about Devon telling classmates he'd answer questions after class instead of during, but Ivy was already forming a plan of her own.

"Then let's practice," she said, standing up. She pointed Devon toward the window, where three kids were crossing the parking lot below. "Pretend they're your class. Give your presentation to them. If your heart starts pounding, that's just the adrenaline, and you keep going anyway." Devon exhaled, rolled his shoulders, and faced the glass. "Photosynthesis," he began, "is how plants make their own food." His voice cracked on the second word, and he kept talking anyway. Ivy sat down to listen, and Mrs. Okafor wrote resilient on her notepad, underlined it twice, and slid it across the desk where Devon could see it when he finished.

Oliver sat in the waiting room with his shirt held out from his armpits, sniffing each side like a detective at a crime scene. Both sides smelled like gym socks that had been locked in a locker over summer vacation. Three weeks ago they hadn't. That was the mystery. He had used the same soap, worn the same shirts, played the same sports, and suddenly, at his eleven-year checkup, he was sitting in the corner seat farthest from the other patients, holding his elbows tight against his ribs.

In the chair beside him, his sixteen-year-old cousin Marco flipped through a magazine about dirt bikes. He had driven Oliver because Mom's car was in the shop. "You keep doing that sniffing thing," Marco said. "You look like a golden retriever."

"Something changed," Oliver said. "I want to know what. I used to be immune to stink. I could run five laps and smell like nothing."

Marco put down the magazine. "Fresh sweat doesn't really have a smell, you know. The stink comes later. Bacteria on your skin break down the sweat from glands in your armpits, and those glands switch on around your age."

Oliver considered this. So the sweat itself was innocent. The bacteria were the culprits. That meant the crime scene was under his arms, and the evidence needed time to develop, like the smell in Marco's hockey bag. It also meant there was a way to test it.

In the exam room, the doctor checked his ears, his knees, and his growth chart, and said he was doing fine. On the way out, Oliver stopped at the drinking fountain and wet a paper towel, then ducked into the bathroom and scrubbed one armpit with soap from the dispenser. The other one he left alone. A scientific control, like in fourth grade. He dried off, rejoined Marco, and rode home with his arms at his sides, breathing through his nose and taking notes in his head.

At home he checked every hour. The washed side stayed plain and unremarkable, like tap water. The unwashed side grew steadily worse, like a sandwich left in a hot car. By dinner he had eliminated every other possible cause. New shirts, no. Different food, no. It was bacteria working on sweat, and the smell took time, exactly as Marco had said. He reported his findings at the table, and his little sister set down her fork and announced she was moving to the garage.

The next morning Oliver used Mom's deodorant from the cabinet above the sink, then walked to school with his arms swinging loose for the first time in weeks. Marcus, who sat next to him in third period, leaned over during attendance and said, "You smell like my dad's gym bag, but in a good way."

"I'll take it," Oliver said. "That's called data."

Victor stabbed his fork into a meatball and pushed it around the plate while his little sister talked with her mouth full of noodles. Everyone at the table was doing that thing where they pretended to eat normally, but really they were all sneaking glances at the trading card he had propped against the salt shaker. It was a Blazetail Dragon, foil edition, and three days ago nobody at Jefferson Middle School would have traded a broken pencil for it.

"Now everyone wants one," his mother said, reaching over to turn the card so it caught the light. "How much did Damon offer you today?"

"His skateboard, his hockey jersey, and forty dollars." Victor could still hear the cafeteria noise around that offer, half the seventh grade crowding the table, someone chanting "foil, foil" until a monitor told them to sit down. "Last month I bought it for two bucks at the garage sale by the library. Two bucks. Because nobody wanted it then."

His grandfather set down his spoon. "Two dollars. And now forty plus a skateboard." He smiled like he was remembering a joke he had played on himself a long time ago. "You know, I did a report on this in school. Not cards. Tulips." He let the word sit there while Grandma rolled her eyes and said, here we go. "In the Dutch Republic, in the winter of 1636 into 1637, prices for rare tulip bulbs soared. People were trading houses for a single bulb. And then in February 1637, it all collapsed, because buyers stopped showing up." He picked up his water glass. "One morning there was no one left to sell to. Just like that."

Victor stopped chewing. He thought about the hallway that afternoon, how he had counted six kids clutching Blazetail Dragons in plastic sleeves, and how Bruno had quietly tried to sell his for ten dollars and gotten no takers. Six dragons. Maybe there were more in lockers. The cafeteria had felt contagious that week, everyone wanting the card because everyone else wanted it, but wanting wasn't the same as there being enough to go around. Or too many. His stomach did a slow flip.

"I almost traded it," he said. "Yesterday. Marcus offered me his whole dinosaur fossil collection for it, and I said I'd think about it." He remembered standing at his window last night, holding the card up to the streetlight, feeling like a genius. Now he felt like the last person at a party who hadn't heard that everyone else had gone home. "What do I do?"

"That's not for me to say," his grandfather said, and Grandma squeezed Victor's hand and said something about how a smart boy figures out what a thing is worth when the crowd goes quiet. Her compassion, Victor thought, was mostly aimed at Marcus and his fossils.

That night, after the dishes, Victor sat at his desk with the card flat under his palm. He could keep it because he loved the way the foil turned green at an angle, or he could take it to school tomorrow and be the first seller in a room full of them. Downstairs, his sister was already asking if she could have it if he didn't want it anymore. He slid the card into a plain white envelope and wrote one word on the outside: "Wait."

"Green Arrow is the fastest car in this whole neighborhood," Declan announced, holding the lime-green car over his head. "Maybe the fastest in the county."

Oliver looked at the ramp they had built against the fence, a long board propped on the old picnic table. Green Arrow had just beaten Oliver's red car, Falcon, by what looked like half a car length. One race. Half a car length.

"That was one race," Oliver said.

"One race that Green Arrow won," Declan said, as if that settled it. He was already lining the cars up again, but this time Oliver stopped him.

"Hang on." Oliver picked up a stick and scratched two columns in the dirt at the bottom of the ramp, one marked G, one marked F. "We race them five times. We count the wins. Then we know."

"We already know," Declan said. "My dad said he'd bet the mortgage on Green Arrow." Oliver's own dad said stuff like that too, usually right before losing the weekly card game to Aunt Rhonda.

"That's not knowing, that's bragging," Oliver said. "Think of it like this. We can't see which car is really faster. It's hidden. So we make a guess we can test. My guess is that Falcon wins more than half the time."

"That's a weird way to say 'I think I'll win,'" Declan said, but he set the cars on the top of the ramp anyway. "Ready? Let go."

They let go together. Green Arrow pulled ahead halfway down and won by two car lengths. Oliver scratched a tally mark under G.

Race two went to Falcon. Race three went to Falcon too, barely, a nose ahead at the flowerpot finish line. Declan crouched down and squinted at the wheels of Green Arrow, spinning them with his thumb. Race four, Green Arrow. Race five, Falcon. The score stood at three to two, Falcon.

"Best out of five," Oliver said. "Falcon wins."

"Rematch," Declan said instantly. "Best out of five again. Different dirt."

So they ran it again. Falcon took three out of five the second time too. On the third set, Green Arrow won the first two races and Declan did a small dance in the grass, but Falcon came back and took the set, three to two again. Same score, three sets in a row.

"That's weird," Declan said, staring at the tally marks scratched across the dirt. "It's the same every time."

"It's consistent," Oliver said. "That's how we know it's real. If we'd only raced once, the first time, Green Arrow won, remember? You'd still be doing your county speech." He pointed at the mark under G. "One race can go either way. It could just be luck. But when it keeps coming out the same over and over, that means something."

Declan sat back on his heels. "So how much faster is Falcon? Like, a lot?"

"We could try to quantify it," Oliver said. "Measure the gaps. My mom has a tape measure in the garage."

Declan was already running toward the garage. "If Falcon loses the measuring, I'm calling for a fourth rematch!"

"Bring the pencil too," Oliver called after him. "And a rag, your car's got mud in its wheel wells."

Jeremy held the knife the way his mom had shown him, curled fingers tucked so his knuckles guided the blade. "Claw grip," she'd called it, and he liked that it had a name, like something a video game character would know. The onion sat on the cutting board, papery skin half peeled, and he scrutinized it, looking for the line where the root end held it together, because his mom had said to keep that side intact while slicing. His first cut wobbled, but the second one landed clean, and the third after that. His eyes burned and he blinked hard, but he kept going, because tonight he was making the sauce himself, all of it, from scratch.

The tomatoes were already bubbling in the pot, and the recipe said to serve it over rice, which confused him at first. He'd expected pasta. But his mom had left a note on the counter that just said: two cups rice, three cups water, one teaspoon salt, lid on, heat low, eighteen minutes. No instructions about draining. That struck him as strange, because every time he'd watched pasta get cooked, the water got poured off through the colander at the end. Rice, apparently, was different, and he wanted to know whether that was a mistake in the note or a real thing.

He measured the rice and water, set the lid, and turned the burner to low. While the sauce thickened, he chopped a small green pepper, slower now, more careful. He was starting to feel competent, like someone who actually knew his way around a knife, when the timer went off and he lifted the rice lid. The grains looked plump and separate, and the pot was dry. Completely dry. No puddle, nothing to pour off.

Still, old habits were strong. He carried the pot to the sink and held it over the colander, tilting it, just in case.

"Whoa, stop," his mom said from the doorway. "You don't drain that."

"Why not? That's what we do with spaghetti."

"Rice isn't spaghetti. It's the absorption method. The rice cooks in a measured amount of water and soaks it all up."

Jeremy looked at the pot again, then set it back on the counter. So the exact cups of water in the note weren't random; they were the whole trick. If the rice had soaked up every drop, then draining would only mean losing rice through the holes, not getting rid of water that wasn't there. He tested the idea with a fork, fluffing the grains apart. They were tender all the way through, each one separate and steaming.

He spooned the sauce over the rice and carried both plates to the table. His mom took a bite, chewed, and nodded slowly. "Okay," she said. "From now on, Thursday dinners are yours."

Tyler kept the box on his lap the whole ride, because the bus was notorious for potholes, and the last thing he wanted was his first phone sliding under a seat. It was a hand-me-down from his grandfather, handed over at the kitchen table that morning while Grandpa ate toast. Grandpa had weighed it in his palm and laughed. "The phone Martin Cooper used for the first handheld cell phone call weighed about 1.1 kilograms. Two and a half pounds, like a bag and a half of sugar." He had set it down gently after that, as if it might bruise.

Now Tyler slid the phone out and it did seem impossibly light, lighter than his math binder, lighter than the sandwich in his backpack. He couldn't feel the difference between two and a half pounds and nothing much unless he had something to compare, so he borrowed Marcus's half-filled water bottle from the seat pocket and held it in one hand and the phone in the other. The bottle was heavier. He added Marcus's science book to the bottle hand and thought about Grandpa holding a brick against his ear the whole walk down a New York sidewalk. His arm would ache before the call even ended.

"I'm doing homework on it," Marcus said, tilting his own screen. "We're supposed to write two paragraphs on a monarchy, any one we pick."

Tyler opened the phone and found the little icon for the web. His parents had made one rule before the bus came: they would permit twenty minutes a day, and they could see the report that showed how much he used. The problem was that this morning the report already said nine minutes, and he had used it for maybe four. Something invisible was eating the time, and he wanted to know what.

He had a theory. Yesterday, while he was figuring the phone out, he had opened a weather app and a game and a music app, and he suspected they were still running in the background even after he closed them, like faucets left dripping. So he tested it. He found each app in the list and swiped it away, all of them, until the screen showed nothing running. Then he locked the phone, set it face down on his knee, and watched the second hand on his watch go around.

At the next pothole the bus jolted and the phone bounced an inch off his leg. He caught it, checked the screen, and opened the report. Still twenty minutes left, all twenty, no seconds ticking away.

"See?" he said, and held it up for Marcus. "It stopped."

Logan stood at the back of St. Brigid's with a folded paper in his pocket, though he wasn't supposed to need it. In three weeks he would stand at the altar for his Confirmation and read the Prayer of St. Francis by heart, and so far he could only get through the first four lines without stumbling. The church smelled like candle wax and old wood, and the afternoon light came through the stained glass in slow colored patches that crept across the floor while he practiced.

Marcus was waiting for him on the front steps, bouncing a tennis ball off the stone railing. Marcus came here every Tuesday because his mother worked late on Tuesdays and Logan's house was between her job and theirs. Usually they walked straight home, but today Marcus had followed him inside, and now he was frowning at the rack of pamphlets by the door.

"What's purgatory?" Marcus asked. He held up a pamphlet with a soft blue cover. "It says souls there are purified before heaven."

Logan took the pamphlet and read the back, which didn't help much, because it assumed you already knew. "It's like a state after death," he said slowly. "You get purified before you go to heaven. Our church teaches it."

Marcus set the tennis ball down on the railing, very carefully, the way he did when he thought someone was pulling a trick on him. "My church doesn't have that at all. My dad would say you either go to heaven or you don't." He squinted at Logan. "Are you making that up?"

"Why would I make it up? It's on a pamphlet." Logan turned it over again. He had heard the word his whole life, at funerals mostly, and never once thought about whether everyone believed the same thing. Apparently they didn't, and nobody had ever mentioned it, which felt strange, like discovering two friends had gone to the same summer camp and never talked about it.

"Let's test it," Marcus said. He was the kind of person who tested everything, which was why he owned three different brands of magnets. "Father Ray is still inside, right? Ask him. Then Sunday I'll ask Pastor Ellie. If they say different things, we'll know." It was a fair plan, and it restrict the problem nicely: one question, two answers, no arguing about who was right.

Logan went back in and found Father Ray folding the pulpit cloths. "Father, does everyone believe in purgatory?" Father Ray said no, that most Protestant churches reject the idea, and went back to folding, as if this were the least surprising news in the world. Logan walked out feeling like he'd solved something, though he hadn't expected the answer to make his own church seem like the exception rather than the rule.

"So your religion doesn't have a monopoly on it," Marcus said on the walk home, spinning the tennis ball in his hand. "That's actually kind of exceptional, finding that out because of a pamphlet." Logan laughed, and while they walked he recited the Prayer of St. Francis out loud, line by line, all the way to the corner where the bus turned. "Where there is sadness, let me sow joy," he said, and for the first time he didn't miss a single word.

Nora spread her survey results across the lab table and tapped her pencil on the edge of the sink. Thirty-two students had answered her question, and the pattern was hard to miss: kids who ate breakfast almost all had better grades than kids who skipped it. Her poster board, half finished, already said "Eat Breakfast, Get Better Grades," in fat blue letters. She had planned to glue on the graph during lunch, but something about the headline was bothering her.

Desmond leaned over from the next table, where he was adjusting the valve on his Bunsen burner. The flame had been sputtering, and when he turned the knob a fraction, it steadied into a neat blue cone. "That's a good graph," he said. "My project is so boring compared to yours. I just burned three kinds of chips."

"It looks good," Nora admitted. "But watch this." She picked up her data sheet and read down the breakfast column. "Tomas doesn't eat breakfast and he gets D's. Priya eats breakfast every day and gets A's." She paused. "But Tomas's family also moved twice this year, and he stays up past midnight. Priya's house is quiet, and she sleeps nine hours." The more she stared at her sheet, the more pairs like that she found. The breakfast skippers were also the kids with long bus rides and lumpy schedules.

"That still counts, doesn't it?" Desmond asked. "They go together."

Nora remembered a word from a science article she had read for the project, and she said it out loud to test it. "Correlation. Two things happening together." Then she added slowly, "But going together doesn't prove one causes the other. Something else might cause both." Tomas's messy mornings and his D's could both come from the same unsettled year, no cereal required. She felt her shoulders drop, relieved rather than defeated, because now she actually had a question worth asking.

She pulled out a fresh sheet of paper and wrote a new survey, one that asked about sleep, bus rides, and homework time along with breakfast. Mr. Okafor walked past and glanced at her revision, but he only raised an eyebrow and kept moving, which she took as a legitimate sign she was on the right track. By the time the bell rang, her poster headline had changed to "Breakfast and Grades: Which Comes First?" and beneath it she had drawn two arrows meeting at a mystery box with a question mark inside. Desmond peered over as he snapped off his burner, and the flame ceased with a soft pop. "So what's in the box?" he asked. "I don't know yet," Nora said, and picked up her pencil again.

The box from his uncle arrived on a Tuesday, and by Wednesday, Nolan was holding a phone for the first time in his life. It was Uncle Dev's old one, passed down with a crack in the corner and a battery that didn't seem to last. Nolan plugged it in overnight, carried it to school on Thursday, and watched it die right after lunch. He told himself it was a fluke. Friday it died during fifth period, before lunch even started.

That night, sprawled on his bed, Nolan typed into the family group chat, which Mom had named "Vasquez HQ." Phone keeps dying by lunch. Is it broken? Uncle Dev replied first with a thumbs-up and then, a minute later, actual words: Not broken. Old. It's a lithium-ion battery, and as it chemically ages it holds less charge. That phone's been through four years of me.

Nolan read the message three times. So the dying by lunchtime wasn't random, and it wasn't his fault, and it also wasn't going to stop. The battery would just keep holding less and less. He started a notes file and tracked it like a science experiment: Saturday, 46 percent by noon. Sunday, 41 percent. The numbers slid downward in a steady line, which meant Monday would be worse, and Mom's birthday dinner was Monday night. He had promised to film her blowing out the candles, and he had a suspicion the phone wouldn't survive until dessert.

He remembered, with a squirm of guilt, the argument in August when he'd said he didn't need a charger in his room because he'd "be careful." He'd thought careful meant immune to stuff like this. Now he understood that being careful had nothing to do with a battery slowly wearing out on its own schedule, whether he deserved it or not. He typed: Dev, do you still have that portable battery pack from the camping trip?

His uncle left it on the porch the next morning inside a plastic bag, along with a sticky note that said, No take-backs. At Monday's dinner, Nolan kept the phone plugged into the pack in his jacket pocket, feeling the small warm weight of it through the fabric like a secret plan. When the cake came out, he propped the phone against the salt shaker and hit record. His mom laughed at the lens, his little sister dove in front of it, and the battery icon held at 38 percent all the way through the candles.

Later, he posted the video in Vasquez HQ with the caption, Evidence that this phone can make it through a whole evening. Uncle Dev replied within seconds: Empathy, kid. I lost plenty of birthday videos to that thing. Nolan started to type back something about trading the phone in eventually, then stopped, thumb hovering, and left the words unsent. He scrolled up instead and watched his mom blow out the candles one more time.

Luke stood at the steel counter in Rossi's kitchen on Saturday morning, an onion in front of him and a very sharp knife in his hand. His mom, the head cook, had finally said he could help make the pasta sauce from scratch, but only if he learned the claw grip first. He curled his fingers like a bear paw, knuckles forward, and narrated each cut out loud. "Claw, tip down, slice." The first piece came out as big as a door hinge, and his mom laughed so hard she dropped her wooden spoon into the sink.

"You're guarding your fingers like the onion is toxic," she said, fishing the spoon out.

"It is toxic," Luke said, blinking hard. "It's attacking my eyes from the inside. That's invisible warfare." But he kept at it, and by the third onion his cuts came out even, small squares falling off the blade like they were supposed to. He swept them into the hot pan and the whole kitchen started to smell like the real thing, garlic and onion sizzling in olive oil.

While the sauce simmered, Luke noticed Dani, the morning baker, mixing up a batch of cornbread batter. She covered the bowl with a towel and then just walked away from it, over to check the oven. That made no sense to him. If the batter was ready, why let it sit? He narrowed his eyes. Maybe it didn't matter. Maybe the recipe was just sloppy. He decided to test it. "Dani, can I put half in the oven right now, and you bake the rest after a few minutes?" She shrugged and said sure, as long as he narrated his experiment to somebody, because she liked a good story.

Both pans went in, one right away and one that had waited. When they came out, Luke cut a square from each and stared. They were both tall and fluffy, not flat and sad like he'd predicted. He tapped the pan with the spoon. "It's double-acting baking powder," he told his mom. "It releases gas twice. Once when it gets wet in the batter, and again when it gets heated in the oven." So the batter could wait, because it wasn't finished rising on the counter anyway. His mom's formula for the pasta sauce was pinned to the wall, and he'd assumed it was some kind of magic. Now he guessed the cornbread had its own rules, too, just ones he hadn't known.

"So you changed your mind," his mom said, handing him a spoon.

"I changed my mind, I chopped three onions, and I still have ten fingers," Luke said. He dipped the spoon into the sauce, blew on it, and took the first taste.

The arena smelled like cold rubber and hot pretzels, and Aaron's whole row of family and friends had turned into one loud, scarf-wrapped blob. His cousin Maya elbowed him every time the home team's defenseman, a big kid named Ruiz with a predatory grin, chased down a breakaway. "Watch him," Maya said. "He hunts pucks like a shark." Aaron's grandpa sat on the other side, wrapped in a coat thick enough to insulate a polar explorer, though the rink was barely cold at all.

Then the disputed goal happened. The puck vanished behind a pile of skates, the goal light flashed, and half the arena screamed while the other half booed. "It never crossed the line!" shouted Uncle Theo. "It did so!" shouted Aunt Regina, and they both leaned toward the jumbotron like it was the last cookie on the plate.

The screen showed the play again, slowed down. That was when Grandpa snorted. "You know, TV couldn't always do that. The first time instant replay was used in a live sports broadcast was by CBS director Tony Verna, during the Army-Navy football game on December 7, 1963."

"Wait," Aaron said. "Before that, people just argued forever?"

"Forever," Grandpa said, "with no proof but loudness."

Aaron grinned, but his mind had already snagged on something else. In the replay, the net looked wrong. Crooked. He couldn't see the puck, but he could see the net's mooring peg, that little thing that holds the goal in place, floating loose on the ice beside the post. His idea: if the net had come off its peg before the shot, the goal might not count even if the puck went in, because a displaced net changes what counts. He grabbed Maya's arm. "Look at the peg. Look at it."

Maya squinted. "The little orange thingy? It's just... sitting there. Like a lost sock."

"On the next replay, watch the post," Aaron said. The screen rolled the play again, and there it was, clear as anything: a defender crashed the crease a full second before the shot, the peg popped loose, and the net slid sideways just enough to swallow the puck. The referee skated to the penalty box, pointed, and waved off the goal. The scoreboard blinked: NO GOAL, NET OFF MOORINGS.

Uncle Theo stood up and bowed to Aaron like he was royalty. Aunt Regina threw a popcorn kernel at him, but she was laughing.

Above them, the big ceiling fan spun with a low hum like a turbine winding up, and the Zamboni rumbled out through the tunnel for intermission. Aaron sat back, satisfied. "See?" he told Maya. "You don't always need to see the puck. Sometimes you just need to see what moved."

"Fine, detective," Maya said. "Next period, tell me where the pretzel guy went, because that one I actually care about."

Colton pressed his nose close to the glass case in the museum's Roman room and frowned. His history teacher had assigned him to explain why people moved west in the 1800s using a real primary source, and the settler diary he'd been given sat photocopies-deep in his backpack, stubbornly silent. He'd read it twice on the bus and still had nothing except a farmer named Amos complaining about money.

Next to him, a younger kid tapped the case. "Why is that one all brown and dull? The other one's shiny."

Colton looked. The kid was right. An early coin gleamed silver-bright under the lights, its emperor's profile still crisp. A later coin sat beside it, coppery, dim, almost ugly. The label between them gave dates and names but no reason.

"Maybe it got old," the kid said.

"It's old either way," Colton said slowly. He leaned closer, and something in his brain turned over like a key. Both coins were supposed to be silver. One shone. One didn't. He crouched, comparing them side by side, then checked a second case, then a third, working down the row in order of date. It wasn't random. The older the coin, the brighter the silver. Somewhere along the line the shine kept fading, coin by coin, until some of the last ones barely looked silver at all.

He found a docent's binder open on a nearby cart and flipped to the coin pages. The words radiate pride of the empire crossed his eye, but the sentence that mattered was plainer: to pay their armies during the crises of the 200s, Roman emperors put less and less silver into their coins, until some held only a few percent silver. Colton read it twice. That was it. That was why the dull one was dull. His instinct had been right that something was off, and now he had proof, checked case by case, systematic as a list.

Then he stopped. Wait. He pulled out the diary pages. Amos the settler kept worrying about paper money going bad, banks failing, his savings turning to nothing in his pocket. Colton read the third entry again, and his stomach jumped. Different century, different continent, but the shape of it was the same. Money that people couldn't trust pushed people to move, whether they were Romans or farmers loading a wagon for Oregon.

At the assignment table by the exit, he spread out the diary and wrote his first sentence: a farmer who no longer trusted money looked for land he could hold in his own hands. He underlined it, then read it aloud to himself.

"Hey," the kid said, appearing at his elbow. "So why was the coin brown?"

"Because the silver was mostly gone," Colton said. "Some of them held only a few percent."

Dominic had one goal for Thursday's session at the tutoring centre: finish his algebra worksheet before the centre's ancient wall clock hit five, so he could grab the good seat, the chair by the window, before anyone else. The worksheet had other plans. Seven problems, all equations with x on one side, and the last one had fractions in it.

"You're doing fine on the first six," said Ms. Okafor, tapping his page. "Whatever you do to one side, do to the other. That's the whole game." She moved on to a girl at the next table, and Dominic got to work. He undid an addition, then a division, and x emerged like a fish pulled out of water, wiggling but caught. He checked it by substituting the number back in, and it fit. He was almost proud of himself, which was rare at 4:41 on a Thursday.

Then problem seven. One quarter, plus a number of sixths, equals x, or something arranged in that neighbourhood. Dominic stared at it. The two fractions sat there like kids from different schools who refused to share a table. He thought about multiplying everything by ten, which worked for decimals, but he suspected it wouldn't accommodate fractions this ugly. He wrote it anyway, then crossed it out.

At the next table, Priya from his math class was doing the same kind of problem. She had multiplied hers by 24 and was now wrestling with numbers the size of locker combinations. Her friend Marcus leaned over and pointed at her page. "You don't need 24. The least common denominator is the smallest number both denominators divide into evenly. For quarters and sixths, it's 12." Priya frowned, tried it, and her whole problem shrank to something a person could actually do.

Dominic looked down at his own page. Quarters and sixths. His denominators were the same pair as hers. He tried 12, multiplying every term on both sides, and the fractions evaporated, leaving a plain equation, the kind he'd already beaten six times. The least common denominator, he thought, was like a rudder: small, invisible in the water, and the only reason the boat went where you wanted.

He finished at 4:58, checked problem seven twice, and carried his worksheet to the window seat. Priya was still erasing. "You're welcome," Marcus told her. She threw her eraser at him.

Ruby sprinted up the driveway with the gift bag swinging from her wrist, because Aunt Hana's dinner started at six o'clock sharp and it was already 5:54. Her mother had sent her ahead with the mangoes while the rest of the family piled out of the minivan, arguing about parking.

At the front door, Ruby stopped so fast she nearly skidded. The porch light showed a neat row of shoes beside the step, all toes pointing outward, and beyond them a lower floor of dark tile inside the doorway. Two pairs of slippers sat waiting on the raised hallway floor, as if they had been set out on purpose.

"That's the genkan," said her cousin Kenta, popping his head around the door. "You take your shoes off there before you come in."

Ruby peeled off her sneakers and lined them up with the others, matching the direction. Then she stepped up in her socks and slid her feet into the slippers, which were a half size too big but felt weirdly official, like a costume. Kenta grinned and led her toward the kitchen, where the smell of grilled fish had taken over the whole house like it owned the place.

"Careful with those," Kenta said, nodding at her bag. "The wrapping paper Aunt Hana likes is kind of flammable, so keep it away from the stove." Ruby clutched the bag tighter. She had learned about wrapping at Grandma's last Thanksgiving, where you handed gifts over with both hands and the receiver set them aside unopened, which had nearly eliminated Ruby's ability to wait, but she had survived. Here, apparently, the mangoes would be presented before dinner, so she had that to look forward to.

At the table, Ruby noticed Kenta saying "itadakimasu" before anyone touched the chopsticks, so she said it too, copying his rhythm, and Aunt Hana beamed at her like she had won something. Then Ruby watched how Kenta held his bowl close to his chin and never stuck his chopsticks upright into his rice, and she decided to test a theory: if she copied him move for move, nobody would correct her once all evening. Bowl up, chopsticks low, quiet slurp of the noodles, which at her own house would have earned her a look from her father but here got Aunt Hana an approving nod at both of them.

"Second helping?" Aunt Hana asked, already reaching for the pot.

"Yes, please," Ruby said, lifting her bowl with both hands.

Landon hunched over the family computer, refreshing his feed for the tenth time. The photo he had posted last night, a shot of his new mountain bike leaning against the garage, should have been safe. His account was private, so only people he had accepted could see it. Yet there it was on a public page called "Bike Spots of Riverside," his bike, his garage door, and the corner of his street sign just visible behind the spokes.

"Maya, come look at this," he said.

His sister wandered in with her phone in one hand and a rice cake in the other. Maya wanted one thing above all else this summer, which was to reach a thousand followers so she could feel like a real artist instead of a kid with a sketchbook. She leaned over his shoulder and frowned at the screen.

"That's your garage," she said. "How did it get on a public page?"

"That's what I want to know." Landon scrolled down. The repost had a caption: "Found this beauty parked on Maple Court, near the school." His stomach tightened. Whoever posted it knew his street.

Maya sat on the edge of the desk chair. "You accepted that guy last week, didn't you? Dev something. He commented on my drawings once."

Landon remembered, and the memory rose up like a flashback from a movie. It was the night he'd gotten the bike, and he'd been so proud that he'd accepted three follow requests in a row without checking any of them. Dev had a profile picture of a skate park and zero posts of his own. Landon had tapped accept in half a second, thinking only that more followers made his page look good, the way Maya was always saying it did.

"I barely know him," Landon said slowly. "But he's a follower, so he can see everything I post." He stopped, turning the idea over. "And if he can see it, he can copy it. Private just means strangers can't walk in the door. It doesn't stop people already inside from carrying things out."

"Ugh," Maya said. "That's like a parasite. It latches on and takes stuff, and you don't even notice."

Landon wasn't ready to accuse anyone yet. He wanted proof, not a guess. So he tried a test, the way his science teacher liked to say, one variable at a time. He posted a new photo of the bike with a caption that read, "Moving the bike to my grandma's porch on Delmore Road for the week." Delmore Road was a real street, but his grandma lived two towns away. If Dev was the one leaking, the leak would follow the fake trail.

The waiting was the worst part. Landon refreshed the page every few minutes, his knee bouncing under the desk. Maya stood behind him, chewing her rice cake down to nothing. The afternoon light shifted across the keyboard. Finally, a new post appeared on Bike Spots of Riverside: Landon's photo, with a caption that said, "This one's hiding out on Delmore now. Grandmas keep the best bikes."

Maya gasped. Landon felt something cold slide through him. Nobody knew about Delmore except his followers, and only one of them had a page full of other people's photos, all reposted, all tagged with locations, as if collecting kids' stuff was a hobby.

Landon clicked to his follower list, found Dev, and removed him. Then he went through every other name, evading the temptation to keep the ones that made his numbers look big, and removed anyone he couldn't say hello to in person. Maya watched him do it, quiet for once.

"I'm not going to accept randoms anymore either," she said at last, sounding more assertive than Landon had ever heard her. "A thousand followers isn't worth it if one of them is a thief."

She held up her phone to show him her sketchbook page, and the follower count sitting at 997.

"Three to go," she said, "but real ones this time."

Theodore had until seven o'clock tomorrow morning to explain the monsoon to his geography class, and so far all he knew was that it involved rain and somewhere far away called South Asia. He was lying on the living room floor at Grandpa's house, leafing through an atlas so old it smelled like a shoebox, when he found a giant map of Asia covered in thin gray lines.

"They're parallels," Grandpa said from his armchair, peering over his glasses. "Lines of latitude. They're called parallels because they never meet."

"Never?" Theodore squinted at the map. The horizontal lines curved across the page like sleepy smiles, stacked one under another. Then he noticed the vertical lines running the other way. "So what are these?"

"Meridians. Lines of longitude."

Theodore snorted. "Meridians. That sounds like a disease. 'Sorry, I can't come to school, I've caught a bad case of the meridians.'"

Grandpa laughed, a wheezy, infectious laugh that made the cat leave the room in protest. "You have five seconds to stop making fun of the atlas or no snack."

The snack arrived anyway, and Theodore spread the map flat between a bowl of peanuts and the remote. He traced his finger along a parallel that ran straight through India, then wiggled it up toward the Himalayas. The land got higher, the lines got squished, and somewhere in his brain two ideas bumped into each other. Sun heats the land all summer, he thought, and land heats up faster than the ocean, so air rises over India and wet ocean air rushes in to take its place, and that air drops its rain when it climbs the mountains. Rain everywhere, for months. Rice loves that. Rice paddies practically sit in water on purpose.

But he wanted to test it before he trusted it. He exhaled slowly onto his bedroom window that evening, watching the glass fog up in a little cloud, then dragged his finger down through it like a raindrop sliding off a mountain. Condensation, cooling air, water letting go. The window was his Himalayas. "Take that, monsoon," he whispered, feeling slightly like a tiny weather god.

At school the next morning, Mrs. Purohit called on him first. Theodore drew the map on the board, sketching the parallels across India. "These are lines of latitude," he said. "They're called parallels because they never meet. The ones going the other way are meridians, and they matter here because the sun heats everything between them all summer long." Then he laid out the rest: hot land, rising air, ocean breeze, mountains, rain, rice. Behind him, his friend Marcus whispered, "Meridians," and stifled a laugh.

After class Mrs. Purohit handed back his notes with a grin. "Best explanation of the year. Where did you learn all that?"

"At my grandpa's house," Theodore said. "From an atlas older than the mountains."

Alexia stood in the laundry aisle with her mother's crumpled list and her own money, feeling like a spy in unfamiliar territory. "Detergent, cold water kind," the list said, and "stain stick." Her mom was away for two weeks, which meant the laundry was Alexia's job now, all of it, sorting to folding. She had watched her mother do it a hundred times, but watching was different from knowing. She picked up a blue bottle, read the back, and put it back. Commerce, she thought, was mostly a trick of making you believe you needed twelve kinds of clean.

Outside, she unlocked her bike and found the back tyre soft as a sleeping cat. She groaned. The repair kit in her backpack had a patch, a pump, and a plastic lever, and she had a vague memory of her cousin fixing a flat once, crouched on the sidewalk like it was nothing. She knelt down and wedged the lever under the edge of the tyre and pushed. Nothing. She pushed harder, and the plastic began to bend. A boy about her age, stacking carts nearby, watched her struggle for a minute before drifting over.

"You're going to snap that," he said.

"It has to come off. That's how you get the tube out." She pointed at the flattened tube, the hidden thing inside the tyre that she couldn't see but knew was there, the thing that actually held the air. She pushed again, and the lever still would not budge, not even a little.

"Maybe it's just stuck," the boy said. "Maybe the whole wheel's a goner."

Alexia didn't answer, because something had occurred to her. The tyre felt stiff all around, tight as a drum even though the tube was flat. What if the leftover air was the problem? Not the tube itself, but the pressure trapped in there, invisible, pinning the tyre to the rim. It sounded plausible to her, and it was testable. She found the valve, pressed the little pin inside it, and heard a thin hiss that went on longer than she expected. She kept pressing until the hiss died completely and the tyre went completely slack.

She slid the lever under the edge again and it moved like a spoon through soup, lifting the tyre off the rim with one easy push.

"Whoa," the boy said. He had clearly changed his mind about the whole wheel being a goner. "You let all the air out first."

"Yeah," Alexia said, already pulling the tube free, hunting for the puncture she could not see yet but would find. She patched it, pumped it firm, and rolled the lever into her pocket like a trophy.

At home, she sorted the laundry into piles on her bed, darks and whites and a hopeful middle pile she decided to call "probably fine." The stain stick even got the mustard out of her green shirt. She folded everything into squares that were not perfect but were hers, and set the last warm stack on the dresser.

Austin had exactly one weekend to figure out why rice farmers in South Asia cared about wind that changed direction twice a year, and his science grade depended on it. He'd read the chapter twice. Something about land heating up faster than water, air rising, moist ocean air flowing in to replace it, rain, months of rain. The words made sense until he closed the book, at which point they evaporated like, well, water.

Then his grandpa mailed him a package. Inside was a folded paper map, creased soft from years of handling, and a note in ballpoint: "Found this cleaning the garage. It's a U.S. Geological Survey 7.5-minute topographic map of the hills behind our old place. Scale of 1:24,000, so one inch on the map equals 2,000 feet on the ground. You always liked that trail. Figured you'd want it before I donate the rest. Love, Grandpa."

Austin scrutinized the map, the way he'd learned to scrutinize things he didn't understand, which was to stare at them hopefully. Brown contour lines looped around the hills, and a dashed line wiggled up the valley. That was the trail he'd hiked every summer, the one where Grandpa always claimed his knees were fine and then sat down on the first available rock. Austin had once asked how long the trail was, and Grandpa had said two miles, give or take his complaining.

Two miles. Austin got a ruler. The dashed line measured a little over five inches, and if one inch equaled 2,000 feet, then five inches was 10,000 feet. He did it twice, because the first time he got the same answer and distrusted it. Ten thousand feet was about two miles. The map wasn't a picture of the trail; it was a promise about the trail, and the promise held. He sat back. Something that looked like nothing but squiggles could tell you something true about a place you couldn't see.

Monday, he stood at the front of the room with the map taped to the board. "This is a topo map of a real place," he said. "One inch on it equals 2,000 feet, because the scale is 1:24,000. I measured a trail I've actually hiked, and the math came out right." Priya, in the second row, raised her hand. "So? What's that got to do with monsoons?"

"Everything," Austin said. "The monsoon is the same trick. You can't see the land heating up, and you can't see the ocean air sliding in over it, but you can see what they do. Every year, the pattern repeats, and it isn't random." He drew two arrows on the board, one pointing toward the land, one pointing back out, almost symmetrical, like the sky breathing in and out. "Rice needs standing water for months. Farmers in India and Bangladesh plant when the monsoon comes, because that rain fills the paddies. When it's late or weak, the crop fails. So they watch for the pattern, the same way I checked the map against the trail. You test the invisible thing against something you can measure."

For his demonstration, he set a baking pan of sand next to a pan of water under the classroom lamp. Within ten minutes the sand was warm and the water was barely changed, and Priya said, "Huh. Okay."

Austin rolled up the map and put a rubber band around it. "Grandpa says his knees are fine, by the way. The map says his trail is two miles."

Harper unfolded the paper on her knees and read the first line out loud. "Meeting of the Maple Street Club, held at Priya's birthday party. Item one: picking the game for the rest of the afternoon." Seven kids sat in a circle on the grass, and Priya's balloons drifted above them in the warm wind. Harper had never run a meeting before, but her paper had a list, and the list said everyone got a turn to speak.

Dex spoke first, arms crossed. "Rock-paper-scissors. And rock, obviously. Rock always wins."

"That's not true," Maya said. "Paper beats rock."

"Okay, but rock is still the best one," Dex said.

Harper looked at her agenda. Item two, she had written, was settling arguments with facts. "We can test it," she said. "Maya, you're up next on the list." She handed Maya a napkin and a pen from the party table. "Play him. Lots of rounds. Write down who wins each one and what they threw."

They played while the others munched cake. Dex threw rock again and again, and the tally crept across the napkin: rock loses to paper, rock beats scissors, paper beats rock, scissors beat paper. After twenty rounds Dex had won eight and lost twelve, and the score kept wobbling around half. Maya held up the napkin. "Look. Rock beats scissors and it loses to paper. That's it. Paper beats rock but loses to scissors, and scissors beat paper but lose to rock. Every choice beats exactly one other choice and loses to exactly one. So no choice is better than the others. Rock isn't special."

Dex squinted at the tally as if a swarm of ants might invade it and rearrange the marks. "Then how come I always used to win with rock?"

"Because everyone thinks like you," Maya said. "They throw scissors half the time, so rock beats them. Then they figure you out."

"You're like a defendant who keeps losing the same case," Priya said from behind her cake, "and keeps blaming the judge."

"That's not even how courts work," Dex said, but he was grinning now.

Harper wrote the verdict at the bottom of the napkin and read it aloud like an official record, and Dex nodded, which she counted as a credible surrender. Then she checked her agenda. "Item three: cake seconds." Everyone raised a hand, so no vote was needed, and Harper crossed the line out with a satisfying stroke of the pen.

The gate of Fairview Cemetery had an abrupt squeak that William heard from fifty feet away, which meant his little sister Ruthie was already inside. He found her standing between two graves, one with a stone cross carved with lilies, the other with a flat marker bearing a Star of David and small pebbles left by visitors. Their grandfather David was under the second one, and their great-aunt Maria was under the first, and William had been arguing with himself all week about which of them, if either, could still somehow see him standing there.

"It's not a contest," his mother had said at breakfast, but William had turned it into one anyway. Aunt Maria's church had taught that souls rise to heaven, whole and awake. Grandpa's synagogue taught something quieter, something William had never quite pinned down, and that was the problem. He had decided the way he decided things in science class: if two ideas explained the same thing differently, look for evidence, or at least for a test. His test was simple, if a little strange. He would stand at each grave and try saying something out loud, something he would only say if he thought someone was listening.

At Aunt Maria's cross he stood a long minute, then said, "I got moved up to second violin." Nothing happened, obviously, and he felt foolish in the hot still air. At Grandpa's marker he was about to repeat it when Ruthie held up a braided candle with several wicks, the one from the spice box their mom kept in the car for Saturday nights. "Mom says I'm allowed to hold the Havdalah candle this week," Ruthie said. "For the first time. And we still have the cup of grape juice and the spices to smell in the bag."

"You brought the whole thing here?" William asked.

"Grandpa would want to smell the spices," Ruthie said, as if that settled it, and William found he could not argue, because in his head the whole ceremony suddenly orbited the idea of separation, the Sabbath ending and the ordinary week beginning, one thing passing into another, the way a conductor lifts a hand and the music shifts into something you didn't expect.

He stood at the marker and changed his test. Instead of speaking as if to someone above, he said, "I got moved up to second violin, and I'm sorry I quit orchestra last year. That was a mistake." The words felt different than they had at the cross, less like sending a message and more like putting a pebble on the stone, which was something he'd always thought was just tradition. Maybe the two graves weren't competing after all. Maybe they were both pointing at something nobody could check from where they stood.

Ruthie tugged his sleeve. "You can hold the candle too," she said, "but only one wick end each."
