Each rectangle had a dark, thick edge, the same border on every single one, and inside each rectangle sat a small dense dot, slightly off center, like a stamp on every brick. Every brick had one. A wall wouldn't do that. She counted five rectangles, then five dots, then five thick borders. The pattern held.

"It's not a wall," she said slowly. "The cell wall is the thick outer border around each onion cell. Each brick is one whole cell. That's why they look like rows of bricks." She grabbed her pencil. The thick border on her diagram, done. The dot was the nucleus, which meant the faint line just inside the border had to be the membrane. She labeled all three, then wrote her name at the top before anything could go wrong.

Desmond took his turn at the eyepiece, still clutching the flashlight, and did not move for a full minute. "Nevaeh," he said finally, "your onion has tiny rooms."

"Cells," she said. "You can keep the spoon."

Alexandre stood at the white line on the track behind the school, breathing into his cupped hands, because Coach Reyes had posted the sign-up sheet for Friday's eight-hundred-metre race and his name was on it, in ink, where anyone could see it. Last year he had gone out like a rocket in this same race and then spent the second half of it jogging with his hands on his knees while other kids streamed past him. He still remembered the exact sound of his own footsteps slowing, slap, slap, slap, like his shoes had given up before he had.

"Track's four hundred metres," said Priya, walking the curve beside him with a stopwatch. "So the eight hundred is exactly two laps. You plan it as a first lap and a second lap, not one long sprint." She was only repeating what the whole team knew, the way she repeated the lunch menu, but Alexandre heard it differently this time, because Friday was coming and his legs already felt tired.

That afternoon he found a folded note taped inside his locker, from his friend Dev, who was home with a broken wrist and apparently too much free time. "Dear Future Champion," it began. "Break a leg. Not like me. Also, I watched your race last year. You ran the first lap like the track was on fire and the second lap like the fire won. P.S. I have started a currency system in math class. One Skittle equals one pencil. The economy is lush and I am rich." Alexandre laughed so hard a sixth-grader turned to stare.

On Friday he made a rule for himself and refused to modify it, even in his head. First lap: fast but not furious. Second lap: everything he had left. At the gun he held back while Marcus from Mr. Okafor's class exploded ahead, arms pumping, and by the backstretch of the first lap Marcus had ten metres on everyone. Coming around into the second lap, Marcus suddenly surged again, threw his head back, and drove across the line, arms wide, shouting before he slowed to a walk.

Alexandre counted the laps on his fingers the whole way. He passed Marcus, who was walking with his hands on his hips near the infield, and heard him mutter, "Wait. That was only one?" Alexandre kept his eyes on Priya at the fence, where she held up one finger, then, a lap later, zero. He emptied everything he had into the last hundred metres, crossed the actual finish line second, and bent over gasping while Dev's crumpled note fell out of his pocket onto the lush green grass. Priya jogged over, looked down at it, and said, "Tell Dev the Skittle economy is doomed."

The morning after Tuesday's practice, Simon's legs ached so much that walking down the bleacher steps felt like stepping onto two bricks. Marco, who caught for the team, climbed up beside him rubbing his shoulder.

"It's all that lactic acid," Marco said. "It builds up when we work hard."

Simon thought about that while they took infield drills. Practice had ended at five o'clock yesterday. His legs had felt fine at dinner, fine at bedtime, fine when he brushed his teeth this morning. The soreness had shown up today, more than a day later. If something was building up during practice, it seemed like it should hurt right after practice, not the next morning. He decided to run a test on himself. At the end of warmups he did ten full sprints from foul pole to foul pole, harder than he ever worked in a game, and then he waited.

An hour after the sprints, sitting in the dugout with his glove on his knee, he flexed his calves. Nothing hurt. He could feel his pulse in them, and they were warm, but the soreness was not there yet. The next morning it arrived, right on schedule, in both legs at once. It was the same pattern as Tuesday. Whatever was making his muscles sore, it was not still sitting in his legs from the exercise, because an hour after he stopped, everything felt normal. On Thursday he found Marco by the equipment shed, pumping up a flat football that someone had left in the bin. The pump handle squeaked with every stroke, and the ball grew round and firm with each push of air.

"Marco, I checked," Simon said. "I did sprints yesterday and felt fine an hour later. If lactic acid were the problem, it would have to stick around a whole day to make me sore this morning. It doesn't. It goes back to normal levels within about an hour after you exercise."

Marco stopped pumping and squinted at him. "Then what's making my shoulder hurt?"

"I don't know yet. But it isn't that."

Coach Alvarez walked past and told them practice was starting, and whether Marco's throw to second was late or on time, that was her call, though Marco muttered that the whole strike zone was subjective anyway, so why bother arguing. The football, fat with air now, sat on the bench forgotten. Simon picked it up, tossed it once in his hand, and handed it back to Marco.

"Hold onto this," he said. "We're testing your shoulder next."

Rosalie slid her binder onto the desk just as Madame Perrin wrote the assignment on the board: a paragraph about your family and pets, then your summer plans, all in French. The room smelled like whiteboard marker and the dusty radiator by the window. Rosalie had seven sentences already, but the last two were the problem.

"You have to use 'voyagerai,'" said Dominic, leaning across the aisle. "Future tense. It sounds way more official."

"It sounds like a robot," said Priya from the next row. "Nobody talks like that."

Dominic flipped through his textbook, hunting for proof. Priya rolled her pen across her desk. Rosalie stared at her own draft, where she had written "Je vais voyager en juillet." She had copied that shape from a poster near the pencil sharpener, one of a boy loading a suitcase, but she had never asked herself why it looked like that. "Vais" was a form of aller, the going verb, and the second word sat there untouched, like an English verb after "to." So the whole thing must mean "I am going to travel," built out of going plus the plain verb. If that was true, she could say almost anything about summer with it.

She tested the idea on the poster sentence, then on her own. She tried "Je vais nager," pointing at Priya. "I am going to swim?" Priya nodded slowly, and Dominic stopped mid-page. Rosalie tried one more, "Je vais adopter un chat," and it held together the same way. Going, then the verb, nothing changing at the end. Dominic read her paragraph over her shoulder and sighed.

"Fine," he said. "Yours sounds like a person. Mine sounds like a narrator reading the news."

"It's still plausible," Priya said generously. "Just stiff."

Rosalie finished her paragraph while the radiator ticked. Her last line was "Nous allons donner le vieux lit du chien au refuge," because her family had agreed to donate the dog's old bed to the shelter once they got the new puppy in June. She read the whole thing once through, quiet under her breath, and liked the sound of it.

When Madame Perrin walked the rows, she paused at Rosalie's desk, tapped the final sentence twice with her finger, and drew a small sun in the margin. Rosalie looked at Dominic and raised one eyebrow. He slid his paper toward her and crossed out "voyagerai."

The trumpet felt like a brick in Anthony's hands, and Mr. Ruiz had already called his name twice. "Measure sixteen, Anthony. From the top." The music classroom smelled like valve oil and old carpet, and the radiators radiated a dry heat that made his fingers stiff. Anthony lifted the horn, blew, and cracked the same high note he had cracked every Tuesday for three weeks.

Beside him, Priya slid her flute onto her lap and leaned over. "You practice, right?" she whispered. "Sunday night? Because you sound great for the first eight measures and then it all falls apart."

"Two hours," Anthony admitted. "Last night. The whole book." He had meant it as proof. Priya's eyebrows went up, and something about her face made him feel like he'd said the wrong thing even though he'd done more work than she had.

At lunch, Anthony sat with his sandwich untouched and thought it through like a math problem. Priya practiced every single day, he knew that, because she'd told the whole section once. Maybe twenty minutes a day. He did two hours in one night. Two hours was six times twenty minutes, so his total time was way more than hers, and yet she played the solo and he cracked notes. Same amount of practice should mean same result. Unless the total wasn't the thing that mattered. Unless the spreading out was the thing. He turned his milk carton around and around. There was only one way to find out.

He made a chart on the back of his science folder and ruled it into small boxes: fifteen minutes before school, ten at night, every day until the next Tuesday. He didn't tell Priya, in case it didn't work. His little sister, Rosa, pounded the piano keys while he practiced, so he started leaving a bag of pretzels on the bench for her, and she settled into playing her own made-up songs at a gentler volume, which helped them both.

The first few days felt slow. He kept missing the same leap in measure sixteen, and his grandfather's old trumpet, a dented brass alloy that had survived two wars and one fall down a staircase, seemed to laugh at him. But on Thursday something odd happened. He picked up the horn, cold, no warm-up except a few long tones, and his fingers found the fingering for the high note before his brain did. He hadn't drilled it harder. He had just... come back to it, again and again, letting each short session do a little work while he slept, ate, walked to school.

On Tuesday, Mr. Ruiz raised his baton. "Measure sixteen. Anthony." The room went quiet. Priya gave him a tiny nod across the stand. Anthony took a breath, thought of nothing at all, and let his fingers go where they had learned to go. The high note came out round and silver, and the kid on trombone, who had declared trumpets obsolete ever since the school bought the low brass section new instruments, said, "Whoa," into his slide.

After class Priya caught him at the door. "So what changed?"

Anthony held up his folder, the chart with its rows of small checkmarks. "Same twenty minutes every day," he said. "Not two hours the night before. Turns out that's the whole trick." Priya grabbed a marker from her pocket and said, "Draw me one."

The photo went up at 9:02 on a Tuesday night: Willow doing her weird victory dance after finishing her science project, socks half off, face scrunched like a raisin. She had meant to send it only to Priya, but her thumb hit the whole group chat instead. Eighteen people. She deleted it within ten minutes, heart hammering, and then sat very still in her dark bedroom, watching the chat scroll on about weekend plans as if nothing had happened. She let herself breathe. Gone meant gone, she decided, and went to sleep.

At lunch the next day, Priya slid her phone across the table. "Look at this." In a different group chat, one Willow wasn't even in, someone had posted the photo with the caption "found this gem." Beneath it, people she barely knew were typing laughing faces and the word "iconic." Willow's stomach dropped. She had deleted it. How could it be here, in a place she couldn't reach?

"I don't get it," she said. "I took it down."

Priya shrugged. "Deleting a post removes it from your page, but anyone who already took a screenshot still has it."

Willow stared at the screen. So that was the rule. It wasn't magic; it was a copy, sitting in someone's camera roll, free to travel anywhere. She scrolled up and found the name of the account that had posted it: a boy named Marcus from her math class. She barely knew him. But the photo hadn't appeared out of nowhere, and somebody had to have passed it along.

That night she ran a test, the way she would for a lab. She posted a harmless picture of her cat to the group chat, waited exactly ten minutes, deleted it, and then texted Priya: "Did you screenshot it before it vanished?" Priya sent back a screenshot, timestamp and all, plus a smug message about how the cat deserved a citation for cuteness. Willow laughed, but her mind was working. The copy survived deletion. That was the whole answer. She couldn't unsend the dance photo, and envying people whose embarrassing moments never surfaced wouldn't help either. What she could do was be objective about the situation, like her science teacher kept saying: state the facts, then act.

The next morning she walked straight to Marcus's table in the cafeteria. "You posted my photo in the other chat," she said, keeping her voice level. "I'm not mad, but I want to know who sent it to you, because I deleted it and it still got around." Marcus looked uncomfortable, then held up his phone. "It was Priya. She thought it was hilarious. She said you'd figure it out eventually." Willow turned around. Priya was standing behind her, grinning, phone raised, and Willow's cat was already on the screen.

The community pool at nine in the morning was almost empty, which was exactly why Beatrice had claimed lane two for her secret project: learning to pace an eight-hundred-metre race even though she was standing in three feet of chlorinated water. Her plan, hatched last night with a notebook and two markers, was to walk one pool length fast, then walk a second length immediately, and feel the difference between starting too fast and starting right.

"Move over, you're invading my coaching zone," said a voice from the fence. It was Dominic from her grade, dragging five plastic hurdles onto the grass beside the pool. He wanted to make the county hurdles team more than he wanted lunch, probably, because he'd been out there every morning all week, crashing into the same hurdle and swearing in a way he thought nobody could hear.

"Why don't you just ask Coach to move them?" Beatrice called through the fence.

"He'd say I'm not ready for race spacing." Dominic wiped sweat off his forehead. "But I asked him yesterday anyway, and guess what. He said yes, backwards." He yanked the first hurdle closer to the second and clicked it down to its lowest notch. "We learn the three-step rhythm with hurdles lower and closer together than race spacing. Then we move them apart as we get faster. So today they're short and squished and I only have to survive."

Beatrice stood in the water with her mouth open. Shorter and closer first. Start with the small version of the thing, then grow it. She thought of last Tuesday's time trial, when she'd exploded off the line, led the whole first lap, and then her legs had turned to something molten, like her muscles had melted inside her skin, and three girls had passed her before the final curve. Her coach had said "save something," which had meant nothing to her at the time, like being told to save money when you couldn't see the money.

But pacing was a thing you couldn't see, and that was the problem. Speed you could see. Energy left in your legs, you could not. So maybe, like Dominic's hurdles, she needed the squished-together version. She set her goggles, pushed off, and swam one length flat-out, then tried to immediately swim a second. Halfway down the return lap her arms felt like wet noodles and she had to grab the lane rope, gasping, while a lifeguard gave her the look you give a drowning hamster. Okay. That was the "too fast first lap," demonstrated in a place where she could stop and think about it instead of collapsing on a track in front of everyone.

Second attempt. She counted her strokes on the first length, deliberately holding back, and it felt almost boring, like walking when you wanted to run. Then the second length, and her arms still worked, still pulled, and she touched the wall breathing hard but whole. Through the fence, Dominic cleared all five low hurdles in a row without touching one, and threw his arms up like he'd won the Olympics.

"Did you see that?" he shouted.

"I saw it," Beatrice called back, grinning into her goggles. "Now move them apart."

Wyatt jogged to the fence line of the outdoor court, where Coach Reyes had chalked a wobbly oval that looped the blacktop. Eight times around made eight hundred metres, and next Saturday was his first real race. His best friend Dez was already there, spinning a basketball on one finger.

"Eight laps, remember," Dez called. "Not a sprint war."

Wyatt ignored him and took off like the race started today. His sneakers slapped the asphalt, arms pumping, and the wind pushed cool against his sweaty neck. He finished the first lap in what felt like record time. By lap three his legs were full of wet sand. By lap five he was walking, hands on his knees, lungs burning like somebody had lit a match inside them.

"That went great," Dez said, grinning.

"It did not." Wyatt gulped air. But something nagged at him, something he couldn't see. He hadn't slowed down because he was tired all at once. The tiredness had been building quietly the whole time, hiding behind his fast first lap like a trick. If spending everything early created the wall later, maybe the opposite was true too. He had to test it. "One more. Timer on."

This time he ran the first lap deliberately neutral, not slow, not fast, just steady as a metronome. It felt almost too easy. He held the same rhythm through lap two, lap three. When lap five arrived, the wall didn't. His legs still had juice, so he pushed harder, and the steady rhythm propelled him through the final two laps faster than his old sprint pace. He leaned against the fence, laughing and gasping at the same time.

While he caught his breath, Dez and two other boys, Marcus and Theo, started a two-on-two game. Marcus had the ball at the top, and Theo ran toward Wyatt's fence side, planting his body like a wall in Marcus's defender's path. The defender bumped off Theo and stumbled, and Marcus darted around them toward the hoop. But a different defender, Theo's man, was suddenly waiting for him under the basket.

"Hey, that's not fair!" Marcus complained, whirling around.

"It's a switch," Dez said, tossing him the ball back. "The two defenders trade the players they're guarding."

Marcus frowned at Theo's screen, then at the two defenders, and Wyatt watched the whole thing click together in his friend's face. It was like his race, Wyatt thought. The move you could see was only half of it; the real play was the hidden exchange happening behind it.

"Again," Marcus said, pounding the ball hard into the asphalt. "This time I'll read the switch and slip the other way."

Wyatt checked his watch and bounced on his toes at the chalk line. "You guys figure out your trick plays. I've got four more laps to run."

"Race you to the fence," Dez said.

Riley pressed three tomato seeds into the dark soil of her aunt's farm and patted them down like she was tucking them into bed. She had claimed the plot behind the barn on day one, and by June the seedlings were knee-high, and by July she had green marbles swelling on every branch. Her plan was simple and enormous: sell her tomatoes at the farm stand by the road, next to her aunt's jam and eggs.

The trouble started at the stand on Saturday. A man in a sun hat picked up one of Riley's ripe red tomatoes, weighed it in his palm, and said, "You've got these in the wrong bin, kid. Tomatoes are fruit. They belong with the peaches."

"They're vegetables," Riley said. "They go in the salad, not the fruit bowl."

"Fruit," the man insisted. "Seeds on the inside. That's a fruit."

Riley's cousin Marisol leaned over the cash box. "Then cucumbers are fruit too. And peppers. And pumpkins."

The man laughed. "Pumpkins? Now you're being ridiculous."

Riley wanted to win this. More than that, she wanted to be right, which she had learned was not always the same thing. That night she borrowed her aunt's laptop and typed one question: is a tomato a fruit or a vegetable. The answer made her sit up straight. Botanically, a tomato was a fruit, full stop. But in 1893, the US Supreme Court had ruled in a case called Nix v. Hedden that for import taxes, tomatoes counted as vegetables. She read it twice, then read it to Marisol over the phone.

"Nix v. Hedden," Marisol repeated slowly, like she was chewing it. "So the Court decided taxes, not lunch."

"So both of us were right," Riley said, "and both of us were wrong. Wait till Sun Hat Man hears this."

Sunday morning, Riley made two signs on cardboard, testing her idea before anyone could argue. One read FRUIT, SCIENTIFICALLY SPEAKING. The other read VEGETABLE, ACCORDING TO THE SUPREME COURT. She set them on either side of the tomato bin with an arrow pointing between them. Her aunt walked by, paused, and said, "Very sophisticated display. Now wash your hands, stand hygiene, customers are watching you handle their food."

The man in the sun hat came back for more tomatoes. He read the signs, read them again, and rubbed his jaw. "Huh. I was scientifically right."

"And I was legally right," Riley said. "The Court said they could enforce the tax that way. So the vegetable side wins for money, and the fruit side wins for science."

He bought two pounds and told two other customers on his way out, loudly, that he had lost an argument to an eleven-year-old and enjoyed it. By noon the tomato bin was empty, and Marisol was drawing a third sign that said SOLD OUT, SCIENTIFICALLY AND LEGALLY. Riley ran back to the garden to count what was still ripening on the vines.

"Ten more turning red," she called. "Tell everyone to come back next Saturday."

The trail climbed through pines that smelled like warm resin, and Kayla stopped every few steps to shove the folded papers deeper into her backpack before they could escape. She had printed two climate graphs, one for a desert and one for a rainforest, because Monday's assignment demanded a real comparison, and she was tired of guessing.

"Are you hiking or doing homework out here?" her friend Priya asked, hopping over a root.

"Both. My teacher said learn it however we want." Kayla pulled out the desert graph and held it up so Priya could see. The rainfall bars were so short they looked like a row of fallen eyelashes. Then she flipped to the rainforest graph, where the bars shot up like a fence. "Look at this. Same planet, and one place gets this," she tapped the eyelashes, "while the other gets a wall of rain every single month."

"That wall one looks familiar," Priya said.

"It should. It's Kerala, where my Ammachi lives." Kayla smoothed the paper against a boulder and squinted at the tall June bar. Something tickled the back of her brain. Every June, without fail, her grandmother sent a photo of the first rain hitting the courtyard, and every June, Kayla's mom would say, right on time. But how could rain have a time?

She called Ammachi right there, because the trail had one bar of signal and Kayla was not the kind of person to waste a miracle. "Ammachi, quick question. Does the rain actually have a schedule?"

Her grandmother laughed so loudly that Priya heard it from a foot away. "Of course. The India Meteorological Department gives June 1 as the normal date for the southwest monsoon to reach Kerala." Down the line came the sound of a calendar page being tapped. "I mark it every year, like a birthday."

Kayla scribbled the date on the edge of her graph. "The monsoon," she repeated, tasting the word. "Okay, that clarifies everything, actually." Because there it was, hiding in plain sight: the June bar wasn't tall by accident. The rainforest graph was a picture of something you could set a calendar by, and the desert graph was a picture of a place where nothing ever arrived on schedule, or at all.

"Wait, say that as a poem," Priya demanded, taking a drink from her water bottle. "One stanza. 'In Kerala, the rain keeps appointments.'"

"In the desert," Kayla countered, "the rain ghosts you for the whole year."

They both cracked up, and a startled jay scolded them from a branch overhead. Kayla folded the graphs with the care of someone holding treasure, shouldered her pack, and marched up the trail. "I'm putting the calendar thing right in my conclusion," she announced. "And Monday, I'm asking my teacher if she knew that rain could be punctual."

The bleachers in the gymnasium smelled like floor wax and popcorn, and Victor sat on the front row of seats going over his word list one last time. He had lost the school bee last year on the word "bite," of all things, because in his head he spelled it the way it sounded and forgot the silent e. Ever since then, English spelling felt like a practical joke someone was playing on him.

Two nights before, he'd almost quit studying. He had thrown his pencil across the kitchen table and told his older sister, Dee, that English made no sense and he was going to postpone the whole thing until a language that made sense came along. Dee, who was frugal with sympathy, slid an old library book across the table instead of a speech. "Look at page forty," she said. So he did, and the page told him something he had never heard before. Between about 1400 and 1700, English vowel sounds changed in the Great Vowel Shift, and the shift happened after spellings had already started to become fixed. That, the book said, was a major reason English spelling often doesn't match pronunciation. Victor read the paragraph three times. The letters hadn't been lying all those years. People had just changed the way they said them, like a town that stays on the map after the frontier moves past it. He didn't suddenly like spelling, but he stopped feeling tricked by it, which turned out to matter more.

Now the principal stood at the microphone on the gym floor. "Contestant twelve, Victor Reyes." Victor walked out, his shoes squeaking on the varnish, and stood beside the judge's table.

"Your word is 'subtle.'"

Of course it was. A word with a silent b, sitting there like a taunt. Victor closed his eyes for a second and ran the pattern through his head: old spelling, shifted sound, the b had probably once done its job before the vowels moved on without it. It wasn't a guess anymore. It was the way the language was built.

"S-U-B-T-L-E," he said. "Subtle."

The judge checked her card and nodded. "Correct."

Victor grinned and walked back to his seat. On his way past the folding chairs he caught Dee's eye in the crowd and mouthed, "Great Vowel Shift." She gave him a thumbs up, and the principal cleared her throat for the next word.

Luca set the last cup on the folding table at the edge of the gymnasium, right under the banner that read Science Fair: Set Up by Noon. In front of him stood nine bean plants in paper cups, each one labeled with a sticky note. Three said Fertilizer A, three said Fertilizer B, and one just said Water. His best friend Marcus leaned over the table and squinted.

"Why does that one only get water?" Marcus asked. "That's like entering a race and not running."

"It's called a control group," Luca said. "It gets no change at all, so I can compare everything else against it."

The trouble was the control group was embarrassing him. Every other plant had grown at least a little, and his plain-water bean sat there with the same two sad leaves it had three weeks ago. Priya from his science class walked past, slowed down, and pointed.

"That one's dead, Luca."

"It's not dead, it's the baseline." He said it with more confidence than he felt. For weeks he had wondered whether his fertilizers were actually working. Fertilizer A plants were tall, B plants were medium, and the control was tiny. If he had no control, he would have nothing to measure against. Now he could see that A had grown twice as much as the plain-water plant, and B about half again as much. The tiny plant was doing its job by doing nothing.

Then Judge Okafor stopped at his table, and Luca's reputation as a kid who glued things together the night before felt suddenly endangered. But the judge picked up the control cup and turned it in his hands.

"Tell me about this one," she said.

"It gets no change at all," Luca said. "Plain water, same light, same everything. The tested groups only make sense if I can compare them against it."

The judge nodded slowly and wrote something on her clipboard. "Most students forget that part," she said, and moved on.

Marcus clapped him on the shoulder. "So the dead-looking plant is actually your best one."

"It's the most important one," Luca said. He watered all nine cups, saving the control for last, and straightened its sticky note so the word Water faced the aisle.

Camille counted her coins twice at the Saturday farmers' market, because the tomato seedlings had to go in the ground before the end of the weekend, and she only had six dollars. "How much for two?" she asked the man at the plant table.

"Three dollars, but I have to warn you," he said. "These are the same variety your mom bought last year, and hers didn't do well."

"My tomatoes got brown spots and fell over," Camille said. "All of them. In the back corner, by the fence."

The man rubbed his chin. "You plant tomatoes in that corner every year?"

"Every year. It's the sunniest spot. What else would I put there?" She waited, but he only shrugged and handed her the seedlings, so she paid and carried them home, frowning.

That evening, she sat on the porch steps and thought about her grandmother's farm, which she visited two summers ago. She remembered walking between the long rows while her grandmother pointed. "Tomatoes here this year, beans here, cabbage there," her grandmother had said. "Next summer, they orbit around, each row takes a turn somewhere new." Camille had thought it sounded tedious, all that moving and mapping. Now she wondered why her grandmother bothered.

On Sunday morning, Camille knocked on Mrs. Petrov's door, because Mrs. Petrov had the best garden on the street. "Can I ask you something?" Camille said. "If somebody plants tomatoes in the same corner every year, and they start getting sick, is it the corner's fault?"

Mrs. Petrov set down her watering can. "It could be. My father rotated crops, always, so the same plant family was never grown in the same spot year after year. He said it keeps the soil from making trouble." She tilted her head. "You know what family tomatoes are in?"

"No."

"Same family as peppers. Not the same as beans, or carrots, or lettuce."

Camille walked home fast, carrying the idea like a full bucket. She dug up the wilted tomato stems from the corner and dropped them in the compost pile, where the decomposers would break them down into dark, crumbly soil over the winter. Then she planted her new seedlings in the middle bed, where the beans had grown last summer. It wasn't the sunniest spot, but she could see it from her window, and she marked the corner with a stick.

All through June she measured the plants with a ruler and drew a map of the yard in her notebook. In the top corner she wrote "tomatoes, last year, sick." In the middle bed she wrote "tomatoes, this year," and every week the number of green dots on her sketch grew. On the last day of school, she counted fourteen little hard green tomatoes hanging from healthy stems.

She ran inside to get her brother. "Come look," she said. "And next spring, the tomatoes move again."

Lea's grandmother lived at the end of Ash Street, a street so long and straight that on hazy afternoons it seemed to fold into the sky. Lea sat on the porch with a sketchbook, a pencil, and one burning ambition: by Sunday, she would draw Ash Street so real that her cousin Marco would swear it was a photograph. The trouble was that whenever she drew it, the houses tipped sideways like drunk dominoes, and the road refused to narrow into the distance the way real roads did.

In the kitchen, Grandma was humming over a sheet of watercolour paper. "You look defeated," she said, without turning around.

"My street looks like it got hit by an earthquake," Lea admitted. "Marco says perspective is mandatory if you want anything to look real. He says artists have a secret trick with lines."

Grandma tapped her own drawing, a row of cottages marching toward a pencil dot she had planted in the middle of the sky. "I learned a trick like that from your great-grandfather. He called it a vanishing point. Everything runs toward it." She would say no more; she claimed mysteries were bad luck if explained, and went back to her paint.

Lea stole the idea and tried it herself. One dot on the horizon. Then she drew lines from the dot outward, like sunrays, and let the edges of roofs and fences lie along them. When she stepped back, the street lay flat and deep, the houses shrinking politely toward the dot as though bowing to it. It felt like a magic spell disguised as homework. Marco was going to lose his mind.

To console him in advance, she decided to make the drawing even crueler: a watercolour, painted at her grandmother's elbow. She wet her brush and painted the dark shadowed roofs first, planning to add the pale sunlight on the walls afterward as a final flourish. But when she swept the light yellow wash over a dark patch, the dark stayed dark, staring up through the yellow like a cat through a window. She tried white. The dark still glared through. "It won't cover," she muttered.

Grandma glanced over and gave a low whistle. "Watercolour is transparent," she said. "Every wash lets the ones underneath show through. That's why we work light to dark. A dark wash can't be covered by a lighter one."

Lea stared at her ruined rooftops, then at her grandmother's painting, which was pale as morning and would grow darker layer by layer, never the reverse. She turned to a fresh sheet, painted the whole sky the lightest water-thin yellow first, then added the shadows after, and watched them sink into place like night following day. "Ash Street, take two," she announced, and set the vanishing point down in the middle of the pale gold sky.

Livia wanted her street drawing to look real, not flat like a map. Every time she drew the bakery on the corner, it stood straight at the viewer like a poster, and the road beside it refused to slide back into the distance. Today, at the community art studio on Delancey Street, she had promised herself she would fix that.

The studio smelled like pencil shavings and turpentine. Livia claimed the table by the window and taped down a fresh sheet. Her friend Marcus slid into the seat across from her, holding a print he had taken from the studio's pile of art posters. "Look at this one," he said. "It's old. Like, really old."

The print showed a painted archway with a man standing beneath it, columns rising on both sides. Marcus read the label at the bottom. "Masaccio's Holy Trinity, a fresco in Florence, painted around 1427." He tilted the paper toward the light, and for a second the surface caught the window glare and went transparent, the image washing out to pale gray.

Livia took the print and stared. The ceiling of the painted arch was made of square panels, and something about them pulled her eyes backward, deeper into the picture. She held her pencil above the print, hesitating, then laid the pencil flat along one edge of a ceiling panel. "I have an idea," she said. "Watch." She dragged her fingertip along the panel's line, then along the next one, and the next. All the lines leaned the same way, like they were sliding down an invisible hill. "They're all going somewhere," she murmured. "Somewhere specific."

She borrowed Marcus's ruler and kept tracing, extending each ceiling line with light pencil marks, then the lines along the floor. At first the marks crossed each other like scattered spaghetti. But when she extended the lines far enough, they all crashed together at one single point, right at the level of the painted figures' feet. "There," she said, tapping it. "One point. Everything aims at it." Marcus leaned in and frowned. "So that's how the road works. The edges have to run to the same spot, or the street looks like the sidewalk is eroding away on one side."

Livia went back to her own paper. She drew a small dot in the middle of the page, then let both edges of her street run toward it, the bakery shrinking as it went. When she held the drawing up, the road actually went somewhere. She grinned and slid the Masaccio print across the table to Marcus. "Trace the ceiling yourself," she said. "I want to see if you land on the same dot."

Maeva stood in the kitchen with one sock on the tile and one bare foot in the air, frozen mid-step. The school dance was in three hours, and she had a problem with a name: Daniel Okafor. He'd asked her, she'd said yes, and then he'd texted, "Actually I don't know how to dance with a partner. Sorry." She'd stared at the phone so long her mom asked if the screen was broken.

"It's not broken," Maeva said. "It's just wrong."

Her little brother Theo, who had recently convinced Dad to install a basketball hoop over the garage door, was dribbling a ball against the refrigerator. "Dances are controversial anyway," he said. "Jayden says you have to hold a girl's hand and it's a hygiene hazard."

"You don't know anything."

"I know you're standing on one foot."

She put her foot down. Then she picked up her phone again, not for Daniel's text, but to search. Last summer at the community picnic she'd seen everybody from grandmas to six-year-olds doing the same steps in rows, and nobody had seemed paired up. She found a video from the picnic and watched it twice. Every person faced the same way, toward the picnic table with the lemonade. Every person repeated the same set of steps, over and over, a grapevine to the right, a clap, a stomp, a quarter turn. Nobody touched anybody. She tested her idea right there on the kitchen tile: she followed along, stumbled, tried again, and by the fourth repeat her feet knew the pattern without her watching.

"Whoa," Theo said. "What's that?"

"It's called a line dance," Maeva said. "A whole group does the same steps, facing the same direction, and you don't need a partner at all."

"Prove it."

She held out her hand for the ball, set it on the counter, and started the video from the beginning. "Just copy me." Theo knocked over a chair on the grapevine and laughed so hard he missed the clap, but on the second run he made it all the way to the quarter turn. On the third run they did it without the video, both facing the window, both stomping at the same moment.

At the dance, the gym was hot and loud and half the seventh grade stood along the wall like wallpaper. Daniel was there, arms crossed, alone. Maeva took a breath, walked over, and said, "You don't need a partner. You just need about four steps. Watch my feet."

The DJ started a song with a beat she knew. She stepped out onto the floor, faced the stage, and began.

"Like this?" Daniel said, two beats behind her.

"Just like that."

Chloe had one afternoon to figure out the onion cells, because on Monday her science teacher would collect lab notebooks, and Chloe's page was still blank except for the title she'd copied off the board: "Cell wall, membrane, nucleus." She was staying at her aunt's farm for the weekend, which meant no school microscopes, only the dusty old one her cousin Ruth had left in the barn loft next to a crate of empty jars.

"Good luck with that thing," Aunt Delia said when Chloe carried it down to the kitchen table. "Ruth used it to look at pond scum. Maybe pond scum is all it's good for."

The letter from her lab partner, Marcus, was folded in Chloe's back pocket, and she read it again while she peeled a papery skin off one of the onions hanging in the pantry. Marcus wrote: "You left before the teacher explained the stain, so here it is. Put a drop of iodine on your slide. It makes parts of the cell show up. Also, the nucleus isn't always where you expect. Don't give up." He had drawn a tiny onion cell in the corner with the wall, the membrane, and the nucleus labeled, but his drawing was so smudged it could have been anything.

Chloe made her first slide with plain water, clipped a thin purple sliver of skin onto it, and pressed her eye to the lens. She saw boxes, rows and rows of boxes, like a brick wall. She could label the cell wall, the outside edge of every box. But the inside was pale and empty. No nucleus anywhere. Her first thought was that the microscope was broken, and for a minute she sat back and felt like giving up, because a broken microscope was a legitimate reason to have a blank page.

Then she remembered the science museum in the city, the table where you could line up model finch beaks next to model foods. She had spent an hour there once, matching a thin, pointed beak to insects and a deep, heavy beak to hard seeds, getting it wrong, trying again until every beak sat beside its food. The trick was that you couldn't see the answer on the beak itself; you had to test what it could actually do. So the nucleus might be in her cells, just invisible, the way a beak's job was invisible until you tried it on the right seed.

She set up two slides to be sure: one plain, one with a drop of iodine from Aunt Delia's medicine cabinet. That way she had only one variable changed between them, which Marcus would appreciate. On the plain slide, still nothing. On the iodine slide, small dark dots appeared inside the boxes, one dot per cell, and a thin dark line tracing the inner edge of each wall. The nucleus and the membrane, suddenly plain as seeds in a bird's claw.

Chloe drew both slides side by side in her notebook, labeling the wall, the membrane, and the nucleus, and wrote the date and the words "iodine stain" so anyone reading it could see what she had documented. Aunt Delia leaned over her shoulder, sniffing the iodine bottle.

"You changed your mind about my microscope," Aunt Delia said.

"I changed my mind about the cells," Chloe said, and slid the notebook across the table so her aunt could see the little dark dots, each one sitting in its place.

The last three gummy bears in the bag dwindled to two, then one, and then just a red smudge on Maya's thumb while she stared out the window of the minivan. Her mom was driving them to Priya's house for a sleepover, and her little brother, Theo, was conducting his own campaign from the back seat. "Can we listen to my dinosaur podcast? Please? I've been waiting all week."

"One episode," Mom said, "after Maya tells me why she's smiling at her phone like that."

Maya wasn't smiling at her phone exactly. She was smiling at a thought. Last weekend at Priya's house, Priya had mentioned that her older sister got her first period at fourteen, which had surprised them both, because Zoe's older sister had gotten hers at eleven. Fourteen and eleven. That was a pretty big spread, and Maya couldn't stop wondering about it. Was there a normal age, or was it all just random? She couldn't see the answer anywhere, but maybe she could find it hiding in the pattern, the way you figure out a rule in math class.

So she had made a survey. She had texted ten friends and asked, "How old was your mom or your sister when she got her first period?" The replies had rolled in all afternoon: eleven, thirteen, twelve, fourteen, ten, twelve, eleven, fifteen, twelve, thirteen. Maya counted them twice on the van's armrest. Four of them were twelve, which was more than any other number, so the middle of the pile sat right there. But the edges stretched all the way from ten to fifteen. There was a center, and there was a range around it, wide as a river.

"Mom," Maya said, leaning between the seats, "when you were a kid, did anyone ever tell you the usual age for getting your first period?"

Mom glanced in the mirror. "My health teacher said something once, but I don't remember it. Why?"

"Priya's sister told her that some big CDC survey found the median age is about twelve," Maya said, "with a wide normal range around it. And guess what my survey says."

"Twelve?" Mom guessed.

"Twelve, with a range from ten to fifteen." Maya held up her phone like evidence in court. "My own data matches a giant government survey. Ten whole people." She felt a little thrill, like she had pulled back a curtain on something invisible. Her own body hadn't started yet, and somehow that felt less like being behind and more like being somewhere inside a wide, ordinary river.

Theo tugged her sleeve. "Enough period talk. Dinosaurs. Now."

"One episode," Mom said, laughing, and pressed play.

Theo leaned back, triumphant, and Maya gave his rebellious, podcast-demanding hand a pat. "Fine," she said, "but when it's over, I'm telling you about medians. It's basically the T. rex of numbers."

Kaylee sat on the crackly paper of the exam chair and stared at the chart across the room, where the third line had gone soft and blurry no matter how hard she squinted. The optometrist swung a heavy metal machine in front of her face and clicked lenses into it, one after another. "Better or worse?" she kept asking, and each time Kaylee answered, the world sharpened a little more. When the chair sank with a hiss, Kaylee glanced down and saw a small brass valve on the side, the kind that let air or fluid in and out. The optometrist must have noticed her looking, because she said, "Handy, right? I can lower it for kids and raise it back for adults."

In the frame room afterward, Kaylee tried on pair after pair while her mom watched from a stool by the window. Everything was too big, too round, or too much like something a grandmother would wear. Finally she found a thin wire pair with purple at the hinges, and the optician said they were titanium, durable enough to survive being dropped, which mattered, because Kaylee dropped things constantly.

"These are the ones," she said, turning her head in the little mirror. Then a thought hit her so hard she said it out loud. "Wait. What did people do before glasses existed? Like, in ancient times? Everyone who couldn't see just... couldn't read?"

The optician hummed and straightened a display of cases. "Well, glasses weren't actually that old an invention, if you think about it. The earliest eyeglasses were made in central Italy, around 1290."

"Thirteen ninety?" Kaylee said, gripping the mirror's edge.

"Twelve ninety. Central Italy."

Kaylee did the math, and the math made her dizzy. People had been writing things down for thousands of years before that, and for most of that time, anyone with eyes like hers would have had to hold a page practically against her nose, or give up entirely. She began to elaborate her theory out loud: that must be why some old paintings showed scholars holding books at arm's length, or squinting like she did at the whiteboard last Tuesday when she copied the homework wrong and got a zero she didn't deserve. That zero was the reason she was here. She'd spent a month blaming the teacher's handwriting before admitting the real cause was hiding behind her own eyeballs, invisible until she finally tested the idea by sitting in the front row and getting everything right.

"So for thousands of years," she said slowly, "everyone who needed glasses just didn't get any."

Her mom came over and rested a hand on her shoulder. "And now you do. That's something."

The optician slid the purple-hinged pair into a case and wrote the pickup date on a slip. "Next Thursday, after school."

Kaylee folded the slip into her pocket, right next to the crumpled zero she'd kept as evidence.

"Thursday," she said. "I'm going to see everything."

The bus rattled over the pothole by the mailboxes, and Brooklyn slid an inch toward the window. Three rows back, Devon Wright was telling Felix Ochoa that his backpack looked like something a kindergartner would carry, and half the bus was grinning along. Felix stared at the seat in front of him and pulled the straps tighter, like he could make the bag disappear. Brooklyn watched him, and her stomach did the thing it always did, a slow molten drop, hot and heavy.

Last week she had said nothing. The week before that too. Every time someone got picked on, the whole bus went quiet in a weird, comfortable way, and she had started to wonder why. It was not that nobody cared. Priya bit her lip. Marcus stopped his joke mid-sentence. Even Devon's friend Theo looked away. So why did forty kids sit still like furniture?

She had tested one small idea on Thursday. When Dev had grabbed Felix's hat, she had waited to see who would speak first. She counted, in her head, all the way to thirty. Nothing. When she finally opened her mouth, the words came out too loud and too sharp, and Devon had turned it around on her, calling her the bus police for the rest of the ride. That had made things worse, and Felix had told her later, quietly, that she didn't have to fight his battles. But he said it like he was glad somebody had.

Brooklyn turned the puzzle over all weekend. What she noticed was this: when it was just her and Felix at the science fair, nobody teased him. When it was her and two other kids at the lunch table, still nothing. It only happened in the crowd. And in the crowd, nobody moved. It was almost a rule, like the pattern in her math homework. The bigger the audience, the smaller the chance anybody acted, because each person back there was probably thinking exactly what she used to think: someone else will say something.

Monday morning, Devon started in again before the bus even left the lot. "Nice dinosaur bag, Ochoa. Did it come with the museum?" Laughter rolled down the aisle, thin and nervous. Brooklyn felt the old heat in her stomach, but this time she didn't stand up and shout. She picked up her water bottle, walked back two rows like she had a reason, and sat down right next to Felix.

"Hey," she said, to Felix only, ignoring Devon completely. "Did you finish the inflation math? I got stuck on question four." Felix blinked, then dug out his binder. She asked him to explain how he'd set up the percent change, and he did, in that soft, careful voice that got steadier as he went. Devon said something else about the backpack, but the joke landed in empty air, because Brooklyn and Felix were both looking at the page, and the kids around them suddenly had somewhere else to look too.

By the time the bus pulled into school, Priya had leaned over the seat to ask about the homework, and Marcus was complaining that the vending machine prices had gone up again. Devon was telling Theo about the game last night. The aisle filled up with ordinary noise, and Felix zipped his backpack like it was any other bag, because now it was.

In the hallway, Felix caught up with her. "Thanks for not making it a whole thing," he said.

"I read about it," Brooklyn said. "It's called the bystander effect. That's why nobody moved. I figured if I moved first, kind of sideways, then..." She shrugged.

"Then it's not a thing anymore," Felix said. He held the door for her, and they walked in together.

Jacob wanted the good table, the one by the window with the kettle and the plate of samosas, and the problem was that Table One had already claimed it. The community centre's heritage night had split into four tables for the games, and the split had been done by Mr. Okafor pulling names out of a cereal bowl, which felt fair and turned out not to be.

By seven thirty, Table Two, Jacob's table, was chanting "Two, two, two" at Pictionary. Table Three had a secret handshake nobody could have learned in two hours, because two hours was all that had existed of Table Three. Table Four had started calling Table One "the window hogs." Jacob had been dumped into Table Two between Priya, who was telling everyone about her grandmother's Diwali lamps with meticulous, loving detail, and a kid named Marcus who claimed his family invented barbecue, which Jacob doubted but let slide.

"We've known each other since six o'clock," Jacob said to Priya. "Why are we cheering like we're a tribe?"

"Because we're Table Two," she said, as if that explained anything.

It bothered him the way a loose tooth bothers you. He had read something once, in his sister's psychology book, about a man named Tajfel who ran experiments where people favoured members of their own group even when the groups had been assigned completely at random. Jacob had skipped past it at the time. Now he watched Marcus guard the felt-tip pens from Table Three like they were family heirlooms, and thought: that's us. We're the experiment. So he tested it. He stood on a chair and announced that the tables were random, that Mr. Okafor had drawn every name out of a bowl, that Table Two was not destiny.

It did not help. "So what," Marcus said. "We're still the best random table." Table Two applauded him. Jacob climbed down, the embarrassment warm in his ears, and considered the possibility that knowing about a thing does not switch it off.

But Priya had gone quiet, and when the samosa plate came out, she carried two over to the kids at Table One and asked what was in their dishes, and they turned out to be things their grandmothers made, with stories attached, and Jacob followed her. Mr. Okafor wandered by and tried to incorporate the moment into a speech about community, and Jacob said, "We're just eating, sir." The window table had room after all. Marcus arrived last, plate out, and said, "This doesn't make us friends."
"We're not tables," said Priya. "We're just hungry people near a window."
Marcus bit into a samosa. "Okay," he said. "That one's mine."

The trumpet wasn't working out, so Hailey switched to the flute, and now she had a new problem: reading music. She sat in the corner of the community center music room with a folded sheet of paper, glaring at the five lines and the fancy swirl at the start of every line. Her friend Marisol came over and dropped into the chair beside her.

"You look like the paper insulted you," Marisol said.

"I can find middle C. That's it. Then everything else is guessing." Hailey tapped the swirl. "And this thing just sits there like it's decoration."

Marisol leaned in. "My cousin plays piano. She calls that the G clef."

"The what?"

"G clef. That's the other name for it."

Hailey frowned at the symbol. A clef called G should mean something. She grabbed a pencil and copied the swirl onto her notebook, big and sloppy. Then she laid her flute sheet next to it and traced the curl slowly with her pencil tip, the way you'd trace a maze. The swirl looped around, dipped down, and curled back up, and where it curled it wrapped around the second line from the bottom. She checked her beginner book's note chart. The note on that line was G.

"No way," she whispered. The clef wasn't decoration. It was a marker, curling around the exact line where G lived, like a ring on a finger.

She tested it. G on the line, one space above was A, the line above that was B, and so on up the ladder. She played the little exercise from her book, and the notes came out in the right order for the first time. She played it again, faster, and grinned so wide her cheeks hurt.

Marisol pointed at the door. "Little kids are coming for vaccine day. The nurse is setting up in the big room, so we have ten more minutes before they kick us out."

"Ten minutes is plenty," Hailey said. "It's not trivial to me. This was the whole wall in my way."

A small boy in a dinosaur shirt peeked into the music room while waiting for his shot, looking scared. Marisol waved him over. Hailey held up her notebook, showed him the swirl, and traced the curl around the second line. "See the loop? It's holding one spot so you never get lost." The boy forgot to be nervous long enough to trace it with his own finger.

When the nurse called his name, he walked out taller, and Marisol hurried after him with his jacket. Hailey packed up her flute, but she tore the notebook page out first and pressed it flat inside her book, the page she knew she would cherish on every practice day to come.

"Same time Thursday?" Marisol called from the doorway.

"Bring your cousin's number," Hailey said, tucking the flute under her arm. "I have questions."

Elliot stared at the two columns Mr. Ruiz had taped to the whiteboard, and both looked exactly the same to him. By Friday, every sixth grader had to bring in a chart comparing what fifty dollars would become in a savings account after five years, and Mr. Ruiz had made it clear he would call on people at random to explain the difference between simple and compound interest. Elliot's chart showed the simple kind: two dollars fifty each year, added up again and again, until his pencil marks marched across the page in a flat, even line. The compound column was the one that made no sense to him.

"It's like this," said Maya, dropping into the seat beside him. She opened her notebook to a page covered in tiny sketches of paintbrushes. "The compound one goes up faster. Look, here, and here, and here." Her finger tapped the gaps, which grew wider every year. Maya wanted the class prize, a twenty-five-dollar bookstore gift card, because she'd been saving all fall for a real set of watercolors and was still nine dollars short. A gift card would finish it.

"That's what my dilemma is," Elliot said. "If both accounts pay the same percent, why does one end up with more? It's like the money is growing on money that didn't exist yet." He copied both columns onto graph paper, and then, because he wanted to clarify it for himself, he wrote out every single interest payment, year by year, for both accounts. The simple payments never changed: two dollars fifty, two dollars fifty, two dollars fifty. The compound payments did. Three dollars twelve. Three dollars ninety. Each one bigger than the last, even though nobody ever added a penny to the account.

"Wait," Maya said, leaning over his page. "Say that part again."

"The interest payments themselves got bigger," Elliot said slowly, reading his own numbers. "Even though we added nothing." He underlined the column where each new payment was calculated on the principal plus all the interest already earned, so the interest itself started earning interest. That was the rule. That was the whole difference. The simple account only ever paid on the original fifty, which was why its line lay flat as a ruler while the compound line bent slowly upward.

On Thursday night Maya left a folded note in his locker: "I showed my cousin the chart and she says we're right. She has a savings account and one year her interest payment grew a little even though she added nothing to the account. Want to present together tomorrow? P.S. The art store closes at six on Saturdays." The hallway around the lockers felt almost desolate at that hour, empty and echoing, but Elliot read the note twice and grinned at the ceiling both times.

On Friday they stood at the front with their chart, and when Mr. Ruiz called on Maya to explain the compound column, she pointed at the growing payments and said, "Each one is paid on the principal plus all the interest already earned, so the interest itself starts earning interest." Mr. Ruiz wrote a big check mark on his clipboard. When the bell rang, Maya held up the gift card they'd split toward the watercolors and said, "Saturday, nine a.m., art store. You're carrying the paint."

Jayden tapped the stopwatch on the museum's ramp exhibit and glared at it like it owed him money. His best friend Priya had already measured the speed of the rolling ball, drawn her distance-time graph, and written "7.2 seconds, champion" on the whiteboard beside the ramp, with a smiley face wearing a crown. Jayden refused to resign himself to second place. He was going to time that ball properly, mark where it was at every second, and draw a graph so clean it would make Priya's crown fall off.

The trouble was that speed was invisible. Nobody could see the ball moving 40 centimeters per second; they could only see where it was, and when. So Jayden crouched beside the ramp with a meter stick, ready to drop a penny next to the ball's position each time Priya called out a second. That was his foundation: positions at known times, then connect the dots and let the graph show the speed hiding inside them. "Ready?" Priya asked. "Born ready," said Jayden, which was a naive thing to say, because the ball promptly rolled off the ramp and under a bench.

While he fished it out, he noticed the exhibit next door, a wall of wires and bulbs with a big circuit diagram painted on it. Thick arrows marched along the wires from the positive terminal to the negative one. But a kid standing there was frowning at her book, and she read aloud, sounding annoyed: "Conventional current is drawn from positive to negative, but the electrons actually move the other way, from negative to positive." She looked at the arrows. "Then the arrows point the wrong way?"

Jayden stared at the diagram. The wires sat there doing nothing visible at all, and yet something was flowing through them, backward from the painted arrows, and nobody could watch it happen. It was exactly like his ball problem. You could not see the speed or the electrons; you could only catch the clues they left behind and work out the hidden truth. "The arrows show one thing," he told the girl, "and the real stuff goes the other way, negative to positive. Sneaky." She grinned and wrote it down.

He raced back to the ramp. "Drop the ball, mark every second, no mercy," he said, and Priya held the stopwatch while he slid pennies along the meter stick. At one second the ball was at 15 centimeters, at two seconds 40, at three seconds 66. He plotted the points, drew the line, and watched it climb in a neat, steady slope. The invisible speed had finally shown its face on paper.

"Six point four centimeters per second per second," Jayden announced. "It's speeding up. Your crown is in danger." Priya leaned over his graph, checked his dots twice, and sighed. "Fine. Best of three. And you're fetching the ball when it rolls under the bench again." She hit the release lever, and the ball rolled, and Jayden dove.

Blake spread his notebook across the kitchen table and clicked his pencil three times, which was his habit when a problem refused to behave. He had forty dollars from mowing lawns, and he wanted it to grow into enough money for a used skateboard by next summer. The trouble was figuring out where the forty dollars should live.

"Simple interest," his sister Priya said, leaning over his shoulder, "is like a dog that sits. Compound interest is a dog that fetches more dogs." She stole a grape from his bowl and chewed it loudly.

Blake wrote out both cases. At simple interest, the same amount landed in the account every year, flat and boring, like identical pancakes stacked on a plate. With compound interest, the interest itself earned interest, so the pile grew faster each year. Over five years the difference was small, but it was real. He ran the numbers twice and drew a little arrow where the two totals split apart, and Priya traced the widening gap with her finger and said, "There. That's where the magic happens. It's not magic, but that's where it happens."

Then came the harder question. Blake had read a forum post where someone bragged about doubling money in a risky app, and he wanted that speed. He carried his notebook to the porch, where Grandma Ruth was shelling peas into a blue bowl, the pods snapping like tiny green knuckles.

"I could put my money somewhere risky and get more," he confessed, sitting on the step below her.

She shook one pea loose and studied it. "My emergency savings sit in Treasury bonds," she said. "They're backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government. They're considered among the safest investments in the world. I keep them there instead of stocks." She flicked the pea into the bowl. "Risky places can vanish overnight. Safe places just sit there being safe."

Blake thought about the skateboard. If he lost the forty dollars, there would be no skateboard, no second chance, and a long summer of watching Priya roll past on hers. He felt a stab of empathy for his future self, broke and skateboardless, and decided that guy deserved better.

"So the plan is," he said later at the bank counter, sliding his forty dollars and his notebook under the glass, "compound interest in a savings account for five years, and when I have real savings someday, Grandma's bond trick." The teller read his arrow diagram, smiled, and stamped the deposit slip. Blake pocketed the receipt and, outside, ran his finger over the number like it was already the skateboard's grip tape.

Kaitlyn stood at the front of the empty auditorium with her note cards fanned out like a poker hand, and for the third time that afternoon she forgot her own argument. Marcus sat in the third row, drumming his pencil on the armrest. "Your warrant," he said. "You gave the claim and the evidence, but you never explained why the evidence proves the claim."

"I had it right here." She flipped a card. She was building her first real debate case for Saturday's tournament, three points about the school switching to a later start time, each one needing a claim, evidence and a warrant. The trouble was that only her middle point was any good. It had a study about sleep and grades, a clean piece of evidence, everything. Her first point was weak and her third was mostly a hypothetical about buses that she'd made up on the bus herself. "I'll just put the sleep one second," she said. "It's the middle of my case, so it holds everything together."

Marcus frowned. "Wait. Try it once and let me listen like a judge." She ran the whole case, and afterward he closed his eyes and tried to list her points back to her. "You said something about attendance first, and your bus thing last, because I'm still laughing at that. The sleep one, the one with the actual study? Gone. I lost it completely." He opened his eyes. "Yesterday you made me memorize a grocery list for practice, and I remembered eggs and apples because they were first and last. Same thing just happened."

Kaitlyn sat down hard on the edge of the stage. "The first and last items in a list. That's the ones people remember best." She grabbed her phone and typed it in, and the search gave it a name, which she read out loud. "The serial position effect. It's why openings and closings matter." She looked at her cards, then spread them across the stage floor and moved the sleep point from the middle to the front, where it would hit the judges before their attention drifted. "Okay. New order. Don't presume I know what I'm doing, either. Tell me if it falls apart."

She ran the case twice more, and the second time Marcus listed everything back without a single gap. "That was a real case," he said, standing up and applauding once, like a judge who'd made up his mind. "You might even build a reputation at this tournament." Kaitlyn gathered her cards, squared the edges, and grinned at the empty seats that would be full on Saturday. "First and last," she said, and tapped the top card. "The judge remembers this one, or nothing."

The train from upstate pulled into the dilapidated platform fifteen minutes late, and Grandpa Ray stepped down carrying one battered suitcase and a paper bag of maple candies. Vincent had been waiting for an hour, holding a sign he'd made that said WELCOME GRANDPA in marker. He waved it so hard the paper tore at the corner.

"I thought we'd lose you to that delay," Vincent said, grabbing the suitcase handle.

"Trains run when trains run," Grandpa said. "No use opposing it. Where's your mother's car?" On the way home, Vincent noticed Grandpa hadn't touched the water bottle Mom had packed, and he noticed it again at dinner, and again the next morning when the orange juice sat untouched beside Grandpa's plate.

On Tuesday they went to the park, and it was the hottest day of the week so far. Grandpa sat on a bench in the shade while Vincent did three trips across the monkey bars. When Vincent came back, dripping, Grandpa's face was flushed and his eyes looked heavy, but he said he was fine. Vincent fetched two waters from the fountain anyway and pressed one into his grandfather's hand. "You haven't had anything to drink since breakfast," he said. "I've been counting."

"I'd tell you if I were thirsty," Grandpa said, but he drank the whole bottle, and then a second one Vincent brought back. Ten minutes later he sat up straighter and said the bench felt cooler, which it didn't, because the sun hadn't moved. Vincent made an inference from that: something was off in Grandpa's own alarm system, not in the day itself. He called his mom at work and asked one careful question, and she said yes, the body's sense of thirst weakens with age, so older people can become dehydrated without ever feeling thirsty. Vincent hung up and made a decision on the spot.

For the rest of the week, he carried a water bottle everywhere and refilled Grandpa's glass at every meal without being asked, and he set a timer on his watch that buzzed every hour. Grandpa grumbled about being managed, but by Friday he was walking the whole loop around the pond without stopping, planning to teach Vincent chess that evening and to beat him, he claimed, in under twenty moves.

On Saturday morning, back at the same train station, Grandpa handed Vincent a fresh bottle of water before boarding. "For the walk home," he said. "You've got the habit now. Keep it." Then he stepped up onto the train, and Vincent stood holding the cold bottle until the last car disappeared around the curve.

The group chat lit up at 4:02 on a Saturday: "Dude, why are you at GameStop? I thought you were broke." Brayden stared at his phone. He had told nobody he was going to the mall. He had left the house saying he was "going for a walk," which was technically true if you counted walking to the bus. He typed back, "how do u know where I am," and Marcus answered with a screenshot of a map. There was a little cartoon face on it, standing right on top of the GameStop dot at the Westfield mall. Brayden looked at the ceiling of the store, then at the exit, as if the answer might be floating somewhere between them.

"Bro, that's the Snap Map," Marcus wrote. "It shows your real-time location to your friends on a map." Brayden read it twice. Real-time. He thought about all the times he'd wandered around after school, killing time before his mom got home, and how somebody could have been watching a little cartoon version of him do it the whole while. Weird feeling, like discovering his shoes had been narrating his day out loud.

He decided to test it. It seemed like an inevitable part of figuring things out; you couldn't just panic, you had to run an experiment. His technique was simple: he would walk from GameSpot to the pretzel stand two stores down, and if the cartoon face moved too, then the map was tracking him right now, not showing some old, harmless record. He bought a pretzel he didn't even want, mostly for cover, and stood under the big yellow sign eating it with the concentration of a scientist. Marcus sent a new screenshot. The face was on the pretzel stand. "Enjoy your pretzel," he wrote, adding three crying-laughing faces.

Brayden nearly choked. "This is so creepy," he typed with one thumb, pretzel in the other hand. But another thought itched at him, the curious kind. If it knew where he was, who else could see it? Marcus was his friend, sure. But the settings had layers, he'd heard people mention "friends of friends" like it was nothing. Somewhere out there, maybe strangers were watching the little cartoon face eat its little cartoon pretzel. He wondered how many eyes a dot could collect before the dot's owner even noticed.

Back home, he dug into the app's settings until he found the map options and switched his sharing to Ghost Mode. Then he typed into the group chat, "ok new rule, if anyone knows where I am, it's because I told them." Marcus replied with a single face, the one wearing sunglasses, and a message: "Meet me at the arcade in ten?"

Brayden grabbed his jacket. "Bring quarters," he wrote back, and hit send.

Lily sat cross-legged on Maya's bedroom floor with Maya's phone balanced on her knees, tapping through photos from Saturday. There was the one of Maya at the ice cream place, grinning with a double scoop. There was the one at the mall fountain. And there was the one Lily had taken of Maya outside Maya's own front door, because Maya had insisted the lighting was perfect.

"Send me the fountain one," Lily said, then stopped. "Wait. How many people can see these?"

"Just us. And my cousins. And probably the group chat." Maya flopped backward onto her pillow. "And that game I play, Frost Fox. It kind of posts stuff sometimes."

"Frost Fox posts your photos?"

"No, no. It posts where I am. Like, 'Maya unlocked the Glacier Zone at Maple Mall!' My aunt commented on it from two states away. She said, weren't you supposed to be at soccer?"

Lily scrolled to the game. A little map pin blinked beside a picture of a fox in a scarf, and next to the fox, Maya's last three locations were listed like trophies. Lily thought about the coyote that had wandered into their neighborhood last winter, how it had seemed to hibernate somewhere unseen all day and appear only at dusk, always knowing exactly which trash cans to visit. Someone had told her the coyote followed patterns, not luck. This felt like that, but backwards: the fox was following Maya.

"Can I check something?" Lily asked. She opened the phone's settings and hunted through screens until she found a list of apps with little arrows beside them. She recognized one arrow right away, because her dad had pointed at his own phone once and said, "That arrow means an app knows where you are." She tapped Frost Fox.

Three choices sat on the screen. Never. While using the app. Always.

"It's on Always," Lily said slowly. "That means it knew where you were even when you weren't playing."

Maya sat up so fast her ponytail whipped around. "You can pick?"

"You can pick for every app, one by one." Lily turned the phone so Maya could see. "My phone asks me the same thing. I always hit Always because I don't read the box. I just want the game to start."

"That's why Frost Fox knew I skipped soccer," Maya said, sounding both horrified and delighted. She jabbed the screen and switched the game to While Using. Then, defiant, she switched it to Never, just to watch the little map pin blink out.

Later, Lily texted her from home: did the fox die? Maya sent back a photo of Frost Fox wearing a blindfold, standing in an empty snowfield, with the caption "he asks where u at and I say none of ur business." Lily laughed out loud, then opened her own phone and went down her list of apps, one by one, arrow by arrow.

The last one, before bed, was a flashlight app. Always.

She stared at it. "You don't even know where I am," she told it, and pressed Never.

The cardboard box on the passenger seat tipped sideways twice on the drive home, and each time Alyssa's hand shot out to steady it. Inside, tangled in an old flannel shirt, was a six-month-old mutt from the shelter, brown with one white ear, whom she had named Biscuit an hour after meeting him. Her mother kept her eyes on the road and said, "He's your responsibility, you know. Food, walks, everything." Alyssa nodded, though she was barely listening. She was busy wondering what he was thinking behind those wide brown eyes, and whether a dog could miss a place he'd only lived in for six weeks.

That first evening, Biscuit explored the kitchen like a detective, nose down, tail up. Alyssa followed him, cataloguing his discoveries. He was curious about the refrigerator, terrified of the ceiling fan, and completely fascinated by the space under the couch, where he stayed for ten full minutes. When her friend Priya knocked on the door, Alyssa grabbed the bag of trail mix she'd been saving and Biscuit trotted after her into the backyard.

They sat on the porch steps, and Biscuit sat too, staring at the bag with an intensity that made Alyssa laugh. She picked out a raisin and held it out. "Want a treat?"

"Stop!" Priya's hand shot across, almost knocking the raisin into the grass. "Grapes and raisins can cause kidney damage in dogs. They should never be given as treats."

Alyssa froze with her hand in the air. "Seriously? They're just dried grapes."

"Seriously. My aunt's a vet tech. It's one of the first things she told me."

Alyssa looked at the raisin, then at Biscuit, who was drooling hopefully. A cold thought slid into her mind. The bag of trail mix had been sitting on the coffee table all afternoon, and the zipper had looked open when she picked it up. She tried to interpret the evidence calmly, the way detectives did in the books she liked. An open bag, a dog alone in the living room for hours, a dog who adored nosing under furniture and into things. She couldn't see what had happened while she was in her room. But she could test it.

She carried the bag to the kitchen table and counted. Yesterday there had been a big clump of raisins stuck together at the bottom; she remembered picking around them because she liked the almonds best. Now the bottom of the bag held only almonds, peanuts, and two chocolate chips. The raisins were gone. Every single one.

"Mom!" Her voice came out higher than she intended. "Biscuit ate raisins. A lot of them, I think. From the trail mix."

Her mother appeared in the doorway, dish towel over her shoulder, and studied the bag. Then she was already dialing the animal clinic, giving Biscuit's weight and the approximate number of raisins, while Alyssa knelt beside the dog and ran her hands over his warm sides, feeling for anything wrong. There was nothing to feel, of course. Whatever was happening inside him was hidden, and the probability that he was fine felt, to Alyssa, like a coin she couldn't see. The vet's voice crackled through the phone, calm and steady, and her mother said, "Bring him in now."

Alyssa had a sudden flashback to the shelter that morning, the moment Biscuit had pressed his nose against her palm through the bars of the kennel, deciding something about her in a single sniff. Now she scooped him into the cardboard box, flannel shirt and all, and held the box on her lap in the back seat the whole way there. Somewhere outside, the streetlights were flickering on, and a raccoon she'd watched raid the trash cans all summer, strictly nocturnal, was just beginning to stir. Biscuit burrowed deeper into the shirt and let out a small, uncertain whine.

"Almost there," Alyssa whispered. "And after tonight, no more raisins. Ever. Deal?"

Alexis had spent every summer at Abuela's house since she was six, and every summer the streets had felt like a map she carried in her head. This summer Abuela had moved to a new neighborhood, and the map was gone. On the first morning, Abuela handed her a canvas bag. "Take these to the donation bin on Calle Rosa," she said. "And take the phone. In case."
