Maybe it was step one.

She crossed out "wren," wrote "FINCH," and drew the beak again, thicker this time, with an arrow pointing to it and the word "fundamental clue" beside it. "Your turn," she said, handing Marcus her pencil. "Draw the frog's mouth. Big or small? Wide or narrow? It matters, I promise."

Marcus took the pencil, raced down the boardwalk toward the pond, and skidded to a stop with his nose an inch from the water. "Huge," he reported. "It's a mouth finch."

The bell over the door had barely stopped jingling when Jeremy started alphabetizing the antacids. He helped out at Reyes Pharmacy every Saturday because his mother worked the register, and because Dr. Reyes herself, an eccentric woman who wore a different vintage hat for every holiday, had told him that a shelf in perfect order could signify a mind in perfect order. Jeremy wasn't sure his mind was in order. For two weeks he'd been snapping at his mom, staring at his ceiling until one in the morning, and getting stomachaches before school, and he didn't know why.

He found a pamphlet in the rack beside the register, the one about stress. It said to watch for tight shoulders, short tempers, and wrecked sleep. Then it gave him an idea he could actually test: breathe in slowly for four counts, hold for four, let it out for four. Three rounds. He stood between the cough syrup and the foot powder and tried it, feeling like an idiot, but by the second round his shoulders had dropped an inch. He tested it again that night, and instead of lying awake he was asleep before his phone's second reminder. So the pattern was real. Something he couldn't see, tension he couldn't point at, could still be measured and loosened.

Then Tyler's message arrived on Sunday, and Jeremy read it three times before answering. "Can I crash at your place soon? Home is bad right now. Don't ask why." Tyler, who always joked in class, who never typed anything shorter than a paragraph, had sent eleven words. Jeremy remembered the pamphlet's list, and now the signs weren't his. They were Tyler's, and Jeremy hadn't spotted them sooner because he'd been too busy cataloguing his own.

He tried the breathing at the pharmacy counter while his mom rang up a customer, because his chest had gone tight the way the pamphlet described. While he breathed, he thought. He couldn't fix whatever "bad" meant at Tyler's house. He didn't even know what it was, and Tyler had said not to ask. But the pamphlet's back page had one more line he'd skipped, about worried friends, and it listed who could be told: a parent, a teacher, a school counselor, the school nurse, or a doctor. Jeremy looked up. Dr. Reyes was standing right there, counting pills, and the plaque on the wall behind her said Doctor of Pharmacy.

"I have a friend who seems scared all the time," Jeremy said. "I don't know what's going on, but I don't want to just sit on it."

Dr. Reyes set down her tray and studied him over her hat brim. "You're not sitting on it. You're telling somebody, and telling somebody is the whole job."

"I'm telling you first because you're here," Jeremy said. "Monday I'll tell my homeroom teacher too. Maybe the counselor."

"Then you've already done the hard part." She pulled a stool over beside the counter and patted it. "Sit down and breathe, kid. In for four."

Jeremy sat, and he breathed.

The letter was waiting on Grandpa's kitchen table when Noah arrived, and he tore it open before he even unpacked his bag. "Noah," Grandma had written from her sister's place, "take care of Grandpa. Count the cigarette packs in the bin for me. I'll be home Sunday. P.S. Try the breathing trick I taught you when your head gets loud." Noah read it twice. Grandma never asked him to count anything unless she was worried, and his stomach did a small flip.

By Wednesday evening he had counted four empty packs, when last summer there had been only one a week. That night he lay awake in the guest room, heart drumming, thinking about it. This was the same jittery feeling he'd had after his concussion in the fall, when the doctor had told him to isolate himself in a quiet room until his head healed. Grandma had shown him back then how slow breaths could settle a racing body, in for four counts, out for six. He tried it now, ten slow breaths, and his thoughts stopped sprinting. Sleep came easier than he expected.

Thursday morning he rode his bike to the pharmacy in the affluent neighborhood across the highway, the one with the fountain out front, because Grandpa needed his blood pressure pills anyway. While the pharmacist, a woman named Dana, filled the order, Noah blurted out his question. "My grandpa smokes way more than he used to. Does smoking change how much you need?"

Dana looked at him carefully. "With regular use, the brain adapts to nicotine, so a person needs more of it to feel the same effect," she said. "It's called tolerance." She handed him a pamphlet about quitting support. Noah gripped it like treasure. So the packs weren't just Grandpa being careless. The habit itself was growing, like a plant nobody pruned.

He tested his idea that evening. "Grandpa," he said at dinner, "how many did you smoke when you started?" Grandpa thought, fork halfway to his mouth. "Two a day, maybe. Navy days." "And now?" A pause. "Don't count, kid." But his ears went red, and Noah had his answer.

Later, on the porch, Grandpa lit another one and Noah sat beside him. "Grandma's home Sunday," Noah said. "Want to talk to her about the pamphlet? I'll do the breathing stuff with you if it gets hard." Grandpa stared at him for a long moment, then laughed and stubbed the cigarette out after only three puffs. "You count my packs," he said, "I'll count your slow breaths. Deal?"

Hazel stood on the back porch of Marisol's birthday party holding a paper with six numbered lines on it, because tomorrow she had to run the first Nature Club meeting of the year and she had never run anything except a lemonade stand that failed. Marisol had offered her party as a practice audience. "Pretend we're the club," Marisol said, waving a forkful of cake at the six kids scattered around the porch. "You be the conductor."

"Conductor of what?" asked Theo.

"Of the meeting," Hazel said. "Like an orchestra, except with people who all want to talk about salamanders at once." She read the first line of her agenda. "Item one: does anyone actually want to sell candy at the fall fair, or was that just Mr. Ruiz's idea?" It went surprisingly well for two items. Priya argued, Dev made a joke about the treasurer's report, but everyone got a turn, and Hazel started to believe she could do this.

Then item three fell apart because of the laughing.

A boy named Quinn was standing near the snack table, and two kids from another school, Rex and some kid Hazel didn't know, were circling him. "Nice shoes," Rex kept saying. "No, really. Nice shoes." They said it in that voice that meant the opposite, and Quinn's ears went red, and every time Rex spoke, the second kid laughed like a drum machine.

Hazel's first idea was to say something sharp to Rex. She even opened her mouth. But then she noticed something she couldn't see directly, only its shadow: Rex kept glancing sideways before each joke, checking whether the porch was still watching. It was like watching a performer count his audience. The laughing kid was the audience. Take away the audience, she thought, and what's left?

She revised her plan mid-breath. "Quinn!" she called, loud and casual. "Come on, let's go. I need help with the snacks in the kitchen." Quinn blinked, then pushed off the table and followed her through the screen door. Rex opened his mouth for another "nice shoes," but there was nobody left to hear it except his one friend, and somehow that wasn't enough. When Hazel peeked back through the window thirty seconds later, Rex was standing there looking bizarre, like a magician whose trick had ended early, and then he wandered off toward the bounce house.

In the kitchen, Quinn dumped chips into a bowl without being asked. "Thanks," he said. "That was getting old."

"That's the whole trick, I think," Hazel said. "They need people watching. No watchers, no show." She looked at her agenda, all six items, and realized item three had taught her more than items one and two put together. Tomorrow she would write the meeting plan differently, with room for whatever actually happened. "Okay, back to the porch," she said. "We never settled the candy question, and I still have three items left. Bring the chips."

Norah pressed her face to the airport window and counted the planes lined up on the tarmac. Seven of them, gleaming in the morning sun. In an hour she would be on the eighth one, flying to the coast for a whole week of beaches and cousins and salt-water taffy. Nothing could hinder a day like this, she told herself, except for one small problem: the drive to the airport had gone badly.

"Are you going to be sick on the plane too?" her little brother Sam asked, chewing a pretzel with annoying calm. He had watched Norah go pale in the back seat of the rental shuttle while she tried to finish two chapters of her library book. The road had curved and curved, and by the end she had her head against the window, swallowing hard.

"I don't know," Norah admitted. She hated not knowing. She stared out at the runway and turned the morning over in her mind. In the shuttle, she had been reading, so her eyes were fixed on a page that never moved. But her body had been swaying and bumping and curving with every turn in the road. Her eyes had said one thing, still, and her insides had said another, moving, and the two messages had crashed into each other somewhere behind her eyes. She felt a spark of excitement. It was a clue.

"Boarding group two," their mom announced, and they hurried down the jet bridge, Norah carrying her library book like a science experiment. She settled into the middle seat and made a decision. "Sam, I'm testing something. If I read during takeoff and my stomach gets bad again, then I'll know the book is the problem." She opened the book anyway, because a good scientist needed proof. The plane roared down the runway, tilted up, and her stomach did a slow, sickening roll while the words on the page wobbled in front of her.

She shut the book and looked out the window instead. Clouds, wing, the tiny houses of their town shrinking away. Her stomach settled like a pond after rain. "It worked," she whispered. Out the window her eyes could see movement everywhere, so nothing was fighting. When the drink cart came, she asked the flight attendant for ginger ale and a napkin, and wrote a note to herself in looping letters: NO READING IN MOVING CARS.

Sam leaned over. "What's motion sickness even called? Like, does it have a name?"

"Motion sickness," Norah said, and clinked her ginger ale against his apple juice. "And I beat it. Watch out, ocean, here I come."

Zack spread his blank essay packet across the library table and stared at the prompt: Should the town build a skate plaza in Milliken Park? The trouble wasn't the topic. It was line one, where his teacher had written in red, "Thesis first. Three points. Outline before drafting." Zack had never done it that way, and his first draft had come back looking like a ransom note of half-ideas.

Priya dropped into the chair across from him, hugging her own folder. She wanted the history essay prize so badly she'd been carrying her research everywhere for two weeks, even to lunch. "You look like your brain hurts," she said.

"It does. I wrote the whole essay, and Mr. Okafor circled the first paragraph and wrote 'flat.'" Zack turned the draft so she could see. "Flat. Like a deflated basketball." He flipped to his favorite part, where he described a skater named Dario sailing over a nine-stair set on opening day. "This part is the best thing in it, and it's at the beginning. I don't get why that's wrong."

Priya tapped the page. "Maybe because it's like telling the punchline first." She was already opening her own folder, hungry to get back to her gold-rush sources, but she paused. "In my book club book, everything terrible happens before the big scene at the end. My sister said that's called rising action." She said it like she was tossing him a key she'd found on the ground. "The problems pile up so the big scene matters."

Zack sat back. Complications, stacking like quarters, before the climax. So what if he saved Dario's flight for the end of the essay and put the buildup first: the cracked sidewalks that made skaters dodge walkers, the tickets, the petitions with their frail, curling edges? Each one was a complication that raised the stakes. He grabbed a fresh sheet and wrote "Thesis:" at the top, then "Point 1, Point 2, Point 3" down the margin. It felt strange, building the frame before the walls, but his intuition said the bones mattered. "So point one is the safety argument," he muttered, "point two is cost, and point three keeps the park busy instead of empty after dark."

He remembered fourth grade then, when Danny Ruiz had ridiculed his book report in front of the whole class, calling it "one big spoiler," and Zack hadn't understood until this moment what Danny meant. He'd opened with the last scene of the book and read it aloud first. No wonder everyone had glazed over.

"Hey Priya," Zack whispered, already filling in point three. She looked up from her folder. "The outline's working. It's like scaffolding." He slid his pen down to the final line and wrote, fast, before the idea could escape him: Save Dario for last.

Layla had claimed the scruffy plot at the far corner of the community garden because nobody else wanted it, and now she knew why. Every morning her seedlings leaned sideways like they were trying to escape. Her beans flopped over in a tangle. Her squash sat there looking depressed. Meanwhile, Mrs. Okafor's plot next door was so vigorous it practically hummed.

"Your beans need something to climb," Mrs. Okafor said, snapping a pea pod. "Come look at my plan."

Taped inside Mrs. Okafor's shed door was a hand-drawn map with circles inside circles. Corn in the center, beans around it, squash around everything. At the top, in curly letters, it said Three Sisters.

"That's what it's called," Mrs. Okafor said. "My grandmother planted it this way." She tapped the map with a soil-crusted finger. "Corn supports the climbing beans, and the squash leaves shade the soil against weeds."

Layla squinted at it. The corn was a fence post you could eat. The beans were the climbers. The squash was, what, a living mulch? She couldn't see any of that happening underground, or in the future, which was the problem with gardens. You had to bet on a pattern you couldn't watch.

So she tested it. She planted her remaining corn seeds in a tight cluster in the middle of her plot, bean seeds in a ring around them, and squash seeds along the outer edge. Her little brother Dev helped by naming every squash. "This one's Gary," he announced. "Gary is going to be enormous."

For two weeks nothing proved anything. Then, in July, the corn shot up, and the beans did exactly what Mrs. Okafor's map had promised. They wrapped around the cornstalks and climbed, one curl at a time, using the corn like a ladder. When a storm rolled through and cracked a branch off the mulberry tree, the corn bent but held. Not one bean pole, because there were no poles. The beans just held on tighter.

But the squash worried her. Three of them wilted, and she couldn't figure out why until she got a letter from Mrs. Okafor, who had gone to visit her sister in Ohio. It read: "Layla, water deep, not often. Squash roots fracture easy if you yank weeds beside them, so mulch instead. Your corn is taller than mine. I am pretending I am not jealous."

Layla watered deep and mulched around Gary and his friends, spreading straw with Dev, who insisted on tucking it in like blankets. By August the whole plot was a jungle. The squash leaves had spread so wide that the shaded ground underneath was bare, while weeds sprouted happily everywhere else. Dev pulled one weed, purely to prove it existed.

At the harvest dinner, Layla served corn, beans, and roasted Gary. Mrs. Okafor took seconds of everything.

"Admit it," Layla said. "Mine's better."

Mrs. Okafor chewed slowly. "I'll admit Gary," she said, and reached for a third helping.

Matteo sat cross-legged on the living room rug with his laptop balanced on the coffee table, glaring at a spreadsheet with four hundred rows of survey answers. His class had asked the whole school, "What's your favorite school lunch?", and somehow he had volunteered to summarize the results by grade. His sister Priya, home from college, was doing something on her phone nearby, occasionally flourishing a pretzel at the screen as if celebrating herself.

"I can't do this," he said. "There are too many rows. I'd have to count forever."

"That's why you use a pivot table," Priya said without looking up. "Drag grade into rows, lunch into columns, and it counts for you."

He tried it, and the numbers snapped into place like magic. Sixth grade loved pizza; eighth grade, weirdly, loved the salad bar. He was about to email the file to his teacher when a box popped up on his laptop: someone was trying to log in to his account, and the attempt came from another country. A second later, Priya's phone buzzed. She held it up. "This is your account asking for a code. Why is your account texting me?"

"That's not me," Matteo said, his stomach dropping. "Someone has my password."

Last summer flashed into his mind: he had used the same password for a game site that later got hacked, and he'd never bothered to change it anywhere else. He'd thought, at the time, that nothing important was attached. He was wrong now, and he knew it, watching the login box glow on his screen.

Then he noticed something. The login attempt hadn't gone through. Instead of letting the stranger in, his account had asked for a code sent to a phone, and the code had gone to Priya's phone, not the stranger's. Priya read the message aloud. "Two-factor authentication," she said. "It wants a second proof, a code sent to a phone, so a stolen password on its own is not enough to log in."

"So they can't get in," Matteo said slowly. "Even with my password."

"Correct. Now change your password before they try anything else, and this time make it a legitimate one, not your dog's name."

He changed it, and while he was at it, he checked the login history. The attempt had come from a country he'd never visited, at an hour when he'd been asleep. He copied the details into an email for the survey file instead, then paused, because something about the timing itched at him. He pulled up the survey spreadsheet and made a new pivot table, this time summarizing who had answered the survey and when. The suspicious login had happened three minutes after he'd emailed the file link to his group chat, which included a kid named Devon, whose family had just moved from Portugal. Matteo built a quick filter, then another, testing his idea, and the pattern held: the only person who could have seen the link and had any reason to guess Matteo's password was someone who'd watched him type it during agriculture club, where they shared the greenhouse signup computer.

"It was Devon," Matteo announced. "He saw me log in at the greenhouse. He probably just wanted to read the lunch results early, so he'd know whether pizza won before anyone else."

Priya lowered her pretzel. "So your grand mystery was a nosy kid and a salad bar?"

"And I still have to finish the report," Matteo said, and dragged one more field into the pivot table.

The counselor's poster said Know Your Stress Signs, and Zoey had copied the list into her notebook on Monday: tight shoulders, snapping at people, trouble sleeping. By Thursday she had checked off all three, because the science fair was in six days and her model of an estuary, where the river met the sea, still looked like a puddle of glue. At lunch she stared at it and realized her hands were shaking. She excused herself to the hallway, sat against the lockers, and breathed the way the poster showed, in for four counts, out for four, until the hallway stopped buzzing.

That was where Marcus found her. He plunked down beside her with his gym bag, and Zoey noticed something right away: two sixth graders walking past turned their heads and drifted to the far side of the hall, the way you'd steer around a spill. Marcus had come straight from basketball practice, hair still damp with sweat, and he had that slumped look Zoey recognized from her own bad days.

"Nobody's sitting with me in the caf," he said. "Third day in a row. I keep thinking it's something I said."

Zoey breathed out slowly, thinking. It wasn't something he said, because he'd said plenty on Monday and people had laughed. It had started after practice resumed this week, and only around Marcus, only in the afternoons. A pattern like that pointed to one hidden cause, and she tested her idea out loud. "Did you change anything this week? Like, are you showering after practice?" Marcus admitted the new coach didn't enforce it, so he'd been skipping and just changing shirts, figuring a quick rinse at home would cover it.

"Showering with soap after exercise washes away the sweat and bacteria that cause body odor," Zoey said, quoting her health teacher's handout, which she'd stuffed in her notebook on Tuesday. "A dry shirt doesn't." Marcus groaned but looked almost relieved, because a shower was a fixable problem, unlike everybody hating you.

That night Zoey wrote him a note and slipped it through the vent of his locker the next morning, since his phone was confiscated until his math grade improved. "Report: I slept eight hours last night because I put my estuary model away at nine and did my breathing thing. You? Shower with soap after practice, then tell me if people stop edging away. Meet me at lunch, either way. Signed, a fellow work in progress. P.S. My stress shoulders are 50 percent less tight."

At lunch Marcus dropped his tray across from her, hair curling and clean, smelling of soap instead of gym. Two sixth graders sat down at the end of the table without steering around anyone, and Marcus grinned and held up a folded reply note. "Eight and a half hours," he read, "and nobody moved away. Testing continues tomorrow."

The sign outside Dell's Gas and Go had slushies for a dollar, and Lucy wanted one so badly she could already feel the brain freeze. Her little brother Marcus wanted one too, plus a bag of chips, plus a lottery scratcher he was not going to get. But between them they had exactly one dollar and forty cents, and Lucy's dollar was spoken for.

"Look at that line," Marcus said. Seven people were crowded at the slushie machine, and the sound of the motor grinding ice filled the whole store. The kid ahead of Lucy, Devon from her science class, filled his cup to the very brim, then filled a second cup for his mom.

When Lucy finally got her turn, the machine sputtered and went quiet. Dell came out from behind the register, tapped the tank, and shook his head. "Machine's out of syrup till my delivery Friday. That's the last of it."

"Great," Lucy said. "So no slushie at all."

Dell shrugged. "Unless somebody wants to pay for what's left in the cup tray. I'm charging three dollars a cup now."

Marcus gasped like she'd asked him to hand over a kidney. "Three dollars? That's robbery!"

But Lucy was watching, not listening to Marcus. Of the seven people in line, only Devon and one trucker actually paid three dollars. The other five put their cups back and drifted toward the soda cooler, grumbling. Lucy chewed her lip. Fewer buyers, higher price. She'd seen the flip side that morning at the farmers market, when the peach lady dropped her price at closing time and got mobbed.

"Hey, Devon," she said. "In social studies, isn't there a name for that? When the price goes up and people buy less?"

"The law of demand," Devon said. "When prices rise, people buy less. When they drop, people buy more."

"That's it." Lucy turned to Dell. "What if you tried one dollar a cup instead? I bet more people would buy what's left, and you'd clear it out before Friday."

"I don't need a jury of thirteen-year-olds running my store," Dell said, but he was rubbing his chin, and the stack of unsold cups wasn't getting smaller on its own. "One hour. Dollar a cup. If it works, you get the first one free."

It worked. Lucy stood by the door and counted, because she wanted her numbers to be consistent before she claimed anything. In forty minutes the tray was empty, and a man in a lawn-mower company truck bought the very last two cups at once. The one thing Lucy couldn't see, the invisible rule underneath the buying and the selling, had behaved exactly the way she predicted, and that felt better than the slushie.

Dell handed her a free cup, cherry red. Marcus held out his hand, eyes enormous.

"You were going to intervene on my behalf, right?" he said. "Because I'm your brother? Because family?"

Lucy sucked down a long, cold sip, considered him over the rim of the cup, and handed him exactly one third.

Bentley unfolded the agenda he had written on the bus that morning, smoothing the crease with his palm. The robotics club met in the art room after last bell, and today, for the first time, he was in charge. Ms. Okafor had left a note on the whiteboard: "Bentley runs it. I'm at a district meeting." He read it twice, then pinned his paper to the easel.

"First item," he said. "Fundraising. The hardware store sponsor pulled out because of the recession, so we need two hundred dollars for parts before the regional meet." He looked around the circle of chairs. "Priya, you had an idea?"

Before Priya could answer, Dex snickered. "Two hundred dollars? Maybe Priya can sell some of her thirty-seven pencils." A few kids laughed. Priya stared at the floor, and Bentley noticed something he had noticed for weeks without really seeing it: after every joke, Dex glanced over at whoever had laughed, quick as a reflex, checking his audience like a satellite checking its orbit.

Bentley had laughed along last week. He remembered it now, the way the sound had come out of him easy and warm, not because the joke was funny but because sitting in the laughing group felt safer than sitting outside it. Dex had grinned right at him afterward and doubled down on Priya's pencil case.

"Fundraising ideas," Bentley said again, keeping his voice level. This time, when Dex cracked a joke about Marcus's laces, Bentley kept his face still. He caught Priya's eye and gave a small shake of his head, and she pressed her lips together and didn't laugh either. Marcus rubbed his sneaker and stayed quiet too. Dex's next joke came out quieter. The one after that trailed off halfway through, and Dex pulled his phone from his pocket and scrolled instead, glancing up once at a circle of faces that gave him nothing.

Priya cleared her throat. "Car wash," she said. "Two Saturdays from now, in the faculty lot. My uncle has hoses."

They voted, and the car wash won by a margin significant enough that they moved straight to item two, assigning jobs. Priya took posters, Marcus took towels, and Dex, without being asked, said he'd handle sponges.

That night Bentley lay on his bed and texted Priya: "Did you see that? He stopped when nobody laughed." Her reply came fast: "I saw. Last year I laughed too. Every time. I keep thinking about that." Bentley typed and deleted three different answers, trying to decide whether to tell her he was thinking about it too. The cursor blinked. Downstairs, the dishwasher hummed into its rinse cycle.

Priya, as it turned out, made the first move. A folded note landed on his desk the next morning in science class. He opened it under the desk. "Next meeting," it read, "I'll hold the agenda sheet while you talk. Then you can watch the room instead of the paper. P.S. Nobody's laughed at Dex since Tuesday. He sat with Marcus at lunch."

Bentley read the last line twice. He looked across the room to where Dex was leaning over Marcus's notebook, pointing at something and asking a question in a low voice. Bentley slipped the note into his binder, between the pages of his lab report where it wouldn't get crushed, and raised his hand to answer the question on the board.

The lobby chat scrolled fast in bright blue text. DragonGrl99 had typed R U SERIOUS in all capitals, which Emilia had learned meant either excitement or fury, and a player named BeefWizard was typing what looked like a memoir, line after line about a match gone wrong. Emilia despised lobby chat on nights like this. Anyone could read it, anyone could jump in, and the tone flipped from joking to toxic in about four messages. She kept her own words short there: gg, ready, brb.

A private message popped up instead, quiet green text that only she could see. It was her cousin Sam, eleven years old and three states away. "I can't get in. It keeps asking for my birthday and then it says I can't make an account."

Emilia opened voice chat and invited him to a private room, because in the lobby everyone could hear you, but in a room only invited players could. "What did it say exactly?" she asked.

"It said I have to be thirteen. I put my real birthday and it kicked me out." Sam's voice went smaller. "Is it because they think eleven-year-olds are annoying?"

Emilia frowned at her screen. She thought about her own signup a few months ago. The same question, the same rule. Her friend Theo had grumbled about it too, and he had said something she half remembered. She typed to Sam, "Wait, don't make a new account yet. I'm going to test something."

She opened the signup page in another tab and filled it out with a fake name and a birthday that made her twelve. Sure enough, the page stopped and asked for a parent's email for permission. She closed the tab without submitting. "It's not about being annoying," she said. "Watch what happens when I say I'm twelve." She told him about the parent email screen.

"So they need a grown-up to say yes?"

"That's what it looks like." Emilia searched the rule on her phone and read the first line out loud. "It's a U.S. law from 1998. Sites have to get parental consent before they collect personal information from kids under thirteen. That's why they make you be thirteen."

Sam was quiet for a second. "So I just have to wait, or get Mom to sign?"

"Or get Mom to sign." In the lobby behind them, DragonGrl99 was typing in all capitals again. Emilia muted it.

"Fine," Sam said. "I'll go ask her right now. Stay in the room."

The game lobby glowed on Sofia's screen like a luminous fish tank, full of usernames drifting in and out. Her best friend Raj's tag, TurboPlumber42, popped up in the chat, and below it a message in bright orange: "SOS. Emergency. Meet me in party."

She clicked him into a private voice channel, which was the whole point of private, because in the public lobby anyone could read your business. "What's wrong with you?" she asked.

"I posted the video," Raj groaned. "The one of me singing the marshmallow song in my brother's shower cap. On my clan page. And then I deleted it. But people saw it, Sofia. Kwon saw it. He screenshotted the page before I took it down, and now everyone says the clan page is haunted because the video 'vanished.'" His voice dropped to a whisper. "Somebody named GhostLily left a comment saying she can still find it. How? I deleted it. It's gone. Deleted means gone, right?"

Sofia frowned at her screen. She thought about how her hamster could hibernate in one corner of his cage for days, invisible but absolutely still there, and how the pipes under her kitchen sink kept leaking even after her dad said he'd "fixed the plumbing." Things didn't always disappear just because you stopped looking at them. "Deleted from where?" she asked slowly. "The clan page is public, right?"

"Public. Anyone could see it."

"Then wait. My cousin showed me this thing once. Hang on." She opened a browser, typed the clan page's address, and then, remembering, went to a site her cousin had bookmarked. "The Wayback Machine has saved more than one trillion web pages, so something deleted from a public website can sometimes still be found," she recited, half to herself, half to Raj.

"Trillion? That's a number with, like, all the zeros."

"Shh. I'm being a detective." She pasted the clan page's address into the search bar and hit enter. A little calendar appeared, dotted with dates like spots on a ladybug. She clicked the most recent one, right before Raj's deletion. The old page loaded, and there it was: a post titled "MY GREATEST WORK," with Raj in a shower cap, mid-note, luminous with steam.

"It's back," Sofia said. "It never left, really. It was just hibernating."

Raj made a sound like a deflating balloon. Then he brightened, which was very like him. "Wait. This means I can see stuff other people deleted, too."

"That's not the lesson here, Raj."

He was already typing.

"Raj. Rude."

On the screen, TurboPlumber42's tag flashed once and went dark, like a fish ducking behind a rock.

Maelie pressed her ear against the metal trash can in her grandfather's garage workshop and tapped the side with a screwdriver. A dull thud answered her, nothing more. For three nights the strange scratching had come from somewhere in the garage, and every morning the traps she set stayed empty.

"You're going to catch it eventually," her cousin Theo said from the workbench, where he was lettering her science fair board in thick blue marker. He had steady hands, and she envied him that, because her own letters always slid downhill. The board needed a section labeled "Hypothesis" and she had asked him to leave space for it.

"Not eventually," Maelie said. "Tonight. I think I know what it is." She stood back and looked at the garage the way her grandfather had taught her, watching for the paths things took. The scratching happened only after dark, always near the back wall, always above the shelf where he kept his old maps of the river estuary, those curling charts of where the current met the sea. Nothing that scratched could be seen by day, so it had to be something hidden, something with a reason for coming out only at night. Her guess was that a mouse had found the bag of birdseed on the top shelf, but guesses were not enough for a science fair.

She looked up "hypothesis" in the dictionary on the workbench and frowned at what she found. "It comes from ancient Greek," she read slowly, "and it literally means 'putting or placing under.'"

"Under what?" Theo asked.

"That's all it says. Putting or placing under." She copied it onto an index card. A hypothesis, she decided, was like the board's foundation, the guess you placed under everything else, and the experiment stood on top of it. If the experiment collapsed, you had guessed wrong.

That evening she set two traps. One went beside the birdseed on the top shelf, where her mouse idea said it belonged. The other went under the trash can, in case the sound was traveling along the wall from somewhere lower and fooling her ears. Sound could do that, bounce and mislead. In the morning she found the top trap sprung, a seed hull beside it, and a gray whiskered shape gone, but the trail of hulls led up behind the maps and through a gap into the ceiling. Her guess had been placed in the right spot after all, and it had held.

At the fair, the judge paused at her board. "So your hypothesis was supported," she said.

Maelie touched the index card glued beneath the title. "It means putting or placing under," she said. "The Greek. I looked it up." She thought of her grandfather, who had wanted her to keep the workshop, and how she had almost said no; that choice still sat with her, not fully settled. The judge smiled and moved on, and Maelie straightened the card so it sat exactly under the words above it.

Lincoln stood at the edge of the school auditorium stage, holding a stack of note cards so tightly that the corners bent. In three weeks he would debate the meatless Mondays plan in front of the whole sixth grade, and his partner, Priya, had just flipped her cards facedown on the folding table. "We have a problem," she said. "Read our first point out loud."

Lincoln read it. His cousin Marco had gone vegetarian last spring, and by June he was tired all the time and quit. Our claim is that meatless Mondays make kids unhealthy, and this proves it. He looked up at the empty seats, then at the banner from last year's debate finals still hanging crooked over the stage. "It sounded good when we wrote it," he said. Priya tapped the card with two fingers. "Every point needs a claim, evidence and a warrant. The claim is fine. But watch what happens when I argue back." She cleared her throat like a lawyer on TV. "My cousin went vegetarian and felt great, so vegetarian eating is healthy. Now what?"

Lincoln paced across the boards, his sneakers squeaking. Both cousins could be real, and they pointed in opposite directions, so a single story could not settle anything. That had to be a rule, a pattern he could not see directly but could infer from the way the arguments crashed into each other. "So one person's story, whichever person it is, can't prove a general trend," he said slowly. "Marco might just be Marco." Priya nodded. "It's called anecdotal evidence. Our whole case is anecdotal evidence, one cousin tall."

They went to work. Priya pulled up the lunch counts on the library tablet while Lincoln searched for a real study of school menus, and they rebuilt each point the right way: claim first, evidence that covered many students, then the warrant explaining why the evidence supported the claim. When Lincoln got stuck on his second point, he tested the warrant out loud like a hinge. "Kids need protein to focus, and the study shows focus dropped at schools that cut protein. That connects." It did connect. His shoulders came down an inch.

At rehearsal the next day, Ms. Okafor sat in the third row eating carrot sticks and played the opposing team. She fired the cousin argument at them, the same trap that had eaten their old case, and Lincoln answered without reading a card. "One story cannot prove a trend, because a single case may not be typical. Our study looks at thousands of students." Ms. Okafor raised her carrot like a gavel and called the round for them. Walking offstage, Lincoln straightened the old banner so it hung level, then turned to Priya and said, "Same time Thursday? I want to work on the rebuttals."

Lillian's grandmother had always made dinner look easy, but tonight Lillian was alone in the kitchen with three recipes and one oven, and nothing about it felt easy. Her brother Devan sat at the counter doing homework, which mostly meant watching her.

"You're going to burn something," he said.

"I'm not. I'm going to prioritize." She tapped the printed recipe she'd found on an American website. "Rice takes twenty minutes, the curry simmers for thirty, and the flatbread bakes at 350 degrees Fahrenheit for twelve. The problem is our oven only shows Celsius. It doesn't say Fahrenheit anywhere."

Devan leaned over the recipe anyway, because what he really wanted was for dinner to include the flatbread. He'd been asking for it since Tuesday, and he didn't care about temperatures, only that the bread came out warm and puffed instead of flat and sad. "So what's 350 in Celsius?"

"That's what I have to figure out." Lillian had a candidate answer from a conversion chart printed in tiny letters at the bottom of another recipe page: 350 degrees Fahrenheit was about 175 to 180 degrees Celsius. But she didn't fully trust a chart she'd found by accident, so she decided to test it before the bread went in.

She set the oven to 175 Celsius and put in a spoonful of butter on a scrap of foil. In her grandmother's oven, at the right heat, butter melted and browned gently in about two minutes; too hot and it hissed and scorched almost at once. She watched through the glass. The butter slid into a golden pool, quiet and slow, no smoke. She tried 180 and watched again. Same gentle melt. Somewhere between those two numbers, she decided, the American recipe lived. "One-seven-five," she said, setting the dial back. "Maybe one-eighty. It's a range, not one exact number."

Then she worked backward through the timing, because everything had to land on the table at the same moment. She started the curry first, since it needed the longest, then rinsed the rice and set it bubbling, and only when the rice had ten minutes left did she roll the dough and slide the flatbread into the warm oven. Devan abandoned his homework entirely and stood beside her at the oven door.

"Is it supposed to puff like that?" he asked.

"That's exactly what it's supposed to do." She pulled the bread out, checked that the dish towel she'd left near the burner was nowhere near the flame, since cloth was flammable and she'd nearly learned that lesson the hard way last month, and carried everything to the table in one careful parade.

Devan tore the flatbread in half before she'd even sat down. Steam curled out of it. "Okay," he said, mouth already full. "You can prioritize dinner every night from now on."

Brody sat on the flat wooden bench behind the baseball diamond, his right arm sweating inside its white cast. Six weeks, the doctor had said, and that was two weeks ago. Across the field, Coach Delgado was running drills, and Brody watched every throw like he could absorb it through his eyes.

His grandfather lowered himself onto the bench beside him with a grunt. Grandpa's left wrist wore a cast too, tan colored and dented at the thumb. "Ten weeks for me," Grandpa said, wiggling his fingers. "You'll beat me out of mine by a month, I'd wager."

Brody frowned. Same kind of break, he knew that much. He had been there in June when Grandpa tripped on the porch step, and three weeks later Brody had landed wrong diving for a line drive, and the x-rays had looked almost identical, side by side on the light board. Same bone, same crack, same doctor. So why ten weeks for Grandpa and six for him?

That was the question he turned over all through batting practice. It was plausible that the doctor just liked kids better, but that seemed weak. It was plausible that Grandpa's break was secretly worse, except the x-rays had matched. Brody liked explanations he could test.

So he tested one. At halftime of his sister's soccer game the next Saturday, he walked the sideline with a notebook and asked every person he could find who had ever broken a bone: how old were you, and how long was the cast on. Marcus, age twelve, five weeks. Marcus's mom, age thirty-eight, nine weeks. The referee had broken his ankle at forty-five and spent three months in a boot. By the end of the afternoon Brody had twelve names, and the pattern jumped right off the page. Every kid was out of a cast faster than every grown-up.

He showed the notebook to his grandfather on Sunday. Grandpa read it slowly, tapped the column of numbers, and laughed. "Young bones heal faster than old ones. Kids spend less time in a cast than adults with the same break." He shook his head. "Sixty-eight years old and learning it from a thirteen-year-old with a notebook."

The day Brody's cast came off, the nurse cut it away with a little buzzing saw and let the sunlight expose his pale, skinny arm to the air for the first time in a month. It looked strange, like it belonged to a younger kid. Outside, Grandpa was waiting in the truck with the window down and the ball bag already loaded.

"Think that arm still works?" Grandpa asked.

Brody rolled down the window the rest of the way, picked up a baseball from the seat, and fired it straight into his grandfather's glove.

The guest bedroom was the coldest room in the house, and Hazel knew it before she even opened the door. The floorboards chilled her bare feet, and the air smelled like dust and old lavender sachets from the closet. Her grandmother would sleep here for a whole week, starting tonight, and Hazel wanted everything to be perfect.

"You can have my quilt too," Hazel said, dragging the heavy blue bundle down the hall. "It's the warmest thing we own."

"That's kind of you, sweetheart." Grandma set her suitcase on the bed, moving with her usual careful steps. On the first night, Hazel checked on her before bed and found her tucked under both quilts, hands wrapped around a teacup she'd brought upstairs herself, her fingertips pale as paper. Grandma smiled and said the room was lovely. The radiator under the window was barely warm when Hazel pressed her palm against it.

She couldn't stop thinking about it the next morning. She remembered a school trip to the butterfly house two years ago, when the guide had explained that bees pollinate flowers by carrying pollen on their fuzzy legs, and how a small thing doing quiet work could keep something alive without anyone noticing. Her grandmother's cold hands felt like that, a small quiet signal of something bigger. So Hazel typed her question into the library computer, half sure she was being dramatic, and found what she needed in a paragraph she read three times: older adults face a greater risk of hypothermia than younger adults, a dangerous drop in body temperature, and they can get it even in a house that doesn't seem that cold, because they may not complain.

That afternoon she found her father arguing with her uncle on the phone about whether to replace the old furnace, a family controversy that had raged since Thanksgiving. Hazel waited until her father hung up, then showed him the paragraph on her screen.

"Hypothermia," she said. "That's what it's called. Grandma's room is freezing and she keeps saying it's fine."

Her father pressed his hand to the guest room radiator, the way Hazel had, and frowned. "You noticed something I missed," he said. "Let's fix it."

They carried up the space heater from the basement, and Hazel, who was small and agile, squeezed behind the dresser to plug it in where nobody else could reach. When Grandma came up after dinner, the room was toasty, and the smell of lavender had softened into something almost like a garden in July. Hazel watched her grandmother pull off the second quilt and settle in with just the sheet, her fingers pink again as she turned the pages of her novel.

"There was a drafty farm house where I raised your mother," Grandma said, patting the bed beside her. "I survived it, but I'm not sorry to skip that part this time." Hazel kicked off her slippers and climbed up next to her, tucking her cold toes under the warm edge of the blue quilt.

Piper arrived at Mr. Alvarez's studio ten minutes early, holding her grandmother's old guitar by the neck. She had a note folded in her pocket, a message her grandmother had written before her hands got too stiff to play: "The twelfth fret holds a secret. Find it yourself." Piper had read it four times on the bus, and she presumed there was a real answer waiting, not just something her grandmother had made up to keep her practicing.

She tuned the low E string and plucked it once. The open string rumbled through the small room. Then she pressed her finger down at the twelfth fret, the one marked by two diagonal inlaid dots, and plucked again. A note came out that was clearly the same and not the same at all. It rang higher, and it matched something she recognized.

"You found it already," Mr. Alvarez said from his chair by the window. He was sorting sheet music and had not touched her guitar once.

"It's the same note," Piper said. "Only higher. A lot higher." She slid her finger along the string, checking. "The twelfth fret sits right in the middle of the string, doesn't it?"

"Measure it if you want," he said.

She borrowed a ruler from the desk drawer. The distance from the nut to the bridge was sixty-four centimeters. The twelfth fret sat at thirty-two, exactly halfway. She played the open string, then the fretted one, back and forth, listening. Pressing the string at its exact midpoint halved the length that could vibrate, and the note rose by a full octave. She tested the A string next, then the D, and it worked every time.

"I kept messing up at the seventh fret last week and I was starting to feel resentment toward this whole guitar," she said. "But this makes sense. It's not random."

Mr. Alvarez smiled. "Halfway is halfway, on every string."

Piper played the open E, then the octave at the twelfth, then both together. The two notes blended into one wide, ringing sound that filled the studio and hung in the air after she lifted her fingers away. She found her grandmother's note in her pocket, smoothed it out on the music stand, and wrote underneath it in pencil: "Found it. The twelfth fret is the middle." Then she played the pair again, louder this time.

Mya's best friend Priya had been acting strange since Tuesday, and the only clue was a photo. It showed Priya's cat, Mr. Whiskers, sleeping on a windowsill, and Priya had sent it to the whole sixth-grade chat with the message "Guess where I am right now!" Everyone guessed the mall, the new pizza place, the library. Nobody guessed right, and Priya just replied with a smirking face and said "Nope, somewhere I shouldn't be."

That was the problem. Priya was supposed to be at her grandmother's house all week, recovering from the flu. Mya knew it because she had walked Priya's route home on Friday, carrying the homework packet like a good friend, and Priya's mom had said so at the door. So where was she, and why the secret?

At lunch on Thursday, Mya leaned over Devon's shoulder in the cafeteria. Devon was the kid everyone went to with phone problems, the one who could fix a cracked screen with tape and patience. "Can I see Priya's cat photo?" Mya asked. "Not the chat. The actual file." Devon raised an eyebrow but forwarded it, and Mya pressed and held the image until a menu appeared, then tapped the little "i" in a circle. A page of details filled the screen. Date, size, camera model. And then, lower down, a map.

The map had a single pin on it. Mya zoomed in, her heart going quick and light. The pin sat on a street she recognized, because she had walked it on Friday. It was Priya's own street, three houses down from where Mya had stood at the door. The photo hadn't just shown a cat. It had shown exactly where the cat was.

"It's called EXIF metadata," Devon said, peeking over. "My cousin learned about it after a whole controversy at her school. The phone writes the exact GPS coordinates of where the photo was taken into hidden data in the file." He shrugged. "Location services were on."

Mya stared at the pin. So Priya was home after all, hiding out for some reason, and now a whole chat of forty kids could technically see it too. She thought about how Mr. Whiskers would be resilient to this sort of thing, cats never worried about being found, but Priya was not a cat. Mya decided to invest her lunch period in figuring out the rest. She texted Priya directly: "You're on your own street. I saw the map. You okay?"

Three dots appeared. Then stopped. Then appeared again. The reply came before the bell: "Don't tell anyone. There's a fox den in my backyard and I've been filming the babies all week. My mom said no visitors till I'm better. Coming to show you at recess."

Adam had one job at the farmers' market: buy a jar of Mr. Ruiz's wildflower honey before it sold out. His grandmother's birthday was Saturday, and she'd said last month that his honey was the only thing she wanted. The problem was that everyone else's grandmother seemed to want it too, because Mr. Ruiz charged four dollars a jar when the other honey sellers charged nine.

By the time Adam reached the stall, the line stretched past the bread stand and curved around the corner. A woman near the front turned around and called back, "He's down to his last crate!" A groan rolled down the line like a wave. Adam stood on a crate to coordinate with his friend Priya, who was saving spots for each other whenever one of them needed to dash off, and waved to show her where he was. She held up two fingers. Twenty minutes from the front, maybe.

When Adam finally got there, a handwritten sign leaned against the empty crate: SOLD OUT, BACK NEXT WEEK. Next week was after the birthday. He stared at the sign, then at Mr. Ruiz, who was apologizing to person after person behind Adam. "Four dollars is my price," the man kept saying, shrugging. "I sell out by nine every week, and I hate turning folks away, but that's just what happens when more people want it than I've got." Adam walked back along the line, and it hit him: every single person still waiting wanted honey at four dollars. If it cost nine, like at the stall next door, half of them would probably walk away, and there would still be jars left. The gap between the crowd and the crates was the whole story.

"It's called a shortage," Priya said when he told her, still holding her tote bag. "My sister tried to get concert tickets last month. Cheap ones gone in four minutes, and hundreds of fans got nothing. She said that's the word for it, when the price is kept low and more people want the thing than there are things to sell." Adam looked back at Mr. Ruiz's empty crates, feeling the shape of the idea settle into place.

At the next stall, though, a farmer was practically hiding behind towers of zucchini. "Take a bag, take two," she told Adam, dropping the price from two dollars to one, then to fifty cents. Nobody wanted zucchini in August, not this much of it. Priya bought three and didn't even like zucchini. Adam bought a bag too, feeling a small flush of embarrassment for Mr. Ruiz and his stubborn four dollars, but also a plan forming.

"Could you do a trade?" he asked the woman. "My neighbor will trade you zucchini bread for honey. She does it every fall." The farmer thought, then nodded slowly. "Tell her to bring the bread Sunday. I've got jars." Adam texted his neighbor from the corner of the market, and she sent back a thumbs-up and three exclamation points. He walked home carrying zucchini for his grandmother's birthday bread, honey already promised, and Mr. Ruiz's empty crates still in his mind, waiting for next week.

The parking lot was already half full when Adam's mom pulled up beside the gym doors, and his heart started hammering before he even touched the door handle. His stomach flipped too, like something small was doing somersaults in there, and he frowned at his own hands because they wouldn't hold still.

"You okay?" his mom asked.

"Fine," Adam said, which was mostly true. He wanted to go in. He'd wanted to go all week, ever since Priya said she'd save him a dance. So why was his body acting like he was about to be chased by wolves?

His best friend Dex came jogging across the lot, holding his phone up like a trophy. "Mr. Holloway let me plug into the speakers for two songs. Two! I'm basically the DJ generator of this whole dance. If those songs go over, he said maybe homecoming."

"That's huge," Adam said, but his stomach flipped again, harder.

Dex squinted at him. "Dude, you look like you're going to throw up on that car."

"I'm not nervous," Adam said. "That's the weird part. I want to be in there." Then he thought about it, turning it over the way he turned over a math problem. His heart was racing. His stomach felt wrong. If it were actual fear, wouldn't he want to leave? But he wanted to stay. So maybe the nervous part came first, even before he felt nervous, and the rest of him was just catching up. He'd read something once about butterflies, and now he tested it out loud: "Maybe it's just butterflies."

"Butterflies," Dex repeated, nodding like a scientist. "Nervousness gives you that. Your heart goes fast and it pulls blood away from your stomach, so it feels like that."

"So if I get my heart to slow down, the butterflies quit?" Adam didn't wait for an answer. He breathed in slow through his nose, out slow through his mouth, four times, while Dex watched with the fascinated horror of someone seeing a friend do something embarrassing in public.

Halfway through the fifth breath, Adam realized his stomach had stopped flipping. His heart still beat fast, but it was the good kind now, the kind that came from the music leaking out under the gym doors and the laughing inside and the fact that in about nine minutes he would be standing in front of Priya.

"Okay," he said, and pulled his jacket tighter even though it was too thin to insulate him from the October cold. "Let's go make you famous."

Dex's grin was infectious. He shoved his phone in his pocket and pushed through the doors first, and Adam followed him straight into the noise and the lights.

Natalie stood at the pharmacy counter waiting for her mom's allergy medicine, drumming her fingers on a display of copper bracelets. The sign above them said EASES ACHES AND PAINS, and beneath that, in smaller letters, a quote from a man named Dale: "After two weeks, my elbow pain was gone." Dale was holding up his wrist and grinning.

A woman with a shopping basket stopped beside Natalie and picked one up. "My brother swears by these," she said. "He wore one for his knee and says it cured him."

"Did anything else happen that month?" Natalie asked. "Like, did he rest it, or take something?"

The woman shrugged. "He probably did lots of things. He's retired, he golfs less in winter." She turned the bracelet over, checking the price.

Natalie had been arguing with her uncle Ray about this exact thing at Sunday dinner. He'd slapped his leather band on the table and said it fixed his back, and when she'd asked whether his new stretching routine might have helped instead, he'd said, "It worked for me, that's all I know." Her cousin Priya had leaned over and murmured, "That's called an anecdote," and later they'd looked it up: a story about one person's experience. The problem, the article said, was that a story like that couldn't show one thing caused another, because nobody had ruled out the other explanations. Knee pain gets better by itself sometimes. Elbows rest. Winters end.

"My dad's a mechanic," Natalie said to the woman. "He says you can't tell what fixed an engine if you changed three things at once. If you swapped the fuel filter and rebuilt a piston and then it ran, you don't know which one did it, or if it just dried out and started on its own." She picked up a box of the pharmacy's store-brand pain relievers instead. "This one has a little paper inside with studies, comparisons, how they tested it with lots of people, not just one guy like Dale."

The woman laughed and put the bracelet back. "One guy like Dale," she repeated. She squinted at the quote on the sign. "Though I suppose his pain was real to him. How it felt was subjective, even if the bracelet didn't cause it."

Natalie nodded. "The feeling can be true and the cure story can still be shaky." She felt her phone buzz: a text from Priya. Tell Uncle Ray we'll run the experiment. One month, bracelet on his left wrist only, stretches only in week two, diary every day.

Natalie grinned and typed back, "Deal. He has to sign it."

At the counter the pharmacist called her mom's name, and Natalie carried the white bag past the bracelet display, already drafting the first line of the diary in her head.

Anthony slid into the only empty desk, third row by the window, and listened to Ms. Ruiz assign science partners. A girl with a braid down her back turned around before the teacher even finished talking.

"I'm Priya," she said. "We got the decomposer project. Pill bugs, mushrooms, worms, any of those. I've been wanting a partner who actually cares, because last year my partner let me do everything."

"I care," Anthony said, though his mind was still on the moving truck that had left his old street three days ago. He thought about his friend Marcus, who had stood on the curb holding a folded map of the new town Anthony had drawn himself, useless now because Anthony had drawn the school in the wrong spot.

At lunch, Priya spread her notebook between their trays. "We should restrict the project to one decomposer so we can go deep instead of shallow. I vote earthworms."

Anthony nodded, but he was watching two kids at the next table laughing over a phone. He pulled out his own phone under the table. There were four texts from Marcus and he had answered only one, two days late, with a single "cool."

That night he tried to think it through like a lab question. Marcus had been his best friend since kindergarten. But his cousin Dev had also had a best friend once, and after Dev's family moved, the two of them just drifted, until a year later they had nothing to say. What was different about the friendships that survived moving? Anthony made a list on a napkin. The ones that lasted, like his uncle and his army buddy, called every single week. The ones that faded, like Dev's, nobody made the effort. It wasn't some mystery of fate. It was contact, regular contact, or nothing.

He called Marcus right then. It rang so long that Anthony almost hung up, sure this was all in vain.

"Yo," Marcus said. "I thought you forgot me already."

"Never. Look, I figured something out. Friends who move apart and stay close keep in touch regularly. Calls, messages, visits. The ones who don't, fade. So let's not be those guys."

"So what, we just text whenever?"

"No. Sunday, four o'clock, video call. Every week. Put it in your calendar."

"Every single week? For how long?"

"For as long as we want to still know each other," Anthony said.

There was a pause, and then Marcus laughed, the same laugh as always. "Okay. Sunday, four. I'm putting it in now. You better answer."

On Sunday Anthony set his phone against the salt shaker and waited, watching the screen, until the call chimed and Marcus's face filled it, holding up a slice of pizza from their old favorite place. "Wish you were here," Marcus said, "but this screen thing is going to have to do."

"Every Sunday," Anthony said. "Deal."

Claire kept a systematic list in her notebook titled "What Makes a Story Work," and so far it had three items: dialogue goes in quotation marks, each new speaker gets a new paragraph, and something big has to happen near the end. Today was the read-aloud in Mr. Reyes's room, and she had signed up first.

Her story was about a dog named Biscuit who slipped his leash and ran into the woods behind the school. In her favorite part, the narrator waded through brush and found Biscuit hiding under a log covered with a shelf-like fungus, trembling but safe. She had checked every line of dialogue twice. "Come here, boy," the narrator called. "It's okay." Commas, quotation marks, new paragraphs, all correct. She raised her hand when Mr. Reyes called her name.

She read slowly, saving the best part. When she reached the log, the room got quiet. Marcus, who sat in front and usually drew monsters during read-alouds, had actually put down his pencil. Claire's voice sped up. "The branches snapped back as she knelt. 'Come here, boy,' she called. 'It's okay.' Biscuit crept out and pressed against her legs." She stopped. That was the last line on the page, and it felt like landing a jump off a high wall.

Marcus's hand shot up. "What happened to the dog after that? Did she take him home? Did her mom find out she skipped piano to look for him?" Three other kids nodded. Marcus said, "You can't just stop. I'll boycott sharing day if people keep doing endings like that." A few kids laughed, but Claire's stomach dropped. She had spent all her time on the dialogue and the rescue, and she hadn't noticed that the story quit exactly when the exciting part was over.

She sat down and pulled out her notebook. Mr. Reyes was walking around checking drafts, so she tapped Marcus's shoulder. "You said what happened after. Is there a name for that part?" Marcus shrugged, but Priya behind them held up a checklist from the writing folder and pointed to the last two lines. Claire read them, then read them again. "Falling action and resolution," she said under her breath.

At lunch she added to her list, working through it line by line. After the climax, the falling action and resolution show the consequences of what happened and tie up the story's loose ends. Priya's question was still ringing in her ears, so Claire flipped to a clean page and started writing. "They walked home in the dark, Biscuit's leash wound twice around her wrist. Her mom was on the porch, and she was not smiling." Marcus leaned over from the next seat. "Now I want to know what the mom says."

Joshua had been saving for a new bike all summer, and the lemonade stand was supposed to be his ticket there, but by two o'clock on Saturday he had earned only four dollars and a quarter. He was stirring the last pitcher with a long spoon when Marcus, the teenager from three houses down, pedaled up the street and stopped at the curb, looking bothered.

"You got customers?" Marcus asked, mopping sweat off his forehead with his sleeve. "I need cash today. I'm trying to sell a bond my grandpa gave me. Ten dollars for a ten-dollar bond. It's worth ten, so that's fair, right?"

Joshua poured him a cup. "What's a bond?"

"It's like a loan," Marcus said. "The government pays you interest for lending it money. Mine pays a tiny bit. Grandpa bought it years ago. But I've asked six people and nobody will give me ten dollars for it. Not even nine. Best offer was eight." He looked down the street as if another buyer might appear out of the heat shimmer rising off the pavement.

Joshua frowned. Something about that didn't add up, and he wanted to figure it out, because Marcus was promising five dollars to whoever helped him sell the thing, and five dollars plus four twenty-five was almost half the bike. He thought about the lemonade. Yesterday he had charged a dollar a cup, and today Mrs. Delgado had told him the store brand was on sale for fifty cents, so she would only buy his at half price. His lemonade hadn't changed. The other lemonade had gotten cheaper. So the price of his old lemonade had fallen because something new had appeared that was a better deal.

"Wait," Joshua said slowly. "Did interest rates go up lately? Like, did you hear that somewhere?"

Marcus shrugged. "Yeah, my mom was complaining about it. New bonds pay more interest than they used to. Everybody keeps saying that."

"Then that's it," Joshua said. "People can get new bonds that pay more interest, so nobody's going to pay you full price for your old one. When interest rates rise, the prices of bonds that already exist fall." He set down the spoon. "It's like my lemonade. It's the same lemonade, but the competition changed, so my price had to change."

Marcus stared at the cup in his hands. "So my bond isn't broken? It's just... out of date?"

"Right. It's still worth something, just not ten dollars." Joshua wiped his hands on his shorts. "Take the eight. And then come help me run this stand, because my whole network of customers is two families and a mail carrier, and I've been negligent about putting up signs on Elm Street. With two of us, we can sell the rest of this pitcher and regulate the price so we both make money."

Marcus drained his lemonade, slapped eight dollars of future earnings on the counter as a promise, and dragged the folding table into the shade where more people could see it.

Julia stood at the chain-link fence at the edge of the playground, holding the new glasses in both hands like they might bite. Tomorrow was picture day, and if she wore them, they would be in the yearbook forever. If she didn't wear them, she would keep walking past her own friends without saying hi, which was what had happened twice this week alone.

Marcus found her there, bouncing a tennis ball against the blacktop. "You still hiding those? Put them on." He had been the one who figured out something was wrong with her eyes, back in October, when she kept copying his homework because she couldn't read the board.

"I don't want the whole school deciding they're weird." She shoved them into her pocket. "Besides, the eye doctor said I've got twenty forty vision. That's better than twenty twenty, right? Bigger number."

Marcus caught the ball and held it still. "My cousin had that. She said it's the other way around. It means you have to stand twenty feet away to read letters that a person with normal eyesight could read from forty."

"That makes no sense." But even as she said it, Julia thought about the eye chart, about how the big E at the top had been easy and every line under it had dissolved into gray smudges. She remembered squinting, leaning forward, the nurse telling her to stay behind the line on the floor. A normal person, standing twice as far back, would have read those same letters. The number wasn't a score. It was a distance.

"Fine," she said. "Test time." She walked to the far wall of the gym, where somebody had stenciled a small Wildcats logo by the door. "How far back do you think this is?"

"Like forty feet, maybe."

She pulled the glasses out and slid them on. The logo snapped into focus, every tooth in the bobcat's grin sharp and clean. She yanked them off, and it blurred back into a smear of purple. She put them on again. Off. On. It wasn't her imagination; the wall itself was changing, or rather, her eyes were. She thought of the arid blacktop in September, how she'd blamed the heat for the way everything shimmered.

Marcus threw her the ball from across the gym, and for the first time all season, she caught it without flinching, because she saw it the whole way in.

"So tomorrow," he said.

"Tomorrow, in the picture." She aimed the ball at the door and hit the bobcat square between the eyes.

The smell of whiteboard marker hung in the air of Room 12 as Noemie stared at the board. 3x + 4 = 19. She was supposed to do the same thing to both sides, like a scale that had to stay balanced, but the x kept hiding behind the numbers, refusing to show what it was worth.

"How do you know it balances if you can't see inside?" she asked her lab partner, Deshawn.

"You just trust it," he said, tapping his pencil. Deshawn wanted to beat his older brother, who had finished this worksheet in ten minutes flat. He was racing, and racing made him messy.

Noemie tried it anyway. Take 4 from both sides. 3x = 15. Divide both sides by 3. She whispered it aloud, feeling the balance of it, and wrote x = 5. She checked by putting 5 back in, and both sides came out 19, like two doors opening onto the same room. Something she couldn't see had been there the whole time, and she had dug it out.

Then came the next problem, and the trouble. Deshawn grabbed the marker and wrote 2x + 3x + 3 = 23. Under it, fast and confident, he scribbled 5x + 3 = 23, then kept going, but before that he had crossed something out. Noemie leaned over. His first line had said 2x + 3 = 5x, treating the lonely 3 as if it belonged with the x's.

"You combined the 3 with the 2x," she said.

"So? They're all smushed together on the same side."

"But they're not the same kind of thing." She picked up a handful of counters from the bin. Two red counters, then three more red counters. "Two x's plus three x's, that's five x's." She set down a single blue counter. "But this 3 is just a 3. You can't squish it in with the x ones. It's like adding apples to a mystery box."

Deshawn frowned at the counters. "The 2x and the 3x are like terms," he said slowly, as if remembering something. He tried combining the 2x and 3x first, leaving the plain 3 alone, then subtracted 3 from both sides and got 5x = 20. "So x is 4." He checked it, and his face split into a grin. He was still going to tell his brother he'd won.

At lunch, Deshawn pushed his tray across the table toward Noemie, offering half a cookie, a small payment that symbolized more than it looked. "My grandma," he said, "she's a retired teacher. I told her about the apples and the mystery box, and she asked me one thing. She asked, 'What does the x stand for?'"

"What did you say?"

"I said, I have no idea, but it's definitely not a 3."

Noemie laughed so abruptly that milk nearly came out of her nose. "Okay, but seriously. What does it stand for?"

Deshawn shrugged and bit into the cookie. "Grandma says that's the whole game. Find out what's hiding."

Carter slid into his seat in the computer lab just as the bell finished ringing, which he counted as a personal victory. Mr. Reyes had assigned a project on internet safety, which meant a whole period of typing in a room that smelled like warm plastic and old sandwiches. He was halfway through a paragraph about strong passwords when the girl next to him, Priya, made a small choking noise.

"Look at this," she whispered, angling her screen toward him.

It was a screenshot. In it, a kid named Marcus, who everyone knew, had sent a private message to someone named Dylan saying their friend Kaya was "the most annoying person in the entire eighth grade, honestly." Now that screenshot was sitting in a different group chat, the big one with half the grade in it, with a row of shocked-face emojis underneath it.

"Wait," Carter said. "That was a private chat?"

"Dylan must have screenshotted it and shared it," Priya said. "Rough."

Carter stared at the image. He had always thought of private messages like passing a note in class, folded paper that only one person touched. But a screenshot, apparently, preserved the note forever, and the note went wherever the person who got it decided to take it. A private message was only as private as the people who read it. He tested the idea in his head: Marcus sent it to one person. One person showed forty. Yep. That tracked.

He looked at his own screen, where his draft to his friend Theo sat open in the corner. He had typed, "Mr. Reyes's tie today looks like a parrot lost a fight," and was about to hit send. His finger hovered. Theo was reliable. Theo had never leaked anything. But Dylan had probably seemed reliable too, right up until this morning.

Carter deleted the sentence and typed instead, "There is a bird. It is on a tie. That is all I will say publicly."

Theo, three rows over, turned around and mouthed, "Coward."

"You're welcome," Carter mouthed back.

Then something else occurred to him, and it was worse. He had sent Theo a private critique of Theo's book report last week, three whole paragraphs about the ending being "confusing in a way that felt accidental." If Theo ever got annoyed at him, that could end up in a group chat too. Carter opened the chat with Theo, found the message, and typed a follow-up: "Also I reread the ending and it's actually good, ignore all of that, especially the word accidental."

"Too late," Theo replied. "I already screenshotted it for the group."

Carter's stomach dropped for a full two seconds before the laughing emoji arrived.

"Kidding," Theo wrote. "But you should see your face from here."

"It's a very dignified face," Carter typed back, and then, after a moment, deleted that too.

Nolan had wanted a dog for three years, and today the wanting was finally over. His family had adopted a small brown puppy named Beans, and he was carrying her home down Juniper Street in the front pocket of his hoodie, her nose poking out like a joey riding in its mother's pouch. "You're not really a marsupial," he told her, "but you're close enough." Beans yawned at him. The houses along the street were tall and neat, the kind of affluent block where every lawn looked mowed by a ruler, and Nolan walked slowly so the walk would last.

Halfway home, Beans squirmed and whined, and Nolan realized she was chewing something. He tipped her gently out of the pocket and pried her jaw open. A shredded strip of minty wrapper stuck to her lip. His stomach dropped. He mentally ran through his backpack, the one he'd let her sniff at the shelter, the one that had sat open on his bed all morning. There had been gum in the front pocket. He remembered the silver packaging, and he remembered the words on it, sugar-free, because his mom bought that kind now. He dug through the backpack on the spot and counted seven empty wrappers where a full pack had been. She must have swallowed some while he was getting the leash.

He couldn't see inside Beans, so he worked from what he could see. She seemed fine, but that proved nothing, and he'd once read something on a poster at the dentist's office about sugar-free gum and dogs. He couldn't remember the details, only that it was bad, so he deduced the safest move: don't wait for symptoms, get to the vet now. He called his mom, and she turned the car around and met them at the corner.

The vet on Delmore Street took Beans straight back, and Nolan sat on a bench with his knees bouncing until the doctor came out. "Good timing," she said. "It was xylitol in that gum, the sweetener they use instead of sugar. Xylitol makes a dog's body release insulin, and insulin can drop her blood sugar to a dangerous level." She held up a syringe of sugar water. "We caught it early, so she'll be fine."

Nolan watched through the window as Beans, drowsy but awake, licked syrup from a small dish. He had wanted this dog for three years, and for three years he had imagined the fun parts, the fetch, the walks, the sleeping dog at his feet. He hadn't imagined checking backpacks, and he changed his mind right there on the bench about what owning a dog actually meant. It meant paying attention even when nothing looked wrong yet.

When they got home, Nolan emptied the backpack completely, gum and all, into a drawer high above Beans's best jump. He set the empty backpack on the floor and watched her climb inside anyway, tail wagging, her whole body disappearing except one brown ear. "Okay," he said, reaching in. "New rule. Nothing in the bag but you."

The paper was creased into eighths from living in Eleanor's back pocket, and the blessing on it had gone soft at the folds. Her bat mitzvah was in three weeks, and she still stumbled in the same spot every time, right where the melody jumped. She sat cross-legged on her bedroom floor, cat at her knee, and sang it again. "V'ein keil," she began, and then the jump came and she lost her place, and the cat flattened her ears like she'd been struck.

Her mother called up that Rabbi Solomon wanted the blessing memorized before Friday, because after Friday there would be no time to rehearse. Eleanor didn't understand that. Sunday had always been her slow day, the day for sprawl and practice. She went downstairs to argue the schedule, but her mother was on the porch with her calendar, so Eleanor folded her paper smaller and put it away.

Then she remembered she was spending Friday night at Zoe's house. She'd been looking forward to it all week, mostly because Zoe had a new phone and a trampoline. She packed pajamas and her toothbrush, and she slid the creased paper in her bag too, in case there was a quiet moment.

At six o'clock, just as the sky over the hills went orange, Zoe's mother stood in the kitchen doorway and held out a basket. "Phones in here, please, girls. It's Shabbat now." Zoe dropped hers in without complaining, which surprised Eleanor more than the basket did. Eleanor handed hers over slowly. "It starts at sunset," Zoe said, "Friday sunset. It goes until tomorrow night, after it's dark out. Then we do Havdalah and everything comes back on." Eleanor had known the word Shabbat her whole life but she had never watched it arrive before, like weather you could time by a clock.
