That night, after pizza and cards by candlelight, Eleanor sat on Zoe's bedroom floor while Zoe braided and unbraided a length of yarn. She took out her paper and tried the blessing under her breath. Away from her own house, away from the piano where she always got lost, the jump in the melody came easier. "V'ein keil," she sang, and this time she sailed right over the gap, and Zoe said, "Do that part again, it's pretty."

The next evening they stood on the porch waiting for three stars to show, because nightfall, Zoe explained, meant dark, really dark, not just sunset. When the sky finally went black, Zoe's father lit a twisted candle and they passed spices around and said the goodbyes to Shabbat, and then the phones came back and everyone's screens glowed blue all at once. Eleanor checked hers and found nothing waiting that mattered. She walked home through the cold carrying the tune in her head, whole and unbroken, and she sang it all the way up her own front steps.

The auditorium smelled like dust and old curtains, which Connor decided was the smell of drama class in general. Mr. Ruiz had them up on the stage in pairs, and the assignment was simple and terrifying: improvise a scene where you accept every offer with "yes, and." No denying, no changing the subject. Connor's partner, Maya, held an invisible object and said, "I found this compass on the floor of the spaceship."

"Yes, and it's pointing toward the equator instead of north," Connor said, taking it carefully, like it might be fragile. "Yes, and that means we're flying upside down." Maya's eyebrows went up, which he chose to read as approval.

Between turns they sat on the edge of the stage, feet dangling, while other pairs performed. Down in the third row, Connor's grandfather was practicing a speech he was giving at the community center on Saturday, about his old plumbing business. He'd started strong, but halfway through he frowned at his notes and said, "Now, where was I," and then just stopped, staring at the page like it had personally betrayed him. He'd done the same thing twice before, always around the middle, and always with that same lost look.

Connor watched him try again, lose the thread again in the same spot, and started thinking. A speech wasn't a book. Grandpa couldn't flip back a page the way a reader could, so once a listener was lost, they stayed lost. Unless something in the words themselves told you where you were. He glanced at the notes. Grandpa said "next" twice and then just wandered off into a story about a water heater. What if the problem was the wandering, the lack of anything that announced a new part?

Connor slid off the stage, walked down the aisle, and suggested Grandpa mark each part before it started. "First, second, finally," Connor said. "Say them out loud." Grandpa grumbled that he wasn't in kindergarten, but he tried it, and this time when he reached the middle he said, "Second," and his eyes stopped drifting, and the audience of two empty seats and one grandson could follow him all the way to "finally."

Back onstage, Maya was already setting up their next scene. "Okay, new rule," she said. "You keep saying where we are, and I'll keep saying yes."

"So you want signposting words in an improv about a doomed spaceship."

"Obviously," said Maya, and held out the invisible compass again.

Natalie had one day left before her grandmother flew in from Monterrey, and so far she could say exactly one full sentence in Spanish: "Tengo un perro pequeño que se llama Biscuit." She said it to the mirror, to the toaster, and to Biscuit himself, who wagged at anything with her voice attached to it. Her mother, who advocated loudly for family bonds whenever Natalie wanted to skip a call, had made her a deal: describe every person and pet in the house in full sentences by tonight, and she could pick the movie on Friday.

She was working on "Mi hermano Marcus tiene quince años y toca la guitarra mal" when Marcus wandered in eating cereal from the box. "You know what's weird," he said. "In French class we just learned you're supposed to say vous to strangers. Like, always. Madame Perrin made us practice it on the janitor and he looked so confused."

Natalie wrote that down, mostly to make him go away. Then she texted her friend Priya, who took German on weekends, and Priya sent back a single message: "Sie. Same thing. My teacher says you'd sound like a toddler without it." So French had vous, German had Sie, and Natalie had a suspicion her Spanish book was hiding the same rule somewhere. The book only said usted meant "you," which was spectacularly unhelpful, since tú also meant "you." Two words, one meaning, no explanation. There had to be a pattern, and nobody was going to hand it to her.

The doorbell rang before she could stew on it. On the porch stood a small older woman in a raincoat, holding a handwritten address that had clearly survived a washing machine. "Busco Maple Street," she said. "Perdón, ¿dónde queda?"

Here it was: a stranger, a real one, asking directions, and Natalie's mouth was already loading the familiar tú she used with Marcus and Biscuit. She caught it mid-launch. Testing time. "Queda a dos cuadras, señora," Natalie said. "¿Usted busca la casa azul?" The woman's whole face did something warm and unhurried, like a cat settling into sun. She talked for a full minute about her granddaughter, the weather in Guadalajara, and the terrible numbering on Maple Street, and Natalie understood maybe half of it and nodded at all the right gaps. When she left, the woman squeezed her arm and said, "Qué niña tan educada."

Natalie closed the door and stood there feeling extremely spontaneous, in a planned and rehearsed sort of way. Then she went back to the kitchen, erased half her sentence list, and rewrote every line for her grandmother in the usted form, out loud, while Biscuit supervised from the warm spot by the fridge. "Mi abuela llega mañana," she told him. "Ella es la persona más terca que yo conozco." Biscuit yawned. From the hallway, Marcus called, "Was that Spanish or did you hurt yourself?"

"Usted no entiende nada," she called back.

Theo had been looking forward to Marcus's birthday sleepover for three weeks, and then Marcus's elbow knocked Theo's slice of pizza straight off the table and onto the carpet. "Nice one," Theo said, loud enough for everyone to hear. Marcus laughed with the other guys, and Theo decided, right there, that it was on purpose. Marcus had been showing off all night, taking the good controller, hogging the VR headset. This was just the newest move.

He spent the next hour collecting evidence. When Marcus passed the popcorn bowl past him to Dev, that was a snub. When Marcus picked Theo last for the Halo team, that was an insult. Theo's awareness of every little slight felt acute, like a radio tuned to one station: everything Marcus did, Marcus did to him.

At two in the morning, the guys were asleep and Theo was still awake, staring at the glow-in-the-dark stars on Marcus's ceiling. He started to replay the pizza moment, frame by frame, like rewinding a video. Marcus had been reaching across for the garlic knots. His chair legs had squeaked sideways just before his elbow moved. Had Marcus even been looking at Theo? He hadn't. His eyes were on the food. Theo sat up. Maybe he had tested the wrong theory the whole night. His simple idea: rerun each "insult" and ask one question, was there another possible cause? Popcorn bowl: it was on Dev's side. Halo teams: Marcus was balancing skill levels, and Theo actually stunk at Halo. Every clue had a second explanation.

At breakfast, Theo watched Marcus get up for juice, and Marcus's sneaker skidded on a patch of floor near the counter. "Whoa," Marcus said, arms windmilling, and Theo noticed a faint slick spot, probably from the pizza grease tracked off the carpet the night before. It was two feet from the table. Right where a chair pushing back could lose its grip.

"Marcus," Theo said. "Last night. The pizza. Did you slip?"

Marcus set the juice down. "Dude, yeah. My chair totally skated on something. I was going for the knots. Why, you thought I did it on purpose?"

"Maybe," Theo admitted. "Everything you did all night seemed aimed at me. I kept assuming you meant it."

"That's called hostile attribution bias," Marcus said, grinning. "My sister says I have it about my math teacher."

Theo laughed so hard he nearly choked on his waffles. "Okay, but in my defense, you were being annoying about the headset."

"I'll share the headset," Marcus said, sliding the last waffle onto Theo's plate. "Frontier day, my turn to explore new planets. You call shotgun on the goggles."

"Deal," said Theo, and grabbed the syrup.

Sydney was halfway through a video about pad thai when every light in the house quit at once, and the fridge behind her dissolved into silence. She counted to ten in the dark, hoping the power would shrug itself back on, then felt her way to the junk drawer and dug out the emergency candles Grandma insisted on keeping there. Soon the living room flickered with four small flames, and Sydney flopped onto the couch beside her grandfather, who was already grinning like the darkness was a treat.

"Good evening for stories," he said. He leaned toward the candlelight. "Back in 2003, I was working in an office when the power went out, and I had to walk all the way home. It was the Northeast blackout, August 14, 2003, and it cut power to about 55 million people. Whole parts of the northeastern United States, plus Ontario, in Canada, all dark at once."

Sydney sat up. "Fifty-five million? How do you even know it was that many?"

"That's what everyone said afterward. Streets full of people walking home, strangers sharing water bottles, restaurants giving away melting ice cream." He laughed. "Best free cuisine I ever had, let me tell you."

Sydney's phone buzzed with one last text before it died, from her friend Marisol down the block: "Look out your front window!!" Sydney carried a candle to the window, careful not to drip wax on the sill. Every streetlight she could see was dark. Every porch light, every glowing window, gone. But then she noticed something odd. Far off, past the park, the sky had a faint orange shimmer of city light, way over on the east side.

She hurried back to the couch, thinking hard. If the whole grid were down like in her grandfather's story, everything would be black in every direction. But the east side still glowed. That meant the outage had edges, which meant it had a boundary somewhere, and boundaries meant the problem was local, not enormous. She tested the idea out loud. "Grandpa, it's not fifty-five million people this time. I think it's just us, this neighborhood. Maybe one little section."

He raised his eyebrows. "How do you figure?"

"Because I can see lights over east. Fifty-five million people would include them, probably."

Just then a knock rattled the door, and there stood Marisol with a flashlight and a printed flyer from the utility crew on her corner: scheduled maintenance, power back by nine, sorry for the inconvenience. Sydney snatched it and read it by candle flame.

"Nine o'clock!" she shouted. "Grandpa, we have two whole hours. Tell me the ice cream part again."

The paper plate sagged under David's slice of cake as he slid onto the porch bench beside his grandmother, who was holding up an empty mug like a trophy. "Two days ago I had the worst headache of my life," she announced to the whole reunion. "Worse than any in years. Then I drank that new ginger tea my neighbor brought over, and by evening it was gone. I'm telling you, that tea is a miracle." Aunt Rosa immediately asked for the brand name, and Uncle Marcus said he'd order a case. David took a bite of cake and wondered something he couldn't quite let go of: would the headache have eased anyway, even if she'd drunk nothing but tap water?

He couldn't test a headache, but he could test a chart. His grandmother kept a little calendar in her purse, and she let him look at it because she loved showing off her careful penmanship. On it she rated every headache from one to ten, and he copied three months of ratings onto graph paper that evening, using a pencil from his backpack. His cousin Marcus Jr., twelve like him, leaned over his shoulder. Marcus Jr. wanted to be a sports announcer and narrated everything, including this. "David versus the mystery of the tea," he intoned. "The crowd is on its feet."

David drew a dot for each headache, then ran his pencil along a diagonal line from the low ratings in the corner to the high ones. The pattern jumped out at him. The tens, the worst headaches, were almost always followed by fours or fives. The bad days fell back toward the ordinary ones, over and over, like coins dropped from a table always landing somewhere near the floor. He sat back. So the tea hadn't necessarily done anything. When Grandma felt her worst, the next day was bound to be more normal no matter what she drank. His quiet assumption that the tea must have caused the cure suddenly looked shaky.

But there was a twist he hadn't expected. "What did you take for the headaches before the tea?" he asked her. She squinted at the calendar. "Whatever your grandfather handed me. Aspirin, usually." David checked the dates. The aspirin days showed the same slide from bad to ordinary. So the pattern swallowed both remedies. "There's a name for this," he said slowly, remembering a phrase from a library book he'd skimmed. "Regression to the mean. It's called regression to the mean." Marcus Jr. cupped his hands around his mouth. "In a stunning upset, the tea loses to nothing at all!"

Grandma sniffed and lifted her mug again, and the steam rising from the fresh tea seemed to symbolize her stubbornness better than any words could. "You can keep your diagonal line," she said. "The tea stays." She took a long, deliberate sip, and winked at him over the rim.

Alexandra lay on her bedroom floor with a notebook, a pencil, and a grudge against her own science project. The assignment was to study something you couldn't see directly, and for three days she had been trying to observe her own stress, which was like trying to photograph wind. What she did have was data: every time she felt wound up, she wrote down the time. Wednesday, 4:15, felt like screaming. Wednesday, 9:40, stomach in knots. Thursday, 3:50, snapped at the dog. Thursday, 9:55, couldn't fall asleep until after eleven.

Her cousin Marcus, who was seventeen and living in their spare room while he "figured things out," leaned against her doorframe. "You're tracking your freak-outs? That's adorable."

"It's a science project," Alexandra said. "And they're not freak-outs, they're stress responses." The school nurse had shown her class a breathing trick last week, slow breath in for four counts, out for six, and Alexandra had been testing it like a hypothesis. It worked, mostly, but the knot kept coming back, and that was the part she couldn't explain. She was starting to suspect she was biased toward blaming her little brother for everything, since blaming him was easy and he rarely defended himself.

Marcus, meanwhile, was being weird. Alexandra noticed it because her notebook made her notice things now. On Friday he was fine at lunch, cracking jokes, helping Grandma dismantle the broken ceiling fan and put it back together so it actually worked better than before. Then around four he got twitchy. He jingled the coins in his pocket, paced the hallway, and snapped at the dog too. By seven he was calm again, back to jokes. Saturday, same thing. Calm at two, restless and snappish at four, calm again by seven thirty. She flipped back through her pages. Two days, two cycles, roughly two hours between calm and jumpy.

"Marcus," she said Saturday night, cornering him by the fridge, "do you vape?"

He got very interested in the inside of the refrigerator. "Why."

"Because you get restless every two hours, like clockwork. I charted it." She held up the notebook, where she'd drawn his pattern right under hers. "I read that the body clears about half the nicotine in roughly two hours. So a couple hours after you vape, half of it's gone, and you feel the urge for another dose. That's why you keep getting jumpy." She tapped the chart. "The pattern fits."

Marcus stared at the page for a long moment. "You're a menace," he said, but he didn't sound mad. "Coach thought I just had bad nerves. Grandma thinks it's my heritage, her side of the family, all high-strung. I thought I was broken."

"You're not broken, you're on a timer," Alexandra said. "Want to see the breathing thing? It won't fix the, you know, timer. But it might help the jumpy part. It works on my stomach knots about seventy percent of the time, which my teacher says is honestly pretty good science."

So they sat on the kitchen floor, because Alexandra insisted the floor made it more official, and breathed in for four and out for six while the dog watched them like they'd both lost their minds. On the third round Marcus laughed so hard he broke the count, and Alexandra made him start over, which made him laugh again. But after ten rounds he rolled his shoulders and said, "Huh. The jittery feeling's still there, but it's quieter. Like somebody turned it down two notches."

Sunday night, Alexandra added a line to her sleep routine, lights out at nine thirty, no screens, notebook by the bed. Monday after school, Marcus appeared in her doorway holding two mugs of peppermint tea and his phone, which he handed over with a grimace. "Delete the vape shop app," he said. "And chart me again next weekend, science girl. I want proof I'm getting boring."

Alexandra grinned and hit delete. "Boring is the whole goal," she said, and opened her notebook to a fresh page.

Kayla had the best seat in the living room, the corner of the couch where she could see the TV and the door to the kitchen at the same time, and she was wrapped in the striped blanket she used to insulate herself against the draft that seeped under the window every winter. Her uncle had claimed that spot for years, but tonight he was stuck in the folding chair, because Kayla had gotten to the couch first and he had let her keep it. She still remembered that. Last spring, when her team had lost the semifinal, he had given up the seat to a neighbor kid and the team had lost anyway, and ever since he had a theory that seat assignments mattered.

The Wolverines were up by four with six minutes left. Down the block in their affluent neighborhood, half the houses probably had the same game on, and every so often a muffled cheer rolled through the walls like the houses themselves were shouting.

"That's it, they've got it," her cousin Marcus said, bouncing a throw pillow off his knee. "They're unstoppable."

Kayla wasn't so sure. The Wolverines had been shaky all season, and something kept nagging at her. She grabbed her tablet and pulled up the standings, scrolling through game after game. Home games were marked with a little house symbol, and away games with a plane. She started counting.

"What are you doing?" Marcus leaned over, chewing a pretzel.

"Counting. Look." She turned the screen toward him. "At home they've won way more than they've lost. On the road it's the opposite." She had tallied it across a whole page, and the pattern held even though road games and home games were the same sport, the same players, the same rules. Something invisible was tilting things.

"So?"

"So that's why they win here. It's a real thing, it's called home advantage," she said. "In most major sports, home teams win more than half their games."

Marcus shook his head. "That's not why. They won because Coach Bell switched to the press in the third quarter."

"Then explain the pattern." Kayla tapped the tally marks. "If it's just the press, why does it only work at home?"

Marcus opened his mouth, then closed it, then pointed at the screen, where the other team had just cut the lead to two. "Because... watch the game, that's why."

Uncle Ray laughed from the folding chair. "My official diagnosis is that neither of you can enjoy anything." But he was grinning, and he craned his neck to look at Kayla's tally marks, and he didn't argue with them either.

Kayla thought about last spring again, the semifinal loss, how she had blamed the referee for weeks. Maybe the truth was smaller and stranger than that. Maybe there were forces you couldn't see on the court, tilting games one direction, and you could only catch them by counting.

The Wolverines missed a free throw. Marcus groaned and buried his face in the pillow. With two minutes left, Kayla pulled the blanket tighter, set the tablet on her lap, tally side up, and said, "Count with me. If they pull this out, it fits."

Antoine sat at the kitchen computer with a bag of chips and a grudge. His cousin Marcus had commented on the town history page: "Everyone says Riverside was founded in 1871, but my grandpa swears it was 1879. That's just his opinion against yours." Antoine typed back, "No, it's a claim. Somebody's right and somebody's wrong." Then he stared at the screen, because he had no idea how to prove it.

He started with the obvious and set the search to exclude anything written after 1950, which wiped out a hundred tourist sites that all copied each other. What was left was a link to the county library's old newspaper archive, scanned page by page. Mom wandered past with her prescription bag from the pharmacy and said dinner was in an hour. "One thing first," Antoine said, and clicked.

The archive was slow and fussy, and half the pages were just smudges. He tried "1871" and got nothing but grain prices. He tried "founding" and got a flood. There it was, a front page from June 1871 with a photograph of men in dark coats standing around a rough wooden sign that said RIVERSIDE. Beside it ran a letter from the land agent, who wrote that the first lots would be sold in July, and a column of official figures from the county recorder listing the lots and their buyers.

Antoine's heart was going fast. On a video call, Marcus squinted at the scanned page Antoine held up to his webcam. "What am I looking at?"

"A primary source," Antoine said. "A firsthand record from the time itself. The letter, the photograph, the official data. It's the best place to check a claim." He scrolled so Marcus could read the land agent's words himself. "Somebody in 1871 wrote this while it was happening. They couldn't have known we'd be arguing about it."

Marcus was quiet for a second. "Okay. So Grandpa's 1879 thing is wrong." He rubbed his chin. "Unless that's when the town got its charter or something." Antoine pulled up a later page and found it: the incorporation paperwork filed eight years after the founding, in 1879. "You were both a little right," Antoine said. "Your grandpa was remembering the charter year, not the founding." Marcus laughed, and Antoine laughed too, the grudge gone.

They stayed on the call planning a project for the heritage fair, a printed copy of that 1871 front page with a note pinned beside it about the 1879 charter. Antoine bookmarked the archive, then printed the page on the good paper, not the flimsy stuff, because his dad had warned him the cheap sheets were flammable near the space heater. He carried the warm page to his room and taped it above his desk, the men in dark coats still staring out of 1871, waiting for everyone else to catch up.

"Delete it," Marcus said, hovering over Nicholas's shoulder. "Delete the whole group chat before Mr. Herrera sees it."

On the screen, the new class chat was already on fire. Someone had posted forty-seven crying-laughing emojis about Mr. Herrera's mustard-stained tie, someone else had replied in ALL CAPS, and Danny had nominated himself "Supreme Chat Overlord" in a message that scrolled for three paragraphs. Nicholas scrolled slowly, like a person watching a nature documentary. "Did you notice how everyone writes differently in here than they do out loud? Danny whisper-talks in class. In the chat he's basically shouting."

Marcus groaned and dropped onto the beanbag. "That's not the problem. The problem is Mr. Herrera made the chat for the volcano project, and now it's a volcano."

Nicholas kept scrolling, and a question started forming, the kind that itched. Had anyone ever written actual rules for this? Not school rules, but manners, the online kind? He typed it into the search bar while Marcus built a sandwich of suspense, saying nothing, just raising one eyebrow and waiting.

The results loaded. Nicholas blinked. "Okay, this is real. Somebody did write it down. It's called the 'Netiquette Guidelines,' and it was published in 1995 as a document called RFC 1855."

"RFC?" Marcus peered at the phone, a chip halfway to his mouth. "That sounds like a robot's gym locker."

"Probably some official document thing," Nicholas said, scrolling. The old text talked about not shouting in capitals, thinking before you post, remembering a real human reads your words. It was written before group chats even existed, back when phones had cords, and yet it described Danny exactly. Nicholas laughed out loud. "This guy predicted Danny in 1995. That's twenty years before Danny."

"So what do we do, print it and tape it to his locker?"

Nicholas was already typing, borrowing the old rules and rewriting them in Danny's own language. He posted: "Chat Constitution, Article 1: no caps unless spontaneous genuine screaming. Article 2: three emojis maximum. Article 3: volcanoes only."

The chat went quiet. Then Danny appeared in the doorway of Marcus's kitchen, still holding his phone, wearing the expression of a Supreme Chat Overlord who had just discovered he could be overthrown. "Article 2 is tyranny," he said. "I demand a rewrite."

"Nominate yourself to the rules committee," Nicholas said, and held up the phone so Danny could see the yellowed 1995 document on the screen. Danny leaned in, squinted, and read the title twice.

"Wait," he said. "They had internet manners before I was born and nobody told me?"

On the first morning of Grandma's visit, Lea sat on the end of the guest bed while Grandma unpacked her suitcase, and they talked about everything: the flight, the neighbors' new dog, Lea's science project. Grandma answered every question right away, laughing at all the right moments. Lea decided the week was going to be perfect.

The trouble started on Wednesday at the train station. Lea and Grandma were meeting Aunt Rosa, and the station roared with announcements, rolling suitcases, and a man playing saxophone near the ticket machines. Lea said, "Aunt Rosa's train comes at noon, right?" Grandma frowned and said, "Tulips? In June?" Lea tried again, slower, and Grandma guessed "new shoes." After the third try, Grandma just smiled and nodded at whatever Lea said, and Lea felt her stomach drop. At home that same question would have gotten an instant answer.

Lea started testing. In the quiet of the kitchen, she asked Grandma ordinary questions and Grandma caught every word, even when Lea mumbled. In the noisy cafeteria at school, when Grandma came for Grandparents' Day, the same questions fell apart, and Grandma kept leaning in and guessing wrong. Lea wrote her results in her notebook like a scientist. Quiet meant yes. Noise meant no. It wasn't that Grandma couldn't hear, because she heard fine when the room was silent. It was the noise that stole the words away. Her science teacher had once said the class shouldn't be biased toward one experiment, so Lea tried a different place, the loud coffee shop, and got the same result. The pattern held.

That night Lea left a note on the guest bed before Grandma went to sleep. "Dear Grandma," she wrote, "I noticed you can hear me great in the kitchen but the train station was a disaster. I don't think your ears are the problem. I think the background noise is. Want to help me test it tomorrow? We can sit in the park away from the crowd. Love, Lea." In the morning Grandma waved the note at her over breakfast. "So that's why I've been nodding like a fool in restaurants," she said. "My sister figured this out years ago and I never believed her."

They became a team after that. When the family went to the Saturday farmers market, Lea steered Grandma to the quiet end by the flower stall before asking whether they should buy peaches or plums. When Aunt Rosa wanted Grandma to participate in the trivia night at the community center, Lea asked the organizer if their table could be moved away from the speakers, and their team came in second. Grandma's pivot from "I'll just stay home where it's quiet" to "find me a corner seat and I'm in" happened somewhere around Thursday, and Lea knew exactly why.

On the last night of the visit, they sat together on the guest bed with the door shut and the house still. "You solved it," Grandma said. "Nobody ever told me it was the noise. They just kept saying I was going deaf." Lea grinned and flipped to the back of her notebook, where she had drawn a chart with two columns, Quiet and Noisy, full of checkmarks and X's. "Science," she said, and held it up for Grandma to see.

Max stood in front of a painting of a narrow street at the city gallery, his sketchbook clamped under one arm, scowling. His homework was to draw a street using one-point perspective, where every line ran toward a single vanishing point, and his version at home looked like a street designed by a dizzy giant. He had a letter from his art teacher folded in his pocket, and he pulled it out and read it again. "Max," it said, "go find the museum's oldest street painting. Find the point where the buildings' edges would meet if you extended them with a ruler. Then look at the round things. The lamp, the fruit cart, the boy's ball. If a sphere is shaded, the highlight is the brightest spot, and it sits on the side facing the light. Its position shows you where the light is coming from. Copy that, and your street will stop looking flat."

The painting, he discovered, was in a room with a skylight, and it did have a fruit cart with an orange on it. Max found the vanishing point first, tracing the building edges with his pencil in the air until they all aimed at a spot on the far door of the street, like the whole town was sliding toward it. Then he looked at the orange. It had one bright dab of paint on its upper left side, brighter than anything else on it. He held up his pencil as a pretend lamp, imagining the light arriving from exactly there, and checked a marble on the cobblestones nearby. Brightest spot, upper left. The cart wheel's rim caught its shine on the upper left too. It was a rule hiding under the paint, invisible until you hunted for it, and now Max saw little spotlight dots everywhere, like the street was secretly lit by a guild of tiny invisible lamplighters, all standing in the same corner of the sky.

"Excuse me," said a girl beside him, maybe ten, holding her own sketchbook open to a gray circle that looked like a flat gray cookie. "Mine's supposed to be a sphere but it looks like a blob. The docent said I should shade it, but I don't know where."

"Which side is the lamp on?" Max asked. He had decided to pretend he was a gallery wizard, since the skylight made everything glow anyway. "A sphere's highlight is the brightest spot, and it's on the side facing the light. So pick where your lamp is, and put your brightest spot there."

The girl bit her lip, jabbed a finger at the upper right of her circle, and drew one small brilliant dot. The blob popped into a ball so suddenly that she laughed out loud, and a guard three rooms away said "Shh" with impressive authority for someone so far away.

Max sat down on the gallery bench and started a fresh street. This time he drew the vanishing point first, aimed every roofline at it like roads to a castle, and gave each round thing, a lamp, a barrel, a bicycle bell, its brightest spot on the upper left, so that his whole imaginary street was lit by the same invisible sun. He was halfway through when the girl leaned over and said, "Your street looks nutritious enough to eat," and Max, who had been thinking of it as a place, had to admit that a street you could eat was even better, so he added a bakery with round golden loaves in the window, each with one bright spot, upper left, shining.

Autumn pushed through the festival crowd with her cousin Jaylen and their new neighbor, Priya, who had moved to town just last week. The street was lined with booths of latkes, jelly donuts, and crafts, and at the far end, on a long table, someone had set up a huge silver menorah. Priya stopped and stared at it.

"Wait," Priya said, counting the branches with her finger. "Eight nights of Hanukkah, but that thing has nine candles. Somebody messed up?"

Autumn looked at the menorah, then at Priya, then back at the menorah. She had lit one at her grandmother's house every year, but she had never really counted. One, two, three. Priya was right. Nine. Her first thought was that the festival committee had made a mistake, but her grandmother had a menorah at home too, and Autumn was suddenly sure it also had nine. She grabbed Jaylen's sleeve. "Come with me. I need to check something."

They wove back through the crowd to her grandmother's booth, where Bubbe was selling knitted scarves to raise money to donate to the food pantry. "Bubbe," Autumn asked, "your menorah at home has nine candles too, right? Not eight?"

Bubbe laughed. "Look at the ones on the shelf, sweetheart." The small menorahs for sale each held nine candles, and in every one of them, one candle sat higher or off to the side, apart from the row of eight. Autumn picked one up and turned it over in her hands. The odd candle out was set apart on purpose. Someone nearby was explaining to a visitor, and the visitor nodded and repeated the word to her friend: "The ninth one is called the shamash." Autumn held the little menorah up so Priya could see the taller branch.

"So the ninth one isn't a mistake," Priya said slowly. "It's for lighting the others." Autumn grinned. "Eight for the eight nights, plus one helper." She set the menorah down and pointed across the street, where a man was getting ready to light the giant silver one at dusk. "Come on, let's watch. You'll see which candle does the work."

They found a spot near the front just as the man lifted the shamash from its high branch, touched it to the first candle, and returned it to its place above the others. The flame held steady against the darkening sky, and the crowd around them cheered. Priya counted the unlit candles left on the row. "Seven to go," she said. "I'll be here every night." Autumn bumped her shoulder against Priya's. "Save us a spot," she said.

Stella had read the note on the fridge three times before Mrs. Hale left: Charlie, age two, dinner at six, bath at six thirty, no snacks after five. Now the clock said six twenty-eight, and Charlie was standing in the tub patting the shallow water like it was a drum. Two inches of water, Stella figured, maybe three. She knelt beside the tub with the yellow rubber duck and tried to sound like someone who had done this a hundred times.

The phone rang in the kitchen. Stella's stomach tightened, because Mrs. Hale had written "call if anything comes up," and the ring seemed to fill the whole house. Charlie laughed and poured a cup of water over his own head, splashing droplets onto her sleeve.

"Stay right there, buddy," she started to say, and then she stopped. She remembered the safety workshop from last summer, the lifeguard with the whistle, and one sentence that had stuck to her like a burr: a young child can drown in just a few inches of water, and without splashing or crying out, so children should never be left alone in or near a bath. It had sounded impossible then. Two inches of water, and no noise at all? But the lifeguard had been completely impartial about it, no drama, just the facts, and that was somehow worse.

So Stella pulled the big frog towel off the hook, lifted Charlie out of the tub, dripping and squealing, and wrapped him up like a burrito. She carried him down the hall with water soaking through her shirt, the phone still ringing. "Coming, coming," she muttered, shifting Charlie to her hip to grab the receiver.

It was Mrs. Hale, calling to say she'd be home by seven fifteen instead of seven, and traffic was terrible, and was everything all right? Stella said Charlie was clean, fed, and wearing a towel, and she heard Mrs. Hale laugh for the first time all evening. When she hung up, Charlie patted her cheek with a wet hand.

Back in the bathroom, Stella dried him and dressed him in dinosaur pajamas while he tried to steal the rubber duck's hat, which did not exist, which was the whole joke as far as Charlie was concerned. She let him win the argument. Her science teacher would have called her a decomposer of fun, she thought, breaking down perfectly good games into rules, but tonight the rules had felt like the right kind.

At seven fifteen the door opened, and Mrs. Hale stood there with rain on her coat. Charlie barreled into her legs shouting "baff, baff," and Stella stood behind him holding the wet frog towel. "He had a great bath," she said. "He was with me the whole time." Mrs. Hale looked at her for a second, then smiled and said the words every first-time babysitter wants to hear: "Same time Thursday?"

The group chat had forty-seven messages by the time Simon sat down with his toast. It was the chat for the science fair, the one Mr. Okafor had set up, and someone had posted a photo of Maya's volcano display. Under it, from Priya's account, was a single line: "this looks like it was made by a third grader."

Simon read it twice. Priya was the girl who said "excuse me" to doors. She had lent him a pencil on Tuesday and thanked him for returning it as if he had done her a favor. He scrolled up and found three more sharp comments from her that week, each one public, each one aimed at somebody's project. In the hallway that same week she had complimented Maya's poster to her face. Simon had heard it himself.

He typed "why are you being so mean?" and then deleted it, because forty people would read it, and a public fight would just transport the whole mess somewhere worse. Instead he started a private chat. His assumption was that Priya would deny it, so he tested it with something small first. "Hey, was that you on the volcano comment?"

"obviously," she wrote back. "it's true. she glued the lava on crooked."

"Do you tell her that in person?"

There was a long pause, long enough for Simon to eat half his toast. Then: "no. that would be rude."

"Ruder than typing it?"

"typing doesn't count," Priya wrote, and Simon could almost see her shrug. He stared at the screen. It did count, though. The words were the same words; only the room was different.

He searched "why are people meaner online" and the first result was about something a psychologist named John Suler had described in 2004, called the online disinhibition effect: people often say things online that they would hold back from saying face to face. Simon read it twice. That was it, exactly, Priya in one sentence. He pasted the link into the private chat.

A minute passed. Then Priya sent a single defiant "so???" followed by, "ok fine maybe the volcano comment was too much." In the main group chat, a new message appeared from her account: "hey Maya, the lava on your volcano is actually straighter than I said. sorry. also I found out my brain is broken in a normal way, ask Simon for the link."

Maya replied with a photo of her volcano wearing a tiny paper crown, and the caption "the third grader accepts your apology."

Ivy pressed her nose against the fencing of the demo garden at Martelli's Garden Center, where her mother shopped every Saturday for bags of soil and trays of tomato seedlings. Behind the fence grew a squash plant the size of a small tent, its leaves broad as dinner plates and its yellow flowers glowing like tiny lanterns in the morning light. Ivy had counted twenty-one blossoms on it last week, and today she counted again.

"Twenty-six," she reported to Priya, who worked the register and let Ivy hang around as long as she didn't trample anything. "Twenty-six flowers. That's a record."

"Beautiful, right?" Priya said. "That plant's been blooming for a month."

Then Ivy saw something that ruined her whole morning. Beneath the biggest blossom, tucked against the stem, hung a single squash the size of her thumb. One. She searched the entire plant, parting leaves, checking every branch. One squash, twenty-six flowers. "Priya, why is there only one? Something's wrong with it."

Priya came over, wiped her hands on her apron, and peered at the plant with her. "Mr. Martelli says that happens sometimes. He shrugs and says the plant's moody." She lowered her voice. "I think he just doesn't know."

That wasn't good enough for Ivy. She took out the little notebook she carried for garden observations, because she had a concept she was testing: if a plant makes flowers, flowers should make fruit, and if they don't, something hidden must be blocking the way. On Sunday she went back with her mother and stood at the fence for an hour, staring. Slowly she noticed that the blossoms weren't all the same. Most of them sat flat on the stem, thin at the bottom, and when they closed and faded, they dropped off and left nothing behind. A few were different. Underneath them, at the base, swelled a tiny green bump, a miniature squash no bigger than a pencil eraser.

She checked every one. The plain flowers: no bump, no squash ever. The bumped ones: a squash started. And there were only two bumped ones on the whole enormous plant, and one of those had shriveled and turned brown, its little squash shriveling with it. She wrote it all down. The bump flowers were the only ones that could become squash, and even they weren't guaranteed.

She asked Priya to borrow the store's gardening book, and they sat on stacked bags of mulch turning pages until Ivy found a chapter with diagrams. There it was. "They're female," she said, jabbing the page. "The ones with the little fruit at the base. The plain ones are male. Both kinds of flowers grow on the same plant, but only the females can turn into squash." She read on, lips moving. "And the female has to be pollinated, pollen has to reach it, or the little fruit just dies."

"Which explains why Mr. Martelli's plant is moody," Priya said. "Twenty-four males and two females. Terrible odds."

Ivy refused to comply with those odds. The next morning, before the flowers closed in the heat, she came back with a soft paintbrush from her art kit. She found a freshly opened male flower, brushed its center gently, and carried the dust of pollen on the bristles to the one remaining female, with its swelling base, and touched the brush to her stigma, careful as putting on a Band-Aid. She tied a strip of blue yarn below the blossom so she could find it again.

A week later she knelt at the fence, following the blue yarn with her eyes. The flower had faded and fallen, but the little fruit beneath it had grown fat and firm, as long as her hand now, striped green and pale. "Priya!" she called across the lot. "Come see!"

Priya jogged over, looked, and let out a whoop. Then she pointed at the fence gate. "Go tell Martelli. He's been blaming the weather for years."

Layla set the pot of sugar and water on the burner and turned the dial to medium. Her grandmother's caramel recipe had one line of instruction, "Cook until amber," which Layla felt implied a confidence she did not share. Behind her, her cousin Marcus leaned against the counter of the school cooking classroom, watching the pot like it might attack him.

"Is this the same browning as the crust on the roast at Sunday dinner?" he asked. "Because that smells way better than this."

Layla thought about it while stirring. The roast crust had come from meat, and meat was full of protein. The pot in front of her held nothing but sugar and water. If the browning were one single thing, then sugar alone should not be able to do it, since the roast clearly needed something the sugar did not have. She turned the burner up a notch, and the thermostat clicked somewhere inside the stove.

"It can't be the same," she said. "This is just sugar and water. There's nothing else in here."

"So?"

"So the roast has protein in it, and this doesn't. Two different things can't need the exact same stuff to brown." She kept watching, and the pale liquid began to turn gold at the edges, then deeper, without a single speck of anything else in the pot. Sugar alone, browning anyway.

Marcus squinted at it. "Then what do you call this one?"

"Caramelization," Layla said. "The roast one is the Maillard reaction, and that one also needs amino acids." She had read the two terms on a card in her science folder last week, and now, watching sugar turn amber all by itself, the card finally made sense.

The smell hit them both at once, buttery and dark, and Marcus made a sound like a deflating balloon. "That smells amazing. In vain did I resist it," he announced, reaching for a spoon.

"That's not how you use that word."

"Fine. I resisted it, and I failed." He dipped the spoon in anyway, and the caramel stretched off it in a long thread that landed on his sleeve. He shrieked and danced backward into the cart of mixing bowls, which rattled like a passing train.

Layla grabbed the pot off the heat, poured the caramel into a bowl, and handed Marcus the spoon. "You earned that one," she said. "Now hold still while I take the picture for Grandma."

Charlotte wanted the green record card, the one Mr. Dover awarded for a perfect graph, and she had been close twice. Today her plan was simple: roll the steel ball down the long ramp, time it with the electronic timer box, mark distance and time, and draw the graph. Speed was just distance divided by time, and a straight line on the graph would prove the ball kept the same pace. She could already picture the card taped above her desk.

Her friend Dev spread the paper tape along the ramp and pinned it at each end. "One meter, two meters, three," he said, tapping each mark. "You release, I read the timer." The timer box had a thin metal wire stretched across the ramp at each mark, and when the ball bent a wire, the box printed the elapsed seconds on its little screen. Dev blew on his cold fingers and joked that the lab was cold enough to submerge them all in hot chocolate.

Their first run was beautiful. Charlotte smoothed the tape, wrote the numbers, and rolled again. By the fourth run she frowned. The times were creeping. At the one-meter wire the ball that had taken 0.80 seconds was now showing 0.86, then 0.91, though she released it from exactly the same spot, the same angle, the same careful push. "The ball isn't slowing down," she said. "Watch it. It looks identical." Dev agreed, and they rolled a marker pen down the ramp as a test and saw it behave the same every time.

She opened the back of the timer box, because Mr. Dover let careful students look inside, and found the wires ran to a coiled component inside the case. Each wire felt warm, and the coil felt warmer still, almost like a mug of tea gone lukewarm. Charlotte thought about the cooling-beaker demo from last term, where a hot thing changes while it settles. She had an idea, and she decided to test it the way you test anything, by changing one thing only. She took a damp sponge from the sink, the porous kind that drank up water when you pressed it, laid the coil gently against it, and waited for the wires to cool. Then she rolled the ball once more.

0.79 seconds. Exactly where they started.

"Try it again," Dev said, bouncing on his toes. She ran the ball three more times, quick ones, before the box could warm up, and the numbers held steady. Then she left the timer running idle for five minutes, felt the wire warm against her wrist, and watched the times drift upward again. When she pressed the sponge to the coil one more time, the readings came back down.

"It's the wire," she said. "The resistance rises as it heats up, so it only stays steady while the temperature stays the same." Dev repeated the sentence slowly, as if tasting it, then wrote it in the margin of their results table. They took all their measurements in fast bursts with sponge breaks between them, and Charlotte laughed so hard at Dev ceremonially announcing "cooling the component, my lady" that she nearly dropped the pen.

Her graph came out a clean straight line, every dot sitting on it like beads on a string. Mr. Dover pinned it to the board and said the class would copy the method. Then he held out the green card. "One question first. Why the sponge?" Charlotte grinned, picked up the timer box, and held the back of it against his hand.

Alexia sat on a flat rock at the edge of the campsite, turning the safety card from the airplane over in her hands. Around her the pines stood in rows, and somewhere behind the tents a woodpecker knocked at a dead trunk. The card, which she had tucked into her backpack without thinking, portrayed a little cartoon passenger chewing something, and that picture had been bothering her since the flight two days ago.

She let herself go back to it. The plane had been dropping through clouds toward the airport, and her little brother Theo had started crying, pressing his hands over his ears and saying they hurt, they hurt. Their mom had dug through the seat pocket, found a juice box, and handed it to him. He had swallowed three times, and then, like a switch flipping, he had stopped. Alexia had felt her own ears plug up during that same descent, a tight stuffed feeling, and she had yawned because she was tired. After the yawn, her ears had cleared with a soft pop. At the time she thought it was luck. Now, on the rock, she lined the moments up side by side: swallowing, yawning, relief.

"So the chewing on the card isn't about being hungry," she said to Theo, who was poking a beetle with a stick. Theo was six and generally eccentric in his habits, wearing his sweatshirt backward and refusing sandwiches cut into triangles, but he looked up anyway.

"We're driving down the pass tomorrow," Alexia said. "It goes down a long way, and last time my ears did the same thing they did on the plane. I think swallowing or yawning is the factor that fixes it. It opens what the card called the Eustachian tubes, and air gets into your middle ear and the pressure lets go." Theo squinted at her. "You can test it with me," she said. "If I'm wrong, we'll both be grumpy, and if I'm right, we won't."

The next morning the car wound down the pass, and the pressure built just as she remembered, like someone pushing on her eardrums with both thumbs. "Now," she said, and she swallowed, hard, twice. Pop. The full feeling drained away, and the hiss of the tires came back sharp and clear. Theo made an enormous theatrical yawn, jaw stretched wide, and then blinked. "My ears went boom," he reported, "but the good boom."

From the front seat their dad glanced in the mirror and smiled but said nothing, which Alexia appreciated. She watched the valley open below them, the river showing silver where the sun caught it, and she thought about the card in her backpack, the little cartoon passenger chewing away. At the bottom of the pass Theo held up his water bottle, took a long swallow, and announced to the whole car, "My ears feel like butterflies now."

Grandpa Ray arrived on Sunday with one suitcase, one crossword book, and a plastic box with seven little lids, each printed with a day of the week. Cameron's mom put the box on the kitchen counter and said, "Grandpa, your pills are in there, sorted by day. That's the whole system." Grandpa Ray tapped the lids twice, like he was checking that they were real.

The trouble started Monday morning. Cameron was eating toast in the backyard, watching Grandpa Ray water the tomato plants in the arid corner of the garden where nothing ever grew, when Grandpa suddenly stopped. "Did I take my pills this morning?" he asked the tomatoes. Then he asked Cameron. Cameron hadn't seen him take anything, and Grandpa couldn't remember walking back inside, which was annoying, because if he skipped the pills he felt dizzy later, and if he took them twice, Cameron's mom had said, they had to call the doctor.

Grandpa started toward the house to take them just in case. Cameron jumped up from the picnic table. "Wait. Don't take any yet." He was thinking about the box, the way a detective thinks about footprints. If Grandpa had already taken his morning pills, then one lid would be open and one compartment would be empty. If he hadn't, the compartment would still be full. You couldn't see the past, but the box could show it anyway. Cameron ran inside, slid down on his knees at the counter, and flipped open the lid marked Monday. Empty. "You took them, Grandpa. Monday's compartment is empty."

Grandpa Ray squinted at the box, then at Cameron, then grinned. "You solved it before I even broke anything. Remind me to put you in my will." Cameron felt a little swell of pride, which lasted until Tuesday morning, when the same thing happened again, and again on Wednesday. By Thursday, Cameron's pride had started to radiate less warmth and more resentment. He was spending his whole week being a pill butler while his friends were at the pool.

Then came the twist. On Saturday, Cameron opened the Saturday compartment and found it empty, but Saturday's pills were supposed to be filled next. His stomach dropped. Grandpa hadn't taken Saturday's dose. Cameron checked the other compartments and found them all empty too, and then he remembered: Wednesday afternoon, Grandpa had stood at the counter, shaking the box, saying he was "reorganizing for efficiency." He had dumped the pills into his hand, sorted them by color, and put them back wherever he liked.

"Grandpa," Cameron said, holding up the box, "the compartments don't mean anything anymore. You alphabetized your pills."

"I sorted them by color, actually," said Grandpa Ray, watering the tomatoes again. "Reds on the left. Very tidy."

Cameron called his mom at work, and she came home with a new box and a lock for the lid. Grandpa Ray held up the locked box, turned it over, and said, "Well. I suppose I've been outsmarted by a fourth-grader's invention and an eleven-year-old. My week is complete."

Joseph pressed his thumb into the rim of his clay bowl one more time, trying to decide whether to modify the wavy edge or leave it alone. The bowl was his best work all summer, and tomorrow was the firing day at the community art studio.

"That one's coming with us," said Marisol, the student helper, stacking pieces on the cart by the kiln. She lifted a small bowl made by a kid named Theo, then set it back down on the shelf instead. "Sorry, Theo. Yours stays out this round."

Theo's shoulders dropped. "Why? Mine's just as good as his."

"I can't put yours in," Marisol said, and moved on to the next cart.

Joseph watched Theo stare at his bowl, chin wobbling. He knew that look. Last year Joseph had cried in this same room when his coil pot came out of the kiln cracked down the middle, and nobody could tell him why.

He walked over and picked up Theo's bowl. His own bowl, waiting on the cart, had felt light and chalky all the way through when he'd tapped it that morning. Theo's bowl was light at the rim, too. But when Joseph turned it over and pressed his palm flat against the thick bottom, the clay felt cool, almost like a cellar floor. His own bowl's bottom had felt like dry sidewalk.

He carried both bowls to the window and held them side by side in the bright light, using the glare almost like a lens to hunt for differences. Theo's bowl had a dull, darker patch across the base, a shadow of color where his own bowl was evenly pale. Something was still hiding in that clay, something he couldn't see directly but could find by touch and by looking.

"Hey, Theo," Joseph said. "Your bowl isn't the problem. The bottom's still damp. Mine was like that last year, and it cracked in the kiln. Water left in clay turns to steam, and steam can crack or even burst the whole piece."

Theo peered at the dark patch. "So it's not ruined?"

"It just has to dry all the way through first. Leave it on the sunny shelf by the window till next week." Joseph set it there himself, turning the damp side toward the sun. Then he went back for a scrap of paper and wrote FIRING NEXT WEEK, THEO'S BOWL, and propped it against the rim, where nobody could miss it.

"It'll be in the next kiln load," he said. "Promise."

Theo smiled and steadied the sign with one careful finger.

Jordan set up his table between the honey seller and the apple farmer, his mother's folding griddle stacked with mixing bowls, bags of flour, and a jar of yeast he'd carried carefully from home. His plan was simple: bake flatbreads and one real loaf for his family's booth at the market, because tonight was his turn to cook and he wanted it to be bread, real risen bread, the kind his grandmother made. He had promised his little sister a slice still warm enough to melt butter.

He measured the flour, stirred in a spoonful of sugar, and mixed the yeast with water from the market's hot kettle, thinking warm water would wake the yeast up faster. The dough came together smooth and springy, and he draped a cloth over the bowl the way his grandmother did. But half an hour later, when he peeked, the dough sat flat and heavy as a hull of concrete. He waited another half hour. Nothing.

"Your dough's not doing anything," said Marisol from the next booth, leaning over with a crate of plums. "Mine always puffs up when my mom makes it."

"Yeast makes bread rise," Jordan said slowly, mostly to himself. "It feeds on the sugars in the dough, and the gas it gives off, carbon dioxide, gets trapped in little bubbles. That's what pushes it up." He looked at the bowl, then at the kettle still steaming behind the counter. Something was wrong with the yeast itself, something he couldn't see. He tested the only idea he had. He ran fresh water, let it cool until it felt only faintly warm on his wrist, like testing a bottle for a baby, and started a new batch with a fresh spoonful of yeast.

While the second bowl rested under its cloth, he watched the kettle. The first water had been hot enough to sting his fingers when he rinsed them. He cupped a little of the new water in his palm and held it for a full minute. No sting.

"Jordan, look," Marisol whispered, poking his arm. He lifted the cloth. The dough had climbed over the rim of the bowl, rounded and swollen, and when he pressed one finger into it, the dent filled slowly back in. His grin must have been contagious, because Marisol laughed and the honey seller gave him a thumbs-up. He punched the dough down, shaped it into a loaf, and slid it onto the griddle. His sister ran up just as the smell reached the end of the aisle. "Is it ready?" she asked. He wrapped the first slice in a napkin and handed it over, steam curling into the morning air.

The community kitchen on Maple Street smelled like onions and cinnamon on Saturdays, and Dominic liked it better than any place he knew. His mother worked the lunch shift there, and today he had claimed a burner so he could fry chicken for his little sister, Ana, who had asked for it three nights in a row. He set the pan on the stove, poured in oil, and waited, watching the oil shiver and go loose as it heated.

He was cutting lemons when he heard a soft whump behind him. Flames stood up out of the pan, orange and calm, the way a candle is calm, which somehow made them worse. His hand shot toward the faucet, because water was what you threw on fire, everyone knew that. Then he stopped. Last month he had stood beside Mr. Ruiz, the kitchen's head cook, when a pan of oil flared just like this one, and Mr. Ruiz had not touched the sink. He had turned off the burner and slid a lid over the flames, flat and quick, like sliding a card across a table. The fire had gone out under it. A volunteer had grabbed a pitcher of water and Mr. Ruiz had said, "Never pour water on a grease fire," and moved the pitcher away, and that was all he had said.

Dominic reached over and shut off the burner. The flames kept dancing, so that was not enough by itself. He picked up the lid, held it sideways like Mr. Ruiz had, and slid it over the pan. The fire smothered underneath, and the kitchen went quiet except for Ana, who had wandered over and stood frozen with her lemonade.

"You put a lid on it," she said. Not a question, just amazement.

"It works because the fire can't get out," Dominic said. "Water would've made it jump everywhere." He lifted the lid a crack, saw only dark oil, and set it down again until the pan cooled. His mother hurried over from the lunch line, wiping her hands on her apron, and Ana told her the whole thing twice, the flames bigger each time.

Word traveled around the room the way good news does, and soon the volunteers began telling each other to keep a lid by every fry station. Mrs. Okafor, who ran the kitchen, gave his shoulder a squeeze. "You were quick," she said. "That kind of compassion for everybody standing near that stove is contagious, you know."

Dominic dumped the burnt oil, wiped the pan, and started over with fresh oil and the lid sitting right beside the burner, where he could reach it in one second. Ana pulled a stool up next to him.

"Teach me the lid trick," she said.

The meatloaf was half gone when Marcus climbed onto his chair and pointed at the phone propped against the salt shaker. "Dad, it says this quarterback has a perfect rating. But it's one hundred fifty-eight point three. Why isn't perfect one hundred?"

"Finish your green beans first," Dad said, but his eyes stayed on the phone, where the game was muted and a fantasy league deadline glowed in the corner: lineup locked at 8 p.m. It was 7:41.

Gabriella reached over and slid the phone toward herself. Last summer, at the lake, Uncle Ray had leaned back in a folding chair and read numbers off the radio like they were a weather report: completion percentage, yards, touchdowns, interceptions. She had thought it was strange even then, that one number could stand in for all of those. "I think I know," she said. "Remember Uncle Ray? He said one number smushed everything together." She scrolled, and there it was on the stats page, rows of passing numbers stacked under a single figure at the top. "See, they take a bunch of passing stats and combine them into one number. That's why it's weird. It's not out of a hundred because it isn't counting one thing."

Marcus squinted at the screen. "One hundred fifty-eight point three out of what?"

"Out of zero up to the maximum," Gabriella said. "Zero is the worst, one hundred fifty-eight point three is the best there is. It's called a passer rating."

Dad set down his fork. "So a perfect game isn't a hundred, it's one fifty-eight three."

"Right. Zero to one fifty-eight point three." She tapped the little bar graph beside it. Each passing stat was a separate component, and the app showed them stacked like layers before they got squashed into that single score at the top.

Marcus picked up a green bean and studied it like it was the last puzzle piece. "So one number is like, lots of games all pressed into one?"

"Lots of throws, lots of games, everything," Gabriella said. She remembered her class project in the fall, when she had averaged her five math quizzes and the average made one bad test look not so bad and one great one look smaller than it felt. Numbers did that. They took a whole messy season and pressed it flat, like flowers in a book.

Dad glanced at the clock. 7:52. His fantasy decision was due in eight minutes, and his old quarterback had a rating of 71.2 while the new one sat at 104.8. "Help me," he said. "Is higher better?"

"Higher is better," Gabriella said, "as long as it's the same kind of number." She pulled the phone closer and started comparing the rows underneath, the completions and yards that the ratings had compressed. Marcus leaned against her arm, breathing meatloaf breath, and slid his empty bean plate to the far side of his tray like a prisoner hiding evidence.

At 7:58, Dad tapped start on the new quarterback. The screen flashed green, then the kitchen light refracted off the phone's glass and threw a small wobbling rainbow across the tablecloth. Marcus laughed his infectious, squeaking laugh and chased the rainbow with his fork, and Dad stood up to get the ice cream, which was his way of saying thank you without saying it.

Kate had one hour before the planetarium's Junior Explainer tryout, and her ball still did not work right. She stood under the dome with a lamp, an orange painted like Earth, and a golf ball on a stick for the Moon, while Marcus from her science class leaned against the console eating pretzels.

"Remind me why I'm here," Marcus said, "instead of at the arcade winning a giant banana."

"Because you owe me for the volcano incident," Kate said. "And I need an audience." Her tryout talk was about the tilt of Earth's axis, how summer and winter come from which way the planet leans as it travels around the Sun. She could say it fine. The problem was the question afterward, the one Dr. Okafor always asked the candidates, the one nobody ever seemed ready for. Last year a boy had walked out mid-answer. Kate refused to be that kid.

She spun the golf ball around the orange to warm up, tilting the orange toward the lamp to show summer. Then she stopped, because something looked wrong. From where she stood, the golf ball showed only a sliver of light, a thin crescent. She moved her head sideways, and the crescent grew into a half, then a bulging globe. She frowned and turned the ball slowly again, watching.

"Move," Marcus said through a mouthful of pretzel. "You're blocking my view of your imminent failure."

"Look at the ball," Kate said. "Not the lit sliver. The whole ball." Marcus squinted and came closer, pretending he hadn't. Kate held the ball still between the lamp and herself. Half of it was bright. She rotated the stick without moving it out of that line, and the bright half stayed bright, exactly half, always. The crescent was just the part of that lit half facing them. "Half of the Moon is always lit by the Sun," she said slowly. "The phases show how much of that lit half faces Earth. It's never actually a dark ball with a light stuck on it."

"So all those crescent drawings," Marcus said, "are just the moon being shy."

"Basically." Kate felt something click into place, the way a puzzle piece does when you stop forcing it. If Dr. Okafor asked about phases, she could infer the answer from what she was seeing, not from a memorized line. For a moment she had felt real despair standing under that dome with a broken model and one hour. Now she had a working one and forty minutes.

Dr. Okafor came out early, arms crossed, and pointed at the golf ball. "Suppose, hypothetically, I asked you why the Moon looks full tonight. What would you tell me?"

Kate lifted the ball into the light and turned until the whole lit half faced her.

"Oops," said Marcus. "I dropped my pretzel."

Sofia set out the last four jars of honey on the folding table, wiped the dust off the sign, and counted her cash box for the third time. Fifty-eight dollars. The bike at Reba's resale shop cost two hundred, and it might be gone by August. "You could put your money in the credit union," her mother had said that morning, but the whole idea felt as dry and arid as the August air blowing across the market lot, stirring grit between the stalls.

The vendor across the aisle, a teenager named Marisol who sold goat cheese, leaned over. "Slow day?"

"Somebody haggled me down on the honey and I said yes too fast," Sofia said. "I need to categorize my customers better. People who want a deal, people who just want honey." She said it like a joke, but the mistake still stung. She had studied percentages in math all spring, and knowing six percent of eight dollars should have taken her two seconds. The humiliation of freezing up in front of a stranger had kept her awake half the night.

"Six percent," Marisol repeated, fanning herself with a paper bag. "That's what my account pays. I put my cheese money in every summer."

Sofia pulled her notebook from under the table. She had been saving one hundred dollars of birthday money, and now she wrote it out right there among the jars. If the account paid six percent simple interest, that was six dollars every year, and after five years she would have one hundred thirty dollars. That she could see plainly, like rows in a garden. But her mother had said to pick the compound kind, and compound was the strange one, where the interest earned its own interest. Sofia tried to picture money growing on money and got nowhere. It was invisible, a rule hiding under the numbers.

"Twelve years," Marisol said, reading over her shoulder. "That's when mine doubles. It's called the rule of 72. Divide 72 by the yearly percentage rate, and that's about how many years it takes to double."

Sofia had guessed doubling would take maybe ten years, because ten times six felt close to a hundred. Now she tested Marisol's rule against her own paper, scribbling year by year, letting each year's interest pile onto the last. After five years the compound account crept past one hundred thirty dollars, only a few dollars ahead of the simple one, which surprised her. But the gap kept widening, and somewhere near year twelve, her pencil crossed two hundred. She checked it twice.

"Seventy-two divided by six," she said slowly. "Twelve. You'd be what, twenty-nine?"

"Twenty-nine and rich in goat cheese," Marisol said.

The honey customer from that morning came back down the aisle, and Sofia straightened her sign, decided to hold her price this time. "Six dollars a jar," she said, "and every dollar goes in the compound account on Monday."

"Make it five and I'll take two."

"Five fifty," Sofia said, and held out her hand.

Alexis pressed the sustain pedal too hard, and the last chord of "Sunrise on the River" clanged instead of fading. He lifted his hands off the keys and stared at the sheet music, where the composer had written a mysterious instruction: hold the final chord for eight full beats, growing softer until it disappears.

The problem was that the chord kept dying at beat five. He had tried pedaling differently, holding his hands flatter, even leaning his whole weight into the keys, but nothing worked. He needed to diagnose the trouble before Friday, when he and Priya would play the duet for the whole sixth grade.

Priya arrived with her flute case and flopped onto the bench beside him. "Still dying at five?" she asked.

"Every time. Maybe the piano just can't do it."

Priya hummed the note, then stopped to breathe, then hummed again. "You know what reminds me of this? Last year in choir, when we held one note for a whole phrase. Remember?"

Alexis did remember. He had been standing in the back row, sure they were about to run out of air, when he noticed something odd. The kid next to him turned his head and snatched a quick breath, but the note never wavered, because Alexis himself was still singing. Then Alexis needed air, and by the time he turned, someone two rows up had already refilled. The sound stayed strong the whole way through even though nobody could have held it alone.

"Staggered breathing," Priya said. "That's what we called it."

Alexis looked at the duet part again. Priya's flute line held the same chord while his piano part faded. "So if I get quieter a beat before you do, and then you fade after me, the sound never fully..."

He set the metronome, counted them in, and played. At beat four he let his volume drop to almost nothing, and Priya's flute carried the chord alone, thin and clear like light through water. At beat six she tapered off just as he pressed the pedal deeper, letting the strings shimmer underneath. Eight beats. The chord dissolved exactly as the composer wanted, into silence.

"That was significant," Priya whispered. "Like, actually significant."

They played it three more times to make sure it wasn't luck. It wasn't. On Friday, when the last chord faded into the hushed gymnasium, nobody clapped for a full second, and Alexis grinned at Priya across the keyboard.

"Same time tomorrow," she said. "I want to try it even slower."

Christopher carried the folding chairs two at a time across the grass, because if he made three trips instead of five, he could get back to the pavilion before Aunt Ruth finished arranging the Seder plates. His family had claimed the corner of the park with the big oak trees, and long tables stretched under the branches where the Seder would happen, the whole meal that told the story of the Jews leaving Egypt, escaping from slavery under the pharaoh. "That pharaoh was like the worst landlord in history," Uncle Danny had joked that morning. "Wouldn't let his workers go no matter what." Christopher had laughed, then wondered what it would feel like to work for someone like that.

The real problem was Zoe. His cousin was seven, the youngest able child at the table, and all week she had been practicing the Four Questions on index cards she kept losing. She practiced them in the car, at breakfast, even once into the bathroom mirror while Christopher waited outside the door. At the Seder, the youngest one asks the Four Questions, and Zoe had whispered to him, "What if I freeze and everybody stares?"

He had an idea, and he wanted to test it before the meal started. His theory was that Zoe froze only when she felt alone, like the time she forgot her line at the school play. If she had someone to aim her words at, just one face instead of forty, maybe the words would come out fine. So while the grown-ups poured grape juice and set out the parsley and salt water, Christopher pulled two chairs behind the oak tree.

"Practice on me," he said. "Pretend everyone else is furniture."

Zoe narrowed her eyes at him. "Furniture doesn't eat karpas."

"Fine, very hungry furniture." She laughed, and then she asked him the first question, her voice wobbly at first, about how this night was different from all other nights. He noticed something: her hands stopped shaking when he nodded along, and by the third question she was looking straight at him, steady as a held note.

When the time came, the gradual fading of the afternoon light made the park smell like cut grass and someone's charcoal grill nearby. Aunt Ruth tapped her glass. Zoe stood up, and Christopher watched her scan the tables, watched panic flicker across her face, and then he caught her eye and gave one small nod, the exact nod from behind the oak tree. She took a breath, turned toward everyone, and asked all Four Questions without stopping once, her voice carrying past the tables toward the playground where kids on the swings went quiet to listen.

Afterward, Grandma Miriam squeezed Zoe's shoulder and said, "Some years these questions make me cry." Christopher bit into his matzah, which crumbled all over his shirt, and thought about how a person could grow like the oak overhead, thriving in good soil. Then Zoe plopped down beside him and whispered, "Same time next year?"

"Only if I'm still furniture," he whispered back.

Payton had one job: record a ninety-second video for the museum's junior docenct contest, explaining how a river carves a canyon over millions of years. The prize was a real badge and a backstage tour of the bat cave exhibit. Her little brother Dewey had one job too, which was to stand there holding the phone and not touch the giant erosion table in the Discovery Lab. Dewey's own plan, as far as she could tell, was to touch the erosion table as much as possible.

The table was a long slope of layered sand and clay with a hose dripping at the top, and it drained toward a bin marked DEPOSITION ZONE. "Okay, rolling," Dewey said, aiming the phone at her. Payton launched into her speech about water carrying sediment away, grain by grain, over millions of years. Then the drips found a channel and the whole slope began to slump, and her speech collapsed with it.

"Stop the water," she said. Dewey turned the valve the wrong way and the drip became a small flood. The top layer of clay melted back into a gentle slope, but beneath it a slab of packed wet sand stood out over the cut like a shelf. Payton crouched down and stared at it. The wall of the little canyon wasn't smooth. It was stepped. Some layers jutted out in steep little cliffs, and the softer layers had worn back into gentler slopes beneath them, like a staircase built by accident.

"That's it," she said. "That's why the Grand Canyon looks like that." She rebuilt the slope, pressing the clay layers hard so they'd hold firm and leaving the sand loose between them. "Dewey, water on. Slow this time." She pointed the camera at the model instead of herself. "The river keeps cutting, millions of years, and the hard layers make the steep cliffs, while the soft ones wear back into slopes. That's what gives the walls their steps." She turned the model toward the poster of the canyon on the plateau above the table, where the real stepped walls ran down to the river. If the judges were going to exclude anything, it wouldn't be because she hadn't shown them something true.

They ran it three more times, and the steps appeared every time, which made her explanation seem probable even to Dewey, who had opinions about nothing. On the last run he whispered, "Do the flood again," and she let him open the valve wide just once, after the phone was safely in her pocket. The whole plateau collapsed into the bin at the bottom.

"Deposition," Payton said, pointing at the heap of sand where the river had dropped everything it carried.

"Can we keep it?" Dewey asked, already reaching in.

Alexis had never swept a gravestone before, and she was surprised at how carefully she did it, as though the granite might notice sloppy work. It was the fourth of April, the first spring since Grandpa died, and her mother had flown them to China to be with the cousins for the day. "What's today called again?" Alexis asked, working the broom into the carved grooves of his name.

"Qingming," her cousin Mei said, kneeling in the grass with a damp cloth. "It falls on April fourth or fifth. Families come to their ancestors' graves to clean them and leave offerings." She set out a bowl of rice, a few oranges, and a paper lantern folded into the shape of a bird.

Alexis looked at the offerings, then at the clean stone, then at the rows of other families along the hillside, every one of them sweeping or wiping or setting down food. A question tugged at her. Grandpa couldn't eat the rice. He couldn't see the swept stone. So what was all this for? She tested her first idea out loud. "Is it for him, or for us?"

Mei tilted her head, considering. "Maybe both."

"That's a paradox," Alexis said slowly, turning the word over. The rice was for him and not for him. She decided to run a second test. She took the last orange from the bag and placed it at the base of the stone, but then she spoke to it. "You always stole my orange slices at lunch, Grandpa. You said I had to earn them back in a staring contest." Around her the hill smelled of rain that had come overnight and would come again; the ground was saturated, dark and soft, and her sneakers sank a little with each step.
