Priya tilted her head. "When my grandfather died last year, I learned a shloka for him. It took me eleven days." She tapped the paper. "It's gradual, like anything. One line locks in, then the next. My teacher says a neuron fires the same path every time you repeat something, and the path gets stronger."

"Eleven days," Chase groaned. "I have twenty-one." He stared at the page, then looked up. "Can I ask you something weird? Where do you think Grandpa Joe went? Like, actually went."

Priya set down the plate. "In Hinduism, the soul passes through samsara. That means a cycle of birth, death and rebirth, around and around." She traced a circle in the air with one finger. "And karma decides the direction. Karma is the results of a person's actions, and those results shape the next life."

Chase turned that over while he stole a laddu. A hidden rule, like gravity: you could not see it, only the effects. He wondered if it could be tested the way you test anything invisible, by watching what it did. "So if somebody was kind all the time, the kindness would... land somewhere?"

"That's the idea," Priya said. "Grandpa Joe gave my mom his winter coat the day they met. That kind of thing counts."

That night Chase tried something new. He drew the prayer as a circle instead of lines, arrows curving from each phrase to the next, so that the end flowed back to the beginning like Priya's finger in the air. When he forgot the middle, he could travel the loop the other way and arrive from the far side. By bedtime he had the whole thing, and the words no longer felt like a wall but like a path he had walked twice.

At the ceremony, three weeks later, he reached the fourth line and felt his mind go blank. He pictured the circle, traveled backward from the end, and the missing words appeared exactly where the arrows said they would be. He finished strong, and in the front row Priya drew a slow circle in the air.

Penelope slid into her seat in the art room just as the bell rang, pulling her sketchbook out before her backpack even hit the floor. Today was the day. Mr. Ruiz had promised they would finally learn to draw a street that looked real, the kind that seemed to go back and back until it disappeared, and she had been waiting all week.

"Vanishing point," Mr. Ruiz announced, tapping a single dot he had drawn on the whiteboard. "Everything heads there. Now here's your challenge. Draw your orthogonals first."

Around her, pencils hesitated. Marcus leaned over and whispered, "Ortho-what?" A few kids just started drawing buildings and hoped for the best. Penelope stared at the dot. Orthogonal had to be a name for something, and she had one clue: Mr. Ruiz had said "everything heads there." So an orthogonal was probably a line that ran back toward the vanishing point. But which lines? That was the hidden part. You couldn't see the rule sitting on the desk; you had to hunt for it.

She decided to test an idea. In her mind she walked down her own street, the one with the crooked mailbox and the bakery on the corner. What lines seemed to run away from her as she walked? The edges of the road, for sure. She drew those first, two lines slanting in toward her dot. Then she guessed the curbs, and added them. Too timid. She erased and made them bolder, so eager she nearly tore the paper.

"Mine looks like a sandwich that got stepped on," Marcus groaned behind her, holding up a drawing where his buildings floated like parade balloons.

"You're drawing the fronts first," Penelope said. "Try the lines that go back. Roofs count. Watch." She flipped her sketchbook around. Her rooflines, her curbs, her road edges all marched toward the dot like they were in a line for the bakery. Marcus frowned at it, then at his paper, then grabbed his eraser so fast it flew out of his hand and rolled under Devon's chair.

"Road edges, curbs, rooflines," Marcus muttered as he drew, tapping each one. "Orthogonals."

"Exactly," Penelope said, and her chest did a small proud flip. The erosion of her doubt was complete; every line she put down now looked like it belonged. Windows appeared along her walls, each one smaller and closer together as the street ran back. She even added the bakery sign, squashed tiny near the dot, and it worked. The street wasn't flat anymore. It went somewhere.

Mr. Ruiz stopped behind her desk. "Now that," he said, "generates a whole neighborhood. Where's the next street go?"

Penelope grinned and put her pencil back on the paper. "Right there," she said, and added a corner.

Sara got to the science room early to claim the lamp, because the whole grade would be presenting season models that afternoon and the good equipment went fast. Marcus arrived two minutes later with their globe tucked under one arm, and he stopped in the doorway when he saw her, like he had forgotten they were still partners.

"Your mom signed the form," Sara said, not looking up. His mother worked nights at the hospital and had missed the last two permission deadlines, and Marcus had spent those trips sitting in the office, which everyone pretended not to notice.

"She did." He set the globe on the table. Heat began to radiate from the lamp as it warmed, and Sara angled the shade so the light fell across the tabletop like a small sun. She had taped a red X over their town on the Northern Hemisphere, and Marcus's job was to walk the globe in a circle while she talked. They had rehearsed once, badly, mostly in silence.

The problem showed up immediately. Every time Marcus carried the globe around the lamp, he turned it so the X faced the bulb, the way a person naturally aims the front of something at a light. It looked right, too, which was the annoying part. Bright side, warm side. Sara stopped him on the second lap.

"You're spinning it," she said. "The axis has to point the same way the whole time. Like it's pinned to the wall behind you."

Marcus frowned at the globe. "But then the X ends up tilted away from the lamp over here." He walked it halfway around, holding the top steady toward the back wall, and the red X leaned out into the dark side of the orbit.

"Exactly," Sara said, and then she heard it, the whole thing snapping together in her head. "So for this part the Northern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun, and over there it leans away. Same tilt, different part of the orbit. It never changes direction."

"That's why you don't turn it," Marcus said slowly, walking it again, slower this time, keeping the top aimed at the back wall like a compass needle. The X tipped toward the light, then away, then toward again as he completed the circle.

They ran it three more times until he could do it without drifting, and by then the room was filling and the hallway outside had gone quiet and almost desolate while everyone crowded in to watch the first presentations. Sara looked down at her peasant blouse, the good one she had saved for today, and realized she had leaned against the chalk tray and streaked the sleeve white. Marcus noticed and offered her the only thing he had, a nub of pencil eraser, which of course made it worse, and they both laughed, quietly, for the first time in weeks.

They went third. Marcus walked the globe around the lamp with his arm locked steady, and Sara said, "The axis points the same direction in space all year, so for part of the orbit the Northern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun, and later it leans away," and pointed to the X tipping into shadow as the room watched the little world turn slowly through its year. Afterward Ms. Okafor wrote something in her binder, and Marcus whispered, "We nailed it," and Sara looked at the chalk mark on her sleeve and said, "Say that louder."

The power died with an abrupt click at half past eight, right in the middle of Ryder's game, and the whole house at Grandpa's went black except for the thin gray line of the window curtains. Ryder sat very still and listened. No furnace hum, no refrigerator drone, nothing. From downstairs, Grandpa's voice drifted up the stairs, calm as ever. "Well. Guess the county's having fun tonight. Candles are in the sideboard, third drawer."

Ryder felt his way down, bumping his hip on the banister, and found Grandpa already striking a match in the kitchen. The flame caught, and Grandpa set a stubby candle on the counter, then another on the table, converting the bright, familiar kitchen into something from an old photograph, all shadows and warm little pools of light. "You okay on your phone?" Grandpa asked. "Dead," Ryder said. "I forgot my charger." He'd been planning to charge it at home tomorrow. Now the screen was a dark black rectangle, useless as a brick, and something in his chest tightened at that.

Grandpa took a long flashlight from the mudroom shelf and nodded toward the back door. "Come on. When I was a kid, blackout nights were the best ones. Let's see if they still are." Outside, the whole street was dark, every porch light and window out, and the sky above them was not the sky Ryder knew. It was crowded. There were so many stars it looked almost messy, a spilled bag of salt, and across the middle of it ran a pale, hazy river of light he had never once seen from any city or suburb in his life.

"That's the Milky Way," Grandpa said quietly. "Haven't seen it from this yard since I don't know when." Ryder kept staring. He kept thinking there must be something wrong with his eyes, some smudge on his glasses, but no, it was real, and it was enormous, and it had apparently been hanging over his head his entire life without him ever knowing. Then he remembered where he'd seen something about this, a library book about the night sky he'd flipped through last month and mostly ignored. He'd skipped the paragraphs and read only the fact boxes. One of them had stuck anyway. "There was this atlas," he said slowly. "A world atlas of light pollution, from 2016. It estimated about eighty percent of North Americans can't see the Milky Way from where they live, because of artificial light." He checked Grandpa's face to see if he'd remembered it wrong, but Grandpa just nodded.

"Go get my laser pointer," Grandpa said. "Top drawer of my desk, the little silver one." Ryder fetched it, and Grandpa thumbed it on and traced a slow line up the black sky, pointing out Vega, then Deneb, then the whole glowing river itself, the green beam looking almost like it touched the stars. Ryder wanted to test something. If all that glow in the sky was really stars that the streetlights normally drowned out, then a single porch light coming back on should erase at least part of it. He stood squinting at the Milky Way, waiting for some house somewhere to flicker back to life so he could watch the stars vanish in real time. Nothing came on. The whole neighborhood stayed dark, and the sky stayed crowded, and the wait itself felt like its own strange gift.

The streetlights snapped back on all at once around ten, so sudden that Ryder flinched, and the Milky Way disappeared like breath wiped off glass. Only a dozen of the brightest stars survived. He hadn't even gotten to finish his test, but he'd seen enough: the stars had been there the whole time, waiting behind the porch lights and the glowing windows, and all it took to hide an entire galaxy was ordinary electricity. He'd spent the whole evening mad about his dead phone, and now, staring up at the washed-out sky he used to think was normal, he couldn't decide whether he wanted the power back or not.

"Same time next blackout?" Grandpa said, pocketing the laser pointer. Ryder watched the porch light buzz and steady itself, steady and bright and ruinous. "Yeah," he said. "But I'm bringing a blanket."

The assignment was due on Friday, and Landon had spent three days avoiding it. Now he sat in the school library at four o'clock, a blank page in front of him, and the clock above the biography shelves ticking like it was counting down a siege. He had to write a short story with dialogue, and the dialogue had to be punctuated right, and the whole thing needed a climax. Ms. Ferrante had circled his last attempt in red and written "See me" at the top, which was worse than any grade.

He tried a sentence. "Where are you going," He asked. It looked wrong the moment he wrote it, but he could not say why. His friend Priya slid into the chair across from him with her own paper and a granola bar. She leaned over his shoulder.

"Question mark," she said, tapping the page. Landon frowned. He flipped through the class packet of examples until he found one: "Where are you?" he asked. There it was, the question mark sitting inside the quotation marks, and the tag after it starting with a lowercase h. That seemed backwards to him. He asked was its own kind of sentence, wasn't it?

"Watch," Priya said. She took his pencil and wrote the whole thing out plain, without any marks: Where are you he asked. "Now decide where the question ends. Is He asked part of the question?" Landon stared at it. The question was only the part in the guy's mouth. The tag belonged to the narrator. He tried it both ways on the page, once with a capital H, once without, and read them aloud. The lowercase version sounded right, like one breath instead of two broken pieces. He erased the capital.

His old ideas for the story, a spaceship battle, suddenly felt dormant, like something that had been sitting too long in the dark. He had wanted a siege scene with robots. Instead he started writing about two brothers in a treehouse, one hiding something, and by the third line of dialogue he was writing fast, punctuating the questions without slowing down. Priya had moved on to her own paper, but when he read a line out loud she laughed once, quietly, and the librarian glanced over. Landon felt his ears go hot.

The problem was the climax. He wrote four versions where the brothers argued, and each one fizzled out. Then he tried having the younger brother finally ask the question he had been afraid to ask all story long: "Why didn't you come to Mom's funeral?" he asked. The older brother went silent on the page, and then Landon knew exactly what happened next, because the whole story had been waiting for that one question. He wrote the ending in a single sitting, twenty minutes, his hand cramped around the pencil.

When he read it through, though, the robot siege was gone for good, and he felt a small pang about that, the way you do when you trade something loud and fun for something quieter and harder. Priya packed up her bag and paused at his table. "Read it to me tomorrow before class?" she said. He slid the paper into his folder, smoothed the crease flat with his palm, and said, "Only if you fix my commas first."

Luca stood at the canoe launch with his duffel at his feet, waiting for the camp van, and tried to look like a kid who had done this a hundred times. He had never been to summer camp. His cousin Diego had spent a month at one last summer and came home telling stories about a lake, a rope swing, and something he called the frontier, a stretch of woods at the edge of the property where the older campers got to hike. Luca wanted that more than anything, and he'd said so on the ride up, so many times that his mom laughed. Now he watched the driver load his bag beside seven others and climbed in anyway.

The first week was good, until Tuesday night, when cabin inspection turned into tick check. The counselor handed each boy a flashlight and told them to line up, and a kid named Marcus groaned loudly. "We didn't even hike today. Why bother?" He flopped onto his bunk and pulled his sleeping bag over his head like a tent.

Luca had been scratching behind his knee since the afternoon trail walk, and while Marcus complained, he thought about it. He hadn't hiked Monday either, but today they had cut through a field of tall grass to reach the swimming dock, off the trail, because it was faster. The itching had started after that. He couldn't see the back of his own knee, but the fact of the itching was data, like a footprint. He grabbed the kid next to him, a quiet boy named Owen. "Can you check behind my knee with the flashlight? We went through that tall grass by the dock."

Owen shined the light and went still. "There's something there. Small. Like a poppy seed with legs." Luca's stomach dropped, but he made himself think instead of panic. Marcus peeked out from his sleeping bag, suddenly interested. "Is that a blacklegged tick?" he asked. "My sister got one at her camp. She said they're also called deer ticks, and they can spread Lyme disease, so everybody had to check every night."

"Then check everybody," Luca said, pulling his pant leg down. "Especially anyone who was in that grass." Marcus sat up, all complaints gone, and helped Owen run the flashlights along ankles and hairlines and behind ears. They found two more ticks among the six boys who had taken the shortcut, and the counselor got them off properly and logged it, while Marcus explained to the next cabin over why the nightly check existed. "I take back what I said," he told them. "This is the most sophisticated reason to make us line up I've ever heard."

By Friday, the whole cabin had a system. Lights out, then flashlights on, then a rotation where each boy checked the boy behind him, faster every night, until it consumed barely five minutes. "Efficient," Owen said, with a small proud smile, and Marcus gave Luca a fist bump. On Sunday, the frontier hike opened for the older campers, and Luca's name was on the list. He caught up to the group at the trailhead, boots already dusty, and Marcus tossed him a spare flashlight. "For after," Marcus said, and Luca grinned and tucked it in his pocket as they stepped into the trees.

Georgia had one job at the polling station: hold her grandmother's place in line while Gran fetched her glasses from the car. But the line was slow, and beside the door somebody had taped up a poster of the town charter, all forty rights printed in tiny columns. Georgia started reading to pass the time.

She was halfway through the list, lips moving, when a man in a green jacket came out of the voting hall. She recognized him. Councillor Ruiz, the one from the newspaper photo. He had voted against the bylaw that banned skateboarding in the library plaza, the bylaw that had emptied the plaza and pushed every skater in Georgia's grade onto the cracked lot behind the gas station.

"You're Councillor Ruiz," she said. "You said the plaza ban was wrong. So when are you changing it?"

He smiled, but not much. "I can't change it alone. A single councillor can't change a bylaw alone. A change needs a majority vote of the whole council."

Georgia stared at him. "But you agree it's a bad rule."

"Agreeing isn't voting power. There are seven of us."

She looked back at the charter poster. Right there, near the top: the right of citizens to gather peacefully and to petition their government. She'd read it twice without really reading it. Now she said it out loud, slowly, testing it. "So we can ask. Together. That's not just a decoration on a wall."

"That's the idea," Ruiz said. "Petitions matter. Voters matter. Today, especially."

Georgia's mind was moving fast. This was polling day, and the whole town was walking past this door. People who cared enough to vote cared enough to sign something. That was the hidden pattern: the ban hadn't been defeated by one enemy, it had passed because nobody had shown up to argue, and now the people who could argue were all standing in one line. She ran to Gran's car, grabbed the notebook from the back seat, and tore out six pages.

"Sign here if you want the plaza bylaw reconsidered," she called, standing where everyone had to pass. A woman with a stroller signed. Two teenagers signed without asking questions. A man in a volatile mood, red-faced about parking tickets, refused, but then a library volunteer signed right after him and told him the plaza used to be full of kids before the ban. He scowled and kept walking, but slower.

By the time Gran came back with her glasses, Georgia had ninety-three signatures. Ninety-three, in one hour, from one line. She counted them twice on the bench by the door.

She had wanted Ruiz to fix it, one important person snapping his fingers. Now she wanted something different: seven votes, and a stack of paper heavy enough to matter. She folded the pages, squared them against her knee, and walked the stack straight back to Councillor Ruiz.

"You said majority," she told him. "So start counting."

Lucas stood in the hallway outside room 412 with his grandfather's watch already on his wrist, though he could not remember deciding to put it there. His hand had gone to his back pocket for the tissue and come back with the watch instead, like a reflex he hadn't known he had. Inside the room, his grandmother was folding the blanket at the foot of the empty bed, smoothing it flat, then smoothing it again. The air smelled of antiseptic and the faint orange peel his grandfather had always kept in his shirt pocket, even in here, even at the end.

"Grandpa would've wanted you to have that," she said, nodding at the watch.

Lucas turned the cracked leather band with his thumb. Last summer his grandfather had caught him messing with it and smacked his hand away, laughing. Now nobody would smack his hand again, and that thought made his throat hurt. But something else bothered him too, a worry he couldn't shake. His school counselor had said the word "moving on" about his dog that died in fourth grade, and Lucas had gotten the idea stuck in his head that grief was like a hallway you walked down, and if you stopped to hold on to things, you never got out. Wearing the watch felt like stopping. He tested the idea quietly, taking the watch off and setting it on the bedside table, the way you might exclude a bad-luck charm from your pocket before a test. The room felt colder. He picked it back up.

While his grandmother signed papers at the nurses' station, Lucas wandered down to a small room with a sign that said FAMILY RESOURCE SHELF. He expected pamphlets with clip-art teddy bears, but the shelf held real books. One was thin and serious, nothing like the contemporary covers with bright cartoons in the bookstore, and the spine said Continuing Bonds, 1996. He pulled it down and read the back, mouthing the words. It said the book had argued that keeping a connection to someone who has died, through memories, objects, or traditions, could be a healthy part of grieving. He read it twice, then a third time, pressing the words into himself.

He carried it back down the hall, the watch ticking against his wristbone. "Grandma," he said, "did you know some people think you're supposed to keep stuff? Like wearing his watch isn't, like, cheating?"

She looked at the book, then at him, and something in her shoulders let go. "Continuing bonds," she said. "Your grandpa kept his own father's pocket knife in the garage drawer for forty years. Never sharpened a thing with it."

Lucas slid the book back onto the shelf outside room 412, where his grandmother was waiting with the car keys. He wound the watch the way he'd watched his grandfather do it a thousand times, crown between thumb and finger, slow, until it resisted. "Tuesday pancakes," he said. "Grandpa's recipe. You keep the buttermilk in the garage fridge, right?"

"Back shelf," she said, "behind the soda water." She took his hand, and they walked past the nurses' station toward the elevator doors, the watch ticking the whole way down.

Ariana set her trumpet on the music stand and glared at the twelve-bar blues chart like it had insulted her family. "You're going to improvise a solo today," Mr. Ruiz had said, which was easy for him to say, since he wasn't the one who had to invent notes in front of the whole jazz band. She'd practiced the chord progression until she could play it asleep, but the moment she tried to make up a solo, everything came out in a panicked rush, notes tumbling over each other like they were fleeing the scene.

"You're rushing again," said Marcus from the piano bench, grinning. "That solo lasted about nine seconds."

"It did not." Ariana checked the clock. It had, in fact, lasted about nine seconds.

Marcus reached into his bag and pulled out a small wooden box with a sliding weight and a pendulum. He wound it, and the thing began to tick, steady as a dripping faucet. "Try it under this." Ariana assessed the little machine, turning it over, watching the weight slide up and down its scale. "Where did you even get this?"

"My grandpa. He says it's older than jazz itself." Marcus tapped the lid, where a worn brass plate read Maelzel. "Johann Nepomuk Maelzel patented the mechanical metronome in 1815. A ticking device that sets a steady tempo." He said it the way Grandpa must have said it to him, like a magic password.

Ariana had a sudden flashback to fourth grade, when she'd played "Hot Cross Buns" at approximately the speed of a hummingbird's heartbeat, and her teacher had gently suggested the audience might enjoy hearing some of the notes. So rushing was an old habit, a hidden pattern inside her that she couldn't see, only hear from outside, like a voice recording that sounds nothing like you. But the metronome could see it for her. That was her idea, and it was simple: if she played with the ticking, either the tick would slow her down or she would prove the tick wrong.

She lifted her trumpet, set the pendulum swinging, and started the solo again. The first four bars felt like walking a tightrope, her fingers wanting to sprint while the tick kept saying not yet, not yet. By bar eight something clicked, or rather stopped clicking out of turn, and her notes landed square on the beats. On bar twelve she ended on a low note that bent downward, the way she'd heard on old records, and let it hang there.

Marcus played a little ta-da chord. "Nine seconds of glory, no more. Well, more like thirty."

"Consumer of my solos, you are a negligent audience," Ariana said, pointing the trumpet at him. "That one deserved applause."

"Fine." He gave her three slow, sarcastic claps, perfectly in tempo with the ticking box.

Every morning that week, Victoria found the kitchen floor wet in the same spot, a shallow puddle by the window above the sink. Her mother blamed her for spilling water. Victoria was tired of being blamed, and more than that, she wanted to know what was really happening, because nothing in the house leaked as far as anyone could tell.

She made a guess: condensation was forming on the cold water pipe that ran behind the wall, and it dripped down through a gap in the floorboards. It was a guess about something she could not see, since the pipe was hidden, so she needed a way to test it. If the pipe was the cause, she reasoned, the puddle should form even when nobody used the sink all night. She taped a paper towel over the gap in the boards, taped another to the wall near the window, and marked the spots with pencil so she could tell them apart.

The next morning both paper towels were dry and the puddle was back. Her guess about the pipe was wrong, and she said so out loud at breakfast, which surprised her brother, Dean, who was building an intricate model bridge out of toothpicks for his own project. "You sound happy your idea failed," he said. "It's not fun," Victoria said. "But at least I know something now." Dean looked up from his bridge, which had reached a plateau in its construction, and shrugged.

While hunting through the hall closet for a flashlight, Victoria found a box of her father's old college books. One, a battered paperback with a cracked spine, had a chapter with a sentence she read three times: a philosopher named Karl Popper had argued, in a book first published in 1934, that an idea is scientific only if some possible observation could prove it wrong. She carried the book to the kitchen and read the sentence to Dean. "So my pipe idea counted," she said. "There was a result, dry towels, that could knock it down. And it did."

"Then what's your next one?" Dean asked. Victoria looked at the window above the sink, at the puddle below it, and at the tarp-covered grill on the patio just outside. Her new guess was that dew was collecting on the tarp at night and running off its lowest corner, which hung a few inches above the window ledge. If that was true, the puddle should vanish if the tarp's corner was moved. It should also mean wet streaks on the ledge itself, which she had not checked.

That evening she slid the tarp's corner a foot to the left and propped it on a bucket, so any runoff would drip onto the patio stones instead. She set a cup on the window ledge to catch anything that touched it. Then she went to bed and lay awake for a while, turning the philosopher's rule over in her mind. An idea you could not test, she thought, was just something you liked believing.

In the morning the floor was dry. The cup on the ledge held half an inch of water, and the patio stones under the tarp's old corner were dark with moisture. Victoria called her mother into the kitchen and showed her the cup, the dry floor, and the sentence in the book, bookmarked with a toothpick. "I was wrong about the pipe, and I almost let you humiliate me about spilling," she said. "It was the grill tarp the whole time."

Her mother leaned over the cup and laughed. "So what do we do about it?" "Move the tarp for good," Victoria said, "or hang a gutter on it." She was already pulling on her boots to go outside and slide the whole tarp farther down the patio.

Flight 47 to Phoenix was delayed again, and Florence spread her science homework across two plastic seats in the gate area. Her graph for the Sonoran Desert showed rainfall bars so short they looked like a typo, while the rainforest graph she'd copied from the library book had bars like a row of broken teeth, tall and constant. She had to compare them using temperature too, and the assignment sheet called for a paragraph she had not yet managed to formulate.

Her little brother Theo leaned over her shoulder with a topographic map of the mountain near Grandma's house. "You said we'd go sledding when we land," he said. "Pick the hill before Mom changes her mind."

"Mom already changed her mind twice," Florence said. "Once about the window seat."

The map was covered in wiggly brown lines, close together in some places and far apart in others. Checking each line against the height numbers printed on it was tedious, and Florence kept losing her place whenever the gate agent announced something nobody listened to. She traced one slope with her finger where the lines bunched up like angry eyebrows, then another where they were scattered wide, and a third where they marched down the page at regular intervals, like fence posts.

"That one," Theo said, poking the regular one.

"Why that one?"

He shrugged. "It looks calm."

Florence frowned. The lines on that slope were evenly spaced, each one the same distance from the last, all the way from the top of the hill to the creek. On the other slopes the spacing changed, tight then loose then tight again. She thought about what the spacing might be hiding, since the map could not show her the actual ground. Wide spacing had to be one steepness and narrow spacing another, so if the spacing never changed, then the steepness never changed either. "Contour lines spaced evenly apart," she said slowly, "show a slope that has the same steepness all the way along it."

"So no surprise cliffs?"

"No surprise cliffs." She drew a red circle around the slope and wrote GO HERE under it, then held the map up to the window. Beyond the tarmac, a fuel vessel sat parked beside the plane, and a man in orange ear protection was checking its gauge.

She turned back to her graphs, and now the comparison wrote itself almost without her. The desert's temperature line swung up and down with the seasons while rainfall stayed nearly nothing; the rainforest stayed warm and soaked month after month. Two places, two patterns, and you could read the whole climate off the shapes. She finished the paragraph, then looked at the clock and at the map.

"Forty minutes till boarding," she said. "Enough time to check the map for a backup hill, in case the first one is full of kids who also like calm."

Cole lined up five glasses on the kitchen counter like a scientist preparing a difficult experiment, which was exactly what he considered this. In the first glass he poured lemon juice, in the second water with a pinch of baking soda, and in the third a splash of cola. His friend Marcus sat on a stool, spinning a strip of litmus paper between his fingers.

"Bet you the lemon and the cola test almost the same," Marcus said. "It's not like one's a laser and the other's a flashlight. pH three, pH four, what's the difference? One number."

"One number on a scale where each whole step is a tenfold change," Cole said, but he said it quietly, because he was not entirely sure he remembered it right. His science notebook was upstairs, and going to get it would mean admitting he needed to check. Instead he took the strip from Marcus and dipped it into the cola. It came out red. Red meant acid. The lemon juice turned its strip red too, but somehow a deeper, angrier red, and Cole felt something tighten in his chest.

He remembered his grandfather's old garden kit in the drawer under the phone, a box with numbered color cards from pH one to pH fourteen. He dug it out and held the wet strips against the cards, tilting them toward the window light. Cola matched the card for four. Lemon matched the card for three.

"See?" Marcus said, leaning over his shoulder. "One apart. Only a little more acidic."

"No." Cole's mouth was dry. "Each whole step on the pH scale is a tenfold change, so pH three is ten times more acidic than pH four. The lemon isn't a little more acidic than the cola. It's ten times more acidic." He watched Marcus's face go through disbelief, then doubt, then the slow widening of eyes that meant the math had landed. Ten times. From one number.

"In vain did Marcus search the counter for some flaw in the cards or the strips," Cole wrote later in his notebook, because his teacher wanted full sentences. But right then he was busy pouring water into the lemon glass, testing again, accommodating every strip the kit had left until the color crept from three toward four. Marcus grabbed the last strip and dipped it into the baking soda glass himself, where it turned blue as a summer sky.

"Wait," Marcus said. "So two steps would be a hundred times?"

Sawyer spread his poster board on the folding table beside the samosa booth and frowned at his bar graph. He had counted the origins listed for his town on the census website, the same numbers his teacher had shown the class, and turned them into percentages. Scottish, eighteen percent. Chinese, fourteen. Cree, eleven. Métis, nine. Indian, eight. Ukrainian, seven. He added them twice on his calculator, and both times the total came out to ninety-seven percent, which would have been fine, except he still had six more bars to count. By the end he was at a hundred and forty-three percent, which was impossible. People did not just appear out of nowhere, and the festival around him was proof: the whole town square was booths and flags and food steam, maybe two thousand people, definitely not two thousand eight hundred and sixty.

He decided to test it the direct way. At the Ukrainian booth, a grandmother in an embroidered shirt was handing out perogies, so he asked her what she would write on the census for origin. "Ukrainian and Scottish," she said. "My mother's family came from near Kyiv, my father's from Glasgow." At the next table a girl about his age, Priya, was taping up a banner that said Trinidad AND Portugal, and she laughed when he raised his eyebrows. "My dad's side is Indo-Trinidadian, my mom's Portuguese. It's all me." Sawyer wrote both answers down. Three booths later, a man selling bannock told him, "Cree and Irish, on my mother's side and my father's," and pointed at his own display, which showed two family trees side by side.

Sawyer sat back down and tried to clarify the pattern in his notes. Nobody had picked just one origin except a few people, and that was what he needed to check. He walked the booths for another hour, asking his question at every table, and the answers stayed consistent: most people gave him two, some gave him three. That was the hidden cause. The census numbers were not counting people. They were counting origins, and the same person could be in more than one bar on his graph.

When he got home he searched the census pages until he found the sentence, and it matched exactly what the booths had shown him. People had been able to report more than one ethnic or cultural origin since 1981, which meant the origin totals added up to more than the whole population of Canada. His graph was not broken. His arithmetic was fine. The bars were simply overlapping, the way Priya's banner overlapped two countries.

The next morning at the festival, Sawyer added a strip of paper above his bars: One person can be in more than one bar. That's not a mistake. He watched a man stop, read it, and trace the Scottish and Cree bars with one finger, nodding slowly. "My kids are all three of these," the man said, tapping Ukrainian too. "Draw me in there twice."

The assignment sheet said one thing in bold: you must use a primary source. Lucy stood in the second-floor gallery of the county history museum, where a glass case held a copy of an 1846 settler's diary, its brown ink faded to the color of weak tea. Her friend Devon was supposed to be helping, but he had wandered three cases down to a giant timeline of empires and was now pointing at it.

"Look at this," Devon called. "It says the Roman Empire ended in 476. But this other label says the eastern half kept going. That makes no sense."

Lucy leaned over the timeline with him. The map showed the empire split in two, and the eastern portion, shaded green, stretched forward across the centuries while the western part stopped dead.

"That's the Byzantine Empire," Devon said, reading the small print. He tapped the last green date. "It says the Ottoman Turks captured Constantinople in 1453." He counted on his fingers, twice, because the number seemed wrong. "That's almost a thousand years longer than the western half lasted. How can an empire fall twice?"

"Maybe the whole thing didn't fall at once," Lucy said. "The western half fell, and the eastern half just kept going. Empires aren't one block." She looked back toward the diary case, and something clicked. If an empire could split and one piece survive, then a story people told about the past could also be only half of it. Her textbook said people moved west for "opportunity," but that word covered everything and explained nothing. She needed the diary to tell her which half of the story was true.

She went back to the case and read the transcription card mounted beside it. The settler, a woman named Ruth Ellery, wrote that her husband's mill had failed after two bad harvests, that the land they rented in Ohio had grown "thin and tired," and that a letter from her brother in Iowa described soil "so dark it stains the wagon wheels." Lucy tested a simple idea against the words: if people moved because the East was worn out, the diary would complain about the land before it ever mentioned adventure. It did. Ruth wrote nothing about starting fresh or seeking fortune. She wrote about exhausted fields and a brother's letter. Lucy copied the three best lines onto her notecard, then held them up next to the museum's wall map of migration routes. The routes ran away from the older states and toward the newer ones, like water finding a downhill path, though she reminded herself that was a simile, not evidence.

"Can I see?" Devon said, coming over. He read her notecard. "So the book says opportunity, but she says the ground gave out."

"That's what I'm going to argue," Lucy said. "The source beats the summary."

Devon frowned at her notecard, then back at the timeline. "So maybe I could argue the timeline the same way. One piece of Rome died in 476 and the other piece, the Byzantine Empire, lasted until 1453 when the Ottoman Turks took Constantinople. Almost a thousand years longer."

"Then the sign upstairs isn't wrong, it's just vulnerable," Lucy said. "It only shows the western half."

A museum guard started toward them, and Devon stepped away from the case so fast his elbow knocked the rope stand. Lucy grabbed the stand before it tipped, her notecard still pressed flat against her chest.

The Tuesday book club met in the library's back corner, between the biography shelves and a radiator that clanked like it had opinions. Mila had read "The Lighthouse Keeper's Daughter" twice, once diligently with a pencil and once in a blanket fort, and she came to the meeting with a theory she was almost proud of. On page twelve, the keeper's lantern had a crack in the glass. On page forty, a ship vanished. Everyone at the table knew what that meant. The keeper had let the light fail. He was guilty.

"Obviously he did it," said Devon, who had read only the back cover. "The cracked lantern is foreshadowing. It's practically a confession."

Mila wanted to agree. The crack was the kind of detail teachers circled in red pen. But something bothered her, the way a pebble in a shoe bothers you only when you stop walking. The crack was mentioned once and then never again. The keeper repaired it on page thirteen, cheerfully, humming. Real foreshadowing, she thought, should lean forward, pointing at something ahead, not sit there like a forgotten sandwich. So she tried an experiment. She wrote the clue on an index card, flipped it over, and wrote on the back: what if this is here to make me look the wrong way?

The librarian, Ms. Okoye, wheeled past with a cart of returns and paused long enough to hear Devon declare the keeper guilty beyond doubt. "You should finish chapter nine before you vote," she said, and kept rolling, which was the most anyone at that library ever interfered with anything.

They read chapter nine. The ship had not vanished at all; it had detoured around a storm and docked two towns over, and the keeper's log proved his light burned all night. The crack on page twelve had done exactly nothing. Devon stared at his copy like it had lied to him personally. "Then why was it in there?"

"To fool you," Mila said. "It's a red herring. A false clue, put in on purpose so readers leap to the wrong conclusion." She held up her index card, front and back. "Not every hint is real foreshadowing. Some of them are traps."

Devon argued for a while, then ceased, because Ms. Okoye had returned and was standing there with the sequel, which she placed gently in front of him. On its cover, a herring, bright red, and a lighthouse with glass so clean it could have passed a hygiene inspection.

"The new one has a clue about a leaking boat," Devon said warily.

Mila sharpened her pencil. "Then we'd better decide if that boat leaks on purpose."

The bus smelled like sunscreen and pine air freshener, and Cooper had been riding it for two hours with his duffel wedged under his knees because the overhead rack was full. He had wanted to stay home. That was the truth he hadn't told his dad, who had been so cheerful at the curb that morning it was almost bizarre, like he was the one getting shipped off for a month. Cooper's actual motivation for going was simpler and more embarrassing: Maya Delgado from his science class had said camp was where she'd learned to find her way around the night sky, and he wanted to be able to do that too.

The boy across the aisle, a wiry kid named Theo who talked with his whole face, leaned over. "You nervous? You look nervous."

"I'm fine," Cooper said, which was mostly a lie. He was fine about the ropes course and the lake. What worried him was the dark, specifically being the only one awake in a cabin full of strangers and not knowing which way anything was.

The first night, after lights out, Theo nudged him and they snuck down to the dock with two other boys, Asher and Ravi. Asher held up his phone, then made an angry sound. "No bars. No compass, no nothing."

"So we point north using the stars," Theo said, squinting up. "That's a thing people do."

"Which stars?" Ravi asked. "There are approximately a billion of them."

Cooper lay back on the warm boards and found the Big Dipper almost immediately, the shape Maya had traced on the classroom window with her finger in April. He remembered her saying something about it, and the memory came back in pieces, the way a photo develops. He found the bowl, then the two stars on its outer edge, and drew a line in his mind, stretching them upward and away.

"I think those two stars point to the North Star," he said slowly. "The ones on the outside of the bowl. They call them the pointer stars."

"You think, or you know?" Theo asked.

Cooper followed the line and there it was, a modest, steady star that didn't look special until you reached it. "That one. That's got to be it."

Asher held his dead phone flat and spun it like a compass card until its top edge lined up with the star. "So that's north. Congratulations, we're officially not lost."

Then Theo laughed, a strange held-in kind of laugh, and pulled a real compass from his sock. "My grandpa made me swear I'd carry it. I've had it the whole time."

Ravi stared at him. "The entire bus ride? The entire hour of us being dramatic about no signal?"

"Your motivations for not mentioning it remain unclear," Cooper said, and everyone groaned at him.

Theo flicked the compass open. The needle swung, shivered, and settled.

It pointed straight at Cooper's star.

Grayson's sneakers squeaked on the gym floor as he lined up with fourteen other boys for the last day of basketball tryouts. His friend Priya sat on the bleachers with a stopwatch, waiting for her turn to help Coach Herrera record sprints. She was only there because she had missed the swim team cutoff by half a second, and she hadn't wanted to go home and stare at the notice on her fridge.

"She said my time didn't make the top eight," Priya said quietly while the coach set up cones. "But I swam the hundred in Texas this summer, and I was faster than that. I got slower. That's what doesn't make sense."

Grayson took a drink from his water bottle and thought about it while he jogged in place. He had seen Priya race in the summer too, at the big aquatic center where her club practiced. Their school's own pool was so short that when he counted the lane ropes, you touched the wall almost before you got going. If the Texas pool was longer, then swimming the same distance there would mean fewer turns, and fewer turns meant you couldn't push off and glide the way you could at school.

"Wait," he said. "Was the Texas pool the big one? The fifty-meter one?"

Priya nodded. "Long course. That's what it's called. Our pool is short course, twenty-five yards." She turned the stopwatch over in her hands. "Coach Benson said her club times can't be compared directly with her tryout times. That's why I had to swim again here."

Grayson chewed on that. So Priya hadn't gotten slower at all. Her tryout time just couldn't be stacked against summer races, because the pools weren't the same distance end to end, and the cutoff list had been built from numbers that didn't match. His mind drifted to the previous spring, when he had quit track after one bad meet and told himself he was simply not a runner. He wondered now whether he had quit over one false measurement too.

"Go!" Coach Herrera shouted, and Grayson burst down the court. His legs were heavy from two days of drills, and fatigue hindered his footwork on the crossover, but he forced himself to keep his eyes up and find the open teammate. The ball left his fingers and dropped through the net without touching the rim.

After the drill, he jogged back to Priya. "Tell Coach Benson you want to swim the hundred again," he said. "Or ask her to convert your long course time. You're not slower. You were just measured in a different pool."

Priya looked at the list of names the coach had started writing on his clipboard, then at the gym doors. "I almost didn't come today," she said. "I thought it was permanent, that cut."

"It's not," Grayson said. He picked up his ball and squared his shoulders toward the hoop. "Nothing's permanent until the roster goes up on that door."

The fruit fly problem started at Avery's kitchen table, where her little brother Dex had left a bruised peach in a bowl for two weeks. "Fruit makes them," Dex insisted, pointing at the tiny flies circling the bowl. "The peach grows them by itself." Avery had her doubts, but she had no proof, and Monday's science class gave her an idea for getting some.

Mr. Okafor's room smelled like pencil shavings and the rubber gaskets from the sink sprayers. At the front counter sat a stack of clean jars, a square of wire gauze, and two slabs of raw meat wrapped in paper. The lab sheets were blank except for one line: a question about where maggots come from. Avery raised her hand before anyone else could. "My brother says rotten food makes flies by itself. Can we settle it?"

"Then formulate a guess we can test," Mr. Okafor said. "Something the jars can confirm or knock down." Avery wrote her guess at the top of her sheet: flies come from outside, from other flies, not from the meat. If she was wrong, the jars would show it either way, which was the whole point of setting them up.

Her group put meat in four jars and left two of them open. They stretched gauze over the mouths of the other two and wound string around the rims so nothing could crawl in. Avery pressed her eye to the mesh on the covered jars. She could see the meat clearly, gray and glistening, but the gauze kept anything the size of a fly from reaching it. "Same meat, same shelf, same air," she said. "The only difference is the cover." By Wednesday, white specks no bigger than grains of rice had appeared along the edges of the meat in the open jars. By Friday, the specks had become maggots, and flies had found the open jars too, landing and lifting off again like they owned them. The covered jars sat clean. Nothing grew on that meat at all.

"Look," said her lab partner Naomi, holding up both lab sheets. "Open jars, maggots. Gauze jars, nothing." Avery turned to the history poster on the back wall, the one with the timeline of scientists, and stopped at a name she had walked past a hundred times without reading. "Francesco Redi," she said slowly. "1668. He put meat in jars, and maggots grew in the open jars, but not in the jars covered with gauze that kept flies off the meat." She had done his exact experiment without knowing it, and his result matched hers jar for jar. "That's like testimony," Naomi said. "Somebody tested the same guess three hundred fifty years before us and got the same answer."

At home, Avery carried the peach bowl to the back porch and set it on the railing. Dex watched from the door. "You're letting them out?" he asked. "No," Avery said. "I'm letting you watch." She pointed at the peach, where a fruit fly was landing on the bruised spot, and Dex leaned in close, his nose almost touching the bowl.

The projector hummed while Mr. Reyes took attendance, and Jacob slid into his seat at the back computer lab station, opening the message app before the teacher even finished calling names. He wanted one thing this morning: to find out who had leaked his photo. Two weeks ago he had posted a picture of himself at the hospital, right after his brother's surgery, with a caption about being scared. His account was private. Yet yesterday a kid from another school, someone Jacob had never met, had walked past him at the mall and said, "Hope your brother's okay." His brother was fine. Jacob was not.

He started with his follower list. Eighty-three names. He scrolled slowly, tapping each profile, looking for anyone who might have passed the picture along. Most were kids from his grade. A few were cousins. Then he found one he barely recognized: Derek, a boy from his old elementary school who had followed him three years ago, back when Jacob accepted almost anyone. Derek's page was public, and near the top, Jacob found it. His hospital photo, reposted without the caption, with a joke attached. The room noise, keyboards and chairs and someone's sneaker squeaking, seemed to drop away.

Jacob tested the idea forming in his head. He created a second account under a fake name and tried to view his own page. Nothing. The private setting held, and he could see nothing at all. So the leak had not come from the outside. It had to be someone already inside. He tried once more with a third fake account, just to be sure, and again the wall held. The only people who could have seen the photo were the followers he had already accepted. Derek fit, and Derek's repost fit too.

He walked over to Marisol's station, because she had been friends with Derek's younger sister. "Can you message him for me?" he asked. "Tell him to take it down."

Marisol pulled off one earbud. She had her own project on screen, a photography portfolio she'd been building all semester for the district contest. "Why should I? Derek's been trying to get views all month. He'll listen if it helps him, not if it helps you."

"Tell him I'll give him credit if he ever wants to use one of my brother's drawings. Or tell him everyone at school will think he reposts old stuff because he can't make anything new." Jacob watched her weigh it, watched her lens of attention shift from her portfolio to him. "It's not trivial to me," he added. "That photo was just for people I know."

Marisol sent the message. In five minutes, Derek replied: the post was gone. But when Jacob checked his follower list again, he understood the other half of it. He removed Derek, and then he kept going, tapping remove on name after name, kids from elementary school, strangers, people whose faces no longer coincided with anyone he actually talked to. The list shrank from eighty-three to thirty-one.

Mr. Reyes called for attention, and Jacob closed the app. On Marisol's screen, her contest portfolio glowed, and she was still smiling at her own good news. "Thirty-one," Jacob said quietly, counting what was left of the list he used to brag about.

"It'll grow again," Marisol said. "Only slower this time."

He looked at the empty seat where the projector light fell, then logged off the computer entirely.

Alexis sat on the end of the hotel bed with one sneaker on and one in her hand, listening to the rain hammer the window. When the storm rolled in that afternoon, Dad had bailed on the campsite in a rush, dragging everyone and half the gear into the van, and now they were thirty minutes away in a room that smelled like carpet cleaner. Her little brother Theo was trying to see if he could fit entirely inside the hotel ice bucket, which he could not.

"Dad," Alexis said. "The fire pit. It was still warm when we left. I put my hand over it before we got in the van."

"It's pouring," Dad said from behind his phone. "Nothing's surviving that."

But Alexis kept thinking. Rain falls on the top of a fire pit, and the top is ash, and ash is like a blanket. Under the blanket, something could stay hot and dry while everything above it soaked. She couldn't see under there, which was exactly the problem. She thought about how the coals had looked last night, how the orange had gone gray but lumpy, like the heat was hiding rather than gone.

"Rain covers the ash," she said. "It doesn't necessarily get underneath it. Remember when it rained at home and the inside of the woodpile stayed dry?" Theo's head popped out of the ice bucket. "Are you saying the fire is a secret agent?" he asked. "Yes," Alexis said. "A secret agent of arson." Dad sighed the sigh of a man still paying the mortgage on a house he did not want to burn down along with half a state park, and reached for the van keys.

At the campsite the rain had thinned to a drizzle, and the woods around them looked lush and steaming, every leaf shiny. The fire pit was a black, soggy lump. Alexis fetched the big water jug from the van and poured the whole thing over the pit until water overflowed the stone rim. Then she grabbed a stick and stirred the drowned ashes, digging down through the layers, and a hiss rose up and a curl of steam escaped from the middle, exactly where she had guessed the blanket had been doing its job. "Ha," she said. "There you are."

She stirred until the whole pit was a cold, gray soup, then poured a second jug of water over it, because once felt like not enough. Then she did what she'd been planning the whole drive over. She pulled back her sleeve and pressed her palm flat against the ashes, holding it there. The mix was soggy and gritty and completely cool to the touch, no warmth anywhere, not even down deep where she pushed her fingers in. Theo did the same on his side and made a face. "It's like cold oatmeal," he said. "Cold oatmeal that used to be a criminal."

Back at the hotel, they came through the door dripping, and Dad went straight for the free cookies on the front desk while Mom handed out towels. "So tomorrow," Mom said, "we drive home with no secret agents?" "None," Alexis said. Theo held up his palm, still gray with ash, and said, "I kept the evidence."

Rachel's cousin Marcus had been holding court by the potato salad for ten minutes, and she was tired of it. "My coach's sister took that new cold syrup and was better in two days," he announced. "It works. Case closed."

"It's not closed," Rachel said. "That's one person. Grandma got over her cold last week with no syrup at all."

"Grandma is a tank," Marcus admitted, and half the picnic table laughed, because Grandma was currently beating Uncle Ray at arm wrestling.

Rachel wanted to settle it, and she had a tool: her science homework, an article about a real study of that exact syrup. She fetched the printout from the car, dodging Aunt Denise, who tried to delegate dish duty to her on the way past the kitchen window. "After," Rachel promised, which was what everybody said and nobody meant.

She read the article while Marcus chewed. The researchers had given the syrup to some people and a lookalike, tastelike nothing to others. What stopped her was one line: the people in the study hadn't chosen which one they got. They were assigned to their groups at random, like a coin flip, so that differences like age or health were likely to be spread evenly between the groups instead of piling up on one side. "Why random?" Marcus asked, spraying crumbs. "Why not let people just pick?"

Rachel thought about it, turning her cup around and around. "Because if volunteers picked, the healthy people might all grab the syrup, and then the syrup group would look great even if the syrup did nothing. If you flip the coin, both groups get the same mix." She looked up, pleased with herself, then less pleased. "Which means your coach's sister proves nothing. She just picked herself."

"So we test it," Marcus declared, undeterred. He stood on the picnic bench like a tiny general. "Everybody who had a cold this winter, raise a hand!"

Eleven hands went up. Rachel made two columns in her notebook, syrup and no syrup, and hunted down the details like a monsoon rolling through the party, relentless and slightly damp, since it started raining and she kept going anyway under the porch roof. Uncle Ray had taken the syrup and been sick for a week. Little Jo had taken nothing and bounced back in three days. Aunt Denise, Grandma, two second cousins, all with intricate stories of honey, soup, and one questionable sock soaked in vinegar.

The results were a beautiful, useless mess. Two of the syrup people got better fast, two didn't, and Grandma, still syrup-free, demanded to know why anyone would drink "that swamp water" when soup existed.

"So we learned nothing," Marcus said, flopping onto the bench beside her, rain dripping off his hair.

"We learned one thing," Rachel said. "Next time, we flip a coin first."

Grandma slammed down Uncle Ray's arm one final time and called across the yard, "That's my girl. Now somebody dry off the potato salad."

The cafeteria had a new poster by the milk line: JOIN THE MILLIONS WHO ALREADY SWITCHED TO VOLT SODA. Alice stopped in front of it with her tray, because beneath the giant smiling face of the pop star Dree Santino, there was nothing else. No flavor, no price, no reason at all.

"Millions," said Priya, reading over her shoulder. "That's a lot of people."

Alice frowned. "Switched to it from what? And why?" The poster didn't say. It just assumed that if everyone was drinking Volt, you would want to drink Volt too, so you wouldn't be the one person standing outside the crowd. She thought about that all through lunch, turning her carton of plain milk over in her hands like it might hold an answer.

After school, media club met in the library, and Mr. Okafor had put out stacks of magazines for their ad-cutting project. Alice flipped through them with Priya and Marcus, hunting for examples. "Look at this one," Marcus said, holding up a page. "Nine out of ten teens choose Fizz Blast." Priya found another: "Don't be the last one on your block without a Snack Rocket." It was the same trick over and over, and once Alice saw the pattern, she couldn't stop seeing it, like when you learn a word and suddenly it's everywhere.

"It's called a bandwagon appeal," Alice said, reading from a list of techniques on Mr. Okafor's handout. "It urges you to do something because everyone else is doing it. It never tells you what the thing actually does better." She tapped the Volt poster she'd sketched into her notebook. "The Dree Santino part is a celebrity testimonial too. He's probably paid to smile like that."

"Maybe," Marcus said. "But Dree is genuinely good. I'd still buy it."

For the club's bulletin board, Alice made her own counter-poster: VOLT SODA. WHAT DOES IT DO BETTER? NOTHING ON THE POSTER SAYS. She pinned it up in the hallway on Friday morning, feeling proud. By afternoon, someone had drawn a mustache on Dree's face on the original poster and written VOLT TASTES LIKE BATTERY ACID underneath, which was not what she'd meant at all. Mr. Okafor took both posters down and told her the hallway wasn't the place for unapproved materials, even clever ones.

Still, on the bus home, Priya slid into the seat beside her. "I asked my brother what Volt actually does better," she said. "He said nothing, it's just soda. Then he asked for a sip of my water." Alice laughed, but she kept looking out the window at the billboard of Dree's enormous smile going by, still promising millions, still selling nothing.

Rachel lined up the meter stick along the lab bench while her partner Marcus held the steel ball at the top of the ramp. Their assignment was due at the end of the period: measure the speed of a rolling ball using distance and time, then draw a distance-time graph. The graphs did not intimidate Rachel the way they seemed to intimidate half the class, but today the numbers were refusing to cooperate.

Marcus released the ball and Rachel clicked the stopwatch, calling out the time each time the ball crossed a chalk mark: one meter, two meters, three. They ran it three times, wrote the times in their table, and Rachel plotted the points on graph paper. Most of them climbed in a neat diagonal line. But between two meters and three meters, the points went sideways, the same distance for a whole stretch of seconds.

"Your timing is off," Marcus said, peering over her shoulder.

"My timing was fine." Rachel tapped the flat stretch with her pencil. "Same distance, different times. Something happened to the ball right there."

She looked down the bench. Halfway along, someone had left a lump of dried glue near the two-meter mark. She crouched until her eyes were level with the surface. The glue sat exactly where the graph went flat.

They ran it again with Marcus watching that spot instead of the stopwatch. The ball rolled, hit the glue, wobbled, and sat there for a moment before creeping over the edge. It was stuck, briefly, in the same place while time kept going.

"That's it," Rachel said. She marked the glue spot in her notes, then scraped the lump off with a spatula and wiped the bench down. "Do it again."

The fourth run produced a clean set of points. Rachel plotted them, and this time the line climbed steadily from corner to corner, no flat part anywhere. She calculated the speed by dividing the distance by the time and got nearly the same answer for every stretch of the run. Marcus leaned over to check her arithmetic and frowned at the earlier graph still lying beside it.

"So that flat part," he said, "what does that even tell you?"

"It means the ball wasn't moving," Rachel said. "Stuck on the glue, not going anywhere."

She stapled both graphs to their lab sheet, the flat one and the clean one, and wrote a sentence under the first: ball caught on glue between two and three meters. Then she flipped the glue lump into the trash with the spatula.

"Same time tomorrow?" Marcus asked, packing up his bag.

"Bring your own stopwatch," Rachel said. "And somebody should warn the sixth period class about that bench before their turn."

Blake had saved twenty-two dollars from mowing lawns, and he intended to spend every cent on the one thing he had wanted since March: a plush shark from the kiosk near the food court. He walked past the transparent glass of the aquarium store, where a wall of fish tanks emitted a soft blue glow, and smelled popcorn and soy sauce drifting from the food court. Then he saw the kiosk, and he saw the price sign, and his stomach dropped. The shark, which had cost eighteen dollars in April, was now thirty-five. A line of six kids stretched from the counter toward the pretzel stand.

"You're kidding," Blake said to the kiosk owner, a woman with gray braids.

"Everyone wants them since that video," she said. "I only get ten a week from my supplier. When I run out, people offer me more than the sticker price just to hold the next one."

Blake walked away with his money still folded in his pocket. At the far end of the food court, farmers had set up long tables for a weekend market inside the mall, which happened once a month. He drifted toward it because it was quieter there, and because a crate of strawberries caught his eye. A hand-lettered sign read: Two baskets for four dollars. He blinked. In April, at the market by his grandmother's house, one small basket had cost four dollars.

He picked up a basket and turned it over. The berries were dark red all the way to the stem, and the whole table smelled sweet, like jam before it cooked. Behind the strawberries, a fish farmer was laying out salmon on ice, and Blake overheard him tell a customer, "It comes from the estuary, where the river meets the sound, so it's fresh as anything."

"Why so cheap now?" Blake asked the strawberry farmer, a man with dirt still under his fingernails. "These were double the price last month."

"It's the peak of the local harvest," the farmer said. "I've got more than I can pick."

Blake stood there holding his basket, and an idea began to form, quiet and slow, the way the light from the tanks had glowed. Six kids had lined up for ten plush sharks. Here, a whole table sagged under more strawberries than the farmer could pick. Scarce and wanted meant expensive. Plentiful meant cheap. He wanted to see if the idea held somewhere else, so he walked back toward the pretzel stand, where a vendor was throwing away a tray of day-old cinnamon twists. "A dollar each," the vendor called to anyone passing. "Way less than lunchtime, before they ran out by one o'clock." An hour ago, Blake remembered, that same tray had emptied fast at full price.

He carried his two baskets of strawberries to a table by the tanks, where his friend Marisol was doing homework. He set one basket in front of her.

"Those cost four dollars?" she said. "For both?"

"Peak harvest," Blake said, and ate a strawberry, which was warm from sitting in the sun of the skylight, and so sweet he closed his eyes for a second.

The spelling bee was held in the back corner of the public library, between the biography shelves and a radiator that clanked like it had opinions. Sofia sat in the second row, mouthing words to herself. Her real problem was sitting in the first row: Marcus, whose cousin lived in Canada, and who had spent all week insisting that "colour" was the correct spelling and that Americans had ruined everything.

"Round three," announced the librarian, Ms. Okafor. "Sofia. Your word is 'condense'."

Sofia pictured steam turning to droplets on a cold window. "C-O-N-D-E-N-S-E. Condense."

"Correct." Ms. Okafor shuffled her cards, then paused. "Interesting. Round four will be our vocabulary bonus round. The word is 'arid'. Use it in a sentence to earn two extra points."

"Arizona is so arid that even the cactuses look thirsty," Sofia said, and half the audience laughed.

Marcus got "intestine," spelled it, and whispered, "You're going down," as he passed her chair. Then Ms. Okafor said the word Sofia had been dreading and hoping for at the same time.

"Colour."

The room went quiet. "Color," Sofia said slowly. "Or colour? Which country are we in?"

"Spellers may ask for the word's origin," Ms. Okafor said cheerfully.

"Origin, please."

"This spelling comes to English through French."

Sofia's brain spun. French spelling would be "colour," with the u. But Marcus kept saying his Canadian cousin spelled it that way, and Canada used British spellings, and they were not in Canada. She had a theory, and only one way to test it. "C-O-L-O-R. Color."

"Correct."

Marcus shot up from his seat. "That's wrong! My cousin Dara spells it colour! She says Americans just randomly dropped the u!"

Sofia marched to the reference shelf, pulled down the big dictionary, and flipped until she found the word history box beside "color." Marcus leaned over her shoulder, still fuming.

"Look at this," Sofia said. "Noah Webster's 1828 American Dictionary of the English Language promoted simpler spellings like color instead of colour. And those spellings became standard in the United States."

"So it wasn't random," Marcus said slowly.

"Nope. It was Webster. You can be mad at a person, which is way more satisfying."

Marcus studied the page, then grinned. "Fine. But Dara's still going to say Webster was wrong."

"Tell her to take it up with the radiator," Sofia said, and patted the clanking pipe like an old friend.

Arthur slid the chicken breasts out of the refrigerator and lined them up on the counter like pale little pillows. Family dinner night had been his idea this semester, ever since his grandmother announced she would retire from cooking the Sunday meal and hand the job to whoever wanted it. His sister wanted takeout. Arthur wanted to cook it himself, in the school's kitchen classroom, where the ovens actually worked and there were drawers full of real tools.

He found the tool he wanted right away: a digital thermometer with a thin metal probe. His grandmother had always judged chicken by slicing it open and checking that the juices ran clear and the meat looked white. But Arthur had read the guidelines taped inside the cabinet door, and he kept turning one line over in his mind: U.S. food safety guidelines say poultry is safely cooked when its thickest part reaches 165 degrees Fahrenheit, or about 74 degrees Celsius, measured with a food thermometer. Not color. Not juices. A number, checked in the thickest part. Could the outside look done while the inside was still dangerous? He wanted to find out.

He set the oven, laid the chicken in a baking dish, and slid it in. While it cooked, his classmate Marisol came over to watch. "My mom just pokes it with a fork," she said.

"That's guessing," Arthur said. "The thermometer measures the actual temperature in the middle. That's where the chicken is thickest, so that's where you check." He tapped the cabinet card. "It has to reach 165 degrees Fahrenheit, which is about 74 degrees Celsius."

He was hesitant at first about where to stick the probe, worried he would hit the pan and get a false reading. So he tried a small experiment. He slid the probe into the side of one breast, angling it toward the center of the thickest part, and watched the numbers climb: 130, 148, 157. He pulled it out, wiped it, and tested a second breast, then a third. They read 160, 155, and 161. Same oven, same pan, different temperatures. The pieces weren't cooking evenly, and guessing by color would never have caught that.

He slid the pan back in for five more minutes and tested again. This time all three probes settled at 165 or higher, and the smallest one read 170. He wondered whether the big pieces had hidden cold spots too, so he checked each one twice, in different spots, like a doctor double-checking a diagnosis before telling anyone the news. Every reading held.

At home that evening, his family gathered around the table. His grandmother cut into her chicken, looked at the white meat, and raised an eyebrow at him.

"Tested it three ways," Arthur said, and set the thermometer down beside her plate. "It hit 165 in the thickest part. You can check."

Elijah got to the park ten minutes early, which he decided was exactly the wrong amount of early, because now he had time to think about everything that could go wrong. Maya was meeting him by the fountain at two. He had rehearsed a list of questions on the bus, and at the top of it was the one he was surest about: Do you like school?

She showed up right on time, and they walked to the coffee kiosk by the playground. He bought two hot chocolates even though it was eighty degrees out, because it was the first thing he'd planned and he couldn't think fast enough to change it.

"Do you like school?" he asked as they sat down on the bench.

Maya shrugged. "Yeah."

"Do you like this park?"

"Yeah. It's nice."

The conversation kept dying like that, question, one word, silence, question, one word, silence. Elijah could feel the afternoon leaking away. He stared at the fountain and tried to figure out what was happening. It wasn't that Maya didn't want to be there, he thought, because she kept glancing at him like she was waiting for something. The trouble seemed to be with the questions themselves, though he couldn't see that directly. He ran back through them. Do you like school. Do you like this park. Do you like hot chocolate. He noticed a pattern: every question he'd asked could be answered with a single word and then it was over, like a door that only opened one inch.

He decided to test it. "What's a class you'd take if school let you invent one?" he asked.

Maya put down her cup. "That's actually a good question. I'd take a class on propaganda, like how ads and posters get you to believe stuff without you noticing. My grandpa has all these old posters from a country that doesn't even exist anymore, and some of them are beautiful and completely terrifying." She talked for two whole minutes, and then she asked him a question back, and he elaborated on his answer about a class on haunted bridges until she was laughing so hard she nearly spilled her hot chocolate.

"Okay, your turn to answer the class one," she said, tapping his arm. "For real."

"A class on how to talk to people," he said. "Because apparently yes-or-no questions are terrible and I only just figured that out."

Maya stopped laughing and looked at him strangely, and for one long second he worried he'd said something wrong. Then she said, "Wait. You did that on purpose? You changed your questions halfway through?"

He nodded, bracing himself.

"That is the nerdiest, most impressive thing anyone has ever done on a date with me," she said, and grabbed the last of his hot chocolate, and pointed toward the playground. "Race you to the swings."

The candle flames fluctuated every time Isaac's little sister, Prue, breathed, which she was doing on purpose. "Stop huffing at the candles," he said. "The power's already out. You don't have to blow out the rest of it."

"I'm not huffing. I'm sighing. It's different." She sighed again, and two flames wobbled in agreement.

Isaac leaned back on the couch and thought about why the whole street had gone dark at exactly 7:04. It hadn't flickered or faltered the way it did in ordinary storms, dropping out in stages as the voltage seemed to fluctuate before failing. This had been one clean cut, every house at once, like someone had snipped a single thread. A single thread meant a single point of failure somewhere near the top of the street. He had a guess about exactly where.

"That face you're making," Prue said, "is your detective face. It's not robust enough for a real mystery. You look like a kid who lost a sock."

"It's not a sock." He got up, took the flashlight from the drawer, and angled it out the front window. Halfway up the block, right where the big oak leaned over the road, something thin and black lay draped across the sidewalk. He felt a cold little jolt in his stomach. He and his friend Marcus had walked under that oak at 6:50, fourteen minutes before the lights died.

"Stay here," he told Prue, and he went out the front door and stood at the edge of the porch, well back from the sidewalk, and called Marcus.

"You seeing what I'm seeing?" Marcus answered on the second ring.

"The wire across the walk. Marcus, we walked right past that spot before the lights went out."

"So it fell after us. Lucky us. I already told my dad and he called it in. He says a fallen line can still be deadly even when it's not sparking. Treat it as live, stay well away, get it reported." A pause. "Which we did. So technically I solved the mystery before you even made your detective face."

"You can't see my face over the phone."

"I can hear it. It's not robust."

When the utility truck finally came, its amber lights sweeping the candles in the living room into a slow gold tide, Prue tugged Isaac's sleeve. "So the wire was the whole problem? One wire?"

"One wire that looked dead and wasn't taking any chances," Isaac said. "Some things you don't poke to find out."

"Like you," said Prue, and huffed out a candle.

Madison wanted one thing before lunch: to post the selfie she had taken on her front porch that morning, the one where her new braces made her grin look lopsided in a way she actually liked. She sat down at the computer lab's last open machine, opened her photo folder, and got the picture on screen. Behind her shoulder, blurry but there, stood the blue mailbox at the end of her driveway.

"You going to post that?" Deshawn asked from the next seat, spinning his chair around.

"After I check it," Madison said. She zoomed in on the background. On the porch railing, plain as anything, sat the little metal numbers her dad had screwed in when they moved in. 314. Behind those, at the curb, the green street sign read ELMONT ST. She sat back. She had learned the hard way, from a cyber safety assembly video two weeks ago, that a stranger could work out where a photo was taken from exactly this kind of thing, a street sign, a house number, even a school logo on a shirt.

She opened the image editor and cropped the picture tight around her face. The railing, the numbers, the sign all dropped away, and the photo transformed into something she felt okay about.
