Then she tested her idea the way the video had suggested. She picked a random picture from the class trip album on the shared drive, a group shot outside the science museum, and zoomed in. There in the corner was the museum's banner with its address printed along the bottom. Anyone looking at that picture could figure out where forty kids from her school had been standing on a Tuesday morning. She deleted her copy of the album and messaged Priya, who had taken it, to do the same.

"That's the whole mechanism," Madison said to Deshawn, pointing at the banner on screen. "It's not some invisible tracking thing. It's just stuff in the background."

Deshawn leaned over and looked for a long moment. "Huh," he said. He pulled out his phone, found the selfie he'd posted that morning, and stared at it. In the background, over his shoulder, his little brother stood grinning in front of their front door, wearing his soccer jersey with the Riverside Middle bobcat stretched across the chest.

"Take it down?" Madison asked.

"Already did," Deshawn said, still tapping. He held up the phone to show her the delete confirmation, and behind it, on his screen, sat a comment from an account with no picture and a name she'd never seen: "Nice house on 314 Elmont, by the way."

Justin sat in the back row of Room 12 with his ankle propped on his backpack, the brace stiff against his swollen tendon. He had skipped basketball practice, which was voluntary anyway, but the whole day felt like a list of things taken away from him. Now Mr. Okafor had assigned an essay: explain why people moved west in the 1800s, using one primary source. Justin had picked the fattest book off the cart, a modern textbook with a shiny cover and a chapter called "Westward Expansion."

"You grabbed the wrong thing," said Priya, leaning over from the next desk. "That's not what he means."

"It's got everything. Maps, dates, a whole section on reasons." Justin flipped pages at her. "Land, gold, jobs."

Priya shook her head. "My cousin had this assignment last year. A primary source is something made at the time by a person who lived through an event, like a settler's diary. A secondary source is written later by someone studying it. Your textbook is the second one."

Justin looked at the shiny cover, then at the cart, where a thin pamphlet with a brown spine sat ignored at the bottom. He pulled it out. It was a copy of a diary kept by a woman named Harriet Lane, who had walked part of the trail in 1852 with her husband and two boys. He started reading, mostly to prove Priya wrong.

The first entry talked about rain and mud. The second mentioned that their wheat had germinated in the wagon after a soaking, and how Harriet's husband laughed because it meant they'd been carrying wet seed for weeks. Then, deeper in, Justin found what the textbook never said. Harriet's husband owed money to a bank in Ohio, and one of the boys had a cough that wouldn't clear in the damp river town. "We do not go for gold," she wrote. "We go because the debt man comes on Fridays and the doctor says drier air. Isaac cries at night and pretends he doesn't."

Justin copied the line into his notebook. The textbook said "economic opportunity," which covered the debt but not the crying, not the doctor, not Fridays. The diary showed the reason from inside a person who was actually there, and he could suddenly see the pattern the textbook flattened out: the big words were made of small ones like these. He raised his hand and asked to change his source, and Mr. Okafor nodded and made a note on his clipboard, which meant someone else would have to fight over the remaining diaries.

At the last bell Priya found him at his locker. "So I was right," she said.

"You were right," Justin admitted. He handed her the pamphlet, since he'd already photographed the pages he needed, and she grinned and hurried off down the hall. He stood there a moment, weight on his good foot, thinking of Harriet's boys coughing in the mud while seeds sprouted in the wagon bed. His essay would be the best thing he'd written all year, and he'd never play in Friday's game. He zipped his backpack, swung it over one shoulder, and limped toward the doors.

Hannah stood at the edge of the gymnasium in her one nice dress and watched the fog machine do its work under the basketball hoop. The thermostat on the wall said the custodian had lost some kind of war, because the room was freezing and half the dance committee was huddled near the speakers like penguins. She had wanted to come to this dance for one reason: Priya was going to be there, and Hannah had spent two weeks deciding whether to say anything about that, and had settled on the brave strategy of standing near the punch table and hoping fate would handle it.

Fate, so far, had handled nothing.

Then Marcus appeared at the door with a box of glow stick bracelets for the seventh graders, and one of them wasn't working. He snapped it, shook it, held it to the light like it owed him money. "Where's the light even coming from in these?" he said. "There's no battery."

"Maybe you cracked it wrong," said his friend Dominic.

Hannah took the bracelet and turned it over. She bent it slowly and felt, inside the plastic, a tiny stiff thing give way with a click, like a small bone. The tube lit up green along half its length. She bent the dark half the same careful way and felt a second click, and the whole bracelet glowed.

"There's a little glass vial inside," she said. "Bending breaks it."

"That's it?" said Marcus.

"And the vial has hydrogen peroxide in it. When it breaks, it mixes with other chemicals and a dye that are in the rest of the tube. That's the light."

"Does that have a name?" Dominic asked. "It feels like it has a name."

"It's called chemiluminescence," Hannah said. "My cousin worked at a party supply store and said it about forty times."

Marcus began snapping bracelets with scientific interest, and the sound began to irritate Ms. Reyes, who was guarding the door, because every seventh grader in a ten-foot radius now wanted one and the box was not infinite. Hannah flexed the bracelet onto her wrist and noticed Priya had drifted over to watch the snapping.

"You broke it and it got better," Priya said.

"Only works once," Hannah said. "Then you just have to enjoy the glow while it lasts."

Priya held out her wrist, the unbroken bracelet dangling. "Show me?"

Hannah clicked it green, and the two of them walked out onto the floor under the hoop, where the fog was finally doing something beautiful.

The food bank shared a parking lot with the seniors' residence, so Gavin's mom dropped him at the front door of the residence first, where a volunteer named Dora was pushing a cart of grocery boxes down the hallway. "You must be the new helper," she said. "We're doing deliveries today. Some of the folks here can't carry a box up the stairs, so we bring it to them."

Gavin took half the stack and followed her. He had expected the food bank to be a warehouse with long lines, and he'd pictured something quieter too, a building full of people who never spoke. That second picture fell apart at the second door, where Mr. Hall greeted them with a joke about the elevator being slower than his old tractor.

At the fourth door, a woman named Mrs. Okafor counted the cans in her box twice. "Tuna, beans, rice, peaches," she said. "Same as last month. And the month before." She didn't sound ungrateful, but she didn't sound happy either. On the walk back, Gavin noticed she was the only one who had counted.

He wondered about that the whole afternoon. Maybe she was worried the supply was running low, or maybe she was checking whether anyone had taken something out. He couldn't see the reason directly, so he tested a simple idea: he asked Dora what Mrs. Okafor liked to cook. "Soups," Dora said. "But she never says so, because she thinks complaining about a free box sounds rude."

The next week, Gavin slipped a note into the signup sheet the food bank used for donations, marking Mrs. Okafor's building for a soup drive. When the boxes went out again, hers held broth and barley and a bag of dried lentils. She counted the cans as usual, then stopped at the lentils and smiled at them for a long moment. "Well," she said. "Somebody was paying attention."

In the hallway afterward, Mrs. Okafor caught up with them. "Can I ask you something, dear? How long have food banks existed in this country? I came here in the seventies, and I don't remember any." Gavin had looked this up at the library only the day before, hoping someone would ask. "Canada's first food bank opened in 1981," he said, "in Edmonton, Alberta." She repeated the words like she was tasting them. "Eighty-one. I'd been here ten years by then."

The following Tuesday, Mrs. Okafor was waiting by the door with a pot of lentil soup, enough for the whole hallway. Mr. Hall brought spoons from his room. Gavin carried the pot carefully to the common room, both hands steady, and set it in the middle of the table.

The gym smelled like floor wax and old sneakers, and Dominic sat on the bleachers with his laptop balanced on his knee, trying to build his first debate case before Friday's round. The resolution was about building wildlife corridors so animals could move between fragmented forests. He knew what he wanted to argue. He just couldn't figure out how.

"You're staring at a blank page," said Priya, dropping onto the bench beside him with her own notebook. "Claim, evidence, warrant. Remember?"

"That's the problem. I have the claim. Corridors help the ecosystem recover. I have the evidence, the study showing more species survived where corridors were built. I don't have the warrant."

"Then write down why your evidence proves your claim."

He tried. He typed, deleted, typed again. Then he flashed back to Tuesday's practice round, when Marcus from the other team had stood up and told a long story about a single mountain lion that died trying to cross a highway. The room had gone quiet. Everyone felt terrible for that mountain lion. But then Dominic's team had read three statistics about survival rates, and the judge had voted for the numbers anyway. Marcus had slammed his notebook shut and said, "I don't get it. My story was better."

Dominic had gotten it wrong too, at first. He'd thought the judge was being cold. But his sister, home from college, had glanced at his notes and said, "Aristotle figured this out a long time ago. In his Rhetoric he described three ways to persuade: ethos, the speaker's credibility; pathos, the audience's emotions; and logos, reasoning and evidence." She'd tapped his page. "Marcus had pathos and nothing else. You had logos. That's why you won."

Back in the gym, Dominic looked at his blank warrant. He tested an idea. If he wrote, "The study shows survival rates rose when corridors existed, therefore corridors cause survival to rise," that was a warrant, but a weak one. He frowned at it. Maybe the problem was that his evidence only matched his claim if the reader accepted that what happened in the studied forests would happen everywhere. So the warrant had to say that. He typed: places with similar conditions produce similar results, so evidence from comparable forests applies to the plan in the resolution.

"Got it?" Priya asked.

"Test it," he said. "Hit me with an objection."

"The study's from another country. Doesn't apply here."

"That's an attack on my warrant," Dominic said, and grinned. "Last week I wouldn't have even known that's what you were doing. You'd have just sounded stubborn."

"Obstinate," Priya said. "The word is obstinate."

"Fine. You're obstinate, and I answer it." He held up his screen. "Same climate, same species, same road density. It applies."

Priya read the page, then nodded once. "Okay. Now do the mountain lion story."

"For pathos?"

"For the judge who's also a person," she said, and turned her laptop toward him. "We'll put it last."

Dominic dragged the story of the mountain lion to the end of the case file and hit save.

Mrs. Ortega had said little Sophie would be asleep by eight, and she was, so Megan stood alone in the lamplit living room with forty minutes of quiet and her phone at nine percent. She was supposed to be reading for English, and instead she was doing what she always did in a strange house: looking at everything.

The coffee table held a mug of cold tea, a scatter of mail, and a bottle of children's vitamins, orange and shaped like bears, sitting right at toddler height. Megan remembered her mother dragging a chair to the pantry one afternoon, muttering that medicines and cleaning products belong up high and out of reach, because little kids explore by putting things in their mouths. Megan had rolled her eyes at the time, thirteen and full of small rebellions, and had not helped move the bottles. She picked up the vitamins now and looked around the room. Under the sink she found dish soap and a spray bottle of cleaner, crouched there like they were hiding. She carried everything to the highest kitchen shelf, the one perpendicular to the doorway where Sophie could not see it even if she stood on a chair. Then she sat back down, feeling both pleased and slightly ridiculous, since Sophie was asleep and would probably stay asleep.

Twenty minutes later Sophie appeared in the hallway, barefoot and wailing, and Megan's ridiculous feeling evaporated. She scooped the girl up, found the sippy cup, and walked her slowly around the living room to settle her. Sophie stopped crying almost at once. Then she leaned over Megan's arm and reached, with the calm certainty of someone who knew exactly what she wanted, toward the empty spot on the coffee table where the vitamins used to be. She opened her mouth and made a little chomping motion, like a goldfish.

"So that's where they always are," Megan whispered. Her whole body went cold and then hot. She had moved the vitamins because of something her mother once said, without really believing it mattered, and now the proof was dangling from her arms, smacking her lips at a bare patch of wood. Sophie had been sneaking bears off that table all along, quietly, whenever someone left them out. Probably not enough to hurt her. Probably. Megan made a note to tell Mrs. Ortega exactly where the bottle had been sitting, and how many might be missing, even if it meant admitting she had gone through the cupboards.

She rocked Sophie until the girl's eyes closed, then lowered her into the crib with the care of someone defusing a bomb. When Mrs. Ortega's headlights swept the window, Megan was sitting on the couch with her English book open, though she had read the same page three times.

"Everything okay?" Mrs. Ortega asked, keys still in her hand.

"Mostly," Megan said. "But we should talk about the vitamins."

Mrs. Ortega's eyes went straight to the empty coffee table, and she said, "Oh no. Not again."

Arthur had forty minutes before the book club's shared folder locked at four o'clock, and his paraphrase of Macbeth's "Tomorrow" speech was still a mess. The five of them met in the corner of the school library every Thursday, and today Ms. Okonkwo had told them their written responses had to follow proper MLA format when they uploaded them. Arthur didn't know what that meant, exactly, but Priya did, and Priya noticed everything.

"You quoted the whole speech inside your sentences," Priya said, leaning over his laptop screen. "It's swimming."

"It's my favorite passage," Arthur said. "I want all of it in there."

"Then you can't keep it inside a sentence." Priya scrolled through her own response until she found an example. "Watch. In MLA style, a prose quotation longer than four lines is set as an indented block, half an inch from the margin, without quotation marks." She highlighted her block, and Arthur saw the passage sitting alone on its own lines, pushed inward, with no quotation marks anywhere around it. "Long ones get their own room. Short ones live inside your sentence."

Arthur tested it right away. He copied the speech into a draft and counted lines on his screen. It ran past four lines, so he hit Tab once, watched the whole thing slide half an inch from the margin, and deleted the quotation marks. Then he counted again to be sure. Four was the cutoff, and he was over it. "So if I trimmed it to exactly four," he said slowly, "it could go back inside the sentence?"

"If it fits," Priya said. "But why would you cut your favorite part to squeeze it into a sentence?"

She was right, and Arthur knew it before he finished nodding. Instead of trimming the quote, he worked on the paraphrase beneath it. That was the actual assignment: take Macbeth's speech and say it in modern English. "Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow" became "one day after another after another, dragging along." He tried to condense the whole speech into a few plain lines, the way Dex had done with his scene from Romeo and Juliet last week. Dex had made the balcony speech sound like two kids texting, which everyone agreed was terrible and also, somehow, completely authentic to the way people actually talked.

Arthur kept circling one part. Macbeth says life is "a walking shadow, a poor player that struts and frets his hour upon the stage and then is heard no more." Arthur wrote and crossed out three versions. It wasn't just about a bad actor. It was about everything ending, the way a species can vanish into extinction and leave nothing behind but a gap where it used to be. Macbeth was saying people were like that too. He wrote, "We're shadows that walk around for a while, make noise, and then nothing."

Dex read it over his shoulder. "That's grim."

"It's the play," Arthur said. "It's already grim. I'm just translating."

The clock on the wall read 3:47. Priya checked the folder, Marcus uploaded his, and then it was Arthur's turn. He looked once more at his block of quotation, indented half an inch from the margin, no quotation marks, four-plus lines on its own. The paraphrase sat under it in his own words. He hit upload, and the progress bar crawled toward done.

"Thirteen seconds to spare," Priya announced.

Arthur closed the laptop. "Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow," he said, "except there's no folder after today."

Alexa needed the green pen. Mr. Okafor had promised the two students who wrote the most accurate product reviews for the class energy-unit project a chance to test the new solar panels after school, and Alexa had wanted to touch those panels since September. The problem was the worksheet, which asked them to sort sentences from real reviews into two piles: facts you could check, and everything else. She had underlined half of her review and could not say why.

Beside her, Marcus was already on his third review, tapping his pencil like a drummer. "This one's easy," he whispered. "It says the hand-crank flashlight is the best on the market. Best. That's just somebody talking." He moved on before Alexa could ask how he knew.

Alexa stared at her own page. The rechargeable battery pack review said the design was beautiful, the instructions were boring, and the company should include a spare cord. Beautiful. Boring. Should. She said the words under her breath and felt something click, the way it did when a graph finally showed its pattern. Those words were judgments. You could not check them the way you could check "the battery holds 2,000 milliamp hours" or "the cord is one meter long." If a sentence leaned on best, worst, beautiful, boring, or should, it was almost always someone's opinion dressed up as information. "Judgment words," she murmured, and circled every one.

She started generating sentences to test the idea, one plain fact and one judgment word, over and over, like mixing chemicals to see which combination reacted. "The fan runs at two speeds" went in the check pile. "The fan is the worst gift ever" went in the other. It worked every time. She raised her hand so fast her chair squeaked, and when Mr. Okafor called on her, she laid out her rule in forty seconds flat. He asked her to write it on the board for the class vote, since they graded each other's projects by simple democracy, hands up, majority rules.

The vote was close. Marcus got the second panel slot by one hand, and it was Alexa's own friend Priya who raised it, because Priya's review was the one Alexa had gently pulled apart in front of everyone, all those shoulds and bests laid bare on the overhead projector. Priya had laughed, but not really.

At three o'clock Alexa stood at the window watching Marcus clip the panel to its stand outside, his breath fogging the glass. The class had asked to borrow her list of judgment words, and Mr. Okafor had called her method legitimate, which was worth more than a slot on a Wednesday afternoon. Still. She pressed one finger against the cold pane.

"Save me a turn," she called through the crack in the window, and Marcus, without looking up, tilted the panel half a degree toward her.

Alex had promised Mr. Delgado he would finish his history project today, which was why he was sitting on the cold steps of the war memorial with a photocopied settler's diary spread across his knees. The assignment seemed fundamental to his grade: use a primary source, an actual person's own words, to explain why families moved west in the 1800s. The diary's handwriting slanted and cramped, and the wind kept lifting the pages like it wanted them to go west too.

"Careful, that paper's older than my knees," said Mr. Okafor, the volunteer who polished the memorial plaques every Saturday. He set a smooth stone on the corner of the pages and settled onto the step beside Alex. His hands were trembling a little today, so Alex held the polish cloth while Mr. Okafor guided the rag in slow circles over the bronze.

Alex read aloud a line where the settler wrote that his brother's farm had failed and prices had fallen so low that staying meant losing everything. "That's it," Alex said. "Hard times pushed them. But how do I prove that's a pattern and not just one grumpy guy?" He flipped to the back of the packet, where a second family wrote almost the same thing, and a third. Same push, different pens. That felt like evidence, not luck.

Then his eye caught the longest plaque, the one Mr. Okafor was polishing. Names from two wars, and at the bottom an inscription about the peace that followed the first. "Mr. Okafor, my great-grandpa's on this wall. After that war, didn't they make Germany shrink its army? How did it get big again so fast for the second one?"

Mr. Okafor tapped the line he'd just cleaned. Alex leaned close and read it aloud. "The Treaty of Versailles limited the German army to 100,000 soldiers and banned Germany from having an air force." He read it twice. An entire air force, gone, by rule. And still, twenty years later, planes everywhere and armies in the millions. "So the rule didn't hold," Alex said slowly. "Somebody broke it, and my great-grandpa ended up on this wall anyway." He copied the sentence into his notebook, word for word, the way he'd copied the diary lines. Two sources, two wars, one habit: go to what people wrote at the time.

"You know what your problem is, Alex?" Mr. Okafor said, and Alex braced himself. "You think you have to finish everything in one day." He nodded at the notebook. "Read it to your grandfather tonight. He knows more about all this than any plaque."

Alex looked down the long list of names, then at the diary pages weighted by the stone, and started folding them into his backpack with the care of someone carrying something borrowed. "Grandpa," he said, testing the plan out loud. "I brought you some homework."

Samantha adjusted the fine focus knob one hair's width at a time, and the onion skin slide snapped into view like magic. Sort of. The cells looked like pale bricks stacked in rows, and she could see the thick cell walls easily, plus the thin membrane hugging the inside edge. The problem was the nucleus. Her lab sheet had a diagram with an arrow pointing to a dark dot, but her cells showed nothing but faint gray outlines.

Maybe her stain had failed. She had dripped the iodine the way the directions said, but the drop had pooled at the edge of the coverslip instead of soaking through. She peeled off the coverslip, added one smaller drop right onto the tissue, and lowered the glass again slowly so no bubbles would sneak underneath.

"You look intense," said Marcus from the next stool. He was already labeling his drawing, smug about it.

"Can you actually see the nucleus?" Samantha asked.

He leaned back from his eyepiece. "Kind of? A speck. I think."

She returned to her microscope. This time, in three cells near the center, dark little spots floated inside the gray. That was it. She drew the cells on her sheet, careful to coordinate the arrows on her diagram with what she actually saw, and not with the printed example. She wrote cell wall, cell membrane, nucleus.

Then she stopped, pencil hovering. "Who figured out that dot was a thing? Somebody had to be the first person to look and say, there's a spot."

Marcus shrugged, but Priya across the table said, "I read about it in a weird old book at my uncle's house. The Scottish botanist Robert Brown described the cell nucleus in 1831 while studying orchid cells." She said it fast, like she was afraid she'd forget a word.

"Orchids," Samantha repeated. "So he saw it in flower cells, not onions."

"Flower cells first. Then it works everywhere."

Samantha tested the idea. There were prepared slides in the wooden box at the front, including one of orchid tissue. If the same dark spot showed up in both the orchid and her onion, then the nucleus wasn't some onion quirk or a mistake in her staining. It was a rule about cells. She carried the orchid slide back, swapped it in, and focused.

Dark spots. Same as hers, just bigger.

"Ha!" She waved Priya over. "Look. Mine and yours match."

Priya bent to the eyepiece and grinned. "You just did what he did, only with two plants."

"Two plants and a lot of iodine," Samantha said.

That evening she wrote her lab report and taped an extra note inside the cover, addressed to her older cousin Elena, who had mailed her the little magnifying glass that started all of it. "Dear Elena," she wrote, "today I saw the same dark dot in onion cells and orchid cells, the one Robert Brown described in 1831. My first slide had no dot at all, so I restained it and it worked. Being a scientist might be feasible after all. Your (possibly future) favorite botanist, Samantha." She drew a tiny cell at the bottom, with three careful labels and an arrow pointing at the dot.

She sealed the envelope and set it on the counter by her lunchbox for morning.

Eve slid her debate notes across the desk and checked the clock above the whiteboard. Fifteen minutes until her turn, and her argument still had a hole in the middle of it. The topic on the board read, "Why do two people watch the same event and walk away certain of different things?" Mr. Reyes had written it up that morning and refused to say more, which Eve thought was unfair, since the whole class kept raising their hands and he kept saying, "Work it out with each other."

"I'm saying the security camera settles it," Marcus whispered beside her. He wanted to win, that was plain; he'd said twice already that he never lost a debate. "The sensor over the gym door recorded the whole thing. Facts are facts."

"But my cousin Priya saw the fight from the bleachers, and she swears Deshawn shoved first," Eve said. "And my other cousin Jamal was standing right next to Deshawn, and he swears Deshawn only put his hands up." She looked down at her notes. Both cousins had been at the same family barbecue afterward, each one calling the other blind or stubborn, and Eve had spent the whole evening wondering how two honest people could end up so angry at each other over one hallway shoving match.

She flipped through her sister's psychology book, which she'd brought because the cover promised something about perception. There it was, a sentence she'd underlined the night before: naive realism is the belief that we see the world as it really is, so people who disagree with us must be uninformed or biased. She read it twice. That was Priya exactly, and it was Jamal too, and if she was honest, it was also her, sitting there certain that Priya was the reasonable one because Priya was her favorite cousin.

"Three minutes," Mr. Reyes called out.

Eve grabbed her pencil. She could incorporate the idea into her opening, right after the camera part, so Marcus's facts wouldn't collapse the moment she mentioned cousins. She scribbled fast, then tapped his arm. "You're doing it right now," she said. "You think the sensor footage is just the truth, so anybody who reads it differently must be dumb or lying. That has a name."

Marcus frowned at her notes. "So what, nobody can be wrong?"

"I don't know yet," Eve admitted. Behind them, Mr. Reyes stood and pointed at the clock.

"Eve and Marcus, you're up."

Marcus grabbed his cards. "Fine," he muttered, "but if the camera says I'm right, I'm saying so first."

Brooke had forty dollars of birthday money in her pocket and a plan: a new backpack from the mall's sporting goods store. But on the way, she passed the bank kiosk near the fountain, where a poster showed two lines climbing side by side over five years. Simple interest grew in a straight staircase. Compound interest curved upward, because each year's interest earned interest of its own. She stared at the graph until her cousin Dana elbowed her.

"You're doing money homework at the mall? Tragic," Dana said.

"There's a difference," Brooke said. She grabbed a flyer and a pen from the counter. "If I put forty dollars in at simple interest, I get the same flat amount every year. Compounding pays me on the whole balance, so it accelerates." She sketched five quick boxes on the back of the flyer, doubling her totals in her head, and the numbers diverged by year three. The compound line pulled away like the fast lane on the escalator.

Then she spotted a display card beside the poster: a corporate bond paying nearly twice the interest of the savings account. Twice. She turned to Dana. "Why would anyone pick the savings account? This is obviously better."

"Nothing's obviously better," Dana said. "When we got our apartment lease, Mom said the landlord had to accommodate her service dog or we'd walk. Landlords who want something from you have to give something up." Dana tapped the card. "So ask yourself what the borrower wants from you and what they're giving up."

Brooke frowned and pulled up a finance page on her phone, typing in the bond's name. The rating was far below the top grades. She read the entry twice. "These are called junk bonds," she said slowly. "Companies that are more likely to fail to pay have to offer higher interest to get anyone to lend to them. That's why it pays double. It's not free money, it's a warning sticker." The page also called them high-yield, which sounded glamorous until she remembered what the yield was compensating for.

"So what do you do?" Dana asked.

Brooke laid the flyer flat on the counter and made two columns. The savings account had a small, certain rate that compounded every year; the bond had a big rate attached to a borrower who might not pay her back at all. She thought of it like a variable in math class: one thing she could hold constant, and one thing that could swing either way. "The credible choice is the boring one," she said. "For now. Maybe when I have more than forty dollars, I can take one small risk."

She walked to the bank desk and asked the teller to open a savings account with compound interest, then fed her two twenties into the bill reader. The receipt printed with a balance of $40.00 and a date five years in the future, when the account would be worth more.

"Backpack?" Dana asked as they headed for the escalator.

"Next birthday," Brooke said, folding the receipt into her pocket. "This one's climbing the curve."

Isla stood in the hallway with her back against the doorframe, holding a pencil flat on top of her head the way her dad always did. He wasn't home yet, so she reached up and made the little line herself, then stepped sideways to look. The mark was barely above the one from September. Barely. She measured the gap with her thumb and it was about the width of an eraser.

Her brother Theo came thudding down the stairs with a folder under his arm. He'd had his knee checked at the doctor's that morning, and he was still telling everyone about it. "They took pictures of my bones," he said. "Actual pictures. Like the bones are glowing."

"X-rays," Isla said. "Everyone's seen those."

"Not of me." He flopped onto the couch and pulled out a dark film, holding it up to the window light. Long pale bones, and near the ends of them, thin darker gaps. Isla leaned in. She'd assumed bones grew from the middle, like a plant shooting up from its stem, but the gaps were all up near the joints.

"That's where they grow," Theo said. "The doctor called them growth plates. Right near the ends." He tapped the film with one finger. "And he said once they close after puberty, that's it, you're done getting taller. He pointed right at mine." He sounded proud, like the closing plates were a trophy.

Isla sat down slowly on the arm of the couch. Done getting taller. She thought about the eraser-width of growth in three months, and about how her jeans from last spring still fit, even though her shoes had gone up a whole size. Her body was clearly doing something, but not the something she wanted. There was no way to see a growth plate on her own legs, no way to peek. But there was the doorframe, with its pencil lines going back to kindergarten, and the date written beside each one. That was her evidence, her pattern, the only record she had.

She went and got the notebook where she tracked everything, hurricane names and homework and now this, and copied the heights onto graph paper. September, October, November, December. The line climbed, small but steady, not flat, not finished. She decided to keep the marks monthly, first Sunday of each, and to exclude any measurement taken with shoes on, since that would ruin the data.

"You're being weird," Theo said, watching her draw.

"I'm being scientific." She snapped the elastic band off the notebook and used it to hang her pencil on a nail beside the doorframe, so it would always be there. Outside, the first thunder of the monsoon season rolled in, and rain started hammering the roof.

"Measure me too," Theo said, getting up. "Right now, before dinner."

Isla pressed the pencil flat against his head and drew the line. "Say the date."

"May eighteenth," Theo said, and she wrote it underneath.

Nathan spread his poster board across the kitchen table and stared at the empty space where his explanation was supposed to go. His science presentation was in two days, and his topic was the monsoon: how the land of South Asia heats up in summer, how air rises over it, how moisture-laden winds sweep in from the ocean and drop the rains that rice fields drink for months. He understood it, mostly, but every time he tried to say it out loud, it collapsed into a jumble of words.

"Say it to me," said his older brother Ravi, who was sitting at the counter with an ice pack strapped to his head. Ravi had taken a concussion at cricket practice three weeks ago, and the doctor said loud noises and screens were off limits, which left him with nothing to do but listen. "If I can follow it, anyone can."

Nathan went to retrieve the globe from the shelf by the window and set it beside the poster. "Okay. In summer, the land gets hotter than the sea, fast. Hot air rises, and that pulls in wet ocean air from the south and west. When that air hits the mountains and the land, it rains for months. The rice needs it." He paused. "But here's my problem. People say it's all about the sun being directly overhead, near the equator. So I figured, near the equator equals monsoon. Then I checked."

He spun the globe and stopped it with his finger. "I looked up capitals to test it. Quito, the capital of Ecuador, lies less than a quarter of a degree south of the equator, so its latitude is almost zero. Zero! Closer than almost any capital on Earth. But Quito doesn't get monsoon rains the way India and Bangladesh do." He tapped the globe. "So latitude can't be the whole answer. It's the difference between land and sea heating up that matters. That's the hidden part, the thing you can't see. Sun, land, sea, mountains, wind. It's a chain."

"Chain," Ravi repeated slowly. "One link pulls the next."

Nathan grabbed a shallow baking pan, filled it with water, and set it in the sun on the windowsill next to a dry ceramic tile. Every hour he touched both and wrote down what he felt. By late afternoon the tile was hot enough to make him jerk his hand back, while the water had barely changed. He was still scribbling the numbers when the sky outside turned the color of wet slate, and rain hammered the window so hard he could barely hear himself think.

The next morning the power was out and school was delayed, and Nathan paced the kitchen with his flashlight, certain the presentation would be canceled after all that work. Ravi came downstairs, ice pack gone, and pushed the poster board toward him. "You're on in front of Mom and me. Full audience." Nathan took a breath and started at the beginning, pan, tile, globe, Quito and its almost-zero latitude, land heating faster than sea, wet winds rising and dropping their rain on the rice. When he finished, Ravi nodded and said, "Understandable even with a concussion. That's a legitimate test."

From the doorway, Mom cleared her throat. "The school called back. Power's restored, and your teacher moved your slot to first period instead of last." Nathan groaned, then grinned, and Ravi said, "At least now you'll be fresh." Nathan looked out at the flooded garden and said, "Great. Now I have to explain a monsoon before the one outside drains away."

Theodore sat on the counter behind the teller line, next to the staff washing machine, holding his pizza-stained shirt at arm's length. The orange blotch on the chest was from the slice he had eaten in the parking lot an hour ago, and it shone even under the break room's dim fluorescent light. His mother had a double shift at the bank, so she had traded him a deal: learn to do laundry, start to finish, and he could use the machine in the back while she worked the window.

First he took a census of the laundry bag she had left him. He counted six dark items, four whites, and one red sock that he set aside like a suspect, since it looked capable of turning everything pink. He sorted, he loaded, and then, before starting the wash, he tried an experiment. Why not just water? Grease was wet, water was wet. He held the stained corner under the tap and rubbed the fabric against itself with aggressive, determined strokes. The blotch dimmed slightly and then stopped, a pale orange ghost that refused to move.

"Why won't you budge?" he muttered.

Ms. Alvarez, the custodian, came in to empty the trash. "Pizza?" she said, nodding at the shirt. "Water alone won't touch that. Use the detergent."

He acquired the bottle from the supply shelf above the sink and squinted at the back label while she waited. "It says here detergent molecules have one end that's attracted to water and another end that's attracted to oil and grease." He looked up. "So one half of the molecule likes my stain and the other half likes the wash water?"

"Grabby little things," Ms. Alvarez said, and rolled her cart out.

Theodore wondered whether it could really work that way, each molecule reaching out in two directions at once, invisible and busy. He drizzled detergent straight onto the blotch, waited while the sink filled with hot water, and pushed the shirt under. Then he watched. The orange ghost loosened at its edges, feathering out like ink in water, and the fabric beneath came back white, thread by thread. He fished the shirt out, wrung it, and held it to the light. Nothing. The stain had gone wherever the water had gone, carried off by its invisible partners.

He ran the full load after that, sorted and soaped and timed, and when the dryer buzzed he folded everything on the break table, matching socks into pairs. He carried the stack out to the teller line and set his clean shirt on top, stain side up.

His mother glanced over between customers. "You actually did it," she said. "What happened to the pizza?"

"The molecules took it," Theodore said.

Harper had decided to paint her grandfather for his birthday, which was ambitious, since she had exactly three weeks and one sheet of printer paper. She laid the first pale wash across the forehead, a colour she called "old lemon," and watched it soak in. So far so good. The second wash, a slightly deeper gold for the cheeks, went on beside it, and the third, a warm shadow under the nose.

Then the paper began to wrinkle. It rose in little waves, like someone had shrunk it in the wash, and her grandfather's face buckled into ridges. His forehead looked like it had grown accordion folds overnight.

"Grandpa's going to think he aged forty years," said Priya, leaning over from the next easel. She was painting a portrait of her cat, which was going about as well as a cat portrait ever goes, which is to say the cat looked like a loaf of bread with ears.

"Very funny. But why is it doing that? I didn't touch the edges." Harper turned the paper over, then back again. It was flat-ish when dry, wavy when wet. She tried an experiment: she painted a small square of wash on a corner of a fresh sheet and watched. Within a minute, that corner alone puckered. So it was the water. But her teacher's demo paper, which had been soaked repeatedly last week, lay flat as a pancake. Same water, different paper. Same washes too. The difference had to be the paper itself.

She carried her ruined grandfather over to Mr. Duffy, the studio volunteer, who was sharpening pencils as though it were a competitive sport.

"My paper's doing a wave impression," she said. "Yours doesn't. What's yours made of, dragon skin?"

Mr. Duffy chuckled and held up his pad, thick as a slice of bread. "It cockles if it's too thin. That's what they call it when it buckles. Watercolour artists usually use the heavy stuff, about 300 grams per square metre." He tapped the cover. "It's also sold as 140-pound paper, if you see that on the label."

Harper traced the number on the pad with her finger, then felt her thin sheet, which was about as substantial as a receipt. "So my paper was doomed from wash one."

"Doomed from wash zero," said Mr. Duffy. "Take a sheet."

Back at her easel, Harper taped the heavy paper down and began again: light lemon first, then the gold, then the shadow, building her grandfather's face in layers from pale to dark. The paper drank the water and stayed stubbornly flat. She was rather vain about her mixing of the perfect grey for his ears, since it took eleven tries, and she made herself sketch the curve of his nose twice, because noses were basically cartilage with ambitions.

Priya drifted over. "Your grandpa doesn't look like an accordion anymore."

"He never did," said Harper, and dipped her brush for the next wash.

Grandpa's porch was the best place in the world to figure things out, and Colton had a big thing to figure out before Monday. His cousin Marcus was visiting too, along with a neighbor kid named Theo, and Grandpa had promised them all lemonade and a chess set older than anyone in the room.

Theo was quiet and wore the same dinosaur shirt two days in a row, which gave Marcus all the material he needed. "Nice shirt," Marcus said, grinning. "Did you dig it out of a museum?"

Theo's comeback was fast and clever. "At least I don't look like a potato with eyebrows."

Colton actually laughed before he could stop himself, and Theo's face went red. Marcus didn't laugh back, though. He leaned forward like a hawk spotting something small and helpless, which was exactly the predatory look the older kids at school got right before things got loud. "A potato with eyebrows?" Marcus said. "Okay, fossil boy. Does your mom still cut your hair with a bowl?"

"Does yours cut yours with a weed whacker?"

By the third round, Theo was shouting, Marcus was shouting, and the chessboard sat forgotten. Colton realized he was watching the exact pattern from school. Last week a kid named Ryan had teased a classmate named Dev, and Dev had fired back a brilliant insult about Ryan's shoes. He'd expected applause. Instead the teasing got ten times worse, and Dev ended up eating lunch alone. Colton had been trying for days to work out why a good comeback made things worse instead of better.

He stared at the chessboard, moving a knight in his head. A clever insult gave the other person something new to attack. That was it. It was like handing your opponent a fresh piece.

"Grandpa," Colton said suddenly, "are you a descendant of any famous chess players?"

"One or two, supposedly," Grandpa said, setting down the lemonade. "Why?"

"Just wondering if it's in the blood." Colton turned to Marcus. "Hey, back off the shirt thing. It's not funny, so stop."

Marcus blinked. His mouth opened, hunting for something to grab onto, and found nothing. "Whatever," he said, and looked at the board instead. "Whose move is it?"

"Yours," said Theo, and for the first time all afternoon he smiled.

They played two full games before the mosquitoes came out. Theo won the second one by sacrificing his queen, which he explained in a whisper while Marcus pretended not to be impressed. On Monday, Colton walked toward Dev's table in the cafeteria with his tray, already deciding exactly what he'd say if Ryan started up again. Short, calm, nothing new to fight about. He sat down across from Dev and said, "Save me a seat tomorrow?"

Jack had the assignment taped to the fridge: pick one right from the country's charter, put it in your own words, and take one real action about it by Monday. He'd chosen the right to contact your elected representative, because his street lamp on Crescent Road had been dead for three months, and his little sister Maya had to walk home from her friend's house in the dark on Tuesdays. His dad had once called the city about it and gotten nowhere, but the assignment said representatives had to respond to citizens. Jack wanted to test that.

First he tried the city website and found a wall of forty-some councillor names, each with a photo and an email. He couldn't email forty people. He noticed, though, that every name had a small label beside it, a number and a name like "Crescent Heights." He got out a street map his mom kept in the junk drawer and made a meticulous list of nearby street names, matching them against the labels. A pattern emerged: the labels weren't random. Each councillor was attached to one specific area of the city.

"That's a ward," Maya said, reading over his shoulder while eating toast. She'd learned it on a field trip. "Each councillor is elected to represent one ward."

"So I just need ours," Jack said. He typed their address into the site's ward finder, and up came Ward 9, Riverside, with a photo of Councillor Amara Odell. One name instead of forty. That was the hidden rule he'd been looking for, the thing that made the whole task possible, and it had been sitting in plain sight the whole time.

He drafted an email, deleted it, and drafted it again. He wanted it to signify a serious request, not a kid's complaint, so he stated the facts plainly: the lamp had been out since November, the street had no other lighting, and a twelve-year-old walked there every Tuesday. Maya leaned against his chair.

"Say there's a motion sensor on the back porch across the street and it doesn't reach," she offered. "So it's really all dark."

"Good," Jack said, and added it. He hit send at 8:52 on a Thursday night, and then there was nothing to do but wait. He checked his inbox Friday at recess, and again after dinner, and found only a notice that the basketball team pictures had been rescheduled.

On Saturday morning Maya shook him awake, holding the tablet in both hands. "You got mail. Real mail." Councillor Odell had written three paragraphs, thanking him for the detailed report and saying she would ask Public Works to inspect the lamp, and could he confirm the nearest cross street. Jack typed back "Crescent and Fifth" before he was even fully out of the blanket, then read the email aloud a second time while Maya toasted them both an English muffin.

Tuesday night, they stood at the window. A city truck rolled slowly down Crescent Road, its beacon circling, and a worker in an orange vest raised a long pole toward the dead lamp. It flickered, blazed, and steadied, laying a clean square of light across the sidewalk.

"It works," Maya said, and pressed her palm flat against the cold glass.

Riley set her debate packet on the library table so hard that the pages fanned out like a dropped deck of cards. Her assignment sheet said, in Ms. Okafor's looping handwriting, "Thesis and three-point outline before any draft. No exceptions." Riley had a draft already, two pages of it, written last night in one long sprint about why the school should start a recycling program. The problem was that her draft said three different things, and she could not tell which one she actually believed.

Across the table, her friend Devon was marking up an essay with a green pen, circling words one by one. Riley watched him fix "recieve" to "receive" and "there" to "their" and move a comma.

"Is that revising?" she asked.

"Yep," Devon said. "Revised it twice already."

Riley slid her laptop toward him. "Can you look at mine, then? Just tell me what to fix."

He read for a minute, then turned the screen back to her. "There's like one spelling error. Congrats. But your first paragraph says recycling saves money, your second says it saves the planet, and your third says it teaches responsibility, and then they all just kind of wander off."

Riley exhaled slowly and stared at the ceiling tiles. "So if fixing spelling is revising, what's this other thing called, where I have to take my own argument apart?"

Devon shrugged. "My tutor says the word 'revise' comes from the Latin revisere, meaning 'to look at again'." He went back to his green pen. "So real revising is supposed to be seeing the draft again, like a civilian who never met you, not fixing typos like a machine."

A civilian who never met you. Riley sat with that. She opened a new document and typed one sentence at the top: "The school should fund a recycling program because it saves money, builds student responsibility, and sets an example for the district." Then she made three headings and dragged chunks of her draft under each one. Under "saves money," she found she had almost no evidence, just enthusiasm. Under "responsibility," she found her strongest paragraph, the one about the sixth graders who ran the cafeteria compost bins. Interesting, she thought. The outline was like a map of her own brain, and apparently her brain had been marching in three parallel directions at once.

She deleted her entire second point. It hurt a little, like throwing away a drawing she'd spent an hour on, but the map was clearer with two roads instead of three, so she split the responsibility point into two halves and rebuilt.

At 3:45 Devon packed up. "How's the typo situation?" he asked.

"Extremely bad," Riley said. "I just cut two hundred words and moved everything." She turned the screen toward him. "But I looked at it again. First time, actually."

He leaned in, read the new outline top to bottom, and laughed. "Riley. Your thesis says the program saves money."

"It does."

"Your evidence is a compost bin run by sixth graders."

Riley looked at her outline, really looked, and the flaw opened up under her eyes like a pothole. "Okay," she said, cracking her knuckles. "Round two."

Kate had been stuck on the same eight measures for forty minutes, and Mr. Alvarez had stopped counting her mistakes out loud, which was worse than counting them. "Again," he said, and she played it again, and her left hand still fumbled the third note every single time, like a foot catching on a loose stair.

"Enough for today," he finally said. "Same piece Thursday." He closed the lid over the keys, gently, as if the piano were something durable that would outlast both of them. On the drive home Kate sat with her hands in her lap and didn't let her mother console her, even when her mom said maybe the passage was just too hard for now. It wasn't too hard. She could play every note separately. It was only the sequence, the order, that fell apart.

That night she slept nine hours, mostly out of sulking, and in the morning she came downstairs early, made toast she didn't eat, and sat down at the kitchen keyboard just to prove the passage was still broken. Her left hand played all eight measures straight through, clean, twice in a row. She stared at her own fingers like they belonged to somebody else.

She thought back to the summer, when she'd had her vaccine shot and a sore arm and had skipped cello practice for two days, and the day she came back her bowing on the hard etude had been smoother than before she stopped. She'd assumed her teacher had been wrong to call it a coincidence. Now she wasn't sure. The pattern was the same: practice, then sleep, then sudden improvement with no extra practice in between.

So she tested it. She picked a new six-note pattern she had never played, drilled it until she was missing it about half the time, wrote down exactly how many mistakes she made on ten tries, and then refused to touch the keyboard for the rest of the day. Six mistakes out of ten, recorded on a napkin and folded into her pocket. At school she caught herself tapping the pattern on her desk and sat on her hands.

Thursday she got to the studio fifteen minutes early and played the old passage first, to warm up, and to show off a little. It was still clean. Mr. Alvarez raised an eyebrows. "When did you practice this?"

"Monday night. Then not at all. I slept on it." She unfolded the napkin and played her new test pattern ten times, counting under her breath. Three mistakes. "Yesterday it was six."

He leaned on the piano. "Out of ten tries?"

"Out of ten. Same pattern, same hand, no practice since."

He looked at the napkin, then at her. "Do it again," he said. "I want to count."

Charlie carried the sack of flour across the farmers' market like it was a sleeping cat, careful not to jostle it. She had spent her last twelve dollars on it because tonight she was making bread for her family, all by herself, the way Gran used to. At the egg stall she paused to read the note tucked in her pocket again, the one Gran had mailed from the hospital before she got better and moved away to Aunt Ruth's.

"Ten minutes of kneading before it rises," the letter said. "No cheating. The proteins in the flour wake up when they meet water, and kneading makes them stronger and stretchier. That stretch is what holds the bubbles. Love, Gran."

Charlie turned that over as she walked past the tomato pyramid. Invisible stuff inside flour, proteins she would never see, doing work she could only feel. It seemed strange that ten minutes could matter so much, but Gran never put numbers in a letter unless she meant them.

At home, the kitchen went quiet except for the radio. Charlie mixed flour and water, then kneaded for about two minutes until her arms ached, covered the bowl with a towel, and left it. An hour later the dough had risen into a soft, lazy hill. She punched it down, shaped it, slid it into the oven, and waited, remembering how Gran had once caught her skipping the kneading entirely. Charlie had concealed that loaf's failure by blaming the oven, and Gran had let her, which somehow felt worse.

The loaf came out flat and dense, like a brick with delusions. Charlie stood over it, thinking. Same flour, same oven. The difference had to be the kneading, because that was the only thing she'd changed from the loaf that worked last month. If the proteins truly got stronger and stretchier with kneading, then two minutes wasn't enough and ten wasn't a random number. There was a rule in there, invisible, and the flat loaf had just proved it.

She started over. This time she set the timer and kneaded the full ten minutes, feeling the dough change under her hands, going from shaggy to smooth to something that pushed back like it was alive. While she worked, her little brother read the note out loud and asked why the market's bread table had a sign that said "no controversy," and Charlie laughed and said that was about the jam judging last summer, not about flour. The dough rose high and proud, and when the second loaf came out golden, she cut the first slice and handed it to her brother.

"Taste it," she said. "Then tell me if you can feel the difference ten minutes makes."

Nicholas sat on his bedroom floor with his laptop open and a peach juice box beside him, which had cost him his last two dollars because he'd spent his allowance Monday on a flimsy dragon kite he never flew. He'd punched his wall that same afternoon, over a game, and his knuckles still stung. That was the strange part. He hadn't even been that angry a second before his fist moved.

His older sister Priya knocked and came in without waiting, the way she always did. She wanted the desk lamp for her room because hers had burned out, and she'd been leaving sticky notes on his door all week, each one more polite and more pointed than the last.

"You can have it after I finish something," Nicholas said.

"You said that Tuesday." Priya sat on the edge of his bed anyway. "What are you even doing?"

"I'm looking stuff up." He turned the laptop so she could see the page he'd found. His cousin Marcus had told him at Thanksgiving that teenagers basically have unfinished brains, and Nicholas had decided to check it, the way he'd once checked whether Marcus was right about hot water freezing faster than cold. That one had turned out mostly wrong. This one seemed to be true.

"It's called the prefrontal cortex," he read aloud. "The part of the brain involved in planning and controlling impulses. It keeps developing through the teenage years and into a person's twenties."

"So you're not finished," Priya said.

"So I'm not finished." He looked at his sore knuckles, then at the kite still folded in its plastic sleeve in the corner, bought with money meant to last the week. It was almost a relief, like finding out the wobbly shelf had never been screwed in right in the first place. Not an excuse. Just a fact he could now see, even though he couldn't see the thing itself.

He decided to test it. If his planning equipment was still under construction, maybe he could build something outside his head to make up for it, the way you'd put a rail on a staircase. He got a marker and a sticky note and wrote "think two seconds first," and pressed it to the wall above his desk where his fist had landed.

Priya watched him, then pointed at the peach juice box, half drunk and sweating on the carpet. "You spent everything you had on that and the kite."

"It's nectar," Nicholas said. "Peach nectar. That's literally what the box says." He handed it to her so she could see, careful not to spill it, thinking two seconds first as instructed.

She read the ingredients, snorted, and set it down. "You're going to be like this until your twenties?"

"Apparently." He unplugged the lamp and held it out to her. "Bring it back when your new bulb comes."

Priya stood in the doorway with the lamp tucked under her arm, its cord dragging behind her like a tail.

Jade pushed the shopping cart past the cereal aisle with the focus of a general planning an invasion. Tonight was her night to cook, her first real dinner since Mom had started working late, and she had decided on potato soup with a mountain of caramelized onions on top. Her little brother Theo trailed behind her, dropping a box of crackers into the cart whenever she wasn't looking.

"Put those back," Jade said, fishing out the third box.

"You can't abandon a cracker family once you've picked it up," Theo said solemnly, holding two boxes together like they were friends.

She grabbed them from him and put them back, but not before he sprinted toward the produce section with the agile speed of a kid who knew he'd win any race in a grocery store. When she caught up, he was holding an onion in each hand and pretending they were arguing with each other.

"One bag," she said. "We need a lot." She counted out onions, checked the potatoes, and grabbed a lemon, because a recipe she'd read at school claimed lemon made everything better. The soup was technically part of a life-skills unit, though Jade privately thought "curriculum" was a fancy word for "make your kid cook dinner so you don't have to."

At home, the kitchen was hers. She set the cutting board down, peeled the first onion, and started chopping. Halfway through, her eyes began to burn. By the end of the onion, tears were streaming down her face so hard that Theo, who had wandered in to steal crackers, stopped in the doorway.

"Why are you crying?" he demanded. "Did the soup die?"

"It's the onion," Jade said, blinking hard. "I'm not sad, it just, ow." She wiped her eyes and stared at the half-chopped pile. A whole onion had sat on the counter all morning and done nothing. The moment she cut into it, her eyes flooded. So something about cutting it had to release something. She picked up a whole onion and held it right up to her face and sniffed. Nothing. Then she leaned over the chopped pieces and her eyes instantly watered again.

"Ha," she said, pointing at the pile. "Whole onion, no problem. Cut onion, waterworks. Cutting it breaks its cells, and that releases enzymes that make a gas. The gas floats up and gets in your eyes, and your eyes water to fight it off."

"That's the weirdest vegetable fact I've ever heard," Theo said. "Can you fight it?"

Jade considered the problem like a scientist with a knife. If the gas floated upward, maybe her eyes just needed to be out of the line of fire. She chopped the second onion with her head turned almost sideways, one eye squeezed shut, which worked about as well as it looked, meaning not at all. Theo laughed so hard he had to sit on the floor. Then she tried cutting the onion near the running faucet, because the recipe blog had mentioned it, and that helped a little, though she wasn't sure why and refused to guess.

For the last onion, she dug the swim goggles out of the pool bag by the back door. They left a red ring around her eyes and steamed up within a minute, but no tears. Theo watched her chop the entire onion, goggled and triumphant, while the onions softened in the pot and the kitchen began to smell like something good was actually happening.

"You look like a bug," Theo announced.

"A bug," Jade said, lifting the lid to drop in the potatoes, "who made dinner."

The food bank smelled like cardboard and apples, and Tyler stood in the doorway with his gloves on before anyone told him where to go. A woman named Rosa handed him a clipboard and pointed to a folding table where three other volunteers were sorting donations from the weekend food drive. His job seemed simple: check the cans and boxes, put good items on the shelf, toss expired ones into the bin. He had signed up to conquer his Saturday boredom, but now that he was actually here, something on the table caught his eye.

A man at the end of the table, Mr. Duffy, held up a box of cereal and frowned at it. "One day past," he muttered, and dropped it toward the trash bin.

"Wait," Tyler said. "Isn't there a difference between a safety date and, like, a quality date?"

Mr. Duffy paused, the box hovering. "What do you mean?"

Tyler had read something on a poster in the lobby while he waited for Rosa, but he wanted to be sure. "I don't actually know. Can I check?" He walked back to the lobby, found the poster by the donation barrel, and read it twice. When he came back, he was almost running.

"In the United States, the USDA says a 'best if used by' date shows when a food will be at its best quality," Tyler said, holding up his phone where he'd snapped a picture of the poster. "It's not a food-safety date."

Mr. Duffy turned the cereal box over. "Huh. Look at that. It says best if used by. Not use by." He set the box back on the table instead of in the bin. "So where'd you learn that, kid?"

"I didn't, really. I just noticed the sign and wondered why there were two different phrases. Isn't that weird, that they'd bother printing different words?" Tyler picked up another box, this one crackers, and studied the date. "It's like a hidden rule. You can't see it just by looking at the shelf, but it changes what happens to every single item."

Rosa came over to see what the small crowd was about. Tyler explained the date thing, and she nodded slowly. "That's a good catch. We've been throwing out a lot of good food, then." She raised her voice to the whole room. "Everybody, from now on, check what kind of date it is before you toss it."

The sorting picked up speed after that. Tyler made a game of it, calling out "quality date" or "safety date" like a referee, and the other volunteers started racing him to spot the difference first. By noon the shelf was fuller than it had been all morning, and the trash bin held only half of what anyone expected. Was this how real scientists felt, he wondered, when some small phenomenon nobody else had noticed suddenly made a messy pile of things make sense?

The last donation bag held a dented can of peaches, robust and heavy in his hand, with no date he could find at all. Tyler turned it under the light, hunting along the seam.

"Found it yet?" Mr. Duffy called over.

"Not yet," Tyler said, and kept turning the can.

Laurence knelt on the stone floor of the temple annex with a folded sheet of Sanskrit verses in front of her. In three weeks she would chant the whole prayer from memory in front of the congregation, part of her coming-of-age ceremony, and so far she could get through four lines before the words slipped away from her.

Her cousin Priya found her there after the morning bells. "You look like you're trying to stare a hole in the paper," Priya said.

"It won't stick. I read it over and over and it just slides off." Laurence flattened the page against the floor. "How did you ever memorize anything for your ceremony?"

Priya sat down beside her. "I didn't memorize for that. I danced. Two hours a day for four years, and last spring I finally did my first full solo performance. It's called an arangetram. It means ascending the stage." She straightened the edge of her shawl. "It marks the end of my first formal training."

Laurence looked at her. "Four years. And you're still the one who complains about practice."

"Exactly because of that." Priya laughed.

That night Laurence thought about the difference between Priya's four years and her own three weeks. Priya hadn't learned her dance by reading it. She had learned it with her feet and her hands, the same movements repeated until her body knew them without the mirror. Laurence had been treating the prayer as something on paper, a thing outside her, instead of something she could carry in her mouth and her breath.

The next morning she tested the idea. She stood in the temple courtyard, left the sheet folded in her pocket, and chanted the first line while touching the pillar nearest the door, the way she had done on her first day. Then the second line at the tulsi planter, the third at the low step. She walked the route six times, tying each line to a place she could walk to.

On the sixth round, her aunt tried to intervene, saying she should come in and eat before the priest arrived, but Laurence held up one hand and finished the verse at the bell rope without a single mistake.

At breakfast her uncle asked why she was grinning at her idli. "I thought memorizing meant being biased toward my eyes," she said. "All reading, no doing. I was wrong. It's in my feet now too." Nobody in the family had paid a single rupee for lessons, unlike Priya's parents, whose income had stretched thin over four years of dance fees, and that made the walking method even better.

On the day of the ceremony she stood before the congregation, closed her eyes, and saw the courtyard in her mind, pillar, planter, step, bell rope. Her voice moved from station to station. When she finished, she opened her eyes, and Priya, in the second row, raised her hands in a dancer's salute.

The onion came out of the root cellar still cold, and Oliver peeled a single layer of skin from its curved side with tweezers, the way the science booklet said, laying it flat on a glass slide. His grandfather's microscope sat on the kitchen table between the salt shaker and a jar of bolts. It had been in the barn loft for years, and Oliver had spent half the morning polishing its little mirror before he could see anything at all.

He wanted this to work. He had written to his grandfather three weeks ago, when the science fair project was assigned, asking if he could borrow the microscope, and yesterday a letter had finally come back. The letter was in his pocket now, soft at the folds from being read too many times. His grandfather wrote about the farm and the weather, and then, near the end, about a summer long ago when he had volunteered in the Galápagos Islands counting finches. That part Oliver had read four times.

First, though, he had to see the cells. He dropped a bead of water and a thread of iodine onto the skin, pressed the cover slip down, and bent to the eyepiece. At first there was only a pale blur. He turned the knob a fraction at a time, the way a careful person turns a key in an old lock. Then the blur sharpened into rows of brick-like cells, each one walled off from the next, and there inside each cell, faintly, a dark dot.

He sat back. He found the diagram in his booklet and matched it piece by piece. The thick outer line of every brick was the cell wall. Just inside it, so thin he could barely tell it apart, was the membrane. The dark dot was the nucleus. He labeled them on his own drawing, and where he could not decide whether a line was wall or membrane, he guessed, and the guess felt arbitrary, so he checked it twice.

Then he took out the letter. "You asked once whether bigger is always better," his grandfather had written. "On the island of Daphne Major, the medium ground finches had big beaks, good for big hard seeds. But after the very wet El Niño year of 1983 brought many small, soft seeds, selection reversed, and smaller beaks were favoured." Oliver read it again, thinking of his grandfather the year he sold the big tractor and bought the small one, and how the neighbors had laughed, and how nobody laughed after the dry summer. He looked back into the eyepiece at the little walled city, every cell the same size, nobody bigger than anybody.

The screen door banged and his mother came in with two buckets of feed. "You find them?" she asked.

"Wall, membrane, nucleus," he said, and slid the letter across the table to her, still open to the last page.

Brayden lay on the couch with a box of tissues, a bowl of crackers, and three days of nothing but game shows. The flu had flattened him on Friday, right before his cousin Marcus's birthday party, which was tomorrow at noon. His mom had made a deal with him: if his fever stayed normal all morning, he could go. He wanted that more than anything, because Marcus had saved him the last slice of pizza every year since they were seven.

He was texting his friend Dev when a thought stopped his thumb mid-word. The sleepover. Dev had been there too, laughing and eating chips and winning every round of the racing game. Dev texted back that he was fine, but Brayden scrolled up in the group chat anyway. Saturday morning, two days ago, Dev had sent a single message: "ugh, think im getting the flu." Brayden stared at it, then counted on his fingers. Dev had been perfectly healthy at the sleepover on Friday night. Then, less than a full day later, he was sick.

Brayden sat up so fast the blanket slid to the floor. People with the flu could spread it starting about one day before they felt any symptoms. That meant Dev hadn't just caught it after the sleepover. He had probably been spreading it while they were all piled on the air mattress, sharing controllers and a bag of pretzels. Brayden's own fever had started Sunday, which was almost exactly one day after the sleepover. It lined up like a laser beam pointed straight at Friday night.

He had to test the idea. He messaged the other two boys from the sleepover. Ten minutes later, both had replied. Tyler: "fine so far." Owen: "my throat kinda hurts today." Owen had been the one who fell asleep with his head on Dev's shoulder during the movie. Brayden read the messages twice, letting the pattern digest. Two out of five boys sick within the same stretch of days, all of them exposed to the same person before that person knew he was sick.

Brayden walked to the kitchen where his mom was cutting fruit. "I figured out where I got it," he said. "Dev seemed totally fine at the sleepover, but you can spread the flu starting about one day before you even feel symptoms. So he was already contagious Friday night. Owen's getting sick too, and he was all over Dev." He took a breath. "So here's the thing. If I go to Marcus's party tomorrow, even with no fever, I might be doing the same thing Dev did."

His mom set down the knife and looked at him for a long moment. "That was an eloquent argument for a kid with a stuffy nose," she said. "Go call Marcus. Tell him the truth, and ask about that pizza."

Brayden dialed, and when Marcus picked up, he said, "I'm going to tell you something weird, and then I'm going to ask you a favor about pizza."

Rosalie stood on the auditorium stage with her scene partner, Dex, and tried to hand him an invisible pizza. "Here's the pizza you ordered, sir," she said. "No," said Dex. "I ordered soup." Behind the curtain, the debate team was rehearsing, and the clock on the back wall said the improv showcase started in thirty minutes. Mrs. Okafor had been clear: pairs who couldn't sustain a scene for two minutes would be cut.

"You have to say yes," Rosalie whispered. "That's the whole thing. You accept the offer and add to it." Dex shrugged, and she noticed he was flexing his right hand like a tendon in his wrist had gone tight from gripping his debate notes all day. "I'm a debater," he said. "My instinct is to argue." She tried again with the pizza. He said no again, and this time added, "You're just an actor, you wouldn't understand blocking an offer."

From behind the curtain, a voice drifted out, sharp and bored. It was the debate judge, a tired senior with a clipboard. "Marcus, when you said 'you're just a sixth grader,' I had to mark that down. That's an ad hominem fallacy. You attacked the person instead of the claim." There was a pause, then a younger kid's voice said, "So it doesn't matter if my argument was right?" and the judge said, "The claim stands or falls on its own. Attack the claim, not the kid."

Rosalie chewed on that. Dex had just done the same thing to her. He hadn't said her idea about saying yes was wrong; he'd said she was just an actor, as if that settled it. She couldn't see the rule of improv any more than she could see the rule of debate, but she could test whether the two corresponded. Maybe blocking a scene and attacking a person were the same move: refusing the offer in front of you by pointing at who made it.

She set down the invisible pizza. "Try this," she said. "When I make an offer, don't tell me what I am. Tell me what happens next." Dex frowned, then rolled his shoulders back like he was starting a rebuttal. "Fine. Sir, the pizza arrived, and it's on fire." Rosalie blinked, then grinned and fanned it with her cape, which she decided she was wearing. "Yes, and the fire spell can only be broken by a debate champion." Dex stepped forward, extinguished it with a wave, and looked almost competent doing it. Mrs. Okafor's footsteps were already coming up the aisle.

They had ninety seconds before she reached the stage. "Ready?" Rosalie asked. Dex raised one hand, palm out, as if holding a very small, very important pizza. "Yes," he said, "and this time I ordered it."

Zoe stood at the boards with the sign-up sheet in her mitten, waiting for Priya to finish her lap. Their winter tournament allowed each team one pick from outside its regular roster, and they had argued about that pick all the way to the rink. "It has to be Dana," Priya said, skating over in a spray of ice. "She scores every single game. Her average is two goals a game." Zoe frowned at the clipboard. "Morgan's average is two a game too. I wrote them both down." Priya snorted. "Then it's a tie, so pick Dana. Everyone ranks Dana higher."

"But that's what's bugging me," Zoe said. "If they're tied on average, why does everyone say Dana is better? Nobody can actually see who's better. We only see the games." Priya rolled her eyes, but Zoe had already flipped her notebook to a page of tiny numbers. She had gone through the league website the night before, eating a nutritious dinner of toast with peanut butter while she copied down every game log. "Look. Dana: two goals, two goals, two, one, three, two, two. Same every night." She tapped the second column. "Morgan: five goals, zero, six, zero, zero, one, two. Same average. But Morgan swings between great and terrible games, and an average hides how spread out the results are." She said it out loud and then checked her math again, because it seemed too strange to be true. Two players, same average, completely different players.

"So which one do we want?" Priya said. Zoe proposed a test instead of an argument. "Next scrimmage, we put Morgan on our line and watch. If the spread thing is real, we should see it." At Saturday's scrimmage Morgan scored four goals in the first period, and Priya threw her arms around Zoe at the bench. In the second period Morgan missed an open net twice and passed to nobody, and Priya groaned. "That was a humiliation," she muttered, pulling her helmet straight. "Mine too," Morgan said, embarrassed, sitting down between them. Zoe slid the water bottle over. "You're still averaging two a game," she said. "That's what my notebook says, and my notebook has never lied to me yet."

By the end of the third period, Morgan had scored twice more, and the swing had shown up exactly as the numbers promised. Zoe did not gloat. Instead she asked Morgan one question: "Tournament games are single elimination. One bad game and we're out. Do you want to be our pick, knowing that?" Morgan thought about it, chipped the ice off her skate blade, and said, "Pick Dana. She never stops at two. I'll take a regular spot if you have one, and I'll work on the zeroes." Zoe crossed off one name and wrote the other.

On the walk to the parking lot, Priya bumped her shoulder. "You solved it with a notebook and toast." Zoe laughed. "The toast was the nutritious part. The numbers did the rest." Inside the rink, the Zamboni began its slow loops, and the noise of the fans would not cease until every last scrap of ice was smooth.
