Priya pointed at the driver's booth, where a new standings sheet had just gone up, team averages printed in tidy rows. "Look at that," she said. "All those games, squished into one number." Zoe grinned and tucked her notebook under her arm. "Not for long," she said, and turned back toward the doors.

The lights went out just as Nora was finishing her homework, and the whole house sank into a blue evening dimness. She found her way to the back door and stepped onto the porch, where her older brother Dev was already standing with a flashlight, shining it at the empty birdbath as if it might explain things. Their little brother Milo was in the kitchen, and Nora could hear the refrigerator door swing open, then shut, then open again.

"Milo, stop that," she called through the screen door. "You're letting the cold out."

"I want the yogurt," his voice drifted back. "I can't find it in the dark."

Nora went inside and held the flashlight while Milo rummaged, but the beam wobbled and he moved containers aside, and she felt the cool air spilling past her ankles like water from a cracked cup. She remembered a poster from the school cafeteria, the one she'd read while waiting in the pizza line: according to the USDA, a fridge keeps food safely cold for about four hours in a power cut, as long as the door stays closed. Four hours, if it stayed shut. Milo was spending those hours a few seconds at a time.

"We get one open," Dev said from the doorway, having apparently been thinking the same thing. "Everybody decide first, then we open it once, grab everything, and shut it for good."

Milo looked ready to argue, but then his lower lip trembled and he sat down on the cold tile. Nora crouched beside him and tried to console him, saying they'd have a yogurt picnic as soon as they planned it right, and after a moment he wiped his nose on his sleeve and agreed. They made their list on the porch by flashlight: yogurt, the leftover noodles, the milk, the cheese, the orange juice Milo pretended not to want. They stacked it all in a cooler from the garage, next to the porous old cinder block that their father used as a doorstop, and then they sat on the steps eating cold noodles with forks, listening to crickets.

The power came back at half past nine, humming through the porch light and glowing yellow against the dusk. Dev stood up, stretched, and opened the refrigerator to put things away, and every bulb inside blazed on cheerfully. Nora laughed so hard she nearly dropped her fork, because the fridge had come back to life precisely when they no longer needed to keep it closed.

"Four hours of careful planning," Dev said, "wasted on ten minutes."

"Get me the yogurt," Milo announced from the steps. "I've decided."

Felix sat at the kitchen table wrapped in a quilt that smelled like the linen closet, staring at a bowl of chicken soup he had no intention of eating. His fever had spiked overnight, and now every joint in his body ached like he had run a marathon in his sleep. His little sister, Poppy, kept orbiting the table with her thermometer, pretending she was a nurse on television.

"Mom thinks we should wait until Saturday to call Dr. Okafor," she reported, tucking the thermometer into her doll's armpit. "Dad thinks you're going to turn into a zombie by Friday."

"I heard that," Mom called from the stove. She stirred something and sighed. "His fever is 102, but it might break on its own. The office is always packed on Thursdays."

Felix pushed the soup an inch away, then pulled it back, then pushed it away again, like the bowl itself was making the decision. His brain felt like wet sand, but something was nagging at him, a memory from a pamphlet he had read in Dr. Okafor's waiting room back in September, mostly because the magazine rack had nothing but golf catalogs. He tried to reconstruct it. The pamphlet had said something about flu medicine, the kind you get with a prescription, and a deadline. Two days. The medicine worked best if you started it within two days after symptoms began.

He counted backward on his fingers, which took longer than it should have. "Mom. When did I start feeling bad?"

"Tuesday night, sweetie. You were shivering during dinner."

"So the clock started Tuesday." He held up two fingers. "Two days. That's my window. If we wait until Saturday, I miss it, and the medicine won't do much." He slid the soup toward her like a lawyer presenting evidence. "Calling today isn't arbitrary. It's the rule."

Mom tapped the spoon against the pot. Poppy whispered "zombie" in a spooky voice.

"You read that somewhere?" Mom asked.

"Waiting room pamphlet. Golf rack, remember."

She laughed, wiped her hands on the towel, and picked up her phone. While she was on hold, Felix took one bite of soup and, to his own surprise, kept going. When Mom hung up, she said the nurse agreed completely and they could come at three.

At the clinic, Dr. Okafor wrote the prescription and said, "Good timing. This antiviral works best when it's started within two days of your first symptoms, so you caught it just right."

"Did you hear that, Poppy?" Felix said weakly from the exam table. "Your almost-zombie brother caught it just right."

On the drive home, he leaned against the window and decided that being right was a kind of currency in their family, worth at least one extra hour of video games. He planned to spend it the moment his hands stopped aching.

Then Poppy leaned over from her booster seat and pressed the thermometer into his ear. It beeped. "Ninety-eight point six," she announced. "My medicine worked. That'll be five dollars."

Grayson spread his Spanish worksheet across the library table with the confidence of a general deploying troops. On it he had written a whole conversation for his pen pal letter: how to order tacos, ask for water, and find out how much the bill cost. "¿Cuánto cuesta?" he muttered, testing it out. "Cuánto cuesta el taco de pescado." Tomorrow was the exchange video call with Mateo in Oaxaca, and Grayson wanted to sound like someone who could actually survive in a restaurant, not like a lost tourist pointing at a menu.

Priya dropped her backpack on the chair beside him and leaned over the page. "Ready for the big call?"

"Almost. I just have to write the last paragraph where I tell him I'll speak Spanish with the waiter." Grayson wrote "hablé con el camarero" and underlined it twice for emphasis.

Priya squinted. "That says you already spoke with the waiter. Past tense. You chopped hablar down to habl- and stuck the wrong ending on it."

Grayson stared at the word. He had been so sure. He flipped back through his notes and found a list of verbs, hablar, comer, pedir, and then, near the bottom, a line he had skimmed: hablaré. He looked at it, then at his own botched attempt, then back again. The whole infinitive was still sitting right there inside the word, hablar plus é, like a train with a new car hooked on the end instead of the engine getting replaced.

"Hablaré," Priya said, tapping the example. "That means I will speak. It keeps the whole infinitive and adds the ending onto it."

"So I don't chop anything off. I just bolt something on." Grayson tested the pattern out loud, quieter and quieter as the kid at the next table glared at him. "Comeré. Pediré. It's the same trick every time." He felt a little naive for having assumed the future would work like the past, but at least he had caught it before Mateo did, which would have earned him a laughing emoji and probably a screenshot.

He rewrote the paragraph. "Esta semana practicaré pedir la comida en español," he read to Priya. "And then I ask how much everything costs, so when I visit, Mateo's mom can't sneak the expensive flan onto my half of the bill."

"Bold plan," said Priya. "Now paraphrase your whole letter for me in English so I know you're not accidentally promising to buy everyone dinner."

Grayson walked her through it, paragraph by paragraph, and Priya delivered her critique: good ordering, decent questions, one word that sounded like he was asking to adopt the waiter. He fixed it, folded the letter into his binder, and headed for the front desk to check out a Spanish phrasebook for extra backup.

At the circulation desk he paused, turned around, and called back to Priya, "¡Pagaré!" Then he patted his pocket where his lunch money lived.

Katherine sat cross-legged on Priya's bedroom floor with Priya's laptop between them, three orange slices deep into an argument about the swim team's points. Priya swore the Dolphins were crushing everyone this season, and she had a spreadsheet to prove it. "Look, I'll show you," Priya said, opening the file. "You type the scores in this column, then in the cell below you put equals, S-U-M, open parenthesis, then drag over the cells you want, close parenthesis, hit enter." Katherine typed it herself, and when the number appeared at the bottom of the column she actually bounced a little. "It added the whole thing. Twelve scores, one click." Then Priya showed her the chart button, and a bar chart sprang up with the Dolphins' bar towering over the Stingrays'.

"That's not right," Katherine said slowly. The Dolphins had 214 points and the Stingrays had 205. She knew that from the paper list on the wall, because she was the one who kept it for the coach. Nine points out of more than two hundred, and on the chart it looked like the Dolphins were double everyone. She leaned in and studied the side of the chart, the little numbers running up the axis. "It starts at two hundred," she said. "Not at zero." Priya squinted. "So?" Katherine clicked the axis, found the scale settings, and changed the minimum to zero. The bars shrank until the Dolphins' lead looked like what it was: a sliver, a margin so thin the season wasn't decided at all.

Priya didn't say anything for a moment. "I made that chart for the team group chat," she admitted. "The vote was unanimous because everyone saw it and figured the season was basically over. We agreed to skip the last meet since we'd already lost." Katherine felt the orange slices turn sour in her stomach. "You didn't lose," she said. "You're nine points back with one meet left. That's nothing. That's catchable."

Priya grabbed her phone and typed fast, sending the fixed chart to everyone with the words "we can still win this, come to practice tomorrow." The replies started coming in within a minute, and Priya's face went from gray to glowing. Katherine was glad, truly glad, but there was a small ache underneath it. She had made the chart honest, and the consequence was that Priya's team would now fight hard in the last meet, the meet Katherine's Dolphins would have to win all over again. She was going to have to swim her best race of the year against her best friend.

"To verify it's really fixed, check the axis on my phone too," Priya said, holding it out. Katherine looked at the little screen, at the honest little bars standing close together, and nodded. "It's fixed," she said, and clicked the button to send it to the coach.

Ariana counted the steps from the cabin to the dock, because if she knew exactly how far the lake was, maybe it would stop feeling like the edge of a map. Camp Wanaset claimed to be the most prestigious canoe camp in the county, and the banners everywhere said so, and her older brother had spent two summers here winning the paddle trophy that sat in the lodge. Ariana had never been away from home before, and today was the day every new camper got in a canoe for the first time.

"New campers, you're with me," said Kaya, who was fourteen and the tutor for beginners, meaning she took them out on the water every morning. Kaya wanted that trophy more than anything, and she kept glancing at the older campers racing near the far shore. "We paddle after lunch. Nobody flips my group."

At the dock, a boy named Dex went first. He stepped onto the edge of the canoe instead of the middle, and the whole boat lurched sideways under him. He grabbed the gunwale, the canoe wobbled again, and Kaya hauled him back onto the dock before he went in. "You're not getting in like that," she said. Dex's face went red, and he muttered something about quitting, because he had told everyone at breakfast he would catch the biggest fish in the lake from a canoe, and now he couldn't even sit down in one.

Ariana watched the older campers next. Every single one of them stepped into the middle of the canoe, and kept low, knees bent, gear centered between them. Nobody had said anything about it. They just did it, like it was a rule written somewhere she hadn't been shown. She looked at Dex wobbling on the dock and made a quiet guess: the boats tipped when weight went onto the side, and stayed calm when weight sat low and centered in the middle.

"Me next," she said. She stepped straight into the middle of the canoe, crouched, and slid onto the seat. The boat barely moved. Dex stared at her.

"How'd you do that?"

"Watch." She nodded at the older campers. "They all get in the same way." Dex tried again, stepping into the middle, low and slow, and this time the canoe held steady under him. He gripped his paddle and grinned.

Later, they would transport their gear across the lake to the fishing spot, and the whole camp would see two first-timers paddling out flat and calm. For now Kaya pushed them off from the dock and jumped into her own boat, eyes already on the far shore.

"Race you to the reeds," Dex called, and dug his paddle in.

Katherine had exactly one class period to finish her shaded sphere for the art show, and her pencil was betraying her. The highlight kept turning gray no matter how lightly she touched the paper. Across the table, Marcus held up two pencils that looked identical, both yellow, both freshly sharpened. "Why does this one draw so dark and this one barely shows up?" he asked. "They're the same size. It's like one of them is lazy."

Katherine took both pencils and scribbled a quick swatch on scrap paper. One left a rich, velvety black; the other left a mark so faint it looked like a ghost of a pencil. She turned them near the window and noticed small letters on each one. The dark one said 4B. The pale one said 4H. "They're not the same kind," she said. "The letters are different." Marcus leaned over her shoulder, nearly knocking her eraser off the table, and she caught it before it rolled away.

"My grandpa has a whole coffee can of these at his house," Katherine said, turning the pencils over. "He told me once what the letters mean, but I forgot most of it." She remembered one part, though, a sentence he'd said while she sat at his kitchen table drawing horses: pencil cores aren't just one thing, they're graphite powder mixed with clay. She frowned at the pale pencil. "So if more clay makes a harder pencil that leaves lighter marks, then this 4H one must have more clay in it than the 4B."

"Test it," Marcus said, always ready for anything that sounded even slightly like science class. Katherine pressed down hard with the 4H, then feather-light with the 4B. Even under pressure, the hard pencil stayed pale, and even with the gentlest touch, the soft one smudged dark. "It's backwards from what you'd expect," she said. "The harder one gives you less." Marcus squinted at his own drawing. "So that's why my clouds look like storm clouds. I've been using the dark one for everything."

He looked so defeated that Katherine slid her 4H across the table to him. "Try this for the light parts. And press less with the dark one for the middle." She watched him shade a cloud so fluffy it looked ready to float off his page, and he grinned like he'd invented weather.

For her sphere's highlight, she finally understood what to do. Instead of pressing the dark pencil lighter and lighter, which only eroded the paper's tooth into a shiny smudge, she used the hard pencil with its faint, pale mark, letting the white of the page glow through at the very top. Her shading curved around the sphere now, giving it real perspective, the way Mr. Okafor kept saying, like it existed in actual space and not just flat on the desk. At the end of class he held up her sphere as an example, calling it "a thoroughly contemporary take on a classic exercise," which made Marcus whisper, "He just means it looks cool."

Katherine wrote 4H on the back of her scrap paper and tucked it in her pocket, next to two pencils she'd decided to keep forever. "Grandpa's going to be proud," she said. "That thing you figured out," Marcus said, gathering his cloud drawing, "can you teach it to my little sister? Her cat drawings look like they got caught in a rainstorm." Katherine laughed. "Bring her a 4H," she said, "and tell her the pale pencil is her best friend."

The kitchen smelled like burnt garlic, and Easton was trying to write an essay at the table while his cousin Mira practiced tinikling between the counter and the fridge. She had two wooden spoons and was tapping them on the floor, and her friend Daisy was stepping in and out of them like her ankles were made of glass. "Tap, tap, clap," Mira counted, loud and nervous, because in the real dance two people tapped bamboo poles on the ground twice and then clapped them together on the third beat, and if Daisy miscounted, the spoons would snap shut on her ankles like a cranky turtle.

"Can you count quieter?" Easton asked.

"Can you write quieter?" Mira said. "Your pencil sounds like a rebellious squirrel."

Easton looked down at his paper. The assignment was to compare how two faiths explained what happens after death, and he had exactly two sentences, one of which was his name. His lola believed in heaven and purgatory, which she described as being made clean before you went home. His friend Tomas's family was Buddhist and talked about being reborn, coming around again in a different form. Both ideas were about something nobody could actually see and come back from to report, which struck Easton as the world's worst homework design.

Then Daisy yelped. Mira had gotten excited on a turn and clapped the spoons a beat early, catching Daisy's sock. Daisy hopped on one foot, laughing, and Mira covered her face. "I'll embarrass myself at the recital," she groaned into her hands.

"No, wait," Easton said, standing up. "Count out loud, like you were doing. You kept her ankles clear when you counted. It went wrong when you stopped counting."

Mira gave him a suspicious look but started again. "Tap, tap, clap. Tap, tap, clap." Daisy's feet flicked in and out, safe every time, like the pattern was a law of nature instead of two wooden spoons.

Easton sat back down and looked at his blank page, and something clicked that felt like a spoon clapping shut. Both beliefs were patterns too, ways of counting past something you couldn't see. His lola's way said you went home after being made clean. Tomas's way said you came around again, like the third beat returning to the first. He couldn't test either one, not the way he'd just tested Mira's counting, but he could set them side by side and watch where they matched and where they clashed. His pencil finally started moving.

"Done!" Daisy announced, arms up like a champion.

"Tap, tap, clap," Easton read aloud from his page, then scribbled a new first line: Life, life, and then what?

Mila had made Grandma Rosa's snickerdoodles three times this winter, and every batch came out the same: dry in the middle, puffy like little cakes instead of flat and chewy. She stood at the counter with the recipe card propped against the flour canister, reading it again. Her dad's voice drifted in from the hallway, where he was on the phone with her uncle about the wind turbine they were helping install at the school, and she half listened while she puzzled over the card. The recipe said two and a quarter cups of flour, the same as always. She hadn't changed anything.

Or maybe she had. She thought about how she measured. She dipped the measuring cup straight into the bag, the way she always had, and the flour came up in a dense block that she leveled with a knife. She remembered Grandma Rosa weighing her flour on the little silver scale instead, and how she used to transmit recipes by letter, with weights written beside the cups. Grandma had texted her the gram amounts last week: two hundred and seventy grams for two and a quarter cups. Mila had never bothered with them. Cups were faster.

She pulled the scale from the top shelf and set the bowl on it, pressing tare until the numbers cleared. Then she scooped a cup of flour the way she always did, packed and leveled, and poured it in. The scale read one hundred and sixty grams, not one hundred and twenty. She frowned and did the next cup. One hundred and fifty-five. She measured the last quarter cup and then checked the total: over three hundred and forty grams. Almost eighty grams more than the recipe meant. Eighty grams was like adding a whole extra half cup that nobody asked for.

"Whoa," her little brother Theo said, appearing at her elbow with his synthetic vanilla-spiked hot chocolate, which Mom had finally bought after the real vanilla bottle ran dry. "Why's the number so big?" Mila tapped the bag of flour. "Scooping straight from the bag packs it down, so a cup holds way more than the recipe wants. That's why they're coming out like little cakes." She dumped the flour back, spooned it gently into the cup, leveled it, and weighed again. One hundred and twenty-five grams. Closer. She did the rest the same way, watching the numbers climb toward two hundred and seventy exactly.

The dough felt different under her hands, softer and slacker, and it spread on the pan in fat rounds instead of sitting stiff. When the timer buzzed, the cookies came out golden with crackled tops, and when she broke one in half it pulled apart in strings. Theo took one before it was even cool. "These are the real ones," he said through a full mouth. Mila set two aside on the good plate and took out her phone to text Grandma Rosa a picture. She typed, "You were right, I weighed the flour," and pressed send. Then she ate the broken cookie standing up, right there beside the warm oven.

Easton spread his bar mitzvah study folder across the synagogue library table and felt his stomach drop. Rabbi Stein had handed him two packets instead of one, and the second packet was thick. "Wait," Easton said. "I thought I only had to chant my Torah portion."

Rabbi Stein was already halfway to the door. "You have the haftarah too," she said. "A reading from the books of the Prophets. Most b'nei mitzvah students chant both."

Two readings. Easton's bar mitzvah was in eleven weeks, and he had promised himself he would master every letter of one reading, not fumble through two. Then he remembered the other promise he had made, to his social studies teacher, Mrs. Okafor, who had assigned a project where students had to categorize how two different faiths explain what happens after death. Easton had picked his own and his friend Deshawn's church, and tonight was his chance to ask questions at the youth group Deshawn had invited him to.

At the church basement meeting, the pastor talked about heaven, about being welcomed home. Easton wrote it down, then asked, "So how do you picture it? Like, what does it look like?" A woman beside him smiled and said everyone pictures it differently, which was not much of an answer. Deshawn leaned over and whispered, "You're asking like it's a place you can visit."

That was exactly what Easton had been doing, and he knew it. His grandfather, a descendant of the synagogue's founding families, had taught him chess and had always said you figure out hidden things by what you can see on the board. Easton decided to test a simple idea: maybe each faith's answer to death was hidden somewhere you could actually look, in their texts and their rituals, not just in what people said out loud.

Back home, a letter was waiting in his grandmother's careful handwriting. "Your grandfather asked me to give you this when you started studying for your bar mitzvah," she wrote. Easton unfolded it and read his grandfather's words: "When I chant the Prophets, I am listening to voices older than me. They disagreed about everything, including what comes after. Argue with them. That is how you honor them."

Easton grinned. His haftarah portion sat right there in his folder, Isaiah, full of images of consolation. He read it twice, then read the pastor's pamphlet from youth group, then drew two columns in his notebook and filled them with what each one actually said. It was like the chessboard: pieces you could see, patterns underneath.

The next Sunday at the library, Deshawn found him still writing. "You solved your afterlife project?"

"Better," Easton said. "I found out I had two readings to learn, not one, and the second one might be the best source I've got." He tapped the Prophets packet. "Want to hear the tricky part? These guys didn't agree with each other either."

Deshawn pulled up a chair. "Read me the part you underlined."

The casseroles kept arriving like a currency nobody had asked for, dish after dish stacking up on Grandma's old kitchen table, and Christopher hadn't touched a bite of any of them. It had been six days since Grandpa died, and in those six days Christopher had slept maybe two hours a night, maybe less. His legs felt hollow. He pushed a fork through the lasagna and watched the cheese go cold.

"You look terrible," his cousin Marcus said, cornering him by the punch bowl.

"Thanks."

"No, I mean it. Are you sick?" Marcus leaned closer. "If you're getting the flu the day before the funeral, my mom will lose her mind. She's already losing it."

That was the thing, the worry that had been circling him all week like a fly he couldn't swat. Because it wasn't just the sleeping. It was that food made his throat close. It was that his hands shook carrying the mail. He had started building a list in his head: mono, or something worse, something they'd catch too late, and he'd be in a hospital bed while everyone was already standing at a grave. Tomorrow. The funeral was tomorrow at ten, and he was supposed to read the card he'd written, and his body was falling apart on a schedule.

He tried an experiment that afternoon. He went into the den where his dad was sorting Grandpa's old photographs, and he said, straight out, "Dad, are you sleeping?"

His dad didn't look up. "Couple hours a night. Maybe."

"Are you eating?"

Dad finally turned. "Your aunt made me finish half a sandwich today. First real thing since Sunday." He squinted at Christopher. "Why?"

Christopher pulled a chair over. "My hands shake. My stomach's wrong. I thought maybe I was getting sick, but." He stopped. "You sleep two hours. You eat half a sandwich. And Aunt Terri looks the same way. And Marcus's mom was awake at three, I heard her in the kitchen."

Dad set down the photo he was holding, one of Grandpa holding a fish the size of a canoe paddle. "Grief doesn't just mess with your feelings," he said quietly. "It can get into your body too. Tiredness, sleep going bad, appetite going strange. It happens."

"So I'm not sick."

"You're not sick." Dad rubbed his eyes. "It's just grief, invading everything, the whole system."

Christopher sat with that. Then he asked about the second part of his test, the part that actually scared him. "Then how do I read the card tomorrow if I'm like this?"

"You eat something small tonight. You sleep as much as your body lets you. That's the fix. Not a radical one, just a boring one."

At the evening meal, in front of everybody, Christopher took a piece of bread and ate it slowly, bite by bite, while his aunts pretended not to watch. It went down. It stayed down. He went to bed at nine and lay in the dark listening to his grandmother's clock tick in the hallway, and he slept four whole hours, which felt like an ocean.

In the morning he put on the gray shirt his mom had laid out and found the card in his jacket pocket where he'd left it. At the funeral home, when the pastor nodded to him, Christopher stood up. His hands were steadier than they'd been all week. He unfolded the card, looked out at the folding chairs and the flowers and his father's tired face, and began, "My grandpa taught me to fish."

"Speak up, buddy," his dad called softly.

Christopher lifted his chin and said it again, louder, to the whole room.

Kayla stood at Grandma Rosa's counter with an onion the size of a softball and a knife she was slightly afraid of. Her older cousin Marco always chopped the onions at family dinners, and everyone laughed about how he cried through every sauce. This year Kayla had asked to learn, and now here she was, being shown how to curl her fingers into a claw, knuckles forward, so the blade could only find the vegetable and never her fingertips.

"Watch," Grandma said, tucking her own hand into the same claw shape. "The knuckles are the wall. The knife rides along them." Kayla copied it, feeling a little like a crab. Her first cut was crooked, but the second was straighter, and by the fifth she noticed a pattern: the closer the tip of the knife stayed to the board, the less the onion slipped. She wondered if that was true for every vegetable, or just onions with their slick skins.

The sauce came together piece by piece. Onions into the oil, then garlic, then the tomatoes Grandma had crushed by hand. Kayla tasted it and frowned. "It needs something," she said. "I want to revise it. More salt? A pinch of sugar?" Grandma slid the sugar jar across the counter without a word, which Kayla took to mean she'd guessed right.

The problem arrived with the rice. Grandma's timer went off while the bread still had ten minutes in the oven, and there was no free burner, because the sauce was bubbling away on the last one. Grandma reached to lift the pot and hesitated. Kayla called her friend Priya, who cooked dinner at her house every Thursday. "Take it off the heat," Priya said, "lid on. It can rest like that for several minutes and the trapped steam finishes it. That frees the stove for other dishes." Kayla reported it, and Grandma raised an eyebrow, wiped her hands, and moved the pot to a cold burner with the lid pressed down tight.

While the bread finished, Grandpa wandered in still taking his antibiotic for his chest, so Kayla pushed the orange juice away from him and poured him water instead. He watched her stir the sauce and asked what was in it, and she told him: onion, garlic, hand-crushed tomatoes, one secret pinch of sugar. She kept glancing at the rice pot, wondering what was happening under that lid that she couldn't see. Was it really still cooking, or just sitting there? When she finally lifted the lid, the grains stood plump and separate, steam curling up past her face. "It worked," she said. Grandma tasted a forkful, nodded, and pointed at the pasta water, which had just begun to boil.

Adam had until Friday to turn in a bar chart showing how many decomposers he had found in each bag of leaf litter, six bags, six counts, and his science teacher wanted the numbers in a spreadsheet with a formula that added the whole column. Adam did not own a computer, so after school he walked to the public library with his crumpled data sheet in his back pocket. He felt that handing in raw numbers scrawled on paper would look negligent, like he hadn't tried at all, and he had tried. He had counted pill bugs, earthworms, and one moldy beetle.

At the first open terminal, Adam searched for a free spreadsheet tool. The very first result, sitting at the top of the page in its own shaded box, said FREE in capital letters, so he clicked it. The page loaded, invited him to start his project, and then asked for a credit card to "verify his trial." Adam stared at it. He was twelve. He did not have a credit card, and even if he had, his mother would not hand the number to a website that shouted FREE at him. The second link on the page, below the first one and without a box around it, led to a plain tool that opened instantly and asked for nothing.

"Not the top one," Adam murmured, making a note of it. The first link at the top of a search page wasn't necessarily the one to trust. He would remember that.

He typed his counts into a grid, one column for each bag, and hunted through the menus until he found a function that would add them. When he typed it in and pressed enter, the total appeared in the cell at the bottom: forty-three decomposers altogether. He highlighted the column, clicked the chart button, and watched six bars rise out of nothing, tall where he'd found the damp corner bag crawling with sow bugs, short where the dry bag near the fence had held almost nothing. He saved the file and then retrieved it twice more, just to be sure it was really there.

Mrs. Okafor came by with a cart of returns and glanced at his screen. "That's a nice chart," she said. "What program is that?"

"The free one from the second link," Adam said. "The first link wanted a credit card."

She smiled and tapped the edge of the monitor. "You know these computers have spreadsheet software installed already? Has for years. It's right there on the desktop."

Adam looked at the little green icon in the corner of the screen, then at his finished chart, and slid his data sheet deeper into his pocket. "Can I print it anyway?"

The last chocolate chip cookie on the cafeteria table was about to cause a war. Rachel watched Danny wave two dollars over it while Priya held up three, and behind them a sixth grader was digging through a backpack with the focus of someone defusing a bomb.

"Sold to Priya for three dollars," said Marcus, who ran the bake sale table like a small corporation. He had one cash box, one price list, and no interest in fairness. Yesterday the same cookies had been fifty cents each, because yesterday there had been forty of them.

"That's not right," Danny said afterward, walking with Rachel down the hall. "The seller just picks whatever number he wants. Marcus decided three dollars."

"Priya decided three dollars," Rachel said. "She offered it. If nobody wanted cookies, Marcus would be giving them away by lunch."

They argued all the way to the library, where Rachel was supposed to be documenting sources for her social studies paper. Instead she typed "who sets prices" into the catalog, mostly to win the argument. One thin green book came up, and she pulled it off the shelf and sat on the floor between the stacks to read it.

"Listen to this," she called to Danny, who had followed her in. "Some economist, Alfred Marshall, wrote it in 1890 in his book 'Principles of Economics.' He said supply and demand are like the two blades of a pair of scissors. It takes both to set a price."

"So neither one alone does it," Danny said slowly.

"So we were both kind of right, which is the worst possible outcome." Rachel checked the page again to make sure she had the year right, because Danny was famous for claiming her sources were biased whenever they supported her side. 1890. The book said 1890. The scissors had been around a long time, cutting prices in half with two blades, and nobody at their lunch table had noticed.

The next morning Rachel brought a test. She baked a dozen cookies at home, with her mother supervising the oven part, and set them next to Marcus's table with a sign that said ONE DOLLAR. Marcus sneered at her amateur operation until fourth period, when his own cookies ran out and hers were the only ones left in the building. By lunch, kids were offering her two dollars, then two fifty, and one boy tried to reserve a cookie by paying in advance, which Rachel declined on the grounds that she was not a bank.

Then came the twist. At the end of lunch, Mr. Okafor, the vice principal, stopped at her table. Rachel braced for a lecture about unauthorized food sales. Instead he bought her last two cookies for three dollars and asked if she would be interested in running the snack table at the spring fundraiser, since last year's organizer had graduated.

"Fundraiser prices go up when it's a big crowd, right?" Rachel said, sliding him his change.

Mr. Okafor looked at her over the cookie. "Who have you been talking to?"

"A dead economist," Danny said, taking another dollar from a kid who had come back for seconds.

The zamboni had just finished its slow lap, and the ice smelled like cold pennies and burnt rubber when Keira laced her skates at the boards. Day one of hockey tryouts, and forty girls were racing lines under the whir of the fans. Coach Reyes skated the perimeter to supervise each drill, whistle in her teeth, stopwatch in her glove.

Keira went all out. She sprinted the lengths, slammed through the checking drill, and won every board battle along the wall. By the end of practice her legs were trembling, but she felt great, and Marisol, her best friend and her rival for the last forward spot, felt great too. They compared notes in the locker room, dripping and laughing. "Tomorrow we do it all again," Marisol said, pulling her pads off. "I feel like a laser. Nothing's slowing me down."

Day two, Marisol hobbled in like a rusty robot. She gripped the rail in the lobby, wincing at each stair, and stared at her own legs as if they'd betrayed her overnight. "I was fine last night," she groaned. "I even did extra jumps in my driveway." Keira frowned. Her own thighs ached too, worse than yesterday, which was strange. If skating had hurt them, the hurt should have shown up right away, not a full day later, like a bill arriving in the mail. Her older brother had once complained he couldn't sit down for three days after his first squat workout, fine the first evening and destroyed on day two. Keira had filed it away as weird. Now she watched Marisol lower herself onto the bench and thought, this is the same thing.

She tested the idea on her own body. Her hamstrings, which she'd stretched gently that morning, ached but worked. Her quads, which she'd hammered, were stiff as boards. So the pain arrived late, somewhere between a day and three days after, and it picked whatever muscles had been pushed hardest. She said it out loud, grinning. "Delayed onset muscle soreness. My brother calls it DOMS." Marisol squinted. "So yesterday's practice is only hitting me now?" "Now through maybe three days from now," Keira said.

Then came the twist Keira hadn't planned. Coach Reyes split them into scrimmage lines and put Marisol on defense, not because she was slow but because her legs couldn't take forward sprinting today. Keira got Marisol's spot at wing, and she hated how she got it. Between periods she skated over. "You should have it when you're whole," she told her. "Coach, can we rerun this Friday?" Reyes raised an eyebrow, then nodded once.

Friday, both girls fresh-legged, raced the length of the ice side by side, sticks clattering, ice chips flying like glass. "Whatever happens," Marisol panted, "remind me never to do driveway jumps after day one again." Keira laughed and leaned into the turn.

Brielle leaned close to the screen so the code seemed to magnify, every line of it jumping out at her. The assignment said her Python program had to ask for a number and print whether it was prime, and she was determined to finish before anyone else in the class. She typed the input line, then a loop that checked each possible divisor, and pressed run.

"Nine," she whispered, typing it in. The screen printed "not prime," and she nearly knocked her chair over. "Yes! It works!"

Then Desmond slid his laptop across the table. His cat sprite walked across a golden coin again and again, and the coin never vanished. "My game is broken," he said. "The cat touches it and nothing happens."

Brielle grabbed the laptop. She clicked the coin's script and stared at the blocks. "Your 'if touching' block is just sitting out there by itself," she said. "It's not in any loop. It only runs once, when the script starts, and then it's done." She pointed at the stack below it. "Put it inside your forever loop. Then it gets checked again and again."

"Forever," Desmond repeated, dragging the block into the loop.

They hit the green flag together. The cat padded across the coin and the coin popped out of existence with a sparkle. Desmond whooped so loudly that their colleague two seats over, a quiet kid named Priya, looked up from her own screen.

"That's the same thing my program does," Brielle said, spinning her chair around. "The loop tries dividing the number over and over. One check wouldn't be enough. You have to keep checking."

Priya frowned at her screen. "Mine says eleven is not prime, but it is prime."

Brielle rolled her chair over. In Priya's loop, the check read the number as text instead of a number, so the comparison came out wrong every time. Brielle showed her the one small fix, and Priya ran it again. "Prime!" it printed, and the three of them grinned like they had won something.

Desmond tested his game one more time. The cat walked over the coin, and this time he collected it. "You want to be my quality tester?" he asked. "Fair warning, my opinion of your testing is subjective. I'll say you're great no matter what."

"Deal," Brielle said, and saved her program with a flourish. Then she leaned toward the screen and typed one more number to test: ninety-seven.

"Prime," the computer answered.

Kaylee had exactly one free period before the photography club's web page had to go live, and the computer lab smelled like warm keyboards and somebody's grape soda. Her plan was simple: a title, a few pictures of lichen from the school nature trail, and a heading that sat dead center instead of hugging the left edge like it was afraid of the page.

"You're still on the heading?" said Marcus, sliding into the seat beside her. He was supposed to be finishing the club's Python quiz program, which kept score but refused, so far, to display anything sensible.

"I'm still on the centering," Kaylee said. She typed `text-align: center;` into the style block, saved, and hit refresh. The heading stayed stubbornly on the left, like a cat that had decided that corner was its corner now.

While she stared at it, Marcus ran his program. A question came up, he answered it, and the score line printed `777`. The half of the club still in the lab gathered around and laughed, because a score of seven hundred seventy-seven was, in Marcus's words, "generous."

"That's not the math," Marcus said. "I added seven three times. It should be twenty-one." He scrolled through his code like he was looking for a burglar hiding between the lines.

Kaylee leaned over. The problem, whatever it was, wasn't something she could see by reading; the code looked fine, which meant the cause was somewhere underneath, like the reason her heading wouldn't move. She had an idea. She opened a Python console and typed it small and quick: `'7' * 3`. The screen returned `777`.

"There," she said. "In Python, multiplying text by a whole number repeats the text, so '7' * 3 gives '777' instead of 21."

"So my sevens are strings?"

"You quoted them when you built the question. So it glued three sevens together." Marcus went back and found it, a pair of quotation marks doing quiet damage, and fixed it. His next score printed 21, and the club applauded like he'd landed a plane.

Kaylee turned back to her own hidden cause. If his bug had been invisible, hers probably was too, so she stopped reading the words and started reading the shape of them. The braces, the curly ones that opened the style rule, didn't match. One opened, and the browser, finding no reason to trust anything after it, ignored the whole thing. She added the missing one, saved, refreshed, and the heading drifted to the middle of the page at last, over a row of gray-green lichen thriving on an old stone wall.

"Beautiful," Marcus said, peering at the screen. "Opaque background, too. Very solid."

"Like my debugging," Kaylee said, and clicked refresh one more time just to watch it happen again.

Mr. Okafor's computer lab smelled like warm keyboards and old carpet, and Zachary had one goal before the bell: get his heading to sit in the middle of the page. He had typed the tag for his heading, saved the file, and opened it in the browser. The words "Zachary's Fossil Finder" sat stubbornly against the left edge, like a kid refusing to move over on a bench.

"Try the style part," said Priya from the next computer. "The CSS. That's what it's for." She turned her screen toward him, showing her own page about anime, its title floating dead centre.

Zachary stared at his file. There were two languages on the screen, one building the bones of the page and one decorating it, and he couldn't see either of them doing anything. The heading only existed because of invisible instructions, and something invisible was keeping it crooked. He had a theory. Maybe the decorating language had a rule for centring, the way a game has a rule for jumping. He tried typing a line that said text should be centered, saved, and hit refresh. The heading slid to the middle of the page.

"Whoa," he said. "It moved."

His grandfather, who was visiting for Grandparents' Day and had been watching from the doorway, wandered over. "In my day we thought coding meant typing walls of letters," he said. "My friend's grandson shows me programs he builds by snapping blocks together."

"That's Scratch," Zachary said. "It came out of the MIT Media Lab. It was first released in 2007." He pulled up the Scratch site on his screen so his grandfather could see the colored blocks clicking together like LEGO.

"Blocks," his grandfather repeated, shaking his head slowly. "So the computer doesn't care whether you type or snap?"

"I guess it all turns into the same thing underneath," Zachary said. He wondered whether that was true, whether every language, even the block one, dissolved into the same invisible stuff before the machine understood it. He refreshed his page again just to watch the heading jump to centre a second time.

Mr. Okafor paused behind them. "Nice work, Zachary. Next week we start storing user answers in a database, so your fossil quiz can remember who took it."

"That's like a file cabinet the page can look things up in," Zachary said, mostly to himself. His mind was already racing ahead, ideas fluctuating between a page where visitors typed in their town and one where the site suggested nearby dig sites. This lab felt fertile, like a place where things you built could grow into bigger things.

His grandfather leaned closer to the screen, squinting at the centred title. "So show me," he said. "Where do I snap my first block?"

Colton sat on the crinkly paper of the exam table with his elbows on his knees, staring at the two dark half-moons under his arms. They had shown up halfway through morning announcements, and PJ Torres had announced them to half the hallway like it was breaking news. Now Dr. Marsh was tapping the screen, and Colton waited for his chance.

"Growing bodies sweat more," Dr. Marsh said. "It's normal." She handed him a sample card. "What matters is what you buy. Check the label."

That was it. No cure, no pill. In the waiting room, Mom flipped through a magazine while Colton's little brother narrated the fish tank, and Colton turned the sample card over and over. Whatever the doctor knew, she had left the actual answer for him to find.

The drugstore was two doors down. Colton stood in the deodorant aisle while his brother wandered toward the candy, and he read labels like his life depended on it, because tryouts were Thursday and the gym had no air conditioning. Two sticks sat side by side. One said antiperspirant, one said deodorant. He had always thought they were just two words for the same thing, but the fine print did not agree. The antiperspirant box said it reduces sweating by temporarily plugging sweat ducts. He read it twice, then turned to the other. That one never mentioned stopping sweat at all, only odor, reducing it or covering the smell.

"Those are opposites, basically," Colton said to his brother, who had drifted back with a pack of gum. "Antiperspirant stops the wet. Deodorant only handles the stink."

"So get the wet one," his brother said, already bored.

It was that simple, and it wasn't. Colton thought about PJ and the hallway jury that had laughed at his shirt. The antiperspirant stopped the actual sweating, which was the whole problem. The deodorant would just put perfume on top of it. His old stick, he realized, had been a deodorant all along, which explained a lot about the last month. Trying to fix it by layering on three swipes every morning had been reckless; it had done nothing but waste time.

He took the antiperspirant to the register with his own five dollars. Thursday afternoon, in the hot gym, he took his shot, ran the lines, raised his hand for the pass, and kept his arms up on purpose. Afterward, he pulled his shirt away from his body and looked. Dry. He walked past PJ on the way to the water fountain and lifted his arm to wipe his forehead.

"Nice tryout," PJ said.

Jonathan had one job at the science fair table: dip the strip, read the color, call it. Mrs. Okonkwo had given him twelve bottles, all labeled with letters instead of names, and a stack of litmus paper, red and blue. His poster explained that acids turn blue litmus red, bases turn red litmus blue, and that the pH scale runs from zero to fourteen, with acids low and bases high. It should have been simple. But bottle H had turned his blue strip red, and his red strip red too, and then, when he tried the second strip from the same bottle, both stayed blue. That could not happen, and yet it had.

He stood very still, holding the wet paper up to the gym lights. Behind him, judges moved down the row of tables. Somewhere a baking-soda volcano burbled. In front of him, his display looked neat and certain, while the evidence in his hand disagreed with everything on it. If the paper was bad, his whole results chart was worthless. If the bottle was bad, then something invisible was going on inside it, something he could not see, only reason about.

"Your table's cool," said Priya from the next booth, where her eccentric model of a chlorine atom hung from a coat hanger, painted balls wobbling on fishing line. Her index card read MASS NUMBER 35, ATOMIC NUMBER 17, and then NEUTRONS, followed by a blank she had covered with a scribbled 20. "I don't get the blank though. My grandma wouldn't just tell me. She had me doing a practice sheet at her kitchen table last night and she said the mass number counts the protons plus the neutrons, so I should be able to figure it out myself."

Jonathan looked at the card, not really meaning to. Then he looked again. If the mass number counted protons plus neutrons, and the atomic number was the protons, then neutrons had to be the part left over. Thirty-five take away seventeen. Eighteen, not twenty. "You wrote twenty," he said slowly. "But the neutrons are the mass number minus the atomic number. That's eighteen."

Priya frowned, checked her card, and erased the twenty with such force the card bent. "Grandma's going to be smug about this."

The movement made her elbow catch her water cup, and water arced across the boundary of their tables and splashed, impossibly, onto the far end of Jonathan's stack of litmus paper. He grabbed the stack. The bottom third was soaked and useless, and there, in the puddle, sat his mystery bottle H, which he had capped badly and left too near the edge. A thin line of liquid had been seeping out along the table all morning, pooling under his paper strips. His first test had been honest. Every test after that had used paper already touched by the leak, and the leak, he realized, was base, because his spare red strip, dipped clean on its dry end into fresh water, turned blue when a drop of the puddle reached it. He had not been testing the bottles. He had been testing his own spilled solution.

A judge stopped at his table, clipboard ready, and asked him to evaluate his results. Jonathan took a fresh dry strip, held it up, and said, "Give me thirty seconds. I have to redo one, and I can tell you exactly why."

On Friday afternoon, room 214 was supposed to be silent for free reading, but the table by the window was not silent. Devon had his Monopoly box open, setting up a game for indoor recess, and Marcus was imitating the way Eli had said "actually" during homeroom, drawing out the word until the boys on either side of him laughed. "Actually, that's not in the rules," Marcus said in a pinched voice. "Actually, actually." Eli stared at his book and turned a page he had not read.

Harper watched from two tables over. She wanted to tell Marcus to knock it off, but last month she had done exactly that in the cafeteria, yelling at a sixth grader for teasing her friend, and the teasing had simply moved targets, landing on her friend for needing a bodyguard. Shouting made it worse. That much she had learned. What she had not figured out was what to do instead, so she sat there feeling useless while Eli kept his eyes on his page.

Then she noticed something. Every time Marcus did the voice, he looked around to check whether people were laughing. When Tyson had smirked and gone back to his comic, Marcus repeated the joke louder. When nobody reacted at all, the joke got smaller. That was her inference: the teasing ran on an audience, the way a fire ran on air. She could not take the air away by ordering people to stop laughing, but maybe she could give the audience something else to do. She had an idea, and it was worth a test.

She walked over, sat down at Devon's table, and said, "Can I play? We need at least three." Devon nodded and handed her the dog. Eli glanced up once. Marcus drifted over too, because a game was starting and nobody was watching his performance anymore.

They played, and on Eli's second turn he landed on Marvin Gardens and passed on buying it. Devon reached for the dice, but Eli said, "Actually, that's not right. The official rules say if a player lands on an unowned property and chooses not to buy it, the bank auctions it to the players." Marcus snorted. "Nobody gets auctioned." Harper flipped the rule sheet out from under the box lid, ran her finger down the column, and turned it so Marcus could see. "It's right here." Marcus read it, shrugged, and said, "Fine, but I'm not investing my money in Marvin Gardens." They auctioned it anyway, and Devon won it for cheap, which made him so pleased he forgot to be lethargic about counting his bills, as he had been all afternoon.

They played until the bell, and Marcus never did the voice again, not even when Eli beat him to Park Place. On the way out, Eli caught up with Harper in the hallway. "Thanks for the game," he said. "You were two dollars short on rent, by the way."

Easton had told his mother he would make dinner for once, and now, at Priya's counter with a whole onion in front of him, that promise felt like a decision made by someone else entirely. Priya's parents would be home at six thirty, which gave them fifty minutes to produce a pasta sauce from scratch and no time to go to the hospital.

"Curl your fingers under, like a claw," Priya said, demonstrating. "The knuckles guide the blade. The fingertips stay out of the way."

Easton curled his fingers and lowered the knife, waiting for the onion to fight back. It didn't. The slices came off thin and even, and he felt briefly like a person who knew things. "This is actually working."

"You look shocked," Priya said, stirring the canned tomatoes they were turning into sauce with garlic and a pinch of sugar. "Don't get cocky. The onion gets harder near the root."

She was right, but only slightly, and by six ten the onion was fully chopped and nobody was bleeding. Easton scraped it into the pan, and the kitchen turned warm and humid with steam while everything sizzled. Priya moved the sauce pot to the back burner and put a tray of garlic bread into the oven.

"Timer's set for eight minutes," she said. "Then we pull the tray."

At six twenty-one, Easton washed his hands at the sink while the pasta boiled beside him. A wave of water sloshed over the edge and soaked the oven mitt hanging on the hook, and he thought nothing of it. When the timer beeped, he grabbed that mitt and reached for the oven door.

"Stop." Priya caught his wrist. "It's wet. Wet oven mitts can burn your hands. The water in the cloth carries heat quickly, and it can turn to steam."

Easton looked at the mitt, then at the red mark already creeping across the heel of his palm where the damp had touched it. So the heat hadn't just sat on the surface of the cloth like it did when the mitt was dry. It had traveled through, fast, carried by the water, and somewhere in there it had boiled. He filed that away next to the onion trick: invisible rules, running underneath ordinary things, waiting for someone to grab the wrong one. Priya interpreted his silence correctly and handed him a dry mitt from the drawer.

The garlic bread came out golden. At six twenty-nine, sauce bubbling, they heard the garage door open.

"Dinner," Easton announced, "made by professionals."

Megan slid her poster board under the lab table and pulled out the two jars she had brought from home. One had held soup left open on the counter for a week, and it was now cloudy and streaked with green fuzz. The other had been sealed since the day she made it, and it looked almost the same as fresh. Her science fair project was due in three days, and she still could not answer the question her little brother had accused her of dodging: "If germs are everywhere in the air, why didn't the sealed jar go bad?"

In the empty science classroom after school, she laid the jars side by side and tapped the sealed lid. Something invisible was the problem, and she could not watch it happen. What she needed was a testable guess, something she could check with an experiment instead of just arguing about it. In class they had called that kind of guess a hypothesis, and Mr. Reyes kept saying a good one could either win or lose, as long as it could lose. "The soup went bad because something from the air got in," she wrote in her notebook. "If I let air in but keep the dust out, the soup should stay clean."

She was on her second try at bending glass tubing over the burner when Marcus from her class wandered in to grab his backpack. "You're going to set off the alarm, being that reckless with a flame," he said, but he stayed to watch. She had drawn a diagram from the old science book on the shelf, the one with the picture of swan-shaped flasks. She told him what the caption said while she worked the glass into a long S-shaped curve. "Louis Pasteur boiled broth in flasks with long S-shaped necks, and the broth stayed free of microbes because dust and germs got trapped in the bend of the neck." Marcus leaned over her shoulder. "So the neck is the whole trick?"

"It's my whole protagonist," Megan said, pointing her pen at the curve in the glass. "The jar that went bad is just the villain." She filled her homemade flask with broth, boiled it on the hot plate until steam rolled off, and set it beside an open jar of the same broth as her control. Then she labeled both and carried them to the windowsill, where they would sit for the next two days.

On Thursday she almost ran to the classroom. The open jar had gone cloudy and sour-smelling, and she held her breath as she lifted the flask with the curved neck. The broth inside was clear, no fuzz, no film on the glass. The bend had done its job while the open mouth had let trouble straight in. Marcus looked over the jars, then at her notebook, where she had written one last line and underlined it twice: hypothesis supported.

Mr. Reyes stopped at her table on his way past the windowsill, picked up the flask, and turned it in the light. Megan stood there grinning, waiting for the question she finally knew how to answer. "So," he said, "tell me why this one is still clean."

Brooke had promised the science fair committee a volcano, and now she regretted it, because everyone built volcanoes, and hers was going to look exactly like the one Marcus Reyes was building two lab tables away.

"You know why they erupt, right?" Marcus said, holding up his vinegar bottle like a trophy. "Baking soda plus vinegar. The baking soda is sodium bicarbonate, the vinegar is acetic acid, and together they make carbon dioxide gas. That's what pushes everything out. Everybody knows that."

"Everybody also builds the same cone out of papier-mâché," Brooke said. She looked down at her own cone, gray and lumpy, and decided she'd rather lose than present a third identical volcano. If the gas did the pushing, then the amount of gas ought to matter, which meant the amount of vinegar ought to matter, and nobody ever checked. She could test it. Three bottles, three different amounts, same baking soda each time, and a ruler taped to a wall behind the volcano to measure how high each eruption reached.

Mr. Okafor wandered past and did not offer help, which was his way of saying he trusted them, or possibly that he was being negligent about supervising the vinegar supply. Either way, Brooke got to work. The first trial, a small splash of vinegar, produced a sad burp that barely reached ten centimeters. The second, half a bottle, shot foam past the thirty-centimeter mark and splattered Marcus's notebook.

"Hey. That stuff hindered my data," Marcus said, wiping off his page.

"Then maybe you should collect some," Brooke said, and to her surprise, he came over. His project, it turned out, was just a volcano with red food coloring, no measurements at all, and the fair was in two days. He had an obligation to his partner too, which he had been ignoring.

They ran six trials together, trading the jobs of pouring and reading the ruler. More vinegar meant a taller eruption every single time, and the numbers lined up so neatly that Brooke wrote them twice to be sure. Marcus copied the last column into his notebook, then looked at his plain red cone the way you look at a sandwich next to a banquet.

"We're combining projects," he announced. "Your measurements, my cone. Mine has better paint."

Brooke considered arguing, but his cone did have better paint. "Fine," she said. "But I'm the one who says how much vinegar goes in the bottle."

"Deal," said Marcus, and handed her the ruler.

Louis sat on the porch steps of Grandpa's house with a sketchpad on his knees, staring at the driveway sketch he'd made the night before. Something about it was wrong, and he couldn't say what. The road looked like it was tipping sideways, like the whole street was sliding off the page.

He was drawing the view because of a promise he'd made at summer camp two weeks ago. Flashback: on the last day of art class, Ms. Reyes had pinned everyone's street sketches to the cabin wall, and Louis's had drawn a groan from the kids. "Your road edges are going three different ways," his friend Devon had said, tapping the paper. "Mine too," Louis admitted, though he hadn't even noticed until Devon pointed it out. Ms. Reyes had said only, "Everything going back into the distance shares one point." She never said where, and the bus home came before Louis could ask.

Now he looked up from the porch at Grandpa's actual street, the one that ran straight back toward the far fence line. He held up his pencil at arm's length, level with his own eyes, and squinted along it. The road's edges, the sidewalk lines, even the cracks between the driveway slabs all seemed to lean toward each other the farther back they went. His intuition told him they weren't really leaning at all. They were parallel, side by side, the same distance apart all the way down. The slant was only in the looking.

He drew a light horizontal line straight across his paper, level with where his eyes would be if he were standing in the picture. Then he marked a single dot on it, right where the road seemed to disappear. From each bottom corner of his road he drew lines up to that one dot, and the same for both sidewalk edges. He checked it against the real street again, then added windows and doorways with lines aimed at the same spot. It was strange, like the dot was a magnet pulling everything in.

Grandpa came out with two glasses of lemonade and leaned over his shoulder. "What's that dot for?" "It's called a vanishing point," Louis said. "Every line going straight back runs to it, right on the horizon, at eye level. One point for all of them." Grandpa squinted at the drawing, then at the street, then back. "Huh. I've lived here forty years and never saw that."

Louis texted Devon a photo of the finished sketch that evening, and the reply came back fast: "NOW it looks real. Do my street next." He grinned and flipped to a clean page.

Lydia leaned over the lab table in room 214, where the radiator hissed because someone had turned the valve the wrong way and steam kept escaping into the already humid September air. In front of her lay two printed climate graphs, one for Cairo and one for Singapore, and Mr. Ruiz had asked the class to decide which place got more rain. The bars for Cairo looked taller in three different months, and Lydia tapped the paper triumphantly.

"See? Cairo wins in March, April, and May," she told Marcus, who sat across from her with his arms crossed. "The bars are right there. Taller means more."

Marcus frowned. "Singapore is a rainforest. My cousin went there and said it rained every single afternoon. Cairo is a desert. Deserts are dry, that's the whole point." He slid the papers closer to himself as if the graph might confess.

"You can't argue with a graph," Lydia said, but a small doubt hindered her from saying it too loudly. Deserts were dry. She knew that. She pulled both sheets back and looked again, not at the bars this time but at the numbers running up the left side of each page. On Cairo's graph, the rainfall axis climbed to 300 millimeters at the top. On Singapore's, it climbed to 400. She found March on both. Cairo's tall bar stopped at about 40. Singapore's shorter-looking bar, on its much taller axis, stopped at 170.

"Oh no," she said. "Look at the axes. The bars aren't on the same scale." She turned the papers so Marcus could see. "A short bar can stand for more rain if the axis goes higher. You can only compare the bars by height if both graphs use the same scale."

Marcus leaned in, traced the numbers with his finger, and sat back slowly. "So Singapore gets more rain in March. A lot more."

"And every other month too," Lydia said, checking the rest of the year and finding the same thing over and over. She had been so sure, and she had been wrong in front of the whole table group. Priya, two seats down, had heard everything and was already whispering it to someone else.

Mr. Ruiz walked by and set a small stack of fresh worksheets on their table, graphs with matching scales printed on both. "Try these," he said, and moved on.

Lydia took the top sheet, but she kept the old ones too, folded into her binder. She wanted to remember being certain and wrong at the same time, so next time she would look at the numbers before she pointed at the bars. "Fine," she told Marcus. "Your cousin's afternoons were right."

"Want to tell Priya that?" Marcus asked.

Lydia looked over at Priya, still whispering, and shook her head. "I'll tell her myself at lunch."

Mathis had been camped on the couch for three days, surrounded by crumpled tissues, a thermometer, and half a glass of orange juice he kept forgetting about. The flu was finally loosening its grip, but his nose still felt like a leaky faucet. His little sister Nadia wandered in, holding her toothbrush, and stood at the edge of his blanket nest.

"Why do you keep telling me to use soap?" she said. "I rinsed my hands with water just now. They're clean. See?" She held them out like evidence.

Mathis squinted at her from under the blanket. "Water just slides off the virus," he said. "Soap breaks apart the fatty outer layer that surrounds flu viruses. That's why washing with soap gets rid of them better than rinsing with water alone."

Nadia blinked. "The virus has a layer? Like a coat?"

"Kind of." He sat up, interested despite himself. "Think of it like grease on a pan. You can rinse a greasy pan forever and it stays greasy. Add soap and it comes apart." He paused. "At least, that's what I think happens. Let me check." He grabbed his phone from the armrest, typed with one thumb, and scrolled. "Huh. Yeah. That's the consensus. Every source says the same thing."

"So my hands are still covered in viruses?" Nadia stared at her palms like they'd betrayed her.

"Probably. I've been sneezing on every doorknob in this house for three days." Mathis pushed the blanket back. "Come on. Let's do an experiment."

In the kitchen, he found the olive oil and a dinner plate. He poured a thin puddle of oil onto the plate. "Pretend this oil is the fatty layer. Dip your finger in water and try to wipe it off." Nadia swiped at the oil. It smeared and stayed, a slick rainbow smear across the white plate.

"Now try with soap." She lathered her finger and dragged it through. The oil broke apart and lifted away, clinging to the foam in little beads. She did it again, and again, watching the plate go clean.

"So the virus just... falls apart?" she said.

"That's the idea. Its coat gets broken up." Mathis turned the plate under the tap, watching the last oily streaks vanish. It was strange to think about, all those invisible things on doorknobs and hands, held together by something so delicate. What else was floating around that nobody could see?

Nadia washed her hands at the sink, properly this time, humming while she scrubbed. Then she pointed at Mathis. "You should wash too. You're the one who's sick."

He held up his hands in surrender and headed for the bathroom. "Fine," he called over his shoulder. "But nobody touches my orange juice."

Hailey slid into her seat just as the last bell finished ringing, and the computer lab smelled like warm keyboards and the janitor's lemon spray. Mr. Ruiz had written one sentence on the whiteboard: "Write a program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime." She had sixty minutes, and she wanted the green "CORRECT" on the checker more than she wanted lunch, which was saying something, because today was pizza day.

She typed fast, her fingers still cold from the walk across the courtyard. She knew the concept: a prime number has no divisors except 1 and itself, so she should try dividing by every number in between. She wrote a loop, hit run, and typed in 7. The screen printed "not prime." She tried 11. "Not prime." She tried 5, 3, even 13, which she had known was prime since fourth grade. Every single one came back "not prime."

"Yours broken too?" whispered Deshawn from the next computer. He leaned over, chewing his pencil. Around them, papers with the assignment began to circulate as students printed their attempts and compared answers in low voices.

"Every number," Hailey said. "Even the primes." She stared at her loop, then at the output, then back at the loop. Something invisible was happening between those two lines of code, and she meant to find it. She added one print statement, a temporary spy: every time the loop found a divisor, it would report which one. She ran it again with 7, and the screen filled with a single line: divisor 7.

"There it is," she said. "It's dividing 7 by 7." The checker's complaint suddenly made sense. Her loop went range(2, n), and that stopped one number short, at n minus 1. At least she thought it did. She tested it with another spy, printing everything the loop actually tried for 7, and out came 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. The number 7 itself never even entered the loop, so her earlier line must have grabbed it some other way. She scrolled up and found her mistake sitting there in plain view, dividing n by n before the loop even started. She deleted it, and range(2, n) did exactly what she needed: it tried 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6, every possible divisor except 1 and 7 itself.

Deshawn leaned over again. "Is that fix going to work, or is the problem more ambiguous than that?" She grinned, typed 7, and hit enter. The word "prime" appeared, small and green on the dark screen. She reached over and tapped his paper with her pencil. "Try 13," she said.

The bean seeds on the windowsill had begun to germinate, tiny green hooks pushing out of the soil, but Samantha barely looked at them. She was still thinking about what she had said in the hallway that morning: that most students at their school walked to school. Marcus had laughed and called it a wild guess, and she had walked away with her ears burning.

Now Mr. Okafor was writing two words on the board: opinion and claim. He would not say much, only that the class would spend the period deciding which of the statements on his desk belonged in each column. Samantha slid her bean tray aside and leaned forward.

"Most students at our school walk to school," Mr. Okafor read aloud. "Opinion or claim?"

"Opinion," said Priya. "Nobody knows that."

"But you could find out," Samantha said, before she could stop herself. "You could ask everybody. Like a survey."

Marcus turned around in his seat. "Nobody has asked everybody."

"So?" Samantha's heart was beating fast. "It can still be checkable even if nobody has checked it yet. If we took a survey, we'd know."

The room went quiet. Mr. Okafor tapped the board. "Could we actually do that?"

"We could count," Priya said slowly. "At the doors, in the morning. Walkers, bus riders, car riders."

They planned it right there. On Tuesday, Samantha stood at the front doors with a clipboard, making a tally mark for every student who arrived on foot. Priya took the side doors and Marcus, who had volunteered before Samantha could ask him, took the gym entrance. By first bell Samantha's fingers were cold and her column of tally marks ran down the whole page.

They typed the numbers into the classroom database, which Mr. Okafor kept for experiments, and the bar chart appeared on the screen. Walkers were the tallest bar. Not by much, though, and the bus bar was close behind. Samantha stared at it, remembering how certain she had sounded in the hallway, how sure. She had been right, mostly, and somehow that felt less like winning than she had expected.

"Well?" Marcus said, leaning over her shoulder at the screen. "Were you right or not?"

"Close enough that it's probable I'd be right again next time," Samantha said. "But I'd have to count again to know for sure."

Marcus grinned and shook the clipboard at her. "Same time Thursday?"

The notification buzzed at 9:47 p.m., and Noah picked up his phone to find the group chat already scrolling fast. "BIO PRESENTATIONS FRIDAY," Priya had typed in all caps, followed by Mr. Kessler's rubric screenshot. Under it, sixteen thumbs-up and one message from Tasha: "not gonna be there friday. doctor thing." Noah frowned. Tasha had a doctor thing for the last presentation too, and the one before that. He scrolled back through the chat history, and the pattern condensed into something he could actually see: every single time a presentation came up, Tasha vanished.

He typed, "u ok?" and then deleted it, because it felt like calling her out in front of everyone. Instead he sent a private message: "hey, you doing the bio slideshow? I can share mine if you want to compare notes." Three dots appeared, vanished, appeared again. "i'm skipping," she wrote. "my anxiety gets so bad before them i feel sick." Noah sat back against his pillow. He got nervous too, stomach flipping, heart loud, but he'd noticed something about his own stress that he couldn't leave alone. When he forced himself through a presentation, the next one felt a little smaller. When he ducked out of one, like the book report he'd faked a fever for in October, the fear afterward seemed to grow instead of shrink, like it was being fed.

He tested the idea out loud, typing slowly. "ok weird question. the ones you skip feel scarier the next time, right? like each one is worse than the last?" A long pause. Then: "yes?? how did u know." Noah's own coping trick was reading in the hallway for five minutes before class, or texting his brother a joke, anything to get his hands busy. "i think skipping gives you relief really fast," he wrote, "but then it makes the anxiety stronger later, because you never get to find out you could handle it." He stared at the sentence, hoping it didn't sound like a lecture from a health pamphlet. Tasha replied with a single shaking-face emoji, then: "friday is in 3 days. i can't."

"you don't have to do the whole thing," he typed. "do the first slide. one slide. i'll stand next to you." He suggested she set a boundary with Mr. Kessler, just tell him flat out she'd present last so she wasn't first up and panicked. The next morning Tasha showed him her slideshow, eight slides about axolotls, and admitted she'd been drafting it for two weeks without telling anyone. "so you already did the work," Noah said. "your brain just keeps saying run." She laughed a small, real laugh and said her mom kept an optimistic sticky note on the fridge that she'd started ignoring.

Friday came. Tasha went second to last, and she stood there with her note card shaking, and she read the first slide, and then the second, and after the axolotl regrowing limbs she looked up and saw Priya mouthing "whoa" in the front row. When she sat down she texted Noah from across the room: "that was awful and i did it anyway." He wrote back, "memoir title. 'awful and i did it anyway.' you're welcome." On the walk to lunch she caught up with him at the water fountain, still pale but grinning. "Next one," she said, "I'm going third."

Elizabeth dragged the garden hose across the backyard and pointed it at the sandbox her little brother Caleb had claimed as his kingdom. He stood on the ladder of the slide with his arms crossed.

"That's my city," he said. "I'm the tenant. I pay rent in candy."

"You're squatting," Elizabeth said. "Move your buildings." She had a science project due Monday: she was supposed to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years, using erosion and deposition, and she refused to just read a paragraph off the internet. She wanted to build the thing.

Caleb slid down and started relocating his plastic dinosaurs while she raked the sand into a smooth slope and turned the hose to a trickle. At first nothing happened. The water spread out and vanished. She narrowed the stream with her thumb and persisted, holding it in the same channel for ten minutes, and a small groove began to cut. Sand lifted from the upstream edge and traveled, then dropped where the flow slowed at the bottom, building a fan-shaped delta. She felt a jolt of recognition. Erosion on one end, deposition on the other, the canyon creeping backward between them. If a trickle did this in ten minutes, a river over millions of years made the carving inevitable.

"But it doesn't matter," Caleb said, kneeling to inspect her groove. "My rocks don't change. This gray one has been gray forever. Rocks are rocks."

"That's wrong," Elizabeth said. She held up two sandbox stones, one smooth, one jagged. She rubbed them together and grit fell onto the sand, the same grit the water was already carrying away. The jagged stone was becoming sand, and sand could press into new rock, and rock could melt or get squeezed and heated until it was something else entirely.

"Any rock can become any other rock," she said. "Melting, weathering, heat and pressure. It's called the rock cycle."

"You're making that up."
