"Look it up yourself." She turned the hose back on, and the water found her groove again, deepened it, and split around a buried rock, leaving it standing on a little column of sand like a tiny mesa. Caleb watched the delta spread toward his last dinosaur.

"That's going to flood my guy," he said.

"Then move him. That's what the river does. It doesn't knock."

The bus smelled like wet raincoats and old vinyl, and Cameron had the letter folded in his back pocket, which meant he'd read it eleven times since breakfast. Mr. Reyes had clipped it from the local paper and dropped it on Cameron's desk with a shrug, saying only, "Thought you'd want this, since you're at that park every Saturday." The letter said the new skate park, which cost two million dollars, is a waste, and Cameron's stomach had been clenched ever since.

He slid into the seat across from Dana, who was nursing a cold and sniffling into a tissue. "Don't breathe on me," she said. "My mom says this virus is going around the whole school." Cameron held his breath for three seconds out of politeness, then gave up. He unfolded the letter and smoothed it on his knee.

"Read this," he said. Dana read it. Behind them, Marcus leaned over the seat, because Marcus leaned over every seat on the bus, that was practically his job.

"Two million dollars," Marcus said. "That's a lie. My uncle works for the city. It was two million." Cameron frowned at the paper. If the number was right, then that part of the letter wasn't a lie at all. You could look it up. You could call the city office, or find the budget online, and the number would either be true or it wouldn't. Dana blew her nose and said, "So the letter's true, then?"

"No," Cameron said slowly. "Not all of it." He read the last words again. A waste. That was the part that had been buzzing in his head since breakfast like a fly against a window. His little sister had asked at dinner whether the park really was a waste, and their dad had said that was somebody's opinion, not a fact, but he'd said it fast and then gone back to his noodles, and Cameron hadn't gotten it until just now, on a bus that rattled over every pothole on Marsh Road.

"Here's the thing," he said, holding up the letter so both of them could see it. "The cost can be checked, but 'a waste' is an opinion." Dana squinted at him. "So?" Cameron tapped the paper. "So when Mr. Reyes asks us Monday about stuff like this, that's the whole trick. One sentence can have both in it. Like if I said the ocean, which covers most of Earth, is boring. The covering part you could check. The boring part is just me." Marcus drummed his fingers on the seat back. "So whoever wrote this could be right about the money and still be wrong about the park."

"Or right about the park and lying about the money," Dana said, and sneezed into her tissue.

The bus groaned around the corner by the field where the last endangered cranes nested each spring, and Cameron folded the letter along its old creases. He was already planning what he'd write back to the paper, something that started with the number and ended with Saturday morning, his board under his arm, the whole park loud with wheels and nobody complaining. "First thing Monday," he told them, "I'm asking Mr. Reyes if we can print both."

Brayden balanced the mixing bowl on the picnic table and checked the recipe again, though he had memorized it by now. Mom's birthday biscuits, the ones his grandfather used to make, and Brayden had promised the whole family a batch at tonight's backyard dinner. The garden behind him was lush after a week of rain, and the grill already smelled like charcoal, but the biscuits were his job alone.

He reached for the tin marked baking powder and tilted it. Empty. A few grains sifted out and that was all. The nearest store was a twenty-minute bike ride, and the potatoes needed watching on the grill, so riding away wasn't really an option. He stood there with the tin in his hand, feeling the old resentment from last summer rise up, the time he'd quit halfway through Grandpa's recipe book and Grandpa had quietly finished it himself. This year Brayden wanted to preserve that recipe, not lose it, and quitting twice felt like the same failure twice.

In the cupboard by the back door he found a box of baking soda and thought, close enough. He stirred it in, cut the dough, and set the tray on the grill's side shelf where the heat was gentle. Ten minutes later he lifted the lid and stared. The biscuits had gone flat and faintly bitter, nothing like the tall golden ones in the photo.

He sat down on the step and turned it over. The pancake batter Grandpa made used buttermilk, sour and tangy, and it always rose high. These biscuits used plain milk. Soda went in where buttermilk went in. Powder went in where nothing sour went in. Brayden stood up slowly. The box of baking soda needed something acidic in the batter to do its work. He grabbed his phone and read the label on a baking powder tin in a photo: it already contained both baking soda and a dry acid, which was why a recipe didn't need anything acidic for the batter to rise.

"Then I'll add the acid myself," he said out loud. He found lemon juice in the fridge, mixed a fresh batch with plain milk, soda, and a careful spoonful of juice, and slid the tray back onto the warm shelf. His little sister wandered over and peeked under the foil.

"Smell like Grandpa's," she said.

"Better," Brayden said, and lifted the lid on eight tall, golden biscuits.

Kate sat at the kitchen table with her laptop open, the cursor blinking in the To field of a new email. Her best friend Priya's surprise party was in two weeks, and Kate wanted to invite the whole science class, all twenty-six of them. The problem was that she only had about nine addresses of her own. The rest lived in a class list Mr. Okafor had sent out in September, and she remembered, vaguely, that his message had come to her with everyone else invisible somehow. She scrolled through her inbox until she found it, but when she opened his email, the To field showed only her own address. Nothing else. That was strange. If he had sent it to the whole class, where were the other names?

Her dad came in and set down a piece of paper on the counter, sighing at it. "Parking citation," he said. "I was four minutes over at the meter." He shook his head and poured coffee. Kate barely looked up. She clicked Reply on Mr. Okafor's message and studied it again. Maybe he had sent the same email twenty-six separate times? That seemed like a lot of work, but it would explain the empty field. She decided to test a smaller version of the idea. She opened a new email to Priya and typed a joke subject line, then noticed, below the To field, two more boxes: Cc and Bcc.

She typed her own address in To and Priya's address in Bcc, just to see, and sent the words "testing, ignore this." Her laptop was quiet except for the refrigerator hum and the soft tick of the wall clock. When the message arrived a second later, she opened it. It said To: Kate. Priya was nowhere on it. She forwarded that message to herself too, and Priya's address stayed invisible. So the Bcc field was the hidden cause, the rule that governed how Mr. Okafor had sent the list without showing anyone's address to anyone else.

She called Priya to check her thinking. "Did you get a weird test email from me?"

"Two of them," Priya said, laughing. Kate smiled; Priya's laugh was exactly her grandmother's, hereditary and unmistakable. "Why'd you send it like that?"

"Bcc," Kate said. "It stands for blind carbon copy. People in that field get the message, but nobody else can see their addresses." She said it out loud and felt it settle into place, like a key turning.

"So you can invite the class without sharing everyone's email with everyone else," Priya said.

"Exactly. Nobody's address gets passed around, and nobody sees who else is invited." Kate started pasting addresses into the Bcc field, one by one, twenty-six of them. Then she typed, in her cheerfully loud party voice, all capital letters and exclamation points, the kind of tone she would never use in a quiet note to her grandmother: SURPRISE PARTY FOR PRIYA!!! Then she deleted it, because Priya was on the phone and could hear her typing. She retyped it as a secret code instead: "Study group at my house, Saturday, bring your periodic table."

"Sounds boring," Priya said. "Perfect."

Kate hovered over Send and double-checked that the To field held her own address, and only hers, a single name standing guard over twenty-five secrets.

Alicia had run the eight hundred metres four times this season, and four times she had sprinted the first lap like a burglar escaping with the good silverware, then shuffled the second lap like a grandmother looking for her glasses. Coach Ruiz kept saying one word at her: pace. But pace was invisible. She couldn't see it, couldn't hold it, and it refused to explain itself.

At Thursday practice she set out to test an idea. Her plan was to run the first lap at what felt almost insultingly slow, the equivalent of jogging while pretending to be busy, then spend everything she had left on lap two. She asked Marcus, a sprint hurdler who was loitering by the water jug, to stand at the two-hundred mark and yell "SLOW" if she went out too fast. Marcus agreed, mostly because he wanted an audience.

Marcus had his own problem. His hurdle rhythm kept falling apart, and while Alicia circled the track he clattered over the barriers, landing heavy every time, like a chair being dropped. On her third lap she slowed to watch him. He rose up tall over each hurdle, chest proud, practically waving to the crowd, then came down dead, all his speed gone.

"You're landing like a piano," she called. "Lean your chest forward over your lead leg when you clear it. Keep your body going that way instead of up."

"Up is where the hurdle is," Marcus said, reasonably.

"The hurdle is only knee-high. You're jumping to the moon."

He looked at his hurdles the way you look at a dog that has bitten you before, and Alicia jogged on, but the idea stayed with her. Marcus's trouble and hers were the same trouble, she thought, running her cooldown. He wasted his energy going up when the race went forward. She wasted hers in the first lap when the race had two. She just couldn't see her own mistake the way she could see his.

At Saturday's meet she went out slow, so slow that the field streamed past her and a man in the stands audibly reassured his daughter that the girl in last would catch up eventually, probably. Alicia stayed calm. Three hundred metres, four hundred, and the bell rang. Then she began passing people, one by one, like she was collecting them. She crossed the line third, which had never happened, and lay down on the infield grass to enjoy the sensation of legs that had betrayed her only partially.

Marcus came over, sweating and grinning. He had run the hundred hurdles and taken two seconds off his best time. "Leaned the chest forward over the lead leg," he reported. "Didn't go to the moon once."

"Coach Ruiz says next time I go out even slower," Alicia said from the grass.

"There's slower than that?"

She squinted up at him. "Burglar walking pace. Bring the water jug."

The essay was due Monday, and Jayden had exactly zero words written. He sat at his grandpa's kitchen table with his laptop open, the cursor blinking on a blank page, while outside the window the garden baked in the August heat. His thesis sat in his head in a hopeless jumble: somehow he was supposed to argue that the town should fix the old public pool, and he had until Sunday night.

His friend Marcus had sent him a strange text an hour before. "Just read the first sentence of each body paragraph. That's the trick. If your argument doesn't hold up that way, it's broken." Jayden had stared at it, suspicious. How could anyone understand a whole essay from a handful of lines? He decided to test it. He wrote his thesis at the top of the page: The town council should repair the Maple Street pool. Then he tried to build an outline around three points, one for each paragraph, and something felt wrong. He had three points but they overlapped, and when he wrote only the first sentence of each planned paragraph, the argument collapsed into mush.

He tried again with fresh points, and this time he made each opening sentence reach back and grab the thesis, the way a rope ties a boat to a dock. Point one: the pool is cheap to fix compared to building new. Point two: it serves the most families in summer. Point three: repairs could be finished before next season. When he read just those three lines, the whole argument stood there like a skeleton, complete. He typed the first sentences to Marcus, and Marcus texted back a single thumbs up. Something in Jayden's chest unclenched, though he refused to be optimistic yet. He was pessimistic about one thing: the body paragraphs themselves, which could still stretch on forever if he wasn't careful.

His grandpa shuffled in, sweating, a hormone-triggered redness still on his face from mowing the lawn, and set down two glasses of lemonade. "How's the paper?" he asked. Jayden turned the screen toward him. "Watch this," he said, and read only the first sentence of each paragraph aloud. His grandpa listened, nodded slowly, and tapped the table. "I understood the whole thing," he said, "and you skipped everything else."

Jayden grinned and started drafting, but he made a rule for himself: no paragraph would run long just to prolong the page count. Every sentence after the first one had to earn its place. Outside, sprinklers hissed over the brown grass, and his fingers were already moving across the keys.

Chase had one goal for the field trip to the Harlow Living History Farm: get through the day without his group's egg basket ending up on the ground. So far, so good. The morning had revolved around chores, and Mrs. Teller had assigned him, Priya, and Milo to the chicken coop, where a dozen hens strutted around like they owned the county.

"Collect the eggs, handle them gently, and bring them to the kitchen porch," the guide had said. Milo immediately dropped his clipboard, which did not inspire confidence.

Chase crouched in the straw, sliding his hand under a speckled hen who squawked at him like he was a parasite who had come to drink her blood. "Easy," he muttered. "I'm not even hungry." Priya snickered behind him, and the first egg went into the basket without incident. By the fourth, Chase felt like a professional.

Milo, holding two eggs up to the light like precious gems, suddenly frowned. "Hey. There's no rooster anywhere. I've been watching. Zero roosters. So if we keep these eggs somewhere warm, will they hatch?"

Chase considered the question while a hen pecked at his shoelace. No rooster, that was true. He tried to picture it: twenty eggs under a heat lamp, and one morning, twenty chicks. Something about it felt wrong, like a vending machine with nothing stocked inside. "I don't think so," he said slowly. "My grandma's neighbor has hens and no rooster, and she sells the eggs as eating eggs. If they hatched, she'd basically be running a chick factory for free."

"So what's the difference?" Milo demanded. "Eggs are eggs."

"Maybe not." Chase looked around the coop again, checking rafters, checking the yard through the wire. The hens were the whole population. An idea formed, simple enough to test. "Every chicken we've seen today came out of an egg. If these eggs could hatch on their own, the farm wouldn't need to buy chicks ever, right? But the guide said they order chicks in the spring."

Priya gasped. "She did! I wrote it down. I write everything down." She flipped her notebook open to a page with the words CHICKS ARRIVE, APRIL underlined twice.

Milo looked personally betrayed by biology. "So without a rooster, the eggs can't hatch into chicks at all?"

"That's my theory," Chase said. "Hens lay them either way. Rooster or no rooster, you still get eggs. But no rooster, no chicks. Ever."

They carried the basket to the kitchen porch, where the guide was demonstrating an old butter churn, its wooden lid so clouded and opaque with age that nobody could see inside. Milo set the eggs down with exaggerated ceremony, like a funeral.

"Good work," the guide said. "Those go to the frying pan tomorrow. We'll have a demonstration about breakfast in the 1800s."

Milo opened his mouth, closed it, and finally said, "So if I had kept one in my hoodie, nothing would ever happen. No matter what."

"Nothing," Chase confirmed, "except you'd smell like egg."

Priya raised her hand anyway, notebook at the ready. "One question. If hens lay eggs no matter what, then what exactly does the rooster do all day?"

From somewhere beyond the barn came a sound that was definitely not a cow.

The train swayed through pine hills, and Elena's little sister Dory kept her fist closed tight on the seat between them. Their family trip was almost over, and Dory had been quiet since they left the park, which was not like her at all.

"Let me see it," Elena said. Dory tried to evade her eyes, staring out the window instead, but slowly she opened her fingers. In her palm sat a chunk of rose quartz, streaked with pink, about the size of a plum.

"Isn't it gorgeous? I found it right by the waterfall. The waterfall was the climax of the whole trip, and this is like a souvenir of it." Dory cupped her other hand over the stone. "It's mine now."

An affluent-looking man across the aisle glanced over the top of his newspaper, and Elena lowered her voice. Something was nagging at her, a memory she couldn't quite see. At the visitor center there had been a display, and the ranger had said the words on it out loud, but Elena had been too busy looking at the wolf skull to pay attention. She thought back. The words had come in a list, she was almost sure, and the list had been long enough to fill a whole poster. She dug through her backpack, pushing aside granola bar wrappers until her fingers found a folded paper: a brochure she had grabbed because it had a picture of a marmot on the front.

She unfolded it on the tray table. There it was, exactly as she remembered, a list of seven principles under the heading Leave No Trace. She read down the numbered lines. Plan ahead and prepare. Travel and camp on durable surfaces. Dispose of waste properly, which explained the ziplock bag of orange peels their dad had carried out. Then the fourth line: leave what you find.

"Seven of them," Elena said, tapping the page. "And number four says leave what you find. That rock belongs there, Dory. If everybody took one, there wouldn't be any left."

Dory's chin wobbled. "But I want to remember the waterfall."

"You can remember it another way. Remember the junior ranger badge you wanted so bad?" Elena leaned closer. "A ranger's job is following these rules. If you take the rock, you can't really call yourself one."

Dory stared at the stone for a long moment, then at the brochure. "Fine," she whispered. "But I'm drawing it first. Every single stripe." She pulled her sketchbook from under the seat and flattened it against the window, and Elena handed her a pencil.

The bus jolted over the railroad tracks just as Norah opened her English book to the scene Ms. Okafor had assigned. Tomorrow each student had to stand up and read a speech from Macbeth, then paraphrase it, which meant saying the same thing in words a normal person would actually use. Norah had inherited her grandmother's old copy of the play, its margins crowded with faded pencil, but so far that hadn't helped her understand a single line.

"To-morrow, and to-morrow, and to-morrow," she read under her breath, hunching so the seventh graders behind her couldn't hear. "Creeps in this petty pace from day to day." She squinted. Creeps was easy. Petty pace, fine, slow. Then the speech turned into candles and walking shadows, and she lost the thread completely.

Dex slid into the seat beside her at the next stop, balancing his trumpet case on his knees. He glanced at her page. "You look like the bus ran over your book."

"Macbeth. I have to paraphrase this speech and I don't even know what's happening. Why is he talking to nobody?"

Dex leaned over and read the stage direction at the top. "It says 'alone.' Huh." He tapped it. "My sister did this play last year. She called that kind of speech a soliloquy. A character, usually alone on stage, speaks their private thoughts out loud so the audience can hear them."

"So it's like thinking out loud?" Norah looked at the page again, and something shifted. If Macbeth was alone and just speaking his private thoughts, then everything he said was a secret. He wasn't performing for anyone in the story. He was telling the audience what he really believed, the stuff he'd never say to his wife or his soldiers.

She tried it as a test, translating line by line in the margin. Tomorrow keeps coming, one day after another, until the end of time. And all our yesterdays have shown fools the way to dusty death. She wrote, our past days just lead stupid people to the grave. Out, out, brief candle became life is short, like a candle you blow out. "He thinks nothing means anything," she said slowly. "That's the secret. He's lost, and only we get to know it."

"That's actually kind of sad," Dex said. He pulled out his own worksheet, which was crumpled at the bottom of his bag. "Can you help me with mine after? Mine's the one where the guy pretends to be a pig farmer."

"It's a disguise, not a soliloquy. You're lucky." She smiled and wrote her last paraphrase at the bottom of the margin, next to a stray pencil note her grandmother had left decades ago: vulnerable when alone on stage. Norah underlined it twice and passed Dex a fresh pencil without his asking.

Isaac sat in the back seat with his knees pressed against the driver's seat in front of him, which had never happened before this summer. Last year his legs had fit the car the way they always had. Now, on the drive to his grandmother's house, he kept shifting because his sneakers jammed into the seat pocket, and when he pulled his knee up to sit cross-legged, his shorts rode up and he saw them: thin lines, pale pink, running sideways across the skin above his knee like tiny scratches that had never bled.

"Stop wiggling," his sister Maya said beside him. She was eleven and had claimed the window seat, an argument Isaac had lost that morning and was still evaluating. Maybe he should have let her have the middle instead. Three hours of a wedged elbow was worse than forty minutes of no window.

"What are those?" Maya asked, pointing at his knee. "Is that a rash?"

"It's not a rash." Isaac bent closer. He turned his leg toward the light from the window. The lines were on both knees, he discovered, almost exactly matched, and he had not fallen, not scraped anything, not even gone through the blackberry bushes behind the gym. So they had come from inside somehow. He thought about his cousin Theo, who was fifteen and had lines kind of like these on his shoulders, and about how Theo had shot up four inches in a single season of basketball. Isaac had grown two shoe sizes since spring. Maybe that was it. Maybe when you grew too fast, the skin got left behind, like a note arriving after you'd already moved.

"I have them too," Maya said suddenly, in a smaller voice. She tugged her waistband down a half inch at her hip. "Right there. I thought something was wrong with me. I've been hiding them at the pool."

Isaac studied hers. Hers were fainter than his, thin pale streaks. "Those are stretch marks," he said. "From growing fast." He remembered then, on his own thigh, marks from two years ago when he'd had his first big growth spurt. He pulled up his shorts to check. You could barely find them now, just ghost-smudges in the light. "Look, my old ones mostly went away. They fade."

Maya inspected his leg, then hers, comparing. In the front seat their dad reached over and tapped the thermostat down two degrees because the sun had shifted onto his arm. "Everything okay back there?" he asked.

"Fine," Maya said, and pulled her waistband back up. "Isaac, tell me again about the fading part when we stop. Slowly. I want to remember it at the pool on Monday."

Sawyer pressed his face close to the display case, where a coil of copper wire sat next to a voltmeter and an ammeter. The sign said YOU MEASURE IT, so he clipped the probes where the arrows pointed and watched the needles jump. Six volts. Half an amp. A third dial showed a symbol he didn't recognize, something like a tiny horseshoe with feet, next to the number twelve.

"Is that a horseshoe?" asked a girl beside him, lanyard swinging. "Like, lucky twelve horseshoes?"

"It's not a horseshoe," Sawyer said slowly, though he wasn't sure what it was. "It's Greek. My math teacher writes something like that on the board." He copied the symbol onto his palm with a finger, wondering what a letter had to do with wire.

The sign above the meters told him only this: divide volts by amps. He tried it in his head. Six divided by half an amp meant twelve, and that matched the number beside the little horseshoe. So the meter had done the same arithmetic he just had. He changed the dial to a thinner wire and the current dropped to a quarter of an amp, and when he divided this time he got twenty-four. The horseshoe number climbed exactly with his answer. It was like guessing there was a rule running quietly behind the glass, invisible until you checked the numbers against it.

He revised his first idea, then. The meter wasn't measuring the wire directly like a ruler measures length; it was figuring the value out from the two things he could see, the volts and the amps, and then displaying the answer with that Greek letter. "Omega," he said out loud, suddenly certain, because he remembered now where he'd seen it, on a worksheet about Greek letters that he'd mostly ignored. "Resistance is measured in ohms," he told the girl, pointing at the symbol. "Ohms, written with omega."

She looked skeptical. "Says who?"

"Says the numbers." He liked that better than any sign. He'd been pessimistic about the whole electricity wing when they'd walked in, expecting walls of paragraphs, but this was more like a detective puzzle where the culprit never shows his face and you catch him anyway. The climax came when he found the display's challenge card: a mystery wire, meters unlabeled, and a blank box for the answer. He measured nine volts and three amps, divided three into nine, and wrote a three in the box, then drew the horseshoe beside it as carefully as he could, feet and all.

When the light above the box blinked green, the girl squinted at his symbol. "Still looks like a horseshoe to me."

Elliot's little sister had been coughing for three nights, and his mother had sent him to the pharmacy on Marsh Street with twenty dollars and one instruction: bring back something that actually worked. He stood in the cold-and-flu aisle between two boxes. The first box, bright orange, had a photograph of a smiling man and the words "I felt better in one day!" printed across the top. The second box, plain white, said "Tested in a study of 420 adults." Elliot turned both boxes over in his hands. Forty-two dollars, though. Way over budget. There was a third option, a store brand for eight dollars with no photograph and no study, just a list of ingredients.

A man in a rain jacket was standing beside him, holding a tube of sunscreen. "Get the orange one," the man said. "That stuff saved me in February. One dose and I was a new person."

"Thanks," Elliot said, but he didn't reach for the orange box. One person. One February. He put the eight-dollar store brand in his basket anyway, because it had the same ingredients as the white one, which he'd checked twice, letter by letter.

At the counter, he counted his money and found he could also afford the sunscreen, which his mother had asked for if there was anything left. The pharmacist, a woman with reading glasses on a chain, rang it up. "Good timing on this," she said. "We ran out all week. Our supplier tested it on volunteers who live right near the equator, where the sun is strongest. They couldn't keep it on the shelf down there."

Elliot looked at the tube. "How many volunteers?"

"About three hundred, the label says." She turned the tube so he could see the small print. "Big studies like that, they're more reliable than one person swearing by something. With enough people, the flukes just even out."

"That's what I was thinking," Elliot said, and he meant it, though he hadn't been able to articulate it that clearly in the aisle. He thought of the man in the rain jacket, one person, one February. He thought of the smiling face on the orange box. Then he thought of 420 adults, all coughing, all taking the same white pills, most of them getting better. Maybe some of them hadn't. But with that many people, the ones who would have recovered anyway and the ones who never improved wouldn't be able to hide the truth. His own idea felt more robust suddenly, less like a guess.

He was almost out the door when he noticed a shelf of cough drops with a sign: "Voted Best by Our Customers." Underneath, in smaller letters, it said "Based on a survey of 350 shoppers." Three hundred fifty people. He imagined his three friends from science class voting on something, all agreeing, and how that could still be wrong. This was different. He picked up a bag of the honey-lemon drops and added them to his basket.

At home, his sister took the syrup without complaint, and the drops turned out to be the real prize. She held one up and studied it like a tiny amber stone.

"Where'd you get these?" she asked.

"The pharmacy," Elliot said. "A lot of people picked them."

Hunter slid his paper menu across the lab table and tried again. "Quisiera el pollo con arroz," he said, and Ms. Reyes nodded, so he pushed his luck. "¿Cuánto cuesta?"

"Ocho dólares," she answered, holding out her hand for the fake money, and Hunter counted out eight paper bills from the envelope. That part was going fine. Ordering the food, asking the price, paying. The part that kept wrecking him was the game at the end, where one student played a waiter giving directions to the restaurant and the other had to walk the route through the classroom.

Last week he had ended up at the pencil sharpener instead of the door twice. His partner, Dana, kept grinning at him, and Hunter was tired of it. His older sister had promised to take him to a real Mexican restaurant on Saturday if he could get through one whole round without a wrong turn, and he wanted that dinner more than he wanted to admit.

He listened while Dana played the traveler for the kid before him. "Sigue derecho hasta la mesa de la maestra," the waiter said, and then, "después gira a la derecha en la silla azul." Hunter watched the kid walk. He went straight past the teacher's desk, then turned right at the blue chair, and ended up exactly at the pretend kitchen door. Interesting. Hunter had heard both those words as the same word before, all one blur of "derecho, derecha, whatever." But the kid had treated them as two different things, and it had worked.

When his turn came, Hunter stood at the back of the room under the paper canopy that the class had hung from the ceiling to make the classroom look like a patio. He gripped his paper menu. "Buenas tardes," said the waiter, a kid named Marco. "El restaurante está cerca. Sigue derecho," and Marco pointed straight ahead, "hasta el escritorio, y luego gira a la izquierda."

Hunter took one step straight toward the desk, then stopped. He wanted to test it. "¿Derecho significa a la derecha?" he asked, tipping his hand toward the right wall, where the supply closet was.

Marco shook his head. "No. Derecho means keep going straight. A la derecha means to the right." He pointed forward, then pointed right, with an obvious difference between the two.

So they really were two words, and the difference mattered. Hunter walked straight to the desk, turned left, and made it all the way to the pretend kitchen door without one wrong turn. Dana clapped once, slowly, like she couldn't believe it. Hunter went back to the counter and ran the whole thing again, this time with the waiter saying "a la derecha" first, and he turned right at the blue chair, then straight, and arrived again.

After class he copied the menu prices into his notebook and converted them in his head, eight dollars to what he'd actually need from his allowance, because Saturday he was ordering for himself, in Spanish, without a script. He wrote the two words at the top of the page in big letters and underlined them both. Ms. Reyes passed his desk on her way out and tapped the page.

"El sábado," Hunter said, and pointed at the underlined words, then at himself.

"Muy bien," she said, and held the door.

Zack sat at the corner table in the school library, a blank page in front of him and twenty minutes until the writing lab closed. His social studies essay was due Monday, and the assignment sheet said he had to state a thesis and outline a three-point argument before drafting a single paragraph. He had picked his topic, that the town should build a bike trail along Miller Creek, but every time he tried to start, his mind went as barren as the empty parking lot outside the window.

He flipped through a folder of sample essays Ms. Okafor had left on the shelf. One was about why the school day should start later, and it moved smoothly from one idea to the next. Another, about school uniforms, was choppy; each paragraph sat alone, like separate islands. Zack read them twice and noticed something. The smooth essay kept using small words at the start of its paragraphs: first, however, furthermore, therefore. The choppy one hardly used any. He set the two essays side by side and traced the words with his pencil. First introduced the opening point. However signaled a turn. Furthermore added something on top. Therefore showed what followed from everything before.

His friend Priya dropped into the chair across from him with a stack of books. "What are you doing, playing connect the dots?"

"Sort of." He slid the choppy essay toward her. "Read this paragraph, then the next one."

She frowned. "They don't go together. It's like the writer teleported."

"Now read it this way." He had copied a paragraph onto scratch paper and added one word at the start, furthermore. Priya read it again and her eyebrows lifted.

"Oh, that's better. Ms. Okafor calls those transition words."

Zack pulled his own paper back and built his outline. Thesis: the town should build the Miller Creek trail. Point one: the census counted four hundred more kids in town than five years ago, so the parks were crowded. Point two: the trail would keep riders off the busy road. Point three: the creek path was already public land, so the cost would be low. Then he added his connectors. First, the town has grown. However, the roads were never widened. Furthermore, the land is free. Therefore, the trail should be built.

He wrote the opening paragraph, and for the first time the sentences came out in order, each one pointing to the next. When the librarian flicked the lights twice, Zack packed his bag slowly, reading the outline one more time on his way to the door.

"Monday, I'm actually ready," he told Priya, and he held up the page so she could see the four little words circled in the margin.

Lauren's flashcards had deteriorated into a curled stack of coffee-stained index cards, and she still could not get past the fourth line of the prayer she had to recite at her confirmation next Sunday. She spread the cards across the kitchen table and glared at them, as if they were hiding the fifth line somewhere under the smudges.

Simran arrived at four o'clock with her backpack and a bag of samosas, because that was the deal: Simran quizzed Lauren on the prayer, and Lauren helped her with algebra. "Ready?" Simran asked, sliding into the chair opposite her.

"Line five keeps disappearing," Lauren said. "I say it ten times, and then it's just gone."

Grandma shuffled through the kitchen, her bad knee popping where the cartilage had worn thin, and set down a plate of mango slices without a word. Lauren watched Simran's hands. They were shaking a little, and Simran kept smoothing her dupatta flat against her notebook even though it was already flat. That was odd. Simran was the calm one, the one who never erased anything.

They drilled for twenty minutes, and Lauren's concentration deteriorated fast. Then she noticed something. "Wait," she said. "I know every single word of forty songs. All of them, no cards. But one prayer, nothing. Same brain. Why?" She thought about what was different. Songs had tunes. The words were tied to something you could hear, not just see on a card. She had a theory and no proof, so she tested it: she picked a melody from one of her favorite songs and sang the prayer's first four lines to it, then kept going. Line five came out on its own. Line six followed. She sang the whole thing.

Simran's mouth fell open. "That's it. Do you know what Japji Sahib is? My part for the ceremony at the gurdwara. It's actually meant to be sung, it's a prayer with a rhythm, and I keep blanking on it like you did, and I was too embarrassed to say so." She laughed and covered her face. "I came here to quiz you and I needed the quiz myself."

"I guessed," Lauren said. "Your hands were shaking the whole time."

"You noticed that?" Simran pulled out her own worn sheet of paper, folded so many times the creases had gone soft. She took a breath. "The tricky part isn't memorizing, it's understanding it. My dad says we believe in rebirth and karma, and Guru Nanak taught that the body takes birth because of karma, while salvation is attained through God's grace." She traced the last line with her finger. "That's what I have to mean when I say it, not just say it."

"Then you'd better understand mine too," Lauren said, "because you're the one who has to sit through it Sunday. Front row."

"Second row, remember? Front row is Grandma's, and nobody argues with Grandma." Simran stood, then winced, pretending her knee had popped just like Grandma's. "See, I'm basically family already."

Lauren grabbed the piano bench and dragged it to the middle of the kitchen. "New deal. You sing yours, I sing mine, and nobody stops until both of them stick." She set the mango slices between them and held up the first card. "Line one, ready?"

Simran straightened her dupatta one last time, and this time her hands were still. "Ready."

Christopher sat two rows behind Marcus and refused to look at him, which was hard, because Mr. Delgado had just asked the class to nominate a partner for the history project. Marcus raised his hand and pointed at Priya. He did not even glance back.

At lunch Christopher didn't sit with him, and at afternoon study hall he wrote in his notebook: Marcus picked Priya, so Marcus is done with me. But the sentence bothered him. Priya had the best notes in the class, and Marcus needed a good grade to stay on the basketball team. Maybe Marcus hadn't picked her over him at all. Maybe he had just picked a good partner. Christopher couldn't see inside Marcus's head, but he could test one idea. He wrote a second line: If I tell him what I think happened, and repeat back what he says, I'll know if he's mad or just busy.

In English the next morning, their teacher mentioned that the term "active listening" was introduced by the psychologists Carl Rogers and Richard Farson in 1957. It means trying to understand the speaker's point of view, Christopher thought, often by repeating their meaning back in your own words. He copied the sentence down, then circled it twice.

He caught Marcus by the lockers after the last bell. "You could've asked me to be your partner," Christopher said. "I was going to, but you skipped lunch on Tuesday and I thought you were avoiding me, so I panicked," Marcus said. "So you felt I was already dumping you as a friend," Christopher said, repeating the meaning back. Marcus's shoulders dropped about two inches. "Yeah. Exactly that."

Christopher had been sure Marcus had chosen Priya because Priya was cooler, or because their friendship was somehow over, and now he could feel that certainty cracking apart. It was strange how a thing he couldn't see, the reason behind one raised hand, could look so dark from two rows back and so ordinary up close. "Mr. Delgado says we can have groups of three," Marcus said. "Priya's cool with it. We're doing descendants of local founders, and apparently one of them had a controversial past, some land dispute thing." "I'm in," Christopher said. "But I pick where we work. My house. Your mom's dog ate my homework once." Marcus laughed and shoved his locker shut. "Deal," he said, and they walked out together into the cold.

Carson had the sheet of paper taped to the refrigerator, right next to the thermostat, where the whole family would pass it a dozen times a day. The words of the ceremony song ran down the page in two columns, left and right, and for three days he had been muttering the left column at the counter while he scrambled eggs. His little sister Zaria kept bumping the paper with her elbow just to annoy him.

"The left side is easy," Carson said on Saturday morning, tapping his pencil against the mug. "It's the right side that falls apart every time." Zaria leaned over his shoulder, chewing a piece of toast. She wanted the solo in her school chorus more than anything, and she had been eyeing the ceremony program like it was a tryout sheet. "Then let me be the right side," she said. "You do the left, I answer."

He sang the first line, cautious as somebody testing ice. Zaria fired back the answering line, loud enough to rattle the cabinet doors. It worked. He tried the second line, she answered, and the whole thing rolled down the page like two people passing a ball. "It's call-and-response," Carson said, grinning. "The leader sings a line and the group answers." He remembered now: Great-Aunt Ruth's old records in the attic, the choir leader throwing out a line and the whole room catching it. She had told him the pattern ran deep in African musical traditions, and in gospel and work songs, the kind her father had sung laying railroad ties. He'd thought it was boring then. It did not sound boring now, bouncing off the kitchen ceiling.

So he tested an idea. Instead of memorizing the song as one long ribbon of words, he learned only his half and let Zaria's half pull his out of him. When he blanked, she hummed the shape of her answer, and his line rose to meet it, like the words were waiting just behind the sound. By noon he had conserved his voice by whispering his lines and still not once lost his place. "You're not even looking at the paper," Zaria said, impressed despite herself.

That afternoon at the community center, the ceremony director asked who would lead the call for the rehearsal. Zaria's hand shot up so fast it nearly knocked over a music stand. Carson's stomach flipped, and his hand went up anyway, reckless and trembling. He stood, faced the rows of folding chairs, and threw out the first line. Forty voices caught it and threw it back. He grinned and gave them the next one.

Emilie spread the poster board across two folding tables at the family reunion, her markers lined up like tools. Her friend Priya's sign-language club needed a banner for the school fair, and Emilie had promised it for Monday. Across the top, in fat blue letters, she had written: PRIDE IN deaf CULTURE. Her cousin Marco leaned over her shoulder, arms crossed, frowning at the small d.

"You got that wrong," he signed, his hands quick and sharp. His mother, Aunt Rena, translated from the lawn chair beside the table. "He says the D should be capital."

"Since when does deaf get a capital letter?" Emilie signed back, slowly, because her signing was still clunky. Marco snorted and wandered off toward the volleyball game, leaving her with the poster and the problem.

She remembered the club's first meeting in September, how Priya had stood at the whiteboard and said her grandmother was deaf and that the club would learn her language. Nobody had mentioned capitals then. Emilie had assumed deaf was like tall or tired, just a description. But Marco had grown up with two Deaf parents. If he was fussy about one letter, the letter meant something, though she could not see what. The rule was invisible; she needed someone to show her where it lived.

She found Marco's mother by the dessert table, filling a plate with lemon bars. "Aunt Rena, why does Marco care about the capital D?"

"Because of something from 1972," Aunt Rena said. "A linguist, James Woodward, proposed writing Deaf with a capital D for the community and culture of sign-language users, and lowercase deaf for the hearing condition itself." She tapped the plate. "Two different things, one spelling apart."

Emilie turned that over while Aunt Rena went back for a second lemon bar. Capital D for the people, the language, the belonging. Small d for the ears. Priya's club was about people and language, so it was Deaf. Marco wasn't being picky; he was being exact, the way Grandpa was exact about calling himself an artisan instead of a hobbyist woodworker, because the word carried who he was.

Back at the table, Emilie tested the rule on every line of the poster. Deaf culture, capital. When the club text mentioned Priya's grandmother losing her hearing, that part was deaf, lowercase, the condition. She filled in the big D with red marker, pressing hard, then held the poster up across the yard so Marco could see it.

He jogged over, studied it, and gave her a slow thumbs-up. "Better," he signed. Then he pointed at her blank bottom margin and grinned. "Now make it beautiful."

"Give me those yellow markers," Emilie said. "And somebody keep Uncle Vic away from the table. Last year he signed my name on my own birthday banner and I was gullible enough to hang it up."

Marco laughed, a sound like two hands clapping, and tossed her the yellow.

The gym smelled like popcorn and floor wax, and Felix had his phone out before the buzzer even started the game. His best friend Dara leaned over from the next bleacher.

"You're checking baseball stats at a basketball game?"

"It matters," Felix said. "My dad says Justice was better than Jeter in the nineties. My uncle says Jeter. I'm settling it." He tapped through the seasons, one by one, and felt his stomach drop a little. In 1995, David Justice had the higher batting average. In 1996, David Justice had the higher batting average again. He scrolled back up to check, then down again, calibrating his eyes to the columns the way he'd line up a free throw. Same result both years.

"Justice," he announced. "Twice. Case closed."

Dara snatched the phone. "Then add them together. Two seasons, one winner." She found the combined numbers and went quiet. Then she turned the screen toward him, and Felix read it twice, but the numbers did not change their minds. Jeter's two-year average was higher.

"That's broken," Felix said. "He lost both years. How does he win the whole thing?" Down on the court, the home team was committing foul after foul, and the crowd groaned with each whistle. Felix barely heard it. He tried adding the averages himself, then multiplying, then starting over, and nothing came out the way the screen said. He passed the phone along the row to his older sister, Priya, who was home from college and only came to games when she wanted the nachos.

"Look at this," he said. "Justice beats Jeter in ninety-five, Justice beats Jeter in ninety-six, and then combined, Jeter's on top."

Priya squinted at it, shrugged, and handed it back. "Numbers are weird," she said, and went back to the nachos. That was the cost of asking Priya anything.

The buzzer sounded for halftime with the home team down by twelve. Felix kept scrolling while the cheerleaders tumbled across the floor. The whole game was numbers too, he realized. Field goal percentage, rankings, that "significant scoring drought" the announcer kept mentioning, as if four empty minutes could be squeezed into one tidy phrase. All those shots, all those misses, pressed into a single figure, like a cliff slowly worn down to one smooth number. Erosion, his science teacher would call it.

The twist came in the fourth quarter, when Dara nudged him, grinning, holding the phone. "I found it. It's a famous thing. Justice, Jeter, all of it."

"Does it say why?"

"Doesn't matter," Dara said. "Your dad and your uncle were both right."

The home team lost by two on a last-second shot that rimmed out. On the walk to the parking lot, Felix texted his dad one line: "Everybody won." The reply came back before he reached the car: "That's not an answer."

Brayden crouched behind the folding table in the gymnasium and rolled a marble down the ramp for the ninth time, muttering, "Two meters, one point four seconds. Come on, be consistent." His graph paper was supposed to show a neat climbing line for the judges, distance on one axis and time on the other, so anyone could read off the speed of his rolling ball. Instead his points scattered like confused ants. He needed this to work because Priya Nair, at the next table, had built a working model of a lock made entirely of popsicle sticks, and he refused to lose to popsicle sticks.

"Your marble hates you," Priya said, leaning over. "That's a scientific conclusion. I can make a graph of it."

"It's not the marble, it's the ramp." He picked up the marble and held it to the light like a suspect. Somewhere behind them, a kid at the physics table was trying to explain why sound traveled, and failing, which gave Brayden a dangerous idea.

He remembered last summer at his grandmother's residence, the old porch with its loose floorboards, when he had stomped his foot at one end and his cousin Marcus, lying at the other end with his ear against the wood, had sworn he felt the thump before he heard it through the air. They had argued about it for an hour. Marcus said the sound was the thump itself sliding down the board, like a hockey puck. Brayden had said that made no sense, because then the board should end up piled at Marcus's ear.

He looked at Priya's table. She had a slinky and a box of dominoes, leftovers from a demo she'd abandoned. He borrowed both. "Watch," he said, and set the dominoes in a line across her table, then flicked the first one. Clack, clack, clack, all the way down. "Sound's like that," he said. "A push goes down the line, but each domino just tips over where it stands. The dominoes don't travel with the sound."

Priya frowned. "So the last domino doesn't slide to my hand?"

"Nope. It only moves back and forth, kind of. Like this." He stretched the slinky between them and nudged his end. A round ripple rolled toward her, and the coils between them just wiggled in place, elastic and shiny, none of them actually arriving anywhere. Priya touched the far end and yelped when the bump reached her fingers.

"So the air between me and Marcus does that," Brayden said, grinning. "Each bit of air wiggles and passes it along. The push travels, the air stays home. Marcus owes me a soda."

"But the push, the wiggle, that's what your graph is missing," Priya said suddenly, jabbing at his paper. "You're measuring total distance at total time, but the speed is the slope. Mark where the marble is at each half second. Little dominoes of data."

He divided his timing into marks, rolled the marble again, and plotted the points. They climbed in a straight, obedient line. A judge stopped, ran a finger along the graph, and said, "Nice slope."

"That's the speed," Brayden said. "One point four meters per second, give or take a marble's opinion." He held up the slinky and gave it one more happy nudge, and the ripple rolled all the way down to Priya's fingers, where it arrived on time.

Alexis had two problems, and both were due on Friday. The first was her health project, a labeled diagram of the brain showing how addictive drugs affect it. The second was Alexis herself: for three nights she had stared at the ceiling until midnight, and by afternoon her jaw ached from clenching it through math class. Her intuition said the two problems were separate. Her intuition, she was starting to suspect, was wrong.

At the library table, she spread out her diagram. She had drawn the pathway with the arrow pointing the wrong way, from the front of the brain backward, and she couldn't figure out why her notes felt off. She traced the labels with her pencil. "It runs from the ventral tegmental area," she muttered, "deep in the brain, to the nucleus accumbens." Her friend Priya leaned over from the next seat.

"That's the brain's main reward pathway," Priya said. "And addictive drugs boost dopamine along it. You've got the arrow backwards, like a dinosaur walking tail-first."

"An extinct dinosaur," Alexis said, and erased the arrow. "Wait. Is that why I can't sleep? My brain's reward thing is all lit up from scrolling?" Priya shrugged, but Alexis decided to test it. She would decompose her evenings into parts, change one part, and see what happened. Like an experiment with herself as the diagram.

That night she plugged her phone in downstairs, an hour before bed, and lay on her floor doing the slow breathing her PE teacher had shown them, four counts in, six counts out. She fell asleep before ten. She woke before her alarm, jaw loose, and the ceiling looked like a ceiling instead of an enemy. The next afternoon in math she noticed her shoulders creeping toward her ears and took three slow breaths, and the tightness loosened. The hidden pattern held: the late scrolling and the clenching and the midnight ceiling-staring were one thing, not three.

On Friday she turned in her diagram, arrow corrected, pathway labeled from the ventral tegmental area to the nucleus accumbens. Her teacher handed it back with a sticky note: "Come see me." Alexis's stomach dropped. In the hallway, the teacher pointed at the corner of the page, where Alexis had taped a chart of her own week, nights on one axis, phone-down times on the other. "This wasn't required," the teacher said.

"It's my data," Alexis said. "Can I present it too?"

"Present it first," the teacher said, and wrote an A at the top of the page.

Rosalie spread her supplies across the picnic table: a stack of square paper, a magnifying lens she used for examining folds, and a bottle of water that was already going warm in the afternoon sun. The library origami club was meeting on Saturday, and she had promised to bring a paper crane that actually stood up. Three cranes lay in the grass, each one slumping over like it had given up.

Her neighbor Marcus climbed over the fence, the way he always did, and picked up one of the failed birds. "Still the same problem," he said, turning it toward the light. "The neck folds are too loose."

"I know that," Rosalie said. "What I don't know is why they keep coming out loose when I do exactly what the diagram says." She flattened the third crane and studied the creases through her lens. Each fold looked sharp on top, but when she held the paper up, she could see faint ghost lines underneath, running the wrong direction. Those hidden creases had been pressed into the paper during her earlier failed attempts. The problem was not in the fold she was making now; it was in the folds she had made before.

She tried to paraphrase the idea for Marcus. "So it's like the paper remembers." He shrugged, so she grabbed a fresh square. "Watch. No practice creases, no reusing paper." She folded slowly, and this time the crane's neck stood stiff and straight, its head pointing at the sky.

Marcus sat down on the bench. "Hey, at the club meeting, Priya said the word origami means something different. She claims it just means folding."

"It's both parts," Rosalie said. "Origami comes from 'ori', meaning to fold, and 'kami', meaning paper."

Marcus frowned. "Then Priya's only got half of it."

"You can tell her Saturday," Rosalie said. "Bring a crane so she knows you actually fold." He borrowed a square of paper and tried to copy her steps, but his bird turned out crooked, and after a minute of pressing and pressing at the wing he gave up and dropped it in the grass.

"That was a vain effort," he admitted, and Rosalie laughed. She lined up her one good crane on the table where the sun caught it, and set a fresh square beside it for tomorrow.

Charlotte slid into her chair just as her mother set down the pasta bowl with a clunk. Her mother had been on the phone all afternoon with the corporation's office in another city, and now she was stirring parmesan into the pot like it had personally offended her.

"You okay, Mom?" Charlotte's little brother Theo asked with his mouth full. He had been building an intricate fortress out of breadstick sticks, and their mother's mood was clearly messing with his architecture plans.

"I'm fine," their mother said, in the voice that meant the opposite. "The merger means half our team might migrate to the Chicago office next spring. I found out an hour ago. My anxiety has been through the roof since."

Charlotte watched her mother's hands, noticed the way she kept checking her phone even though it was silent. She remembered what Zoe had told her at lunch, after Zoe had failed her math quiz. "My counselor says coping means the ways you handle stress or hard feelings," Zoe had said, counting on her fingers. "Healthy coping is stuff like exercise, getting enough sleep, and talking with someone you trust. I used to just stay up scrolling, which is the bad kind." Charlotte had rolled her eyes at the time. Now she wondered.

She decided to test it. "Mom, remember when you made us walk the loop at the park after Grandpa's funeral, and you said moving helps you think?" she asked. "Want to go after dinner? Theo can come."

"I have emails," her mother said.

"Zoe says talking to someone you trust counts as coping too," Charlotte said. "So we could walk and you could talk. That's two healthy ones at once."

Theo looked up from his fortress, which had collapsed during the phone-checking. "I want to come. I'll rebuild the walls outside with sticks."

Their father raised his eyebrows at their mother. "The emails will still be there at nine," he said.

They walked the loop while the sky went orange. Theo collected sticks for a new fortress and their mother talked, haltingly at first, about boundaries she should have set months ago, about saying no to the extra projects that had swallowed her whole spring. By the second lap her shoulders had dropped an inch, though Charlotte noticed she still checked her phone twice at the corner where the signal came back.

At bedtime, Charlotte found her mother on the porch with her laptop, working anyway, because the merger was still happening and a walk could not change that. But she had also left her office chair pushed back from the desk, pointed toward the door, and a sticky note stuck to the screen that said "9:00, park?" Tomorrow the anxiety would be back, Charlotte knew. Still, she texted Zoe: "It worked on my mom. Mostly." Zoe sent back a running emoji and the words "sleep counts too." Charlotte put her phone in the drawer, where it buzzed once, twice, and then went quiet.

The minivan smelled like sunscreen and French fries, and Ariana was pretending not to sniff her own gym shirt when her little brother, Milo, leaned over from the back seat. "You smell like the boys' locker room," he announced, delighted with himself.

"Rude," Ariana said, but she cranked the window down anyway. She had showered after gym. She had even put on the deodorant she'd bought last month, the one with the intricate swirl design on the stick that had fooled her into thinking it was fancy. So why could she still smell herself? She turned the question over while Mom navigated traffic toward Grandma's house.

Then she remembered Thanksgiving, when her cousin Dez had been home from college. Some kid at the adult table had asked why his deodorant suddenly mattered, and Dez had laughed and said, "Fresh sweat has almost no smell. Body odor comes when bacteria on your skin break down sweat from the armpit glands, and those glands don't kick in until puberty." Ariana had been half listening then, busy with pie. Now the words snapped into place like a puzzle she'd finally found the edge of. That was why she'd never needed deodorant before this year. It wasn't that she'd gotten lazy. Her whole armpit situation had been rewritten.

She had a hypothesis, and a hypothesis needed a test. "Milo," she said, spinning around in her seatbelt, "smell my wrist." Mom said, "Eyes forward, please," but Milo was already grabbing her arm and taking a huge sniff. "Nothing," he reported. "Soap, I guess." "Exactly!" Ariana said. "My wrists sweat, but no smell. So it's not sweat itself." She was so excited she nearly bounced off the seat. "It's the armpit glands. Puberty ones. Bacteria eat their sweat and that's the smell. I'm basically running an experiment right now."

"You're basically being weird," Milo said, but he was grinning, already sniffing his own wrist like a detective. Mom muttered something about science happening in the car instead of at the dinner table, and Ariana pulled out her phone to text Dez: "Your armpit speech just solved my whole afternoon." She paused before sending, already anticipating the next problem. If bacteria were the culprit, was her deodorant even the right kind? Maybe she needed the antibacterial one, the one with the ingredient list long as a polymer chain, which was the only thing she'd retained from science class this week. "Next stop, the drugstore," she said to the windshield. Mom sighed. "We're going to Grandma's." "Then after Grandma's. This is important, Mom. This is a matter of reputation." Milo snickered. "Reputation of what, Stinky?" Ariana flicked his cap sideways and grinned at the road ahead.

Hannah spread the photocopy of the charter of rights across her grandfather's kitchen table, next to the toaster and a jar of marmalade. She had a civics assignment due Monday: explain one of the rights in her own words. Her pencil hovered over section 2, freedom of expression, but her mind kept drifting to the notice taped to the fridge. The town council was meeting Thursday night to vote on closing the outdoor rink, and Hannah had signed the petition to save it. A right on paper was one thing. She wanted to see one used.

Last summer, she remembered, the library board had tried the same trick with the reading room. A dozen parents had shown up to speak, and they had been turned away at the door, told the list was already full. At the time Hannah had assumed the board simply didn't want to hear them. Now she wondered. Her grandfather kept old council agendas in a drawer, and she dug one out. Under the heading "Delegations," it said that anyone wishing to appear as a delegation must register with the city clerk's office before the meeting.

So that was the pattern. It wasn't that the council silenced people; it was that there was a procedure, a small step in the hierarchy of rules that ran the town, and the library group had missed it. The reasoning seemed logical to Hannah: if you wanted to speak, you had to get on the list first. She decided to test it. On Tuesday after school she rode her bike to the clerk's office and filled out a form.

At the Thursday meeting, the chamber smelled like floor wax and burnt coffee. When the rink item came up, the chair called for delegations and read out two names. Hannah's name was one of them. A man in the third row stood up too, holding a folder, and the clerk shook her head. "You didn't register with our office before the meeting," she said quietly. "You can speak at the next one." The man sat down, and Hannah's grandfather, beside her, gave her elbow a squeeze.

She walked to the microphone on legs that felt slightly too long. She had her paragraph ready, the one she'd rewritten three times. "I want to demonstrate what the rink means to this town," she said, and she told them about the Tuesday night skate races, the kids who learned to stop and turn there, the fact that it cost less to maintain than one new parking lot. She kept it to two minutes because the agenda said delegations got two minutes, and Hannah had read the agenda.

The vote was postponed for a month. Afterward the man with the folder stopped her in the aisle. "How'd you get on the list?" he asked.

"City clerk's office," Hannah said. "Before the meeting."

He wrote it on his folder, pressing hard.

Easton lay on his bed with three crumpled tissues on the blanket and his tablet propped against a pillow. His cold was almost gone, but his mother had made him stay home one more day, and he had spent most of that day wondering about one thing. Two weeks ago his sister Priya had a cold, and he had caught it from her. Last winter he had caught a different one from his friend Marcus. His flu shot had protected him against the flu every year, so why was there no shot like that for colds?

He typed his question into the search bar. The first answer made him sit up straight against the pillows. More than 200 different viruses could cause the common cold. He read the number twice, then said it out loud to the empty room. Two hundred. And the page said rhinoviruses are the most frequent cause, which meant some little family of viruses he had never heard of was responsible for more of his sniffles than anything else.

Priya appeared in the doorway holding two mugs of tea. "Mom said to bring you this. Why do you look like you solved a mystery?"

"Because I kind of did," Easton said. "I always blamed you for my colds. But you can't make a vaccine that covers two hundred different viruses the way the flu shot covers the flu. That's why nobody's ever given us one." He turned the tablet toward her. "Rhinoviruses. That's what usually gets us."

Priya set the mugs down and climbed onto the end of his bed. "Okay, but here's my problem. I want to stop catching your colds, since you clearly can't stop catching mine." She pulled a marker from her pocket, the special gold one she had been saving for a school poster, and drew a line down the middle of a tissue. "Sick side and healthy side."

Easton tested her idea against what he had just read. "That works for us, but it doesn't work for the world," he said. "We could hide from each other forever and still get colds, because there are so many different viruses out there. Any one of them could be the one that gets you next." Priya frowned at her golden line, clearly wanting a better answer than that.

"Then we do both," she decided. "Tissue rule in this house, and you wash your hands before you touch my mug." She traded him her tea for the tablet and started reading, and after a minute she looked up with an exceptional grin, the kind she saved for good ideas. "I'm going to tell my class this on Monday. Two hundred viruses, and rhinoviruses win. I'll sound like a health diplomat negotiating peace between us."

"Just don't cough on my poster markers," Easton said, and she threw a clean tissue at him, and it landed right on the sick side of the line.

Simon stood at the white line on the track, chest still aching from the time trial. Two laps of the track, eight hundred metres, and he had led the first lap by twenty metres, then died. Marcus had passed him on the back straight like Simon was standing still.

"You went out too fast," Marcus said, catching his breath beside the fence.

"I know that," Simon said. "I can feel it. What I can't do is hold back while everyone runs away from me."

That was the real problem. He could not see the energy he was spending, could not see it running out. He only saw it afterward, in the collapse.

He walked past the pool on his way out and stopped. The swim team was doing front crawl lengths, and one swimmer, a tall girl in lane two, kept beating everyone else by half a length. Simon watched her turn her head to breathe, over and over. The others lifted their whole faces toward the ceiling, pausing at every breath, but she barely turned at all. One goggle lens stayed down in the water, and only her mouth swung far enough to clear the surface. Simon counted. Every single breath, the same small turn, one eye still underwater. The others broke their rhythm and lost speed each time they breathed; she never did.

It reminded him of a video he'd seen in fourth grade about lions chasing gazelles. The lion was the consumer, burning huge energy, and it had to cease the chase after a short burst or collapse. The gazelle conserved and lasted. He had thought it was only about animals. Now he thought: the fast girl isn't doing less. She's doing the same work but spending nothing extra on breathing. Nobody watching could see the difference, but the clock could.

The next trial was Thursday. Simon decided to test one small idea: hold a pace he was certain felt almost too easy for the first lap, like keeping one goggle in the water, saving the turn. At the gun he dropped into fourth place. His legs felt affluent with energy, rich and full, and every metre the leaders paid for their speed. At the bell for the second lap he was still whole. He swung past one runner, then two, and with eighty metres left only Marcus remained ahead.

"Where did you come from?" Marcus gasped.

Simon didn't answer. He just kept turning his legs over, smooth and low, one eye on the finish line.

Hazel stood in her grandmother's crowded living room holding a wrapped box of almond cookies and trying to remember the plan. Her French cousins were arriving any minute, and her grandmother had said the meal would be on the table at six o'clock sharp, which gave Hazel exactly one hour to figure out the kissing thing before she embarrassed herself in front of everyone.

The trouble had started at the airport that morning. Aunt Céline had swept in and kissed Hazel's cheeks twice, left then right, while Uncle Marc had given her three kisses, which meant Hazel had to tilt her head an extra time and nearly bonbed noses with him. Then Coco, who was thirteen like Hazel, had kissed her twice again. Hazel smiled through all of it, but inside she was thinking hard. Her aunt and uncle were from the same family, so why didn't they match?

The doorbell rang, and the room turned turbulent with relatives hugging, untying scarves, and passing gifts. Coco's little brother Théo came in shaking rain off his jacket like a dog, and their grandmother handed out presents, insisting that the smallest children open theirs first, which was different from Hazel's house, where everyone waited and tore in at once. Hazel put her cookies on the gift table, then edged toward Coco in the kitchen, where a pot of mussels was steaming and someone was pulling the black hulls off bread slices that had gone soggy in the rain.

"Can I ask you something?" Hazel said. "At the airport, your mom kissed me two times, but your uncle did three. Did I do it wrong?"

Coco laughed, not meanly. "You did fine. It's called la bise," she said. "The number of kisses depends on where you live in France. My mom's from a place where it's two. Uncle Marc grew up somewhere it's three."

Hazel felt like a code had cracked open. It wasn't about her, or about being polite or rude; it was a pattern, like area codes. She wanted to test it. When Grand-mère Lucie arrived early, before the others, Hazel watched carefully. Two kisses. "You're from the same region as Aunt Céline," Hazel said, and Grand-mère Lucie beamed and kissed her twice more, right there on the spot.

By the time everyone sat down at six, with elbows off the table because in this house hands rested beside the plate, Hazel had counted kisses from four more relatives and gotten every single one right. Uncle Marc leaned over during the salad course and said, "You have conquered the bise, Hazel. Better than my own son." Théo, mid-mussels, protested loudly, and the whole table dissolved into laughter while Hazel ducked her head, grinning, and passed the bread.

Simon had been sitting in the waiting room of Bright Smiles Dental for eleven minutes, and in that time he had said the word "acetylcholine" wrong in his head about forty times. His science-fair partner, Priya, sat beside him with a stack of notecards, because their project was due Monday and this was the only hour they both had free. Simon's little brother was in the back getting a cavity filled, which meant their mom was busy and the two of them were unsupervised with a topic neither of them fully understood yet.

"Okay," Priya said, shuffling the cards like a magician. "Question one. Why is nicotine so hard to quit? Go."

"It's, um, addictive," Simon said. A man across the room looked up from his magazine, and Simon lowered his voice. "I know that part. I just don't know why addictive. That's like saying water is wet because it's watery."

"That's why we're doing this project, genius." Priya flipped a card. "Here's the piece I found. Tell me if my comparison works. I want to say nicotine is like a fake key."

Simon chewed on that. "A fake key for what?"

"Okay, imagine a lock. The lock is on a brain cell, and it's a protein." She tapped her temple. "The real key is a chemical messenger the brain makes itself, and it's called acetylcholine. That's the brain's own key. The lock normally opens for that one. But the lock is called a nicotinic acetylcholine receptor, and here's the trick: nicotine happens to fit it too. Fake key, real lock. The brain cell responds like the real key showed up."

"So the lock doesn't check ID," Simon said slowly. "It just... turns."

"Exactly. You sounded like you knew that just now."

"I didn't know it. I reasoned it. There's a difference, and it's not subjective, it's measurable." He grinned. Priya threw a notecard at him.

The dental hygienist walked by with a tray of tiny mirrors, and Simon watched her fish a dropped pen out from under the chair with a long hooked picker, like a scavenger hunting a prize. "Could we use her in the demonstration?" he whispered. "No. Focus. Fake key, real lock, brain's own messenger is acetylcholine. I can say it now without dying."

At that moment the inner door swung open and Simon's little brother emerged, cheeks puffy, holding a paper cup. "The dentist says I have to resign from gummy worms," he announced gloomily, "effective immediately."

"You can't resign from gummy worms," Simon said. "You can only be fired from them."

Priya wrote "fake key" at the top of a fresh card and underlined it twice. "Monday, we're getting an A. Monday, you're going to say acetylcholine in front of the whole class without tripping over it. Say it once more, right now."

"Acetylcholine," Simon said, just as the man with the magazine muttered, "Kid, I quit smoking eight years ago, and even I never had to pronounce that."

Simon raised the notecard like a trophy. "Fake key, real lock."

Jaxson sat cross-legged on Devin's bedroom floor with his phone balanced on one knee, watching the group chat scroll. Devin's little sister thumped down the hallway outside, and somewhere below them the kitchen TV murmured through the floor. The chat was for planning Saturday at the skate park, but nobody had answered Jaxson's last three messages. He had written "anyone going early?" an hour ago, and it sat there like a coin dropped in an empty well.

Then Marcus posted, "I can come at ten." Right after, Priya posted, "me too, bringing my new board." Jaxson's question had never existed to them. He stared at his screen and thought about it. It wasn't that they disliked him. It was something quieter, something about how a small gray bubble among thirty others just vanished. He needed his message to have weight without being annoying, and he wasn't sure those were even different things yet.

He typed "WHERE ARE YOU GUYS MEETING" and hit send before he could second-guess himself. For three seconds nothing happened. Then Priya replied, "why are you yelling?" Marcus sent a single wide-eyed emoji. Jaxson's ears went hot. Yelling? He hadn't shouted a word out loud. But sitting there on Devin's floor, hearing how loud those capital letters looked against Priya's calm lowercase reply, he could see what she meant. In here, on the screen, caps were a raised voice, even in a silent room.

"It's like you walked into a library and hollered," Devin said, peering over from his bed. Jaxson had to digest that for a moment. The same words could be quiet or loud depending only on their shape. It was a small paradox: he had used the biggest letters to be noticed, and the bigness itself was what made him look wrong. "Sorry," he typed, all lowercase. "ten works for me too. I'll bring the extra bearings."

"finally someone has bearings," Priya answered, and Marcus sent a row of thumbs-up. Jaxson noticed the pattern then. Priya used lowercase even when she was excited. Marcus never used periods unless he was serious. The chat had rules nobody had posted, and he had been reading them wrong this whole time, like standing too close to people without knowing it.

He put the phone face-down on the carpet and listened to the TV muttering below, Devin's sister's footsteps, the radiator ticking. The morning was still going to be awkward maybe. But it was a solvable kind of awkward. He picked the phone back up and typed slowly, in ordinary small letters, "want me to come early and help set the ramp?" Priya's reply came fast: "yes please." Jaxson grinned at the screen and said, "Marcus owes me a soda for the bearings."

The community center gym smelled like floor wax and old popcorn, and Victor liked it best on Tuesdays, when the whole basketball season still stretched out ahead of him. This Tuesday, though, Coach Reyes had something different planned. She dragged a thick rope out of the equipment closet and told them to try tug-of-war before shooting drills, just for fun, just to see. Victor was picked for the six-person side, and even though their team weighed more than the five-person side, they lost. Twice.

"That's strange," Coach Reyes said, coiling the rope. "You all look like you're easing off out there." She didn't say it in a mean way, but Victor felt his ears go hot, because it was true. When he pulled with five others, he couldn't tell if he was pulling hard or hardly at all.

That night he typed tug of war pulling less with more people into the library computer, mostly to prove it wasn't his imagination. He found it right away. "In 1913 Max Ringelmann reported that as more people pulled on a rope together, each person's average pull became smaller," he read. So a bigger team didn't automatically pull harder. Each person's average pull shrank. He wrote it on a scrap of paper and folded it into his sock drawer, then thought better of it and put it in his gym bag instead. The tournament was Saturday, and Coach Reyes had announced that tug-of-war would open it, one pull against the Riverside team to start the day.

At Thursday practice, Victor asked to try something. "Let's pull one at a time," he said. "Watch the rope move each time, so everybody knows what their own pull looks like." Marisol went first, and the rope jerked a clear arm's length. Then Devon, then Victor, each one marked with a sneaker on the floor. After that, when all six pulled together, Victor counted under his breath, one two pull, one two pull, and the rope moved farther than it had on Tuesday.
