"It's like the whole center," Marisol said, wiping her hands on her shorts. "My mom calls it an ecosystem. Basketball, the garden club, us. Everything works when everybody does their part." Devon, who had spent Tuesday sulking that the rope game was pointless and that they'd lost because of Marisol, nudged her shoulder. "Okay, I take it back. You were pulling fine. I just couldn't see it."

Saturday morning came gray and cool, and the permanent trophy case gleamed by the front doors, waiting for a new plaque with the winner's name. Riverside's team was bigger, eight to their six, and their captain grinned like the win was already his. The whistle blew. Victor gripped the rough rope, found the rhythm in his head, and heard five teammates breathing in time beside him. The red flag in the rope's center slid, steady as anything, across the painted line.

The folding tables at the festival smelled like cardamom and burnt samosas, which Marcus decided was not the worst combination in the world. He sat behind the temple booth with a paper of Devanagari script in front of him, supposed to be learning the Gayatri Mantra by heart before his sacred thread ceremony next month. His grandmother had told him twice already that the ceremony would come whether or not he was ready, and she had said it in the exact voice she used when his shoelaces were untied.

"You're mouthing it like a fish," said Priya, his cousin, who was stacking laddus into a luminous golden pyramid nearby. "Fish are organisms, Marcus. You are not a fish. Try again."

"I am a fish," Marcus muttered, "a fish with a memory of at least three seconds, which is more than I can say for this line." He squinted at the words. They slid around on the page like ants at a picnic, and every time he got one syllable locked in, another one escaped.

Then his grandmother appeared with a steel plate piled high with rice, and instead of setting it in front of him she set it in front of the aunties at the next table. She poured herself only fruit and water. Marcus had been noticing this for weeks, actually. At home she skipped rice the same way, always on certain days, and he had never caught which days, because the days themselves seemed to wander.

He counted on his fingers, right there among the samosas. New moon, full moon, and then the eleventh day after each one. It landed twice a month, both halves. It fit every skipped plate he could remember, including the birthday dinner she'd turned into a fruit plate while everyone else had biryani.

"Thaathi," he said, tugging her sleeve, "you skip rice on the eleventh day of each half of the lunar month. Both halves. Am I right?"

She raised an eyebrow at him the way she did when he'd finally found the hidden Diwali sweets. "Ekadashi," she said, patting his head. Then she walked off with her fruit plate, leaving him feeling like he'd solved a riddle nobody had told him was a riddle.

Priya leaned over, grinning. "So if I hide your mantra paper on Ekadashi, will you go hungry too?"

"I'll trade you. You get my paper, I get your whole laddu pyramid."

"That pyramid is a sacred organism. It took me twenty minutes." She hesitated anyway, glancing at it. "Fine. But you have to recite the whole first line without the paper, right now, in front of the aunties."

Marcus stood up, took a breath like he was about to dive into deep water, and began, "Om bhur bhuvah svah," and behind him he heard his grandmother set down her fork to listen.

The highway signs said sixty more miles to the coast, and Luca's little brother Nico had already asked "are we there yet" four times, which had to be some kind of record. Their dad drummed the steering wheel. Their mom read the map out loud even though the GPS was talking too, because she didn't trust it. She said it was biased toward highways.

Luca watched the pine trees flick past the window and thought about last summer, the same beach, the same cramped car. That was the trip when he'd made his big mistake. He'd been in the water when he felt the ocean start to pull, a steady tug out toward the deep, and he'd rebelled against it, swimming straight back toward the sand with everything he had. The harder he fought, the farther out he went, until his arms burned and his dad had to splash in and drag him back. The lifeguard on duty had scolded him gently afterward, and Luca had nodded without really listening, too embarrassed.

"What's that sign say again?" Nico asked now, digging through the photos on Mom's phone. He'd found one from the beach boardwalk, a yellow warning sign with a picture of a swimmer and an arrow.

"Rip current," Luca said. "It's the thing that got me last year."

"What do you do if the water pulls you out? Like, for real?"

Luca was quiet for a second. He'd thought about it all winter, replaying that afternoon, wondering what he should have done instead of panicking. He'd even tested an idea in the pool at school, swimming along the lane line sideways instead of turning against the current the teacher made with the paddle. It was slower, and it felt wrong, like giving up, but it worked. "You don't swim straight back at the beach," he said. "That's what I did, and it just kept pulling. You swim parallel to the beach instead, along the shoreline. The current's narrow, so you get out of it that way, and then you can come in."

"You're sure? You tried it?"

"Sort of. And the lifeguard said the same thing after Dad pulled me out. I just didn't want to hear it back then." Luca shrugged. "Tomorrow you can watch me do it right. If there's even a current."

"There better be," Nico said, "or I'm pushing you in."

The stopwatch came from a drawer marked obsolete equipment, and it looked the part, with a crack across the face and buttons worn smooth. Emily pressed it anyway, because the class had only five working stopwatches and fourteen students, and Marcus had claimed the good ones for his group within four seconds of the bell.

The plan was simple. Emily would release a marble from the top of the lab ramp, and Josh would stand at the end of the hallway, twenty meters away, and shout "go" the moment it left her hand. Then he would click the stopwatch when the marble crossed the tape line by his shoes. They would divide distance by time, quantify the speed, and draw the distance-time graph Mr. Patel wanted by Friday.

The first run gave them a speed of 0.4 meters per second, which would have been fine for a snail, possibly the only organism slower than their marble. They tried again. 0.38. Again. 0.41.

"That marble is not that slow," Emily said, staring at the numbers. Something was hiding in the setup, something they could not see. She paced off the hallway, counting tiles. Twenty meters, same as before. The ramp angle hadn't changed. The only thing between her and Josh was air.

Then she remembered the lesson from last week, the one about sound. Warm air carried it faster than cold air, gaining about 0.6 meters per second for each degree Celsius. If the hallway was warm, Josh's "go" reached her quickly, but on a cold day it would crawl, and her start would be late, which would make the marble seem slow. She checked the thermometer by the door: 26 degrees. She did the arithmetic on her palm with a pencil. At 20 meters, a small delay in hearing "go" added a real chunk of error to every run.

They tested it. Emily had Josh clap hard against the far wall and timed the echo with the cracked stopwatch, once in the warm hallway by the radiators and once in the cold stairwell, ten trials each. The warm trials came back faster, and when she worked the numbers, the difference matched the rule: about 0.6 meters per second for every degree. She drew the graph with corrected times, and the line came out clean and steep and beautiful.

Mr. Patel walked past and squinted at it. "Nice correction for sound delay. Next time, use the light gate instead of shouting. Light doesn't dawdle."

"Light doesn't dawdle," Josh repeated, nodding, and packed up his stopwatch.

Emily carried the ramp back to the shelf. "One question," she said. "When I released the marble, when exactly did you start timing?"

Josh adjusted his backpack strap. "Right after I heard 'go.' Well. After 'go' and one Mississippi. Mr. Patel said always count one Mississippi."

Emily looked at her beautiful graph, then at Josh, then at the drawer of obsolete equipment, which suddenly seemed like the most honest thing in the room. "Give me the stopwatch," she said.

Hunter sat on the low wall by the basketball courts, his right arm wrapped in a bright orange cast that everyone had already signed twice. Three weeks ago he had been racing Devon across the wet blacktop, slipped, and thrown his hands out in front of him the way anybody does. His left palm had skidded harmlessly. His right wrist had taken everything, and now the radius, the bone on the thumb side of his forearm, was knitting itself back together in a sleeve of fiberglass.

The doctor had told him something that kept circling back in his head. "Of all the broken bones we see in kids," she had said, scanning his x-ray, "a fracture of the radius near the wrist is the most common. Almost always from landing on an outstretched hand, like you did." Hunter had nodded then, but now he was watching the playground with new eyes, because Devon was about to test his theory.

"You're going to eat it on that patch," Hunter called. Devon was on his board, rolling toward the spot where the drainage grates made the pavement buckle. The new kid, Marcus, had an opaque monopoly on the good ramp by the fence, hogging it since lunch began, so everyone else had to make do with the broken ground.

"Watch me stick it," Devon said, and of course he didn't. The board shot sideways and Devon went down with both arms flung forward, palms slapping the blacktop. He bounced right up, shaking out his wrists, grinning.

"See?" Hunter said, hopping off the wall. "Everybody catches themselves the same way. Hands out. That's the pattern." He had started allocating his lunch periods to this, standing by the courts with a notebook, tallying every fall he witnessed. Twelve falls so far, twelve outstretched hands, four kids rubbing their wrists afterward. Two of them had ended up in the emergency room like him, one with a swollen wrist and a story identical to his own.

"So what do we do about it?" Devon asked. "Fall on our faces?"

"That's the problem," Hunter admitted. "You can't not put your hands out. It just happens." He looked down at his cast, at the signatures blurred where his thumb rubbed against it, and for the first time the orange didn't seem like a badge from a cool crash. It seemed like the tuition for a lesson he could never quite teach anyone, because the body never listens in the moment.

Devon picked up his board. "Race you to the wall," he said, and took off running.

Hunter ran after him, one-armed and slower, and lost.

Aubrey had been avoiding the periodic table all week, but Friday's quiz left her no way out. She spread her notes on the kitchen table and found the trick her brother had shown her before he left for college: the big number in each box was the atomic number, and that told you the protons. Carbon was six. She checked neon, ten, and gold, seventy-nine, until the pattern felt solid under her fingers.

Then she found the crumpled note Priya had slipped into her locker before moving away. In Priya's looped handwriting it read: "I built a carbon atom for our last project. Six protons, six neutrons. If you build one with eight neutrons instead, is yours still carbon? Text me. I'll wait." Aubrey read it three times. Priya's family had left in October, and this was the first message that felt like they were still lab partners.

Aubrey scavenged through the junk drawer for something to build with. Buttons would work, and dry pasta. She laid out two atoms on the table, using pennies for protons and elbow macaroni for neutrons, keeping the noodles neutral in color so she wouldn't mix them up with anything else. Six pennies in each pile. Six noodles in the first, eight in the second. They sat side by side, clearly not the same.

She stared at them for a long time. If protons made an element what it was, then both piles were carbon, no matter what the noodles said. But she wanted to be sure before she texted Priya, because being wrong in front of Priya had always stung worse than being wrong anywhere else. She decided to invest one evening in finding out: she looked up the two versions in her science book and found them both listed under carbon, side by side.

She grabbed her phone and typed fast. "Mine is still carbon. The protons decide. Yours is carbon-12, mine is carbon-14. They're called isotopes."

The reply came before she finished her water. "I KNEW it was isotopes but I wanted you to figure it out yourself. Show-off." Then, after a pause that stretched long enough for Aubrey to reread the whole exchange: "The new girl here doesn't build atoms with me. It's not the same."

Aubrey picked up the pasta carbon-14 and carried it to her room, where it would sit on the shelf next to the model rocket Priya had left behind. She set the atom down carefully and texted one more line. "Friday night, seven o'clock, my kitchen table. Bring buttons. We'll build the whole second row."

Sebastian had been waiting for this watch party since Tuesday, and now that everyone was crowded into the living room, he could hardly sit still. Chips bowls covered the coffee table, his uncle had claimed the good armchair, and the pregame show blared while his cousins argued about which team would win. Only Grandpa Ray sat quietly near the window, polishing his glasses, and Sebastian noticed he was smiling like he knew a secret.

"You should have seen the very first one," Grandpa Ray announced during a commercial. "I remember it like yesterday. The Green Bay Packers beat the Kansas City Chiefs thirty-five to ten."

Sebastian frowned. Grandpa told great stories, but he also claimed he'd once shaken hands with a president, which nobody in the family believed. The first Super Bowl sounded ancient, older than Dad even. "Wait," Sebastian said, grabbing his tablet. "When was it?"

"January fifteenth, 1967," Grandpa said without hesitating.

Sebastian typed fast. The kickoff show returned on TV, everyone shouting, but he ignored it. If the date checked out, maybe the rest did too. His cousin Dana leaned over his shoulder. "What are you doing? You're missing the highlight reel!"

"Fact-checking Grandpa. He says he remembers the first Super Bowl."

Dana snorted. "Nobody remembers that. He probably made it up, like the president thing."

The search results loaded, and Sebastian froze. January 15, 1967. Green Bay Packers, Kansas City Chiefs, 35 to 10. Every number matched, exactly, with no wobble. He checked a second site, then a third, because a single page could be wrong. Dana kept tapping his arm, saying he should resign himself to the fact that Grandpa exaggerated, that the old man's stories were just an extravagant metaphor for a life he wished he'd lived. Sebastian shook her off.

"Grandpa," he said, standing up in front of the TV, which earned him a groan from his uncle. "It's all true. Every bit."

Grandpa Ray put on his glasses and grinned wider than Sebastian had ever seen. "Told you. And the president thing?" He paused dramatically. "That one's not true." The whole living room erupted, Dana laughing loudest, and she admitted she'd completely changed her mind about Grandpa's stories. She dropped onto the couch beside him and demanded he start from the beginning.

Just then the whistle blew, the game kicked off, and Grandpa leaned forward, pointing at the screen. "Now watch this next play. I've got a feeling about it."

Simon stood at the kitchen counter with an onion, a sharp knife, and a plan: he would make pasta sauce from scratch before Dad got home at six thirty, which gave him exactly fifty minutes. His mom was away for the week, and Dad had promised takeout every single night, which Simon figured he could eliminate if he proved he could cook something real.

First, the onion. The video he'd watched three times said to curl his fingertips under, knuckles forward, so the blade could only nick bone and not skin. "The claw grip," Simon said out loud in a dramatic voice, then actually did it, fingers tucked like a crab. He cut the onion in half through the root, peeled it, and sliced, and the vapor rising off it made his eyes water so badly that he had to walk to the window and blink at the street like a sad owl.

While he sniffled, he got out the scale. The recipe said his sauce needed something called a roux to thicken it, and it said to weigh the butter and flour. He set a knob of butter on the scale. Twenty-five grams. Then he measured out flour. Twenty-five grams. Same number. He frowned at the two little piles, because recipes usually didn't care this much, and this one acted like the amounts matching was a rule.

He called his friend Priya, who had cooked at the community kitchen all summer and acted smug about it. "Why does the butter and flour have to be the same?" he asked. "The recipe just says equal parts by weight and doesn't say why."

"Because it's called a roux," Priya said. "Flour cooked in fat, equal parts by weight. That's just what a roux is. Ours never came out lumpy when we weighed it right." Simon said a rude thing about her smugness, and she laughed and hung up.

So the flour went into the melted butter, and Simon stirred it with a wooden spoon while it bubbled and smelled faintly like toasted bread. It was supposed to thicken things, he knew that much, but he couldn't see how a paste the size of a golf ball was going to turn his pot of watery tomato stuff into actual sauce. He had a test idea: he'd pour in half the tomatoes, watch, then pour in the rest. Science, basically.

The first half of the tomatoes hit the roux and sat there, pale and lumpy, and Simon's stomach dropped. Then he kept stirring, and within a minute the lumps smoothed out and the whole surface went glossy and slow, like lava. He grinned so wide his cheeks hurt. He poured in the rest, stirred, and the sauce thickened right before his eyes, coating the spoon in a way his soup never had. Hidden cause confirmed. He added salt, a pinch of sugar, and the cooked onion, which he'd nearly forgotten on the cutting board.

At six twenty-five, Simon set down two bowls of pasta. Dad walked in at six twenty-nine, sniffed the air, and said, "Who broke into my house and made sauce?" Simon held up his untouched fingers, knuckles still faintly smelling of onion. "Claw grip," he said. "Zero cuts." Dad took a bite, closed his eyes, and pointed his fork at Simon like a judge declaring a verdict. "Takeout is cancelled for the rest of the week. Unanimous."

"There's only two of us," Simon said.

"Unanimous anyway," said Dad, going back for seconds.

Mathis slid into the back seat and pulled the folded paper out of his jacket before his mom had even started the engine. "I got my prescription," he announced. "But there's something bizarre on it. It says minus two point zero zero."

"Minus?" His little sister Lena leaned over from her booster seat, craning to see. "Like you got a negative score on your eyes?"

That was exactly what Mathis had assumed at first, and it had rattled him all through the waiting room. A negative number sounded like failing. He studied the paper again as the car pulled out of the parking lot. At the top it said the prescription measured lens strength in diopters. Below that, next to the word for his right eye, sat the dash and the numbers: -2.00.

"Two diopters," he said slowly. "Not a grade. The minus has to mean something else."

"So what does it mean?" Lena asked.

"I'm testing it." He flipped the paper over, where the optometrist had scribbled a note comparing his lenses with his dad's old pair. His dad was farsighted, and next to his numbers there was no dash at all, there was a plus sign. Mathis traced it with his finger. "Dad's is plus. Mine is minus. They're opposites."

"Opposite how?"

"I can see stuff up close but far away is blurry. Dad's the other way around. So minus goes with mine, nearsighted, and plus goes with his." He grinned. It felt like cracking a code. "The sign isn't good or bad. It's a direction."

His mom glanced in the mirror. "So you're not failing?"

"I'm minus two. That's all it is." He said it out loud twice more, trying the words on. Minus two diopters. It sounded almost official.

At the next red light, Lena dug through the glove compartment and came up with their dad's old sunglasses case. "These could be a candidate," she said, holding them up. "Try Dad's plus ones."

Mathis put them on. The world outside the windshield went soft and wrong, the stoplight smeared into a red smear. He laughed and yanked them off. "Nope. Minus for me, plus for Dad. Confirmed."

"When do your real glasses come in?" his mom asked as the light turned green.

"Thursday." He pressed the paper flat against his knee. "Thursday, I'm finally going to read the scoreboard at away games."

Lena bounced in her seat. "Two diopters of scoreboard."

The sneeze plague hit Kayla's town the same week the oak trees turned lush with pollen, and by Thursday her little brother Marcus was miserable. Their mom clicked onto CareMarket, the online site where neighbors sold extra medicine, and typed in "allergy tablets." Kayla leaned over her shoulder and stared at the screen. The same box that cost six dollars last month was listed for eighteen, then twenty-two, then thirty, each new seller's price higher than the one that preceded it.

"Nobody's going to pay that," Kayla said.

Three of the boxes sold while they watched. A fourth sold in the minute it took Mom to enter their payment information for the one at thirty-one dollars.

That night Kayla sat at her own laptop, where she sold beaded keychains on the same site. Her llama keychains used to go for eight dollars, but lately three other kids had started making llamas too, and the whole page was flooded with them. She dropped her price to five, and hers finally sold. She scrolled back to the allergy listings and frowned. On her page, more sellers meant lower prices. On the medicine page, more buyers meant higher prices. Same website, opposite direction.

She tried an experiment. She listed two llama keychains at nine dollars each, higher than anyone else. Neither sold for two days. She lowered them to four and both sold before breakfast. So people could walk away from keychains. She looked at the medicine page again. The price had climbed to thirty-five, and the little "sold" tags kept appearing anyway.

She messaged her friend Desmond, whose dad was a pharmacist. "Why do people keep buying allergy pills even when the price doubles?" she typed.

"Because they have to," he wrote back. "Dad calls that inelastic demand. Necessities, like essential medicines, barely change how much people buy when the price changes."

Kayla read it twice, then copied it into her notebook under a heading: RULES OF THE MARKET. Rule one: plenty of something, price falls. Rule two: everyone wants something scarce, price rises. Rule three: if people can't do without it, the price can climb and they'll still buy.

The next morning she checked CareMarket before school. The pollen count was even higher, and a new listing had appeared at forty dollars. She watched a buyer snap it up in eleven seconds.

"Forty dollars," Marcus croaked from the couch, wiping his red eyes.

"Next year," Kayla said, "we're buying in March."

Austin slid into his chair just as his mom set down the spaghetti, and his phone buzzed against his leg before he even picked up his fork. It was the group chat. Someone had posted a screenshot of the photo he'd put on his page last night, the one of him asleep at his desk with his mouth open and a pencil stuck in his hair. He had deleted it after only ten minutes. Now here it was again, with a row of laughing emojis underneath.

"That's the third time your phone has buzzed since you sat down," his dad said, twirling noodles onto his fork. "Rule of the table, buddy."

"I know, I know." Austin put the phone face down, but his mind kept snagging on the problem like a sleeve on a nail. He had deleted the photo. He'd watched it disappear from his page himself. So how was it sitting in the chat, crisp and complete, as if it had never left? He took a bite and barely tasted it.

"Earth to Austin," his sister Maya said, waving a garlic bread stick at him. "The jury has decided you're being weird."

"The jury?" he said.

"Maya's class did a mock trial today," his mom explained, sprinkling parmesan. "She's very proud of her guilty verdict."

Austin pushed his plate forward a half inch, thinking. His sister would probably be the perfect person to ask, because she took screenshots constantly. "Maya, when you screenshot something, where does the picture actually go? Like, whose is it?"

She shrugged. "Mine. It's in my photos. It's just a copy I made." She bit the end off the bread stick. "Why? What did you post?"

Heat crawled up his neck. "Nothing. Hypothetically, if somebody deleted something from their page, could it still exist somewhere?"

"Sure," Maya said, like it was the most obvious thing in the world. "Deleting it takes it off your page. Anybody who already took a screenshot or saved a copy still has it."

Austin sat back. The steam from the spaghetti drifted past his face, and somewhere in his head, gears turned over. So the photo had never really vanished. It had just moved, quietly, into other people's phones, like coins slipping between couch cushions. Where else might it be? He started a mental checklist and decided to be systematic about it. Three people had probably been on their phones right after he posted. Ben, for sure, because Ben had liked it. Priya, maybe. And that kid Dylan from science class, whose name he wasn't even sure how to interpret half the time, since Dylan never said anything in words, only in screenshots and stickers.

"Okay, one more buzz and the phone goes in the drawer," his dad said, eyeing him.

Austin finished his water and asked to be excused. In his room, he opened the chat and typed, not mad, just curious: "who sent that, and did you save it?" Ben answered first with a single word: "saved." Then Priya: "me too, sorry lol."

Austin looked at his own empty page, then at the three copies of his sleeping face glowing in three other phones somewhere out in the world. He took out a notebook and wrote at the top, "Who has it?" Under that he started his list.

Sofia spread the short story "The Long Dock" across the library table and put her notebook beside it. On Saturday she had to stand up at the book club and explain one example of foreshadowing and one of symbolism, and so far her notebook held only a list of page numbers. Across from her, Marcus was reading the same story for the third time, because he wanted to be the one who found the best example and got his pick of the donated paperbacks on the prize shelf.

"I've got foreshadowing," Marcus said, tapping page four. "The dock boards creak before anyone even drowns. That's the author warning us." He slid the story toward her. "Beat that."

Sofia read his page, then flipped forward, hunting for something better. On page nine she found a line she liked: "The old lantern's light spread thin and did not reach the end of the water." She wrote down that the lantern meant safety that failed, and that the dark water beyond it was standing in for what nobody could control. Then she found a quote that seemed even stronger. "The sea takes whatever it wants," a boy named Dale says on page twelve, after he pushes his brother's boat out too far. Sofia copied it in big letters and underlined it twice. The author's message, she labeled it.

She read her page aloud to Marcus as practice. "The story tells us the sea takes whatever it wants."

"Who says that?" Marcus asked.

"Dale. It's right there."

"Dale's the one who wrecked the boat and blamed the water," Marcus said. "That's his opinion, not the book's. The whole point is that the narrator says the wind was calm that day."

Sofia checked page eleven. The wind was calm. Dale had said the same thing twice before anything went wrong, and both times he was trying to talk his brother into going out. She crossed out the words author's message and wrote Dale's excuse instead. Her first idea, that the quote was the theme, would have sunk her whole talk like a boat with no rudder, drifting wherever the loudest voice pushed it.

She rebuilt her notes around the lantern and the creaking boards, then practiced once more, quieter, while Marcus radiated satisfaction at having caught her mistake and claimed first pick of the paperbacks. He chose a thick survival novel and held it up.

"Saturday, you open with the lantern," he said, "and I'll open with the boards. Deal?"

Clara leaned closer to the library computer, where her spreadsheet filled the screen. She had typed every answer from the school survey into it: one column for grade, one for favorite lunch, and a count for each. Then she taught herself the formula that added the column, and the bar chart sprang up beside it, tall rectangles for sixth grade, seventh, and eighth. The sixth-grade bar won every single question. "Of course they do," said Marcus, looking over her shoulder. "There are way more sixth graders than anybody else."

Clara stared at the chart. It did seem strange that sixth grade swept all five questions, even "Do you like the school mascot?" She clicked through the menu at the top of the screen, hunting for anything that might make the bars mean something fairer. She was not going to resign herself to a chart that just measured crowd size. Under one menu she found an option labeled "Show Values As," and inside it, something about a percentage of the column total.

She clicked it. All three bars shrank, but not by the same amount. The sixth-grade bar dropped the most, because a big class spread its answers over a bigger total. Now the eighth-grade bar was tallest for the mascot question, even though sixth grade still had the biggest raw count. "Wait," Marcus said, pointing. "Eighth grade won that one. But they have the fewest people."

"That's the point," Clara said. "Show Values As turns each count into a percentage, so grades with different numbers of students can be compared fairly." She tested it on the next question, pizza versus tacos, and watched the bars rearrange themselves again. Sixth grade still won that one, but only by a sliver, not by the canyon of the original chart.

Mr. Reyes, who ran the newspaper club, came by to check her results for Friday's issue. "The principal wanted to know which grade likes the new schedule best," he said. Clara turned the screen toward him and showed him both charts, side by side. "The raw numbers say sixth grade," she said. "The percentages say it's almost a three-way tie." He tapped the second chart and said that was the one to print.

Clara saved the file twice, once on the computer and once on her flash drive, because she had an acute memory of losing last month's survey to a crashed laptop and the small fracture it had put in her deadline. Then she printed the percentage chart, and Marcus carried it to the newspaper room at a run.

Victoria held her slice of cake and watched Dex back away from the picnic table, his ears going pink while Cole and two other boys laughed at his rumpled jacket. "Nice outfit, Dex. Did you dress in the dark?" It was Mara's birthday party, and nobody wanted a scene, least of all Mara, who was already hurrying over with her hands out like a tiny diplomat negotiating peace.

"Guys, come on," Mara said. "It's my party."

"Chill, we're just joking," Cole said. Victoria knew that tone. Joking meant the teasing would restart the second Mara turned around. She'd seen it happen at the science club meeting last week, when Dex tried to suggest a project idea and Cole talked over him until Dex just shut his mouth and stared at the table.

Victoria stepped between the boys and the dessert table. "We're doing a game," she announced. "Round-robin style." Cole groaned. "A round-robin means each person speaks in turn around the circle," she said. "You don't get to skip, and you don't get to talk over anybody." She pointed at the picnic bench. "Sit. Best birthday memory wins the last cupcake."

Cole shrugged and sat, because it was a game and games had rules, and even he followed rules when cake was involved. They went around. Cole told a loud story about a water park. One boy described a snowstorm blackout. Victoria shared the time her grandmother set her own birthday cake on fire with too many candles, and the smoke smell had saturated the whole kitchen for days.

Then it was Dex's turn. He was quiet for a second, and nobody could interrupt, because that was the rule. "My best birthday," he said, "was when it rained and the power went out, and my dad let us build the whole birthday cake out of marshmallows and cereal because the oven was dead." Everyone laughed, the good kind, and Cole said, "Okay, that's actually exceptional," and pushed the last cupcake across the table to him.

Victoria watched Dex break the cupcake in half and hand part of it to Cole, who took it without a word. She turned to grab her drink and found Mara standing beside her, arms crossed, grinning. "Nice game," Mara said. "Too bad you planned it." Victoria frowned. "What?" Mara pointed at the table, where Cole was now asking Dex, quietly, where he'd found the cereal marshmallows. "You invented a game so nobody could tease him," Mara said. "That's the sneakiest nice thing anyone's done all day."

Victoria picked up her cup. "I have no idea what you're talking about." "Then explain why you're smiling," Mara said, and Victoria hid it behind her cup, badly.

Anna wanted the limited-edition hoodie from the mall's skate shop, and she wanted it before her brother Marcus bought the last one, which was why she was half jogging past the fountain with her phone out, snapping a photo of the store window to post to her friends. "First one here," she typed, and added the location tag, because why not.

The comment came in before she reached the door. Not from Marcus, not from Priya, but from an account with no picture and a username she didn't recognize. Seen you at the fountain. Red jacket. Anna stopped walking. She looked around the crowd near the pretzel stand. Plenty of people, none of them looking at her, which somehow made it worse.

She found Priya at the phone kiosk, where Priya was comparing screen protectors. "This account knows I'm here," Anna said, holding up the phone. "Never seen it before in my life." Priya read the comment twice. "Okay, don't panic. Marcus would say this is toxic, but let's just test it." She tapped through Anna's settings like she'd done it a hundred times, which she had, for her mom last weekend. "Every app on here lets you choose whether it can use your location. Always, only while you're using it, or never."

"So?"

"So look at your game." Priya turned the screen around. The game Anna played every day, the one where you catch creatures that appear on a map of your own neighborhood, had its location set to always. Not only while you're using it. Always. Anna stared at it. "It's been on even when I'm not playing." She thought about the trail that would leave: school, home, the mall, the fountain, every Saturday for months, stored somewhere she couldn't see it and shared with who knew who. She set the switch to never, then posted a new photo of a completely different window, on the far side of the mall, with the location tag for the food court.

Then they sat on the bench by the fountain and watched her phone. The stranger account went quiet. No comment, nothing, for ten whole minutes. Priya demonstrated the answer by posting her own picture of the same far-off window, and still nothing arrived. Anna blocked the account, bought her hoodie, and texted Marcus: store's sold out, too slow. As they walked out past the fountain, Priya nodded at the crowd and said, "Tomorrow we're checking every app on your phone."

Eve stood in the kitchen with her hands pressed flat against her sides, whispering the words of the blessing she had to know by Sunday. Her grandmother had written it out for her in careful looping ink, and on Sunday, at the ceremony, she would say it alone in front of the whole family. She had to know it by heart.

The problem was her arms. Every time she reached a tricky line, her hands flew up without asking her, as if they could pull the next word out of the air. She'd clamp them down and lose her place. She tried again in the hallway, and her right hand escaped on "bless the road before me." She growled and started over.

Her cousin Fiona came in carrying her dance bag. "You look like you're being electrocuted."

"I'm memorizing."

"Arms down," Fiona said. "In Irish step dancing, that's the rule. Arms still, feet fast." She dropped into position, hands pressed to her sides, and her shoes hammered out a rhythm on the floorboards, heels and toes chasing each other while her shoulders never moved. It looked almost impossible, like two different people sharing one body.

Eve watched her and a question started forming. Her arms flapped when her brain was hunting for a word. Fiona's feet worked fast while her body stayed quiet. What if the flapping wasn't the problem? What if it was just energy with nowhere to go? Maybe it didn't matter which part of her moved, as long as something did.

"Play the reel," she said. "The slow one you practice to."

Fiona raised an eyebrow but found it on her phone. The fiddle started, infectious even at practice speed, and Eve planted her feet and began the simple steps Fiona had taught her last summer, the ones where you never lift your arms. On the third try, the whole blessing came out in order, word after word, her hands glued to her sides the entire time.

She tried it again to be sure. Then once more without music, just her feet marking time on the tiles. It held.

"Percentage of how sure you are?" Fiona asked.

"Ninety. Ninety-five."

"Grandma's going to ask how you did it. You going to disclose your secret method?"

Eve grinned and didn't answer. She started the steps again, hands pressed to her sides, and the first line of the blessing came out steady and strong.

The restaurant's big screen showed the stadium packed to the last row, and Theodore was halfway through his second basket of fries when the crowd did the wave. Thousands of people leapt up section by section, a ripple of color rolling around the bowl of seats, and the whole restaurant cheered along like the wave might somehow spill off the screen and soak them.

"That's called the Mexican wave," said Priya, his cousin, who had flown in from Manchester the night before and was now stealing his fries with impressive skill.

"The what?" Theodore said. "It's just the wave. Everybody calls it the wave." He looked around the table for backup, but his little sister was busy building a tower of ketchup packets and his dad was arguing with a menu.

"Mexican wave," Priya said again, munching. "That's what we call it at home."

Theodore could not believe two countries could have two names for the same ripple of strangers standing up. He decided to test it, because that was what you did when something sounded wrong. He climbed onto his chair, cupped his hands around his mouth, and shouted "Wave!" at the restaurant. A few people near the screen glanced over. One man in a soccer scarf lifted his arms, then sat back down, looking embarrassed.

Theodore sat, thought, and tried again. This time he yelled "Mexican wave!" The man in the scarf jumped up so fast his drink wobbled. "You know it!" he called back. He stood, raised both arms, and pointed to the left side of the restaurant, where a family of six rose in a soggy, wobbling chain, then the booth behind them, then the birthday party in the corner, all the way around the room until the wave crashed back into the man in the scarf, who sat down flushed and delighted.

"Okay," Theodore admitted, dropping back into his chair. "You win. Different countries, different words." He was already planning something bigger, though. The World Cup final was next month, and Priya would still be visiting. "We should do this at the school assembly," he said. "Half the gym yelling one thing, half the other, and we watch which one gets everyone up."

Priya grinned and pushed the empty fry basket toward him. "You'd better order more ammunition," she said. "You're going to need it."

Noemie spread her debate notes across her grandmother's kitchen table, which smelled like lemon polish and old coffee. Her first tournament was Saturday, and her case was dying. Every card was there, every quote copied neatly, but when she read it aloud to the salt shaker, the salt shaker fell asleep.

"It sounds like a robot reading a phone book," she told her grandfather, who was peeling an orange at the counter with the patience of a man who had nowhere to be. He had acted in theaters for forty years, and Noemie sometimes forgot that, since now he mostly acted like a person who owed nothing to anyone.

"Read me one point," he said. She did, in the flat, tedious drone she'd practiced, and he winced like she'd stepped on his foot. "Do you know what a debate case has?" he asked. "Same as a scene. A character wants something in every scene, and the actor plays every line trying to get it. We called that the objective. So. What do you want when you give this point?"

"To win the round," she said, but that felt too big, like wanting to be warm instead of wanting this blanket. She looked at the first point again and formulated it smaller: she wanted the judge to believe the numbers were real. She read the point again, leaning forward a little, pushing the evidence across the table like it was the last piece of bread and the judge was starving. It sounded different. Interesting, even.

She tested the idea on the next component, her second point, wanting the judge to feel a little alarmed. Her voice sharpened; her grandfather raised his eyebrows over his orange slice. When she tried the third point without choosing anything, it went flat again, which proved the pattern wasn't luck. "So the claim is that knowing your objective fixes a flat speech," she said, hunting for a pencil, "the evidence is three points, two alive and one dead, and the warrant is that the voice follows the want."

"That sounded like a debate case," her grandfather said.

"That was a debate case," Noemie said, writing fast. "You just became my evidence. Don't move."

He put up his hands, orange peel still hanging off one thumb. "I've been typecast before. At least this role comes with snacks."

Eli slid his thumb across the new phone's screen for the tenth time, and for the tenth time the glass answered him with a small, satisfying glow. The phone had cost him two years of birthday money and a summer of mowing lawns, and his mother had made him sit at the kitchen table and sign a paper about screen time before she would hand it over. "You budget your minutes," she had said. "The phone doesn't get to do it for you." He had signed it while the smell of her burnt toast still hung in the air.

By afternoon he had downloaded his favorite game, and by dinnertime a text arrived. YOUR ACCOUNT WILL BE DELETED IN 24 HOURS UNLESS YOU VERIFY YOUR PASSWORD. The message claimed to be from the game's official support team. Eli's stomach tightened. He had spent four hundred hours building that account. He tapped the link, and a login page appeared, gray and plain, asking for his password. He typed the first letter, then stopped. The real game company already had his password. Why would they need him to send it to them?

He tested his idea. He opened the game itself, from the icon, not the link. It loaded fine. No warning banner, no deletion notice, nothing in his inbox. Then he checked the sender of the text. The number had a strange stretch of digits, and the web address in the link, when he looked closely, had an extra letter jammed into the company's name, like a bad photocopy. The salt shaker sat cold under his fingertips as he read it twice.

"Mom," he called. She came in wiping her hands on a dish towel. He showed her the message. "It says verify or be deleted."

"That's phishing," she said. "Somebody pretending to be a company you trust, trying to get your password."

He deleted the text, blocked the number, and reported the message from inside the game's own help menu, which had a button for exactly this. His heart was still beating fast, but the beat had shifted into something steadier. He had almost handed over the keys to four hundred hours of work because a gray page looked official in the right context. He set the phone face-down on the table.

"So how was your first day with it?" his mother asked, sliding a plate toward him.

Eli picked up his fork. "Somebody tried to rob me before dinner."

She laughed. He didn't. He turned the phone back over and moved the phishing report into a folder he named, out loud, "Evidence."

Emily had been sitting at the kitchen table for twenty minutes, trying to write her social studies essay with her left hand, because her right arm was wrapped in a bright green cast from wrist to elbow. The essay was about tariffs, and she had managed one sentence: "A tariff is a tax on goods that come from another country." Her pencil grip was clumsy, and the words on the page looked like they had been written during an earthquake.

Then the itch started. It began as a small tickle under the cast, right near her wrist, and grew into a fire. Emily squirmed. She shook her arm. She pressed her palm against the cast and pushed, which did nothing at all. Her eyes drifted to the plastic ruler lying beside her essay, thin and flat and perfect.

She was sliding the ruler toward the edge of the cast when her little brother Theo walked in, eating a granola bar. "Mom said dinner's in ten minutes," he said. Then he saw the ruler. "Are you going to scratch with that? Mom told me the doctor said not to. She said doctors warn against sliding objects like pencils or sticks into a cast, because they can scrape the skin and damage the cast's lining."

Emily froze with the ruler halfway to her wrist. "Great. Now what do I do?"

"You could bang on it," Theo offered, and he rapped his knuckles on the hard green surface. The vibration traveled down, and for one second the itch faded. Emily grabbed a wooden spoon from the counter and tapped the cast gently, once, twice, like a woodpecker. It worked, a little, but the itch always crept back.

"We need a real plan," she said. She thought about the cool pack of frozen peas in the freezer. Cold might travel through the cast where scratching couldn't. Theo fetched the peas and held them against the itchy spot while Emily kept tapping. Between the cold and the tapping, the fire dulled to a small ember.

"That's the most eloquent solution to an itch I've ever seen," Theo said, mouth full of granola.

"It's not eloquent, it's desperate," Emily said, but she was smiling. "You should advocate for the peas method at school. You could make posters."

"Poster number one: The Ruler Is Not Your Friend."

Emily laughed so hard the peas slipped, and Theo lunged to catch them before they hit the floor.

Sydney sat cross-legged on Priya's bedroom floor with a laptop balanced on a stack of board games, staring at a spreadsheet full of survey answers. Two hundred and six students had answered the question "What should the new school mascot be?", and Sydney's job, as the newly appointed mascot committee data person, was to figure out which choice each grade liked best. The list just went on and on: name, grade, mascot choice, over and over. "There has to be a faster way than counting these by hand," she said. "My eyes feel like they're revolving in my head."

Priya's grandfather, who was staying with them that month and liked to drift past the door offering snacks, leaned in over Sydney's shoulder. "Ah, a spreadsheet," he said. "You know, I remember the first one. VisiCalc. Dan Bricklin and Bob Frankston wrote it, and it came out in 1979 for the Apple II. First spreadsheet program for personal computers." He tapped the screen gently. "I did our household sums on it. Every rupee of our first mortgage, row by row."

"You had a spreadsheet before I was born," Sydney said, "and I still can't make this one count anything." He laughed and shuffled off to the kitchen, offering no more help than the history lesson. Sydney glared at the toolbar until she spotted a button labeled PivotTable. It sounded plausible, at least, like something that would turn a mess into a summary. She clicked it, dragged "Grade" into the Rows box, dragged "Mascot" into the Columns box, and dragged "Name" into Values. The spreadsheet recalculated itself, and suddenly there it was: a clean little grid of numbers, grades down the side, mascasts across the top.

Then she saw the problem. Sixth grade wanted the Honey Badger by a landslide. Eighth grade, her grade, wanted the Thunder Falcon. But one answer showed up as "thunder falkon", another as "THUNDER FALCON", and one kid had simply written "falcon, but the thunder one", so the table had split them into three different columns and made the Falcon look like a loser. "The data's lying," Sydney groaned. "The eighth graders spelled our own mascot wrong." Priya peeked over and said, "To be fair, Kevin spells everything wrong. He wrote ' library ' as ' libary ' on a poster last month."

Sydney fixed the spellings one by one, refreshed the pivot table, and watched the Thunder Falcon column swell until it beat the Honey Badger by eleven votes overall. She copied the grid into the committee report, feeling briefly like a wizard, and then stopped. Sixth graders were going to be furious. They had more voters in the survey than any other grade, and the one-big-table method she'd just built would flatten them completely. Her pivot table had answered the question, all right, but the question turned out to be a trap. She could report the winner, or she could report winners by grade and start a war.

The cursor blinked on the empty line where her recommendation was supposed to go. Priya's grandfather appeared again with two plates of biscuits and set one beside the laptop. "Thunder Falcon," he read off the screen, and then he saw the grade-by-grade rows and raised his eyebrows. "Ah," he said. "In 1979, that little machine did the arithmetic, but the decisions, those it left to me." Sydney pulled the keyboard closer and began to type.

Chase stood in the Kellers' kitchen with a baby on his hip and a note on the counter that read, "Back by nine. Sophie naps at seven." Mrs. Keller had barely reached the front walk before Sophie started screaming. It was a full, red-faced scream, the kind that made Chase's ears ring, and it did not stop.

"Okay, okay," he said, bouncing her the way he had seen his mother do. Sophie screamed louder. He checked her diaper, which was fine. He offered the bottle from the fridge, and she knocked it away with one small furious hand. Through the window he watched Mr. and Mrs. Keller stroll down the sidewalk, completely unaware, and something in his chest went cold. What if something was actually wrong? What if he had to call them back five minutes into his first babysitting job?

Then he remembered his sister talking about her psychology class. "Crying when a parent leaves is called separation anxiety," she had said. "It's a normal stage of development. It usually starts in the second half of a baby's first year." Sophie was eight months old, and this afternoon Sophie had waved bye-bye to a spoon, which meant she was old enough to know exactly who had just walked out the door.

So the screaming had a hidden cause, and it was not a broken anything. Chase looked around the kitchen for a distraction. He restricted himself to three rules: nothing sharp, nothing small enough to swallow, nothing from the top cabinets. That left the wooden spoons and the pot drawer.

He set Sophie on the floor, crouched down, and slid the drawer open slowly. The metal pots caught the light. He banged a spoon against a saucepan once. Sophie's scream broke in the middle, like a dropped plate. He banged again, a little rhythm this time. Sophie stared, then grabbed a spoon with both fists and smacked the pot herself. Within two minutes she was laughing so hard she hiccuped.

When the Kellers came back at nine, they found their living room arranged like a drum set and Sophie asleep in Chase's arms, one spoon still in her fist. "She cried the whole time, didn't she?" Mrs. Keller asked, wincing. "Only at the start," Chase said. "Turns out she's basically the ambassador of pot music." Mr. Keller laughed and paid him, and at the door Mrs. Keller said, "Same time next Friday?" Chase grinned. "I'll bring my own spoon."

Naomi sat cross-legged in the window seat with the photocopied scene on her knee and a deadline breathing down her neck: paraphrase every speech into modern English by Monday, or fail the quiz. Her little brother Theo kept leaning over the back of the couch like a gargoyle.

"You're reading it wrong," he said. "That guy sounds like a robot."

"I'm reading it exactly right. That's the problem." She tapped the page. "Every word is a wall. 'Prithee, good mercutio, let's retire.' What is prithee? Some kind of greeting? A curse?"

"It sounds like a sneeze."

Naomi ignored him and read the line again, slower. Retire had to mean leave, because the characters wanted to get out of the heat. Good was just good. But prithee sat there like a locked door, and the character used it three more times down the page, always at the start of a request. "Prithee, tell me." "Prithee, have done." She flipped to the front of her textbook, where a page of word histories was tucked between the introduction and the play itself. The entry was short, and she read it twice to be sure.

"Prithee is a squeezed-together form of 'I pray thee,'" she said. "It means please."

"So he's not a robot," Theo said. "He's just polite."

"He's very polite. That's the whole trick." Naomi felt something click into place, the way a puzzle piece does when you stop forcing it. The character wasn't being strange. He was asking nicely, over and over, for things that mattered. She grabbed her notebook and started writing: "Please, good Mercutio, let's get out of here. Please, tell me. Please, enough." The speeches stopped being walls and became people talking.

She read her paraphrase out loud, giving Mercutio a robust voice, all swagger and noise, and Theo laughed so hard he slid off the couch. "Do the other one," he said. "The angry one." She did, and she illustrated the speech with a jab of her finger at each insult, like she was dealing cards.

"Monday's going to be fine," she said, and meant it.

"It's a treaty, then," Theo said, holding out his hand. "You help me with my book report, I stop calling Shakespeare a sneeze."

Naomi shook it, then turned back to the page and began the next speech.

Eva dragged the basketball, the flashlight, and two lawn chairs into the backyard before her brother even finished his cereal. Tomorrow she had to explain, out loud in front of the whole class, why summer happens, and she refused to say "because Earth gets closer to the sun," which was what Marcus had said last week and which was completely wrong.

"Earth is closest to the sun during winter in the north," she announced, propping the flashlight on one chair and holding the basketball above the other. "So distance can't be the answer. It's the tilt." She stabbed a sticker onto the top of the ball and angled it sideways. Marcus flopped onto the grass with a sandwich, watching with the expression of someone who found all of this voluntary and would rather be anywhere else.

"Shine the light," she ordered. He pointed the flashlight at the tilted ball. Eva traced the bright patch with her finger. "See? When the north end leans toward the light, the beams hit it more directly, straight on, so that half gets more heat. That's summer. When it leans away, the same light spreads out over a bigger area, so it's colder." She spun the ball slowly, keeping the tilt aimed the same direction, and the bright patch slid from the top of the ball to the bottom. "Six months later, the south end gets the direct beams. That's their summer. It's never the distance. It's always the angle."

Marcus squinted, then started picking at the sandwich. "Fine, but you'll still mess up the rock question. Heat always melts stuff. That's just what heat does."

"It does not!" Eva dropped the ball and marched to the rock garden by the fence. She grabbed a flat gray stone crusted with pale green lichen and scraped a clean spot with her thumbnail. "Grandpa said this one's metamorphic." She turned it over. "It got changed way down deep, by heat and pressure, but it never fully melted. That's the whole point. If it had melted, it would be a different kind of rock."

Marcus sat up, which for Marcus was practically applause. "So it can get hot enough to change and still stay solid?"

"Yes! Heat and pressure, deep underground, changed it, no full melting." She held the stone up so the sun caught its banded layers. "And if you contradict me in front of the class tomorrow, I will throw this at you."

"It's a rock, not a frisbee."

"Details." Eva set the stone on the chair beside the flashlight, angled the basketball one more time, and cleared her throat at the empty yard like it was a classroom. "Okay. From the top. Nobody knows why summer happens. Except me, and this basketball."

Aria sat at the kitchen table with her notebook open to a page that looked like a battlefield. Her English teacher had announced a short story contest, the most prestigious one in the county, and the winning story would be read aloud at the spring assembly. Aria wanted to win, or at least finish, but her draft kept tripping over itself. Every time a character spoke, she lost the thread.

"Who are all these I's and V's?" her little brother Marcus asked, leaning over her outline page. "They look like the numbers on a clock."

"They're Roman numerals," Aria said. "The big points get those. The little details under them get A and B." She pointed at her page. "See? I is the beginning, II is the middle, III is the climax. Under II, there's A, the frog pond, and B, the argument."

Marcus nodded slowly, still squinting at the letters as if they might rearrange themselves. Then he went back to his cereal, and Aria went back to her real problem. Her story was about two sisters who find a dying pond behind their school, an ecosystem slipping away because the water has gone still and sour. The sisters argue about whether to tell anyone. That argument was supposed to be her climax, but on the page it landed flat, like a jump rope with no one turning it.

She decided to test an idea. Maybe the problem was her dialogue. She had been writing, "I think we should tell Ms. Ruiz, said Elena." without punctuation that worked. She tried again, slower this time, saying each line out loud. "I think we should tell Ms. Ruiz," said Elena. "She said the frogs used to sing here." The comma went inside the quotation marks, and the lowercase s on said, because the sentence kept going. She wrote three more exchanges that way, listening to the rhythm. Then she moved a line of dialogue to the very top of section III, so the argument exploded right at the peak instead of drifting there, and she heard the difference immediately, the way a bullfrog can emit one deep note that carries across a whole dark field.

That evening a message popped up on her phone from her friend Dana.

Dana: You still doing that contest? I gave up. My story had no ending, just people talking forever.

Aria: Keep the talking. Move it. Put your loudest argument at the end of your outline, section III, and build everything toward it.

Dana: That's it?

Aria: That's half of it. Fix your commas too. Mine were a disaster until today.

Aria set the phone down, took out a fresh index card, and wrote III at the top, then A and B underneath, the sisters standing at the pond's edge in the last scene. She read her closing line once more, crossed out a comma, and put a new one inside the quotation marks where it belonged.

Jade sat in the exam room with her right arm propped on the paper-covered table, the fiberglass cast scratchy against her chin. Six weeks ago she had broken her radius falling off the garage roof while installing a birdhouse with her dad, and today, finally, the doctor would cut the cast off. In the waiting room she had seen a boy about her age leave with his arm out of a sling, and something about it had bothered her. His newly freed arm hung thinner than the other one, the skin pale, like a stick taped to his shoulder. She kept turning the image over in her mind, and by the time the nurse called her name, she had a guess: an arm that stays completely still for weeks loses something.

"So you think you can keep the muscles working from inside the cast?" her little brother Theo asked from the corner chair. He wanted her home by three, because he had plans for the two of them to build a model volcano before dinner, and every extra minute in this office felt like a stolen one.

"That's the idea," Jade said. "I've been squeezing this." She dug a stress ball out of her jacket pocket with her left hand, the one that had done everything for six weeks, and pressed it into her casted palm. Her fingers curled around it, faint and effortful, like they were moving through syrup. "Ten squeezes, four times a day, since week two. If stillness makes an arm shrink, then some movement should keep it from shrinking so much." She had no way to see inside the cast, which was the frustrating part. She could only measure the results today.

The saw whined, the shell split, and the two halves came away. Jade stared at her right arm and her stomach dropped. It was noticeably thinner than her left, the wrist narrow, the muscle of her forearm soft and small where the other one was round and firm. Her experiment had not saved it. "It's so skinny," she said, holding both arms side by side. "Why is it so much smaller?"

The doctor paused on his way out. "Muscles kept still in a cast weaken and shrink," he said. "That's normal." Then he was gone, and Jade turned back to her arm, flexing it, watching a small tremor run through it.

"Theo, grab my notebook," she said. She wanted to write this down while it was fresh: date, arm measurements, squeeze counts. Physical therapy would start next week, and the therapist had warned her that progress would hit a plateau at some point, where the arm would stop improving for a while no matter what she did. She intended to be ready with data, a whole coherent record from cast to recovery. Theo dug the notebook from her backpack and slapped it onto the table.

"Volcano at three," he said. "Deal?"

"Deal," Jade said, and wrote the first number down.

The lights went out just as Autumn was reaching for the last slice of pizza, and the whole farmhouse dropped into blackness so complete she couldn't see her own hand. "Grandma!" she called, already grinning, because a power cut at their dilapidated old house felt like the start of an adventure, not a disaster.

She heard her grandmother's chair scrape in the dark, then the sound of a drawer opening. "I'll get the candles," Grandma said. "There's a box on the pantry shelf."

"Wait, don't!" Autumn shot up from the table, arms out in front of her like a sleepwalker, bumping the doorframe before she found the hallway wall. She counted doorways in her head, the way she'd memorized them on a boring afternoon last summer, and felt her way into the kitchen. "We're not using candles. Where are the flashlights?"

"The candles are right here, dear. I've used candles in outages since before your mother was born."

Autumn found the drawer by touch, pulled it open, and her fingers closed around the rubber grip of the big flashlight. She clicked it on and the kitchen blazed back into existence, and she felt absurdly proud, as if she'd personally restored electricity. "In fire safety we learned that safety agencies recommend flashlights rather than candles during a power cut," she said, holding it up like a trophy. "A candle can easily start a fire in a dark house."

Grandma paused with the matchbox in her hand. Outside, the wind threw a gust against the shutters, the tail end of the week's storms that had soaked the fields until the ditches ran like little rivers. "Well," Grandma said slowly. She looked at the candle stub, then at the flashlight, and set the matchbox back in the drawer. "I suppose the house has stood two hundred years. I'd like to preserve it a bit longer."

"So it's flashlights?" Autumn was already digging for the second one, the small one with the crank handle that her grandpa kept for camping trips.

"It's flashlights," Grandma agreed, and she laughed. "Look at me, changing my mind at my age."

They carried the lights out to the porch and sat on the swing, watching the stars come out over the dark valley, brighter than Autumn had ever seen them without the porch light washed out. The pizza got cold inside, but Autumn didn't care. She cranked the little flashlight and aimed its beam at the barn roof, then traced it along the fence line toward the road. Somewhere out there the power crews were working, and the lights would come back eventually, but for now the whole dark world belonged to them.

"Want to see how far the beam reaches?" Autumn asked, standing up on the porch rail.

George set the two bean pots side by side on the picnic table, then moved them apart again, because side by side meant the taller one would shade the shorter one, and he wasn't testing shade. His question was simpler: did the plant food he'd bought with three weeks of allowance actually make beans grow faster? Pot A got the food. Pot B got plain water. Everything else, he'd promised himself, would stay exactly the same.

For nine days it worked. Pot A pulled ahead, and George measured both stems every morning with a ruler he kept in his back pocket. Fourteen centimeters versus nine. He wrote the numbers in his lab notebook and tried not to grin, because a real scientist, he figured, would be more like an artisan with data, careful and unhurried, immune to showing off.

Then his little sister Nadia came outside with a popsicle and stopped by the table.

"Why is this one all leaning?"

George looked. Pot B, the plain-water pot, leaned hard toward the fence, its leaves angled sideways like they were trying to escape. Pot A stood straight. He walked around the table twice. Both pots had the same soil from the same bag, the same amount of water from the same cup, the same kind of seeds from the same packet. So why would one lean?

He got down on his knees and scrutinized the yard from pot level, the way a bug would see it. From there he could see it plainly: the picnic table sat half under the big maple, and Pot B was in the shade of the trunk for most of the afternoon, while Pot A caught the window-side sun. Sunlight came from one direction, so Pot B had been bending toward the bright strip along the fence.

He stood up fast. His whole experiment was broken. The fourteen-versus-nine comparison meant nothing, because the pots hadn't been treated the same. One sat in the sun and one didn't, so the difference in the plants could be sun or food or both mixed together, and he couldn't tell which. He pressed his palms flat on the table.

"What?" Nadia said, licking her popsicle.

"Everything was supposed to be the same except the food. That's the whole point. If anything else is different, I can't say the food did anything."

"So make them the same."

He moved both pots to the open middle of the yard, where neither one got shade and neither one leaned anywhere, and turned them so the leaves that had bent all faced the fence. Then he found a scrap of paper and wrote in his notebook: START OVER, DAY 1. FAIR TEST MEANS ONLY ONE THING CHANGES.

The science fair was in eleven days. Not much time, but enough, if nothing else moved. He poured the measured water into each pot, marked the levels with tape, and carried his ruler inside.

"Can I have the plant food for my Venus flytrap?" Nadia asked.

"No." He shut the screen door. "You'll confuse my variables."

The cafe smelled like burnt espresso and cinnamon, and Livia spread her papers across the corner table anyway. Two assignments due Friday: a short story with dialogue, and a rewrite of her school lunch report, which her teacher had handed back with one word in red pen at the top. Report. "That's a grade killer," said Dex, sliding into the seat across from her with an empty smoothie cup. He wanted a refill, but the cashier had told him twice that refills ended at noon, and it was 12:04.

"My report had facts," Livia said. "Prices. Menu items. Six paragraphs." She flattened the page against the table. "Everything true."

"Then what's wrong with it?"

She read her own opening line: The cafeteria serves pizza on Tuesdays and chicken nuggets on Thursdays. Dex squinted at it. "Okay. I know that now. So what?"

"So what," Livia repeated. The question sat there like a coin she couldn't spend. She picked up her story draft instead, the one about a girl who finds a sinister note taped inside a library book, and stared at her dialogue. She had written: Maya said "who put this here". No comma, period in the wrong spot, and every character spoke in the same flat voice. She rewrote it slowly, comma before the quotation marks, new paragraph each time the speaker changed, and the page suddenly looked like a real story. The logic of it clicked. Punctuation was telling the reader who was talking, like a map.

Then she stopped. Her story had no climax. The girl just found the note, showed it to her brother, and went home. She'd ended it too early, before anything exploded. She flipped back to the report. Her problem there was the same problem. She'd listed lunch facts and gone home.

"Dex." She pulled the report toward her. "A persuasive essay's goal is to convince the reader to agree with a position or take an action."

"Not just give information about a topic," Dex said, chewing his straw. "Even I know that. You wrote a menu."

She crossed out her first paragraph and wrote: The school should replace Friday's soggy fish sticks with a build-your-own salad bar. Every fact after it now had a job. The prices weren't trivia anymore; they were ammunition. At the end she added a demand: sign the suggestion sheet outside the gym. Then she went back to her story and gave Maya a choice at the climax, follow the note's directions or hand it to the librarian, and let her choose.

Livia calibrated the last paragraph so the ending landed hard and short, then read both pages over once. She slid the story across the table to Dex.

"Read the dialogue out loud," she said. "Tell me if you can hear who's talking."

Dex read, stopped at the note, and looked up. "Okay, but if Maya hands it in, what happens?"

"Turn the page."

He turned it, and his eyes went wide.

Emile had exactly one hour before the library computers logged everyone off, and his climate project was due tomorrow. He slid into the seat nearest the window, pulled up the rainfall and temperature graphs the librarian had authorized him to print, and spread them across the desk. One graph belonged to a patch of the Amazon rainforest, thick with green bars for rain every single month. The other, from a desert in Australia, showed rainfall bars so short they looked like someone had tapped the paper with a pen. The desert's temperature line jumped and fell like a rollercoaster while the rainforest's stayed flat and warm. That part he understood. What he did not understand was the coordinate his teacher had written on the handout: a number that started with a minus sign.

His project partner, Priya, dropped into the chair beside him and typed the coordinates into the online map, hunting for their exact spot in the rainforest. "Type it exactly," Emile said, because the minus signs felt crucial, like they were part of the address. Priya waved him off and entered the numbers her way. The map spun, zoomed, and landed on a stretch of dry, cracked land scattered with gray shrubs. It looked exactly like their desert graph. Neither of them said anything for a second.

"That's not the rainforest," Emile said. He leaned over and looked at what she had typed. The first number, the latitude, was missing its minus sign. He retyped it with the minus and hit enter, and the map flew north across the equator and dropped them back into solid green rainforest. Priya tried it again on purpose, dropping the minus from the longitude this time, and the map jumped east, all the way to the other side of the world, into Indonesian jungle instead of Amazon jungle.

"So the minus means something," Emile said slowly. He tried their desert coordinates without the minus on the latitude, and the desert became grassland in the northern hemisphere. He flipped the longitude's sign instead, and the desert landed in Africa rather than Australia. He wrote it in the margin of his handout, testing each one against the map like checking answers in the back of a math book. South of the equator, negative latitude. West of the prime meridian, negative longitude. That was the rule the map kept obeying, every single time.

Then came the twist. When he finally typed their rainforest coordinates perfectly, with both minus signs in place, and compared the site's rainfall chart to the one in his handout, the bars did not match. His teacher had copied the rainfall percentages from the wrong column, and half his carefully labeled graph was wrong. The library lights flickered the five-minute warning, and the printer behind them groaned through somebody else's fifty pages.

They divided the work on the walk to the print desk. Priya redrew the rainfall bars while Emile copied out the corrected temperatures, both of them scribbling on the backs of the old graphs because there was no time for new ones. The printout came out warm and smudged at one corner, but the lines were readable. "Tomorrow she's going to ask where we got the fix," Priya said. Emile folded the pages in half and slid them into his backpack, minus signs still showing in the margin. "Then I'll tell her we got lost first."

Charlotte's mistake happened in the second measure every single time. She was practicing the new piece for Monday's audition, the one her piano teacher had marked up with softs and louds and a big ritardando near the end, and she couldn't get past those opening chords. Her younger sister, Dara, sprawled on the couch behind her with headphones half on, humming along anyway.

"You're singing it wrong," Charlotte said, stopping.

"I am not. I'm singing exactly what you're playing."

"It's not the same note. Not even close." Charlotte played the first melody note, a low G. Dara matched it, and it sounded higher, thinner, like a smaller version of the same sound. Charlotte frowned and played it again. "See? Different."

Dara came and stood by the bench. "It's the same, though. It's like the same note but up high. Sing it with me."

They sang together, and the strange thing was that it worked, the way two gears of different sizes still turn the same machine. Charlotte pressed the G below middle C, then the G above it, one after the other, over and over. Same name, same feeling, different height. She pulled her theory notebook out of the bench, the one Mom had left there with her old sheet music, brittle and frail at the corners, and flipped to the back where she kept questions she couldn't answer yet.

"Here's what I think," she said. "When a note is one octave higher, it's vibrating exactly twice as fast. Twice. That's why they sound like the same note at different heights." She tested it the only way she could, by ear, jumping octaves up and down the keyboard and listening for that same-note feeling, and it held every time, low to high, high to low.

"Okay, but does that fix your measure?" Dara asked.

Charlotte looked at the page. The mistake wasn't a wrong note at all. Her left hand kept jumping an octave on the second beat, hitting the higher G when the piece wanted the low one, and because they matched, her ear never caught it. Now she could hear the shape of it, tall and short, and she played the measure six times clean.

"Better," Dara said. "The loud part's still mushy, though."

"The dynamics. I keep forgetting to get soft before the crescendo, so there's nowhere to grow from." Charlotte set the metronome, its brass alloy case still warm from the lamp, and started from the top. Mom would have to authorize her taking that Tuesday slot at the recital, and that meant auditioning on Monday, ready or not.

She played it through, soft where it begged for soft, swelling where it had to, the final ritardando landing like something set down carefully on a high shelf. When she finished, Dara was quiet for a second, then said, "Play it again."

Charlotte's hands hovered over the keys. Mom's notebook lay open on the bench beside her, its penciled notes in a hand she would never hear explain anything again. She lifted her fingers and began.

The living room was so crowded that Christopher ended up on the floor with his back against the couch, wedged between his cousin Marisol's knees and the coffee table. On the screen, the game was tied with two minutes left, and Uncle Ray kept standing up whenever his team scored, which blocked the diagonal view from the armchair where Grandpa sat. During a timeout, a commercial for sneakers came on, and Marisol said, "Wait. Why do they even call it a basket? Nobody's shooting into a basket. It's a hoop with a net."

"Because it used to be a real basket," Christopher said. "A peach basket."

"You made that up," Marisol said, and Uncle Ray laughed from the kitchen doorway, which Christopher took as a signal that the whole room was about to humiliate him if he didn't produce proof. He had read it somewhere, in Grandpa's old sports almanac, but he couldn't remember where the book was now. While everyone argued about whether the referee had missed a foul, Christopher crawled along the floor to the shelf under the window, where the almanac lived between a dictionary and a stack of TV guides. He found the entry under basketball and ran his finger down the page.

"James Naismith invented basketball in December 1891 at a YMCA training school in Springfield, Massachusetts," he read, "using peach baskets as the goals. Peach baskets. That's why it's called basketball. They didn't cut holes in the bottom at first, so somebody had to climb up and get the ball out every time somebody scored."

Marisol leaned over his shoulder to see the page herself. "Huh," she said. "You weren't making it up." Uncle Ray came back in with chips and said, "That's actually true. They used peach baskets." Christopher felt himself grinning, but then the game came back on and Grandpa stood up fast, and the almanac slid off Christopher's lap onto the carpet, page down, spine bent.

Grandpa's team lost by one point on a shot at the buzzer, a long diagonal runner that banked in off the backboard. Grandpa sat down slowly and didn't say anything for a while.
