"She showed off quietly." Her mother knelt and pulled a weed from the base of the stone, then sat back on her heels. "You've been quiet too. Quieter than you think I notice."

Autumn picked at the label on the urn. She could ask now or carry it another week, and she'd already carried it for seven days, and it hadn't gotten lighter. "At the movies I laughed," she said. "Like, a lot. It was three days after the funeral and I laughed until I cried." She stared at the grass. "I keep thinking I did something wrong."

Her mother didn't answer right away. She brushed dirt from her knees and looked at the stone, at PEARL ALVAREZ, 1947 to this year, and Autumn braced herself for a correction.

"Remember when I took that psychology class at the community college, the year you were in fourth grade?" her mother said. "There was a researcher named Margaret Stroebe and another one named Henk Schut. In 1999 they described grieving people as moving back and forth between focusing on the loss and getting on with daily life. They called it the dual process model."

"Dual process model," Autumn repeated. Back and forth. Loss, then daily life, then loss again.

"So laughing at a raccoon is part of it?"

"That's the getting-on-with-daily-life part, yes. And being sad here is the other part. You're allowed to do both. You're supposed to do both."

Autumn thought about testing it, the way she'd test an idea in science class. Yesterday she'd made herself look at Grandma's mug on the shelf and had to sit down from the ache of it. Today she'd hummed along with the radio without noticing until the song was over. Back, then forth. Maybe the guilt was just her misreading the data.

A wind came up the hill and bent the white flowers toward the road, showing off for nobody, and Autumn squatted to turn the urn a little more, just to be sure.

"There," she said. "That's better."

Gavin curled his fingers into a claw, knuckles forward, and set the onion on the cutting board the way Amara had shown him. "The knife rides against your knuckles, never your fingertips," she said, "unless you want to donate blood to the sauce." He laughed, then pressed down carefully, and the onion fell apart into neat little cubes. He was doing this because his mom had worked double shifts all week and he wanted dinner waiting when she got home, something made by him and not microwaved.

Amara's little brother, Amir, sat on a stool stirring the tomatoes with his good arm. He'd had a vaccine that morning, and the soreness in his other arm hindered him so much that he could barely lift the spoon, so Gavin chopped extra slow and let Amir feel like the official stirrer. "Careful with that old pepper in the back of the fridge," Amara warned, holding up a soft, wrinkled one. "Mold can be toxic even after you cut it off. We're using the fresh ones."

Gavin had planned the order himself. He figured the flatbread was the tricky part, the thing most likely to go wrong, so he tackled it first while his hands were steady. He rolled the chapati dough into circles and cooked them on the hot, dry griddle. Each one puffed and browned in only a minute or two, which surprised him. He stacked them on a plate, covered them with a towel, and moved on to the sauce, which had to simmer a long while to get thick.

When everything else was finally ready, he lifted the towel and found the chapatis cold and stiff, more like plates than bread. He frowned at them. The sauce had taken half an hour. The bread had taken two minutes. He turned the fact over in his head: anything that cooks in a minute or two can wait until the very end. "Amara, do you have more dough?" She did, so while she spooned sauce into bowls, he rolled three fresh circles and laid them on the griddle one at a time. Each came off hot, soft, and folded straight onto a plate. Amir grabbed the first one before Gavin could set it down.

At that moment the door opened and Gavin's mom walked in, tired and carrying her coat. "You cooked?" she said, staring at the table.

Amir pointed at the last chapati with tomato sauce on his cheek. "We made the bread last," he announced, "so it wouldn't get cold."

Gavin looked at the empty plate where the warm bread had been. "Then I guess I'm making it last again."

Brooke sat cross-legged on the living room carpet with her laptop on the coffee table, a mug of hot cocoa going cold beside her. Her class had surveyed the whole school about lunch periods, and Ms. Reyes had promised that anyone who summarized the results by grade could present at Friday assembly. Brooke wanted that spot on the microphone more than she wanted to admit out loud.

She built her first pivot table, dragging the grade column into the rows area and dragging the answers into the values area. The counts appeared, and for a moment everything looked perfect: sixth grade, seventh grade, eighth grade, each with its numbers. Then she saw it, a fourth row sitting under the others, labelled "(blank)". She counted the grade rows again, as if counting harder might make the extra one disappear. One hundred and six students had answered, but her table had one hundred and twelve. Six answers had come from nowhere, or from somewhere.

"(blank)," she said out loud, reading the label to the empty room. "What grade is blank?"

Her older brother Dev wandered through on his way to the kitchen, eating cereal straight from the box. "What's blank?" He leaned over the back of the couch, crumbs falling into the cushions, and Brooke pointed at the mystery row. She scrolled back to the raw survey answers in another tab and started scanning the grade column. It took her a minute of scrolling, but there they were: six rows where the grade cell was just empty. She could deduce what had happened. Six students had filled in the whole survey but skipped the grade question, and every empty cell had been gathered into its own group instead of being thrown away.

Dev squinted at the screen. "So the table's wrong?"

"No," Brooke said slowly, "it's right. It's just telling me something I didn't ask for." Last month she had almost deleted a whole column of data because it looked like garbage, and Dev had talked her out of it, which still annoyed her a little. She changed her mind about the "(blank)" row now the same way. Instead of deleting it, she typed a note beneath the table: six respondents skipped this question. At the assembly she could explain that, and it would sound like she had planned it all along.

She counted the rows one last time, then highlighted the mystery group in yellow so she would not forget it. "Hey, Dev," she called toward the kitchen, where he was running water somewhere behind the plumbing under the sink, "guess who's presenting on Friday."

"Wear something without cocoa on it," he called back, and Brooke laughed, an infectious snorting laugh that made him laugh too, all the way from the kitchen.

Georgia set up her easel by the window of the dilapidated community art studio, where the paint-spattered sink dripped and one fluorescent tube flickered. She was painting a sunset over the lake for the studio's fundraiser show. Anything that sold would count toward the studio's revenue for the year, and Ms. Ruiz had said they needed at least four hundred dollars to fix the window in the ceramics room. Georgia wanted her painting to be the one that sold.

She laid in the sky with broad strokes of orange, then began adding the red band above the horizon where the sun sat. Under her brush, the red and orange melted together and turned a dull, muddy brown. She frowned, scraped the area with a palette knife, and tried again with fresh paint. The second band turned brown too, worse than the first. The third attempt looked like gray mud. Her lake was still blue and clean, but the sky looked ruined.

Across the table, Marcus was mixing greens for a forest scene. "What's wrong with your sunset?" he asked. "It looks like dirt."

"I keep adding red and it keeps going brown," Georgia said. She looked at his palette, where his green paint sat next to a tube of red he had used for a barn door. On the studio wall there was an old color wheel chart, its plastic film peeling. She walked over and traced her finger from the red wedge straight across the circle to the wedge opposite it. Green sat there. Then she looked back at the lake in her painting, which she had underpainted with green before adding the blue water on top. Some of that green was showing through where her strokes were thin, right where the red bands turned muddy.

"Complementary colors," Marcus said, squinting at the chart. "That's what they're called. They sit opposite each other on the wheel, like red and green."

Georgia went back to her easel and ran a quick test. On a scrap of canvas she dabbed pure red, then touched green into half of it. The dab turned the same dull brown as her sky. Then she painted a swatch of red over an opaque layer of white, with no green underneath, and it stayed bright. She let out a breath. It wasn't her paint or her brush. It was the green showing up from underneath, mixing into the red as she blended.

She covered the lake area with two thick coats of white gesso, waited for it to dry while she cleaned her brushes in the dripping sink, and then painted the red band fresh over the white. This time it burned clean and bright against the orange. She layered the colors up toward a deep violet, and the whole sky glowed the way it did over the water in September. Marcus came over and stood beside her, brush in hand.

"That one's going to sell first," he said.

Georgia signed her name small in the corner, then flipped the painting around to face the window, sunset light falling across wet paint.

Nathan stood at the edge of his aunt's backyard holding a wrapped box and trying to work out where to put his shoes. Everyone else had left theirs in a heap by the back door, even though they were outdoors, so he kicked his off too and carried the box up the steps. The party was for his cousin's engagement to a woman named Kanya, whose whole family had flown in from Thailand, and Nathan had been told exactly one thing by his mother on the drive over: do not embarrass us.

The greetings were the first puzzle. Kanya's parents did not shake hands the way his uncles did. They pressed their palms together at the chest and bowed slightly, and Nathan copied it, feeling clumsy, and saw Kanya's father smile like the awkwardness itself was fine. Then his grandfather came over and clasped Nathan's shoulder in the big two-handed grip their family used, and Nathan realized that different people in the same backyard were greeting him in entirely different systems, and both systems were correct.

The gift was the second puzzle. His box held a fantasy novel, his favorite genre, chosen because Kanya's little brother Sun, who was nine, had spent the whole week reading on the porch steps. Nathan handed it over the way he would to anyone, but he noticed that Kanya's mother received gifts with both hands and a small dip of her head, and that Sun did not tear the wrapping open at once. He turned the package over and set it aside to open later, which made Nathan feel like a guest in a country he was standing inside already.

Lunch was long and shared, dishes moving in circles. Nathan watched which spoon took food from which bowl, how people served the person beside them before themselves, and how his own loud slurping made Kanya's grandmother glance over, once, without a word. He ceased slurping and took smaller portions, and the grandmother put an extra piece of chicken on his plate, which he decided, being pessimistic by nature, to interpret as forgiveness rather than a test.

The problem came after lunch. His little cousin Mia, who was six and loved Sun already, reached up on tiptoe to ruffle his hair the way she ruffled everyone's hair. Nathan grabbed her wrist before he thought about why.

"Wait," he said.

Mia blinked at him. Sun looked at the hand in Nathan's grip and then at Nathan's face. Nathan let go of Mia's wrist slowly. "In Thailand the head is sacred," Sun said, plainly, like he was naming a street. "So touching someone's head, even to pat a kid, can be seen as rude." Nathan thought back over the afternoon, the greetings, the both hands, the small bows, and saw the pattern running underneath all of it, like a water pipe hidden in a wall.

Mia pressed her palms together and bowed to Sun instead, so solemn that Sun laughed and bowed back even lower. Then she bowed to Nathan too, and Kanya's father, watching from his chair, raised one hand and patted the empty air above Mia's head, touching nothing at all.

The laundromat smelled like warm cotton and machine oil, and Abigail stood in front of three machines holding a garbage bag that held every piece of clothing she owned. Mom was away at a two-week training in Denver, and before she left she had said, "You can live out of the bag or you can figure it out." Abigail had chosen the bag for nine days. On day ten, the last clean shirt, the one with the diagonal green stripes, had come out of the hamper smelling like gym class, and here she was.

Sorting took longer than she expected. She remembered being six, sitting on the dryer while Mom pulled out reds, whites, and darks like a card dealer. "This one pink sock ruined a whole load once," Mom had said, holding up a faded pink sock like evidence in a trial. Abigail had laughed then. Now she turned a purple hoodie over twice, undecided, and finally dropped it with the darks. She fed quarters into the machine like she was paying a toll, poured in the detergent, and settled onto a folding table to wait, her whole cargo of dirty clothes tumbling behind the round window.

The wash took forever, so she read the safety sticker on the dryer while she waited. She read it twice. Failing to clean the dryer is the leading factor in home clothes dryer fires, it said, according to the U.S. Fire Administration, because built-up lint blocks the airflow and lets heat collect. She looked at the dryer's pull-out filter, which stuck out of its slot at an angle like a forgotten drawer.

When her wet clothes finally landed in the dryer, she yanked the filter out and stared at it. The mesh was covered with a thick grey mat of lint, dense as a blanket, and there was more packed behind it, deeper in the slot, where some earlier customer had clearly just pushed it down and walked away. So that was a job nobody had been doing. She peeled the mat off in one piece, like lifting a pelt, and dropped it in the trash. Then she dug out the packed lint with two fingers until air could pass through clean.

While the dryer ran, she thought about whether she should have called Mom weeks ago and asked how all this worked, instead of wearing the same shirt four times. She hadn't wanted to look helpless. But Mom had left a note on the fridge about the tomato plants needing her to pollinate the cherry tomatoes with a paintbrush, since there were no bees on their balcony, and Abigail had done that part without complaint. Maybe laundry was just another paintbrush.

The buzzer sounded. She folded the striped shirt first, sleeves crossed over, and laid it square on the table.

"One load," she said out loud, to nobody, and started on the socks.

Piper sat on the low wall at the edge of the skate park, her left arm in a bright green cast, watching her friend Dara drop into the bowl. Two weeks ago that had been her. She remembered the exact moment her board slipped out from under her on the coping, the way she'd put her arm down to catch herself, and the sound that was not really a crack. More of a bend. Like a stick that doesn't quite snap.

At the hospital, the doctor had looked at the X-ray and said the words that had been circling in Piper's head ever since. "Good news. It's a greenstick fracture, so it's partly broken." Piper had stared at the ghostly image of her own bone and asked, "Partly? How can a break be partly?" The doctor pointed to a line that stopped halfway across, like a crack in a sidewalk that runs out of steam.

Now she couldn't stop thinking about it. She'd asked her little brother to bring her a green branch from the backyard, and yesterday, while nobody was watching, she'd pressed her thumb against it. The bark split on one side only, and the branch bowed away on the other, still connected. That was her bone. That was why kids got this kind of break, the doctor had said, because their bones are more flexible than adults'. Older bones snap clean, like dry kindling. Younger ones bend first and crack on just the one side.

"You're doing the branch thing again," Dara said, rolling up beside her with a clatter. She nodded at the twig in Piper's right hand.

"Watch," Piper said. She bent it slowly, splitting the bark a little more. "One side cracks, the other side bends. I keep wondering if my arm would've snapped all the way through if I'd fallen harder. Or if I was, like, eighty."

Dara laughed, then went quiet, spinning her board under one foot. "I always thought a broken bone was a broken bone. Like, all the way or nothing." She frowned at the branch. "So your arm's not really broken?"

"It is," Piper said. "It's just broken on one side and bent on the other." She set the twig down carefully, the way you'd set down evidence. "I'm going to invest my whole recovery in figuring out how it heals. Does the bent side pull the cracked side back straight? Or does the crack fill in first?"

"That's a lot of thinking for a kid with a cast," Dara said, but she was squinting at the branch now too.

Piper traced a line down the middle of the twig with her finger. "This is like the equator of the branch. One half splits, one half holds. If I taped the split side, could the bendy side still flex?" She looked up at the bowl, where sunlight made a bright curve of the concrete. "Next week I get the short cast, the one that lets my elbow move. Doctor says skating again in a month might be feasible if the X-ray looks right."

Dara kicked her board up into her hand. "Race you to the vending machine, then."

Piper was already off the wall, green cast swinging, running on legs that worked just fine.

The diner smelled like bacon and burnt coffee, and George had never been less interested in food in his life. His dad slid into the booth across from him, cheerful as a game show host, while George's little sister Priya attacked a stack of pancakes like they owed her money.

"Eat something, buddy," Dad said. "We've got four more hours of driving, and the hotel only holds the room until ten."

"That's what I keep telling him," Priya said through a mouthful of syrup. "Ten o'clock. Deadline. Tick tock."

George put his forehead on the cool formica table. It was nine in the morning back home, which meant his body believed it was six, and his body had opinions about six. The weird part was the trip out. Two weeks ago they had flown west to California, and he'd felt fine, practically bionic. They'd landed, retrieved their suitcases from the carousel, and gone straight to the beach. He hadn't been tired at all.

"You were up until two in the morning," Priya reminded him helpfully. "I heard you talking to your shoes."

"One conversation," George said into the table.

He lifted his head and started working the problem like a math sheet, because that was what he did when he felt terrible. Out west, fine. Back east, wrecked. Same kid, same plane, same crummy airline pretzels. The only thing that had changed was the direction. He pulled the paper placemat toward him and drew two arrows, one pointing left, one pointing right. Under the left one he wrote FINE, SUPERHERO, HANDSOME. Under the right one he wrote ZOMBIE.

Priya leaned over. "What's that?"

"Evidence," George said. "Going west, I felt great. Coming home east, I'm a puddle. It's not random. It's a pattern." He tapped the arrows. "I think jet lag is just harder going east than going west."

"That's your testimony?" Priya raised her hand like she was swearing in. "State your name for the record."

"George. Also a zombie."

She giggled, then paused with her fork in the air. "Wait. That's actually a thing? It's not just you being dramatic?"

"It's a thing. I tested it. There were two flights, and I was the experiment." He'd been meticulous about it, in a sleepy way. On the flight out, even the crossing of three time zones hadn't knocked him down. On the flight back, one day home and he was awake at three in the morning, staring at the ceiling, listening to Priya snore.

Dad had been watching the whole performance over his coffee. "So what you're telling me is that next summer we fly west again."

"Forever," George said. "We just keep flying west for the rest of our lives. It's science."

The waitress came by with a plate of hash browns nobody remembered ordering. "Heard the word zombie from three tables away," she said. "These fix most things."

George looked at the hash browns. His stomach considered the offer. Slowly, suspiciously, he picked up a fork.

"Better hurry," Priya said, pointing at the clock. "Nine forty."

George took a bite, then another, and felt something almost like being a person again. "Okay," he said. "New plan. We get to the hotel by ten, I nap like a normal scientist, and tomorrow we take the longest way possible to school. Westward."

"Deal," said Dad, dropping a twenty on the table. "Everybody in the car. Zombie first."

Priya grabbed the placemat with the arrows and folded it into her pocket. "I'm keeping this for the record."

"Objection," said George, and followed her out the door.

Riley's family kept the washer and dryer in the garage, next to a shelf of motor oil and a bicycle pump, and every Saturday her mother had done the laundry there. But her mother was in Toronto for two weeks helping Aunt Carol, which left Riley and her father, and her father had already shrunk one of his own sweaters to doll size. "You're thirteen," he said on the phone. "This can be your job." So on Saturday morning Riley stood in the garage with three hampers, sorting clothes into piles: whites, darks, and one pile she wasn't sure about, a pink sock that had turned the whole load last winter, when it snuck in with the whites and dyed Dad's undershirts a pale blush. She put the doubtful sock in with the darks. She read the detergent bottle, measured it, and set the machine for cold. Then she discovered they were almost out of detergent, one load short, and Dad was at work.

She counted her money. The detergent at Halloran's was marked four dollars and ninety-nine cents, and she had exactly five dollars. She rode her bike the eight blocks, found the bottle on the shelf, and carried it to the register. The screen said five dollars and thirty-four cents. Riley counted again, laid out her five dollars, and stood there while the line built up behind her. "That's all I have," she said, feeling her face go hot. It embarrassed her, standing short in front of a cashier and six strangers.

A voice behind her said, "Where I come from, the price on the shelf is the price you pay." It was Mrs. Ferris from two doors down, holding a box of teabags. "In Britain, and in Europe, the tax is already in the price they print. Here in the States, and in Canada too, the shelf price leaves the tax out, and they add it at the till." She put down thirty-five cents. "I moved here from Manchester, and it caught me the first year, every single time." Mrs. Ferris had been wanting an excuse to talk to somebody all week; her daughter never called, and her kettle worked better with company. "Come by for tea after, and tell me if your load came out."

Riley rode home thinking it through. At the garage she pulled the warm clothes from the dryer and shook out her father's synthetic running shirt, which had come out of the dryer crackling with static because she'd forgotten a dryer sheet, and she made a mental note for the next load. She folded the towels in halves, then halves again, so the edges matched, and she liked the symmetry of the stack. When Dad came home she told him about the shelf prices and the thirty-five cents. "Mrs. Ferris wants tea," she said. "Bring the cookies," he said, "and check the sock." Riley pulled the pink sock from the folded darks. Still pink. The navy towels around it, still navy.

The temple hall smelled of camphor and wet stone, and Stella moved to the beat of the mridangam drum, her anklets ticking like a clock. In three weeks she would dance before the deity at the Navaratri festival, her first real performance, and she knew the whole piece by heart except for one moment that kept sliding away from her.

Her grandmother sat against the back wall, watching with her arms crossed. That was the strange part. Last year, when Stella had performed at the school talent show, Ammamma had applauded everything, even the mistakes. Now, every time Stella reached the fourth verse, the old woman's frown deepened. Stella finished the run-through, wiped her neck with the corner of her practice sari, and walked over.

"Ammamma, is it my footwork? The aramandi?"

Her grandmother shook her head slowly. "Your hands," she said. "You are telling the wrong story."

Stella's mind began to orbit the problem the way it did with a hard math proof, circling it, looking for the angle nobody had shown her. She knew the moves. She could feel them in her wrists. But the frown had appeared only in the fourth verse, and only when her hands did a certain thing. In class, her teacher had said that in Bharatanatyam, a classical dance from Tamil Nadu in India, the symbolic hand gestures called mudras work like words to tell a story. Swap one word and the sentence means something else. Stella had nodded that day and filed it away in her head like an entry in a database, something to retrieve for a quiz. It had never occurred to her that a wrong entry could matter.

She stood in the middle of the hall and danced just the fourth verse, slowly, watching her grandmother's face instead of her own hands. At the half-turn, her fingers folded into a beak shape, the gesture for a bird, and the frown came. She stopped. "This one?"

"That is the crow," her grandmother said. "The verse is about the peacock. A crow pecking at the offering, that is what you showed me."

Stella laughed, then felt her face go warm. She had felt so sure, so untouchable up there on the practice floor, and all along one small finger's difference had been turning a holy verse into a joke about a scavenger. It made her feel strangely vulnerable, like discovering that a door she'd been leaning on was never locked.

They stayed after the drummers left, grandmother and granddaughter, shaping peacocks out of their hands under the dim lights while the bells above the sanctum rang for the evening prayer. Ammamma's fingers trembled with age, but the gesture itself was steady, as if it had been waiting in her hands all these years to be passed on.

"Show me the sixth verse too," Stella said, kneeling beside her. "Before I get that one wrong as well."

Levi locked the bathroom door, faced the mirror, and started his presentation for the third time. "The honeybee population would flourish if cities planted more wildflow." His voice snapped in half on the last syllable, sliding from low to squeaky like a cassette tape gone wrong. He gripped the sink. His hands were damp, his heart was drumming, and a hot feeling crawled up his neck. He knew those signs now, because last week his counselor had made him a card with three questions on it: Are your hands sweating? Is your heart fast? Are your shoulders up by your ears? Two out of three, and his shoulders were practically touching his ears.

He set the card on the edge of the sink and counted. In for four, hold, out for six. He did it five times, watching his shoulders sink in the mirror like ice cream softening. Last night he had tested something else too. Instead of staring at his phone until midnight, he had put it in the kitchen at nine thirty, and this morning his head felt clearer, less like a snow globe someone kept shaking.

The crack itself, though, that was a different problem, and he had a theory about it. He flashed back to Tuesday, standing in front of science class, when his voice had broken right on the word "pollination" and Marcus had laughed so hard he knocked over a chair. Afterward Levi had looked it up on the library computer, hunched so nobody could read over his shoulder. He found that during puberty, a part called the larynx, the voice box, grows larger, and the vocal cords get longer and thicker, which makes the voice deeper, especially in boys. So the crack was not him being nervous exactly, or not only. His throat was under construction, doing a gradual rebuild, and the squeaks were construction noise. His theory: if his voice was going to wobble no matter what, then the thing he could actually control was the stress around it. Tonight he would test the idea with a full run of the presentation, breathing and all.

He started over. "The honeybee population would flourish if cities planted more wildflowers." It cracked twice more, once on "flourish" and once on "biodiversity," but his hands stayed mostly dry and he didn't stop talking. That was the twist, he realized, pulling open the door: the presentation could survive a crack. It couldn't survive silence.

His sister Priya was in the hallway with her earbuds in, and she pulled one out. "Was that you rehearsing? It sounded pretty good."

"It cracked, like, four times," Levi said.

"Pfft. Devon's voice cracks every day and nobody cares anymore." She held out the earbud. "Want to hear the song I think would go good with your slides? You're a strong candidate for background music, since your topic is so dramatic."

Levi took the earbud and listened, and by the second chorus his shoulders were all the way down.

The sign-up sheet at the community center said the Wolves were a brand-new team, and by the second practice Jaxon understood exactly what that meant. Nobody passed to anybody. Marcus, who had told everyone at school he would be captain someday, called for the ball on every possession even when two defenders were draped over him. By the third week, things had begun to deteriorate, with shouting matches in the layup line and one kid, Deshawn, quitting before the first game. After practice Jaxon sat in the center's reading room, pretending to work on his math homework, while the coach's caterpillar tank sat on the windowsill, one fat larva hanging from a twig in its slow way of becoming something else. He pulled a dusty psychology book off the shelf mostly to have something to do, and found a chapter about groups.

A psychologist named Bruce Tuckman had proposed in 1965 that groups go through stages called forming, storming, norming and performing. Jaxon read the sentence twice. Forming, when everyone is new and polite. Storming, when the arguing starts. He thought about last Tuesday, when Marcus and Ravi had gone nose to nose over who should take the last shot in a scrimmage, and Coach Odum had to blow the whistle four times. Maybe the Wolves were not broken. Maybe they were just in the middle of a list.

He remembered the first practice now, back in that warm gym that smelled like floor wax. Everyone had stood in a loose circle, saying "nice pass" and "my bad" in quiet voices, nobody wanting to step on toes. That was forming, he realized, and it had lasted exactly one week before the storm rolled in.

So he tested it. He made a chart in the back of his notebook, a row for each practice, and he marked down the arguments in one column and the assists in another. He said nothing to anyone, because "the team is storming" did not sound like a legitimate excuse for a bad practice, and he figured the guys would laugh at him. The pattern held anyway. Week one, three arguments, two assists. Week three, seven arguments, zero assists. Week five, two arguments, nine assists, and Marcus drove the lane and kicked it out to Ravi for a corner shot without either of them yelling.

Before the game on Saturday, Jaxon finally showed Marcus the chart in the locker room. "A psychologist named Bruce Tuckman said groups go through stages called forming, storming, norming and performing," Jaxon said. "I think we're in the norming one."

Marcus studied the page for a long moment, jaw tight. "So I don't have to call for the ball every time?"

"You can still call for it sometimes," Jaxon said.

Marcus grinned and slapped the notebook shut. "Fine. But after the game, we talk about me being captain."

They ran out through the double doors into the noise of the gym, sneakers squeaking on the bright floor, and the caterpillar on the windowsill hung motionless in its chrysalis, waiting for its wings.

Maya's basement smelled like dust and old carpet, and the only light came from a desk lamp bent over her laptop. Ella pulled a second chair up close, because their history project, a web page for Monday's mock trial exhibit, had to exist by tonight, and so far it existed only in Maya's head. The defendant in their case, a fictional ferry captain accused of scuttling his own boat, deserved better than a plain typed sheet taped to the wall.

"First the skeleton," Maya said, typing. She wrote out angled brackets, and a heading appeared at the top of the page, sitting stubbornly in the left corner like a cat that refused to move. "Now CSS," she said, and typed a few more lines. When she refreshed the browser, the heading stayed exactly where it was.

Ella leaned in. Something had to be wrong in the part they couldn't see, the code itself, and only the screen showed the evidence. She pointed at one line. "You closed the style tag before you wrote the rule. The browser never even read it." Maya moved the tag, refreshed, and the heading drifted to the centre of the page at last, calm and even, like it had always meant to be there.

Then Maya grinned and opened another file. "Watch this. I'm also checking the raffle numbers for my brother's club, and the program tells whether a number divides evenly." She typed quickly and added, "The percent sign gives the remainder, so n percent d equals zero exactly when d divides n evenly." Ella squinted at the little window. She typed 14 and 7, and the program printed True. She tried 14 and 4, and it printed False. From those two results she could infer the rule was doing its job, because 7 went into 14 without anything left over, while 4 left a remainder behind. "Your brother will think this is magic," she said. "He's gullible that way," Maya said. "He believed me when I told him our basement floods with orange soda."

They kept working until the defendant's name sat centred under the heading in tall blue letters, and below it a short paragraph laid out the charge against him, the missing cargo, the quiet harbor, the night no one could explain. Maya read it out loud once, slowly, the way a lawyer might. Ella saved the file twice, just to be sure, and pushed back from the desk as the clock on the wall ticked toward the hour her mom was coming. "Send it to yourself," she said. "Right now, before the wifi does something weird." Maya hit send, and the little paper airplane icon spun once and flew away.

Nicholas ran his thumb along the laminated periodic table taped to his grandfather's workbench, counting squares until his finger stopped on carbon. Six, the box said, in a small corner number he'd never paid attention to before. He was trying to get ahead of Monday's quiz, and his best shot at passing it was this garage, because at home his little brother interrupted every five minutes.

The garage smelled like oil and cut grass. A toaster sat on a crate near the door, left over from the yard sale, still plugged in. Nicholas had brought bread because his grandfather said a person couldn't think on an empty stomach, and he'd been eating slices while he worked out the pattern in the table.

"So the little number tells you protons," he muttered. "Oxygen, eight. Iron, twenty-six." He tested himself, covering the symbols with his palm and guessing from the number alone. He got sodium right, then mixed up neon and nitrogen, both starting with N, and had to check twice.

His friend Marcus shoved the side door open, holding a blackened slice of bread. "Your brother burned this at your house and blamed me. Give me a dollar, I'm starving."

"Toaster's over there. And it's not my fault Denny can't work a dial." Nicholas slid a fresh slice in.

Marcus leaned over the table. "What are you doing?"

"Learning protons. Sixty for neodymium. It's just a code, kind of. Once you see it." He tapped the boxes.

Marcus dropped the burnt slice on the workbench. "That's toast. It's still bread. It just got dark, like when you draw on paper with pencil. Physical change."

"No." Nicholas pulled his own slice out, golden at the edges. "Watch." He held up the burnt piece next to his. "Heat makes new brown stuff in there, that's why it smells different. You can't turn it back into soft bread. It's a chemical change. Once it's brown, it stays brown."

"That's the toast's business, not science."

"It's both." Nicholas took a bite. "Grandpa said heat from that toaster can't insulate anything, it does the opposite, and that's how I knew something had to be happening to the bread, not just to it."

Marcus picked up the burnt slice and squeezed it. It crackled and stayed flat. He dropped it. "Fine. Chemical. What's the criterion, then? How do you tell them apart?"

"If you can undo it, physical. If you can't, chemical. Ice melts back, toast doesn't." Nicholas found the element for gold, seventy-nine, and circled it in pencil. "Also, that's an approximate answer. Grandpa says nothing's perfect."

Marcus grabbed two more slices of bread. "Then I'm testing the chemical change myself. Butter side up."

Nicholas watched the coils glow orange, then pushed the lever down for him.

The lobby filled fast, and Aaron watched the names stack up like seats in a bus. Some players typed in ALL CAPS, some dropped six emojis per sentence, and one kid named PixelFox mimicked the admin's formal greeting style, "Welcome, competitors," copying it word for word until half the room was saying it. Aaron knew the rules of this place: public chat was loud, jokes were subjective, and nothing you typed there belonged to you anymore.

His friend Dex was running late, as always. Their team of five needed a jumper, someone to switch sides and fill the last slot, and the match locked in eight minutes. Aaron opened a private window to their smaller chat, the one just for the team, and typed, "Is Dex coming or should I grab Reena?" Then he made a mistake. In a second private window, meant for only one person, he typed something sharper: "Honestly, Dex has been dead weight all season. We carry him every game."

The countdown hit six minutes when a screenshot appeared in the public lobby chat. It was his message, word for word, his username cropped but his orange avatar icon still visible in the corner. Somebody had pasted it for everyone. The public room, which had been chaotic and silly, went quiet in the way a cafeteria goes quiet when a tray hits the floor. Then the messages came fast: "ooooh," "who sent that," "Aaron is that you?"

He stared at the screenshot and worked backward through what he knew. He had sent it to exactly one person, in a private chat. That meant the screenshot had to come from that person, or from someone looking at their screen, because a private message only stayed private if the person who received it kept it that way. It could be screenshotted and shared by anyone who got it. The only name in that window was Tic. Tic, who had been friendly all week, Tic, who had asked him yesterday what he "really thought" about the team.

Four minutes. Aaron opened a window to Dex and typed fast, a short message on the screen between the countdown numbers: "You'll probably see something about you in lobby chat. It was my worst sentence, not my real opinion. You held the bridge in the semifinal alone. I'm sorry." Then he turned to the public chat, took the sting at his own expense, and typed where everyone could see it: "That was mine. I said it, it was cruel, and I regret it. Dex, the jumper slot is yours if you want it."

Two minutes. PixelFox, still copying people, typed "I'm sorry, Dex," and then everyone was typing it. The lobby door chimed, and Dex's name slid into the last slot on the team list. No message came from Dex, not in public, not in private, not for the whole countdown. Then the loading screen swallowed the lobby, and the match began.

The courthouse smelled like dust and old folders, and Sebastian clutched his notes so hard the paper went soft at the corners. His civics class had been assigned to explain one right from the Charter of Rights and Freedoms in front of a real judge, and Sebastian had chosen section 3, the right to vote. He regretted it now. Last year he had frozen during a speech about recycling and had stood there for forty seconds opening and closing his mouth like a fish, and Marcus Tran still did an impression of it in the hallway. He was not going to be a fish twice.

In the front row, waiting for his turn, he spread out his materials on the wooden bench. He had a printout of Canada's 2015 federal election results, because his grandfather had voted in it and never stopped talking about it. Sebastian ran his finger down the numbers. The Liberal Party had won 184 of the 338 seats in Parliament. He did the division on the corner of the page. That was more than half, which meant a majority, even though the page also said they had gotten about 39.5 percent of the popular vote. He frowned and checked it twice, because those two things seemed like they shouldn't fit in the same sentence. Fewer than four in ten voters had picked that party, and it still got more than half the seats. He tested a simple idea: maybe the seats were just counted wrong. He added the other parties' seats up, 338 total, no mistake. So it wasn't an error. There was some pattern in how votes turned into seats that he couldn't see directly, only see the shadow of, like a landlord you never meet but whose rules you live under anyway.

"Sebastian Marsh," the clerk called.

He walked to the front. The judge, a small woman with reading glasses on a chain, nodded at him. "Your right, please."

"The right to vote," Sebastian said, and then, before his mouth could seal shut, he kept going. "It means every citizen gets a say, and no government can just take the say away. It's yours like your name is yours."

"Can you give it teeth?" the judge asked. "Make it less ambiguous."

He thought of his printout. "In 2015, the Liberal Party won 184 of 338 seats, a majority, with about 39.5 percent of the popular vote. So votes and seats don't match up neatly. Which is exactly why the vote itself matters. It's the one part no one can rearrange after the fact, no matter how the seats come out. Nobody gets to invade that." He heard Marcus snicker at the word invade, and Sebastian grinned for half a second before going on. "My grandfather waited his whole life to use that right in that election. If it can be stretched or shuffled, people still lined up for it. That has to count for something."

The judge took off her glasses. "So in your own words, one sentence."

"Voting is the door every citizen gets a key to, even if the hallway behind it is weird," Sebastian said.

There was a pause that felt like a year. Then the judge wrote something down and looked up. "The hallway is definitely weird," she said, and beckoned the next student forward. Sebastian walked back to his bench, sat down, and smoothed the crumpled printout flat on his knee, running his thumb over the number 184 one more time.

Eleanor's problem had a name, and the name was Mr. Okafor's worksheet: "Use a primary source to explain why people moved west in the 1800s." She sat in the school library with a photocopied page of a settler's diary in front of her, and the diary refused to cooperate. "The land here is flat as a griddle," the settler had written, "and my wife has planted hollyhocks perpendicular to the fence, which she says will fool the wind." That told Eleanor exactly nothing about why anyone had dragged a wagon across half a continent. She flipped the page over. The library's copy machine had accidentally printed part of the next article on the back, something about President Wilson and a peacekeeping body called the League of Nations.

Marcus slid into the chair across from her and stole her pencil. "Still fighting that worksheet? You look like the diary insulted your family."

"It kind of did. This guy writes three paragraphs about hollyhocks." She tapped the back of the page. "But listen to this part. The Senate never ratified the Treaty of Versailles, so the United States never joined the League of Nations. The president helped plan the whole thing, and his own country said no thanks."

Marcus stopped chewing his pencil. "Wait. That's like baking a cake for the whole class and then being the one kid who isn't allowed a slice."

Eleanor laughed, then frowned, then laughed again. "It contradicts everything I assumed. I thought if the president wanted something, it just happened." She copied the sentence onto a sticky note, because it felt like the kind of thing that could sneak up on her later.

Then she went back to the diary with new eyes, hunting for the hidden reason the way she'd hunted for the hidden fact. The settler's grandfather had lost a mill in the East. The land office in Ohio had promised two hundred acres. There it was, buried under the hollyhocks: people moved because of money and land, and the pretty sentences were just decoration. She tested it on the next page. "Sold the clock, kept the rifle, bought seed corn." Money and land again. The pattern held.

"I've got it," she announced. "The diary never says why directly. You have to read past the flowers."

Mr. Okafor wandered by, scanning worksheets like a hawk with a grading pen, and paused at her paragraph. "Evidence?" he asked.

She held up the page. "Lost the mill. Two hundred acres. Sold the clock." Then she added, because she couldn't resist, "Also, the Senate never ratified the Treaty of Versailles, so the United States never joined the League of Nations. Just so you know I know things."

"That's a different unit," said Mr. Okafor, but he was smiling.

"Consider it a preview," said Eleanor, and handed Marcus his pencil back.

The community centre had ice on one side of the building and a pool on the other, and Charlie ran the concrete loop between them, eight laps for eight hundred metres, watching the Zamboni crawl past the boards like a slow white animal. Her problem was simple and stubborn: the first lap always felt so easy that she sprinted it, and the last two laps she died, her legs turning to wet rope while Priya Kowalski sailed past her at every meet. Coach Reyes kept saying "regulate your effort," which Charlie heard as "be someone other than yourself," and she hated it.

Her best friend Marisol swam mornings in the pool, and Charlie watched through the observation window between laps, mostly to avoid looking at the clock. Marisol's head cut through the water and beside her face there was a dip, a little hollow in the surface, and Charlie could see her mouth grabbing air in it. Charlie stopped and pressed her hand to the cold glass. The water elsewhere was flat, level with the tile line, but next to Marisol's cheek it had dropped, and her mouth reached that pocket below the flat surface.

"How do you breathe in that?" Charlie asked afterward, dripping sweat onto the pool deck.

"My head pushes a bow wave," Marisol said, wringing out her cap. "It leaves a dip beside my face. Air comes to me instead of me lifting up for it."

Charlie turned that over all week. Marisol wasn't fighting for air; the dip arrived because she kept moving, because she didn't stop being a swimmer in order to breathe. Running, Charlie figured, might have its own version, some hidden economy she'd been missing. Her simple idea: if she counted her steps on the first lap and held that count on every lap after, the pace would carry her the way the bow wave carried Marisol's mouth. Equivalent effort, lap after lap, instead of a sprint and a funeral.

At the meet she counted. Ninety-two steps the first lap, when her legs begged for seventy. Ninety-two through the second. Priya pulled ahead at the three-hundred mark and Charlie's whole body screamed to chase her, and she didn't, she counted, ninety-two, ninety-two, and on the last lap the counting held her up like a hand under her chin. She passed Priya with sixty metres left and won by half a stride.

She found the note taped inside her locker afterward, in Priya's round handwriting: "You finally stopped going out too fast. Took you long enough. Rematch Thursday?" Charlie smiled, then felt the cost of it, her quads shaking so hard she had to sit on the bench to read it twice. She peeled the note off the metal, folded it into her pocket, and went to find the ice cream money she'd promised Marisol.

Florence sat in the third row of the empty auditorium with the trumpet in her lap, glaring at it like it had insulted her family. In two weeks she had to audition for the community band, and she could play exactly four notes, none of them on purpose.

"How do three buttons make all those notes?" she asked her friend Dez, who was sprawled across two seats eating crackers.

"Maybe you just blow different?" Dez said.

Florence tried it. She blew harder, softer, sideways. The note wobbled but stayed stubbornly the same. Then she pressed the middle valve, the one marked two, and blew. The note dropped, sinking lower like an elevator going down a floor. She let go, and the pitch rose right back up.

"Pressing it makes the note lower," she said slowly. She pressed the first valve alone. Lower again, but a different lower. She pressed one and two together, and the sound sank further, a step she'd never found before.

"Okay, so every button drops the pitch," Dez said, brushing cracker crumbs off his sleeve. "Then how do you go up? Climb a ladder?"

Florence ignored him, because a thought was forming. She had watched the band director play at the last rehearsal, and she remembered something odd. When he played his highest notes, his fingers were flat on the valves, pressing nothing. When he played low, all three fingers were down.

She tried all three at once. The trumpet gave a deep, growling note, the lowest thing she'd produced in her life. "It's not buttons and blowing," she said. "The valves add tube. Press one and the air has to travel through an extra loop of tubing before it comes out. The whole column of air gets longer, and a longer column makes a lower note."

"That's why it looks like a squiggly snake," Dez said. "All that tubing hanging off it."

"So to go up, I press fewer valves, not more." Florence picked out the pattern, valve by valve, crawling up and down a scale. Three valves, and combinations gave her more notes than she'd counted on. Then she hit a snag. The note with the second and third valves sounded wrong, sour and floppy, while the same note fingered with just the first valve came out clean and steady.

"Try that one again," Dez said, sitting up, the suspense of it finally pulling him out of his slouch. "The one and the two-three."

She played them back to forth three times. Different fingerings, same note, but one was brighter. The other one sounded brittle, like it might crack apart if she pushed it.

She wrote both fingerings in her book and circled the better one. Then she started the scale again, this time from the bottom, all three valves down, rising one loop at a time toward the high empty seats of the auditorium. When she reached the top note, no valves at all, she held it until it rang against the ceiling, and Dez stood up and applauded with two crackers still in his hands.

Harrison typed `if n % 2 == 0:` and sat back, certain he had just written the world's most brilliant prime checker. The computer lab hummed around him, twenty machines all running at once, and Mr. Delgado had promised that anyone who finished both parts of the project could test their program on the big projector screen. Part one was the Python program. Part two was a simple webpage explaining it, which was where Priya leaned over from the next seat and squinted at his screen.

"Why is your title in h3?" she asked.

"Because it looks the right size," Harrison said. He had scrolled through the tags, tried h1, thought it looked like a shout, and settled on h3 like a person compromising between a whisper and a yell.

Priya shook her head. "There are six heading levels, h1 to h6. h1 is the most important one. Your page title is the most important thing on the page, so it should be h1."

"Six of them?" Harrison said. "Who needs six sizes of heading?" But he changed the tag anyway, and the title snapped into place at the top, big and unmissable, like it had been waiting for him to get out of its way.

Then he ran the prime checker, and his confidence collapsed. It said 2 was not prime. It said 9 was prime. He stared at the screen, because the bug was invisible, hiding somewhere in the logic where he could not see it, and he would have to hunt it by testing rather than by looking. He tried 3. It said 3 was prime, which was right. He tried 5. Right again. So the program was not completely broken; something specific was going wrong, some pattern he had not noticed yet.

He grabbed a scrap of paper and wrote out what his code actually did, step by step, like reading an X-ray of a program to find the broken bit. His rule checked whether n was divisible by 2, then looped from 3 upward. But 2 itself was divisible by 2, so the program called it not prime. And 9? His loop jumped by twos, checking 3, then 5, then 7, sailing right past the moment when 9 divided evenly by 3. "It skips the very number that catches it," he muttered. Priya snorted so hard she sounded like a goose.

He fixed both problems, one careful line at a time, then tested every number from 2 to 30. All correct. His program was durable now, built to survive even Marcus typing a million into it just to be annoying. When Mr. Delgado called his name, Harrison walked to the projector computer, plugged in his drive, and entered 97.

"Prime," the screen announced.

"Prime," Harrison said, and pumped his fist, and behind him Priya whispered, "And it only took you six levels of thinking to get there."

Camille stood in the wings of the community theatre with her hands trembling so hard that her cue sheet flapped like a small bird trying to escape. She was not even performing tonight; this was only the Saturday improv workshop, and still her fingers shook. Beside her, her friend Priya from science class was bouncing on her toes, and Camille noticed that Priya's script, all two lines of it, was trembling too.

"Yours does that too?" Camille asked, pointing.

Priya nodded and managed a grin. "My mom says it even has a name. Glossophobia. Fear of public speaking. She said it's one of the most commonly reported fears, so basically half the planet feels like us right now."

"That many people?" Camille had assumed she was the only one whose body betrayed her this way. Somehow knowing there was a word for it, and a crowd behind it, made the shaking feel less like a personal failure and more like weather. She flattened the cue sheet against her thigh.

Last summer, she remembered, she had auditioned for the youth production of Peter Pan and frozen mid-sentence, standing on that same stage while the director waited and the silence grew until it felt like the whole impoverished theatre, with its cracked seats and one working spotlight, was holding its breath. She had walked out. She had not come back until Priya dragged her to this workshop.

"I don't get the point of making up scenes in front of people," Camille had told her that morning. "I'd rather memorize lines."

"You'll see," Priya had said, and Camille had changed her mind about at least coming, mostly because Priya had promised her mom's brownies would be involved.

Now the mentor of the workshop, a college student named Ruthie with paint-stained overalls, called them out. "Camille and Priya, you're up. Rule is simple. Whatever your partner says, accept it and add to it. Yes, and."

Priya stepped into the empty stage square and announced, "We're astronauts and the ship is out of fuel."

Camille's mind went blank, then she remembered the rule. Accept the offer. Add to it. "Yes, and we can land on that marshmallow planet."

"Yes, and the marshmallows are radioactive."

"Yes, and they make us grow to the size of buildings!" Camille mimicked a giant, looming over an imaginary city, and Priya shrieked with laughter and mimicked one back. Somewhere in the third or fourth exchange, Camille realized her hands had gone still. She was too busy building the scene to fall apart.

Afterward Ruthie high-fived them both. "Nice work. Same time next week?"

Camille looked at Priya, who was already nodding. "Yes," Camille said, "and we're bringing brownies."

Arthur had exactly forty minutes before his museum workshop started, and he meant to use every one of them. The workshop was called "Build Your Own Atom," and each student had to pick an element, then construct it out of foam balls, wire, and glue. Arthur wanted carbon, because carbon was in pencils and in him, which felt important. The trouble was the instruction sheet, which said: "Find your element on the periodic table and give it the right number of protons." Arthur stared at the giant table painted on the wall. It was a colorful plateau of little boxes, numbers, and symbols, and he had no idea how anybody read it.

A girl named Priya was already digging through the box of wire. "The wire's for the electron rings," she said, holding up a loop she'd bent into a neat circle. "You know electrons go around the nucleus in certain fixed orbits? Energy levels, like little racetracks."

"Sure," said Arthur, though he didn't, exactly.

They found the answer together on a plaque near the atom exhibit. Priya read it out loud: "In 1913, Niels Bohr proposed a model in which electrons travel only in certain fixed orbits, or energy levels, around the nucleus." She tapped the name. "So that's why the wire rings. Bohr was the first to draw atoms that way. I'm going to document this in my notebook so I can prove to my brother I learned something on a Saturday."

Arthur wasn't worried about brothers. He was worried about protons, which nobody could see, and which the sheet demanded in the correct amount. He ran his finger along the carbon box on the wall. There was a big 6 at the top, a C in the middle, and a longer number underneath that said 12.011. Two numbers. Two suspects. He tried an idea: maybe one number told you how many protons, and the other was something else entirely. But which?

He tested it on oxygen, because he knew oxygen was number 8 from a poster in his classroom. The big number at the top of oxygen's box was 8, and the smaller decimal was 15.999. So the top number matched the protons. Then he checked helium, which he knew had 2 protons from a book about balloons, and there it was again: big 2 at the top. The pattern held. The big whole number at the top was the atomic number, and the atomic number was the number of protons. That meant carbon had six protons, six little invisible specks he could now count on his fingers.

He grabbed six foam balls for his nucleus, then bent a wire ring and slid three electrons onto it. "It's sort of ironic," he said to Priya, arranging the second ring. "I'm building the part I can see, the electrons, using a guy's idea from 1913. But the part I really had to hunt for was the part nobody has ever seen." Priya held up her notebook, where she had written Bohr's name twice and underlined it once. "Six protons," Arthur announced to the whole table, holding up his carbon nucleus like a trophy. "Carbon, coming through."

Brooke had been at Dana's kitchen table for an hour, and the history project was due Monday, which gave them one weekend. They were supposed to build a small database of World War II propaganda posters, tag each one, and write about which posters had been most influential in selling war bonds. Dana had nominated Brooke to present it in front of the class, and Brooke had said yes before her stomach could catch up. Now the cursor blinked on an empty screen while Dana went to get snacks.

Through the doorway, Brooke could hear Dana's mother on the phone in the living room, saying something about a doctor's appointment on Tuesday. When Dana came back with a bowl of pretzels, her hands were shaking slightly and she set the bowl down harder than she meant to, scattering salt across the table. "Sorry," Dana said. "The poster with the pointing uncle, is that ours to write up?"

"You did that one already," Brooke said slowly. She watched Dana pick up the same index card she had just filed, read it, and file it again in the wrong slot. That was the third time. Dana wasn't being lazy; something else was going on, something Brooke couldn't see directly. She remembered Dana leaving the cafeteria early all week, and the field trip Dana had skipped in October, and the way Dana's mother had just mentioned a doctor.

Brooke tried an idea out, careful as stepping on ice. "Is Monday freaking you out?" Dana's shoulders went up around her ears. "The presenting part," Dana said. "I stress about that stuff. Everybody does. But mine doesn't stop. It's like a fire alarm that goes off when there's no fire." She rubbed the salt granules between her fingers, and the scratchy sound filled the quiet kitchen. "I finally told my mom, and Tuesday I'm seeing a doctor about it. My cousin did the same thing. Hers was bad enough and lasted long enough that it got in the way of school and everything, so the doctor said it was an anxiety disorder, not just regular nerves. And it's treatable. She's way better now."

"So it's not just you being weird," Brooke said. Dana almost smiled. "No. There's a name for it and stuff that helps. I've been trying my own coping stuff, like breathing exercises, but my mom says the doctor can do more." She glanced toward the living room, then straightened the scattered cards. "Also, I have to say this. You can't text me at midnight anymore about homework. I lie awake staring at my phone. I need some boundaries, even with you."

"Deal," Brooke said. "No texts after ten." Then she slid the pointer card across the table. "I'll present the database part if you take the posters. Fair?" Dana thought about it, tapping the card against the edge of the table, and finally nodded. "Fair." She picked up her pen, and the fire alarm in her head, wherever it was, stayed quiet enough to let her write the first line.

Jace slid his ruler across the paper for the fourth time and erased the line again. The assignment was a street in one-point perspective, every building, curb and power line running toward a single vanishing point that existed nowhere on the real street, only in the drawing. He put a dot in the middle of the page and tried to make the lines obey it. His buildings kept leaning like they had given up on gravity halfway down the block.

"You're guessing," said Priya from the next stool, not even looking up from her painting. "Last week you guessed on the portrait too, and I got a nose."

"You got a nose because you asked for a nose," Jace said. "It was a decent nose."

"It was a nose on my paper without permission." She held up her current piece, a girl in a dark shirt with a small pendant necklace. "Now I'm trying to paint around these tiny highlights on the chain, and my brush is too fat. I keep losing the white."

Jace remembered the nose incident, and before that, the time in seventh grade when he had traded his lunch for what he thought was a lucky eraser and it turned out to be a lump of gray rubber that smeared graphite instead of lifting it. He had a habit of grabbing solutions before checking whether they were real. Maybe that was why the perspective assignment bothered him. There was no guessing allowed. The lines either met at the dot or they didn't, and anyone could see it instantly.

He flipped through the supply cabinet, hunting for anything that could save Priya's necklace without saving his pride along with it, and found a small brown bottle with a battered label. It said the stuff was a liquid rubber you painted onto areas to keep them white. Once it dried, you painted over it, then rubbed it off to reveal the paper. "Hey," he said. "Try this."

Priya read the label twice, which was one more time than Jace had. "So I paint it on the little highlights, let it dry, paint the whole shirt dark over it, and then rub it off and the white comes back?" She looked at him sideways. "Is this another lucky eraser situation?"

"That eraser was one time." He watched her dab the milky liquid onto the brightest links of the chain with a toothpick, since no brush was small enough. It went on looking useless, like school glue, and dried to a faint peachy film. Then she swept the dark shirt color straight across it without dodging at all, which felt to Jace like watching someone walk a tightrope on purpose.

While it dried for the second time, Jace turned back to his street and decided to test an idea instead of guessing. If the vanishing point controlled everything, then the curb, the rooflines and the stripes down the middle of the road should all aim at the same dot, no matter how arbitrary the buildings' sizes were. He drew one line at a time, checking each against the point like he was calibrating a scale. When he finished the roofline on the left side, it landed exactly where he'd wanted. Perspective, he decided, was a fair adversary. It beat you only when you made things up.

Priya rubbed at her pendant with a fingertip. The rubbery mask balled up and rolled away, and underneath it the little links gleamed white against the dark shirt, exactly where she had put them. She held the painting out at arm's length, then closer, then out again.

"Okay," she said. "You can trade me useless art supplies anytime."

Michael sat cross-legged on the rug in Dara's basement, laptop balanced on a stack of board games. The plan was simple: a web page called the Prime-o-Matic, with a giant centred heading and a box where you could type a number and find out if it was prime. He had typed the HTML first, then added the CSS, and the heading still sat stubbornly in the top left corner like it had been glued there.

"Did you save the file?" Dara asked from the couch, where she was rolling a tennis ball along the armrest. "The browser can't retrieve the new styles unless you save first."

Michael clicked save, then hit refresh. The heading drifted to the centre of the page, dark blue and enormous, and he sat back with the satisfied feeling of a door finally swinging open on the second try. The page asked a question in plain grey text: Enter a number. He typed 7, pressed the button, and the page said 7 is prime. Correct. He tried 9, and it said 9 is not prime, also correct. Dara came over and typed 97. Prime. They were halfway to a victory snack when she said, "Try zero."

He typed 0 and pressed the button. The page said, in cheerful green letters, 0 is prime.

"That's wrong," Dara said. "Zero isn't prime. It isn't anything." Michael stared at the green line and felt a small, cold drop of despair, the kind you get when something you built confidently turns on you. The checker worked by trying every divisor starting at 2, so for zero the loop found nothing to reject it with, and the code fell through to the prime answer. He couldn't see the loop failing; he could only see its wrong result, like footprints in snow with no animal in sight.

"Okay," he said slowly. "The loop starts at 2. Zero, and 1 too probably, and negative numbers, they never get tested, they just sneak past." He rolled the thought around, then typed an approximate guess at the fix, a single line near the top of the function, and refreshed. Dara typed 0 again. The page said 0 is not prime. Then 1. Not prime. Then -5, and the page held the line: not prime. All the numbers below 2 got sorted out before the loop even began, which was where they belonged.

"So it only checks real candidates now," Dara said, and typed 11, and the heading glowed blue above the words 11 is prime.

"Boom," Michael said, and reached over to change the heading's colour to green.

The line at Jefferson Elementary School stretched past the bike racks, and Muhammad stood at the very end of it, holding his grandmother's coupon book while she searched her bag for her voter card. A folding table near the double doors held a display he hadn't expected: a large poster titled "Know Your Rights," with articles from the Constitution copied out in careful block letters.

"Read it to me," his grandmother said, squinting at the small print. "My glasses are somewhere in this bag, and we're not losing our place in line."

Muhammad read the First Amendment aloud, then the Fourth, then stopped at one about due process. "It says no state can deprive any person of life, liberty, or property without due process of law," he read slowly. "Baba, what does that mean, really?"

"It means," she said, "you tell me."

He thought while the line shuffled forward. "It means the government can't just take your stuff or lock you up because it feels like it. There has to be a real process. Steps. Like... a foundation under a house. You can't skip it." She nodded but said nothing more, which meant he was on his own.

A man ahead of them was grumbling into his phone. "They passed the water bill, then they didn't pass it. How can both be true in one week? I'm telling you, it's rigged."

Muhammad's ears turned warm. That was the bill his social studies teacher had put on the board Monday. He remembered two different wordings, two headlines, one saying passed and one saying stalled. Something clicked into place, though he couldn't see it yet, like a pattern hiding under a floor.

"Excuse me," Muhammad said to the man. "Was it the House version or the Senate version?"

The man lowered his phone. "House voted Tuesday. Senate voted today on their own copy. Different words in it, the radio said."

"A bill has to pass both the House and the Senate in identical form," Muhammad said, the rule assembling itself out loud, "before it goes to the president. So if the words aren't the same, it's not law yet. Both things you heard can be true."

The man stared at him, then at his phone, then laughed. "Twelve years old and you just untangled the news for me."

The voting machine emitted a low beep as the man stepped up to it, and the line moved again. Muhammad's grandmother had stopped rummaging. She was looking at him with an expression he couldn't read.

"Say the due process one again," she said. "In your own words. My friend Rosa is inside working the table, and she argues with everybody about that one."

"She argues?"

"Every election. You'll see." She took his hand and pulled him toward the doors. "And don't be polite about it."

Blake sat cross-legged on Dara's basement carpet, staring at a laptop screen that stared back with an error message. He had typed nine lines of Python, and the program had refused him nine times.

"It says invalid syntax," he said. "Again."

Dara leaned over from her beanbag, headphones around her neck. "You forgot the colon after the for loop. You always forget the colon."

"I do not always forget the colon." Blake scrolled up, found the missing dot, and added it. The goal was simple: the program would ask for a number, then print whether that number was prime. Dara had bet him a bag of chips he couldn't finish it before dinner. Blake wanted those chips more than he wanted to admit.

He ran the program again. It asked for a number, so he typed 7. "7 is prime," the screen announced. He typed 9. "9 is prime." Blake groaned. "Nine is not prime. Three times three. It's the most not-prime number there is."

"So your checker is broken," Dara said. "It can't see the factors hiding in there."

Blake thought about that. The factors were invisible until you actually divided. That was the whole trick. A number could look prime and secretly be a product of smaller numbers, and the only way to know was to test it. "Okay," he said slowly, "what if I try dividing by every number up to the square root? If any of them divides evenly, it's not prime."

"You're going to replicate the test for each divisor?" Dara asked. "Like, loop it?"

"Exactly like loop it." He rewrote the middle of the program, mumbling to himself, deleted a stray semicolon that had wandered in from somewhere, and ran it again. 9 came back "not prime." So did 15. So did 21, that obstinate little fake. He tried 13, 17, 97. Prime, prime, prime.

"Pay up," Blake said, holding out his hand.

Dara tossed him the chips, then pulled her laptop close and opened Scratch, dragging a sound block into a loop. A record scratch blatted out of her speakers, and she wiggled a sprite back and forth with it.

"You know why it's called Scratch, right?" she said. "DJ scratching. A DJ moves a record back and forth on a turntable to remix sounds."

Blake crunched a chip. "So you're basically a DJ. Except your turntable is code."

"And you're the consumer of my art," Dara said, hitting the green flag again.

The record scratched. Blake typed 2 into his program, and the screen said, "2 is prime."

Jackson stared at the blank page in his notebook and wrote his first line of dialogue: "Give it back," Marcus said. He checked the board twice, making sure the comma sat inside the quotation marks. Ms. Rivera had promised that anyone who punctuated every line correctly and built to a clear climax would get to read their story aloud on Friday, and Jackson wanted that spot more than he had wanted anything since tryouts.

His story was about two friends fighting over a lost dog. The trouble was the fight itself. He had written the shouting match first and the quiet apology after, and when he read it back, the whole thing felt like a balloon losing air. His pencil hovered. Why did it feel wrong when all the pieces were there?

He flipped through his reading binder and found the notes from the debate unit in October. There it was, in his own handwriting: some writers order their points from weakest to strongest, so the argument builds and the reader finishes on the most convincing reason. Jackson sat back. Maybe stories worked the same way. Maybe the quiet apology, the small moment, was the weak point, and the shouting match was the strong one, and he had them backward. It was an inference, not a fact, but it was testable.

He cut the pages apart with Mrs. Chen's scissors from the supply cabinet, taped them in the new order, and read it aloud under his breath in the corner by the window. The small moment came first: Marcus finding the dog's collar on the sidewalk and saying nothing. Then the argument grew, and the shouting cracked open at the end. His skin prickled. It worked.

At lunch he showed the taped pages to Priya, who was still stuck on her own story. "I nominate your ending for best line in the class," she said, pointing at Marcus's last words. She hesitated, then added, "My teacher from last year would say it's too aggressive to end on yelling."

"Yelling isn't the point," Jackson said. "It's the top of the hill. You climb weakest to strongest so the reader finishes on the most convincing part." Priya frowned at her notebook, then grabbed a pen and started numbering her scenes.

On Friday, Jackson stood at the front of the room and read the whole story without tripping once. When he finished the last line of dialogue, "I found his collar the day he ran," Marcus said, and Jackson put the period inside the marks exactly where it belonged, Priya was the first one clapping.

The first night at Camp Windrock, Alyssa lay awake listening to a girl named Priya breathe in the bunk above her. By the second night she noticed the pattern: Priya stopped unpacking whenever the lake test came up, chewed her thumbnail raw, and snapped at anyone who touched her duffel bag. On Wednesday, Priya got aggressive over a borrowed hairbrush and then cried behind the boathouse, and Alyssa sat down next to her in the gravel.

"You get stressed before the swim test," Alyssa said. "I can tell because of your hands."

Priya stared at her. "You noticed that?"

"My mom taught me the signs. Mine is stomachaches. Watch." Alyssa counted Priya's breaths out loud, slow ones, four counts in and six counts out, the way the camp mentor had shown the whole cabin after lights-out. Then she said, "You're not sleeping either. I hear you turning over like the top bunk is orbiting the earth all night."

Priya laughed a wet, hiccuppy laugh. After a minute she whispered, "Sometimes I think about hurting myself. Just to make everything stop. Don't tell anyone. Promise?"

Alyssa's promise rose in her throat and then stuck there. She thought hard. Keeping secrets was a rule she'd always followed, but a promise that could let her friend get hurt wasn't a rule at all, it was a trap. She remembered the counselor saying exactly one thing at orientation: if a friend talks about hurting themselves, you tell a trusted adult right away, even if they asked you to keep it a secret. Alyssa had thought it was strange advice at the time. Now it felt like a flashlight in a dark tent.

"I can't promise that," she said, standing up and dusting gravel off her shorts. "Come with me or I'll drag you. Your choice. I'm very strong, I did the ropes course."

"You're the worst secret keeper alive," Priya said, but she got up too.

They found Counselor Dana by the fire pit, and Alyssa said the whole thing in one breath before her courage escaped. Dana didn't lecture anyone or look disappointed. She put her arm around Priya and said, "I'm really glad Alyssa walked you over. That took guts from both of you." Then she told Priya they'd call her parents together in the morning, and that tonight she'd sleep in the quiet room next to the infirmary, with a fan and no top bunk orbiting above her.

That night Alyssa did her own slow breathing, four in and six out, and made a deal with herself: phone in the duffel at nine, headlamp off at nine-thirty, lights out. In the morning Priya appeared at breakfast with her hair actually brushed and slid a tray of hash browns across the table.

"For the worst secret keeper alive," Priya said. "Extra crispy."

"I'll take it," Alyssa said, and stole her orange juice too.

Emilia stood on the porch of the Tanaka house holding a wrapped box of maple candy from her grandmother, and she could not decide whether to take off her shoes before the door opened. At home nobody cared about shoes. Here, in the entryway, six pairs of sandals sat in a neat line, so she lined hers up too, smallest to largest like at the shoe store, and hoped that was right.

Inside, everyone stood to greet her, even Grandmother Tanaka, who rose slowly from her cushion with a hand on the table. Emilia's own family waved from couches and shouted hellos across rooms. She bowed the way her friend Kenta had shown her in the school hallway, a small dip, and Grandmother Tanaka bowed back even lower, which made Emilia wonder if she had done it wrong. Kenta's mother took the candy with both hands, not one, and said thank you twice, once in English and once in Japanese, and set the box on the shelf unopened.
