At Emilia's house gifts were torn open immediately so everyone could admire them, so she decided they must be saving the box for later, like dessert.

The real trouble began with the ramen. Bowls of steaming broth and noodles appeared, and Emilia picked up her chopsticks carefully, the way she had practiced with two pencils on her desk at home. Then the slurping started. Grandfather Tanaka slurped. Kenta slurped. Even quiet little Suki, who was only seven, drew her noodles in with a sound like a small wave. Emilia froze with her chopsticks halfway to her mouth. At her own table her father gave one look to anyone who made noise while eating, and her grandmother's memoir of growing up on a farm had a whole chapter about manners, including a line she had read aloud at Thanksgiving: "A quiet table is a polite table." Emilia had always believed that. Now she was not so sure.

She decided to verify it, quietly, like a science experiment. She waited until Grandfather slurped again, and she watched every face around the table. Nobody frowned. Nobody glanced at him. Kenta's mother refilled his tea and smiled. If slurping were rude here, Emilia reasoned, someone would react, the way her father's eyebrows reacted at home. Then she tried the smallest test she could manage: one noodle, drawn in quickly. It made a gentle sound, and Grandmother Tanaka nodded at her and said, "Good, good," and slid the plate of egg closer to her side.

"Better flavor when it's loud," Kenta whispered, leaning toward her. "That's how we do ramen. And soba too." Emilia slurped again, longer this time, and the noodles actually did taste better, hot and quick instead of cooled and slow.

When the bowls were empty, Suki climbed into Emilia's lap and asked whether America still had volcanoes that were extinct. Emilia said most of them were, but a few were only sleeping, and Suki found that so funny she laughed until she hiccupped. Grandmother Tanaka pointed at Emilia's bowl, then at the teapot, and raised her eyebrows. Emilia held out her cup with both hands, the way the candy had been accepted, and watched the tea pour.

The library smelled like old paper and lemon cleaner, and Claire had exactly ninety minutes before it closed. She spread the photocopy of Macbeth across the table, scene three, and glared at it. Tomorrow in English she had to stand up and paraphrase every speech into modern English, and right now the lines looked like someone had dropped alphabet soup on the page.

"Double, double toil and trouble," she muttered. Fine, that one she could handle. "Toil means work. Trouble is trouble." She wrote "keep working and keep having problems" in her notebook. But halfway down the page, the script threw a word at her she could not paraphrase at all, because it was not a speech. It sat in brackets, all by itself: exeunt. She flipped back to scene one. There it was again, exeunt, right after the witches finished talking. Then she found exit, once, when a single messenger left the stage. Three different scenes, two different words, and she could not see the difference. It was like a rule someone had hidden inside the script.

Claire got up and pulled the big Riverside Shakespeare off the reference shelf, mostly because it had more scenes in it, more evidence. She laid it beside her photocopy and started counting. Exit appeared when one person left. Exeunt appeared at the ends of crowded scenes where two, three, sometimes a whole mob of characters walked off together. Scene after scene, the pattern held consistent. Exit for one, exeunt for a crowd. She sat back so fast the chair creaked.

Behind her, someone cleared a throat. Marcus from third period stood holding a soda he was definitely not supposed to have indoors. "You've been muttering in Latin for ten minutes," he said. "It's kind of scary."

"It's Latin?" Claire said.

"Obviously. Exit is Latin for he or she goes out," Marcus said, like it was the most normal thing in the world. "And exeunt is Latin for they go out. They use it when two or more characters leave."

Claire stared at him, then at her notebook, then at him again. "How do you know that?"

"My mom makes me read the footnotes." He shrugged and slid into the chair across from her, dragging her Riverside closer without asking. "So what's all this for, anyway?"

She told him: the paraphrasing assignment, tomorrow, out loud, graded. Marcus pulled the photocopy toward himself and read the witches' speech in a dramatic whisper that made a woman at the next table glance over. "Okay, so this part where the witches cook the stuff," he said, "the paraphrase could be, we'll preserve this potion in the cauldron until it's ready." He wrote it down, misspelling preserve twice before getting it right.

They split the speeches between them, trading lines back and forth. When they reached the end of the scene, Claire tapped the bracketed word with her pencil. "Exeunt," she said. "That's them, plural. Both witches, plus Hecate, plus everybody. They go out."

Marcus checked the stage directions against their notes, one scene at a time, and every single one matched. The overhead speaker crackled that the library would close in fifteen minutes. They gathered the papers fast, and Claire copied the two words onto her palm in smudged ink. At the door, Marcus held it open and said, "If Mrs. Pell makes you say the Latin part out loud tomorrow, do the witch voice."

"Fire burn and cauldron bubble," Claire croaked at him across the parking lot.

Sara set two cereal boxes on the kitchen table, then slid them behind the bread maker where nobody could see the labels. Her science fair project was due Friday, and she had one evening left to prove her idea. "Marcus," she called, "I need you in here. Bring your honest face."

Her brother wandered in with a granola bar hanging out of his mouth. Sara took it away from him. "You're a participant now. No snacks before the test." She poured the name-brand flakes into a bowl marked A and the store-brand flakes into a bowl marked B, then shuffled the boxes deeper behind the bread maker so even she could forget which bowl was which. She copied a code onto a folded slip of paper, taped it shut, and set a heavy mug on top of it.

"What's the mug for?" Marcus asked, dropping into a chair.

"So I can't peek. It's a blind test. You don't know which sample is which, so what you expect can't sway your answers." She slid the bowls toward him with a glass of water between them. "Taste A. Swish. Tell me what you think. Then B. No guessing which is the fancy one."

Marcus chewed slowly, like the flakes might lie to him. "A is crispier," he said. "B tastes a little like the box."

Sara wrote it down. That was the answer she had predicted, and it bothered her. She had guessed her brother would pick A because he always begged for the name-brand stuff, the kind with the artisan bakery logo on the front that made everything sound handmade and expensive. If he couldn't tell the boxes apart and still picked A, maybe his tongue actually knew something. She made him repeat the test with fresh pours, swapping the bowls' positions. Again he chose A.

Then Dad wandered through and Sara made him sit down too. He tasted both, tapped the table, and pointed at B. "That one's better. Toastier."

Sara sat back. Two tasters, opposite answers, and no boxes in sight. She unfolded the slip under the mug and stared at the code. Bowl A was the store brand. Marcus had picked the cheap cereal twice, without knowing it, and praised it. Dad had picked the expensive one. Her prediction had been wrong in the most interesting way possible: people's expectations couldn't sway their answers because people didn't know which sample was which, so the answers were all over the place. Taste, not labels, was doing the talking.

She wrote "Trial Three" at the top of a fresh data sheet and looked up at her father. "Dad, there's water in the glass for a reason. You have to do it again."

Oliver sat on the bench outside the pretzel shop with his phone and one bar of wifi, trying to isolate the reason his sister's old blog had vanished. The link she'd sent him was dead. "It just says page not found," he said.

"Exactly," said Dani, dropping onto the bench beside him with her backpack. She worked at the mall on Saturdays, restocking candy, and she wanted a promotion to the register, which meant she needed to prove the candy store's website had once advertised a free-sample policy that the manager now denied. "If I can show him the old page, I get the register. If I can't, I stay on the candy cart."

"But the page is gone," Oliver said.

"Gone isn't the same as deleted," Dani said. She tapped his screen. "Try the Wayback Machine."

He typed it in. A page loaded with a little carousel icon and a place to enter a web address. "It says the Internet Archive has been saving copies of public web pages since 1996," he read. He put in the candy store's address. A timeline appeared, a row of dates going back years. He picked one from two summers ago, and the old page bloomed on his screen, faded colors and all. Right there, in green letters: free sample with every visit.

"You're a candidate for sainthood," Dani said, photographing his screen with her own phone.

Oliver barely heard her. He had typed in his sister's blog address on a hunch. A date appeared. He clicked it, and the dead page came back to life, every post, every photo. There was his own face at nine years old, in front of their old house, and under it his sister had written the street name and the school he attended. Anyone in the world could be looking at this right now. Any stranger. He scrolled down and found a post with the mall tagged, the very bench he was sitting on, dated three years back.

"Your sister should take that down," Dani said, reading over his shoulder.

"She can't take it down," Oliver said slowly, testing the idea as he said it. "It's not on her site anymore. It's saved somewhere else, and that place lets anyone look." He tried closing his sister's blog and typing the address again. Same result. The copy was just there, patient as a filing cabinet.

He texted his sister a screenshot. Then he looked at his own account settings, the ones that let his posts carry the mall's location without asking him, and switched that off, one toggle at a time.

Dani was already walking toward the candy store with her phone held up like a ticket. "Wish me luck," she called.

Oliver's phone buzzed. His sister had replied with three wide-eyed emojis and one line: "Delete it. Delete everything."

Penelope unrolled the climate map across the picnic table and weighted its corners with two flashlights and a bag of trail mix. Tomorrow night, back home, she had to stand up in geography class and explain how a monsoon forms and why rice farmers in South Asia depend on it, and right now she could not make the map cooperate. Tiny letter codes, Af and BWh and Am, were printed in the oceans and across the continents, and she had no idea what they meant. Her little brother, Marcus, leaned over her shoulder with a marshmallow stick still in his hand.

"What do the letters say?" he asked, poking at the Bay of Bengal.

"They say I'm going to fail," Penelope said, and he laughed, which was not helpful.

She pulled out her phone, which had one shaky bar of signal at the edge of the campground, and typed the codes in. The screen loaded slowly, like something dragging itself uphill. The letters, she read, were part of the Koppen climate classification, still used on climate maps today. It had been developed by Wladimir Koppen, a climatologist born in Russia who worked in Germany. She said the name out loud twice so it would stick.

"Koppen," Marcus repeated, chewing his marshmallow stick. "Sounds like a kind of cookie."

The code for the monsoon lands of South Asia was Am, and that was the piece she needed. She thought back to a demonstration her teacher had done in the fall, before the teacher announced she would retire at Christmas. She had set a hairdryer over a pan of sand and a pan of water, and the sand had heated fast while the water had stayed cool, and over the water a little wheel of paper had spun because air was rising there and pulling air in from the sand side. Penelope had understood it then, but standing at a picnic table she needed to test it herself, because tomorrow she would have to make thirty kids see a wind they could not see. She filled one pot from the water jug and left the other empty, set both in the sun on the table, and laid a strip of paper between them, pinned with a pebble so it could swing like a compass needle. Then she waited, drawing the monsoon arrows into her notebook, a symmetrical pair of curves, one pointing toward the land in summer and one reversing in winter, when the land cooled faster than the ocean and the flow turned around. Rice needed the summer flood of rain those onshore winds carried; without it, the paddies cracked dry.

After twenty minutes the paper strip trembled and drifted, gently but definitely, toward the empty pot, the hot dry one. Air over the hot pot was rising and air was creeping in to replace it. It was small, but it was real, and it meant her explanation was true at the scale of a kitchen pot and at the scale of a continent.

"Watch," she said to Marcus, and she cupped her hands and breathed warm air over the wet pot while he shaded the dry one with his jacket. The strip shifted again, wobbling back the other way.

"Did we just make a monsoon?" Marcus asked.

Penelope folded the map, careful with the corners, and grinned at the paper needle still swinging between the pots. "We just made a monsoon."

Madison sat at her grandma's kitchen table with the school's lunch survey open on Grandpa's old laptop, the one that ran hot enough to send up a faint smell like vapor from the vent. The student council meeting was at seven, and she had promised the president she would bring an answer to one question: which grade actually voted for the later lunch? Six hundred students had filled out the survey, and the answers sat in three long columns called Grade, Answer, and Answer again, a wall of rows she could never count by hand.

"Grandpa used to say that spreadsheet could do the counting for you," Grandma said, setting down a mug of cocoa. "He never showed me how, though. He just grinned and clicked."

Madison clicked too. She found something called a pivot table, dragged Grade into the box labeled Rows, and a tidy list appeared: sixth, seventh, eighth. She dragged Answer into Columns, and across the top it read later lunch, earlier lunch, no opinion. The third column of Answer she dropped into Values, and the whole table filled itself in with counts, how many students in each grade gave each answer, row by row.

"There it is," she whispered. She could infer the rest without adding anything up. Eighth grade had picked later lunch by a mile, and sixth grade, her own grade, had mostly wanted it earlier. Her best friend Priya had spent a week telling everyone the sixth graders were the ones pushing for the change, and Priya was wrong. Madison saved the file, then sat back. Winning the argument would cost something, and she could already picture Priya's face.

"You look like your grandpa when he solved something," Grandma said, peering at the screen. "He'd have called that table exceptional."

At the meeting, Madison plugged the laptop into the projector before anyone could stop her. The president leaned forward, reading the rows. "So it's the eighth graders," she said slowly. "Huh. The whole plan was built around the sixth grade."

Madison's hand hovered over the keyboard. Priya was in the third row, arms crossed, waiting. "I can show the numbers," Madison said, "or we can talk about it first."

"Show them," said the president.

Madison looked at Priya one more time, then pressed the key that put the table on the wall.

Jordan had read the text forty times since Friday. "Meet me at the gate at 7," Marisol had written, "my little brother's tagging along, hope that's ok." Then a second message: "don't laugh, he's obsessed with you ever since you taught him that card trick." Jordan had typed and deleted six replies before sending a thumbs up, which now seemed like the lamest response in history.

He stood by the gate with two hot chocolates and one dollar left in his pocket, watching the crowd funnel past the ticket lady whose whole job seemed to be enforcing the no-outside-drinks rule. When Marisol appeared, waving, with a nine-year-old in a puffy coat trailing behind her, Jordan felt as exposed as the away team's kicker, standing alone on the field with everyone watching. His face went hot, and he knew without a mirror exactly how red he looked, because his cheeks felt like they were radiating heat into the cold October air.

"Dominic, you remember Jordan," Marisol said.

"The card trick guy!" Dominic shouted. "Do it again."

Jordan tried the trick. His hands were shaking and he fumbled the double lift, and Marisol laughed, which made him grin, which made his face burn even worse. He turned toward the fence and pretended to study the scoreboard.

"It's blushing," said Dominic, with the authority of a kid who had recently done a report on it. "My science teacher says blushing is when blood vessels in your face widen and more blood flows near the skin."

"Okay, emperor of embarrassing facts," Marisol said, poking her brother, whose coat had a gold collar like the team's penguin mascot, the Emperor.

Jordan half listened, but something snagged in his brain. Widen. More blood near the skin. If widening made red, maybe narrowing made less red. He couldn't see his own vessels, couldn't see blood moving anywhere, but he could test the idea. He pressed the cold hot chocolate cup against each cheek, one, then the other, like a man applying aftershave.

"What are you doing?" Marisol asked.

"Nothing," he said. "Cold cup."

By the third quarter, Dominic had abandoned them for the concession stand and Marisol scooted close on the cold bleacher. "You don't have to hide when you blush, you know," she said quietly. "It's kind of the best thing about you."

Jordan didn't believe her, but he put the cup down anyway, letting his cheeks do whatever they wanted, even when she laughed at his terrible joke about the referee. Then Dominic came sprinting back with a foam finger and a problem: he'd spent their bus money on it. Marisol dug through her pockets and found nothing, and Jordan found one dollar and a lot of silence.

They walked the two miles home in the dark, all three of them, taking turns wearing the foam finger. Marisol held his hand somewhere around the fourth block, and somewhere around the sixth, Dominic snatched the last of the hot chocolate without asking. Jordan let him keep it.

Maya had one job at the Vaisakhi celebration at the cultural center: hold the front banner during the procession through the parking lot. Her cousin Simran had held it last year, and Maya envied her for it, because the banner carrier got to stand right beside the drummers. But this year the aunties had made a rule. The banner went to whoever won the history game at the kids' table, and Maya had been stuck serving langar when the game started.

By the time she reached the table, her little brother Arjun was already there, frowning at a question card. "I can't get this one," he said. "It's about why Vaisakhi matters."

The volunteer running the table shook her head. "You get two tries. Then the next person goes."

Maya leaned over Arjun's shoulder. The card asked what happened on Vaisakhi, and when, and where. She didn't know all of it. She had heard the words Khalsa and Anandpur before, at the gurdwara, but the pieces wouldn't line up. She couldn't see the answer directly, so she decided to test an idea: the story had to be somewhere in the room, because the whole day was built around it.

"Come on," she said to Arjun. They walked toward the courtyard, where the procession was forming. A small boy tugged on the sleeve of Maya's uncle, who was tying an orange flag to a pole. "Why does everybody make such a big deal about today?" the boy asked.

"Because on Vaisakhi, in 1699, Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, founded the Khalsa at Anandpur," her uncle said, still working on the flag.

"Which part is the answer?" Arjun whispered. He had only caught half of it.

"Think," Maya said. "What did you already have on your card?" Arjun said the card mentioned a year and a place. The year had to be 1699, because that was when the Guru founded the Khalsa, and the place had to be Anandpur, because that was where it happened. The rest, the part about Guru Gobind Singh being the tenth Guru, filled in the blank about who did it. Maya checked it against the banner itself, which had the words "Khalsa" stitched in gold thread beside a picture of the Punjabi countryside, and against a display of migratory birds painted on the courtyard wall, labeled with routes people had walked from Anandpur over the centuries. Everything matched.

They went back to the table. Arjun read his answer out loud, and the volunteer nodded. Then she turned to Maya. "Your turn. Same question, different card."

Maya took a breath and said it straight: on Vaisakhi, in 1699, Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, founded the Khalsa at Anandpur. The volunteer handed her the banner pole.

"Wait," Arjun said. "I won too."

"There's one banner and two of you," the volunteer said. "Work it out."

Maya offered a quick negotiation: she would carry the banner for the first loop around the parking lot, and Arjun could take it when they passed the drummers the second time. Arjun stuck out his hand and they shook on it.

The drums started. Maya lifted the pole high, the orange cloth catching the wind, and stepped out in front.

Easton slid the box across the kitchen table until it bumped his milk glass, because if he was going to open it, he wanted to do it slowly enough to remember. Inside was his first phone, dark blue, with a case his mom said was durable enough to survive being dropped off a roof. He turned it on while his little sister Priya leaned her elbows on the table and breathed directly on his shoulder.

"Screen time rules," his mom said, sliding the charger across like a business deal. "Homework first, phone in the kitchen at nine. And you have to let me enroll you in the family safety thing tonight." She said it lightly, but she watched his face while she said it, and he nodded because he meant it.

The first thing he wanted was a flashlight app, since his room's ceiling light flickered like it was trying to quit. He found one with a cartoon bulb icon, tapped Install, and stopped. A box had come up. The app wanted permission to use his camera, his microphone, and all of his contacts. Easton frowned at it. "Why would a flashlight need to hear me?" he asked the kitchen.

"To hear if you're scared of the dark," Priya said solemnly.

He didn't tap Allow. Instead he hunted through Settings, tapping into Apps, then Permissions, because his cousin Malik had once said something Easton only half remembered, something about controlling what apps could touch. What he found surprised him: a list. Camera. Microphone. Contacts. Little toggles beside each one, all off. He tested it. He granted the flashlight permission to the camera, then took it away again with one tap, and the toggle went dark. So apps had to ask first, and he could take the permission back later, anytime, right there in the settings.

He tried two more apps to be sure. A drawing app asked for nothing. A free game asked for contacts, microphone, camera, and something about his location. He denied everything, and the game still worked. "Interesting," he said.

"What's interesting?" his mom asked, coming back with two mugs, setting the cocoa one in front of Priya first.

"The flashlight wanted my contacts. Why does a flashlight need to know Priya's friend Gabby's phone number?"

His mom laughed into her mug. "Maybe the bulb wants pen pals." Then she put her hand briefly on his shoulder, the way she did when he did something right without being told. "Take the permission away, then. You know how now."

He did, one tap, and the flashlight turned on anyway, a clean white beam across the table that made Priya's cocoa steam glow like a tiny ghost.

"It works without asking for anything else," Easton said. "So all that asking was just an illusion, like the app was being polite when it was really just being nosy."

"Like Malcolm at recess," Priya said, and both of them cracked up, because Malcolm asked everyone's business and called it journalism.

At nine that night, the phone went in the kitchen drawer, screen glowing through the gap one last time before it slept.

The propane stove clicked three times before it caught, and Thomas set the heavy pan over the blue flame with the confidence of someone who had watched exactly four cooking videos that afternoon. He had promised his family caramel apples for the last night of the camping trip, and the bag of sugar sat beside him like a dare. His little sister Maya dragged her camp chair close enough to be a hazard.

"Is that how the roast got brown this morning?" she asked, nodding at the pan. "Same thing?"

Thomas started to say yes, then stopped. The roast had browned with nothing but its own juices, no sugar anywhere. This was just sugar, alone in the pan. Something felt different about the two, and he wanted to figure out what before he answered her.

"The roast had meat juices," he said slowly, watching the sugar begin to melt at the edges. "There's no meat juice in here. Only sugar." He turned the flame down a notch, because the videos had all warned him about burning, and tried an experiment in his head. If the two brownings were the same thing, they should need the same ingredients. But sugar alone was browning right now, and the roast had browned without any added sugar. So the reactions couldn't be identical. He remembered a word from one of the videos, half-buried under the instructor's terrible jokes: caramelization. That was this, the browning that happened when sugar alone was heated.

"So what was the roast doing?" Maya asked.

"There was another one," Thomas said. "The Maillard reaction. It also needs amino acids." He pointed at the pan. "This is just sugar. No amino acids in here, so no Maillard, just caramelization."

Maya squinted at the melting sugar as if she could see the difference, which of course nobody could. That was the strange part, Thomas thought. Two brownings that looked alike and happened for different hidden reasons, like two endangered animals that look the same until a scientist counts the stripes. You had to reason it out from what went in.

The sugar went amber, then copper. Thomas swirled the pan and listened to Maya narrate like a sports announcer for what she called the Caramel Dynasty, rulers of all desserts. Then the color deepened too fast, and he yanked the pan off the heat with a clatter.

"Too dark?" Maya asked.

"A little." He stirred it, and the burnt edge mellowed into something smoky but still sweet. Not perfect, but not ruined. He dipped one apple slice, held it out, and waited while she bit down.

"Crispy," she declared, mouth full. "The Dynasty lives."

Elliot had recited the New Year prayer forty-one times in the courtyard of the temple, and he still stumbled on the same line. Behind him, in the hall with the red pillars, drums and gongs and cymbals crashed together, then stopped, then crashed again. His cousin Marcus poked his head around the door. "The lion keeps falling over," Marcus said. "Come watch."

Inside the hall, the lion costume lay crumpled on the floorboards like a pile of laundry. Two boys from the temple's youth group climbed out of it, one from the front and one from the back, and stood blaming each other. "You turned too early," said the boy from the head. "You were late," said the boy from the tail, which contradicted him so flatly that Elliot laughed before he could stop himself. The drum master, Mr. Lou, raised one hand and the noise died away. Elliot had never considered that a lion dance was done like this, two dancers inside one costume, one working the head and the other the tail, moving to the drums, gongs and cymbals. He had always assumed it was one very tired person.

He crouched by the fallen costume and had an idea. "Try counting," he said. "The drums give you a pattern. If the head moves on the beat and the tail moves on the same beat, you can't contradict each other, because you're both following the same thing." It was the same trick his grandmother had given him for the prayer: match the words to the rhythm of the bells, and the line you keep forgetting attaches itself to the sound. The two boys looked at each other, shrugged, and climbed back in.

The next run was not perfect. The lion wobbled, knocked over a folding chair, and sat down hard. But on the run after that, when the cymbals flared, the head rose and the tail followed in the same instant, and the lion leapt onto the bench by the incense burner as if it were buoyant, weightless, alive. Mr. Lou actually smiled, which Marcus whispered had never happened before in the history of the temple.

That evening Elliot stood in the courtyard with his grandmother, the paper lanterns glowing above the stone lions at the gate. He recited the prayer all the way through, riding the rhythm the way the tail had ridden the drumbeat, and did not stumble once. His grandmother folded her hands and nodded slowly. "Again," she said, "but this time with the bells."

Jaxson had signed up for the talent showcase because Mr. Ferro left the sign-up sheet on the auditorium door for two weeks, which felt almost like a dare. Now he stood backstage with the school's borrowed guitar, and the sixth string sounded wrong. Not slightly wrong. Totally, embarrassingly wrong, like a bear groaning while everyone else was singing.

The showcase started in twenty minutes. He had learned three chords over a month of lunchtime practice in the empty auditorium, and his whole song depended on that string sounding right. He sat on the edge of the stage, turned the tuning peg, and the note sank even lower. He turned it again, the same direction, and the note dropped again, deep and fuzzy.

He stopped with his hand still on the peg. Okay, he thought. Something was happening here that he could not see. The string was doing something when he turned the peg, and turning it that way made the sound go lower, every single time. So the direction mattered, and whatever invisible thing made the note was being changed by it. He turned the peg the other way, slowly, and the note climbed, rising tighter and brighter until it passed the right pitch and kept going. He backed off a hair. The string settled into a clear, steady tone, and when he pressed his chord, the whole thing rang instead of groaning.

"Is that the trick?" a voice asked. Priya from homeroom was crouched by the curtain rail, holding a violin case that hindered her view of the stage. She had signed up too, and her hands had been shaking since third period, though she kept her face neutral about it.

"It's a pattern," Jaxson said. "The tighter you make the string, the faster it vibrates, so the note goes higher. Loosen it and the vibration slows down and the pitch drops." He plucked the string, tightened it a touch, and plucked again so she could hear the rise. "I loosened it wrong twice before I figured out which way the peg even went."

Priya set down her case and tried it on her violin's E string, turning her peg a sliver, listening, turning back. Her note steadied, and her shoulders came down an inch. She looked at Jaxson like he'd handed her something. "Play it for me?" she said. "The song. I want to hear it while nobody's out there yet."

He glanced at the half-empty rows of seats, then at the little label on the guitar's headstock that read steel and bronze alloy strings. Fine strings, he decided, even if they took figuring out. He set his fingers on the first chord, and Priya settled into the front row, tapping her violin bow softly against her knee to give him a beat.

The clock above the whiteboard said 11:52, and Piper had already packed her bag. Three days in Marsh Creek and she knew exactly two people's names, both of which she had learned by reading the sticky labels on their desks. She had inherited her grandmother's habit of arriving early and leaving exactly on time, but today she slowed down, because the girl in the second row, Marisol, was still copying homework.

"Lunch?" Piper asked. It came out flatter than she meant.

Marisol shrugged. "Sure."

At the table, Marisol talked about the soccer team and a teacher everyone called the Reptile. Piper laughed in the right places. When the bell rang, Marisol said, "See you," and walked off toward the gym without looking back. Piper sat alone with her tray for a second, then dumped it.

That night she found the article her history teacher had assigned, a stack of photocopied pages about friendship research. She read one line three times: a 2018 study by Jeffrey Hall of the University of Kansas found that it takes about 50 hours together to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend. Fifty hours. She did the math on her notebook cover. One lunch was thirty-five minutes. Fifty hours was like eighty-five lunches, almost a whole school year of them, and that was only to reach casual.

So she stopped waiting for friendship to happen and started building it like a project. She sat with Marisol every day. She showed up at soccer practice with water bottles. She kept a tally in the back of her notebook, small pencil marks, five minutes at a locker, forty at lunch, ninety at a Saturday game. By the third week she had eleven hours and a pretty good idea of which jokes worked.

Then Marisol grabbed the notebook to borrow a pen and the pages fell open. She stared at the tally marks.

"What is this?"

"Nothing. A count."

"You're counting our hangouts?" Marisol's voice went sharp enough that two girls at the next table turned around. "Am I homework?"

Piper's face went hot. "It's not like that. It's a thing I read. Acquaintances aren't friends yet, that's all. There's a, a number of hours." Even she could hear how it sounded.

Marisol dropped the notebook on the table and left. Piper erased the tally that night, every mark, until the paper was gray and soft. She left the count alone but kept sitting at the table anyway, because the hours didn't care whether she tracked them.

Two weeks later, her mom sent her to the pharmacy to pick up her little brother's antibiotic, and Marisol was at the counter, waiting on a prescription of her own.

"Middle aisle," Marisol said, tilting her head toward the candy. "They still have the sour ones."

Piper followed her. Marisol tore open the bag outside and held it out without a word, and Piper took one, and they walked home the long way, arguing about whether the sour ones were actually better than the chocolate.

The meatloaf was still steaming when Dad turned up the TV volume so they could hear the ad over the sound of forks. "Nine out of ten dentists recommend this toothpaste," a deep voice announced, "and studies show it fights cavities better than any other brand." Dad snorted. "Sure they do." But Hailey's little brother Ben swallowed a whole piece of broccoli just to talk faster. "Grandma says that brand is the best one. She read it somewhere." Hailey put down her fork. "Grandma thinking it's the best is her opinion. The ad saying it beats every other brand is different. That's like... you could actually check it." Ben rolled his eyes so hard she could practically hear it.

"That's not different," he said. "It's all just what people think." Dad carried his plate to the counter, chewing the end of a thought, and Hailey noticed he did that whenever he was actually listening. "Your sister has a point," he said. "One you can look up. Her arthritis prescription says something similar on the information sheet, and the pharmacist had actual study numbers behind it. That's a claim with evidence." Hailey grabbed Dad's phone off the counter, careful of the gravy smudge, and typed in the toothpaste claim while the kitchen still smelled of onions and burnt edges.

The results loaded slowly, the way they always did at the far end of the table. Then she found it: a fact-checking site called PolitiFact, founded in 2007, that rates claims people make in politics and ads. "They call their rating scale the Truth-O-Meter," she said, reading aloud. "It goes from True all the way to a rating called Pants on Fire." Ben laughed so hard milk came out of his nose, which ruined the tablecloth Mom had just washed.

But Hailey wasn't laughing. She scrolled, and there it was, a toothpaste study claim from a few years back rated Pants on Fire, because the "nine out of ten dentists" survey had asked dentists to pick from a list that company itself had made. The word "plausible" appeared in the write-up, and it fit exactly: the ad sounded plausible, but it fell apart when someone checked. "Ben," she said, "Grandma's opinion is that it tastes good. That can't be wrong because it's hers. But this company said their study proved something, and PolitiFact could refute it with the actual survey." She slid the phone across the table so the bright screen stopped right beside his plate.

Ben wiped his nose with his sleeve and stared at the little cartoon of pants literally on fire. Then he picked up his fork, jabbed a piece of meatloaf, and said, "Grandma's going to be mad." Hailey was already dialing.

The bus home from Marsh Creek Elementary had eleven minutes of road between the last stop and Edouard's, and he had decided those eleven minutes would be the new meeting room for the Chess Club. He stood at the front, holding his notebook open against a pole, and read from the page he had titled "Agenda."

"Item one," he said. "The problem of Marcus and Devon."

The two boys glared at each other from opposite seats. Marcus had accused Devon of taking the club's good clock, the one Edouard had saved four weeks of allowance to acquire, and Devon swore he had only borrowed it for his cousin's birthday party and brought it back with a cracked corner. Nobody had seen the crack appear. The club had been fighting about it for so long that Ms. Ruiz called it "chronic" and had threatened to shut the club down if they couldn't settle it themselves.

"I just want us to be friends again," Marcus said, arms crossed. "Can we just do that? Be friends again?"

Devon shrugged. "Fine. Friends."

Edouard wrote "friends again" in his notebook and felt uneasy, though he couldn't say why. It seemed too easy. He kept thinking about it while the bus rattled over the railroad tracks, and finally he flipped back a page. At his grandfather's church, when two neighbors quarreled, they didn't just say sorry. There was a meeting, and at the end each person agreed to specific actions they would each take, so each one knew exactly what he had promised. That was the part Edouard had thought was boring. Now it didn't seem boring at all. It seemed like the missing component, the piece that made "friends again" actually stick.

"Wait," Edouard said. "Marcus, what will you do tomorrow? Say the exact thing."

"Be nice to him, I guess."

"That's not a specific action. Say what, exactly."

Marcus blew out a breath. "Fine. I'll stop calling him Clock Thief at lunch. Out loud, anyway."

Devon looked at the floor. "I'll ask before I take anything from the club box. Every time. And I'll bring my dad's screwdriver Thursday to try to fix the corner."

They both said it again, slower, so Edouard could write it down word for word. He tore the page out, split it in half, and handed each of them the piece with his own promise on it. "Now you each know exactly what you promised," Edouard said. "Item two. Tournament snacks." He tapped his pen against the notebook and waited, but both boys were still reading their half-pages.

Marcus folded his and put it in his shirt pocket, patted it once, and said, "Thursday. Screwdriver. I'll hold you to it."

The basement smelled like dust and orange soda, and one bare bulb swung whenever the furnace kicked on. Asher set his laptop on the ping-pong table beside his friend Dante's, between a shoebox of insulated wires from Dante's uncle's old electronics kit and a poster of a symphony conductor that had come with the house. Dante was already typing.

"Okay," Dante said. "You said you wanted a program that asks for a number and says if it's prime. So start with input."

Asher typed. His first attempt just printed "prime" for everything, including 9. He stared at the screen, then got a piece of scrap paper. "Nine isn't prime," he muttered. "So something in my loop is wrong. Three times three is nine, so my program should catch that." He read each line slowly, tracing with his finger, and found he had written `if number % 2 == 0` and then given up too early. Even numbers got flagged, but odd composites like 9 slipped through.

"So you have to try every divisor, not just two," Dante said, spinning a marker between his fingers.

"Right. From two up to, like, the square root of the number. If none of them divide it evenly, it's prime." Asher rewrote the loop with a flag variable he called `is_prime`, set it to True, and flipped it to False the moment a divisor worked. He ran it. Enter a number: 9. Not prime. He tried 7. Prime. He tried 97, 100, 51, which fooled him for a second until the program said not prime, and he checked: 3 times 17. The program was faster than he was.

While Dante tested more numbers, Asher pulled up their old Scratch project, the one where a cat collected coins and a score went up. Except the score wouldn't go up. The coin sprite had its own copy of the number that never changed. Asher clicked through the menus until he found it. The variable had been made "for this sprite only," so the coin had its own and couldn't touch the cat's.

"Try making it for all sprites," Dante said, leaning over. "Then every sprite can use it."

Asher deleted the old variable and created the score again, choosing "for all sprites" this time. He clicked the green flag, ran the cat into the coin, and watched the score climb from zero to one, then two.

Just then his phone buzzed. A text from his cousin Maya: "Did your prime thing work? Send me the code, I want to try 31." Asher grinned, copied the file, and typed back, "It works. And I fixed Scratch too. Come over Saturday."

Dante was already loading a harder challenge on his screen. "Ready for the next one?"

Asher cracked his knuckles and started typing.

The card table sat under the big oak near the craft cabin, and Addison had claimed it every afternoon since Monday. Today three boys from her cabin had taken it over, and they had dragged Theo's cards away from him because, as Drew said, "slow players ruin everything." Theo had a stutter that came out worst when he was rushed, and everyone at the table knew it, which was exactly why they rushed him.

Addison stood a few feet away with her water bottle, watching. Last summer she had snapped at kids who teased her little cousin, and it had gone badly; the teasing just moved indoors and got quieter. This summer she wanted a different result, and she turned the problem over while she unscrewed the cap. If she made the boys feel accused, they would dig in. She needed a way to stop the game itself, not the players.

"You're dealing wrong," she said, walking over. "That's not how you deal for whist."

Drew looked up. "It's just cards."

"Whist has real rules," Addison said. "My grandpa plays it every Sunday, and he deals it two cards at a time, face down, clockwise. He says it has to be done according to Hoyle." She let the name sit there, and when Drew squinted at it, she went on. "Hoyle wrote the book. Edmond Hoyle. His book from 1742 set down the rules of whist, so when Grandpa says 'according to Hoyle,' he means following the rules exactly." She laid her hand flat on the deck. "So if you want to play here, you play it right, or you're just slapping cards around."

"Who even are you?" Drew said, but the boys at the table were already arguing about whether dealing two at a time was faster, and Theo had slid back onto the bench without anyone noticing him arrive. Somebody asked Addison to demonstrate the deal, and she did, slowly, so that Theo could see where each card landed.

By the time the bugs came out, they had played two full hands. Theo called trump twice, and though his words caught on the first one, nobody said anything, because everyone was busy counting tricks. Drew even asked Theo which suit to lead, which was more than Addison had hoped for. Walking back to the cabins in the fading light, she noticed the lettuce seeds she had planted in the camp garden had begun to germinate, tiny green loops pushing out of the soil. Something about that made her think of Theo at the table, quiet and steady now, no longer looking like he might bolt. The guilt she had carried around all last summer, watching her cousin get picked on, loosened a little and let go. The old oak's frail lower branches swayed as the evening breeze came through, and behind her she heard Theo call out, "Same table tomorrow?"

"You copied that print line ten times?" Priya leaned over Henry's shoulder, laughing so hard she knocked over her can of root beer.

Henry stared at the laptop screen in the glow of Priya's basement string lights. He had come over hoping to build something impressive before Monday's coding club meeting, a program that asked for a number and printed whether it was prime. He had the prime part figured out: check whether the number divided evenly by anything from two up to the number itself. But his screen was a wall of identical print statements, one for each count of divisions he had found, copied and pasted until his eyes hurt.

"It worked, didn't it?" he said, though a flicker of guilt crept in, because it hadn't quite worked. When he tested the number 7, three of his print lines fired instead of one, and he couldn't tell which.

"That's a chronic problem with your code," Priya said, tapping the screen. "You paste the same line over and over, then one of them is wrong and you can't find it. There's a better way. Watch."

She deleted almost everything he had typed. Henry winced, but she was already typing something short: for i in range(1, 11): followed by one indented line.

"Try that first," she said. "Just make it print i. Run it."

He ran it. The screen filled with numbers, 1 through 10, one after another, and Henry felt the way he did when a magic trick got revealed and it turned out to be almost insultingly simple. "Wait. That's it? One line did all ten?"

"One line, ten times," Priya said. "A Python for loop runs its indented block once for each value, so for i in range(1, 11) runs that line ten times."

"Once for each value," Henry repeated, and the whole wall of pasted prints suddenly looked absurd to him. He thought about the mystery of the number 7, the three print lines that had fired. He couldn't see which line had gone wrong, but if the loop ran the same line for each value, then the loop itself could tell him. He could print i right next to the count, and the pattern of the numbers would expose the hidden culprit without him hunting through pasted copies.

"Give me the laptop," he said, already reaching for it.

He rebuilt the program in five minutes, the loop checking each possible divisor, then a single print statement at the end reporting prime or not prime. His hands were shaking a little as he typed 7 and hit enter. NOT PRIME, the screen announced. Henry frowned. He poked through the loop, and there it was: he had written a greater-than sign where an equal sign belonged, and the count was coming out wrong for the number 1. One fix, one run. PRIME.

"Yes!" He threw both fists in the air and nearly knocked the root beer off the table again.

"Now test nine," Priya said, arms crossed, grinning like she was trying to provoke him on purpose.

Henry typed 9 and hit enter. NOT PRIME. He checked it in his head, three times three. The program was right, and it was right every time, and it was short enough to actually read.

"We still have two hours before my mom drives you home," Priya said, sliding the laptop back toward him. "So. What number do we throw at it next?"

The book club met in the back corner of the library, where the radiator clanked and Mrs. Okafor's supply cart blocked half the window. Grayson spread his notebook on the table and slid his answer sheet toward Priya. On it, under "Theme of 'The Skylark,'" he had written one word: friendship.

"That's not a theme," Priya said. "That's a topic." She tapped the page with her pencil. "A topic is a subject a novel is about, like friendship. A theme is a full statement of what the novel says about that subject."

Grayson stared at his word. Last week he had skipped the reading and guessed on everything, and Mrs. Okafor had written "See me" in red pen, which he still hadn't done. Maybe if he'd actually read the story, he would know what it said about friendship instead of just slapping the word down like a label on a jar.

"Fine," he said. "So what does it say?"

"That's the part you have to figure out." Priya pushed the paperback across the table. "Try again."

He opened the story to the first page, where the fisherman's wife keeps a chipped blue vessel on the shelf and polishes it every morning even though it's empty. Grayson had skimmed right past that on his first attempt, back when the whole assignment had seemed like a barren stretch of busywork, nothing growing in it for him. Now he read slower. On page three, a bird lands near the window. On page five, the wife says the vessel belonged to her sister, "before she went away." Grayson sat up.

"Wait. The bird shows up three times before the sister is even mentioned. That's foreshadowing. The bird is like... her." He flipped pages to check, and there it was again, the skylark on the windowsill the morning the letter arrives. "And the empty vessel isn't just a jug. It's the space the sister left."

"So what's the theme?" Priya asked. "Make it a whole sentence."

Grayson wrote, erased, wrote again. "Friendship needs to be nurtured, or it becomes an empty space you keep polishing." He read it aloud, and Marcus, who had been drawing a dragon on his folder, actually looked up. Priya nodded slowly, the way she did when she was deciding whether to argue.

Mrs. Okafor came by and picked up the sheet. "Interesting," she said. "The author never says the sister was ever a friend. Read page two again." She set the sheet down and moved on toward the cart.

Grayson turned back to page two, finger on the first line, and Priya leaned over his shoulder.

The porch boards of the meeting house were warm under Camille's bare feet, and beyond the carved doorway the valley lay green and fertile, stitched with sheep and a single winding river. She had the prayer folded in her back pocket, though she wasn't supposed to need it by Sunday. Her coming-of-age ceremony would be held right here on the marae, in front of everyone, and her part was a karakia she had to carry in her head, word by word, the way her grandmother had carried it before her. She kept forgetting the middle stanza. Every time she reached it, the words scattered like birds.

Hemi found her there after school, sweat-dark shirt sticking to his back. He was practicing the haka his kapa haka group would perform for the school welcome on Friday, and he wanted an audience. "Watch my stance," he said, dropping low, fists against his thighs. "I had to modify it. My knee." He launched into the chest-slapping, foot-stamping chant, and though Camille had heard Ka Mate a hundred times at rugby matches, she realized she had never once wondered what the words actually meant. She only knew they made the hair on her arms stand up.

"What are you saying?" she asked when he finished, breathless. "In the words, I mean."

"Ka mate, ka mate, ka ora, ka ora," Hemi said. "It was composed around 1820 by Te Rauparaha, the Ngāti Toa chief. He was hiding from enemies who were chasing him, and when he came out alive, he made the haka to celebrate surviving." He wiped his face with his shirt hem. "It's about being afraid and then not being dead. That's the whole thing."

Camille sat with that. She had always thought the haka was about power, about being terrifying, but underneath the stomping it was about hiding in the dark and coming out. She remembered, suddenly, being nine and refusing to speak at her grandfather's funeral because she was scared of crying in front of everyone, and how her mother had carried her sorry little note to the front instead. She had never decided whether that had been wisdom or cowardice, and she still couldn't. But Te Rauparaha had been chased and had hidden, and the hiding had not been the end of his story. That felt like something, though she couldn't have said exactly what.

She pulled the prayer from her pocket, looked at the middle stanza once, then folded it away and stood up. "Do it again," she said, "and this time I'll do the words with you." When Hemi shouted the first line, Camille's voice cracked on it, then steadied, and the sound they made together rolled out over the porch and down toward the river, which caught the late light and held it like a blade. Behind them, high on the ceiling of the porch, the old electric fan spun its slow propeller circles, pushing the warm air around and around.

On Sunday she would stand in that doorway with nothing in her pockets at all.

The food bank shared a basement with the public library, which meant Aria had walked past its door a hundred times without ever going in. Today she went in, signed the volunteer sheet, and was handed an empty crate.

"Sort cans by type," said Marcus, the other volunteer, a boy from her school who had been coming since September. "Soup, fruit, pasta, beans. Mrs. Okafor will check it after."

Aria worked fast, but something bothered her. The shelf marked SOUP had a gap in the middle, clean and square, as if someone had lifted out exactly twelve cans in a neat block. The shelves on either side were packed tight. She checked the fruit shelf. Another square gap. Pasta, same thing.

"Inventory already counted this morning," Marcus said when she pointed at it. "Don't worry about it."

But she couldn't stop thinking about it during break. The break room had a corkboard, a microwave, and a framed poster on the wall about the history of food banks. She read it twice. The first food bank, St. Mary's Food Bank in Phoenix, Arizona, was started in 1967 by John van Hengel. The idea had spread from there, all the way down to this basement under the library.

"John van Hengel," Marcus said behind her, reading over her shoulder. "That's the name on the big plaque upstairs, by the donation box."

Aria went still. The donation box. A square box, big enough to hold twelve cans in a neat block. She climbed the stairs, crossed the library's quiet carpet, and found the box by the front desk. It was empty, but the floor around it held a scatter of dust and one dried bean. Somebody had been taking the donated cans before they ever reached the basement. The gaps hadn't evaporated on their own. They had been lifted out, whole squares of them, by someone who knew the box wasn't watched in the afternoons.

She stood where she could see the box and the reading chairs at the same time, pretending to browse, and waited through what felt like the least leisurely leisure reading of her life. After twenty minutes an eccentric old man in a rain hat, though the sky was clear, shuffled over, lifted a square of cans from the box, and slid them into a shopping bag.

"Excuse me," Aria said, louder than she meant to. "Those go downstairs. To the food bank."

"The food bank has plenty," the man said, not slowing down.

"They don't. I just sorted what's left, and there isn't much."

He stopped. He looked at the bag, then at her, then at the plaque on the wall. He read it slowly, moving his lips. "Started in 1967," he murmured. "By John van Hengel. One man. Huh." He set the bag down on the desk. "Take them down, then. I'll carry the second trip."

Aria grinned and picked up the bag. "Race you to the stairs."

Lillian spread the agenda for the Science Club's first ever proper meeting across her kitchen table, weighting the corners with salt shakers so the paper wouldn't curl. Three members were coming to her house: Marcus, who had a hundred ideas an hour, Priya, who wanted to discuss the fundraiser, and Dexter, who nobody ever wanted in their group because he wore the same dinosaur shirt every single day and talked like a documentary narrator. She'd invited him anyway. Now she just had to keep the meeting from collapsing before it started.

The problem showed up in the first four minutes. Priya was explaining the bake sale budget when Marcus slammed his fist gently on the table, the way he did when an idea landed on him. "Wait. Wait. What if our fundraiser mascot was a capybara? Capybaras are the most chill herbivore on Earth. Everyone loves them. I'm thinking plush toys. I'm thinking a costume." Dexter opened his mouth, and Lillian knew exactly what was coming, because everyone at school did the same imitation of his voice, slow and floaty, like a nature film. She felt her face go hot on his behalf before anyone even spoke.

"Lillian," Priya said, pointing at the clock, "we're supposed to vote on the bake sale in ten minutes."

Instead of snapping at Marcus, which would only provoke him into defending the capybara for the rest of the afternoon, Lillian grabbed a sticky note and a pencil. She wrote capybara mascot? in her neatest letters and slapped it on the refrigerator door. "It's a parking lot," she said. "Off-topic ideas go there so we can discuss them later instead of derailing the current item." She'd found the trick in her mom's book about running meetings, and she'd been dying to try it.

Marcus tilted his head, considering the note like it was a strange artifact. Then, remarkably, he sat back down. Dexter raised his hand, which nobody had asked him to do, and said, "I move that we discuss the capybara after the budget vote." A motion. He knew meeting procedure, it turned out, better than all of them, probably from watching town council videos for fun. Priya seconded it just to be efficient.

They voted on the bake sale, chose lemon bars, and only then did Lillian peel the note off the fridge. "Parking lot time," she announced. Marcus launched into the capybara pitch, and Dexter interrupted, in his documentary voice, "Actually, capybaras are semi-aquatic. They nap in water. Sometimes birds sit on them." For once nobody made a face or whispered. Marcus leaned forward like Dexter was the most interesting person in the room, which, right then, he kind of was.

They voted the mascot down, seven plush toys to none, but made Dexter head of fact-checking for the whole club. Priya drew a little capybara on the corner of the agenda anyway, and when they passed around the plate of crackers, Dexter took two, symmetrical stacks, and said, "The herbivore snacks."

Lillian wrote parking lot on a fresh sticky note and put it in the drawer for next time.

Avery knelt in the dirt beside the tomato plants and counted the wilted leaves again, even though she already knew the answer was seven. Something was stealing water from the bed near the fence, and the thief was invisible. The soaker hose ran the whole length of the garden, but the far end had gone dry, and only the tomatoes on the north side drooped. "It's a reasonable guess," she said to the dog, who panted at her hopefully. "If I say the hose is blocked somewhere in the middle, and I cut the water on and feel along the line, the guess either works or it doesn't."

Her little brother, Marcus, wandered out with a popsicle, which began to irritate her immediately, because he had a way of leaning over her shoulder and dripping. "Miss Kaylee at the science centre says the hose thing is called a hypothesis," he said, as if this settled something.

"You didn't even go to the science centre."

"I did. On the field trip. The guide asked if evolution was real and Thomas said it's 'just a theory,' and the guide said no, a theory is not a guess, it's an explanation that's been tested over and over, and it's been supported every time. A hypothesis is the idea still being tested. Thomas got so red." Marcus licked his popsicle with enormous satisfaction.

Avery turned that over while she ran her fingers along the hose, one knuckle of rubber at a time. Her blocked-hose idea was still just a hypothesis until the test came back. If she found a kink, the test would support it. If the hose ran clear all the way to the end, the idea would be overturned, and she would need a different explanation entirely, maybe a root crushing the pipe under the fence. She kept pressing forward, wetter and wetter, and just past the basil she felt a hard, folded lump where the hose had doubled back under a stone.

She moved the stone and straightened the kink, and by the time the popsicle stick was dry, water had reached the far end and darkened the whole strip of soil. The climax came at sunset, when the seven wilted tomatoes lifted their leaves like hands unclenching. "So my guess was supported," Avery said. "I tested it once. I'd have to test it a lot more before it turned into anything like a theory."

"Like a tomato theory," Marcus said.

"Sure," she said, and wrote "hose hypothesis, day one" on a plant tag with a stub of pencil, then pressed it into the mud beside the fence.

Madison set the mashed potatoes down hard enough to rattle the salt shaker. Her little brother Theo had ruined her whole afternoon, and now she had to sit through dinner pretending everything was fine.

"Pass the green beans," Theo said, mouth already full.

"After what you did today? You told everyone in class the Eiffel Tower is in Berlin."

Dad looked up from his plate. Mom stopped cutting her chicken.

"It's my opinion," Theo said. "You can't argue with somebody's opinion. That's what Mr. Randall says. Respect the opinion."

Madison gripped her fork. She had replayed the moment all through last period, her face hot while kids snickered. She wanted to prove him wrong, but she wasn't sure how to fight a word like opinion. It seemed like a shield you could hide anything behind. She pushed a bean around her plate, thinking so hard she barely tasted her food.

"But it's not an opinion," she said slowly, testing the idea out loud the way she'd test a loose tooth. "Pineapple pizza tasting good is an opinion. Nobody can check that. But the Eiffel Tower being in Berlin, that's something you can look up. You can find the tower, find the city, and see they don't match." She pointed her fork at him. "It's still a claim even though it's wrong. It's just a wrong claim."

"That's a hard shot," Dad said, half smiling.

Theo slumped. "So my report is a wrong claim?"

"Your whole poster," Madison said. She remembered the glitter he had used, three evenings of it, and felt a small sting under her victory. He had been proud of that poster.

Mom cleared her throat. "Well, since we're being careful with facts, we need to talk about the science curriculum money. The school board wants to cut the wetland field trips to conserve funds." She and Dad started trading worried numbers, and Madison let their voices wash past her while she watched Theo. He was quietly moving his beans into a pile, not eating them.

Later, while Mom loaded the dishwasher, Madison found Theo's crumpled poster in the trash can by the back door. The Eiffel Tower stood in silver glitter above the word BERLIN, and along the border he had drawn a flock of migratory birds flying south, because his teacher had said every city poster needed one real fact about the place. He had gotten that part right, at least. She smoothed the paper against her knee, thinking she might help him fix the tower part tomorrow, if he'd let her.

She carried the poster upstairs and taped it above his desk, glitter flaking onto the carpet. When Theo came in and saw it, he stood in the doorway for a long moment.

"Paris," he said finally. "It's in Paris."

Lydia had forty-three dollars in her savings account and a plan that would take five years, which felt roughly as long as the line outside the phone store she was standing beside. Her mother had offered a deal: if Lydia saved half the cost of the new phone, her mother would pay the other half. Lydia had asked the bank teller that morning which account earned more, and the teller had said the compound one, so Lydia had chosen it, though she couldn't have said why. Simple interest paid on what you deposited. Compound paid on what you deposited plus everything it had already earned, which meant the money made money on its own money, quietly, for years, without her doing anything.

She was working this out on a napkin at a food court table when her friend Dev slid into the seat across from her. He leaned over her scribbled columns and frowned.

"You're doing math at the mall," he said. "Voluntarily."

"Five years," Lydia said. "The simple account would give me the same flat amount every year. The compound one starts slower and then curves upward. By year five it's ahead by enough to matter." She tapped the napkin. "I can't see the curve. That's what bothers me. I have to trust it."

Dev stole one of her fries and pointed at the fruit stand two tables away. "You want to see something you can't trust, look at that. Strawberry smoothies are four dollars more this month."

They walked over. The stand's sign listed strawberry everything, and as they stood there, Lydia noticed the smoothie cart near the escalator, which hadn't sold strawberries a week ago. Beyond it, the yogurt place had a new strawberry banner. She counted three stands in one corridor selling the same fruit that had just gotten expensive.

"Wait," she said. "The price went up, and now there's more of it for sale everywhere?"

"That's supply," Dev said with his mouth full of stolen fry. "Price up, sellers pile in."

Lydia looked down the corridor at the three stands. None of them obstructed her view of the yogurt place, which was a small mercy, since the mall's newest tenant had apparently decided strawberries were worth the rent. She thought about her compound curve, invisible inside her account, doing whatever it did while she slept.

"So if lots of people sell them," she said slowly, "does the price come back down?"

Dev shrugged, being optimistic about nothing in particular. Lydia folded the napkin into her pocket, next to her phone money math, and headed back toward the bank. She wanted to see the teller's face when she asked whether the curve ever curved the other way.

The gym had flooded on Tuesday, so Coach Ruiz held the basketball tryouts in Alex's backyard, which meant Alex couldn't be late even if he tried. He stood at the fence in his sneakers, watching nine other kids dribble around the folding chairs Coach Ruiz had set up as cones.

"You're lucky," said Marcus, jogging over. Marcus lived two streets down and had walked over eating a bagel, which he was still finishing. "Tryout at your own house. Home-court advantage."

"You can't have home-court advantage on grass," Alex said.

Marcus shrugged and sat on the porch steps to watch the others, saving his legs, as he put it. He wanted to see who his competition was before wasting any energy. Alex had done something like that once, at last year's tryout, sitting out the warm-up to study the other kids, and then running his sprints like his shoes were full of wet sand. He still didn't know exactly what had gone wrong, and it bothered him the way a loose tooth bothers you.

So the night before, he'd run an experiment. His sister Priya had timed him on her phone while he sprinted the length of the backyard cold, and he'd done it in a time neither of them wrote down because it was too depressing. Then he'd tried a gradual warm-up, easy jogging and moving stretches, the kind where you walk and reach and swing your legs rather than hold a stretch still, until he could feel his heart working faster and his legs warmed through. After that, the same sprint was nearly a full second faster. Same boy, same grass, same shoes. The only thing that had changed was the warm-up. Priya had made him do it twice more to be sure, which he suspected was mostly because she enjoyed bossing him around, but the numbers held.

"Line up," Coach Ruiz called. "Shuttle runs first, then layups."

Marcus stayed on the porch steps, observing. Alex started the light jog around the chairs, then the moving stretches, keeping it easy, nothing dramatic. He could feel it happen again: his heart rate climbing, his legs going warm.

"You're going to be tired before we even start," Marcus said from the steps.

"I'm warming up," Alex said. "Light jogging, moving stretches. Gets the heart rate up and the muscles warm."

"That sounds like extra work."

It did sound like extra work, which was maybe the point. When the whistle blew, Alex ran the shuttle like the grass owed him something. His legs answered on the first step instead of the fifth. Marcus, meanwhile, went from sitting to sprinting with nothing in between, and by the third shuttle he was moving like a different, slower boy, one whose shoes were, presumably, full of wet sand. He kept glancing at his own legs with an expression approaching despair.

At the layup station, Marcus missed his first four, all of them short, clanging off the front of the rim. On the fifth he banked it in and raised both arms as if he'd solved something.

"Tired already?" Coach Ruiz asked him.

"Unlucky rims," said Marcus. "Homemade."

Coach Ruiz looked at the portable hoop, then at Marcus, and wrote something on his clipboard that was probably not "unlucky rims."

At the end, Coach Ruiz read the list of names for the travel team. Alex made it, third from the top. Marcus did not make it, and stood by the porch steps staring at the grass like it might apologize.

"I had a bad day," Marcus said.

Alex picked up the folding chairs and started stacking them. "Come over tomorrow. We'll warm up first."

"Warm up," Marcus said, as if the word tasted like the bagel had probably tasted. "Fine. But only because your rims are weird."

Mia had never said a rude word to anyone, as far as Victoria knew. She held doors, she thanked the lunch ladies, she even complimented people's braces. So when Victoria opened the comments under the science fair photos and saw "nice volcano, did a preschooler make it," signed with Mia's username, she read it three times. Then she walked straight to the computer lab after last period.

She printed the page, folded it, and found Mia by the water fountain the next morning. "Did you write this?" she asked, holding it out.

Mia looked at the paper, and her face went pale. "It was supposed to be a joke," she said quietly. "People say stuff like that online all the time. It doesn't count."

"It counts to me," Victoria said. She watched Mia's hands shake a little, and she noticed something odd: Mia could not even look at the comment, as if reading it out loud in a hallway made it too real. Victoria walked away without an answer, because she didn't have the right question yet.

At home she searched the words from her own experience: why do nice people write mean comments online. The third result changed everything. A psychologist named John Suler had described it back in 2004 and called it the online disinhibition effect: people often say things online that they would hold back from saying face to face. Victoria leaned closer to the screen. That was it, exactly. The screen was a private space even when the whole world could see it, and Mia's politeness in the crowded hallway was the public version of her, a complete contradiction living in one person.

Victoria tested her idea the next day, carefully, like a real experiment. She posted a reply to the comment: "Would you say this to my face at school? If yes, meet me at lunch." She sat at her usual table at noon and waited, her tray in front of her, her stomach doing flips. The cafeteria noise seemed to dissolve when Mia appeared at the end of the table, holding her own tray, not sitting down yet.

"I couldn't sleep," Mia said. "I kept imagining you reading it alone in your room." She set her tray down across from Victoria. "I'd never say it out loud. Not to anyone. I don't know why the typing made it feel like it wasn't me." She pulled a folded paper from her pocket, the printout of her comment, and tore it in half. "Can I fix it? I already wrote a new comment saying the volcano was actually great, and that I'm sorry. Want to check it before I post it?"

Victoria slid her chair over so they could read it together on Mia's phone, side by side at the lunch table, where everything was face to face.

Eli had forty dollars and one goal: a Slither Snake keychain, the holographic kind that had sold out at three stores already. He'd commuted to the mall on the early bus just to beat the Saturday crowd, and the fourth store, a cramped shop near the food court, still had a sign in the window that read HOLOGRAPHIC SNAKES HERE.

The shopkeeper lifted the last one off the hook behind the counter. "Thirty-five dollars," she said, watching him count.

"That's double what they cost last month," Eli said.

"They're scarce now. Everybody wants one." She set it on the glass, and a girl behind him in line sighed loudly.

Eli paid, mostly to stop the sighing girl from grabbing it, and walked out holding the little bag like it might dissolve. In the atrium he passed his friend Marcus, who was sitting on a bench with a shoebox full of homemade woven bracelets. A hand-lettered card leaned against it: BRACELETS $8.

"Eight?" Eli said. "Maya sells hers for five."

"Maya sold out twice," Marcus said. "Hers are the cool ones now. I figured if hers go for eight at the fair, mine could too." He had sold exactly nothing so far, and his shoulders said so.

Eli sat down beside him and turned the keychain over in his fingers, thinking about the line behind him at the shop, the empty hooks, the sign in the window. Something was connecting itself in his head, a pattern he couldn't quite see yet, like a rule working behind the glass where nobody watched. High price, sold out, everybody wanting one. He looked at Marcus's bracelet box again, then at the wide mall hallway stretching toward the food court.

"Stay here," Eli said. "Watch my snake."

He walked the length of the hallway and back, slow and observant, like a detective in one of the memoirs his grandmother kept lending him. In front of the fountain, two more kids had set out boxes of woven bracelets, nearly identical to Maya's style, each marked $8. Near the escalator, a third. An older girl with an agile, quick-fingered weaving style was working a loom right on the floor, threads flying, a finished stack beside her. Eli counted the bracelet sellers he could see from one spot. Seven.

He came back and put the box lid on Marcus's bracelets. "Follow me," he said, and carried the box to the fountain, where he set it down beside the older girl's stack. "How many have you sold?" he asked her.

She squinted at him. "You're the fourth person to set up in the last hour. I've sold two since noon." Around the fountain, buyers strolled past boxes that now outnumbered them, and Eli watched one kid walk the whole circle, comparing, and buy nothing.

Then Maya herself appeared, coming down the escalator with an empty tray and a look of disbelief. "I sold out at eight dollars," she said, "so I raised to ten. But look at this." She waved a hand at the crowded circle of sellers. "Where did all these come from?"

"Sellers usually offer more when the price rises," Eli said. "Making and selling them gets more profitable, I guess. So everybody jumped in."

Maya bit her lip. "Then ten dollars is wrong now."

"Five is wrong the other way," Marcus said slowly. "When there's this many, cheap wins."

Maya flipped her sign to four dollars, and within minutes a small knot of kids had gathered at her table, because hers were the originals and everyone knew it. Eli leaned against the fountain's cool stone, holding his snake keychain in plain view.

A boy elbowed his friend and pointed. "Whoa, a holographic one. What'd that cost you?"

Eli looked at the bag, then at the crowded fountain behind him, and said, "Thirty-five. But if I were you, I'd wait two weeks."

"Two weeks for what?"

Eli held up the snake so it caught the light and shimmered. "For everybody who saw me buy this to start making them."

Grace watched the class group chat blow up during lunch. Someone named DragonRider42, who had to be Marcus because he never shut up about dragons, had typed "SURE. WHATEVER." at Priya after she suggested a meeting time for the history project. Priya had replied with three sad faces and then gone silent. Now half the chat thought Marcus was furious, and the other half thought Priya was overreacting, and Mrs. Okafor had already posted "We will discuss this tomorrow."

The problem was that nobody could tell what anyone meant. Grace scrolled back through the messages. Marcus used all caps for everything, even "GOOD MORNING." Priya used exclamation points the way some people waved. And a kid named Devon had typed just "k" an hour ago, which somehow made the whole thread feel desolate, like a hallway after the last bell. Same chat, same words, but each person carried a different tone into it, and the tone vanished the moment they hit send. That was the hidden thing Grace wanted to catch.

She hypothesized that the trouble wasn't the people. It was the missing signals. In person, Marcus said "sure, whatever" in a joking drawl and Priya laughed. Online, the drawl disappeared, leaving only the skeleton of the words. If she could prove that, then the fix wasn't apologies. The fix was rules that put the signals back.

After school she found Marcus at his locker and read his own message out loud in his exact joking voice. "Sure. Whatever." He grinned. "That's how I meant it. I say everything like that." Then she read it flat and cold, the way Priya must have heard it, and his grin faded. "Oh," he said. "That sounds terrible."

That night Grace searched whether anyone had ever bothered to write down official online manners, because it seemed like the kind of problem adults would have noticed decades ago. They had. One of the first written guides to online manners was called the Netiquette Guidelines, published in 1995 as a document called RFC 1855. She sat back. That was older than her parents' marriage. People had been fighting about all caps since before she was born.

The next morning she got to Mrs. Okafor first. "Can I set the rules for the chat?" she asked. "There's a real thing to base it on. One of the first written guides to online manners was published in 1995, a document called RFC 1855." Mrs. Okafor raised an eyebrow. "You looked that up?" "Last night. It has a principle I like. Assume the reader can't hear your voice, so don't send anything your face wouldn't survive."

Marcus posted an apology before homeroom, in normal lowercase, and Priya answered with a thumbs-up and "thanks!" with the exclamation point, which Grace now knew was Priya's wave. At the end of the period Grace added one line to the pinned rules: if you mean it as a joke, say so out loud someday, where people can hear you smile.
