Mia pressed her pencil so hard against the sketchpad that the gray ball she had drawn looked like a flat gray circle wearing a smudge. Around her, the community studio at the back of the gallery hummed with quiet pencil sounds, and Ms. Okafor had just announced that today's exercise was mandatory for everyone who wanted a spot in the youth show.

"Start with your sphere," Ms. Okafor said, "and find your terminator."

Mia's hand froze. "Like a robot movie?" she whispered to Theo at the next easel.

Theo shrugged. "Maybe your ball grows armor."

Ms. Okafor placed an orange on each table and clicked on a small lamp, and Mia noticed that one side of her orange glowed almost white while the other side sank into darkness. Between those two halves ran a soft edge, a curving line where the glow simply stopped, as if someone had drawn a border the light was not allowed to cross.

That was the line. She turned to Theo. "The terminator," she said, pointing at the orange. "It's the line on a sphere where the lit side turns into the shadow side. It's where the direct light stops reaching."

"So your ball does grow armor," Theo said, and Mia laughed so hard she nearly knocked over the lamp.

She tested the idea instead of guessing. First she drew the terminator as a curved line, then shaded everything on the far side of it, keeping the near side pale. When she wanted to check her work, she isolated the orange from everything else by propping two sketchbooks around it like walls, so she could see only the light and the dark and the edge between them. Then she added the shadow the orange threw onto the table, stretching away from the lamp, and one small bright spot for the highlight.

Ms. Okafor stopped at Mia's table and held the sketch up to the light. "Now that's a ball you could pick up," she said.

Mia grinned and drew three more spheres on a fresh page, each one with its own terminator waiting to be found.

"Next stop, robot armor," said Theo.

"Orange armor," said Mia, and switched on the lamp again.

Emile stood barefoot on the lanai of his Auntie Leilani's house, arms heavy, feet tangled. In three weeks he was supposed to dance at the community festival, and so far he could not get through a single verse without stopping.

At home he had practiced by humming the melody the way he practiced songs for choir, finding the tune in his head and letting it carry him. His cousin Nalu sat on the steps watching, shaking her head. "That's why you keep losing your place," she said. "You're not dancing to a song. This is hula kahiko. It goes with chanting and a gourd drum, not a sung melody."

Emile frowned. Last summer flashed back to him: Auntie pounding a rhythm on a hollowed gourd while the older kids danced, their movements sharp and grounded, and no music at all, just voices rising and falling in a chant. He had thought then that they were dancing without music. Now he understood the chant was the music, and his humming was a different song entirely.

So he tested it. Instead of humming, he chanted the words out loud, quietly, and let Auntie's drum, the deep boop and slap of the gourd against the mat, be his only clock. When his knees kept sinking low on the wrong beat, he guessed the problem: he was counting in his head instead of listening. He stopped counting. He followed the drum alone, letting the chant's words tell his hands where to go. The movements that symbolize wind and rain began to feel like wind and rain, not like a list of positions.

"Better," Nalu called out. "Your timing is consistent now. You're with the drum."

Auntie brought out a folded mat for the cold evening, wrapping one edge around Emile's shoulders like insulation against the trade wind, and he laughed and shook it off, because he was warm from working.

He started the verse again, feet striking the boards in time, and this time when the drum paused for a breath, he paused too, arms still, waiting for the chant to rise.

"One more time," said Auntie, lifting the gourd.

Hudson had exactly forty minutes before his dad picked him up, and one worksheet that said, in cheerful teacher handwriting, "Explain the pyramids AND the Nile. In your own words." He stood in front of a model of Giza, all sand and tiny stone triangles, and felt his brain begin to decompose on the spot.

"The gift shop closes at four," said his sister, Priya, who had her own agenda and had stated it eleven times since the parking lot.

"Two minutes." Hudson circled the model. The pyramids sat on the west side of the Nile, and the little farms sat right on the river's edge, green strips squeezed against blue. That was the pattern. The fields needed to be near the water because the water was everything, and the tombs rose on the far bank like they'd been parked there on purpose. Floods, he guessed, were a signal, the calendar the whole country ran on. When the river rose and then dropped, it left wet soil, and the farmers planted in that. But the river dropped a lot. How did a field get water when it sat higher than the water did?

The next room answered him, though not in words. A tall pole was pivoted on a wooden frame, with a rope and bucket hanging from one end and a blob of clay on the other. A plastic tub of water sat below it, a raised sandbox above. A sign gave one line: Try it. A docent leaned against the wall looking impartial, as if this were not the most interesting object in the building.

Hudson pulled the rope down. The bucket dipped into the tub. When he let go, the clay end dropped and the whole thing swung up, and the bucket of water rose without him doing anything. He swung it over the sandbox and tipped it into the sand, which darkened in a spreading circle.

"It's called a shaduf," the docent said. "The weight does the lifting."

Priya appeared beside him, gift shop apparently forgotten. "Let me do one." She pulled the rope, hauled up a bucket, and dumped it on Hudson's shoe.

"That was the field," Hudson said, wringing out his sock. "Very fertile."

Kate stood at the soup vendor's table at the Saturday farmers' market, holding a wooden spoon like it might bite her. Mrs. Okafor had shown her how to stir flour into melted butter until it smelled nutty, and Kate was supposed to add milk and cheese for the sauce that went over the roasted cauliflower samples.

"You did this at home already?" Mrs. Okafor asked, dumping cheese cubes into a bowl.

"Sort of," Kate said. She was remembering last Tuesday, when she'd stood at her own stove, stirring and stirring while the butter and flour turned the color of toast, then peanut butter, then something like an old penny. Her little brother had wandered in and said the pot looked like mud, and he was not wrong. The sauce that came out of it had been cheese-flavored water. Her brother had dipped a carrot in it, held it up dripping, and announced, "It's a beverage."

Here, Kate stirred faster this time, waiting for the nutty smell. But she kept thinking about the weirdness of it. At home the roux was dark and the sauce never thickened. Mrs. Okafor's roux was pale gold, and her sauces clung to a spoon like syrup. There had to be a rule hiding in there.

"I want to try something," Kate said, pulling the pot off the heat early, when the paste was barely deeper than the butter itself. She whisked in warm milk, and the suspense lasted exactly four seconds, because the sauce thickened almost immediately, smooth and glossy, and the cheese she stirred in melted into it without a single lump.

"Look at that," Mrs. Okafor said. "No lumps at all."

Kate stared at the pot. "So the darker I cook it, the less it thickens. The browning must break down the flour's starch." She said it slowly, testing the idea against Tuesday's cheese water, and it fit.

"Then your penny-colored pot had nothing left to give," Mrs. Okafor said, laughing.

Kate ladled sauce over cauliflower and handed the first sample to an old man with a cane, because he'd been waiting longest. He took a bite and gave her a thumbs-up with his whole arm.

"Free beverage with every sample," Kate whispered to Mrs. Okafor, and they both laughed until the next customer cleared his throat.

Emmett stood in Grandma's kitchen holding a spoon like a microphone, and for the fourth time he forgot his own second sentence.

"Grandma, can I practise on you again?"

She set down her crossword. "Again and again until it's boring. That's how your grandpa learned his wedding speech, and he only forgot the ring, not the words."

The problem was real. Tomorrow night Emmett had five minutes at the township council meeting to argue against the new bylaw that would tear out the community garden behind the recreation centre, where he had grown the lush rows of beans and zucchini that had won him a ribbon at the fall fair. The bylaw said the land would become extra parking. Emmett had learned, from a page on the township website he'd found while sulking about it, that residents could ask to speak briefly at a council or committee meeting. It was called appearing as a delegation. He'd filled out a form, emailed it in, and gotten a reply giving him a spot. Five minutes, no more.

"You're pacing," Grandma said. "Why don't you stand still and imagine the councillors are bean plants? You've talked to bean plants all summer."

"I have never talked to bean plants."

"You narrated to them. I heard you. You said, and I quote, grow, you stubborn little polymer sacks of water."

Emmett laughed so hard he lost his place on the notecards again. "Cells aren't polymer sacks. Well, the cell walls sort of are, actually. Cellulose is a polymer." He frowned at the cards. "That's not the point. The point is I keep trying to memorize every word, and then one word falls out and the whole speech collapses like wet cardboard."

He thought about the fair, back in September, when the judge had asked him a question he hadn't prepared for. What had he done? He hadn't recited anything. He'd just answered, plainly, about how he'd composted and watered. It had worked because he was talking about something he actually knew.

"Grandma, what if I don't memorize it? What if I just know three things I want to say, in order, and say them like I'm answering the bean question?"

"Then say them to me right now, and I'll be a grumpy councillor who wants more parking."

Emmett put the notecards face down on the counter. "Councillors, seventy families grew food in that garden this year. Parking is something we can generate anywhere, but that soil took us eight years to build. Tomorrow I'm appearing as a delegation, so you have to hear me out, and here is why you should keep the garden."

He went through it twice more, no cards, once while Grandma heckled him about parking. When he finished, she stood up and applauded with her oven mitts.

"I have my own request, by the way," she said. "While you're at that meeting, ask them to fix the streetlight at my corner. I've written three letters. Maybe a delegation gets somewhere."

"Deal," Emmett said, and picked the spoon back up.

The petition lay flat on the counter at city hall, all four pages of it, held down by Jaxson's elbow so the fan by the clerk's window wouldn't flip it over. Behind him, Mira and Devon shifted from foot to foot in their school backpacks. They had collected one hundred and six signatures in eleven days, standing outside the library and the corner store with clipboards, asking people to sign so the city would put a crosswalk on Hartley Road where the middle school kids jaywalked every afternoon because the nearest crossing was three long blocks away.

"I can't take that here," the clerk said, tapping her pen toward a doorway marked Council Services. "Third floor. Ask for the clerk of council." Jaxson picked up the pages. The top sheet had gone slightly translucent from the drizzle that morning, and you could see the signature on the reverse side showing through, backward, like a ghost of itself.

On the third floor, the clerk of council read the pages slowly, and Jaxson's stomach knotted, because he had written the request himself and he was suddenly sure he'd done it wrong. "You've got signatures," the woman said, "but you haven't said what you want them to do. A petition is a written request, signed by many people, asking a government body to take a specific action. Yours says the road is dangerous. That's a complaint, not a request."

Devon made a small noise, and Jaxson felt heat crawl up his neck, the embarrassment of having walked a hundred and six people into a dead end. But then he thought about it the way he thought about math problems, backward from the answer. They had the signatures. Those were still good. What was missing was only the specific action, the exact thing being asked for. That part he could fix without going door to door again.

"Could I write it now?" he asked. "Like, 'We, the undersigned, request that city council install a marked crosswalk with pedestrian signals at Hartley Road and Kemp Street.'" The clerk slid a blank sheet across the counter. He wrote it out, then paper-clipped it to the front of the signed pages, so every name now belonged to a clear request. "You can contribute it at Tuesday's council meeting," she said. "There's an open session at seven. Sign in at the desk, and you'll have five minutes to speak."

They rode the escalator down in silence until Mira said, "Tuesday. That's three days." Jaxson folded the petition into his backpack, careful along the crease. "Three days to figure out what I'm going to say." At the big front doors, Devon stopped and looked back up at the third-floor windows. "One hundred and six people," he said. Jaxson nodded and pushed the door open into the afternoon light.

Gavin's stomach growled so loudly that his cousin Dana snickered across the table. Shabbat had started at sundown the night before, and this was his first time trying to keep the whole day of rest, no snacks between meals, no video games, no rushing around. His little sister Ruthie had done it plenty of times, but Gavin had always quit by noon.

He had devised a plan at breakfast: whenever he wanted his tablet, he would find one person at Aunt Miriam's house and ask them a question instead. It had worked six times so far. The seventh time, he asked his grandfather why the day of rest ended with a whole ceremony instead of just, well, ending.

"You'll see," Grandpa said, which was the most annoying answer in the world.

After dark, everyone crowded into the kitchen. Uncle David poured a small cup of wine, and Grandpa got one of grape juice for Ruthie and the cousins. Then Grandpa brought out a candle, but not a normal one. It was braided, several wicks twisted together at the top, and it looked like a rope that had decided to become a candle.

"Ruthie," Aunt Miriam said, "you're old enough this year."

Ruthie held out both hands. Her chin was up, but Gavin could see her fingers trembling as the flame caught and light jumped against the cabinets. Gavin realized he was holding his breath, as if he were the protagonist of a story who had to protect something fragile. He moved closer so his shoulder was near hers.

They passed around a little silver box of fragrant spices, and Gavin breathed in cloves and something sharp and sweet. The smell was supposed to carry you through the week, Dana whispered, like saving up the rest day in your nose.

Gavin thought about his empty morning, the hungry hours, the six questions. It had felt like nothing was happening. But something had been happening the whole time, the way the braided candle had one flame made of several wicks, and you couldn't see where one part ended unless you looked hard.

Ruthie dipped the candle into the wine and the flames hissed out.

"I did it," she said. "Next year, can I hold the cup too?"

Raphael stood on Mr. Lin's porch with a crumpled note in his pocket and a bag of dumplings in his hand. His friend Dara had gone inside already, and now Mrs. Lin was talking to him in quick Mandarin that flew past like sparrows. He caught nothing. Last summer he had nodded along at his grandfather's market walks, pretending to understand, and the memory of that humiliation still made his ears hot. This time he wanted real words.

"Zǒu ba," Dara called, waving him toward the door. "That means let's go."

They walked to the market behind Mrs. Lin, who carried an empty basket on her arm. When they reached the corner, she stopped and asked Raphael a question with a rising twist at the end. He heard two words he almost knew, but the market had two doors, one to the left and one to the right, and he had no idea which one she meant. Dara looked at him, waiting.

Raphael thought back to those walks with his grandfather. There had been a game of it, once: the old man pointing left and saying "zuǒ," pointing right and saying "yòu." The words had not sounded the same at all, and Raphael had always assumed that was just his bad ear. But now, listening to Mrs. Lin repeat the question, he noticed something. One word dipped down like a slide, and the other rose and circled. Maybe each direction had its own sound, its own tune, and the tune was part of the word itself. That was a pattern he could test.

He pointed at the left door and said, carefully, the dipping one: "Zuǒ?"

Mrs. Lin's whole face opened. "Duì! Zuǒ means left," she said, and she pointed with him, then swung her finger the other way. "Yòu means right." She said it again, slower, and Raphael heard the rise and circle of the second word clearly now, as if the sound itself were pointing.

They went in the left door. The market smelled like ginger and dried mushrooms, and Mrs. Lin filled her basket with bean sprouts that rattled like rain. Raphael tried his two words at the tea stall, pointing at jars: zuǒ, yòu. The stall keeper laughed and slid him a cup of something sweet. He had spent a whole summer nodding and understanding nothing, and he wondered, holding the warm cup, whether that had been his fault or just a choice he could make differently now. He could not decide, and it did not seem to matter as much as it once had.

On the walk home, Dara tested him at every turn. "Which way?"

"Zuǒ," Raphael said, and turned left, and behind them Mrs. Lin called out, "Yòu! Your house is on the right," so he laughed and turned the other way.

Luca knelt at the edge of the inflatable pool his dad had set up on the lawn, holding a garden hose he'd stretched along the grass. Twenty-five metres. That was the distance, and next Saturday was the club's test to move up from the beginners group. The pool wasn't even three metres long, so swimming it here was impossible. He would have to figure out the hard part, the side breathing, some other way.

The hard part was this: every time he turned his head to breathe, he swallowed water instead of air. He had a theory about why. Maybe the problem wasn't the turning. Maybe his arm was splashing water right where his mouth went, so the water was already there before he turned. He couldn't see it himself, but his little sister Priya was watching the Olympics on the tablet on the porch, and she could watch him.

"Why does everyone in that race do the same stroke?" Luca asked, nodding at the screen. "It says freestyle. I thought that meant you could pick any one."

"You can pick any one," Priya said. "Almost all swimmers choose front crawl because it's the fastest of the competitive strokes."

Luca stared at the swimmers churning down the lanes, all of them rolling their heads sideways like gears in a machine. Then he looked at the pool. "Priya, come here. Watch my right arm when I breathe. Tell me if it splashes."

He lay flat in the shallow water and mimicked the stroke in slow motion, pulling his arm, turning his head. Priya leaned close, frowning like a scientist. "It's not the arm," she said. "You're lifting your head up first, then sideways. Your face is going forward and up at the same time. That's why you get water."

Lifting then turning, instead of just turning along the water like the Olympic swimmers did. That was a pattern he could test. He tried again, keeping one cheek pressed to the surface like a pillow, one goggle in the water and one out. Air came in. Real air, no coughing. "It worked," he said, spitting a little grass out of his mouth anyway.

Afterward he sat dripping on the step and helped Priya retrieve the tablet charger from under the couch cushion on the porch, since she'd promised to time him in exchange. "When I pass the test," Luca said, "I'll be in the older group. Real laps, real races."

"Will you do freestyle like everybody else?"

Luca thought about it. He had always imagined doing something different, a fancy stroke nobody expected. "I changed my mind," he said. "If almost everyone picks front crawl because it's fastest, then that's the credible choice, isn't it? You'd have to have a really good reason not to."

"You could have a good reason," Priya said. "You could want to lose slowly in style."

Luca laughed so hard he fell backward into the pool, and came up doing three strokes, breathing sideways, all the way to the far wall.

Max had signed up for art elective the moment the signup sheet went up, because today was the day they got to draw with real charcoal, and he'd been talking about it since breakfast. He claimed a picnic table under the oak tree by the craft cabin, set his sketchbook down, and waited for the instructor to bring out the supplies.

"Everyone gets a Styrofoam ball and a lamp," Dana announced, plunking a box of balls on the table. "Today we're drawing spheres, and the goal is to make them look solid. Not like flat circles. Like balls sitting on the table."

Max grabbed his ball and set it on the picnic table while Dana positioned the lamp at the side. The light hit the ball on the upper left, leaving a bright spot there and a darker curve opposite. He squinted at it, then at his page, and started drawing. Circle first. Then he shaded the right side darker, kept the upper left light, and smudged everything with his thumb until it looked smooth.

"What do you think?" he asked his friend Theo, who was sitting across from him drawing his own ball.

Theo leaned over. "It's good, but something's weird. Yours looks like it's floating. Like a planet."

Max held his drawing up next to the real ball. Theo was right. His ball looked round, sure, but it hung above the table instead of resting on it. He hadn't even drawn a shadow yet. He sketched a gray oval spreading out from the base and filled it in lightly.

"Still floating," Theo said.

Max frowned at the real ball again. The lamp came from the side, so the shadow stretched away from it, but it wasn't all the same gray. He crouched down until his eyes were level with the tabletop. Right where the ball curved down and met the wood, the shadow went nearly black. He looked at his own drawing. He had made his shadow oval one even, symmetrical gray, like a sticker.

He pressed his charcoal hard onto the page right at the point where his drawn ball touched the drawn table, then dragged it just a tiny bit sideways, fading quickly. He lifted the paper.

"Whoa," Theo said. "It's sitting. It's actually sitting on the table."

Max laughed out loud. "The darkest part is right where it touches! Almost no light gets into that little gap!" He shaded his floating-looking first attempt the same way, dark at the contact point, and watched that one sit down too.

At the end of the session, Max petitioned Dana to let the class hang their spheres on the craft cabin wall, and she said yes before he even finished asking. He pinned his drawing up, stepped back, and grinned at the ball that finally, definitely, was not going anywhere.

Tyler had forty minutes before his grandmother arrived to drive the volcano to the science fair, and the volcano had fizzed exactly once all afternoon. He stood at the kitchen counter between a box of baking soda and a bottle of vinegar, glaring at both of them like they owed him money.

His little sister Nadia sat on the counter, allegedly helping. "Do it again," she said.

"I can't just do it again. The fair starts at seven." Tyler peered into the bottle. The baking soda had slid down in a wet lump, and the bubbles had vanished like they were never there. He thought about the iron gate behind the garage, the one he'd photographed in September for his poster. In September it had been gray. By December the bottom rungs were orange and flaky, and no amount of scrubbing had turned the orange back to gray. That was the whole reason he'd picked this project: some things you could undo, like melting butter and pouring it back into a dish to harden, and some things you couldn't. He'd tested the butter on Tuesday and his mother had tested his patience on Wednesday when she found the dish.

"The bubbles," Nadia said, pointing at the dead bottle. "Where'd they go?"

"Out. Bubbles go out."

"Where'd they come from?"

Tyler opened his mouth to say something and found nothing in there. He'd watched the fizz rise a hundred times in videos, and he'd never once asked himself where it began. The poster on the table had a section he'd labeled with duct tape: WHAT PROVES A CHANGE IS REAL. Under it he'd glued the gate photo and a drawing of butter. Nothing about bubbles. Nothing about the one thing his volcano actually did.

He grabbed the tape and peeled the section off, then wrote a new heading: SIGNS OF A CHEMICAL CHANGE. He set out two cups. In the first he put a spoon of butter and softened it in his hands, because he still needed the melt comparison, and the oven took too long. In the second he dropped a pinch of baking soda and drizzled vinegar over it. Fizz. He drizzled more. Fizz, fizz, a robust column of it, better than the volcano had ever managed.

"There," Nadia said. "Do the bubbles mean it's working?"

"They mean the stuff turned into new stuff." He held the cup out to her so she could see the bubbles climbing the sides. "Gas bubbles when two things mix, like baking soda meets vinegar, are a sign a chemical change happened. That's what the fizz is. It's my proof."

"That's it? That's the whole proof?"

"That's the whole proof, and it's better than my butter."

The clock said 6:22. He funneled fresh baking soda into the cone, positioned the vinegar, and carried the poster flat like a pizza. At the door he stopped, went back, and dropped a carrot into his backpack, because the class rodent, Biscuit, was riding along, and Biscuit did not care about chemical changes, only about dinner.

"Start the car, Grandma," he called. "I'm bringing the volcano, the butter, and a rodent."

Autumn had read The War That Saved My Life twice, and she was sure the theme was about courage, but Mr. Delgado had written one word on her last English essay: evidence? So tonight at book club, in the corner of the library with the squishy blue chairs that smelled faintly of orange cleaner, she was going to find a quotation that proved it.

She flipped through her paperback, past the dog-eared pages, until she found the passage she loved, the one where Ada finally rides Bones across the field even though her conscience tells her she'll be in trouble if her mother finds out. It was beautiful. It was also, she realized as she copied it into her notebook, extremely long. She counted the lines. Nine. Far more than four.

"What are you frowning at?" asked Priya, leaning over with a granola bar in one hand. "Did the book kill somebody again?"

"Worse. MLA," Autumn said, and Priya snorted so hard a crumb landed on the chapter list. Last month Autumn had assumed she could just stuff any quotation inside a sentence with quotation marks around it, like a marshmallow in a s'more. Mr. Delgado had circled her giant quotation and written see me, which was scarier than any villain in the novel.

So she tested it. She wrote her two favorite lines inside her paragraph with quotation marks and it looked fine. Then she wrote out the full nine-line passage the same way, and it was a disaster, a wall of quotation marks that swallowed her whole sentence like a python swallowing a beach ball.

Priya grabbed the MLA handbook from the shelf behind them and thumbed through it, chewing. "Here. In MLA style, a prose quotation longer than four lines is set as an indented block, half an inch from the margin, without quotation marks."

"No quotation marks at all?"

"Not one."

Autumn tried it. She moved the whole passage onto its own lines, indented half an inch from the margin, and took off the quotation marks. Suddenly her paragraph could breathe, and the passage just sat there, eloquent and sure of itself, backing up her theme like a friend standing behind her.

When it was her turn to share, Autumn read her theme, then the blocked passage, then said, "Courage isn't the absence of fear. It's acting anyway."

Mr. Delgado, stacking chairs nearby, looked over. "Evidence?" he asked.

Autumn held up her notebook and tapped the indented block. "Right there."

Zoey had promised her little brother that his favorite game, Squid Invasion, would be ready by his birthday, which was tomorrow. The plan was simple: enemy squids would invade the reef, and every time the player's shark zapped one, the score went up. In theory. In practice, her test squid drifted ten steps across the stage and then just stood there, lethargic as a garden ornament, while the shark circled it mockingly.

"Even the squid is bored," said her brother, leaning over her shoulder in the kitchen. "It's just sitting there."

"I see that." Zoey squinted at her blocks. She had dragged a stack under a blue block that read repeat 10. She clicked the green flag again and counted the squid's tiny slides, whispering, "One, two, three." It stopped at ten, exactly where it had stopped last time.

She scrolled through the menu and found a different block, orange instead of blue, with a word on it she'd skipped before: forever. She snapped it into place where the repeat 10 had been, dumping her movement blocks inside it. When she clicked the flag this time, the squid kept gliding, on and on, no freezing.

"Wait, so what's the difference?" her brother asked.

"Repeat 10 runs what's inside it ten times," Zoey said. "Forever keeps going until you stop the whole program." She felt like she'd found a secret lever behind a wall. The squid would now invade endlessly, and her if-then block, the one that checked whether the shark was touching it, would finally get a chance to do its job.

She clicked the flag, dove the shark into the squid, and held her breath. The score flickered from 0 to 47.

"Okay, that's a new problem," she said, and reached for the keyboard.

Mia pressed her nose against the case of rocks outside the planetarium's geology lab, trying to figure out which pile was which. The sign said SORT THEM: IGNEOUS, SEDIMENTARY, OR METAMORPHIC, but the labels had been knocked face-down, and the volunteer had her hands full helping a boy whose paper had ripped.

"I wanted to win the mineral kit," Mia whispered to her friend Theo. "But I can't tell anything about these rocks. How they formed happened millions of years ago. Nobody saw it."

Theo held up two samples from the igneous pile, one pale and speckled, one dark and plain. "These two are supposed to be the same kind. Weird, right? This one's all sparkly, like my aunt's kitchen countertop, and this one's just dark."

Mia turned the sparkly one in the light. She could perceive individual glittering flecks, each big enough to see without squinting. The dark one looked dull and uniform, almost like it had been poured out smooth. She rolled the idea around, then tested it against the show they had just watched. "The presenter said the universe is expanding, and we know because of the recession of the galaxies, the light stretching as everything drifts apart. We can't see it happen, but we can read it in the clues." She tapped the sparkly rock. "So the crystals are the clue here. Big crystals mean the rock cooled slowly, somewhere deep underground. Tiny ones mean it cooled fast, up at the surface."

"So the granite countertop is the slow one," Theo said, "and my dark basalt pebble cooled fast?"

"Granite, basalt," Mia confirmed, sorting the stones into slow and fast stacks. Piece by piece, she worked through the rest, and the cumulative effect of each small correct choice was a full tray, finished before the timer buzzed.

The volunteer flipped the labels upright. Every stack was right. She smiled and set the mineral kit in front of Mia, then slid a spare magnifying glass across the table toward Theo. "For your pebble," she said. "Take a closer look at those tiny crystals."

Clara spread her poster across two folding tables at the community centre, weighting the corners with paper cups because she despised curling paper more than almost anything. Her diagram showed a bill travelling through the legislature: first reading, second reading, committee, third reading, then the Senate, and at the end a big blank box with a question mark.

"That's the hole in my project," she told Priya, who was building a diorama of the Arctic tundra for her own booth, complete with a muskox made from a pompom and two buttons. "I know the bill has to be approved at the end, but I don't know who actually does it. I can't draw a question mark. That looks like I gave up."

"You could draw a crown," Priya said, holding up the muskox. "Does this look scared? It's supposed to look scared of wolves."

Clara frowned at her poster. The queen didn't personally approve every bill, surely. Somebody had to do it for her, but who? She turned the question over while she helped Priya glue tiny white paper hares onto the frosted cardboard, because the tundra needed prey or the wolves made no sense at all.

Then she remembered the field trip in October, when their class had visited the courthouse and a clerk had mentioned something odd. Clara found the pamphlet in her backpack and flipped to the page she'd folded over. There it was. She grabbed a marker and wrote "royal assent" in the blank box, then drew the Governor General beneath it, and beside him a figure in judge's robes.

"Wait," Priya said, leaning over. "A judge?"

"A Supreme Court justice can be a deputy," Clara said. "They can stand in and give royal assent to a federal bill on behalf of the monarch." She drew a little arrow from the judge to the crown so nobody would think the judge had become king.

Priya stuck the pompom muskox on the tundra and stepped back to check it. "Good. Now it looks distinct from the rocks." Then she pointed at Clara's poster. "You should draw the judge giving a thumbs up."

Clara laughed and drew it, right there in the last box.

Florence sat in the plastic chair at Wanderlust Travel while her mother compared packages at the front desk. Behind the agent's computer hung a huge world map with faint lines drawn across it, and along the top and sides ran numbers: 0, 30, 60, 90, 120, 150, 180. A small monitor on the counter listed flights, and next to each city was a pair of numbers. Lagos: 6, 3. Kathmandu: 27, 85. Honolulu: 21, 157.

Her grandmother lived in Kathmandu, and Florence wanted to find it on the map before Mom finished paying. She picked up the ruler from the agent's desk drawer, held it against the map, and tried to calibrate it against the numbers along the top, matching one ruler mark to every ten degrees. But which number was which? The screen gave her 27 and 85 with no labels at all.

She traced the horizontal lines first. They were numbered from 0 at the equator up toward the poles, and Lagos sat at 6, near the fat middle of Africa. So the first number on the screen matched those. That left 85 for the lines that ran up and down. She counted them out from the line marked 0, which the map labeled the prime meridian, and they climbed to 90, then 150, then 180, and on the other side of the map they climbed again from 0 to 180 the other way.

"So that's longitude," she said, mostly to herself.

The agent looked over. "That's what it's called," she said, and went back to the paperwork.

Florence followed the up-and-down line numbered 85 east of the zero line, then the horizontal line numbered 27, and where they crossed she found Kathmandu, a dot inside Nepal. She put her fingertip on it just as her mother turned around.

"We leave in March," Mom said. "Three weeks."

"Good," Florence said. "I already know right where she is."

William's cousin Kayla had a credit card balance of two hundred dollars, and she had stopped using the card entirely, but somehow the balance kept growing every month. "It's like the debt is alive," she told him at lunch, slamming her locker in the hallway outside the cafeteria. William couldn't stop thinking about it through math class. Something invisible was feeding it.

That afternoon, Mr. Ruiz assigned a project: compare the cost of borrowing money on a credit card with saving up first. William chose the skateboard he wanted, one hundred eighty dollars, as his example. He spread his notes across the library table and drew two columns. If he saved twenty dollars a month from mowing lawns, he'd have the board in nine months, and it would cost exactly one hundred eighty dollars. If he borrowed the money on a card instead, he'd pay interest every month he didn't clear the balance. He copied the numbers down, month by month, his pencil slowing.

Then he saw it, and his stomach dropped. The first month's interest got added to what he owed. The second month, interest was charged on that bigger number, which meant interest was being charged on interest. Each row of his table grew by more than the row before it. The debt wasn't just growing, it was accelerating, like a seed that had germinated in the dark and was now pushing up faster every day. He tested it twice, redrawing the table on a fresh sheet because he was sure he'd fractured one of his own calculations somewhere. Both tables came out the same. The numbers didn't lie.

He found Kayla by the buses after school. "The interest they add becomes part of what you owe," he said. "Then the next month's interest is charged on that interest too. That's why your balance climbs even though you never use the card." Kayla stared at him, then at her phone, where her statement confirmed every step.

"So it's not extravagant spending anymore," she said quietly. "It's the debt feeding itself."

William folded his tables and put them in his backpack. "Save first," he said, and started walking home to plan his lawn schedule.

Chase had until Saturday, three days away, to get his monologue ready for the community theatre's audition, and so far he could only rush through it like a kid reading a cereal box. He stood on the small stage in the drafty rehearsal hall, flung his arm out for the line "But soft, what light through yonder window breaks," and heard his own voice trip over itself like sneakers on stairs. "Faster is not better," said Mrs. Okafor from the front row, tapping her pen against the table in a slow, steady beat. "Try again. Follow my tapping." Chase tried again, and this time something odd happened: when he matched her rhythm, the words seemed to carry themselves.

He sat down next to her, puzzling over the page. The tapping had gone da-DUM, da-DUM, da-DUM, and the line had fit it exactly. He counted the syllables on his fingers, twice, because he didn't believe himself the first time. Ten. Every line he checked came out to ten syllables, five pairs, with the strong beat landing second in each pair, like a heartbeat. "It's iambic pentameter," said Priya, the eccentric girl in the rainbow scarf who ran the light board, looking over his shoulder. "My grandma recites it while cooking." Chase stared at her, then back at the page, feeling like he'd found a trapdoor in the floor.

"So the pauses aren't random," he said slowly. "The rhythm tells me where to breathe." He stood up and tried the speech again, letting the pattern hold him back at the soft beats and push him forward on the strong ones. Where the rhythm broke, like at "It is my lady," he stopped dead, and the sudden silence felt enormous, like the whole hall leaned in to listen. Priya clapped once, loud in the empty seats. "Do that on Saturday," she said. "Exactly that."

The next day he made a deal with his little sister, a negotiation involving two hours of her choosing the TV shows in exchange for her sitting through the monologue five times. On the fourth run-through she stopped chewing her granola bar and said, "Wait. Say the part where you whisper again." He said it again, softer, holding the pause before it, and she actually shivered. Chase grinned so hard his cheeks hurt.

Saturday morning, backstage in the smell of dust and paint, he heard his name called. He walked out, planted his feet, and did not rush. He let the hidden pattern carry him, ten syllables at a time, and when the broken rhythm came he stopped and let the silence sit there like a held breath. From the dark rows, someone tapped a pen against an armrest, da-DUM, da-DUM, keeping time with him.

Everly's mother taught driving lessons in a small storefront between a laundromat and a diner, and after school Everly sat in the back room doing homework beside a molten puddle of July sunlight on the carpet. Today, though, her mother handed her a five-dollar bill and a short list. "You're ready," she said, squeezing Everly's shoulder. "Corner store, one carton of milk, and walk straight home. You're my best candidate for this, you know. You've never once gotten lost."

The store was four blocks away. Everly counted the crosswalks, waited for the walk signal at each one, and felt the five dollars crinkle in her pocket like a small transmitted message from her mother. On the shelf, the milk was marked $3.99. She did the math twice on her finger on the way to the register: five dollars minus $3.99 left one dollar and one cent. The cashier, a woman with a name tag that said Rosa, rang it up, and the screen showed $4.31.

"Wait," Everly said. "The shelf says $3.99." Her cheeks went hot. She had counted, she had checked, and she was thirty-two cents short of what she'd expected, even though she still had enough. Rosa pointed at the receipt line that said TAX. Then a man behind Everly, holding bread, leaned in with a gentle smile. "Happened to me for years," he said. "I moved here from England. In the UK and EU, the price on the shelf already includes VAT, so what you see is what you pay. Here in the US and Canada, shelf prices leave out sales tax, and they add it at the till."

Everly stared at the numbers. So that was the rule: the shelf price was only part of the truth, and the till finished the sentence. She tested it in her head with the candy bar by the register, marked $1.00. If the same rate applied, it would cost $1.08 at the register, not a dollar even. She had a dollar in quarters in her other pocket, and she slid them across the counter. The screen read $1.08. "I'm eight cents short," Everly said. Rosa popped the candy into the bag anyway. "For walking here all by yourself," she said.

Everly carried the milk home past the crosswalks, the receipt folded in her fist so she could study the little TAX line again. At the driving school, her mother was standing beside a student car, waving. Everly held up the receipt like a trophy. "Shelf prices lie," she announced, "except in England."

Emilie stood on the coffee table in the living room, holding a note card so tightly it bent. Her little brother Theo sat on the couch with a stopwatch, because Theo wanted to be a race announcer when he grew up, and he considered timing things his official job. "Speech is Friday," Emilie said. "Two minutes, and Miss Okafor is strict about it." Her best point, the story of Grandpa's old propeller plane and the day he landed it on a frozen lake, was buried in the middle, but she didn't know that yet.

She gave the speech to Theo. She opened with a boring question, "Have you ever wondered about aviation?", then talked about three points, then closed with a shrug and the word "anyway." Theo clicked the stopwatch and frowned. "Two minutes and six seconds," he announced. "But Emilie, what was your speech about?" She told him again. "No, what you said. I remember the question at the start and 'anyway' at the end, and the rest is just... fog."

Emilie sat down on the rug. Theo looked lethargic, slumped sideways like the speech had drained the energy right out of him, and that gave her an idea. She needed to isolate the problem, so she gave the speech one more time, exactly the same, except this time she started with the propeller plane story and ended with it too. Theo sat up straight. When she finished, he could name all three points in order. "The middle one I only sort of remember," he admitted, "but the first and last, those are stuck in my head." Emilie grabbed her note cards. "Then that's where the good stuff goes. Miss Okafor said people remember the first and last items in a list best. It's called the serial position effect." Theo repeated the words slowly, like a race announcer saying a new driver's name. "Serial position effect. Sounds fast."

On Friday morning Emilie practiced one last time in the living room, opening with the frozen lake and closing with the propeller spinning in the cold air. Theo clicked the stopwatch at exactly two minutes and raised both arms. "And the winner, by the power of the serial position effect, is Emilie!" She laughed, gathered her note cards, and walked out the front door with her chin up.

Hazel's little brother, Gus, had one mission at the science museum: find the ice cream machine before their parents finished the space exhibit. Hazel had a different mission: beat the "Matter Mixer" quiz at the back of the chemistry hall, which nobody in her class had ever beaten without missing a question. The prize was a sticker that read MOLECULE BOSS, and she wanted it stuck to her binder by lunch.

The hall smelled faintly like pennies. Near the entrance, a display called the tundra table held a tray of ice cubes under a warm lamp, slowly slumping into puddles. Beside it stood a chunk of iron fence, speckled orange and crumbling, with a sign that said it had come from a dilapidated lighthouse up the coast. Farther along, a sealed case let visitors press a button and watch a strip of magnesium flare into blinding white powder, then cool into ash. Hazel pressed it three times, partly for science and partly because it was spectacular.

The quiz machine flashed its first question: Ice cubes melt in the sun. Did anything new get made? Hazel stared at the puddle tray. She crouched, dipped a finger in, and touched it to her tongue. Water. Just water, the same stuff as ice, only sloshier. "So that's a physical change," she muttered. "The shape changed, but the substance didn't." Then she looked at the rusted fence, flaking orange under the lights, and the ash in the case. Those were different. If she scraped the rust off, it wouldn't be iron anymore; if she tried to burn the powder back together, it would just laugh at her. Something new had been made there. She answered: nothing new. The machine chimed.

Gus appeared at her elbow, breathing hard. "No ice cream machine," he reported grimly. "But there's a slushie stand, and slushie is basically ice plus syrup, so technically I'm still on mission." Hazel answered six more questions, missing only the one about burned toast, and the machine spat out her sticker. She slapped it on her binder, then held it up so the lamp light could expose its glittery gold letters. "Say it," she told Gus. He sighed like a man on the tundra surrendering his last sandwich. "Hail the Molecule Boss." She handed him a napkin for the slushie he was already planning.

Christopher sat on the back step with his sketchbook, a golf ball, and a flashlight propped against a flowerpot. His assignment was to draw the ball so it looked round instead of like a flat white circle, and so far he had four flat white circles to prove how hard that was.

His little sister Nadia wandered over, licking a popsicle. "That's a nice cookie," she said, pointing at his latest attempt.

"It's a sphere," Christopher groaned. "It's supposed to look three-dimensional."

"Then why doesn't it?"

He tapped his pencil against his chin. Maybe the problem was that he had shaded everything the same gray, like the ball was made of the same stuff all the way around, which it was, but that wasn't the point. He looked at the real golf ball under the flashlight. One side of it gleamed. Not all of it, just one small bright spot, sitting on the side that faced the light.

Nadia leaned in and squinted at his drawing. "Which side is the lamp on?"

Christopher opened his mouth to answer and then stopped. He couldn't answer. In his drawing there was no side facing the light, because he hadn't put a brightest spot anywhere. He grabbed his eraser and rubbed out his careful gray wash until the paper looked rough and porous, like a worn-out kitchen sponge.

"That's backwards," Nadia said. "You're erasing your homework."

"I'm eliminating the flatness," said Christopher. "Watch."

He studied the golf ball again. The brightest spot sat right where the ball faced the flashlight, so he made one small bright patch on the upper right of his sphere and left it almost untouched, then let the shading grow darker toward the far side, until the shadow the ball threw onto the flowerpot behind it made a long dark tail.

"Which side is the lamp on now?" he asked.

Nadia pointed at the bright patch without hesitating. "That side. It's like the ball is telling on the flashlight."

Christopher held the drawing up next to the real thing and grinned. "A snitching sphere."

"Draw a face on it," Nadia said, "and make the face look guilty."

He laughed and turned the page, already sketching a lumpy, sneaky-looking ball with the highlight gleaming on its shining, tattletale side.

Dominic had been rehearsing his speech the whole bus ride to the town hall, and by the time he pushed through the big wooden doors, he could say "petition" without tripping over it even once. He wanted the town to change the bylaw that banned skateboards in Riverside Park, and tonight he was going to tell them so. He clutched his petition, forty-two signatures in blue and green ink, plus one in purple crayon from his little sister, who had signed it "Trixie, age six, skateboarder at heart."

The meeting room smelled like coffee and old carpet. Dominic found a seat near the front, next to Councillor Ruiz, who had once helped him rescue a kite from a tree. "Perfect timing," she whispered. "Public petitions come first on the agenda."

Dominic marched to the microphone. He explained that skateboarders were getting chased to the parking lot, which was honestly more dangerous, and that a park should be versatile enough for soccer players and skateboarders both. He held up his pages of signatures like a trophy. The room clapped, and one man in a flannel shirt called out, "The kid's got stamina! I gave up on petitions years ago!"

Councillor Ruiz stood up, and Dominic grinned. She was going to fix it right now. "Thank you, Dominic," she said. "I'd love to change this bylaw myself, but I can't. A single councillor can't change a bylaw alone. It needs a majority vote of the whole council."

Dominic felt like a goalie who had just watched the ball sail past him. Then he thought about it. Majority. He counted the councillors at the long table, eight of them, plus Councillor Ruiz. A rule nobody could see was standing between him and the park, and rules like that had to be moved a different way, not by one friendly grown-up but by enough votes stacked together. He had one signature on the council, sort of. He needed five.

So during the break he went to work. He walked the whole table, showing each councillor his purple crayon signature, asking if they had questions, offering to collaborate on a plan for a skate corner with a fence so soccer balls wouldn't get flattened. Councillor Okafor, who looked grumpy all night, actually laughed. "You've done more homework than most adults who show up here," she said.

When the vote came, Dominic sat on his hands to keep from drumming the armrest. The clerk read the names one by one. Yes. Yes. No. Yes. Yes. Yes. Councillor Okafor paused, looked straight at Dominic, and said, "Yes, for the crayon signature alone."

The gavel came down, and the whole room turned toward him. Dominic raised both fists in the air, and Trixie's purple crayon, held high like a torch, caught the light.

Charlotte was supposed to be helping Mom distribute flyers for the neighborhood cleanup, but she had stopped at the coffee table, pencil tapping her chin. A song was stuck in her head, three words of it, and she could not remember the rest. She had tried humming it to her little brother, who just laughed, and now she was staring at her mom's laptop like it might blink first.

She typed purple October cat and pressed enter. The results were useless. A pet store, a Halloween costume, an eccentric artist who painted everything violet. Then she remembered something her cousin had said last summer, messing around on the computer: "Put quotes around it and it has to match." At the time Charlotte had shrugged and gone back to her popsicle. That had been a mistake, she decided now. She should have paid attention.

She typed "purple October cat" with the quotation marks around the phrase, all three words inside them, exactly as she remembered them. The page changed. Every result now contained those exact words in that exact order, and the fourth one down was the song. She clicked it, and the missing words came flooding back with the tune. On the TV in the corner, a courtroom show droned on, a defendant in a wrinkled suit insisting he had returned the ladder.

Then something else caught her eye. At the top of her results sat a shiny box that said Ad in tiny gray letters, promising purple cat sweaters for October. She looked at it, then at the plain results below. So that was the trick. The real answers looked boring, and the fancy box just wanted her money. She thought about how many times she had clicked the fancy box before, without ever noticing the tiny gray word.

She pulled a flyer from the stack to show Mom, then typed one more search, in quotes, just to watch the list snap into order. "You found the song?" Mom called from the kitchen. "Third result," Charlotte said. "The real one, not the ad."

Mason wanted the last spot on the science demonstration team more than he wanted lunch, and lunch at his school was actually pretty good. The tryout was simple: bring a change, show it, and say whether it was physical or chemical. Priya, who sat in front of him, wanted the spot too, and she had brought a tray with an ice cube melting on it, plus her older brother's good flashlight. Her cube was already shrinking under the lamp, and she looked calm, which made Mason's stomach tighten.

He had planned to burn a strip of paper, but Coach Reyes had banned matches, so all he had was his grandfather's old letter about last summer's campfire, folded in his pocket like a secret weapon. He read it to the class.

"Dear Mason. You asked me why I couldn't save the burnt logs for next year, the way we froze the leftover lemonade. Here is what happened. The wood combined with oxygen in the air and turned into ash, carbon dioxide, and water vapour. The smoke you watched drift up was some of those gases going away. You cannot scoop them back and remake the logs. That's the whole answer. Grandpa."

A boy in the back raised his hand. "But my ice pop melts and I refreeze it all the time."

"That's the difference," Mason said. "Melting is physical. The ice is still water, just loose. Refreeze it and it's ice again. Burning is a chemical change. The wood turns into new stuff. Those three things. And it can't turn back into wood, ever."

Priya touched her melting cube, then looked at her tray in a new way, almost disappointed, as if her clever trick had shrunk to something small. But she had no resentment; she scribbled a note and slid it across. "Ash, carbon dioxide, AND water vapour? I only said physical. You got it." Mason wrote back one word: "Team?" She underlined it twice and added a smile.

Coach Reyes walked over carrying the scorched pan from the supply closet. "Somebody burned popcorn in this last year. Explain it."

Mason grinned. "The kernels combined with oxygen. The pan can transport the evidence to the trash, but nothing will turn it back into popcorn." Then he paused. "Could we weigh ash before and after, to see where the rest went?"

Rachel read her race scene aloud to the writing club and watched Marcus's face go politely blank. The paragraph described Tessa "running very quickly down the very steep hill, her heart beating really fast." It was supposed to feel breathless. Instead it sounded like a grocery list.

"Read it again," said Priya, tapping the table, "but this time cross out every word like very and really before you start." Rachel scanned the page. There were eleven of them. She drew a line through each one, and when she read the scene a second time, something odd happened: it got faster, not weaker. She frowned at the page as if it had tricked her.

Then she came to the part where Tella "ran very quickly" toward the finish line, and the whole race still felt slow. She stared at the two words, ran and quickly, and thought about her track meet in September, when she had hung back too long on the final curve. What had she actually done in that last stretch? She had sprinted. Rachel crossed out three words and wrote one. "Sprinted," she said out loud. "It says more than ran very quickly." Marcus sat up. Priya grabbed her own draft and started hunting through it like each verb was a candidate for firing, which, Rachel realized, was exactly what they were.

She broke her long sentences apart too. Short line. Then a longer one that gathered speed and carried the reader down the hill without stopping. Priya's pencil hovered over her page. "My narrator's mood is volatile in chapter two," she said. "One minute calm, the next furious. Think I should do this there?" Rachel looked at her own before-and-after pages, unsure which version a stranger would believe was written by someone who had actually run a race. "Try it," she said. "Read both out loud. If the angry one still sounds calm, cut harder." Priya flipped to chapter two and began reading, and the room went quiet except for pencils.

Grandpa's laptop sat on the kitchen table between a plate of peanut butter toast and a glass prism that caught the morning light and threw little rainbows across the wall. Alice had claimed the laptop the moment she arrived, because today she was going to finish her Scratch game, the one where a cat trotted around a garden collecting golden coins.

She dragged a coin onto the stage, then clicked the cat and built her script. "When the green flag is clicked, move with the arrow keys, and if touching the coin, change score by one," she muttered, reading her blocks out loud like a spell. She clicked the flag and steered the cat straight over the coin with her agile fingers on the arrow keys. The score stayed at zero.

"That coin is being stubborn," said Grandpa, leaning over her shoulder with his toast. "Try again." Alice circled the cat around the coin, then back over it. Still zero. She frowned and clicked the flag again, and this time she watched very carefully as the cat crossed the coin. Nothing happened. No pop, no point, nothing.

The problem had to be invisible, somewhere in the blocks themselves, and that gave her a funny feeling. It reminded her of last summer, when the porch light flickered every night and Grandpa blamed moths until Alice stood out there for ten whole minutes and discovered it was a loose bulb, twisting in the wind. You couldn't see the cause; you had to hunt for it. "Same thing," she told herself. "The bug is hiding in the script."

She read her blocks again, one at a time, like a detective. The "if touching coin" block sat there at the bottom, all by itself, outside everything. Maybe, she thought, it only got one chance to check, right when the script started, and after that it went to sleep. So she tried something. She found the "forever" block, dropped it around her movement blocks, and tucked the "if touching" block inside the forever loop. Then the cat would cross the coin, and the check would happen again and again, over and over, instead of just once.

She clicked the green flag and steered the cat onto the coin. The score jumped to one. "Grandpa! It works!" She bounced the cat around the garden like a small moon in orbit, collecting coin after coin, watching the number climb: two, five, nine. Grandpa tapped the screen. "Eleven coins? I demand a rematch after lunch." Alice grinned and hit the green flag one more time.

Emily sat on the fence rail at her grandfather's farm, a blank page on her clipboard, trying to formulate her science homework into something she could actually draw: a food chain that started with the sun and ended with a top predator. Sun, grass, grasshopper, frog, snake, hawk. That part was easy. The hard part was the second question: what happens when one link disappears?

She kept thinking about the science museum in town, the trip her class had taken last spring. There had been a big arch of wooden blocks, and a boy named Danny had pulled out the middle top stone. The whole arch had come down, blocks clattering everywhere, even though that one stone looked exactly like all the others. Emily had written about it in a postcard to her friend Rosa, and she dug it out of her pocket now, reading her own words again: "Danny pulled one stone and the arch fell. The guide said that stone was the keystone. One block, whole arch down."

She looked out at the hay field. A hawk circled low, then dove. "Grandpa," she called down the hill, "what if all the snakes around here disappeared? They're not that many." Her grandfather leaned on his rake and considered it. "Snakes eat frogs," he said. "Frogs eat grasshoppers."

Emily drew arrows in her mind. No snakes meant more frogs at first, then fewer grasshoppers, then the grass would grow unchecked, and the hawks that hunted snakes would go hungry or leave. The whole field could change from one missing link. It was like the arch, except the arch was blocks you could see, and this was a pattern you had to reason out. She could not watch it happen directly, but she could test the idea on paper, pulling one link out of her chain and following the arrows one at a time.

She wrote her answer: a species whose removal changes its whole community far more than its numbers would suggest is called a keystone species, and her example was the snake. Then, to keep herself objective, she tried removing the grasshopper instead, and the chain barely wobbled, because grasshoppers were numerous enough that the frogs would find other insects. Danny's stone had taught her something after all. She slid off the fence and ran down the hill to show her grandfather the page, waving it over her head.

"Look, it's the arch," she said.

In the market square in Sevilla, Arianna clutched her notebook and tried to remember why she had ever agreed to speak only Spanish for a whole day. Her older brother, Marco, had promised her ten euros if she could describe the entire family to their host, Señora Reyes, using full sentences before sunset. Ten euros was real income for a twelve-year-old with her eye on a leather journal in the shop by the cathedral, so she marched up to the kitchen table, sat down, and opened her notebook to the page of sentences she had written on the plane.

"Mi hermano Marco es alto," she began, pointing at Marco, who was leaning in the doorway looking smug. "Mi madre es simpática. Mi padre es muy alto también." Señora Reyes nodded along, smiling, and then asked the question Arianna had been dreading. "¿Tienes mascotas?" Arianna did have pets, two of them, and she flipped to her notes. She had written "un negro gato" for Midnight and "una blanca perra" for Pepper, because that was how you said it in English, black cat, white dog. She read the words out loud, and Señora Reyes tilted her head the way people do when something sounds wrong but they are too polite to say so.

Arianna's face went hot, but she refused to give up ten euros to embarrassment. She thought about the signs she had seen all morning, the bakery with "pan fresco" painted on its window, the stall selling "naranjas dulces." The describing word came second, every single time, like a rule hiding in plain sight. That had to imply something about her own sentences, so she tested it right there at the table. "Un gato negro," she said slowly, watching Señora Reyes's face, "y una perra blanca."

"¡Perfecto!" Señora Reyes clapped her hands. "Un gato negro," she repeated, and Marco, who had wandered over pretending to be indifferent, actually wrote it on his own hand.

By sunset Arianna had earned her ten euros, describing every cousin, every aunt, and even the neighbor's indifferent orange cat, and she marched straight to the shop by the cathedral. "Quiero el cuaderno negro," she told the shopkeeper, and when he handed her the exact right one, she grinned all the way to the door.

Justin spread the parts across the workbench in his grandfather's garage: marbles, wooden beads, a bag of tiny silver ball bearings, and a loop of stiff wire. The science fair was on Thursday, and his model of a helium atom had to be right.

He glued two marbles and two wooden beads together for the middle, then bent the wire into two rings around it. For the electrons he chose two more marbles, white ones, because they matched. He was reaching for the glue when his older sister Nadia came in to borrow the duct tape.

"Those are your electrons?" she said.

"Yeah, so?"

"Look it up." She tossed him her phone and took the tape.

Justin typed in the mass of a proton versus an electron. The number came back: a proton has about 1,836 times the mass of an electron. He read it twice. His white marbles were basically the same size as the marbles in the nucleus. He tried to picture what 1,836 marbles would look like, and the picture failed. The nucleus would weigh more than everything on the workbench put together.

So almost all of an atom's mass was packed into that little lump in the middle, he thought, and the electrons were almost nothing at all. His model said the opposite. He stood there holding a white marble in each hand, feeling like he'd built the whole thing backwards.

He tested it. He set one marble, for a proton, on the scale from the fishing tackle box. Then he tried to weigh a single ball bearing. The scale didn't even twitch. He added bearings one at a time, counting under his breath, and quit past fifty because his eyes were giving out and the needle had barely moved. That settled it.

He pried the marble electrons off the wire with a screwdriver and replaced them with two ball bearings, so small he had to glue them onto loops of thread to keep from losing them. The marbles and beads stayed in the nucleus, where the mass belonged. Then he made a card for the table: helium, two protons, two neutrons, two electrons, and underneath, in his most careful printing, that a proton has about 1,836 times the mass of an electron.

On Thursday a judge stopped at his table, a man with gray hair and a veteran air force jacket. He read the card, then picked up the model and turned it over in his hands.

"The kid who made this one," he said to the other judge, "actually looked it up instead of guessing." He set it down and tapped the nucleus with one finger. "Start here. Almost everything is in here."

Justin's face went hot, but not in a bad way. He glanced at the two ball bearings glinting on their threads and said, "They're the smallest parts I could find, and even they're way too big."

The judge laughed and wrote something on his clipboard.

Emily noticed it the way you notice a drip behind a wall: not all at once, but once you heard it, you couldn't stop. Maya, who used to demolish a whole slice of pizza at lunch and talk the whole time, now picked at crusts and said almost nothing. She'd stopped coming to Emily's house after school, too, and her texts had gone from long messages to one word: "busy." Emily kept a note in her binder and wrote down what she saw, dates and everything, because her mom called that kind of note-taking an analysis and said it helped you see patterns you'd otherwise miss.

The pattern was ugly. Maya's hands shook when the teacher called on her. She went to the bathroom three times during one math class. On Thursday, she left her lunch untouched and spent recess standing alone by the fence, staring at the field like it was a mile of open water she'd been told to swim.

Emily had a theory, and she knew it was a naive one, the kind you'd be embarrassed to say out loud: maybe Maya was just tired. But tired didn't explain the fence, or the shaking, or the "busy." So she decided to test it. She wrote a note and slipped it into Maya's locker, because Maya wouldn't look at anyone long enough to talk.

The note said: "You don't have to answer this. But if something's wrong, I won't tell the whole grade. I'd only tell one grown-up, and only if you said it was okay. Is something wrong? Circle yes or no."

On Friday morning Emily checked the locker slot between classes, her heart going like a drumroll. The note was there, folded into a tight square. Inside, in Maya's careful handwriting, a "yes" was circled so hard the pencil had torn the paper. Underneath: "I can't stop thinking bad stuff is going to happen. My cousin had this. He got help. Can you come over?"

They sat on Emily's porch after school, the wood warm and smelling like summer even though it was October, a jar of lemonade sweating between them. "My cousin sees a counselor," Maya said. "It's called cognitive behavioral therapy. It teaches you to notice the anxious thoughts and change them. He says it's one of the most effective treatments, and it works, because anxiety disorders are treatable." She took a breath. "I want that. But I'm scared to tell my mom."

"You wrote me a note because talking felt too big," Emily said. "So we'll do it smaller." She slid her binder across the porch, open to the page of dates and observations. "Show her this. You don't have to say anything first. She can read."

Maya's mom read it that evening, standing in the kitchen with flour still on her hands. When she finished, she sat down, pulled Maya's chair closer, and picked up the phone.

"Mrs. Alvarez, hi. I'd like to ask about scheduling an appointment."

Sawyer discovered the pimple on Tuesday morning, right in the middle of his chin, and school photos were on Friday. He leaned close to the bathroom mirror and prodded it, which only made it redder. In the kitchen he found a note from his mom, who had already left for work: "There's five dollars on the counter. The pharmacy on Miller Street has face wash. Ask the pharmacist if you're not sure which one. Love, Mom."

At the pharmacy, Sawyer stood in the aisle reading labels, feeling like his stamina for weird grown-up words was running out fast. Salicylic acid, benzoyl peroxide, oil-free. He finally carried two bottles to the counter, where a pharmacist with reading glasses on a chain looked up from a box of prescriptions.

"First one?" she asked.

"First one," Sawyer admitted. "I don't even get where it came from. I washed my face yesterday."

"Yesterday's not the problem," she said. "During puberty, hormones tell your skin's oil glands to make more oil. That oil is called sebum, and it can clog your pores. Clogged pores cause acne."

"So it's happening under there," Sawyer said slowly, "before I can even see it."

"Exactly." She tapped the smaller bottle. "This one, once a day. Be patient."

He tested the idea like a science experiment. Each morning he washed his face and swiped on deodorant, because if puberty was making oil glands work overtime, other changes were probably happening too, and his gym teacher had made some very explicit comments about the class needing showers after practice. His armpits had their own opinions now. He kept a chart on the back of his notebook, marking the pimple's size with a pencil dot each day. Wednesday, big dot. Thursday, smaller dot. Friday morning, the dot was barely a speck.

At photo time, Sawyer stood in line and turned his chin toward the camera anyway, just slightly, the way he'd practiced. The photographer counted down. Right before the flash, the kid behind him whispered, "Nice shirt."

"Thanks," Sawyer said. "Washed my face, too."

Naomi sat on the fence rail outside the barn with her science homework flattened against her knees. Sun, grass, grasshopper, frog, hawk: she was supposed to draw a food chain from the sun all the way up to a top predator, then explain what would happen if one link disappeared. She had the drawing part done. The second part made her stop. Would one missing link really change anything? Her cousin Theo, who was splitting wood nearby, was skeptical too. "It's a big farm," he said, resting the axe against the stump. "Take away one kind of bug and everything else just shrugs."

Naomi thought about the tide pools she had visited last summer on the Washington coast, and about the ranger there, an old man who had leaned on his walking stick and told them about a scientist named Robert Paine. "He took the starfish off a stretch of this shore," the ranger had said. "The starfish eat mussels. After that, the mussels took over the rocks and crowded out many other species." Naomi had stared at the wet stones that day, trying to picture the change, and now she knew exactly what to write.

But she wanted to test it, not just copy it. Theo followed her to the vegetable garden, where two rows of bean plants stood side by side. On one row, aphids clustered on the undersides of the leaves, thick as green sand. On the other row, ladybugs prowled the same leaves, and the plants looked clean. Last month, Uncle Ray had sprayed the far row and let the near one alone, and Naomi had decided back then not to intervene on either one, just to watch. The result was standing right in front of her.

She flipped her paper over and drew two arrows instead of one, from the sun to the beans to the aphids to the ladybugs, and then a heavy line through the ladybug link. She held it up so Theo could see. "This row is the shore without its starfish," she said, pointing at the crawling leaves.

Theo looked at the paper, then at the beans, and set the axe down for good. "Okay," he said. "Show me which one to draw first."

Parker slid into the booth at the Snowcap Cafe with his notebook, two pencils, and a hot chocolate so tall it could insulate an entire village against the February tundra outside. His older sister Dana dumped her own essay onto the table and stole a marshmallow off his whipped cream.

"You're doing my least favorite thing today," she said. "Five paragraphs. Introduction, three reasons, conclusion."

"Mrs. Okafor says the introduction grabs you like a fishhook," Parker said, "and the conclusion is where you let the fish go, but in a good mood."

"That's suspiciously poetic." Dana tapped his page. "What's your topic?"

"Longer recess. Obvious choice."

He wrote his three reasons in his messiest handwriting: kids focus better, kids get more exercise, kids stop going rebellious by fourth period. Dana read over his shoulder and made a sound like a deflating balloon.

"This is fine," she said, "but it's all one-sided. Nobody who disagrees with you is going to flip sides just because you listed three things they already decided to ignore."

"Then what's the point of the whole essay?"

Dana grinned, which was never a good sign. "Here's the weird thing I learned the hard way. You have to put in the best argument against you. State it fairly, like it's actually a good point. Then answer it. That answer is called a rebuttal. My English teacher circled mine in red and wrote 'finally' next to it, which was either a compliment or an insult."

Parker frowned at his page. "So I write that teachers say recess wastes class time, and then I knock it down?"

"No knocking. Fair first, then answer."

He tested the idea right there, reading his new paragraph aloud over the hiss of the espresso machine. "Some teachers argue that longer recess takes away learning time, which matters because our school days are already short. But students who get more breaks focus better afterward, so the time we lose comes back to us doubled." He looked up. "Dana. That sounds like I know what I'm talking about."

"You kind of do. Terrifying."

Parker copied the whole paragraph into his notebook, then drew a fishhook on the introduction and a small victorious fish on the conclusion. His hot chocolate had gone lukewarm, so he wrapped both hands around it anyway.

Dana slid his notebook back across the table. "Congratulations. You now write better than half of ninth grade."

"Only half?" Parker said. "I'm aiming for at least two-thirds by Friday."

He flagged down the cashier and ordered a second hot chocolate, for research purposes, and got back to work.

Jessica's problem was that Mrs. Okafor had written "Is it a physical change or a chemical change?" on the board, and Jessica's reflex was to guess chemical, because chemical sounded like the fancier answer. She had guessed chemical for melting ice, chemical for tearing paper, and chemical, most extravagantly, for dissolving salt in water. Three red X's in a row.

"It's a physical change," said her lab partner, Dex, who was careful with his goggles and even more careful with his answers. "Melting, tearing, dissolving. The stuff is still the stuff."

"Salt disappears, though," Jessica said. "That's not still the stuff. That's gone."

Dex shrugged, which was his way of saying he had done the reading and she had not.

Jessica refused to lose the argument on a shrug. She got two beakers, filled them with water, and stirred a spoon of salt into each one until the grains vanished. Then she covered one beaker and set the other, uncovered, on the sunny windowsill behind the aquarium. She wrote her name on masking tape and stuck it to the glass, because someone in third period had a habit of claiming every interesting experiment as their own.

For three days she checked the window. The water level crept down. On Friday the beaker held only a damp white crust along the bottom, and when Jessica scraped it with the spoon, the crystals crumbled exactly the way salt did, sharp and gritty on her fingertip. She touched her tongue to it, just barely, and winced.

"Dex," she said, holding up the beaker. "It came back."

He leaned over. "Same salt?"

"Same salt. Evaporating the water leaves it behind." She tapped the glass. "So it's physical. The water went somewhere, but the salt never turned into anything else. It was just hiding."

Mrs. Okafor walked past, looked into the beaker, and wrote something in her binder without a word. Jessica decided that was probably a good sign.

She poured fresh water onto the crust and watched the salt slip away into it again, invisible, patient, ready to argue with her some other day.

The clock above the whiteboard showed four minutes left when Mrs. Okafor dropped the bomb. "Last problem of the day," she said. "First correct answer earns the resilient green trophy, and it stays on your desk all week."

Colton's pencil was already moving. The problem was 1/3 + 1/4, and fractions with different bottom numbers had beaten him before.
