In October, on a worksheet he still remembered, he had written 2/7 and handed it in feeling proud, only to find a big red circle around it. His grandfather had looked at that worksheet that night and said only, "Sevenths and thirds don't speak the same language, kiddo. Find a language they both speak." Colton had stared at the page until bedtime without finding it.

Now Marcus across the table was scribbling fast, and Priya had her hand halfway up already. Colton felt his heart hammering against his ribs like something trying to escape.

Different denominators. Same language. What language did thirds and fourths both speak? He gripped his pencil. Twelveths, a voice in his head whispered, and he almost wrote it, but he didn't know where the whisper came from, so he tested it the way his grandfather tested a fence post, by pushing.

Three times four is twelve. A third of twelve is four, so 1/3 equals 4/12. A fourth of twelve is three, so 1/4 equals 3/12. Four twelfths plus three twelfths, seven twelfths. His hand shot up so fast he knocked over his eraser.

Priya had written 7/12 too, but her scratch paper was blank. "How?" she whispered as Mrs. Okafor checked both papers.

"I multiplied the denominators," Colton whispered back, keeping his voice low so Marcus couldn't steal it. "Three times four is twelve, and twelve works for both."

"Then why is yours crossed out?" Priya pointed. Colton's paper showed 7/12, then 7/12 again in bigger print, because he had checked it twice before raising his hand.

Mrs. Okafor held up both papers. "Both correct. But Priya, show us yours." Priya stood frozen, her blank scratch paper glowing under the lights like snow on the tundra, wide and empty and offering nowhere to hide.

"He taught me," she blurted, pointing at Colton. "Just now. Multiplying the denominators always gives you a number both fractions can use."

Mrs. Okafor raised an eyebrow. "It always works," she agreed, "though you don't always get the smallest one that way. Sometimes you'll have to simplify afterward. Priya, how did you get seven twelfths with no work shown?"

The room went quiet. Priya looked at the floor, then at the poster that depicted the fraction wall, thirds in one row, fourths in the row beneath, and the two rows meeting exactly at twelve.

"I counted the bricks on the poster," she admitted.

Mrs. Okafor laughed and set the little green trophy down between them. "Then share it. Colton gets it Monday, Wednesday, and Friday."

"Deal," Colton said, and slid it across the table to Priya first.

Gavin had been sitting on the floor between the shelves of Second Story Books for forty minutes, and his worksheet still said the same thing: "Find the theme of your novel. Support it with one quotation." The novel was The Castle on Vale Street, and the quote he'd chosen was "Some families are just born bad, and nothing can change that." It felt strong. It felt like the whole point of the book. But something about it tickled at him, like a word he'd almost remembered.

Across the aisle, Priya was flipping through a nature magazine, reading about birds that migrate across whole oceans every autumn. Gavin crawled over to her and held out his worksheet. "Does this work? The theme is that some families are born bad."

Priya squinted at the quote. Then she tipped her head. "Who says it in the book?"

"The grandmother," Gavin said. "Right before she locks the gate."

Priya laughed and tossed her magazine aside. "She's the villain. She's the one the whole story is fighting against."

Gavin sat back on his heels. Was that how it worked? Could a book put a character's opinion in your mouth only to knock it down? He raced back through the chapters in his head. The grandmother said it, yes, but then Rosa spent the entire book proving the opposite, teaching her little brother to read, breaking the lock on the gate. Maybe the author had planted the grandmother's cruel idea there on purpose, the way a magician plants a card, so the ending could flip it over.

He smelled the dusty vanilla of the old shop and pulled the novel back off the shelf, hunting for Rosa's line near the end. He found it on page 198: "We are not what we inherit. We are what we do next." Hereditary bad luck, the grandmother had claimed, and Rosa had answered her anyway.

Gavin copied the new quote in his best handwriting. "So the theme is whatever the book argues for," he said slowly, "not whatever a character argues for."

"Exactly," said Priya, and pointed at his pencil. "Now underline it before you forget."

Peyton stood in the doorway of Ratskeller, the German restaurant her mother had picked for her birthday dinner, and realized the plan had a flaw. Her mother had disappeared toward the back, the hostess had vanished with a tray, and Peyton had no idea where anything was. Every sign was in curly German letters she couldn't read.

It wasn't that she knew nothing. Every Tuesday in German class, Frau Bell had them play a game where one kid wore a blindfold and a partner steered them around the room using only three words. Peyton had been the guide last week, marching her blindfolded friend Maya between the desks. "Links means left," Peyton had said, turning Maya by the elbow. "Rechts means right. And geradeaus means straight ahead, so walk, don't wobble." Maya had giggled the whole way and walked straight into the recycling bin anyway. Peyton had laughed too, but the words had stuck like gum to a shoe.

Now she hovered near the kitchen, feeling like she was on a scavenger hunt with no clue sheet. A waiter rushed past carrying two enormous plates, and behind him a man with silver hair leaned toward a woman at the register and asked a question Peyton caught only pieces of: "Wo ist ... ?" The woman answered quickly, "Durch die Tür, dann links, und geradeaus." Door, then links, then geradeaus. Peyton's heart sped up. Left and straight ahead, she thought. That's the pattern. A bathroom was usually down a little hallway like that, and if the man was asking, the answer had to be directions.

She followed the silver-haired man at a distance, past the kitchen door, then watched him turn left and head straight down a narrow corridor. She counted the words against his feet. Links when he went left, geradeaus when he kept going. It matched. But at the end of the hall he didn't stop at any bathroom door. He pushed through the last door on the right, and light and music spilled out, and a dozen voices shouted something in German that ended with her mother's name.

The room was full of her mother's friends, a cake in the middle of the table big enough that a whole basketball team could consume it in one sitting. "Surprise," her mother said, switching to English and grinning. "Happy birthday, Peyton." The silver-haired man turned around, and Peyton saw he was her uncle from Hamburg, the one who always sent postcards. "You followed me," he said, raising his eyebrows. "The whole way?"

"Links, then geradeaus," Peyton said. "Though I was hoping for a bathroom."

Her uncle laughed and pointed back down the hall. "That one is rechts, first door." He held out a slice of cake taller than her hand. "But eat first. Whether it is the best cake in the family is subjective, and your grandmother has been arguing about it all afternoon."

Nicolas raised his hand in health class so fast his chair squeaked. "Question. Why do we suddenly smell? Like, what actually happens?"

Ms. Reyes pointed at the diagram on the board. "Sweat glands switch on during puberty. Sweat itself doesn't smell much, but bacteria on your skin eat it, and that's what smells."

"Bacteria," Nicolas repeated. "So the smell is basically bacteria leftovers."

"Basically, yes."

"Then the principle is simple. Kill the bacteria, or wash them off, every day. Showers and deodorant." He said it like he'd discovered electricity.

Behind him, Marcus muttered, "We know, dude. We've been using deodorant since September."

"Have you, though," said Priya, waving a hand in front of her nose. "Because there's an objective way to test it. I can smell you from here."

The class laughed. Marcus turned pink. "Okay, fine, I keep forgetting it. My brother says I don't need it yet."

That afternoon, Nicolas sat in Dr. Okafor's office for his sports physical. He'd been thinking about Marcus all day, and about himself, because his own voice had done a weird squeak during announcements that morning. "Can I ask something off topic?" he said. "Marcus thinks nothing's happening to him yet, so he doesn't need deodorant. And I'm the shortest kid in class and nothing's happening to me either. Is that normal, or are we broken?"

Dr. Okafor shook her head. "Puberty usually begins between ages 8 and 13 in girls and between 9 and 14 in boys, and starting anywhere in that range is normal. You're eleven. You've got time."

"So some kids start at nine, some at fourteen, and it's all fine?"

"All fine."

Nicolas walked back to school to meet Marcus, who was waiting by the gym doors. "Good news," Nicolas said. "We're not broken. You could start at nine or all the way at fourteen, still normal."

"Cool," said Marcus. "So I don't need deodorant."

"No. The bacteria don't care about your schedule." Nicolas pulled a stick of deodorant out of his backpack and held it out like a trophy. "Stolen from my dad's drawer. It's yours. I'm enforcing the principle."

Marcus sniffed it, shrugged, and swiped it on right there on the gym steps.

Emily stood in the steamy bathroom, holding the deodorant stick like evidence in a case she was trying to solve. Three days ago her older brother, Josh, had walked past her room, wrinkled his nose, and said, "Shower much?" She had thrown a sock at him, but later, in the dark, she had sniffed her own armpit and understood he wasn't just being a jerk. Something had changed, and she wanted to know what, and whether she could do anything about it.

She remembered the appointment last spring, when Josh had asked Dr. Patel the question straight out: "What actually tells the body it's time for puberty?" Emily had braced for a lecture, but the doctor had just said, "The pituitary gland in the brain signals the ovaries or testes to make more estrogen or testosterone." That was it. Josh had nodded like it was obvious, but Emily had chewed on it for weeks. A tiny gland, sending a chemical message. Nobody could see it happen. You could only see the results, the same way you couldn't see the rain coming but could watch the gutters fill.

So the smell wasn't a personal failure, she reasoned. It was a message from her own brain, and sweat glands reacting to it, and bacteria having a party in a warm damp armpit. That was the hidden cause, and hidden causes could still be interrupted. She had a simple idea to test: if she showered every morning and used deodorant right after drying off, before the bacteria could settle in, would the smell stay gone?

Her plan had two components, the daily shower and the deodorant, and she'd taped a checklist inside the medicine cabinet to keep herself honest. Day one had been easy because it was new. Day two, she'd almost skipped it, wanting ten more minutes of sleep, and had regretted that choice by lunch when she caught herself keeping her arms clamped to her sides in science class. Maybe she should have just gotten up. Maybe it didn't matter that much. She still wasn't sure.

Today was day three. She turned off the water, dried off, and swept the deodorant on before her skin had even finished cooling. The clean scent rose up sharp and minty through the steam. She pulled on her shirt, sniffed the collar once, and flipped the checklist to mark the square. From the hallway, Josh banged on the door. "You alive in there?"

"Busy," Emily called back. "Science experiment."

At Sunday dinner Adam could hardly sit still, because he had a message on his phone and he was dying to tell everyone. His cousin Marcus had texted him: "You won't believe it. Two kids at my party fought over the last piece of cake, and their dad just cut it himself and both kids screamed. How do you split cake without a war?" Adam had pushed his mashed potatoes around his plate all through dinner, thinking about it, and now he set down his fork.

"Marcus needs help," he announced. "Two kids fighting over cake. If you just cut it, someone always yells that the pieces aren't even." His dad started to say something, but Adam held up a hand. "Wait. I have an idea." He grabbed the leftover garlic bread, tore off a chunk, and put it in the middle of the table. "Okay, Dad, you and me. You split this into two parts, and I pick first." His dad cut it, eyeing the knife carefully, and Adam grabbed the bigger piece immediately. His dad groaned. They tried it again with Adam as the cutter, and this time he measured and turned the bread, slowing down, until the two parts looked exactly alike, because if he didn't, his dad would grab the better one.

"It's called divide and choose," Adam said, bouncing in his chair. "One person splits, the other picks first." His little sister demanded a turn, so he halved a dinner roll for her and she studied both halves like a judge before choosing. She pronounced them fair. Adam summarized the whole thing in a text back to Marcus: "Don't cut the cake. Let one kid divide it and the other kid picks first. Divider makes it equal or loses out."

"Smart," his mom said, collecting plates. "Your grandfather settled fights that way for years. That man ran this family like a dynasty, and that was his only rule that never failed."

"It's not arbitrary," Adam said, typing fast. "It actually works."

Then he hit send and ran for the phone to call Marcus.

Emilie arranged the strawberry baskets in a neat pyramid, the way Mrs. Okafor had shown her on her first Saturday at the farm stand. It was her third weekend working the counter, and she had begun to classify the customers in her head: the ones who bought two baskets without asking the price, the ones who squeezed every basket first, and the ones who walked away slowly, glancing back as if the strawberries might call after them.

That morning Mrs. Okafor had taped a new sign to the register. "Four dollars a basket today," she said, rubbing her hands together. "The winter crop cost me double what the summer one did, so the price is double too." Emilie remembered July, when the baskets had been two dollars and the line had stretched past the honey stand, ten and twelve people deep all morning. Her instinct had been to wave customers over the moment she spotted them.

Nobody waved today. A woman in a green coat picked up a basket, turned it over, looked at the sign, and set it back down. A man asked whether the price was a mistake. By eleven o'clock the line was gone, and the pyramid of baskets stood untouched except for one lonely sale. "I was pessimistic about the whole day anyway," Mrs. Okafor said, counting the register. "I always am when I have to raise prices."

Emilie couldn't stop thinking about it. Nothing else had changed: same berries, same stand, same Saturday crowd. Only the price had moved, and the buyers had vanished. She turned the idea over while she restacked baskets, and then she had it, the shape of a rule she couldn't see but could watch working. When the price of something rises, people buy less of it, as long as nothing else changes. She wanted to test it before she trusted it.

"Can we try something for the last hour?" she asked. "Put the price back to two dollars, just to see what happens." Mrs. Okafor frowned at her, then at the full crates that would spoil unsold. "We'd lose money on every basket," she said, but she was already peeling the old sign off the register.

They taped up a new one. Emilie stood at the counter with her heart tapping, and within ten minutes a boy from her science class was buying two baskets, then the woman in the green coat came back, then a family of four. The line rebuilt itself, basket by basket, stretching toward the honey stand just like July. Mrs. Okafor watched from behind the register, arms folded, saying nothing, and Emilie slid the last crate forward to face the crowd.

"Funny thing," Mrs. Okafor said at closing, counting a register that was fuller than the morning's. "In summer I sell cheap and sell out. In winter I sell dear and sit here all day." She held up a worn dollar bill. "Same rule both ways, isn't it?"

"That's the whole thing," Emilie said, snapping the lid on the empty crate. "Price goes up, buying goes down. Price goes down, and look at that line."

Mrs. Okafor laughed and dropped the bill into the drawer. "Then you'd better be here next Saturday."

Aiden had exactly one week before the astronomy club's night hike, and the telescope at Hendricks' Hobby Shop was on sale for one hundred fifty dollars. He had forty-two. His mom had said something careful about money being tight this month, so Aiden went to his friend Priya, who was drawing bats on her binder.

"You could put it on your mom's credit card and pay her back later," Priya said.

"That's what I thought too," Aiden said. "Then I found her card agreement in the junk drawer, that whole contract thing they send in the envelope. It said twenty-four percent interest if you don't pay it all off."

Priya wrinkled her nose. "Twenty-four percent of what, though? That's like, twenty-four cents on a dollar. That's nothing."

Aiden had thought the same thing until Thursday, when he was killing time in the library and found a book about money with a whole chapter on debt. He read one line twice, then carried it to Priya's table and read it out loud. "It's called the rule of 72," he said. "Watch. You divide 72 by the yearly interest rate, and that's about how many years money takes to double."

Priya grabbed his pencil. "Seventy-two divided by twenty-four is..." She counted on her fingers, then wrote the number three in the margin of her notebook. "Three? So if your mom couldn't pay it off, the hundred fifty dollars would turn into about three hundred in three years?"

"That's the part I got wrong," Aiden admitted. "I thought interest just sat there. It grows." He copied the math onto his hand so he wouldn't forget it. "So the telescope costs one hundred fifty dollars, or it could cost three hundred. Saving up first is the real sale."

That night a message was taped to the fridge in his mom's handwriting. "Aiden, if you're serious about the telescope, here's my offer. I'll cover the rest, but only after you've saved your share, and only if it comes with a warranty in case you drop it off a hill. Love, Mom. P.S. Who ate the last of the cheddar? Owls are nocturnal. So, apparently, are cheese thieves."

Aiden laughed, then checked the club schedule and groaned. The night hike was Saturday. He had four days and one hundred eight dollars to go. He shoveled two driveways, sold three old graphic novels to the used bookstore, and helped Mr. Hendricks stack boxes behind the shop for ten dollars and a promise not to tell anyone he'd cried during a planetarium show in fifth grade.

On Saturday, Aiden counted out crisp bills at the register while his mom watched with her arms crossed, smiling. Mr. Hendricks slid the box across the counter, tapped the warranty card stapled to the receipt, and said, "You're the first kid all year who paid cash. What's your secret?"

Aiden hefted the box onto his shoulder. "Seventy-two divided by twenty-four."

The geology hall had a contest table set up beside the gift shop, and Landon spotted the sign right away. Sort twelve mystery rocks into igneous, sedimentary, or metamorphic before the three o'clock buzzer, and your name went into a drawing for a summer science scholarship to the museum's day camp. It was 2:37. His cousin Maya grabbed his sleeve. "We can do this. You're the one who reads all those rock books."

Landon picked up the first rock, dark and speckled, and dropped it into the igneous bin. "Cooled from melt," he said. "The speckles give it away." The second one had stripes, like somebody had folded chocolate into vanilla dough, and he hesitated. Heat and pressure did that, so it went to metamorphic. Then he hit a problem: a gray rock with layers, but the layers looked kind of melted and swirled at one end. Layered said sedimentary. Swirled said igneous. He set it on the table between the bins and frowned at it like it was trying to trick him.

"You're stuck," Maya said. She wasn't teasing; she was watching the clock, which now said 2:52.

"It's violating my system," Landon said. "I thought each rock was one thing, forever and always." Then he looked up. Behind the contest table hung a big wall poster with arrows looping every which way, and at the bottom, in curly letters, it said that in the rock cycle, any type of rock can become any other type, through melting, weathering, or heat and pressure. "Maya. Look. Any rock can become any other. Sediment can squeeze into sedimentary, that can melt into igneous, that can get cooked into metamorphic, and around again. This one's caught mid-way, maybe sedimentary that got squeezed." He dropped it into the metamorphic bin and it felt right in his hand.

They sorted the last three rocks with two minutes to spare, and the volunteer at the table, an influential geologist whose name was on half the plaques in the hall, leaned over their bins. "Eleven of twelve," she said. "That swirly gray one. Bold guess. Tell me why." Landon took a breath and pointed at the poster. "Because nothing stays just one kind of rock forever."

Muhammad stood at home plate gripping a bat he wasn't going to swing, because today the diamond was his pretend pool. His swim test was on Saturday, twenty-five metres of front crawl with side breathing, and every time he took a breath in the real pool he lifted his whole face out of the water, splashed, and stalled. His best friend Danilo sat cross-legged on the pitcher's mound, watching him pivot his head side to side.

"Slower," Danilo said. "You look like you're checking for rain."

Muhammad stopped and thought about the fastest kid in their lane, a boy named Sam who swam like a motorboat. Yesterday, from the bench, Muhammad had noticed something odd. Every time Sam breathed, half of his face seemed to stay down. One goggle lens stayed under the water while the other popped up, and he turned only far enough for his mouth to clear the surface. Muhammad had been hoisting his whole face to the sky, and every single breath cost him speed. He cherished that observation, because it was the first clue he'd found in three weeks of sinking.

"Okay, new idea," Muhammad said. He dropped the bat, lay down in the dusty infield grass, and paddled his arms in slow motion. "My left goggle stays in the water. I turn just enough to get my mouth out. Just enough. Not to the sky." He rolled his head, keeping his right ear glued to the water that wasn't there, and made a snapping little breath through the corner of his mouth. Then his face went right back down.

Danilo counted for him, calling out strokes from the mound, and on the fifth breath Muhammad's roll was smooth enough that Danilo clapped. "That looked spontaneous," he said, "like you weren't even thinking about it."

"That's the whole point," Muhammad said, breathing again, faster now, arms wheeling through the dust. The team had a hierarchy for the Saturday lanes, slowest swimmers in lane one, and Muhammad was tired of lane one. He rolled, breathed with one goggle up, dropped his face, and kept his windmill arms turning all the way to the make-believe wall at second base.

On Saturday morning, Muhammad pushed off and counted his strokes, and at the first breath he kept his left lens in the water, turned only far enough for his mouth to clear the surface, and felt himself keep moving. When he slapped the far wall, Danilo was leaning over the lane rope, holding up two fingers.

"Lane two," Danilo shouted. "I heard Coach say it."

Colton had one job at the town hall meeting: narrate the slide show while his class presented their project on how laws get made. He stood at the front, clicker shaking slightly in his hand, while half the town sat on folding chairs eating cookies his grandmother had brought because she knew everyone would be hungry after school.

"First," Colton said, "a bill gets introduced in the legislature." He clicked to his drawing of a bill trudging up some stairs. He had given it a sad face and a briefcase, and a few people laughed, which made him feel warmer. "Then it gets debated. Then it gets voted on."

His classmate Priya leaned over and whispered, "You're missing a whole house. Federal bills have to pass the House of Commons and then the Senate."

Colton stared at his slide. His bill was only climbing one staircase. He thought about the provincial bill they had read about in the paper, the one about bike helmets. It had gone to the legislature, then it had become law, and he could not remember any second vote. Federal bills crossed two houses like two bridges. The bike helmet bill had only crossed one.

He clicked forward anyway. "But a provincial bill," he said, pointing at his drawing, "only passes one chamber. One staircase. Then the lieutenant governor gives royal assent." He looked at his teacher, who was holding two fingers up, then folding one down, like a referee confirming a score.

"That's right," his teacher said quietly, and Colton let out a breath he had been storing since the monsoon of nerves that hit him backstage, the kind that had soaked his shirt before a single word.

Afterward, an old man in a rain jacket, still damp from the drizzle outside, tapped Colton's shoulder. "Frugal government, one staircase," he said, smiling. "Want a cookie? Your grandmother's been saving the biggest one for you."

Colton took it in both hands.

Alex had one job at the Saturday community kitchen: bake the blueberry muffins all by himself, start to finish, while his grandmother ran the front table. The recipe card sat propped against the flour canister, soft from years of use. He measured, he cracked eggs, he folded berries in with a gentle wrist. Then he read the first line again. "Preheat oven to 375 degrees." He glanced at the clock. The lunch rush started in fifty minutes, and the oven took forever to heat up. Nobody would know if the muffins went in while the oven was still cold. They would just bake and heat at the same time, and he would save ten whole minutes.

He slid the tray in and pressed the button. Ten minutes later, the kitchen smelled right. Twenty minutes later, he pulled the tray out, and something was off. The muffins were pale on top, flat, and dense in the middle, nothing like the golden domes his grandmother made. "Huh," Alex said to the empty kitchen. He turned a muffin over and studied the pale bottom.

His friend Marisol came through the swinging door carrying an empty bread basket. "Whoa. What happened to those?" She picked one up and squished it gently. "These look sad." Alex explained that he had put them in before the oven finished heating, to save time. Marisol raised an eyebrow, her skepticism plain on her face. "My mom calls that skipping preheating," she said. "The batter has to go in only after the oven has reached the set temperature, so baking starts at the right heat." She shrugged. "That's all I know, but she says it like it's a law."

Alex looked at the recipe card, then at the wall clock, then at his flat muffins. Maybe the oven's slowness at the start had changed how they baked, even though the heat eventually arrived. He had a test for that idea. He still had enough batter for a second batch, and this time he would follow the first line exactly, no shortcuts, and see if the results came out distinct from the first batch or exactly the same. If they were the same, Marisol's mom's law was wrong. If they were different, he had found the problem.

He set the oven, and while it climbed toward 375 he washed the mixing bowl and lined the second tray with paper cups. The little indicator light glowed until, with a soft click, it went out. Alex opened the door and felt the wave of heat roll over his wrists. He slid the tray in and set the timer.

Twenty minutes later the muffins stood tall and golden. Marisol came back for the bread basket and stopped in the doorway. "Now those are muffins." She stacked two on a napkin for the front table and handed one to Alex, still warm. He took a bite, and before he could say anything, she said, "I'm officially boycotting the flat ones."

Eli crouched at the edge of the pond with his notebook, trying to draw a food chain for science homework. Sun, then algae, then a mayfly larva, then a frog, then a heron. He kept messing up the heron's beak so it looked like a shovel, like the bird planned to excavate the whole pond.

His little sister Josie plopped down beside him, chewing a granola bar. "That's not a heron. That's a pickle with legs."

"It's a top predator. Eat your snack." Eli frowned at the page. The assignment had a trick question at the bottom: what happens if one link disappears? He'd written "the frog goes hungry," but that felt too small, like saying a bridge falls down because one person trips.

"Every food chain starts with the sun," Josie said, reading over his shoulder. "We learned that in third grade."

"Obviously," said Eli. Then he stopped. Had he actually checked? He tested it right there on the bank, tracing his chain backward: heron, frog, larva, algae, sun. Worked. But was it a rule for everywhere, or just here?

"Except the dark ocean," said Josie, waving her granola bar. "We watched a movie about it. In 1977, scientists in a submarine called Alvin went down and found whole communities of animals living around deep-sea vents, pitch black, no sun ever. Totally radical."

"Submarine?"

"Submersible. Alvin. 1977. It was in the movie, I remember everything." She tapped her temple. "The food chains down there start with bacteria that use chemicals from the vents. Chemicals, not sunlight."

Eli sat back. The willow canopy dappled the water where his algae floated, sun-fed and green. Miles below some ocean, bacteria ran a whole neighborhood on vent chemicals instead. So his chain wasn't a universal law, just a local one, which felt both annoying and excellent, like finding a secret door in his own house.

He wrote his answer: here, remove the algae and the frog, the heron, everything above it collapses, because at this pond the sun is the bottom link. Then he drew a tiny Alvin at the corner of the page, just to show the teacher he knew about the exception.

"For the pickle heron," Josie said, "you should draw it eating a sea pickle."

"Sea pickles are real, Josie."

"Then draw two."

Daniel had a reputation in math club for being the fastest at times tables, but fractions with different denominators made him freeze like a deer on a road. Today Mrs. Okafor had posted the problem 1/4 plus 1/6, and Daniel wanted more than anything to be the one who solved it on the board, because last week Marcus had beaten him twice.

Daniel tried adding straight across, and got 2/10. He stared at it. Two tenths was smaller than one quarter alone, which could not be right. Something hidden was going on, some rule he could not see, and he decided to test an idea. He drew two candy bars on scrap paper and cut one into fourths and one into sixths. The pieces did not match up. Fourths were fat, sixths were skinny. He needed slices that fit both bars, so he kept cutting until the fourths split into three parts each and the sixths split into two parts each. Both bars now had twelve slices. He wrote 3/12 plus 2/12 equals 5/12, and his hand shot up.

Before Mrs. Okafor could call on him, Priya passed him a folded note, which was against the rules but everyone did it. In round handwriting it read, "I used 24 for the denominator and got 10/24. Did you get that too?" Daniel frowned. His answer was 5/12. He checked whether both numbers matched by cutting his paper bars again, and 5/12 and 10/24 named the same amount, but his numbers were smaller and simpler. He wrote back, "Try 12. It works." Priya's eyes went wide, and she raised her hand too.

"I found twelve," Daniel said at the board, "because the least common denominator is the smallest number both denominators divide into evenly." Priya nodded and added, "For quarters and sixths it is twelve. Twenty-four works, but twelve is smaller." Marcus, who had been smug all month, slid his chair backward and migrated to their table to see the candy bar drawings.

Mrs. Okafor smiled and put a new problem on the board. It was inevitable that harder ones would come, but Daniel had his paper and his scissors, and he was already drawing.

Clara pressed her nose against the glass case outside the school library, where a purple mountain bike sat on a folded towel with a price tag that read one hundred eighty dollars. She had counted her savings twice last night: forty-one dollars and some coins. Her mother had said, maybe for your birthday, but her birthday was in March, and the trails behind the school turned golden in October.

At dinner, her uncle Ray was squinting at a piece of paper and shaking his head. "Every month I send them money," he muttered, "and this bill barely shrinks. It's like pouring water into a bucket with a hole in it."

Clara slid into the chair across from him. "How much do you send?"

"Twenty-five dollars. That's the minimum they ask for." He tapped the paper. "But most of it, they keep. It's interest, and it's been years now."

Clara frowned. That didn't seem possible. Twenty-five dollars a month, month after month, and the number hardly went down? She took the bill to the kitchen table and did what her math teacher called a test: she circled every payment on the page, then beside each one she wrote the amount the balance had dropped. Eleven dollars. Nine dollars. Ten and a half. The rest of every payment was going somewhere she couldn't see, month after month, so the paying off just kept stretching out longer and longer, like taffy.

"Uncle Ray," she said slowly, "if you paid more than the minimum, would it end sooner?"

He rubbed his chin. "Wouldn't it be the same either way? Twenty-five is twenty-five."

She slid her paper toward him. He looked at her circles, then at the bill, then at her again. "Huh," he said. "All those years, I could have been done by now." He laughed, a short surprised sound, and folded the bill into his pocket like it was something new.

The next morning Clara stood at the case again. Eighty dollars meant waiting, and waiting was a real cost too, she could feel that. But the probability of the bike still sitting there in October seemed better than the probability of her uncle's bill ever disappearing at twenty-five dollars a month. She could ride the trails this fall owing nothing to anyone, or she could have the bike now and a shadow trailing behind it for years.

A sixth grader wandered up beside her and pointed at the price tag. "My dad just puts stuff like that on a card," he said.

Clara looked at the purple frame, the clean silver spokes, and thought of her uncle's bill, going on and on. "You know," she said, "the minimum payment is a trap. I'd save up first."

Noemie's book club met Saturday morning, which gave her exactly one evening to figure out what she wanted to say about The Great Gatsby. Her mother had promised she could stay up until ten, and the kitchen clock already said 7:42. She spread the library's battered copy across the table, next to a bowl of pretzels she was eating more out of stress than hunger.

The problem was Ms. Okafor's assignment: track one symbol across the whole novel and explain how its meaning changes from chapter to chapter. A symbol, Noemie had decided by dinnertime, was the sneakiest thing in fiction. It looked like an object, but it was secretly carrying ideas around, the way her landlord carried a clipboard that seemed to convey the message "I can raise the rent whenever I want." Objects that meant things. Fine. But which object, and what did it mean, and when?

She flipped back to chapter one, and there it was. On the very first night of the story, someone in her book club had noticed, Gatsby stands in his yard reaching his arms out toward the water. Noemie reread the page, and her pencil stopped. A green light glows at the end of Daisy Buchanan's dock, across the water from Gatsby's house. Gatsby is reaching toward it. "Okay," she said to the pretzel bowl. "That's the symbol."

Now she needed the change. She made three columns on a sticky note: chapter one, chapter five, chapter nine. In chapter one, Gatsby stretches toward the light like it's something he can grab. She wrote "wanting." In chapter five, she found the scene where he shows Daisy the green light from his own yard, and it suddenly seemed smaller, almost ordinary, like a firefly that had gone extinct somewhere between chapters. She wrote "having, sort of." Then chapter nine gave her the line about the green light, the enormous thing Gatsby had yearned for, and she sat back. The light hadn't moved. The dock hadn't moved. Gatsby's whole life had moved around it, and that was the trick. She wrote "too big to hold," underlined it twice, and looked up at the clock. 9:51. Nine minutes to spare.

At book club the next morning, Marcus went first and talked about cars for six straight minutes. When Noemie's turn came, she held up her sticky note, which had lost a corner to the pretzel bowl. "It's the green light at Daisy's dock," she said. "Same light every time. It's the guy looking at it who changes."

Ms. Okafor tapped her pencil once against her chair. "And in the last chapter?"

"It outgrew him," Noemie said, "or he outgrew his own idea of it." Marcus, who had not read the last chapter, quietly turned to the back of his book and started skimming.

Piper had been at Camp Blue Heron for eleven days, and she had skipped the shower nine times. It wasn't laziness, exactly. The showers were cold, the line was long, and nobody had ever told her why it mattered. Then, on Tuesday, her bunkmate Dahlia leaned over during lunch and whispered, "Piper, you might want to try the deodorant in the camp store. My mom packed me two sticks because she said I'd need them." Piper had smelled it herself that morning, a sour whiff that came and went, and she'd wondered where it came from, since she couldn't see anything on her shirt.

That night she stood in line for the shower after all, testing an idea. The smell wasn't in her clothes, because her clothes were clean from home. It came from her, but only after she'd sweated, and it got stronger on the days she skipped washing. Something invisible was happening on her skin, and washing and deodorant were changing it. She tried both, morning after morning, and by Friday the result was consistent: shower plus deodorant equaled no sour smell. She felt like she'd solved a mystery with clues nobody could see.

But Friday also brought a red bump on her chin, right before the end-of-session party with the boys' camp across the lake. Piper locked herself in the bathroom stall with her fingers already raised to squeeze it flat. "Stop!" said a voice. It was Josie, the oldest girl in her cabin, a fifteen-year-old on a scholarship who wanted to be a nurse someday. "Squeezing or popping pimples can push bacteria deeper into the skin and can leave scars," Josie said through the door. "Trust me. Ask my chin from last summer."

Piper lowered her hand. "Then what do I do?"

"Wash it, leave it alone, and let it dissolve into your good looks by morning," said Josie. "Come on, they're doing the bonfire songs early tonight."

Piper looked at the bump one more time, then opened the door and followed her out toward the fire.

Savannah stood in the empty community theatre with her script rolled in one fist, waiting for Mrs. Okafor's verdict. She had performed her monologue three times, and three times the director had said the same thing: "It's all one speed, Savannah. Where do you stop to think?" Savannah wanted the role of the lighthouse keeper more than she had wanted anything since the summer her family almost moved away, and she could not figure out what she was doing wrong. The words were right. The feelings were right. Something invisible was missing.

In the third row, chewing a straw, sat Marcus, the eighth grader who had been in eleven plays. He flipped through his own script, and Savannah noticed something she had never seen before: pencil slashes cut across the pages, a dozen on some pages, like little fences between the lines. "What are those?" she asked. Marcus shrugged. "Beats. A new beat starts wherever the character's thought or tactic changes. The pause is where you switch." Savannah frowned. "But a pause is just... nothing. Empty air." Marcus grinned. "That's what everyone thinks at first."

She took her script to the lobby and read it like a detective. The lighthouse keeper begins by begging the storm to spare her sister's boat. Then, halfway down the page, the keeper stops begging and starts bargaining, offering herself instead. Savannah read the speech aloud in a whisper and found it: the thought changed right after the line "Take me instead of her." She drew a slash there, and two more, one for every place the keeper's mind turned. Then she abandoned her old plan of rushing through the whole speech before she lost her nerve, because now she could see the speech had doors in it, and she was allowed to stand in each doorway.

The twist came at the next rehearsal. Savannah paused after "Take me instead of her," and Mrs. Okafor called out, "Perfect. That's exactly the beat." But when she paused again after "I have kept this light for thirty years," the director tilted her head. "Why are you stopping there?" Savannah froze. She had marked it because it sounded like a big line, but the keeper's thought hadn't actually changed there; she was still bargaining, just louder. "I don't know," Savannah admitted. "I think I put a slash where it just felt dramatic." Mrs. Okafor laughed. "Then erase it. A pause without a reason is just dead air."

Savannah erased the slash, and the monologue snapped together like a lock. In the performance, when she reached the bargaining line, she let the silence stretch until she could hear someone in the second row hold their breath, and only then did she say, "Take me instead of her." Afterward Marcus found her by the snack table, where they split a stale pretzel like it was a treaty ending a long war. "You paused forever," he said. "I thought you forgot the line." "No," Savannah said, and held up her script, slashes showing faint through the stage lights' glow. "I was just changing my mind."

Emily sprinted the last twenty feet and jumped onto the bus just as the doors hissed shut. She dropped into the seat across from Marcus, who was already tearing a folded note out of his notebook.

"Read it before you laugh," Marcus said.

The note was from their book club president, Priya, and it read: "Book club meets tomorrow at lunch. Everyone must state the theme of The Kayak Race with one quotation to prove it. No exceptions. Signed, Priya, President." Emily read it twice, and her stomach did a flip, because she had written "the theme is friendship" on her worksheet and she had a bad feeling it was not enough.

"Friendship," Marcus said. "That's obviously it. The two main characters are friends, they fight, they make up, done."

"Then why do I feel like we're missing something?" Emily pulled out her battered copy of the novel and flipped to the scene where Jax lends Devon his lucky paddle. She read it out loud in a low voice so the driver wouldn't hear. The bus rattled over the railroad tracks, and the whole vehicle lurched so hard that Marcus's backpack bounced off the seat.

"Whoa," Marcus said. "The bus is buoyant today."

"The bus is not buoyant, it's just bumpy," Emily said, but she was laughing. Then she stopped laughing, because she was staring at the page. "Wait. Every single chapter, somebody gives something up for somebody else. Jax gives up the paddle. Devon gives up the race. Even the little sister gives up her seat on the team."

Marcus leaned over. "So friendship isn't just the answer. It's like the topic."

Emily grabbed the pen off his ear, where he kept it like a tiny hierarchy of pens, the blue one always on top. She wrote on the back of Priya's note: "A topic is a subject a novel is about. A theme is what the novel actually says about that subject." Then, underneath, she wrote, "The Kayak Race says a real friend will give up winning to keep the friendship," and next to it she copied the line where Devon slows down and lets Jax take the lead: "You don't leave your partner behind, not even for a trophy."

"That's it!" Marcus shouted, and three sixth graders turned around, so he lowered his voice to a whisper-shout. "Priya is going to freak."

At the next stop, their classmate Theo climbed on, heard the word "theme," and immediately tried to intervene with his own theory, which was that the theme was "kayaks." Emily held up the note, pointed to the difference between topic and theme, and Theo sat down, looking like a man who had just learned kayaks were not the point.

Tomorrow at lunch, Emily was going to read that quotation out loud and watch Priya's face. She practiced the words one more time under her breath as the bus pulled up to the school.

"Not even for a trophy," she said.

Emilie slid the last flat of strawberries across the counter at Mateo's berry stand, where she worked every Saturday morning for four dollars an hour. She was saving for a telescope, and at this rate she'd have it by October. The flats were made of porous cardboard that soaked up the juice if a basket leaked, so she lined each one with wax paper before filling it, breathing in the sweet, green smell of the stems.

The sign made her stop. Last week the berries were three dollars a basket. Today it said five. "Mateo, did someone make a mistake?"

He shook his head and pointed toward the hills, where the fields flourished in rows all summer. "Frost on Tuesday night. Took out half the crop." He lifted a basket so she could see it. "These are what's left."

Emilie frowned. Five dollars was what people paid in winter, when berries came from far away in trucks. In summer they were cheap because the fields were full of them. She turned the idea over while she restacked the baskets, testing it the way she tested everything, out loud, in a whisper, so nobody could hear her being wrong. Fewer berries to sell. Same number of people wanting them. So each basket left is worth more. The frost didn't make the berries better; it made them fewer.

The first customer of the day was a woman with two kids, one of them clutching a refugee teddy bear that had clearly survived a washing machine or two. "Five dollars?" the woman said. "They were three last Saturday."

Emilie took a breath. "There was a frost. It ruined half the crop, so there aren't as many berries, and the ones that are left cost more."

The woman looked at the baskets, then at her kids' faces, and bought two anyway. "Good explanation," she said, counting out the bills.

Emilie wrote FROST on the little chalkboard by the register, so the next customer wouldn't have to ask. Mateo grinned and slipped an extra basket into her tote at closing time. "For the telescope fund," he said.

The classroom smelled like pencil shavings and the grape candy Ms. Ruiz kept in a jar on her desk, and Matthew stared at his copy of "Because of Winn-Dixie" like it had insulted him. Find the theme, the board said, and back it up with a quotation. The theme part he could handle. He thought the book was about how people hide their loneliness, like his own father had hidden his for a whole year after Mom left, going dormant, waking up only to make pancakes on Sundays. Matthew wanted to write about that. The problem was the quotation.

The best line was on page 134: "He sat alone behind the counter." But "he" meant Otis, the pet store man, and if Matthew just wrote "he," his reader might think it meant the preacher, or even the dog's owner. He flipped through his notes, tapping his pencil against the desk until Priya whispered, "You're going to break that."

"Look," he whispered back, and showed her the page. "If I use this quote, who's he?"

Priya squinted. "In MLA style, square brackets go around any word you add to a quotation, to show it wasn't in the original text."

Matthew wrote it out: "[Otis] sat alone behind the counter." The brackets looked strange at first, like little fences around the name, but they made the sentence say exactly what he needed. He tested it once more with a different quote, adding "[loneliness]" where the book only said "it," and watched the whole paragraph snap into focus, the way his father's face had snapped into focus that Sunday morning when he finally said he missed her too.

Ms. Ruiz walked past and paused at his paper. "Nice work. Though you might want to double-check page 134."

He checked. The line was on page 143. He had been so sure. Matthew laughed at himself, erased the number, and wrote the right one, the grape candy smell drifting over his shoulder as Ms. Ruiz moved on.

Victor sat at his grandpa's kitchen table with a pencil, an eraser, and a stubborn problem: the art club needed a shaded sphere by Friday, and his looked like a flat grey cookie. He had filled in the whole dark side with the same even grey, exactly like the handout said, and somehow it had come out worse than a blank circle.

He grabbed an orange from the fruit bowl and held it under the lamp. Maybe drawing from life instead of memory would nurture a better result than guessing had. He squinted at the dark side. "Huh," he said out loud. "It's not the same grey all over."

His grandpa shuffled in, sneezing twice. "That cat of yours. I swear I've developed an allergy to her since you brought her for the visit." He set down his tea and looked over Victor's shoulder. "Don't ask me. I can't draw a straight fence post."

"I wasn't going to ask," Victor said, though he had been about to. He turned the orange slowly. The brightest spot sat right where the lamp hit it. Then came a curving edge where light gave up, and just past that edge, on the side away from the lamp, ran the darkest band of all. Farther around, near the far edge, the grey actually got lighter again, like something was faintly glowing back into it.

Victor leaned close, testing his idea with the pencil tip hovering over his paper. He shaded his sphere's dark side in bands: light near the far edge, and darkest in one curved stripe just past where the light stopped. "The darkest band on the ball itself," he murmured, drawing it in. He tapped the stripe. "It's not the edge of the shadow. It's just past it."

The cat leapt onto the table and batted the orange, and it rolled right off the edge and under the radiator. Victor stared at his finished drawing, a real sphere now, round and solid on the flat page, and laughed. "Fine. You can keep the model."

Eli stood at the shallow end of the community pool, gripping the gutter with both hands, watching the lane ropes bob like green snakes. Twenty-five metres. That was the whole test: one length of front crawl, breathing to the side whenever he wanted. His problem was that whenever he turned his head, water went straight up his nose, and he had to stop, coughing, while the other kids in Level Four swam on without him.

"You're almost there," said Priya from the next lane, treading water. "You've got the arms."

"It's the breathing," Eli said. "If I lift my head up to get air, my legs sink. If I keep my head down, I drink half the pool."

Priya laughed, then stopped, because she could see he wasn't. "Want me to watch you do one length and see what happens?"

He pushed off and swam. Three strokes, then a fourth, and on the fourth he twisted his whole face up toward the ceiling, gasped, got a mouthful of chlorine, and stood up coughing. His eyes stung. The water's smell hung around him like something corrosive, sharp enough that he could almost feel it eating at his good mood. He wiped his face on his shoulder and thought hard.

Here was the strange part. When he'd watched his friend Marcus swim, Marcus barely seemed to turn his head at all. His cheek just touched the water and somehow he got air. Eli had also noticed something in his own swimming, though he'd never thought about it until now: when he blew out underwater, little bubbles rushed past his ear, and there seemed to be a small pocket of air, a little dip in the water, right beside his face. His own head, plowing forward, was pushing a bow wave, and that wave left a lower spot next to his cheek. The water there sat below the level of the flat surface. Which meant his mouth didn't have to reach up to the flat water at all. The air was already down there, waiting beside him, like a moon keeping a tiny orbit around his head.

"Watch this," he said to Priya. "I'm going to try keeping one goggle in the water and one eye out."

He pushed off again. Stroke, stroke, stroke, and then, instead of lifting, he just rolled his head, keeping his cheek low, letting his mouth hang in that little dip. Air. Clean, cold, real air, without his legs dropping like stones. He blew bubbles underwater, rolled again, breathed again, and kept going, all the way to the far wall, where he grabbed the gutter, gasping and grinning.

"Twenty-five metres!" Priya shouted from three lanes over. "I counted!"

Eli looked back down the lane at the water he'd crossed. Somewhere out there, microbes too small to see were probably having a fine afternoon, and he had just out-swum every single one of them.

"Same time tomorrow?" Priya called as she climbed out.

"Tomorrow I try fifty," Eli said, and shook the water from his hair like a dog.

Quinn slid her math notebook across the counter of her grandfather's corner store, between the register and a rack of gum. The last customer of the afternoon had just left, and the only sounds were the hum of the drink cooler and rain ticking on the front window. "Grandpa, before you check it," she said, "I want to check it myself. But I don't know how."

Her grandfather was meticulous about homework; he read every page with a pencil in his hand and circled anything that looked off. Last week he had circled three problems, and the guilt Quinn felt about those three circles had kept her up past bedtime. This week's page was two-step equations, and below them, a small coordinate grid where she was supposed to plot the line y equals 3x plus 4.

"Well," he said, peeling an orange, "you solved for x in the first three. What did you get?"

"For the first one, x equals 5. The equation was 3x plus 4 equals 19." She said it fast, the way you say something you're not sure of.

"Here's a trick my teacher taught me, back when the store was just a fruit cart," he said. "Take your answer and put it back in place of x. If both sides come out equal, the answer is right."

Quinn frowned at her notebook. "Put it back in? Like... I solved to get rid of it, and now I put it back?"

"That's the whole trick. Try it out loud."

"Three times 5 is 15. Then 15 plus 4 is 19." She paused. "And the other side already says 19. They're both 19." She looked up. "So it's right? Both sides came out equal, so it's right?"

"You tell me."

She tried the second one, 2x minus 7 equals 9, with her answer of 8. Two times 8 was 16, minus 7 was 9, and the other side was 9. Equal again. Her spine straightened a little. But the third one, 4x plus 5 equals 17, with her answer of 3, gave her trouble: 4 times 3 was 12, plus 5 was 17. Equal. That was right too. Then why had she felt so unsure?

The fourth one stopped her cold. 5x minus 6 equals 14, and she had written x equals 2. Five times 2 was 10, minus 6 was 4. The other side said 14. Four did not equal fourteen. Her pencil hovered. Somewhere she had gone wrong. She redid the steps slowly, adding 6 to both sides to get 5x equals 20, and then dividing, which gave x equals 4. She put 4 back in place of the variable: 20 minus 6 was 14, and the other side was 14. Equal. "It's 4," she said, crossing out the 2. "The old answer failed the check."

Then she turned to the grid. If y equaled 3x plus 4, she could pick x, work out y, and plot the point. She tried x equals 0, which made y equal 4, and marked the point. Then x equals 1 gave y equals 7, so up went a second point. She drew a line through them and noticed it climbed three squares for every one across, just like the 3 in the equation. On a hunch she checked her line against the equation: the point where x was 1 should sit at y equals 7, and 3 times 1 plus 4 made 7. Equal. The line and the equation agreed with each other.

Her grandfather set a peeled orange slice on the corner of her notebook, right beside the grid. "So it's a picture," she said, tapping the sloping line. "The equation and the graph both depict the same thing, just different ways."

"Good as any poster in here," he said, and turned the sign on the door to CLOSED.

The automatic doors of First National Bank hummed shut behind Ethan, and the smell of floor wax and cold air hit him at once. He clutched a sealed envelope with the stand's earnings and the deposit slip his mother had signed. Behind him, through the glass, his best friend Rosa guarded two nearly full jugs of strawberry lemonade and a hand-lettered sign that read "Cups $3.00." The bank closed at noon, and the clock above the teller counter read 11:41.

Ethan had set the price himself. Last summer, when strawberries were everywhere, their lemonade sold out at one dollar a cup, and there was never a drop left. He remembered standing in Rosa's grandmother's backyard in August, juice running down his wrist, watching the rows of strawberry baskets at the farm stand sell for two dollars a basket because there were so many. But that was then. In February, a single basket had cost six dollars, and Rosa had said, "See? Everybody wants them and there aren't any, so the price goes up." Ethan had turned that over all winter. More people buying than selling pushed prices one way; more selling than buying pushed them the other way. So this morning he had reasoned that three dollars a cup, fancy strawberry lemonade on a hot day, would make them rich.

It had not. At noon they had sold nine cups and poured the rest into jugs. Rosa's grandmother, waiting in the parking lot, had looked at the jugs and then at the sign. "You held your price too high," she said simply. "At three dollars, you offered cups all day long, but buyers didn't want that many at that price. Now look what's left." Ethan had stared at the jugs. It wasn't that people hated lemonade, or that the day was cold, or that the two things merely coincided to ruin their sale. It was something underneath, invisible, like the lichen spreading gray-green across the north side of the bank's stone wall, slow and steady where no one watched. The price itself had made the extra pile up.

"Next," called the teller, and Ethan stepped forward on sneakers that squeaked against the tile. He slid the envelope under the glass. The teller counted the bills, and the machine made its dry clicking sound as it stacked them.

"Deposit for the lemonade stand?" she asked.

"Yes, ma'am. Nine dollars." Ethan glanced back through the glass at Rosa, who was tapping the jug with one finger and had begun crossing out the 3 on the sign, drawing a big number 1 over it. "Tomorrow we sell it cheap," Ethan said. "We're not carrying those jugs home again."

Dominic sat at the kitchen table with three blank pages in front of him and a pencil he had already sharpened twice. The assignment was due Monday: a five-paragraph persuasive essay, with an introduction, three reasons, and a conclusion. He had chosen the most important topic in the world, convincing his mother that he should be allowed to walk to school by himself. He wrote the first reason fast, because it was obvious. Reason one: everyone in fifth grade walks to school alone. Even the kids from the affluent streets up the hill, whose parents had every gadget money could buy, let them go. He filled two pages and then leaned back, satisfied, while his little sister Mira nibbled toast across the table.

Mira pulled the pages toward her and began to narrate his essay out loud in a dramatic voice, the way she narrated cartoons. "Everyone walks alone, so I should too." She stopped and squinted at him. "That's your big reason? Everyone?"

"So what?" Dominic said. "It's true."

"You always say Ethan's wrong about stuff even when everyone agrees with him," Mira said. "Remember when everyone said Billy took the class snacks, and you figured out it was the substitute teacher?" She slid the pages back. "Lots of people doing something doesn't make it right. That's called the bandwagon fallacy." She went back to her toast like she hadn't just knocked over his whole essay.

Dominic stared at the pages. He wanted to tell her she was wrong, but his brain kept snagging on the snack mystery. Being popular hadn't made the accusation true. So maybe being popular didn't make his reason true either. He decided to test it, the way he tested everything, on an easier target first. He wrote a new one-paragraph essay arguing that Mira should let him have the last cookie because everyone in the house wanted him to have it. He read it to her. She laughed and ate the cookie herself in one enormous bite.

"See?" she said, crumbs flying. "Nobody cares what everyone wants."

Dominic spread his three pages back out and crossed out his first reason with a long dark line. Then he wrote a new one: he knew the route, there were two crossing guards, and his friend Devi walked the same way, so they could go together. He worked until the pencil was a stub, and when his mother came home, he read the whole essay to her, introduction to conclusion, standing straight like a lawyer in a show.

She read it twice herself, silent, tapping the counter with one finger. "This is actually a real argument," she said slowly. "Saturday, we'll walk it together. If you don't forget one single safety rule, Monday you walk with Devi."

Dominic pumped his fist. Behind him, Mira whispered, "You owe me a cookie."

Brielle sat at Grandma's kitchen table with a blank page in front of her and a problem the size of the whole page. On Monday, Miss Ortega had assigned a five-paragraph persuasive essay with a real introduction and a real conclusion, and it was mandatory for everyone in the class. Brielle had to persuade her readers of something, and she had chosen the hardest thing she could think of: her mother should let her adopt the stray cat that had been thriving in the alley behind the school since October.

"You've been staring at that paper for a long time," Grandpa said, setting down two mugs of cocoa.

"I know what I want to say. I just don't know how to make anybody believe it." She slid her notes across the table. On them she had scribbled three words she'd copied off a library book when she was hunting for essay tips: ethos, pathos, logos.

Grandpa squinted at the words, then smiled in a way that made his whole face crinkle. "Ethos, pathos, logos. My old philosophy professor would be proud. In his Rhetoric, Aristotle described three ways to persuade: ethos, the speaker's credibility; pathos, the audience's emotions; and logos, logic and evidence."

Brielle wrote fast, then stopped. "Wait. That means there's more than one door into somebody's head." She looked at her notes again. Her first attempt had been all pathos, she realized. The cat is cold. The cat is lonely. The cat has sad eyes. Her mother would just say, "There are sad cats everywhere, Brielle," and close the door. But what if she arranged the doors differently?

She decided to test it. For her introduction she would use ethos: she would explain that she had researched cat care for three weeks, that she knew the cost of food and litter, that she had already talked to the vet on Elm Street. Then logos, with evidence: the vet said a spayed cat could live fifteen years indoors, and the shelter fee was only thirty dollars, which she had saved from raking leaves. Only in the fourth paragraph would she let the cat's sad eyes appear, one paragraph of pathos, placed like the last stair at the top of a staircase.

She wrote the whole draft that afternoon, five paragraphs, and read it aloud in the living room while Grandpa listened with his hands folded. When she finished, he didn't say anything for a moment, and her heart dropped. Then he said, "If I were your mother, I'd already be looking for a litter box."

"Really?"

"You made me believe you first, then feel, then agree. That's a hard thing to do at any age." He stood and went to the hall closet and came back with a thick old book, its cover soft and worn at the corners. "This was my professor's copy. He'd want a descendant of mine to keep it."

Brielle held the book in both hands. It was heavier than it looked. "Can I read just the part with the three words?"

"Page two hundred and thirty-five," Grandpa said, tapping the spine. "Start there. Aristotle was a better teacher than I'll ever be."

She opened the book and began to read.

Dominic had fasted before, but only until lunch. This year, at Grandma Ruth's apartment, he was determined to make it all the way to sundown like the grown-ups, and he announced this at breakfast the night before while everyone was still eating. His cousin Talia, who was twelve and had diabetes, gave him a look over her glass of juice but said nothing.

The next morning the apartment smelled like nothing cooking, which felt strange. Talia sat at the table with a piece of toast, and Dominic stared at it. "You're not even trying?" he asked, feeling his stomach growl like an accusation. Last summer he had quit halfway through the day and told everyone he had a headache, and the memory still humiliated him. He wasn't going to be that kid again.

"I have to eat," Talia said. "Rabbi Felsen told my mom that when fasting would be dangerous for someone's health, Jewish law waives it. In that case, eating isn't allowed to be skipped. It's actually required." She took a bite. "So I'm doing the religious thing right now, with my toast."

Dominic tested this idea the way he tested everything, like turning a lens to see if the light would focus. If skipping the fast could be the commandment, then the day wasn't really about being hungry. He thought about his headache excuse from last summer and how he'd decided, in secret, to feel sick. He didn't say any of that out loud.

At noon, Talia checked her numbers and wrote a note on the pad by the fridge, the way she did so Grandma Ruth could see she was taking care of herself. Dominic picked up the pen and added a line below hers: "I'm still going for sundown. But if I get sick for real, I'll eat. Deal?" Talia read it, slid the pad back, and drew a small check mark with an arrow pointing at his words. Then she poured him a glass of water, set it beside his elbow, and walked away.

Rain hammered the windows of Room 12 like a monsoon that had lost its way from somewhere tropical, and inside, the chess club had dwindled to four players. Rose had spent two weeks trying to recruit new members with posters featuring a knight in sunglasses, which had attracted exactly one sixth grader named Priya, who mostly came for the snacks.

Rose was beating Marcus in six moves when he reached out, picked up his knight, studied the board, and set the knight back down on its original square without moving it. Then he reached for his rook instead.

"No," Rose said. "You touched it. You have to move it."

"That's not a rule. That's a rule you invented to win." Marcus crossed his arms. Priya stopped chewing her crackers to watch.

Rose was sure she was right, though she could not have said where she'd learned it, which bothered her the way a loose tooth bothers a tongue. She got the club's dog-eared rulebook from the shelf and flipped through it while Marcus drummed his fingers. There it was, in a paragraph about formal chess: if you deliberately touch one of your own pieces, you must move that piece, if it has a legal move.

"Touch-move," Rose read aloud. "It's called touch-move."

Marcus looked at the page for a long moment, then at his knight, which had exactly one legal move, straight into the path of her bishop. He sighed like a man carrying groceries up three flights of stairs and pushed the knight forward. "Fine. But now I know it too, and next week it's your hands I'm watching."

"Deal," Rose said, and captured the knight.

Penelope spread her homework sheet across the kitchen table, next to a plate of toast crumbs shaped, if you squinted, like a hockey rink. "Assignment," she announced to her brother Max, who was rolling a tennis ball against the thermostat on the wall. "I have to explain how a regular citizen petitions a councillor to change a bylaw. And I want to actually do it, not just write about it."

"Petition to change the bylaw that says we can't put the hockey net on the street," Max said instantly, abandoning the thermostat mid-bounce. "I've wanted that my whole life." His whole life, Penelope noted, included eleven years, four of them spent pining over that net. She pulled the city website onto her laptop, found a page listing the councillors, and picked the one whose photo had the friendliest smile. She drafted an email, added three reasons why street hockey should be legal with supervision, and hit send before Max could drip jam on the keyboard.

Two days later the reply landed. "Thank you for your message, but I'm afraid I don't represent your area," the friendly-smiling councillor wrote. "You'd need to contact the councillor for your ward." Penelope frowned at the screen. "Ward?" Max said, licking jam off his thumb. "Like a hospital?" "No, it's what the areas of the city are called," Penelope said. "I think each councillor is elected to represent one area." She tested the idea like poking a loose tooth: she typed their address into the city's ward finder, and sure enough, a map bloomed on screen, their street sitting inside a green blob labeled Ward 5. Councillor Okafor, whose photo showed a woman holding a cat, apparently belonged to them.

So Penelope conquered her embarrassment, wrote to Councillor Okafor, and mentioned that the reply had come from a councillor across town whose cat looked distinctly unimpressed. Max insisted on adding a paragraph about proportional punishment, claiming that confiscating a hockey net for a street violation was like jail for jaywalking. Penelope edited it down to one sentence. The house smelled like burnt toast again because Max had been celebrating potential victory with celebratory bread.

On Saturday, an actual letter arrived, paper and everything. "Please come to the community meeting on the twelfth," it read, "and bring your neighbours. Ten signatures will get your proposal on the agenda." Max ran upstairs yelling for their mom. Penelope counted on her fingers: the Hendersons, the Nguyens, the twins who lived in the blue house, and, if she promised to shovel their walk, old Mr. Petrakis, who yelled at the net every single winter.

"Nine," she said. "We need one more."

Max grinned and raised his hand. "I'm a citizen too, you know. I checked."

Florence wanted her pencil drawing of an orange to look round instead of flat, because Grandma had promised to hang one of her drawings in the front hall if it was good enough. Grandma had a chronic habit of saying "good enough" about almost anything Florence made, but the front hall was where guests actually looked, and Florence wanted the orange to earn its spot for real.

She set a tennis ball on the kitchen table and propped her sketchbook beside it. Her first try looked like a flat circle with a gray smudge, so she clicked on the old desk lamp and dragged it close to the table. The ball lit up with a bright highlight on one side, a soft shadow underneath, and a long dark shape stretched across the table behind it. She had never noticed that before. When she raised the lamp high over the ball, the cast shadow shrank to a small puddle at its base. When she lowered it again, the shadow stretched out long and thin, like it was trying to escape across the tabletop.

"Grandma, come look at this," Florence called. Grandma came in from the garden, wiping dirt off her hands. "Watch the shadow. Low lamp, long shadow. High lamp, short shadow." She moved the lamp up and down like a slow elevator, and the shadow grew and shrank each time.

Grandna laughed. "Your grandfather used to do that with his reading lamp and his coffee mug. He'd besiege me with shadow monsters at breakfast."

Florence sharpened her pencil and started the orange again. She imagined a lamp sitting low, just past the edge of the table, and drew the cast shadow stretching far to the right, long enough to nearly touch the bowl she had added behind it. She left a small pale spot for the highlight where the imagined lamp would emit its brightest light, and she pressed harder and harder with the pencil as the shadow curled under the orange's belly.

Grandma leaned over her shoulder, still holding the gardening rag. "That one goes in the hall," she said. "Right where the light from the front window hits the wall."

Hunter wanted the last open swing before the bell, and so did Marcus. They stood toe to toe in the wood chips, neither one moving.

"Rock-paper-scissors," said Marcus. "But I always throw rock. Rock wins."

"That's not how it works," Hunter said. "Watch. Rock beats scissors, but scissors beats paper, and paper beats rock. Every choice beats one thing and loses to one thing. So rock can't be the best one, because there's no best one."

Marcus squinted at him. "Says who?"

"Let's try it. You throw rock every time. I'll figure out the pattern." Hunter could perceive the plan forming before Marcus even raised his fist, because a boy who announces rock always throws rock. They played three rounds. Rock. Paper. Marcus lost. Rock. Paper. Lost again. On the third round Marcus switched to scissors at the last second, and Hunter's paper won anyway.

"Okay," Marcus said slowly. "Okay, but that's because you're some kind of mind reader."

"It's because you told me your move. Your testimony, bro. You testified against yourself."

Marcus laughed despite himself, but then his shoulders sagged. "So what do we do? We both want the swing and we can't both have it."

Hunter picked up a stick and scratched two lines in the wood chips. "Here's the problem, named: one swing, two kids, four minutes till the bell. Now we make a rule that fits it. Two minutes each. Loser of one fair round goes second, but the winner has to swap when I count to a hundred and twenty."

"Fair round means I can throw anything?"

"Anything. Rock is versatile if nobody knows it's coming."

They shook fists. Marcus threw paper, Hunter threw rock, and Marcus whooped so loud a first grader looked over from the slide.

"Count fast," Marcus said, already pumping his legs toward the sky.

Paisley stared at the recipe card on Nova's kitchen counter like it was a treasure map with the X smudged out. "Step one says preheat the oven to three seventy-five," she read. "We have to be walking to the bus stop by noon, or we miss the bake sale." Nova's little brother, Bram, who considered himself the first tenant of every room he entered because he never left it, leaned over their shoulders to supervise.

They measured and mixed, arguing only once about whether an egg with a wobbly shell still counted as an egg. "It contributes the same amount of egg," Nova said, cracking it with a flourish. Paisley folded in the blueberries, dropped the batter into twelve cups, and slid the tin into the oven just as the clock said eleven twenty. Then she sat on the floor and watched the oven light like it was television.

At eleven fifty the timer beeped. Paisley pulled the tin out, and both girls frowned. The muffin tops looked pale, not golden like the picture on the card. "They can't be done," Nova said. "But the timer said." Paisley gazed at the pale tops and considered the issue. The outsides were clues, but the real answer was hidden inside, where no one could see. She grabbed a toothpick, pushed it into the centre of the tallest muffin, and pulled it out. Wet batter clung to the wood. "Not done," she announced, feeling like a detective. She set the timer again and put the tin back in.

The second time, the tops had browned, and when she pushed a toothpick into the centre of another muffin, it came out clean except for a few dry crumbs. "Done!" Nova cheered. They wrapped the muffins in a dish towel and sprinted for the bus, arriving with one minute to spare. At the bake sale, the muffins sold out in twenty minutes, leaving behind only an impoverished plate of crumbs. Bram looked at it and said, "I'll take those."

Anthony's speech was a cargo ship, and he was its captain. That was the game he had invented on the bus to the tournament: the two minutes were the harbor, his three points were cargo holds stuffed with treasure, and the judges were dockworkers who had to unload everything before the tide went out. In practice his grandfather had listened from the kitchen table, nodding along, and then halfway through he had squinted and asked, "Wait, which point is this now? Am I still on the first one?" Anthony had frozen. He knew the speech was good. He could see every argument on the page in his head, perfectly arranged. His grandfather could not. It hit Anthony like a cold splash: a listener cannot flip back a page the way a reader can. Whatever his grandfather heard was all there was. If Anthony lost him, there was no going back for the missing cargo.

In the hallway outside the debate room, Anthony tested a small idea on his teammate Priya. He delivered his opening hook, then said, "First, the plan costs too much. Second, nobody wants it. Finally, it breaks the rules." Then he asked her to close her eyes and narrate it back to him, hold by hold. She got all three, in order. He tried again without the first, second and finally, mixing them in plain sentences, and she stumbled, unsure whether the cost point came before or after the rules point. Anthony grinned. The words were working like lights on a dark channel, marking each hold so the dockworkers always knew where they were.

Room 4 was sparse, just two long tables, a clock, and a judge with a clipboard. Anthony stood, took a breath, and imagined the ship sliding into harbor. "First," he said, and watched the judge's pencil drop to the page. "Second," and it dropped again. When he finished his closing and sat down, the judge had three neat lines on the paper, one for each hold, all unloaded.

His grandfather was waiting by the water fountain. "I didn't get lost once," he said, tapping his temple. "First, second, finally. I knew where I was the whole time." Anthony said, "Hold three is still full, Grandpa. Come on, I'll unload it for you in the car."

Noah had been dreading Thursday choir practice ever since the music room got picked for renovation, because now forty kids crammed into the cafeteria, which smelled like Tuesday's mystery cuisine and echoed like a gym. Mr. Reyes wanted the two groups to sing "Row, Row, Row Your Boat" as a round, and Noah's group kept crashing into the other group's line.

"It's not a contest," Mr. Reyes called out. "Group One, you begin. Group Two, you wait for my cue."

Group One started. Noah counted quietly, waiting, but when his group came in, his ears played a trick on him.
