Nobody moved. There were maybe fifteen kids in that yard, and every one of them suddenly found something fascinating about their shoes or their punch cups. Matthew started forward, then stopped, because last month he'd tried this exact thing in the cafeteria. He had shoved Marcus's shoulder and yelled at him, and it had gone badly: Marcus had turned on him, the teacher had punished both of them, and Eli had ended up more embarrassed than before. Matthew had spent a long time replaying that day, wondering where he'd gone wrong.

He looked around the yard again and noticed something odd. When Marcus teased Eli in the cafeteria, forty kids watched and nobody helped. Now fifteen watched and nobody helped. It wasn't that they were all cruel. He tested a small idea: what if everyone was waiting, assuming somebody else would step in? His older sister had read about that once. "It's called the bystander effect," she'd said, shrugging, and gone back to her book. He hadn't understood what she meant until right now, standing in a dry backyard full of frozen people.

So instead of charging over alone, Matthew walked to Jada first. "Go stand next to Eli," he said quietly. "Just talk to him." Then he tapped Dev on the shoulder. "You too. Bring cake." Jada blinked, then crossed the yard and asked Eli something about the history project. Dev followed with two plates of cake, and suddenly three kids were over there, and then Dana went too, because three people made it easy for a fourth.

Marcus kept talking for a few seconds, but he was teasing a boy who now had friends around him and cake in his hand, and it sounded silly even to the boys beside him. One of them laughed at Marcus instead of at Eli, and Marcus went quiet, his ears red.

Eli took a bite of cake and looked over at Matthew. "Wind it up later," he said, nodding at the wrapped box. "I want to see that propeller spin."

Lincoln had been playing saxophone for four years, and he had never once made anything up on the spot. Every note he knew came off a page. Now Mr. Ruiz had assigned the seventh graders a blues solo over the twelve-bar chord progression, and the page was empty.

His dilemma was simple: he wanted to improvise, but every time the backing track rolled, he froze and played nothing. After school on Thursday, he stayed in the music room with Priya, who ran the chord track on the room's ancient speaker while he practiced. He tried running scales, and they coincided with the chords perfectly, every note safe, every note boring. "That's not a solo," Priya said. "That's a warm-up."

On his fifth attempt, he got reckless. He closed his eyes, leaned into a big wailing note, and lost count of the bars somewhere in the blur. The chords underneath him shifted, and suddenly nothing he played fit anymore. He stopped, cheeks hot. "I don't even know where I am in the form," he said.

Priya paused the track. "Listen to the end of it again," she said, and played the last two bars. "That part's called the turnaround." Lincoln listened. The chords there had a pull to them, like a door swinging open back toward the beginning. He counted it out in his head, twice, and his eyes went wide. The turnaround landed on the V chord, and it yanked the music right back to the start of the next chorus. It was like a homing signal. If he got lost, all he had to do was wait for that pull and he would know exactly where the form began again.

They ran the track a sixth time. Lincoln wandered off course in bar eight, the same place as before, but this time he didn't stop. He held a low note, kept his ears open, and waited. The turnaround arrived like a wave lifting him up, and when the twelve bars rolled back to the top, he came in on the one with a riff he had never played before in his life. Priya hit the table with her palm. "Again," she said, and reached for the play button.

The drama room smelled like dust and old curtains, and Joshua stood in the middle of it with his hands in his pockets, wishing he had signed up for robotics instead. Ms. Reyes had written two words on the whiteboard: yes, and. She said every offer your partner makes, you accept it and add something. Easy, Joshua thought. Then she paired him with Deshawn and said, "Your scene takes place in a garage. Go."

Deshawn rubbed his hands together and said, "Wow, look at all this stuff." Joshua said, "Yeah, there's a lot of stuff." They shuffled in a circle. Deshawn picked up an invisible thing and said, "Check this out." Joshua said, "Cool." Cool was not yes, and. Cool was a dead end, and the scene lay there like a dropped sandwich while the rest of the class shifted in their seats. Ms. Reyes called time.

Sitting against the wall, Joshua chewed on what had gone wrong. It wasn't that they had blocked each other. Every offer had technically been accepted. The problem felt hidden, like a rule of an ecosystem he couldn't see, where some things fed the scene and others starved it. What exactly had Deshawn handed him? An invisible thing. A nothing. Joshua wondered whether the size of the offer mattered, whether a small vague thing could only ever grow into a small vague thing. He decided to invest his next thirty seconds in testing one idea: make the offer big and exact, and see if Deshawn could build on it.

Second round. Same garage, and this time Joshua went first. He gripped an invisible handlebar and said, "Careful, that's Grandma's red bicycle. She rode it across two states when she was our age." Deshawn's whole face changed. "Wait, Grandma Ruby? She told me she buried a tin of money somewhere along that route." "She did," Joshua said, "and the map is taped under the seat." Within a minute they had a shovel, a suspicious neighbor, and a chase down a driveway, and when Ms. Reyes called time, a girl in the front row actually groaned, "No, keep going!"

Afterward Deshawn bumped his shoulder. "Grandma's red bicycle," he said. "That was, like, a whole meal." "Vague stuff is junk food," Joshua said. "Looks like something, but it isn't nutritious." Deshawn laughed and pointed at the whiteboard. "Next scene, you start again." Joshua walked back to center, grabbed the invisible handlebars, and rang the bell.

Ethan ran laps around the cracked asphalt beside the basketball court, counting each one under his breath. His cousin Jaden sat on the rusted hoop pole, spinning a ball on one finger. "You're doing it wrong," Jaden said. "You sprint the first lap like a maniac, then you die. My coach calls it burning the tank." Ethan stopped, breathing hard. He wanted to beat Marcus Delgado at the county meet on Saturday, and Marcus never faded. "So how do you pace it?" he asked. Jaden shrugged. "You figure it out. I already know my plan." He would not say what the plan was, which annoyed Ethan all afternoon.

That evening Ethan ran the court's perimeter with a stopwatch, testing an idea. If he ran the first circuit steady instead of fast, could he finish the second one faster? He tried it four times, and every time the second circuit was quicker when the first was slower. He was beginning to deduce something he could not actually see: the race was lost in the legs before it was lost in the lungs. It felt like a hidden rule, invisible until you broke it.

At the meet, the track looped wide and red around a football field. Ethan overheard two officials doing a census of the entries, calling names down a clipboard, and he counted thirty-two boys in the 800, eight heats. In the warmup area, one boy jogged backward and waved his arms in wide eccentric circles, and Jaden laughed. "That guy's a legend. He ran a whole race backwards once." Then an official called their heat to the line. "Remember," Jaden whispered, "the plan." Ethan had no idea what that meant, and there was no time to ask.

The gun cracked. Ethan held himself back even though every muscle screamed to chase Marcus, who was already three strides ahead. At the bell, he still felt strong, and he began to reel Marcus in, stride by stride. Then, ahead of them both, the backward-jogging legend suddenly surged, arms pumping, face wild, tearing past everyone. The crowd roared. He crossed the line with his hands up.

Except the race did not end. No finish tape waited. Ethan saw the official standing perfectly still, red flag down, and it hit him. On a standard 400-metre outdoor track, the 800 was exactly two laps, and the bell meant one lap still remained. The legend had kicked for the finish one lap too early, and now he was staggering through the second lap while runners poured past him. Jaden, fifty meters back, shouted, "It's two laps! TWO!" Ethan leaned into the final curve with everything left in his tank, drew even with Marcus, and pushed. He crossed the real line half a stride ahead. Jaden caught up afterward, pale and shaking his head. "I nearly did the same thing," he admitted. Ethan grinned and pointed at the lane. "Then my plan worked better than yours."

The kayaks glided across the lake, but Jasmine was barely noticing how tranquil the water looked this morning. Her eyes kept drifting to the dock, where a circle of older campers had gathered around a boy named Owen from her cabin. She caught words like "milk carton" and "crybaby," and she saw Owen's shoulders curl inward like a paper bag being crushed.

Jasmine had spent the first week of camp learning to paddle, to build a fire, to tie a bowline knot. But this was different. Last night she'd watched two girls tease Owen at the campfire, and she had done nothing, and the nothing had sat in her stomach like a swallowed rock. Her first instinct was to march over and shout at the teasers, but she had tried that once at school in the spring, and it had only made everything louder and meaner.

She paddled closer, her brain working fast. What did the teasers actually want? Not Owen, she realized. They wanted the circle. Every head turned toward them, every laugh fed them. The teasing seemed to run on an audience, the way the camp lantern ran on batteries. Take away the audience, and maybe the whole thing would flicker out.

She beached her kayak and jogged up the dock, heart hammering. "Owen!" she called, loud and cheerful. "They need help carrying the snacks to the craft shed. Like, right now. Come on, let's go." She grabbed his sleeve and pulled him toward the path, waving at the circle as if they were all in on some wonderful plan.

Owen stumbled along beside her, and behind them Jasmine heard the circle break apart, voices scattering toward the lake. Nobody followed. Nobody shouted after them. On the trail through the pines, Owen finally spoke. "There weren't any snacks, were there?"

"There were if we make some," Jasmine said. "We can petition the kitchen staff for extra trail mix. I bet if we ask nice, they'll say yes. They liked my fire-building." By the time they reached the craft shed, Owen was laughing, and the two of them were already planning a snack-delivery service for their whole cabin, first customers at lunch.

The next afternoon, when a boy by the canoes started mocking a younger kid's goggles, Jasmine didn't freeze up. She skipped over, hooked her arm through the kid's, and said, "Come on, let's go, I'll race you to the diving platform." They ran the whole way, and behind them the dock went quiet.

"You're fast," the kid puffed at the water's edge.

"Race you back," Jasmine said, and dove in.

Bentley had come to the community centre on a Saturday morning for the pizza promised at the end of math club, and he was starting to suspect the pizza was a trap.

Miss Okafor had handed out worksheets with pairs of triangles on them, and the deal was simple: prove the triangles congruent, or at least prove you had tried. Bentley's paper had two triangles, each with tick marks showing matching sides, and a note in tiny print that said one angle was shared. Shared with what, the paper did not say.

"I can't do side-angle-side," he told Priya, who sat beside him dismantling her pencil eraser. "I've got two sides on each triangle, but no angle between them. It's like being given bread and cheese and told to make a sandwich with the bread invisible."

Priya leaned over. "The angle is somewhere. It's always somewhere." She said this the way people say the remote is always in the couch, which was to say, unhelpfully and with total confidence.

Bentley stared at the diagram. The two triangles overlapped in the middle, their sides crossing like an X, and the tick-marked sides ran along the four arms of the X. The missing angle, he decided, was at the crossing point, right where the lines made their four sharp corners. He could see the top corner and the bottom corner, the left one and the right one, and the triangles each grabbed a different pair of corners.

He devised a test. On scrap paper he drew a big X with a ruler, careful and slow, then measured the top angle with his protractor. Forty-three degrees. He measured the bottom angle, the one directly across the crossing point. Forty-three degrees again. He drew another X, sloppier this time, at some eccentric angle he picked by flinging his pencil. Sixty-one and sixty-one.

"They're the same," he said, louder than he meant to.

"Vertical angles," said Priya, without looking up from her eraser. "That's what those are called. The opposite ones at a crossing."

He checked her tone for mockery and found none, which was almost disappointing. He went back to the worksheet. If the vertical angles were equal, then one triangle's top angle matched the other triangle's bottom angle, and that angle sat exactly between the two tick-marked sides on each triangle. Side, angle, side. He wrote the proof out in four lines, added a fifth line that said therefore in his most confident handwriting, and carried the paper to Miss Okafor's desk.

She read it, drew a small check mark, and slid the paper back. "Nice work. You found the hiding spot."

"There's a hiding spot?"

"There's always a hiding spot," she said, and called the room to attention for the next worksheet.

Bentley returned to his seat slowly, the way a person walks when they realize the pizza was never the trap, the worksheets were, and the trap had worked. Priya held out her diagram, which had three X shapes on it and a hopeful expression.

"Show me the hiding spot," she said.

Eli typed the last line of his program into the club laptop just as Ms. Ruiz called for demos. The code was supposed to ask for a number and print whether it was prime, and on his first three tries it had refused to comply, printing error after error because he had forgotten the colon at the end of his if statement. Now it ran, and he wanted it perfect before the coding club voted on whose project to enter in the district showcase.

Marcus went first. He was running for club president, and the ballot for the election sat folded in his pocket, though everyone knew he wanted more votes than anyone had ever gotten, a record. His program drew a spiral on the screen, and people clapped. Then Eli stood up.

"Type a number," he said. Priya shouted nine, and the program printed "not prime." Twelve, "not prime." Thirteen, "prime." So far his code seemed immune to bugs, which surprised him, since nothing he wrote ever worked the first day.

"Try one," Marcus said.

Eli typed 1. The program printed "prime."

"That's wrong," Marcus said, leaning over the laptop. "One is not a prime number. Mathematicians exclude it so every whole number has only one way to be written as a product of primes."

"How do you know?" Eli asked.

Marcus shrugged. "My cousin argued about it for a week." He went back to his seat without explaining further.

Eli sat down and stared at the screen. His loop checked whether any number from 2 upward divided the input evenly, and since nothing divided 1, the loop finished and his code declared it prime. He couldn't see the rule itself, only what his program did, so he tested an idea: he added a check at the top, before the loop, that printed "not prime" if the input was less than 2. He typed 1 again.

"Not prime," the screen said.

He tried 2, 3, 4, 25, 97. All correct. Priya typed 100 and got "not prime," then 101 and got "prime."

Ms. Ruiz collected the ballots. When she read the results, Marcus had eleven votes, the most anyone could remember. He stood, grinning, and held up the folded slip of paper from his pocket, the one he had printed as a sample so people would know exactly how to mark theirs.

"Adjourned," he said, and dropped the sample ballot into the recycling bin.

Nolan's older brother Dario had a poster of a toucan taped above his desk and a packing list spread across his bed, because in eleven days he was flying to a rainforest with his summer program. He held up a fleece jacket and raised an eyebrow at Nolan. "It's a rainforest. Why would I bring this?"

Nolan had no answer yet, but he had something better: a climate project due in science class on Friday, and it was the same day Dario had to finish packing. Mr. Okafor had handed out two sets of graphs, one for a desert and one for a tropical rainforest, and told the class only to compare rainfall bars and temperature lines and report what they noticed. "The graphs will tell you," he said, and refused to say anything else, which Nolan found annoying and then, later, kind of great.

In the library that afternoon, Nolan laid out the desert graphs first. The temperature line jumped around like a squirrel, hot months and cooler months far apart, and the rainfall bars were almost invisible except one skinny spike. Then he turned to the rainforest sheets. The rainfall bars were tall and steady all year, and the temperature line ran flat, nearly the same in the warmest month as in the coolest. That made sense. Hot and wet all year, he thought, no jacket needed.

But Priya, working across the table, was squinting at a small printed box under her graph. "Look at this part," she said. "They wrote in the day temperatures and the night temperatures separately." Nolan pulled his sheet closer and read the numbers, then read them again. Between day and night, the temperature dropped several degrees. Between the warmest month and the coolest month, it barely changed at all. He grabbed his pencil and did the subtraction twice, because it seemed backwards.

"Wait," he said. "The swing between day and night is bigger than the swing between months. So it's the nights that change, not the seasons." Priya checked his arithmetic and nodded. Nolan copied both comparisons into his project, drew arrows on the graphs, and underlined the numbers. On the walk home he stopped in the driveway, took out his phone, and called Dario. "Bring the fleece. It's warm every month, but the nights cool down more than the seasons ever do. Trust the graph."

Dario paused on the other end. "You're sure?"

"I tested it twice," Nolan said. "Pack the sweater."

Later that week Dario, who had appointed himself Nolan's unofficial mentor ever since he taught him to whistle in second grade, admitted over dinner that he'd almost cut the jacket to make room for bug spray. "I have to confess," he said, sliding the packing list across the table, "you saved me a cold night. Now help me decide what to leave behind instead."

Nolan picked up the list and ran his finger down it. "The matches," he said. "Half this stuff is flammable and you're going somewhere with more water than you've ever seen."

Dario laughed and crossed out the matches, and Nolan folded the list into his pocket to tape above his toucan poster after dinner.

Lily found the stone on the second morning of the camping trip, in the shallows of the river below their site. It was gray and shaped like an egg, so smooth it felt like soap. Her cousin Marco wanted it for his collection the moment he saw it.

"That's my stone," Marco said. "I found the first smooth one yesterday, so the river's smooth stones are mine."

"You can't claim a whole river," Lily said. Marco was nine and had brought an egg carton with twelve labeled slots, one for each stone he planned to take home. He had three so far. Lily held the stone up to the light and wondered what had polished it, because the other rocks along the bank were rough and cracked.

That afternoon she sat on a flat rock with her notebook and the stone and tried to work it out. The river was cloudy with sand, and she could hear small pebbles knocking along the bottom when she put her ear near the water. She scooped a jar of river water and let it sit. Sand settled out, a full finger of it. On the bank she found a boulder with a shallow groove on its downstream side, smooth inside, curving away like the river itself. She remembered a sign at the overlook that said this valley had taken millions of years, and that a canyon got its shape from erosion and deposition, the river carrying material away in some places and dropping it in others. But what actually did the cutting? The water alone felt too soft for that. Her idea: the river was not empty water, it was water full of tools.

She tested it with two rough pebbles from the bank and a scoop of coarse sand in the empty jar. She shook the jar hard for a long time, then poured everything out through her bandana. Both pebbles were duller, with fresh flat patches rubbed onto them. When her dad walked past and asked what she was doing, she said, "The sand did this. The river cuts downward because the sand, pebbles and boulders it carries grind against its bed. That's called abrasion." He said he hadn't known that, and kept walking to the fire.

That evening Marco left a note folded into her boot, because he was sulking and wouldn't talk. It said, "You can have the gray one. My want is the banded one under the log, the one with the white stripe. If you see it, don't take it." Lily read it twice, then went looking. Under the log, half buried in mud, was a rough rock with a white stripe, jagged and dull. She carried it to Marco at the fire.

"This one's yours," she said. "But if you leave it in the river a few million years, it'll look like mine."

Marco turned it over in his hand and dropped it into slot four of the egg carton.

Sophie stared at the laptop screen, where her short story about a lost dog named Biscuit sat unfinished at the moment the neighbors pulled him shivering from the storm drain. "You generated three whole pages," her mom said, passing behind with a basket of laundry, "and now you've stopped cold." Sophie scrolled up and down, wondering what was missing. The big rescue scene had dialogue, commas, quotation marks, everything her rubric demanded. So why did the story feel like it dropped off a cliff?

Her little brother Theo leaned over her shoulder, chewing a granola bar. "Wait, the dog gets rescued and then what? Does he go back to the kid? Does the kid's mom stop being mad about the muddy paw prints?" Sophie opened her mouth to say those questions didn't matter, then stopped. "Actually," she said slowly, "I don't know what happens after." Theo shrugged and wandered off, but the questions stuck to her like burrs. She pulled up her teacher's assignment sheet and reread it, hunting for clues. There it was, one sentence she'd skimmed past: after the climax, the falling action and resolution show the consequences of what happened and tie up the story's loose ends. She read it twice. "The climax," she said to Biscuit's picture on the screen, "is the rescue. That's the peak. Everything after it has to show what happens because of it."

She decided to test the idea like a science experiment. Loose end number one: the muddy paw prints. Loose end number two: the kid, Marcus, who had lied about closing the gate. If the rescue was the turning point, then each loose end needed a consequence that flowed from it. Sophie typed a new scene where Marcus's mom, now impartial about the whole gate argument because the near-loss had scared everyone equally, sat Marcus down and he confessed. Then Biscuit, freshly bathed, curled up on Marcus's bed as if the storm drain had never happened. It was only two paragraphs, but when she reread the whole story, the cliff was gone. The ending landed on solid ground.

Then came the twist. Theo came back and read the new version with his mouth full. "Better," he announced. "But you forgot the biggest loose end." Sophie felt her stomach tighten. "Which one?" He pointed at a line near the top, where Marcus had given Biscuit half his sandwich before the gate was left open. "The other dog. The one that dug under the fence and lured Biscuit out. You never said where it went." Sophie scrolled and, sure enough, there it was, a stray mentioned once and then abandoned. No wonder Biscuit kept barking at the fence in her head.

She added one more paragraph, a final scene where the stray appeared at the gate, and Marcus's mom, in a last line of dialogue, said, "Well, I guess we just became a two-dog family." Sophie saved the file, sat back, and smiled. Theo tugged her sleeve and asked, "Can I pick the next loose end?"

Samantha had rewritten her triangle proof three times, and the red mark on her homework still said the same thing: Not the included angle. Her mother had tried to console her with cocoa, but cocoa could not argue with Mr. Delgado's grading pen, and Samantha was beginning to think nothing could.

She spread her homework on the kitchen table next to the dishwasher's gentle hum. Two triangles, ABC and DEF. She had shown that AB matched DE and BC matched EF, and then she had grabbed angle A and angle D, because they were sitting right there, easy to find. Mr. Delgado had circled her angle pair and written one word in the margin: included?

"Fine," she said to the triangles. "What do you want from me?"

Her little brother Theo wandered in, hunting for crackers. "Why are you yelling at paper?"

"I'm not yelling. I'm reasoning." She pulled two straws from the drawer and a strip of paper with a fold in it. Theo leaned over her shoulder, cracker crumbs already falling.

"Is this your whole curriculum?" he asked.

"Very funny. Watch this." She laid the straws in a V, hinged together with a twist tie, so the two sides stayed a fixed length. "These are my two sides. Now the angle between them, the one right here where the straws meet." She opened and closed the V a few times. "See? If the angle between the sides matches, the whole triangle snaps into the same shape. Side, angle, side. Boom, congruent."

"So you're done. Eat dinner."

"No, because I used the wrong angle." She traced angle A on her paper, the one up at the far end of side AB, not between her two sides. "I picked one out in the corner somewhere. Here, look." She kept the straws the same length but slid the fold around, making a different angle sit at the top instead of between the straws. The triangles that came out were not the same shape at all. "Two sides and some other angle, and you can get triangles that don't match. That's why he marked it."

"So it's like following a recipe and dumping the salt in the wrong bowl?"

"Worse," Samantha said, but she was already writing. She crossed out angle A, wrote angle B, and drew a small arrow pointing at the space squeezed between sides AB and BC. She added one sentence, her most vigorous handwriting of the week: Angle B is the included angle, between the two given sides.

Theo ate another cracker over her paper. She slid it away from the crumbs.

"There," she said, and signed her name at the bottom like a judge.

The swim test at Camp Winnow was on Friday, and Felix had been dreading it for eleven days. He knew eleven was right because he had counted the mornings he woke up with his stomach knotted, and by Wednesday he was so tired from lying awake that he capsized a canoe during a calm-water drill.

Last summer, before he'd quit swim lessons, his instructor had pulled him aside. "You're not bad at this," she had said. "You panic before you even touch the water." Felix had thought about that moment all year, and now it was happening again, except this time nobody was saying it out loud.

He found a folded note tucked into his bunk after lunch. It was from Priya, his tentmate. "My sister used to feel sick every single morning for a whole month," she had written in looping pencil. "She talked to the camp nurse and it got better. But Coach Dez told me my jitters before the relay are normal, that a little stress right before a race actually sharpens you. Yours has lasted for days, though. That's different. Come find me?"

Felix sat on the bunk and stared at the word "different." His stomach had been knotted for eleven days, not eleven minutes. The jitters Priya got showed up right before a race and then left, like a wave that came and went. His had moved in and stayed. Maybe they weren't the same thing at all.

He found Priya at the dock, and they formed an alliance of two nervous swimmers, agreeing to check on each other every day. She taught him what the nurse had taught her sister: breathe in for four counts, hold for four, out for six, three times through. That evening he budgeted his time so lights-out came an hour early, keeping to the same routine every night, no whispered jokes after nine, just his sleeping bag and slow breathing until his eyes closed on their own.

By Friday morning he had slept through the night twice, and when he stood at the lake's edge in his swim trunks, his heart hammered, his hands shook, and the test was imminent. But his stomach was only tight now, not knotted, and the tightness felt almost like readiness. He did the breathing pattern once, watched the water sparkle, and decided the wave had come and it would go.

"Ready?" Priya asked, bumping his shoulder.

Felix stepped off the dock and dove.

Alexis had promised herself she wouldn't just sit in her mom's office playing games on Bring Your Kid to Work Day, and so far she had kept that promise for almost forty minutes. The thermostat on the wall read 68, and she was still cold, but she didn't say so. Instead she stared at the spreadsheet on her mom's spare monitor, where a list of donations sat in columns: names down the left, dollar amounts filling columns B, C, and D.

"There's a department meeting at eleven," Mom said, gathering her notebook. "Can you total those columns for me? The instructions from Mr. Ruiz are in that sticky note on the keyboard."

The note read: "Put =SUM(B2:B10) in B12, then copy it across. It should work for all of them. Gracias." Alexis had never written a formula in her life, and the string of letters and numbers looked like something designed to intimidate her. She typed it anyway, pressed Enter, and watched the column add itself: 1,248.

Then came the puzzle. If she copied the formula into C12, would it add column B again, or column C? She couldn't see inside the computer to know. She thought of last summer, when she'd guessed which door led to the beach and picked the wrong one, and how Aunt Rosa had said, "You could have just knocked." She'd never liked guessing blind. But she could test this, the same way she'd once tested whether the toaster was broken or just unplugged.

She clicked into C12 and typed =SUM(B2:B10) by hand, to see what a wrong answer would look like. It gave 1,248 again, exactly the same number, which meant it was still adding column B. So she deleted it, copied the original formula from B12, and pasted it into C12. The number changed to 956, which matched the total of column C when she added it herself on paper. She pasted it into D12 too, and that column summed as well. The formula had shifted by itself.

"Mom," she called toward the hallway, "Mr. Ruiz's note was right. Why did it change?"

Mom leaned back from her desk chair. "They're called relative references. That's all I know, honestly. Your grandfather tried to teach me this once and I told him spreadsheets were too invasive, that they'd take over my whole job." She smiled a little, as if she were weighing whether that had been a smart stand or a lazy one. "Now look at me."

Alexis highlighted the three totals and clicked the chart button, and a bar chart sprang up on the screen, three fat bars rising at different heights. She screenshotted it and sent it to her dad with the message: "Made this in 10 minutes. Ask me what a relative reference is."

Then she turned back to the chart and dragged its corner until the bars filled the whole screen.

Alyssa hunched over the microscope and adjusted the fine focus for the third time. The onion skin cells lay in neat rows like bricks in a wall, and she could label the cell wall easily, but the lab sheet also wanted the cell membrane and the nucleus, and she could not find either one. Mr. Reyes had written on the board that any slide left unlabeled by the end of the period would earn a zero, and the clock above the door showed nine minutes left. Her lab partner, Desmond, was already sketching his own diagram with annoying confidence.

"It's not fair," Alyssa muttered. "The wall is right there. The other stuff is invisible."

"It's not invisible," Desmond said without looking up. "It's just see-through. Like my grandmother's memoir, the one she keeps saying she'll finish. The story's in there somewhere."

"That's not the equivalent of helpful," Alyssa said, though she smiled despite herself. She tried eliminating possibilities, one by one. Maybe the light was too bright. She closed the iris diaphragm a bit, and the image dimmed, but no membrane appeared. Maybe the stain was weak. She added another drop of iodine to the slide edge and watched it soak under the coverslip, but the cells stayed stubbornly smooth-edged, their insides a uniform pale gold. Four minutes left.

Desmond leaned over. "Try this." Before she could stop him, he placed a single drop of salt water at the edge of the coverslip.

"Hey, you'll ruin my slide!"

"Look first," he said.

Alyssa put her eye to the lens. Inside each brick-like cell, something was pulling inward. The pale inner lining was shrinking away from the outer wall, curling back like a curtain being drawn, and for the first time she could see the membrane itself, a distinct dark outline hugging a smaller shape within the wall. At the center of that shape sat a dense round dot. The nucleus. It had been there the whole time, hidden against the membrane until the salt water drew the water out of the cells and pulled everything apart.

"Whoa," she whispered. "Desmond, look."

He bent to the eyepiece, then straightened up, flipping through the textbook's index. "It's called plasmolysis," he read aloud.

She grabbed her pencil and drew fast, labeling the wall, the membrane pulled inward, the nucleus plain as a coin. Mr. Reyes called two minutes, and Alyssa finished her last arrow just as the bell rang.

"I'm framing this page," she said, holding up the lab sheet.

Lea had signed up for the debate tournament expecting resolutions and rebuttals, but when she checked the schedule in the loud gymnasium, her name was listed under something called Improv Pairwork. A woman at the sign-in table handed her a card. "Your partner is Priya," the woman said. "Room 4. You build a scene together, one minute, judges score it."

Priya was already inside, bouncing on her heels beside a row of folding chairs. She launched straight into their first practice. "We're astronauts," she announced, "and the ship is out of fuel."

"Okay," Lea said.

Priya waited, then rescued the silence herself. "Look, a planet made of cheese!"

"Sure," Lea agreed. "Okay. Cool."

Priya's shoulders dropped. She tried again on the walk to the practice room, a haunted house, then a jungle, and each time Lea agreed with everything and added nothing, and each time the scene sagged like a tent with one pole missing. Priya finally flopped into a chair. "You comply with everything I say, but the scene keeps dying, and I don't get why."

Lea stared at the floor between her sneakers and ran her analysis. It wasn't a disagreement problem. She had never contradicted Priya once. So the hidden cause had to be somewhere else, some rule about what a scene needs besides agreement. She thought about the card in her pocket and turned it over. On the back, in small print, were the scoring criteria. One line read: "Partners must accept what the other has established, then add something new."

That was it. Agreement alone was negligent, like being handed a rope and refusing to pull. The scene needed two builders, not one builder and one nodding statue. "I think I've been doing half the job," Lea said slowly. "It's not just yes. It's yes, and."

They ran it once more in the hallway by the water fountain. "We're pirates," Priya said, "and the treasure map is blank."

"Yes," Lea said, "and I remember the island, because I dreamed it three nights in a row." Priya's grin came back like a lamp switching on. "Yes, and the dream had a warning in it," she said, and they were off, trading offers back and forth until a monitor told them to save it for the judges.

In Room 4, the judge turned out to be a tired man with a clipboard, and the twist was that they knew each other. He was Mr. Okoye, who had coached Lea's debate team two years ago and had once told her she argued like a wall. Lea and Priya built a scene about two librarians discovering a dragon sleeping in the returns bin, and every offer landed and every add lifted it higher. When the minute ended, Mr. Okoye looked up from his clipboard and said, "Who taught you that?" Lea glanced at Priya. "Nobody," she said. "We found it on the back of a card."

Tyler had exactly one campaign promise, and it was a good one: more pizza at the monthly assemblies. His best friend Marcus had almost the same promise, except his said "better pizza," which Tyler argued was a downgrade because you cannot get better than pizza. On Friday, both of them planned to run for class rep, along with Priya, whose posters said "Vote Priya: Structural Improvements," which nobody could explain, including Priya.

Before the real vote, Ms. Okoye announced a practice election in social studies so the class could compare two ways of counting ballots. She would say nothing else about it, which she claimed was "the whole point." Tyler thought that was like handing someone a dilapidated bicycle with two flat tires and saying, "Notice things."

"Everybody gets to enroll as a voter," Marcus announced at the cardboard booth, stamping people's hands with a smiley face because he had lost the ink pad shaped like a star. "Step right up. Democracy smells like grape jelly today." That part was true; the stamp pad was grape scented, and by lunch the whole class smelled like a sandwich.

The practice vote happened with paper ballots. Tyler got 11 votes, Marcus got 10, and Priya got 12. Priya did a small spinning dance, then stopped. "Wait. I won with twelve. But you two got eleven plus ten. That's more than twelve." She said it slowly, like she was poking something with a stick to see if it moved.

Tyler grabbed the ballots and spread them across his desk. He and Marcus had promised the same thing, pizza, so almost everyone who liked pizza had to pick one of them or the other. Their supporters were split between two nearly identical choices, while Priya's supporters all landed in one pile. He counted again, then a third time, hoping the numbers would get embarrassed and change. They did not. "So under this system," he said, "two similar candidates can split their supporters' votes, and a third candidate wins with fewer votes than their combined total." Priya wrote that on her arm with a marker, which she claimed was structural improvement.

Then Ms. Okoye had them recount the same ballots the second way, where the seats got handed out in proportion to the votes. Under that count, the pizza side, with twenty-one votes together, came out ahead, and Priya's side got its fair share too. "So the same votes, counted two ways, give two different winners," Tyler said. "That's either amazing or a crime." Marcus suggested they compromise: run as a pizza team, one candidate, slogan in two colors.

On Monday, Marcus tore down his own poster and drew an arrow on Tyler's, pointing to a new line that said "Co-Reps: Pizza Alliance." Priya taped a structural improvements plank next to it, just to see what would happen. Ms. Okoye walked past the dilapidated poster, now held up with three kinds of tape and one bandage, and said, "Best civics lesson I never taught." Tyler held up the stamp pad. "Grape jelly," he said. "That's our second promise."

Annabelle crouched at the top of the skate park's shallow bowl with a stopwatch in one hand and a marble in the other. Her science project was due tomorrow morning, and she still needed three good runs of data. Her cousin Milo, who had come to practice kickflips before his competition at four o'clock, leaned on his board and watched her chalk a line every meter down the smooth concrete.

"Could you hurry up?" Milo said. "I need this bowl in twenty minutes."

"Then help me," Annabelle said. "You call the seconds, I roll the ball." She set the marble on the slope, and Milo counted each second out loud while she marked where the marble was. When she connected the marks on her graph paper, she frowned. The first run had produced a wobbly, curving line, and she could not tell if her timing had been off or if the marble had actually sped up and slowed down.

She tried again with a tennis ball on the flattest, smoothest stretch of floor beside the bowl. This time she measured the distance at every second and plotted the points carefully. When she laid her ruler across the dots, they fell almost perfectly straight, sloping up from the corner of the page. "Look at this," she said, holding the paper out to Milo. "It's a straight line, and it slopes up. So what does that even mean?" Milo shrugged, still balancing on his board, but Annabelle stared at the graph and turned it over in her mind. If the line was straight, the ball must have covered the same distance in every second. "A straight sloping line means it was going at a constant speed," she said slowly. "The whole way."

Milo rolled over and squinted at the page. "So my marble run yesterday, the curvy one, that was speeding up?"

"That's what I want to find out," Annabelle said. She was beginning to think her first wobbly graph was not a mistake at all. Maybe the bowl itself had made the marble change speed, and the curve was trying to tell her something she could not see directly. She wondered what other hidden rules a graph could reveal, and whether she could justify her guess by testing the marble in the bowl again with better timing.

"Ten minutes," Milo warned, glancing at the clock by the snack shack. "Then this floor is mine." He had changed his mind about her project, though; instead of pacing at the edge, he crouched beside her, holding the stopwatch. "You know my grandma's always saying her pension doesn't stretch far enough, so I can't get a tutor for math," he said. "Maybe graphs like this could help me pass after all. Endangered species, that's what my grade is."

Annabelle laughed and positioned the marble at the top of the bowl. "On three," Milo said, thumb hovering over the button. "One, two..."

The flat happened right outside First National Bank, where Bentley had stopped to wait for his mom. He heard the soft hiss while rolling to the rack, and when he looked down, the back tyre was sagging like a deflated balloon. His repair kit sat in his backpack: two new tubes, three tyre levers, and a hand pump he had never once used. "This could plague me all afternoon," he muttered, because his mom had already said they were going straight to his cousin's birthday party after this.

He knelt on the wide stone steps and jammed the curved end of a lever under the edge of the tyre. It would not budge. He pushed harder, then tried a second lever beside the first, then a third, until all three were wedged in a row like plastic spoons in a jar. The tyre stayed sealed to the rim as if it had been glued there. A security guard leaned out the door. "Need help, champ?" Bentley shook his head. "I'm supposed to be learning this myself," he said, and he meant it. His uncle had refused to nominate anyone else to teach him, saying a boy ought to know his own bike.

He sat back and stared at the wheel. The tyre still had a little roundness to it, he realized. Not much, but some. He pressed the valve stem and let out a long slow whisper of air until the tyre went completely soft and floppy. Then he slid the lever in again. This time it slipped under the edge like magic, and when he pulled back, the whole side of the tyre came loose from the rim in one satisfying pop. "Letting all the air out first," he said quietly, "that's what makes it loose enough."

He worked the rest of the tyre off, felt around inside for the thorn that had caused the trouble, and found it lodged near the valve. He pressed the new tube in, tucked the tyre back over the rim, and pumped until the wheel stood firm and round again. His mom came down the steps, receipts in her hand, and stopped mid-sentence when she saw the bike.

"Did somebody fix that for you?"

"Nope," Bentley said, spinning the wheel with one finger. "Sophisticated work, actually. Watch it go."

The rain hammered the windows of Grandpa's farmhouse, and Charlotte spread her notebook across the kitchen table, staring at the page where her story had stalled. Her assignment was due Monday morning, and her teacher had written one comment at the top of last week's draft: "Your dialogue punctuation is breaking the rules." The story was about a peasant girl who hid a stolen horse in a stable, and the whole middle of it was people talking.

"The stable boy asked the girl a question," Charlotte muttered, reading her own line aloud. She had written: "Where is the horse?" He asked. That capital H looked right to her, the way a new sentence always starts with a capital. But she remembered, suddenly, a Tuesday in September, her teacher's red pen circling the same thing on a different page, and the whole class groaning because nobody understood the mark on the board. Charlotte had copied it down wrong that day. She'd been too busy passing a note, and when the bell rang, she'd shoved the notebook in her bag and never fixed it.

She pushed the memory away and pulled the notebook closer. Instead of guessing, she decided to test it. Grandpa was in the doorway, drying his hands on a dish towel, and she waved him over.

"Read this out loud," she said. "Where is the horse?" He asked. Then read it this way: "Where is the horse?" he asked."

Grandpa read both versions slowly, and his eyebrows went up at the second one. "The second one flows like a person talking," he said. "The first one sounds like two separate people." Charlotte wrote both versions again and stared at them. The question mark sat inside the quotation marks in both. But in the one that sounded right, the word after it started with a lowercase letter, because "he asked" wasn't a new sentence at all. The question mark belonged to the quoted words, and the tag came after, quiet, like a shadow following the line.

She tried it in three more places. "Did you see anyone?" she asked. "Who would believe a peasant?" the miller demanded. Each time she checked: question mark inside, lowercase after. She could almost watch the rule circulate through her whole story, fixing every conversation, the way the heater pushed warm air around the cold kitchen.

By nine o'clock the rain had thinned to a whisper, and Charlotte read her final page to Grandpa by lamplight. The stable boy discovered the hidden horse at the climax, just as the story demanded. Then she flipped back to her September notebook and looked at the old mistake she'd never corrected, still sitting there in her messy handwriting.

"I should have asked somebody back then," she said.

Grandpa tapped the page. "Fix it now," he said, and slid the pen across the table to her.

Asher had his science notebook open on the waiting room bench, but he was staring at the parakeet carrier on the counter instead. His mom was inside with the dog for a checkup, and he had exactly one hour to figure out his homework question before the bus to the regional science meet, where a jury of judges would quiz him on adaptation. The question read: "How did natural selection change the beak shapes of Galápagos finches on different islands?" He had gotten it wrong once already. His first answer had said finches chose their beaks, and his teacher circled it in red.

The vet tech, Denise, came out with a chart and glanced at his notebook. "Finches, huh? We've got a finch in the back, seed stuck in its throat. Want to see?"

"Yes," Asher said, grabbing the notebook.

The little bird had a deep, heavy beak, almost like a pair of pliers. Denise held up the seed that had lodged in its crop, a hard round thing like a tiny stone. Asher wrote "deep, heavy beak" and drew the seed beside it. Then he thought about the other islands he had read about, where the birds ate insects off bark and leaves. A beak like pliers would be useless, practically obsolete, for wiggling a grub out of a crack. You would need something thin, like tweezers.

"Can I test this?" he asked. Denise raised an eyebrow, then laughed and handed him a box of different foods from the shelf: soft mealworms in a cup, hard dry seeds, a strip of millet. Asher found two pairs of forceps in the drawer, one thin and pointed, one thick and stubby. He tried to pick up a mealworm with the thick forceps and dropped it three times; the thin ones snatched it instantly. Then he squeezed a hard seed with the thin forceps and it shot across the table. The thick ones cracked it clean in half. He was writing so fast the pen skipped.

"So on islands with hard seeds, the birds with deep, heavy beaks survived and had chicks like them," he said, mostly to himself, "and on insect islands the thin-beaked ones did." He had changed his own mind in ten minutes. The finches hadn't chosen anything. The islands had done the choosing, quietly, over endless generations.

"You should nurture that idea a little longer," Denise said, tapping his page of drawings. "Draw the two beaks side by side. Judges love that."

Asher grinned and started sketching, thin beak beside the mealworm, heavy beak beside the seed, just as the clinic door swung open and his mom appeared with the dog. "Ready for the bus," she said. He held up the notebook, the cracked seed still sitting in the middle of the page.

Isabella had enrolled in the after-school science club mostly because her friend Marisol had, but now the club's project was due Monday and she was stuck. The assignment was to roll a ball down the hallway, measure its distance every second, and draw a distance-time graph from the numbers. The graph was supposed to show the ball slowing down as it rolled across the carpet. Hers showed something strange.

"Watch," she said to Marisol, who had come over Sunday afternoon. Isabella crouched at the end of the hallway with a stopwatch and a marble. "I roll it, I call the seconds, you write the distance." She flicked the marble. It zipped along the wood floor, hit the rug by the bathroom door, wobbled, and stopped. Every time she tried it, the marble died in the same spot.

They collected the numbers at the kitchen table. Isabella drew the axes, marked time across the bottom and distance up the side, and plotted each point. From two seconds to four seconds, the points sat at exactly the same height: thirty centimeters, thirty centimeters, thirty centimeters. She connected them with a straight, level stretch of line.

"That part looks broken," Marisol said, poking the flat section. "The rest of your line climbs, then it just goes sideways."

Isabella looked at the stopwatch log, then down the hall at the marble still sitting on the rug. It hadn't moved between those seconds at all. The line wasn't broken. "It's not climbing because the ball isn't going anywhere," she said. "A flat line means the ball stopped." She picked up the marble and rolled it again, slower, watching the rug. The marble's own fuzz of dust clung to the carpet fibers, and it sank in and stayed. That was it, not her timing, not her measurements.

For Monday's graph she traced the flat stretch with a red pencil and wrote "ball stuck on rug" above it in small letters. Then she rolled the marble one more time down the hall, but this time she lifted the corner of the rug and let it fly onto the bare wood.

"Now watch it climb," she said.

The tutoring centre smelled of pencil shavings and old carpet, and Isabelle had claimed the corner table by the window because the afternoon sun landed right on her workbook. Her tutor, Mr. Okafor, had shown her one trick, which was to do the same operation to both sides of an equation, and then he had been called away to the front desk. Isabelle practiced alone: if x + 3 = 10, subtract 3 from both sides, and x = 7. If 2x = 14, divide both sides by 2. Each solved problem went into her binder, a cumulative stack of small victories she planned to show her brother, who had bet her five dollars she would quit by October.

Across the table, a younger boy named Dev was bent over a single problem, groaning. "This one's broken," he said.

"Nothing's broken," Isabelle said. "Watch. You can migrate the numbers across the equals sign, as long as you do the same thing to both sides. It's like a seesaw. You subtract here, you subtract there."

"I've been subtracting for ages." He turned his paper toward her. On it, in wobbly handwriting, was x + 1 = x + 2, surrounded by crossed-out attempts, arrows, and one small angry doodle of a burning calculator.

Isabelle reached for her pencil, then stopped. Something about the shape of it made her fingers hover. She tested her idea the only way she knew how, by trying a number. "Okay, say x is five. Then the left side is six, and the right side is seven. Not equal."

"Try a hundred," Dev said.

"One hundred and one, and one hundred and two. Still not equal." She tried zero. One and two. She tried negative numbers until Dev complained she was wearing out the eraser. The gap never closed. It was as if the equals sign were a door that looked open but had a wall behind it, invisible until you walked at it.

She sat back, and Mr. Okafor's voice drifted over from the desk, where he was explaining to a parent that some students develop a bias against maths after one bad year. Isabelle stared at Dev's paper. Her heart beat faster than a subtraction should have made it.

"Dev," she said slowly, "I don't think we can't find the number. I don't think the number exists. No number can be one more and two more than itself at the same time."

Dev looked at his paper, then at her. "So the puzzle's cheating."

"It has no solution. Write that."

He wrote it in careful letters, boxed it twice, and slid it across the table. "Is that allowed?"

Isabelle grinned and pulled her binder toward her. "Let's find out," she said, and raised her hand for Mr. Okafor.

Alexis pushed the cart past the cereal aisle with the list her mother had taped to the handle, reading aloud in her most competent voice. "Dad's laundry lesson starts tonight, so grab what you need." She was going to do an entire load from start to finish, sorting to folding, because she had decided she was tired of wearing shirts that fit her little brother better than they fit her.

"That's the spirit," her mom said, steering toward the cleaning aisle. "We're also doing the big clean tomorrow, so we need window cleaner too."

At the cleaning aisle Alexis picked up a jug of chlorine bleach, because whites, and her mother grabbed a bottle of window cleaner that smelled sharp and clean in the store's fluorescent light. Somewhere near the fish counter, the whole store emitted a smell like low tide, which made Alexis hold her nose and mutter "parasite" at the salmon, thinking about the tapeworm diagram due in science on Monday.

"Hand me the bleach," her mom said, tucking the window cleaner under her arm and reaching to pour a splash of bleach into a nearly empty bottle in the cart, the one Dad had left half full from the garage cleanout.

"Wait." Alexis pulled the bleach back. She had actually read the label while waiting in line, mostly because the jug had a warning box nearly as big as her science quiz, and it said never mix with cleaners containing ammonia. She turned the window cleaner around. Ammonia, right there in the ingredients. Then she looked at the half-empty bottle and squinted at the sticky residue on its side, cloudy and faintly blue.

"That one had ammonia cleaner in it," she said. "If they mix, they release chloramine. It's a toxic gas."

Her mom froze with the bottles three inches apart. "Huh. I was about to make a chemical weapon in the cereal aisle."

"Congratulations on almost being a supervillain, Mom."

The fish guy two aisles over laughed so hard they heard him over the intercom.

They bought the bleach and a fresh, clearly labeled bottle, plus laundry detergent, because that was the whole point. At home that evening, Alexis dragged the overflowing hamper into the hallway and began sorting, which was when she made her first real discovery: one red sock, hiding inside Dad's whites like a tiny criminal, would have turned every shirt pink.

"Sorting isn't just a rule adults made up to torture us," she announced. "It's detective work."

She ran the whites, moved them to the dryer, and folded everything into squares that were only slightly lopsided. Her dad inspected a towel, nodded slowly, and said, "You'll be doing my laundry forever now, you realize."

"No," Alexis said, holding up the red sock like evidence in court. "But I am keeping this one in a jar as a warning to the others."

The community kitchen on Harlow Street smelled like onions and warm spice, and Lucy had been assigned to the whole meal, not just one dish. Rice, curry, flatbread, all finished at the same time, so the plates went out hot. The teacher, Ms. Okafor, called this "real cooking," and Lucy had been proud of the word until she stood in front of three burners and realized she had no idea how to make three things land together.

She started with the rice, since it looked like the slowest. Wash, water, pot, lid, flame. Then she mixed curry paste and coconut milk in a second pot and set it on low. The flatbread dough she would roll and cook last, in a dry pan, quick as anything. On the wall above the stoves hung a faded map of the river delta where Ms. Okafor had grown up, and the label on it read "estuary," the wide mouth where the river met the sea. Lucy traced it with her eyes while she stirred and wondered whether food from a place like that tasted like both river and salt.

Beside her, a boy named Devon kept lifting the lid off his pot of rice. Peek, stir, lid. Peek again. "I just want to see if it's working," he said, a little embarrassed.

"Rice isn't much to look at," Lucy said, but she was thinking harder than that. When the class did a trial run the week before, Devon's rice had come out crunchy in the middle while everyone else's was soft, and he had shrugged and blamed the bag. Lucy hadn't shrugged. She kept turning the question over. Same rice, same water, same stove. The only thing different she could remember was Devon, hovering and lifting, again and again. Could she deduce the cause from that? If the difference wasn't the rice or the pot, it had to be something Devon did, and the one thing he did more than anyone was open the lid.

She didn't say any of this out loud. Instead she made a plan for her own pot, a small test. She would not lift the lid at all, not once, from the moment it started steaming until the timer rang. Her curry needed stirring, and the flatbread needed her full attention with the rolling pin, so her hands were busy anyway. The hardest part was her own worry, the itch to check. She pressed the lid down a little firmer, like sealing a promise.

While the bread bubbled on the dry pan, she counted backward from the clock to figure out timing. Curry off the heat now, bread in thirty-second rounds, rice resting with the flame off and the lid still on. When everything was down to the last minute, she finally lifted her lid. Steam rolled out in one white cloud, and underneath, the grains stood plump and separate and fully cooked, all the way through.

Devon leaned over and looked at her pot, then at his own, which he had peeked at four more times. "Yours didn't crunch," he said.

"Don't lift the lid while it simmers," Lucy said. "Every peek lets the steam out, and then the rice can end up undercooked."

Devon squinted at his pot as if it had betrayed him personally. "So I did this to myself."

"Try one with the lid staying shut," Lucy said. "I'll roll you a flatbread while you wait."

He refilled his pot, set the lid on carefully, and then sat on his hands.

Sara curled her fingers into a claw above the onion, knuckles forward, exactly the way the chef's poster showed, and brought the knife down in slow, parallel cuts. The kitchen of Uncle Ray's restaurant smelled of garlic and scorched tomato from the batch before hers, and her eyes were already stinging. "Keep your fingertips under," said Marcus, the dishwasher's son, who wanted to be a line cook someday and never let anyone forget it. "You slice a thumb in here, my dad says you mop the floor for a week." Sara adjusted her grip and wondered whether the cooks who never cried at onions had simply stopped noticing, or whether their knives were sharper than this one.

Her task was real: the Saturday sauce. Uncle Ray had put two pounds of pasta on to boil for the dinner rush and told her the sauce had to cling, not slide, or the plates would look like soup. She crushed the canned tomatoes with her hands, which felt satisfyingly against the rules, and added her chopped onion to the hissing oil. It smelled like a real kitchen, like the one she imagined when she wrote stories, where the narrator always knew what everyone was tasting.

The sauce simmered, but when she dragged a spoon through it, the tomato part stayed thin and watery, and a slick of oil floated beside it, refusing to join. She tasted it and frowned. Something was wrong, and she could not see what. She checked the heat, lowered it, tasted again. Thin, still thin. She began to wonder whether the problem was not what she had added but something she had left out, some invisible ingredient the recipe assumed.

Then Marcus called from the sink, where he was about to dump the giant pot of cloudy pasta water down the drain. "Wait," Sara said, hurrying over. The water was milky white, not clear, and she dipped a finger in and rubbed her fingertips together. Slick. She remembered the water turning that way as the pasta cooked, and she thought, this water changed while the pasta was in it. "The pasta releases starch into the water," she said slowly, half asking herself. She ladled out a cupful before Marcus could tip the rest away. "A splash of this might help a sauce thicken and cling to the pasta. That's what cloudy means here."

She stirred the splash into her sauce and watched. Within a minute the spoon left a clean trail, and when she lifted it, the sauce hung on, thick and glossy, the oil no longer swimming apart from the tomato. She tasted it and grinned at Marcus, who leaned over her shoulder and sniffed. "Okay, I confess, I thought you were ruining it," he said. She dipped two clean spoons into the pot and handed him one. "Try it before the dinner rush does."

Alexandre had finished dead last in the first eight-hundred-metre time trial, and he knew exactly why: he had sprinted the first lap as if it were the only lap. By the final straight his legs felt like they belonged to someone else, someone slower, and three boys had passed him one after another while he watched them go. That night he wrote an email to his friend Priya, who missed practice because her family had gone to visit her grandmother.

"You will laugh," he typed. "Coach timed us, and I ran my first lap ten seconds faster than my second. TEN. I was the early leader for about ninety glorious seconds, and then I became a statue with legs. Dylan passed me. Then Marcus. Then a kid I have never spoken to in my life, who said 'good race' in a pity voice. Tomorrow I am going to try something: run the first lap slower on purpose, a pace I can actually hold, and see what happens to the second lap. If this fails too, I am taking up chess."

Priya's reply came the next morning, printed out and folded into his shoe, which was her idea of a mailbox. "Chess is a sport for people who fade on the final straight," she wrote. "But modify your plan slightly: don't run the first lap slow like you're strolling through a lush garden. Run it even. Save the speed. Also, your shoe-mail system needs work, my note smells like your gym bag."

At practice, the track was bright after rain, and Coach Russell waved them to the line. Alexandre hung back when the gun went off, letting Dylan and Marcus charge ahead. His legs begged him to chase them, but he counted his steps and kept the pace steady, even, holding it the way Priya had said. Down the first back straight Dylan was five metres up and pulling away, and Alexandre felt the old pull to follow. He let Dylan go.

Then the second lap began, and the race turned inside out. Dylan's shoulders dropped, his stride shortened, and he slowed sharply, as if the first lap had cost him something invisible that was now gone. Alexandre came past him on the final bend, and Marcus too, whose early lead had evaporated the same way. Alexandre crossed the line second, gasping but upright, and Priya's note was still crumpled in his shoe.

"Good race," Dylan panted, leaning on his knees, and this time it didn't sound like pity at all. Alexandre grinned and pulled the soggy paper from his shoe, holding it up like a medal.

Jaxon stood at the kitchen counter with his laptop open and a pile of index cards beside the fruit bowl. Tomorrow he had to stand up in health class and explain how nicotine hooks the brain, and every time he tried to say it out loud, the words tangled like earbuds in a pocket. His mother stirred soup at the stove, and the window above the sink held the last gray light of the afternoon.

"Explain it to me," his mother said, tasting from the wooden spoon. "I'm your practice audience."

He took a breath. "Okay. There's this part of the brain called the reward pathway. It's what makes you feel good when you eat a good meal or win a game. Nicotine tricks it. It gets into the brain and pushes that pathway to release dopamine, which is a chemical that signals, hey, that was great, do it again."

"And that's the trap," his mother said.

"Right, because the feeling fades fast, so the brain keeps asking for more." He shuffled his cards, then stopped, because the cards weren't the problem. He remembered Tuesday's class, how Mr. Reyes had put a number on the board without a single comment, just the number, and let the room sit with it. Nearly 9 out of 10 adults who smoke cigarettes daily first tried smoking by age 18. Jaxon had copied it down slowly, and around him kids had stopped whispering. That was the fact he wanted to end with, but he wasn't sure yet how to make it land. He decided to test it, the way he tested things, on his little sister.

Nia was at the table drawing cats with brown whiskers. He sat down across from her. "Nia, quick question. If nine out of ten grown-ups who smoke every day, almost all of them, first tried it by age eighteen, what does that tell you?"

She looked up, pencil paused. "That they started when they were kids. Like, my age almost."

"Exactly like your age almost." He turned back toward the stove, feeling something click into place, quiet and certain. It wasn't a random fact to stick on the last slide. It was the whole point. The brain builds its want early, and nine out of ten times it starts before anyone is old enough to know better.

That evening, after the dishes, he narrated the presentation twice in his room, start to finish, pacing between the bed and the closet. It had become a small ritual: cards down, lights low, speaking to the desk lamp as if it were the class. On the second run he didn't stumble once. He finished with the number, held up both hands with nine fingers spread, and said, "Nine out of ten. Before eighteen." Then he picked up his cards, squared their edges, and set them by the door for morning.

Nevaeh had the kitchen table to herself for exactly one hour, because that was the deal. Her brother Dex, who was nine and had negotiated hard, wanted the microscope for his "mystery puddle water" after dinner, and Mom had said one hour each, no appeals.

The onion sat on the cutting board like a small, smelly prisoner. Nevaeh's assignment said she had to find the cells in a piece of onion skin, draw them, and label the cell wall, the membrane, and the nucleus. The assignment did not say how to do any of that, which she assumed was part of the challenge. She peeled a paper-thin layer off the inside of an onion ring, laid it on the slide, dropped on a coverslip, and pressed her eye to the lens.

She saw purple. Then she saw purple swirls, like turbulent water in a tiny river, and then she saw nothing but her own eyelashes. She spun the focus knob back and forth. Nothing. She checked the slide. Still there. She checked the onion. Still an onion. The cells, according to the diagram in her book, should look like neat little bricks in a wall, and there was not one brick anywhere in the purple storm.

Dex wandered in with his puddle water in a jelly jar. "My turn yet?"

"Forty-five more minutes."

"Mrs. Tanuya lets us look at parameciums in science. She says you have to find them on the little lens first, the low power one, and then switch to the big ones after." He shrugged. "I don't know why. It's just the rule."

Nevaeh looked at the microscope. There were three lenses on the rotating nosepiece, and she had, without thinking, started with the longest one, the biggest, the one that seemed like it ought to show the most. She rotated to the shortest lens, the lowest power, and pressed her eye to the glass. Bricks. Rows and rows of pale, wobbly bricks, like a wall someone had built while tired. She focused slowly, and the edges sharpened, and there in each brick sat a small dark dot, round and stubborn. The nucleus. The wall was the brick edge itself, and the membrane hugged it from the inside, thin as a rumor.

"Ha," she said.

"You found them?"

"Found them, drew them, labeled them." She was already sketching fast, because a rule discovered at minute forty of a forty-five minute turn is a rule discovered barely in time. Dex hovered behind her, holding his jelly jar up to the window light.

"Can I do the low-power thing on my puddle?"

"You can do the whole thing on your puddle." She slid the microscope across the table to him. "Start with the smallest lens."

"Which one's that?"

"The one closest to the slide," Nevaeh said, "that looks like it can't possibly be useful."

Jade had one week to get the duet right before the family reunion at Grandma's house, and the piano was not helping. Grandma's old upright had a sticky E key and a bench that wobbled, but it was the only piano for miles, so Jade spread her music on the rack and practiced until her fingers ached. Her cousin Marco was supposed to play clarinet with her, and he had texted that morning: "Question. On measure 32 there's 'rit.' and on measure 48 there's 'accel.' What do those even do? Also why does your grandma only have saltine crackers?"

Jade wrote back a letter, because Grandma's internet only worked in the kitchen and Jade refused to drag the whole music binder in there. "Dear Marco," she wrote. "Grandma is frugal, that's why the crackers. Stop eating the crackers and practice. For the other thing, I'm working on it." She was not entirely working on it. She had played the piece twenty times, and every time something strange happened at measure 32, like the song lost its balance, and she could not see why. The notes were right. The counting was right. Something invisible was hiding in the music, and she wanted to find it more than she wanted lunch.

She found the first clue by accident. When she slowed way down on purpose at measure 32, just to read a tricky fingering, the weird feeling vanished. The music suddenly made sense, like it wanted to ease off there. That gave her an idea she could test. She played the whole piece again and slowed gradually at the word "rit.," a little more with every beat, then sped back up gradually after it. It worked. At "accel." she did the opposite, pressing faster by small degrees, and the ending swept up like a wave. She jumped off the bench and shouted to Grandma in the kitchen, "It's a secret message in the sheet music!"

The second clue came from an old recording Grandma had of the piece. Jade played it three times, tapping her foot against the wobbly bench, and sure enough, the pianist on the recording slowed at exactly measure 32 and sped up near the end. When Marco video-called that evening, clarinet in hand, Jade was ready. "Watch me," she said, "and do what my hands do." They started together, and at measure 32 they both stretched the beat out, then pushed it forward again at the end, and they finished at the exact same moment. Marco lifted his clarinet overhead like a trophy.

"So that's it," Marco said, grinning through the screen. "Ritardando means gradually slowing down, and accelerando means the opposite." Jade nodded and flipped the page. "Same time tomorrow. Grandma says she'll delegate snack duty to Aunt Renee, so there might be actual food."

"Also," Marco added, "I'm basically a herbivore, so tell Aunt Renee I want the veggie tray." Jade laughed, set her hands on the keys, and counted them in: "One, two, ready, play."

The pool parking lot had been turned into a squiggly eight-hundred-metre loop with orange cones, and Beatrice stood at the start line in her flip-flops, switching to running shoes with the speed of a firefighter answering a bell. Today was the Summer Splash Classic, and today, she told herself, she would not die on the second lap.

Last year she had died on the second lap. The memory invaded her mind every time she smelled chlorine: her at the front, sprinting like a maniac on lap one, then her legs turning to wet noodles while Priya Chandra floated past her looking fresh as a lemonade stand. Priya had won the giant plastic trophy, a gold cup the size of a birdbath, and had carried it around the pool all summer like a queen.

"I'm winning that trophy this year," Priya announced now, stretching against the chain-link fence. "My grandma's coming. She thinks I'm bad at sports." Priya's want was so loud Beatrice could practically see it in the air, glittering.

"Beatrice, you can't sprint the whole thing," her friend Milo called from the lifeguard chair, where he was selling juice boxes to spectators. "It's two laps, not one."

"I know that," Beatrice said. She did know it. The problem was that knowing and doing were two different animals. Then the wind gusted across the lot, rippling the pool beyond the fence, and Beatrice noticed something: the flags snapped hard on the back straight, right where the course curved past the deep end. Wind. That was a thing you had to fight. Fighting took energy. Energy was exactly what she'd been spending too early, like a kid who eats all the pizza before the guests arrive.

The starter raised a whistle. "Runners, two laps, first lap pacing!"

They took off, and Beatrice made herself hold back even though everything in her screamed to fly. On the back straight the wind hit her like an open oven door, molten air pushing against her chest. Priya was three steps ahead, arms pumping, cutting through it. So Beatrice slid in directly behind her, tucked close, and suddenly the push was gone, like walking behind a big kid in a hallway crowd.

"Quit following me!" Priya shouted over her shoulder.

"It's not personal!" Beatrice shouted back. "It's just easier back here!"

They came around into lap two, and Beatrice still had legs under her. Real legs, springy ones. She swung out on the final bend, the wind behind her now, and poured everything she had left into the straight. Priya's grandmother stood on a lawn chair screaming in two languages. Milo spilled a juice box. Beatrice hit the cone line half a step ahead and collapsed onto the hot asphalt, laughing.

Priya flopped down beside her, gasping. "Okay, teach me the following thing."

"Tomorrow," Beatrice said, staring up at the birdbath trophy gleaming on the picnic table. "Tomorrow I'm going to hold it over my head in the shallow end."

Rosalie sat near the window in Spanish class, tracing the edge of her notebook while Señora Vega wrote family words on the board. Outside, someone was pushing a mop across the courtyard, and the smell of floor cleaner drifted in through the cracked window. Today's assignment was to describe your family and pets in full sentences, out loud, in front of everybody. Rosalie had a dog named Baxter and no siblings, which made her sentences short and, she thought, a little boring.

Marisol went first. She stood up, folded her hands, and said, "Tengo dos hermanos y un gato."

"Two brothers and a cat," said Theo, translating for himself under his breath. "Lucky. I only have one hermana."

Marisol shook her head. "No, no. One brother, one sister."

Theo frowned at her. "But you said hermanos. Hermanos means brothers. So that's two brothers." He turned to Rosalie as if she were the judge of the class, which she found funny, since she had gotten a C minus on the last quiz.

Rosalie thought about it. She remembered the vocab list, and how "hermanas" had meant sisters, and "hermanos" had just been labeled brothers in her messy handwriting. But Marisol was from a family that spoke Spanish at home, and she didn't seem embarrassed or corrected, only impatient, like Theo was the one missing something obvious.

"Wait," Rosalie said slowly. She flipped back a page in her notebook. "Is it like, the plural hermanos can be brothers, or brothers and sisters together? So Tengo dos hermanos might be one brother and one sister?"

"Exactly," Marisol said, sounding relieved. "Two hermanos can be two boys, or a boy and a girl."

Theo sat back, still skeptical. "That seems confusing. How do you know which one somebody means?"

"You ask," Mariola said with a shrug, and the girl next to her laughed.

When it was Rosalie's turn, she stood and gave her sentences one by one. "Tengo un perro. Se llama Baxter." Then, feeling bold, she added, "No tengo hermanos," and she liked how it sounded, like a small complete picture of her life. After class, Theo cornered her at the door with a question about how the plural worked, and instead of explaining, Rosalie pulled out her notebook. "Say your sentence," she told him. "I want to hear if it sounds plausible."

"Um. Tengo dos hermanos," Theo said.

Rosalie grinned and raised one eyebrow, exactly the way Marisol had. "Interesting. Which kind?"

Wyatt had been beating the same six guys all summer, but every single time trial ended the same way: first place for four hundred metres, then legs like wet noodles, then guys streaming past him on the final curve. Today, at the cracked courts behind Riverside Park, he meant to fix that. His friend Marcus had marked a rough four-hundred-metre loop with chalk arrows on the pavement, starting at the fence by the basketball court and winding around the tennis courts and back, and the two of them had agreed to run it twice without stopping.
