He thought of the letter folded in his pocket, the words "slow down," and how tonight he would stand at the kitchen table and decide whether to hand it over before or after he showed the slide.

He carried the microscope out into the evening light, Marisol walking beside him with the onion skin still thin and curled in the jar. "Draw it one more time," she said. "From the side, so you can see the angle." Oliver took out his pencil.

Katherine sat cross-legged on Priya's bedroom floor with Priya's laptop balanced on a stack of board games, staring at a column of numbers. They had spent the whole week selling lemonade at the end of Priya's driveway, and Priya had typed each day's earnings into the spreadsheet: Monday in B2, Tuesday in B3, all the way to Sunday in B10. Katherine wanted a chart to show their class which day earned the most, but first she had to add the column, and she was not going to punch seven numbers into a calculator like a little kid.

"Try the equals sign," Priya said, chewing the end of her pencil. "My cousin does something with an equals sign."

Katherine typed =SUM(B2:B10) into an empty cell, copying it from a smudged index card her cousin had left at their lemonade stand. When she pressed Enter, the number 47.25 appeared. It looked right, but she wanted to verify it, so she added the seven numbers by hand on paper. Forty-seven dollars and twenty-five cents. The formula had done it in one step. She narrowed her eyes at the colon in the middle. "So B2 colon B10," she said slowly, "that must mean everything from B2 down to B10. All of it."

"That's why it worked and my way didn't," Priya said. Earlier she had typed =SUM(B2,B10), and the spreadsheet had answered 14.75, which was only Monday plus Sunday, as if the week had lasted just two days. The consequence of skipping the middle days would have been telling their class they earned barely anything. Katherine deleted Priya's version and kept her own, then clicked through the menus until a bar chart bloomed on the screen, seven bars, with Sunday towering over all the rest.

Then came the twist. Katherine pointed at the tall Sunday bar. "Why is Sunday so big?" Priya went quiet and pulled a folded twenty from her pocket. Her grandmother had bought six cups on her walk home from church, and Priya had written it down without saying anything. "I was going to split it with you," Priya said. "I just forgot to tell you." Katherine did the math in her head. Without Grandma, Sunday was the same as Saturday, and their whole total dropped to about twenty-seven dollars.

"So we made less than we thought," Katherine said, "but now we know the spreadsheet catches things." She updated the chart and printed two copies, one for each of them. The bars looked smaller than before, honest and a little disappointing, but the paper was still warm from the printer, and Priya handed over her half of the twenty without being asked. Katherine folded it into her pocket next to the index card. "Next week," she said, "we track expenses too."

Rosalie stood in the wings of the school auditorium with forty minutes until the improv demonstration for the seventh graders, and her partner, Marcus, was reading the rules off a crumpled handout. "Accept every offer," he said. "You have to say yes, and. So if I say we're in a submarine, you say yes, and the sonar is beeping." Rosalie nodded, though she privately thought the rule sounded too simple to be the whole game.

Their first practice scene collapsed in seconds. Marcus opened a refrigerator, so Rosalie opened a mailbox, and they stood in two different worlds until the scene just stopped, like a watch with a broken spring. "We have to agree on where we are," she said. "That's the yes part. But there's something else." She watched the older kids from drama club warming up on stage, the way one girl would say "Doctor, my arm hurts" and suddenly the other kid checked the elbow, pressed a tendon near the wrist, and acted like a physician. The words themselves seemed to hand over a role, like passing a baton.

She tested it. In the next scene Marcus froze, blank as a dropped curtain, so Rosalie turned to him and said, "Captain, the engines are failing." His posture changed before his face did. He gripped an invisible wheel, barked orders, and steered them through a meteor shower. When they finished he blinked. "You made me the captain. How?"

"It's called endowing," said Priya from the front row, without looking up from her phone. "You give your partner a role through what you say."

Rosalie turned it over while Priya called five minutes. Every time a scene had worked this afternoon, somebody had endowed first. The doctor, the captain, one kid who got called "the world's most competent window washer" and immediately began spraying an imaginary squeegee. The pattern corresponded so neatly to success that she wondered why nobody had mentioned it sooner, then remembered that the handout was crumpled in Marcus's pocket and probably had three more rules they'd never read.

At the demonstration, the two of them walked out under the hot lights. Marcus leaned toward her. "You start," he whispered, which was dangerous, because if she opened a scene wrong they'd both freeze in front of two hundred seventh graders. Rosalie thought of the doctor, the captain, the window washer. She took a breath and pointed at the empty space beside her.

"Museum guard," she said, "the dinosaur skeleton is walking out the front door."

Marcus squared his shoulders. "Then we'd better catch it before it reaches the parking lot."

Grayson slid his French textbook across the library table and glared at it like it had insulted his family. On Friday, his class was going to a French café where everyone had to order lunch in French, ask the price, and get the bill, all without switching to English. His friend Priya had already promised to film anyone who froze mid-sentence, so the stakes could not have been higher.

"Ordering food is easy," Priya said, dropping into the chair across from him with her own book. "The hard part is the bill. What do you even say?"

Grayson flipped to the back of the book, where the vocabulary lists lived. "La facture," he read. "That's invoice. Or la note. That's like a note." He wrote both on a scrap of paper, feeling pleased with himself. How hard could it be? You pointed at cake, you said the price, you asked for the note. It felt almost too easy, which should have been his first warning.

Priya leaned over and squinted at his paper. "La note? That sounds like something you pass to someone in class." She grinned. "Are you going to ask the waiter for a secret message?"

"That's a naive thing to say about French," Grayson said, jabbing his pencil at her. "Words have more than one meaning. Fine is an English word and also a penalty. It's a pattern." But even as he said it, a small doubt wiggled in the back of his mind. French restaurants were probably not full of people asking for invoices. There had to be a restaurant word, something he was missing, and it was hiding somewhere outside the vocabulary chapter.

He marched to the computer catalog, typed in "French phrasebook," and found a skinny orange book shelved in travel. He carried it back, sat down, and ran his finger down the restaurant section. There it was, printed in bold: L'addition, s'il vous plaît. Underneath, in smaller type: The bill, please. Not la facture. Not la note. Addition. He said it out loud three times, quietly, because the librarian had already given him one warning look.

"Find it?" Priya asked.

"If you'd asked for la facture," Grayson said, "the waiter would probably think you wanted paperwork." He copied the phrase onto a menu he'd drawn himself: a croissant, a sandwich, and one suspiciously large slice of cake. Then he paraphrased the whole exchange into the simplest possible version so Priya could practice too. "You say je voudrais, then the food, then combien ça coûte, then l'addition, s'il vous plaît. That's the whole show."

Priya picked up the paper menu and gave his drawing a serious critique. "The croissant looks like a deflated seashell. Otherwise, perfect."

Grayson snatched it back, cleared his throat, and delivered his order to the pencil sharpener as if it were a Parisian waiter. "Je voudrais le gâteau. L'addition, s'il vous plaît!"

From three tables away, the librarian called out, "En français, s'il vous plaît," without looking up, and Priya laughed so hard she slid halfway under the table.

Easton spread his notes across the kitchen table like a general planning an invasion, which would have looked more impressive if half the notes were not covered in orange juice from the glass he had already knocked over once. His world religions teacher had assigned a compare-and-contrast project: pick two faiths and explain what each one says happens after death. Easton had picked Islam and Hinduism, mostly because his friend Dev claimed his grandmother knew everything about reincarnation and Easton's own neighbor, Mrs. Haddad, was coming over that afternoon to drop off a casserole dish. Research through casserole delivery struck him as efficient.

The problem was that the two ideas refused to line up. Dev had explained, mouth full of pretzels, that in Hinduism the soul comes back again and again, living many lives until it finally gets things right. Easton had written LIFE, THEN ANOTHER LIFE, THEN ANOTHER, PROBABLY TIRESOME on one index card. For Islam he had only a half sentence from his textbook, and the half sentence refused to cooperate. He flipped the card over, squinted at it, and ate a pretzel in a rebellious manner, as if the pretzel itself had opinions about theology.

When the doorbell rang, Easton answered it still holding his cards. Mrs. Haddad handed him the dish, spotted the cards, and read the half sentence upside down, which is a skill grandmothers and neighbors develop automatically. "Oh, you're stuck on the Judgment part," she said.

"Kind of. The book says something about a day and being raised, but it cuts off," Easton said. "Is it like a do-over day? Like, if you mess up one life, do you get another one?"

Mrs. Haddad laughed so hard she had to set the casserole on the counter to steady herself. "No do-overs, habibi. In Islam you get this one life. At the end there's a Day of Judgment. We call it Yawm al-Qiyamah." Easton scribbled it down, syllable by syllable, and underlined it twice, then a third time for luck.

That was the piece he'd been missing. One faith gave you many lives to improve; the other gave you a single life and then a verdict. He tested it right there at the counter with two glasses of water as stand-ins: the glass that kept getting refilled, and the glass that got poured once and then judged on whether he had drunk it politely or spilled it like an untrained golden retriever. Mrs. Haddad watched this demonstration with great seriousness. "The spilled glass goes to hell?" she asked.

"The spilled glass gets a stern talking-to," Easton said, mopping the counter. Dev was going to be so embarrassed that his pretzel-based lecture had left out the entire comparison. Easton could hardly wait to tell him.

Kayla stood at Grandma Rosa's counter with an onion in front of her and a knife in her hand, and she had one goal: make a pasta sauce good enough that her cousin Marco would stop bragging about the jar sauce from the store. Marco claimed nobody under seventy could cook from scratch. Kayla intended to prove him wrong by Saturday dinner.

"Curl your fingers under, like a claw," Grandma said, chopping air with her own hand to show her. "Knuckles guide the blade. Fingertips stay out of the way." Kayla curled her fingers and pressed her knuckles against the flat of the blade. The first cut wobbled and the half onion skidded toward the edge of the counter. The second cut landed clean, and the third after that. She could feel the rhythm of it, like a pattern hiding inside the onion, waiting for her hand to find it. She wondered if every skill had a hidden pattern like that, something you couldn't see until your fingers discovered it.

Then the worst thing happened. She reached for the salt shaker and her elbow knocked the knife. It slid off the counter, spinning, and every instinct in her screamed to grab it. Instead she jumped backward, and the knife hit the floor with a clang and lay there, gleaming and harmless. Her heart hammered. Grandma didn't even look up from her pot. "Good," she said. "If a knife starts to fall, you let it drop. Trying to catch a falling knife is how people get cut." Kayla picked it up, washed it, and set it flat in the center of the cutting board where it couldn't slide again. She noticed she had already revised her whole setup in her head, moving the salt to the other side too, so nothing else lived near the edge.

They crushed tomatoes with their hands, and Kayla watched the seeds pool at the bottom of the bowl like tiny amber beads. Grandma stirred, then held out the spoon. Kayla tasted. It was thin and pale and disappointing. "It tastes a little impoverished," she said. "Like it's missing something." Grandma laughed. "Salt, a pinch of sugar, and time. Flavor you can't rush." Kayla thought of Grandpa in the garden, who claimed onions were practically an antibiotic and would fix anything from a cold to a bad mood. She wasn't sure she believed him, but she sliced another onion anyway, claw grip and all, and stirred it into the pot.

By Saturday, Marco took one bite, paused, and took another. "This is from a jar," he said. Kayla set the knife down flat in the center of the counter and smiled. "Prove it."

The folded note landed on Easton's shoe during the car ride, passed back from his best friend Marcus, whose church youth group was visiting the Hindu temple the same morning as Easton's social studies class. "Bet your grandma says people get reborn and that's the best part," Marcus had written. "Ask her if we'd WANT that." Easton grinned and wrote back, "Watch me."

Inside, the temple smelled of incense and flowers, and shoes sat in rows by the door like sleeping animals. Easton's grandmother, who taught the comparative religions unit at the community center and was considered something of a prestigious scholar in their neighborhood, had come along as a guide. Easton kept his notebook ready. He had decided to categorize everything he heard today: beliefs about heaven in one column, beliefs about rebirth in another, and a big question mark for everything else.

"That bell means the priest is waking the deity for the morning," his grandmother said, tilting her head toward the shrine. After the arati, when the flame circled and everyone sang, she answered questions from the group. A girl asked what happens when people die, and his grandmother said some here believe the soul is born again into a new life, and that this continues in a great cycle.

Marcus elbowed Easton hard. Easton raised his hand. "So being reborn, is that something you hope for, or something you want to get out of?"

"That's the question, isn't it?" his grandmother said, eyes sparkling like he'd won a prize. She turned to the priest's assistant, a young man arranging fruit near the altar. "Would you say it?"

The young man smiled. "Moksha is liberation from the cycle of rebirth," he said simply, "and it is the highest goal of human life."

Easton scribbled fast. No heaven column. He drew an arrow with LOOP crossed out next to it. Marcus leaned over and whispered, "So the best thing is to escape the loop? Our pastor says the best thing is going to be with God forever." Easton looked at his two columns, then at his question-mark column, and made a third heading: THE GOAL. Under rebirth he wrote "escape it"; under heaven he wrote "reach it." The arrow went the same direction on both, away from here, toward something higher. He practically bounced in his seat.

Back at the shoe rows, Marcus dug in his pocket. "Almost forgot. Second note." This one said, "My mom says ask your grandma if she'll do a swap, you come to our Easter service, I come back here." Easton looked up, and his grandmother was already reading over his shoulder.

"Tell his mother yes," she said. "And Marcus, you're a descendant of question-askers, all of you. That's the best lineage there is." She held the door, and the morning light hit the temple steps. "Next time, you two ask the questions together."

Adam slid into the seat beside the reference desk, where the library's only free computer waited, and pulled his crumpled worksheet from his backpack. The science club needed a chart of how much cafeteria waste each grade produced last month, and Mr. Ruiz had said whoever brought the best chart would get to present it at the assembly. Adam wanted that spot more than he wanted lunch, which was saying something.

He opened the spreadsheet and typed the numbers from his worksheet into column B, one row for each grade. Then he clicked the empty cell below the last number and typed SUM(B2:B10), exactly the way the handout showed. He pressed Enter. The cell did not show a total. It showed SUM(B2:B10), the letters sitting there like plain text, refusing to be anything else. Adam checked the handout three times. He had not mistyped anything.

He leaned toward the next computer, where a girl from his class, Priya, was typing fast. "Did your total work?" he asked.

She glanced over. "You forgot the equals sign. Every formula has to start with it. Without the equals sign, the cell just shows what you typed." She turned back to her screen, where a neat column of numbers already added itself.

Adam sat very still for a second, feeling both foolish and relieved. He deleted the cell, typed =SUM(B2:B10), and pressed Enter. The number 412 appeared instantly. He checked it against his worksheet, adding the rows by hand, and it matched. One small symbol had been the difference between words and a number. He was not going to forget it.

Then he highlighted the grades and their totals and clicked the chart button. A bar graph appeared, and the sixth-grade bar towered over the others because sixth graders threw out the most apple cores. Adam thought of the compost bin project, the one where worms and other decomposers turned food scraps into soil, and decided his chart should go right next to it. He saved the file, then went to retrieve his flash drive from the bottom of his backpack, digging past a smashed granola bar he had been negligent about cleaning out for weeks.

When he plugged in the drive and hit save again, the screen went gray. Priya looked over and laughed, not unkindly. "Autosave," she said. "Mine's been in the cloud the whole time."

Adam stared at the frozen screen, finger hovering over the power button, and whispered, "Please still be there."

Brielle slid into the seat at the far computer in the lab and typed her program before the bell even finished ringing. It asked for a number, then tested every divisor from 2 up to the number itself, printing "prime" or "not prime." It worked on 7. It worked on 31. Then Marcus, her project colleague on this assignment, leaned over and typed 982,451,653.

The cursor blinked. And blinked. Brielle stared at the frozen screen. "It's stuck," she whispered.

"It's checking every single number up to nine hundred million," Marcus said. "We're going to be here until graduation."

Brielle grabbed her notebook. First fix: stop testing at the square root, since anything past that would have already found a partner. She added that, and the program sped up, but 982,451,653 still took a slow crawl. She squinted at her loop, counting on her fingers. Skip the even divisors, she thought. After checking 2, why test 4, 6, 8 at all? An odd number can never be divided evenly by an even one. So if the number isn't even, the program only needs odd divisors. She deleted half the checks and started the loop at 3, stepping by 2. She saved the file and held her breath.

The answer flashed back in under a second: not prime. "Look at that!" she said, loud enough that two kids at the next monitor turned around. "Twice as fast. We halved the work." Marcus magnified the timing numbers on his screen so the whole row could see the before-and-after, and he was already planning their next test. "Give me your phone number," he said. "If it's nine or ten digits, we can check it for prime factors before the bell."

Brielle started to laugh, then stopped. She typed her own number in, and the program thought for a moment and printed "prime." She tried her mother's number: prime. Then she typed the number from the gym locker she'd been assigned that morning, 316, and the program answered instantly, "not prime." She tried dividing it in her head by odd numbers after 2, the way the program did, and landed on 4 times 79. That meant her locker combination, which was supposed to be random, came from a number that factored neatly, and if it factored, someone with the same program could break it.

She looked at Marcus. "Tomorrow we test every locker number in the school."

The gymnasium smelled like vinegar and poster glue, which Jonathan took as a good sign, since his project involved both. His display read ACIDS, BASES, AND THE SECRET LIFE OF pH, and beside it sat twelve labeled cups: lemon juice, soap water, baking soda mixed with water, cola, milk, and seven more he had collected from his kitchen at midnight like an eccentric chemist raiding his own refrigerator. Each cup had a strip of litmus paper taped beside it, red where the paper had turned and blue where it hadn't. His plan was to let the judges evaluate his results themselves.

Marcus from fourth period strolled over with his own poster under his arm. He squinted at Jonathan's chart, where every cup had a number next to it. "What's the pH of that lemon juice?"

"Three," Jonathan said.

Marcus pointed at the cola cup, which read four. "So the cola's basically the same. Three and four, that's only a one apart." He smiled the way he did when he thought he'd caught something. "Your whole chart says lemon juice and cola are both just sour."

Jonathan looked at his chart, then at the two cups. Something in his stomach went tight, the way it did before a test he hadn't studied for. He had written the numbers down three days ago, but he had never really thought about what jumped between them. A one didn't look like much. He needed a way to show Marcus, right here, right now, with a judge already moving down the aisle toward them.

"Wait," Jonathan said. He pulled out his science notebook and flipped to the back page. "Every whole step on the pH scale is a tenfold change." He wrote 3, then 4, then drew an arrow between them and wrote x10 beside it. "So pH 3 is ten times more acidic than pH 4. Not one more. Ten times."

Marcus frowned. "Ten times? From one number apart?"

"Ten times," Jonathan said. "That's the whole trick of the scale." He tore two fresh strips of litmus paper from his kit, because he wanted Marcus to see the numbers weren't just marks on a poster. He dipped one strip in the lemon juice and one in the cola and laid them side by side on the table. Both turned pink, but the lemon strip went deep red almost instantly, faster than the cola strip, and Jonathan felt his pulse slow down for the first time all morning. "It isn't a ladder where every step is the same size," he said. "It's more like each step is a whole flight of stairs."

Marcus leaned in so close his nose nearly touched the paper. "So my poster's wrong," he said quietly. "I wrote that pH 5 and pH 6 aquarium water are close enough."

The judge stopped at their table, clipboard ready, and tapped the lemon juice cup. "Walk me through your method."

Jonathan took a breath. "First I dip the litmus paper, then I read the color against the chart, then I record the pH number. Same steps every time, same order." He straightened the two pink strips next to each other, deep red beside pale rose, and slid them toward her. "See for yourself."

The teasing started right after lunch, at the long table by the windows. Dex had knocked over his milk, and now Braden was drawing it out. "Nice job, spill king," Braden said, and two kids at the end of the table laughed. Dex stared at his tray and mopped at the puddle with one slow, lethargic swipe of his napkin.

Harper's first idea was to tell Braden to knock it off. She had tried that in October, when he was on Marcus about his shoes. Braden had just turned it around and started on her for a week. So she sat there and thought instead. Why did some teasing stop on its own and some keep going? She ran through the times she'd watched it. Once, when Braden was ragging on Priya's drawing, Ms. Okafor had walked past, and he'd quit instantly, but that was fear, not a fix. Then she remembered something odd from the fall party. Braden had been teasing Dex about his old backpack, and right at that moment Liam had shouted that the cake was being cut, and everyone had stampeded to the front of the room. When they came back, the teasing was simply gone. Nobody had challenged anybody. The distraction had eaten it.

She turned that into an inference: if teasing needs an audience and momentum, then breaking the momentum might work better than attacking the teaser. She decided to invest one try in testing it, today, at this table. If it failed, at least she'd know.

Braden leaned over Dex's tray. "Hey, spill king, you want a bib?"

Harper stood up fast and pointed at the window. "There's a hawk on the fence," she said, loud enough for the whole table. Heads swung. A big bird sat on the chain link by the portables, gray-brown, turning its head. Three kids got up to look, then five, then most of the table was crowded at the glass. Someone said it might be a Cooper's hawk, and an argument started about Cooper's hawks versus red-tails, and Dex came to the window too, milk forgotten.

By the time the hawk lifted off toward the track, lunch was nearly over and people were collecting trays. Braden got pulled into a debate about whether the bird was even real or just a pigeon. He never came back to the milk. On the way to fifth period, Dex fell into step beside Harper.

"Was there really a hawk?" he asked.

"There was," she said. "I just didn't expect it to matter."

"Next time," Dex said, "you could invest in something closer to the ground. I hear the fourth graders are releasing crickets in the gym on Friday."

Louis sat at his grandfather's kitchen table with a pencil, a ruler, and a blank page that seemed to be mocking him. His art teacher had assigned a drawing of a street, and he wanted it to look real, not like a flat cartoon road. He drew two lines that ran straight down the page, side by side, and frowned. It looked like a ladder lying on the ground.

He carried the paper out to the porch, where his grandfather was shelling peas. "What's wrong with it?" his grandfather asked.

"It doesn't look like it goes anywhere," Louis said. "It's just two lines."

His grandfather set down the bowl. "When I was about your age, I used to stand on the footbridge behind the church and watch the trains. My brother swore the rails got closer together far down the line. We nearly fell off that bridge arguing about it."

"Did they?" Louis asked.

"Go see for yourself."

Louis walked the dirt path to the footbridge and leaned over the rail. The two rails left the bridge beneath his feet, perfectly parallel, as wide apart as they always were. But down the line, a quarter mile away, they seemed to draw together, tighter and tighter, until they touched at some point he couldn't quite name. He stayed there a long time, watching, and an intuition took shape in him: the rails never actually moved, but they looked as if they met in the distance. His brother had been fooled by looking; his grandfather, he guessed, had been right.

Back at the table, Louis tried an experiment. He drew a dot in the middle of his page, then ran two lines from the bottom edges of the paper straight toward that dot, like the rails converging under the bridge. He added windows and doorways with their tops and bottoms angled toward the same spot. The street suddenly stretched away from him, deep and solid, as if he could walk down it. He erased the dot itself, since you couldn't see it in real life, and the drawing held anyway.

"Better," his grandfather said over his shoulder. "You've stopped being negligent about the far end of things."

"It's called a vanishing point," Louis said, tapping the spot with his pencil. "The rails look like they meet there, even though they never touch." He turned the page toward the window, checking his lines one more time, then wrote his name in the corner.

Easton had forty minutes before Maya's parents got home, and the onion was winning. Every time he pressed the knife down, the cutting board skated three inches toward the edge of the counter like it was trying to escape.

"Stop moving," he told it.

"Boards don't listen," said Maya, who was browning garlic at the stove and had appointed herself head chef despite contributing mainly commentary. "Also you're holding the knife like it insulted you."

"I'm holding it exactly how the video said. Claw grip, fingertips tucked, knuckles forward." He curled his left hand over the half onion like a bear paw with a manicure. "The problem is the board, not me."

The board disagreed. He sliced, it skidded, and the onion chunk shot off the counter and landed near the dog bowl, where it would soon be found by a golden retriever who interpreted every dropped object as a gift. Easton retrieved it and considered the situation. The board slid every single time he pushed down, but it never slid when Maya stirred something on the far side. He stared at the counter, then at the thin wet ring the onion had left behind, then had an idea that felt almost too simple.

He wet a dish towel under the tap, wrung it out, and spread it flat under the board.

"Now you're just decorating," Maya said.

"Watch."

He set the knife down and pushed the board sideways with his palm. It didn't budge. He pushed harder. Nothing. It was as if the counter had decided to hold on.

"Huh," said Maya.

"That counts as a victory," Easton said, and got back to the onion. With the board finally sitting still, the claw grip actually worked, and thin half-moons of onion started stacking up in an orderly little pile instead of scattering like startled fish. He swept them into the pot with the garlic, where they hissed and softened. Maya crushed the canned tomatoes with her hands, which she claimed was authentic and he suspected was just fun.

"Technically an onion is a decomposer's dream," Maya said, sniffing the steam. "Humid in there, warm, full of sugar. Fungi would move in within a week."

"Then let's not give them a week."

They plated the pasta at 6:28, sauce still bubbling, two minutes to spare. When her parents walked in, her dad sniffed the air and said, "Something smells like an actual restaurant."

Maya pointed her fork at Easton. "He tamed the cutting board."

"It was the wet towel," Easton said, and went back for seconds.

Lydia slapped her pencil down on the climate graph and pointed at the tall blue bars. "No way this place is a rainforest. Look at October. The rain practically stops."

Marcus leaned over her shoulder, blocking the fluorescent light. "You're only looking at the bars. Check the line, the temperature one. That's the part that hinders your whole theory."

She traced the red line across the months with her finger. Every city on the worksheet had two graphs side by side, one for a desert and one for a rainforest, and their teacher had said only one thing before turning them loose: use the numbers, not the pictures. The room was warm and slightly humid from the radiator, whose valve had been dripping steam all week, and Lydia wiped her palms on her jeans before picking the pencil back up.

"Fine," she said. "October's line is at twenty-one degrees. And the bar shows... sixty-two millimeters." She wrote both numbers in the margin. November: twenty degrees, seventy millimeters. December: nineteen degrees, sixty-one. She worked down the whole year, month by month, while Marcus read the numbers out loud and she recorded them. Somewhere in July she started slowing down, hoping to find one month that would break the pattern, one month below eighteen degrees or under sixty millimeters of rain. There wasn't one.

"Ms. Okafor said this is the Koppen system," Marcus said, chewing his pen cap. "Every month over eighteen degrees and at least sixty millimeters of rain, and it counts as tropical rainforest."

"Then it counts," Lydia said quietly. She looked at the desert graph beside it, where the temperature line swung like a jump rope between blazing summer and freezing winter, and where half the bars were barely whiskers above zero. She had been so certain, so ready to argue in front of the class that the flat-looking graph was the dry one, that the truth landing on her desk felt like losing something.

She raised her hand anyway. "I want to change my answer. The second graph is the rainforest."

"Because of the rule, or because Marcus talked you into it?" Ms. Okafor asked from the front.

"Because of the rule." Lydia slid the paper forward, all twelve months tallied in the margin, and heard Marcus exhale beside her, half relieved and half like he'd already moved on to arguing with the next pair. The radiator hissed, and a drop of water fell from the valve onto her shoe.

Elizabeth turned the hose on low and aimed it at the mound of dirt she had spent an hour piling at the low end of the yard. The water slid down the slope in a thin ribbon, no wider than her thumb.

"That's it?" Marcus said from the fence. He was the neighbor's kid, and he had laughed when she told him what she was doing. "You said you were going to make a canyon. That little trickle couldn't carve anything. The Grand Canyon is a mile deep."

"It's not about one day." She nudged the hose a degree to the left. "The Little Colorado River isn't some giant, either. It just never stops."

Marcus climbed the fence and dropped into her yard. "So your hose is going to run for millions of years?"

"No. But I can speed everything else up." She had built the mound loose on purpose, half dirt and half sand, so the water could bite into it fast. In real rock, the same thing took ages. She had read about a Scottish geologist, James Hutton, who argued way back in 1785 that slow, everyday processes like erosion, working over immense time, shaped Earth's surface. No flood, no catastrophe. Just ordinary water, refusing to quit.

"You mean like a tenant who stays in a house so long the house wears out around him?" Marcus said.

"Sort of, except the river is the tenant and it never moves out." She let the water run. The ribbon found a groove, deepened it, collapsed a chunk of bank, and carried the sand downhill in a muddy cloud. At the base of the mound the water slowed, and the sand settled out in a small fan, building a flat delta an inch at a time. Deposition, right there on the grass. "See how it drops the sand when it slows? That's the other half. The river takes material from one place and dumps it in another."

They watched for twenty minutes. A trench opened down the middle of the mound, deep enough now that the water ran shadowed inside it, curling around a pebble that had become a boulder in the streambed's scale. Marcus crouched and pressed his finger into the fan of sand.

"Okay," he said. "So if a drip of water can do that in an afternoon, a river with a few million years." He didn't finish it. He put his hand into the current and dammed it. The water pooled behind his fingers, then spilled over the top and cut a new channel around his knuckle.

"Exactly," Elizabeth said. "It finds a way around everything. It's basically inevitable." She pulled his hand out, and the flood chewed the new channel twice as deep in under a minute.

Hailey sat in the back corner of the computer lab, tapping her pencil against the desk while the projector hummed at the front of the room. Mr. Reyes had written one task on the board in green marker: write a program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime. She had typed the first two lines easily, n = int(input("Give me a number: ")), but after that her screen showed nothing but a blinking cursor, and the bell was twenty minutes away.

The problem circled in her head like a wasp. A prime number has no divisors except one and itself; she knew that part cold from math class. But how could a computer tell if a number divided evenly? When she did it by hand, she could see the answer come out with no remainder. The machine couldn't see anything. It just calculated.

Across the aisle, Deshawn was already testing his program, and the sound of his keys clicking made her jaw tighten. She leaned over. "How'd you do the dividing part?" she whispered. He turned his monitor toward her. "You don't divide, really. You use percent." She read his line: if n % d == 0. "Percent like percentage?" she asked. That seemed ambiguous, like it might mean something about ratios. "No, it's the remainder," Deshawn said. "In Python, percent gives you the remainder." She stared at the symbol, and the concept landed all at once, like a light snapping on in a dark hallway.

Her fingers started moving. She built a loop with d counting up from 2, and inside it she wrote the check: if n % d == 0, then n had a divisor that split it evenly, so it wasn't prime. She tried 9 first, and the program printed "not prime" because 9 % 3 came out to nothing left over. Then she tried 7, and every remainder showed up stubborn and lopsided, so it printed "prime." She smelled the dry, dusty warmth of the lab's old computers and grinned at her screen.

Then she typed 1, and the program said "prime," which she knew was wrong. She chewed her thumbnail. One wasn't a special mystery; her loop never even ran for it, because it started counting at 2. She added a quick check at the top: if n < 2, print "not prime." When she tested 2 and then 1 again, both answers came out right.

Mr. Reyes passed behind her and paused, reading over her shoulder. He didn't say anything at first, just tapped the edge of her desk twice and moved on. Deshawn raised his hand to ask about 1, and Hailey turned around in her seat. "I already fixed that one," she said. "Wanna race on 999,983?"

The first time Alicia ran the eight hundred metres, she sprinted the first lap like a burglar fleeing a crime scene, then spent the second lap moving at a speed roughly equivalent to a shopping cart with a bad wheel. Coach Reyes timed her anyway, out of politeness. She collapsed on the infield grass and watched her shoelaces rotate slowly, like they were the ones who had run.

"There has to be a secret," she told Marcus, who was folding himself into a hamstring stretch nearby. Marcus wanted one thing in life, which was to beat his older brother's four-hundred time, and he talked about it so often that Alicia could recite it. Right now he was not thinking about the eight hundred at all.

"The secret is don't do it," Marcus said. "Eight hundred metres is the worst race. It's too long to sprint and too short to rest."

That night Alicia watched the 2012 London Olympic final, David Rudisha's world record run, on her mother's laptop. She timed the laps herself, thumb on her phone stopwatch. First lap, then second lap. She sat back. His first lap was more than two seconds faster than his second. The fastest man ever to run the distance had not run it evenly. He had spent more than he kept.

The next morning she told Marcus, who was doing starts in lane four whether anyone had asked him to or not.

"So even Rudisha went out fast," he said, "but not stupid fast."

"Two seconds isn't nothing," Alicia said. She had a theory now, which was that the first lap was a fire you had to light at exactly the right size, and the second lap was what happened when it burned down. Too big a fire and there was nothing left but smoke and apology.

At Thursday practice she tried it. First lap controlled, arms loose, breathing like she'd practiced in the hallway until her mother asked if she was okay. Coming off the final bend of lap one, her legs sent up their usual complaint, and she half expected them to fracture on the spot, though she knew that wasn't how fractures worked. She ignored the complaint. She had budgeted for it.

On the second lap she was still passing people. One of them was a girl from another school who said something unrepeatable, and Alicia found that very reassuring, actually.

At the line she was eight seconds faster than last week. She bent over, hands on knees, and checked her stopwatch twice in case the first reading was a lie.

"Three-oh-two," Marcus read over her shoulder. "That's two seconds off my brother's pace. For the four."

"Wrong race," Alicia said, still gasping.

"I know what race it is." He was already walking to the starting line, shaking out his arms. "Watch my start. Tell me if my first thirty metres look like yours."

The blank document had been open for forty minutes, and the cursor blinked at Jayden like it was timing him. The essay was due Monday morning, and it had to be persuasive, with a real argument, and his teacher had said something about a thesis that he had half heard from the back row. He was at Grandpa's house for the weekend because Mom's work trip got prolonged by three days, and the Wi-Fi was so slow in the den that the page kept freezing.

"Still staring at nothing?" Grandpa asked, carrying two glasses of lemonade. He set one down next to the laptop and nodded at the screen.

"I don't know how to start," Jayden said. "I keep trying to write the first sentence and it's all garbage."

Grandpa pulled a battered shoebox from the shelf behind the desk. Inside were hundreds of index cards, soft with age, each one holding a single line in cramped pencil. "I never started with sentences," he said. "First I decided what I wanted to say. Then I worried about words." He tapped a card. "Thesis. That's the whole point of the thing, in one line." Then he laid three more cards on the desk in a row, side by side. "Three reasons under it. That's how I did every report for thirty years."

Jayden picked up the cards. Grandpa's handwriting was small and sure. Each card said only what it meant, not how it would sound. He grabbed a stack of fresh index cards from his backpack and wrote one word at the top of the first one: TREES. Then, without letting himself think about sentence style at all, he scribbled a single line: "The oak in Grandpa's yard should not be cut down." Under it he made three cards: shade, history, animal homes. His hand moved fast because nothing had to sound good yet.

He was halfway through filling in the third card when he noticed a yellow sheet stuck to the refrigerator through the doorway. It was a work order from a tree removal company, dated Friday. His stomach dropped. He walked over and picked it up, and his eyes went to the address line, which matched the house number on the mailbox outside. "Grandpa," he called, holding the paper up, his voice strange in his own ears. "This is your address. What's happening Friday?"

Grandpa came in drying his hands, read the sheet, and sighed. "Council says the roots are cracking the sewer line. I didn't want to tell you before your visit."

Jayden looked from the work order to his three cards lying in a row on the desk. "Then my essay isn't practice anymore," he said slowly, an idea forming. "Grandpa, do you have a copy machine?"

"Down the hall, under the coupon drawer."

Jayden gathered his cards and headed for the hallway. "The parks office is open Monday, and I'm going to make sure this is on top of the stack."

Sawyer pressed the multimeter probes against the fat copper wire and squinted at the screen. The exhibit card said "Measure It Yourself," and it wasn't kidding: two wires sat side by side on the table, a thick one and a spaghetti-thin one, both hooked to batteries. His little sister Priya wanted to move on to the static electricity ball, but Sawyer had a plan. He was going to figure out the resistance of each wire all by himself, the way a real engineer would.

First he measured voltage, which meant clipping the probes across each wire while the battery pushed current through it. Then he clipped the meter in line with the wire to read the current. He wrote both numbers on the back of his ticket stub. "Voltage divided by current," he muttered. "That gives resistance." The thick wire read 6 volts and 2 amps, which worked out to 3 ohms. Easy.

The thin wire gave him trouble. He measured it twice because the current looked wrong somehow, too small, and he was starting to feel pessimistic about his whole method. Maybe the battery was dying. Maybe he had clipped something backward. He checked everything, then did the math anyway: 6 volts, 0.5 amps. He frowned at the stub. "Twelve ohms? That's four times the thick one. Same battery, same length. How can one wire be that much harder to push through?"

Priya leaned over his shoulder. "Maybe the skinny one's just worse," she said.

"But why would it be worse?" Sawyer turned the thin wire in his fingers. It was the same copper, the same silvery shine, the same length coiled beside its partner. Nothing he could see was different except the size. And you couldn't see resistance at all. It was like guessing what was inside a wrapped present from how heavy it felt. He wondered if that was the whole answer hiding in plain sight. He pulled a volunteer's clipboard toward him and sketched two circles, one wide, one narrow. "If current is like a crowd trying to get through a hallway," he said slowly, "a fat hallway is easy and a skinny one is a traffic jam."

He had to revise his ticket-stub notes now, because he'd labeled the wires A and B in the wrong order. He crossed them out and rewrote: thick, 3 ohms; thin, 12 ohms. When the museum lights flickered for the four o'clock show in the planetarium, Priya tugged his sleeve, but Sawyer grabbed one more reading first, probes steady, eyes fixed on the little screen. "Just once more," he said. "Science."

Lauren stood in the kitchen doorway with the reading folded in her hand, watching her grandmother press dough flat with the heel of her palm. Her grandmother pressed slowly, the way she did everything since the doctors said the cartilage in her knees was wearing thin, and Lauren felt a flash of guilt for even asking.

"Abuela, did you have a quinceañera?"

"I did. In Guadalajara." Her grandmother dusted flour from her fingers. "It started at church. It always starts that way, mija. A Mass of thanksgiving, first thing, before any dancing."

Lauren's stomach dropped. She had been planning for the party, the dress, the waltz. Now her mother was telling her that in three weeks, at the beginning of the Mass, she would stand in front of everyone and deliver a reading from memory. In Spanish. She had tried learning it silently on her bed for two nights, and every time she got to the fourth line, the words deteriorated into a jumble, like wet sand slipping through her fingers.

"Abuela, how did you memorize things? For school?" She was guessing her grandmother had a method, some hidden trick she had never been taught. Her grandmother laughed and tapped her own ear.

"I couldn't read then, not well. I learned everything by hearing it. My mother would say a line, and I would say it back, out loud, until my brothers begged me to stop."

Lauren tested the idea that same afternoon. She recorded herself reading the passage on her phone, then played it in a loop while she swept the porch, saying each line out loud right after her own recorded voice. By dinner she had eight lines solid. Out loud worked. Silent staring did not. There was a rule hiding in that, she was sure, something about the ears being a legitimate second memory, a door the eyes couldn't open.

The twist came on Sunday. Her mother sat beside her at the kitchen table and picked up the paper. "We should practice," she said, but her voice was strange, thin, and she turned the page sideways as if admiring the margins.

"You're nervous," Lauren said.

"Spanish Mass readings were never my thing." Her mother's cheeks went pink. "I was going to quietly hand the paper to the lector and let him read it for you."

Lauren stared. All week her mother had been drilling her, timing her, and now it turned out her mother had been ready to let the whole thing slide? Then Lauren slid the phone across the table, pressed play, and said, "Then you learn it my way. Line by line, out loud. You say it, I say it back."

Her mother pressed record, took a breath, and began.

Norah balanced her backpack on her knees as the bus rattled past the hardware store, trying to read the wrinkled handout without letting it touch the sticky seat. Mrs. Okafor had assigned the balcony scene from Romeo and Juliet, and by tomorrow each pair had to paraphrase every speech into modern English and perform it in front of the class. Norah's stomach dropped every time she thought about standing up there, so she figured she would at least get the words right.

The trouble was that the words made no sense. She read Juliet's line again. "O Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo?" She scribbled underneath: Romeo, Romeo, where are you, Romeo? That seemed obvious. Juliet was on the balcony, Romeo was hiding in the garden, so of course she was asking where he was.

Deshaun slid into the seat across the aisle, his own copy folded into a paper airplane. He saw her pencil hovering and leaned over. "You stuck already?"

"Juliet's looking for him," Norah said. "She wants to know where he is."

Deshaun unfolded his page and ran his finger down to a note in the margin, one Mrs. Okafor had circled in red. He read it, then looked up with a grin that made Norah suspicious. "She's not asking where. Wherefore means why."

"Why?"

"Yes. Why. Like, why do you have to be Romeo?" He tapped the next lines, where Juliet begs him to deny his name. "She just found out the guy she likes is a Montague, and her family hates Montagues. So she's going, why him, of all people? Why did I have to fall for the one boy I can't have?"

Norah stared at her own paraphrase, where are you, Romeo, and felt her ears go hot. "That completely changes it," she said slowly. "She's not searching the garden. She's arguing with the universe."

Deshaun laughed. "Arguing with the universe. That's good. Write that down."

She crossed out her line and started over. Why do you have to be Romeo? Take the name off and be somebody else. Then a thought hit her, and she sat up straight. "Wait. This is the whole scene. She's saying the name is the problem, not the person. He could just... not be Romeo." She tested it against the rest of the speech, and it held. Every line was about names, about what you inherit from your family whether you want it or not. Her family had inherited her grandmother's house, and nobody had asked Norah's opinion about the ugly green kitchen either.

"I get it now," she said, and copied the new version in her best handwriting.

Deshaun pulled out a granola bar, broke it in half, and handed her the bigger piece. "You look kind of shaky," he said. "Sugar helps. So does knowing your stuff, and you know it."

"Mostly I'm scared of messing up in front of everyone," Norah admitted, taking the piece. "I feel like the second I stand up, I'm completely vulnerable."

"Then don't stand up," Deshaun said. "We'll sit. Downstage, whatever that means. Mrs. Okafor never said we had to stand."

Norah looked at him. "You'd really do the scene sitting down?"

"I'd do it lying on the floor if it helps you talk." He took a bite of his half. "Besides, I still have to paraphrase my whole speech, and you're the only one on this bus who knows wherefore means why."

"Deal," Norah said, and handed him her pencil.

Carson stood in Grandma Ruth's kitchen with the paper shaking in his hand. In three weeks he would stand in front of the whole congregation and recite the blessing from memory, and right now he could remember exactly one line out of eleven.

"You've walked from my front door to this kitchen a thousand times," Grandma said, sliding a tray of mandelbrot into the oven. "Use that."

"Use walking? That's not a thing."

"It's called the method of loci," she said, tapping her forehead. "Old as Rome, so don't tell me it's not a thing." She refused to say more, which was her way of making him figure it out, and she went back to checking the thermostat, muttering that the oven ran hot and she had to conserve the little patience the machine had left her.

Carson frowned at the paper. Fine. If each line of the blessing lived somewhere along the route, then walking the route in his mind would hand him the lines back, one after another. He tried it right there in the kitchen. The first line went by the crooked mailbox at the front gate, because both felt like a beginning. The second line he set on the porch swing, third on the coat hooks shaped like ducks, and he kept going, hallway, staircase, the doorframe with Grandpa's pencil marks from every birthday. When he reached the eleventh line, he gave it to the sugar bowl on the kitchen table. Then he closed his eyes and walked the whole route without moving his feet, and the whole blessing poured out in order.

His little sister Mira had been watching from the counter, where she'd been building a tower out of cinnamon sticks all afternoon. "Do my spelling words next," she demanded. "I have a bee on Friday and I am going to win it."

"Only if you promise not to be reckless with my route," Carson said. "Don't go moving lines around in my head." He pointed at the sugar bowl. "Line eleven lives there. If you memorize the word 'onomatopoeia' into my sugar bowl, I'm doomed."

"Deal," Mira said, and she screwed her eyes shut and started walking an imaginary hallway, mouthing the first letters of every word. Grandma Ruth pulled the mandelbrot out of the oven, set the tray down, folded her arms, and said, "From the top, Carson. No paper."

He took a breath, thought of the mailbox, and began.

Hunter had exactly one hour to learn how to order lunch in Spanish before his Spanish club walked to the little restaurant on Maple Street for their end-of-term practice session. He sat at a desk in the back of Mrs. Alvarez's empty classroom, hunched over a menu she had photocopied for him, converting English phrases in his head into the new words he'd memorized that week: el sándwich, la sopa, ¿cuánto cuesta? He could ask how much it cost. He could name the food. What he couldn't figure out was why Mrs. Alvarez kept writing "para llevar" in the margins of his practice sheet, next to every order he'd drafted.

His real problem was bigger than the assignment. His bus left at 3:15 for his brother's soccer tournament, and the club's lunch reservation was at 2:30. If he wanted to eat anything, it would have to be on the bus, wrapped up, not on a plate at a table. He had no idea how to say that.

He tried a test. He asked his friend Daisy, who sat two rows over working on her own menu, "What do people say when they want the food to go? Like, wrapped up, not eaten there?"

Daisy shrugged. "Beats me. I'm just ordering the soup and staying put."

So Hunter hunted through the photocopied menu. Near the bottom, in small print, he found a line: "Precios para llevar: $4.50." The takeout prices, Mrs. Alvarez had said, were cheaper than the sit-down ones. That meant "para llevar" had something to do with taking food away instead of eating it there. He wasn't sure, but it was the only pattern he could find, and it showed up next to every boxed-meal price on the page.

At the restaurant, the smell of toasted bread drifted under the canopy of faded umbrellas out front. Hunter got in line behind his classmates, watching them order one by one. When his turn came, the man at the counter waited, pencil ready.

"Un sándwich de pollo, por favor," Hunter said. Then he pointed at the wrapped sandwiches in the glass case and took his best shot. "Para llevar."

The man's pencil paused, then he nodded and reached into the case instead of toward the plates stacked behind him. He wrapped the sandwich in white paper and slid it across the counter.

"Cuesta cuatro cincuenta," the man said, and Hunter recognized the number from the menu's small print, the cheaper takeout price. He counted out the bills, gripping the warm package. It had worked. He had guessed the rule from the prices, and the man's nod had proved it.

He jogged out to the bus stop with the sandwich tucked under his arm, tearing one corner of the paper as he climbed the steps. His classmates, still settling their plates back at the restaurant, would eat slowly under the umbrellas, but he would eat too, somewhere past Maple Street, on the road toward the game. He took a bite and grinned at the window. "Para llevar," he said to his reflection, and the bus rumbled forward.

The essay prompt sat on Zack's desk like a dare: should the town keep its old movie theater or sell it for a parking lot? He had strong feelings, but when he tried to start writing, his page stayed barren except for his name. He had two pages due Friday, and it was already Wednesday study hall in the library, where the radiators ticked and dust hung in the slanted light near the window.

His friend Priya slid into the chair across from him with a stack of books and a granola bar. "Stuck?"

"I know what I think," Zack said. "I just can't get it to make sense on paper. And my thoughts keep running into each other."

Priya tapped his blank page. "So don't write the essay yet. Write one sentence that says what you think and why. One sentence, three reasons."

Zack stared at the window, where a crow was walking the ledge. He tried it out loud. "The town should keep the theater because it brings people downtown, it's the cheapest thing for families to do, and it's the only old building left on Main Street."

"That's a thesis," Priya said. "Now make each reason its own paragraph."

"Paragraphs already? I haven't written anything."

She pulled his paper toward her and folded it into rough columns with her finger. "Watch. Give me three reasons and a made-up first sentence for each one."

He tried the first. "The theater gets people to come downtown, because on census weekends the diner says it's full after the late show."

"Okay. Now say how it connects back."

He tried again, slower, testing the idea the way he'd test a stick on thin ice. "Because bringing people downtown is one reason to keep the theater." It felt almost too simple. He wrote it down anyway.

Priya leaned over and read only the first line of each paragraph he drafted, skipping everything else, humming to show she wasn't peeking. Then she sat back. "Keep the theater, downtown business, cheap family nights, last old building. I got your whole argument without reading a word in between."

Zack looked at his paper, surprised. "Just from the openers?"

"Every paragraph starts with its own topic sentence," Priya said, "and the topic sentence hooks that point back to your thesis. So I could follow it like a trail of bread crumbs."

He read his three opening lines again, then crossed out one and wrote a sharper version, because now he could hear where his own argument wobbled. The page was filling up, column by column, and the crow on the ledge lifted off into the gray afternoon.

"One more paragraph," he said, and clicked his pen.

Brayden's project sat at the end of table six: a ramp, a marble, and a stopwatch borrowed from his gym teacher. The whole point was to measure how fast the marble rolled by timing it at different distances, then draw a graph. The only problem was his graph, which currently looked like a seagull having a bad day.

"You drew that with your eyes closed, right?" said Priya from the next table, leaning over. She was showing an elastic band car, and the rubber bands kept snapping off and attacking judges.

"I drew it with my eyes open and my brain off," Brayden admitted. He'd marked the seconds going up the side and the distances along the bottom. When he connected his points, the line bent backwards halfway across, as if the marble had rolled uphill, gotten confused, and teleported.

He sat back and remembered science class in the fall, the day Mr. Okoye had made everyone chant it while flapping his arms like a windmill. Brayden had laughed so hard he'd knocked his pencil into the residence of the class hamster, Rocket, who chewed it in half. What had the chant been? Something about the axes. He stared at his ruined seagull. His points made sense as numbers. The line was nonsense. So the numbers weren't the problem; the placement was.

"Wait," he said. He flipped the paper over and started again, writing seconds along the bottom and distance up the side. One, two, three seconds. Twenty centimeters, forty, sixty. He connected the dots and the line climbed steadily, neat and straight. "Time goes along the horizontal axis and distance goes up the vertical axis," he told the graph, feeling slightly like Mr. Okoye. The marble hadn't teleported at all. It had rolled the same speed the whole way, and now the paper proved it.

Priya wandered over with a rubber band stretched between her fingers like a tiny slingshot. "Fixed it?"

"Fixed it. My marble rolls at a steady twenty centimeters per second." He pointed at the slope. "You could mediate an argument between my data points now. They all agree."

Judge Alvarez appeared at the table, clipboard first. He looked at the ramp, then the graph, then Brayden. "Show me," he said, and tapped the stopwatch.

Brayden set the marble at the top of the ramp. "Three," he said, "two, one, release." Priya leaned in so far her rubber band twanged against the table edge.

Alexis had failed the last two multiplication quizzes, and tomorrow was the unit test. Her stomach hurt every time she thought about it, and last night she had lain awake until midnight, listening to the furnace tick. She told her friend Priya about it on the bench by the gym.

"It's like my body is stressed even when I'm just sitting there," Alexis said. "I want to figure out what's causing it."

"Maybe it's the test," Priya said. "Obviously."

"No, I mean the stomachache part. I can't see what's making it." Alexis frowned. "My intuition says it's not the food. It happens at the same time every day, right before math."

Priya pulled a crumpled paper from her backpack. It was a handout from the counseling office that had gotten mixed into her folder, titled "Stress Signs and What Helps." Alexis read down the list: tight shoulders, upset stomach, trouble sleeping, racing thoughts. All of it matched.

"Look at this part," Priya said, pointing. "Belly breathing. It's also called diaphragmatic breathing."

The paper said to check whether the belly rises as you breathe in instead of the shoulders lifting, because that lets the lungs fill more deeply. Alexis put one hand on her stomach and one on her shoulder and took a breath. Her shoulder hand moved. Her stomach hand didn't move at all.

"You try," she said. Priya did the same thing, and her shoulder hand rose too.

"So we're both doing it wrong," Priya said. "Which means this is a thing you can actually get wrong. It's a skill."

They practiced through lunch. Alexis breathed in slowly through her nose and watched her hands until the stomach one finally lifted and the shoulder one stayed still. The tight feeling in her chest loosened a little. She tried it four more times to make sure it wasn't a fluke, and each time the belly rose first.

That night she followed the second half of the handout, a sleep routine: same time every night, no screens, backpack packed before bed. She did three slow belly breaths with her hand on her stomach, and she was asleep before she could count the furnace ticks.

The next morning, her stomach was quiet. She took the test, and when she got to problem nine she felt her shoulders creep up toward her ears. She set her pencil down, put a hand on her belly, and breathed until she felt it rise.

After class, Mr. Roark handed back the quizzes. "Alexis, see me a second."

She stayed, expecting the worst, imagining her grade decomposing into a pile of missing assignments. He turned her paper over. Problem nine, the one she had breathed through, was the only one marked wrong.

"That's the twist," Priya said later, laughing. "You got a ninety-four, and the one you missed was the one you relaxed on."

"That's not the twist," Alexis said. "The twist is my stomach didn't hurt at all."

Hannah spread her homework across Grandpa's kitchen table: a photocopied page of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and a blank sheet for her explanation of one right. She had picked Section 8, protection against unreasonable search, because it sounded dramatic. Grandpa set down two mugs of tea and pulled a chair around beside her instead of across the table.

She read the section out loud twice, then wrote her first sentence: "This means nobody can ever search you." Grandpa tapped the page. "Read it again. Which word are you skipping?" She found it: "unreasonable." Her teacher wanted them to explain a right in their own words, and hers had quietly changed the rule.

The memory came back to her then, from last fall. She had marched into a convenience store with her backpack and the owner had pointed at a sign that said NO BACKPACKS. She had said, "That's against the Charter. I have rights." The owner had just looked at her, and her friend Priya had dragged her outside before it turned into a real argument. At the time she had decided the owner simply didn't know the law.

She pulled out her phone and searched for "Charter who does it apply to." The results were consistent. She read one line, then another, frowning. "Grandpa," she said, "it says the Charter applies to governments and their actions. Not to private businesses or individuals. Not directly."

"So was the store owner breaking the Charter when he banned backpacks?"

"No," Hannah said slowly. "No, he wasn't. That's a different kind of rule, like a store policy. I was wrong." She sat back. "Priya's going to hear about this." Then she thought of a way to test it, because it seemed too strange to accept from one search. She imagined the same sign posted at the public library, run by the city. The sign at the store was a policy; a government doing something similar would touch the Charter. It was a logical distinction, and once she saw it, the whole thing held together.

She rewrote her sentence: "The Charter puts limits on what governments can do, so a rule that's fine for a private store might not be fine for a public one." She underlined it. Then she turned to Grandpa. "You knew the whole time, didn't you? At the library last month, when I complained about the backpack thing." He raised his mug. "The Charter keeps a certain hierarchy in place," he said. "I wanted you to demonstrate you could climb it yourself." She took her tea out to the porch and texted Priya: "I owe the store an apology."

Emily's problem was simple: the ball rolled across the lab table so fast that nobody could time it, and the graph she was supposed to draw had exactly three sad dots on it, all clumped at the far end.

"It's over before I even click the stopwatch," said Marcus, her lab partner, clicking the stopwatch anyway.

Emily looked at the blank grid on her worksheet. To draw a distance-time graph, they needed to quantify how far the ball went in a measured time, several times, at marks along the way. That was the whole assignment. She glared at the ball, which sat at the end of the table looking innocent, like a small round organism that had evolved specifically to ruin her grade.

Then she remembered the field trip in October. At the science museum there had been a long, gentle ramp with a ball you could release yourself, and a plaque she'd only half read while waiting for her turn. She'd thought it was just a slow, boring version of a slide. But the ball on that ramp had crept down so gradually that even the kid behind her, who spent the whole visit dropping his juice, could have timed it. The plaque had said something about a man named Galileo. She closed her eyes and pulled the words back up: Galileo studied motion by rolling balls down gentle ramps, which slowed the motion enough for him to time it.

"Get the board," she said.

They propped one end of the whiteboard on a stack of three textbooks, making a shallow slope, and let the ball roll down its smooth back. Now they could time it. At twenty centimeters, their stopwatch said one point four seconds. At forty, two point seven. At sixty, four point two. Marcus called out numbers; Emily plotted them, and the dots fell into a line so straight she checked twice to make sure she hadn't drawn it with her ruler by accident. The line climbed steadily upward. Speed, drawn from nothing but distance and time, was suddenly sitting on her paper.

Mr. Okafor stopped at their table and picked up the worksheet. "Nice line. Where'd the ramp idea come from?"

"A dead guy," Emily said. "Kind of obsolete, but his ramp worked."

He handed it back, and his eye drifted to the corner where a motion sensor sat plugged in, the one that had been broken since September. He jiggled its cord, and the little green light flickered on.

"You could have just used this," he said.

Marcus looked at the stopwatch, then at the sensor, then at their beautiful hand-drawn line. "We like the ramp," he said, and set the ball rolling again.

Simon crouched behind the start line at the far end of the field, flipping his race number over in his hands. Coach Reyes had said the words once, in the gym, and walked away: "Three minutes if you want the record." Simon had no idea what that meant for his legs.

He found a pencil stub in his sock, the one he kept for math class, and wrote on the back of the number. Three minutes for eight hundred metres. He chewed the pencil. Then he remembered the chalk line Coach had pointed at on the track, halfway around, and the way she had counted the curved sections out loud last week. The track was four hundred metres all the way around. He stopped chewing. Four hundred went into eight hundred twice, so if the whole race took three minutes, then each lap had to take half of that. Ninety seconds. He wrote "90" in big numbers and underlined it twice.

Last spring flashed back at him, sharp as a starter's gun. The district meet, his first eight hundred. He had sprinted the first lap like it was a hundred, arms pumping, passing everybody, feeling like a king. Then his legs had turned to rope in the second lap and four runners had gone past him before the finish. He had stood with his hands on his knees and watched their backs. His problem had never been speed. It had been something he couldn't see, hiding in the way he spent his legs too early.

"Simon, heat two," called the timer, a kid from the affluent side of town whose parents bought the team all its stopwatches. "You're the only consumer of lane one today, so enjoy it."

"Whistle me the ninety," Simon said. "First lap."

The kid frowned. "You want me to yell at ninety seconds?"

"Just do it."

The gun cracked. Simon counted his steps and held back, even when Darrell from Jefferson surged ahead. Sixty, seventy, the pack stringing out, his chest telling him to go, go. Then the whistle: "Ninety!" Simon crossed the line right on it, Darrell three seconds up, and Simon smiled, because Darrell was already breathing like a punctured tire.

Simon did not cease moving, did not sprint yet, just lifted his knees a little more. By the final curve the gap had shrunk to a stride. Simon heard Darrell's ragged breath beside him, felt the number flapping against his chest with "90" pressed to his skin, and drove for the line.

"Two fifty-eight," the timer shouted, thumb on the watch. "Who taught you that?"

Simon turned the number over so the pencil side showed. "Nobody," he said. "I did the math."

Simon sat in the dentist's waiting room with a poster rolled under his arm and a note card balanced on his knee. Tomorrow he had to explain to his class how nicotine hooks the brain, and his plan so far consisted of the words "reward pathway" written at the top of the card and a drawing of a brain wearing a fishing hat. "You look like a man about to resign from school entirely," said Marisol, dropping into the chair beside him with a magazine she had no intention of reading.

"It's invisible," Simon said. "That's the problem. I can't show them a molecule walking into a brain and flipping a switch." He tapped the card. "Nicotine gets in, and the brain releases dopamine, this feel-good chemical, in the reward pathway. The brain notices, decides it likes nicotine, and starts demanding more. But nobody can see any of that happen. I need proof you can't see." Marisol flipped a page. "Then prove it the way my brother proved the dog was stealing socks. He couldn't see it either. He set up a camera, kind of, and then a trap with a sock and a door."

Simon thought about that all through his cleaning, even with the hygienist poking around like a scavenger hunting for one last popcorn kernel. His idea formed somewhere between the flossing and the rinse. A hidden cause still leaves a pattern, and you can test a pattern. He would draw two brains on his poster and show what repeated nicotine did to the pathway over time, then show what happened when the nicotine stopped. If the demands got louder before they faded, that was the invisible hook leaving a visible mark.

In the parking lot afterward, Marisol's cousin Devon was leaning against the fence, and he held out a small pen-shaped thing with a grin. "One hit," he said. "It's watermelon. Barely even counts." Simon looked at it, then at his poster tube. "Nope," he said. "The brain keeps developing until about age 25. That makes teenagers more vulnerable to nicotine addiction than adults." Devon blinked. "So my brain is literally still under construction, and you want to pour nicotine on the construction site?" Marisol snorted. "He's been rehearsing all afternoon. It's kind of subjective whether that was for you or for his presentation."

"It was for both," Simon said. "Consider it a free preview." Devon pocketed the vape with theatrical sadness and muttered something about nerds with posters. Simon unrolled the poster on the hood of his mom's car, spread it flat with both hands, and held up his marker. "Now help me draw a brain in a hard hat."

The bunting over the festival stage had snapped loose on one side, and every time the wind lifted, the whole banner flapped like a luminous orange fish trying to escape. Marcus watched it while his grandmother steered him by the elbow toward the langar tent, where the smell of cardamom and fried dough made his stomach growl loudly enough that two aunties laughed.

"You have to know it by Sunday," she said. "All of it. Not mostly it."

"I know, Bebe. Mostly is almost all."

"Almost is not all." She set down her plate. "Your uncle will be there. He will listen."

Marcus groaned. Japji Sahib was long, and the Punjabi words slipped out of his memory the way water slipped off a duck. He had been repeating it for two weeks, in the shower, on the bus, once out loud in math class until Priya Nair leaned over and whispered, "Buddy, you're chanting." He could not figure out why it had to be word-for-word perfect when nobody was even testing him on the meaning yet.

He found his cousin Simran near the kite stall, arguing with a kid about whether a kite was technically an organism. "It eats wind," the kid insisted. "It breathes."

"It has no cells," Simran said. "Case closed. Marcus, tell him."

"It has no cells," Marcus agreed, then slumped onto a hay bale. "Simran, why does Bebe want Japji Sahib exactly right? It's just my Sunday thing."

Simran snorted. "Sunday thing? Uncle Harjit is taking Amrit. At the Khalsa initiation ceremony. It's called Amrit Sanchar. And Japji Sahib is recited there too." She picked up the kite string. "So when you say it at home, and he says it there, you're saying the same thing at the same time. Sort of."

Marcus sat up. Same words, same morning, two places. That was the point. It was not a test of his memory. It was a rope you held from your end while someone else held the other. He tested it right there, closing his eyes and reciting the first verse, and when he stumbled on the fourth line, he felt the wobble like a dropped stitch.

"Simran," he said, opening one eye, "if I mess up on Sunday, does Uncle feel it?"

"He'll console you with jalebi, probably."

Marcus grinned and started the verse again, slower, letting each word land like a foot on a narrow bridge.

"Better," Simran said. "Now say the next one."

Aubrey spread the printed periodic table across the kitchen table and glared at it like it had insulted her. Tomorrow's quiz would ask her to find the number of protons in an element, and she could not make sense of the little numbers at all. Gold had a 79 somewhere near its name, and iron had a 26, and she could not tell which number meant protons, which meant something else, and which one she was supposed to hunt down like a scavenger digging through a junk drawer.

Her little brother Theo wandered in holding a postcard from their class trip to the science museum, which had happened two weeks before Aubrey got sick and missed it. He slid it across the table. On the front was a photograph of an old handwritten chart, faded and crowded. "That's from the timeline wall," he said. "The Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev published an early version of the periodic table in 1869. I copied it off the plaque because it looked like a cool cheat sheet."

Aubrey frowned at the postcard. The old table looked nothing like the neat colored grid in front of her. Some squares were empty, as if Mendeleev had simply left room for elements nobody had found yet. She flipped the postcard over and found a message she had written to herself the morning of the field trip, before she knew she would be home with a fever instead: "Dear Aubrey, sit in the front for the chemistry exhibit. Take notes. You will thank yourself during the quiz." She had never gotten the chance. Her stomach did a small, sour flip, and she decided she would invest the whole evening in figuring this out on her own, postcard and all.

She started with the one thing she remembered from before she got sick: the atomic number. She traced her finger down the grid, hunting for the pattern. Hydrogen, number 1. Helium, number 2. Lithium, number 3. She tested an idea against iron. If the big number, 26, was the atomic number, and if the atomic number counted protons, then iron should have 26 protons. She checked gold, at 79, and oxygen, at 8, and the rule held every single time, like a lock accepting one key. The atomic number was the proton count. That was the whole secret, and nobody had needed to tell her.

"Twenty-six," she said out loud, tapping iron. "Iron has twenty-six protons." Theo, who was dunking a cookie in his milk, looked up. "That's it? That's the hard thing?" She threw a folded napkin at him, but she was grinning.

There was still a cost, and she knew it. She had missed the museum, the front row, the exhibit where a docent let kids hold a sample of real gold, and no amount of kitchen-table work would give that day back. But she pulled a blank index card toward her and wrote "Au, 79" in careful letters, then "Fe, 26" beneath it, building her own small timeline from Mendeleev's ghost of a table to this one.
